papers.title: Transfer Learning for Power Outage Detection Task with Limited Training Data
papers.abstract:
Early detection of power outages is crucial for maintaining a reliable power distribution system. This research investigates the use of transfer learning and language models in detecting outages with limited labeled data. By leveraging pretraining and transfer learning, models can generalize to unseen classes.
  Using a curated balanced dataset of social media tweets related to power outages, we conducted experiments using zero-shot and few-shot learning. Our hypothesis is that Language Models pretrained with limited data could achieve high performance in outage detection tasks over baseline models. Results show that while classical models outperform zero-shot Language Models, few-shot fine-tuning significantly improves their performance. For example, with 10% fine-tuning, BERT achieves 81.3% accuracy (+15.3%), and GPT achieves 74.5% accuracy (+8.5%). This has practical implications for analyzing and localizing outages in scenarios with limited data availability.
  Our evaluation provides insights into the potential of few-shot fine-tuning with Language Models for power outage detection, highlighting their strengths and limitations. This research contributes to the knowledge base of leveraging advanced natural language processing techniques for managing critical infrastructure.
papers.summary: Detecting power outages early from social media posts is hard when there is little labeled data. The authors test zero-shot and few-shot learning with pretrained language models on a curated, balanced dataset of outage-related tweets and compare them against classical baseline models. Classical models beat zero-shot language models, but small amounts of fine-tuning change the picture: with 10% of the data used for fine-tuning, **`BERT` reaches 81.3% accuracy (+15.3 points)** and `GPT` reaches 74.5% (+8.5 points).

papers.title: Multi-LLM Systems Exhibit Robust Semantic Collapse
papers.abstract: Whether machines can originate novel content has been debated for nearly two centuries, from Lovelace's assertion that no engine can "originate anything" to Turing's question of whether a machine can amplify ideas brought in from outside. Interacting multi-LLM systems, increasingly deployed for autonomous generation, reopen this question empirically. Here we show that such systems exhibit semantic collapse, systematic convergence in semantic representations despite apparent lexical variation, with no retraining or weight updates. The pattern holds across model families and over 200 to 1,000 rounds. Thirteen intervention implementations tested, spanning decoding parameters, prompt design, agent composition, activation engineering, and reinforcement learning, did not reliably restore semantic diversity. Mechanistic analyses suggest that semantic collapse is not solely attributable to the alignment or conformity biases examined here, but is consistent with intrinsic properties of autoregressive generation. Our results point to persistent constraints on the ability of multi-LLM systems to sustain open-ended exploration in closed-loop settings.
papers.summary: When several LLMs interact in a closed loop to generate content on their own, they show what the authors call semantic collapse: their outputs converge in meaning even though the wording keeps varying, and this happens without any retraining or weight updates. The effect holds across model families and over runs of 200 to 1,000 rounds. **None of the thirteen interventions tested reliably restored semantic diversity**; these covered decoding parameters, prompt design, agent composition, activation engineering, and reinforcement learning. Mechanistic analyses suggest the collapse is not explained only by the alignment or conformity biases the authors examined, and is consistent with intrinsic properties of autoregressive generation.

papers.title: Transformer-based segmentation of prosodic boundaries in Brazilian Portuguese
papers.abstract: Automatic prosodic segmentation identifies boundaries between speech units from acoustic and linguistic evidence. Although recent deep learning approaches have produced strong results for English, automatic segmentation for Brazilian Portuguese (BP) still relies mostly on rule-based or traditional machine-learning methods. This paper presents SAMPA, a Whisper-based segmenter that transcribes BP speech while inserting explicit markers for terminal prosodic boundaries. We fine-tune Whisper large-v3 on manually segmented recordings from the NURC-SP dataset and evaluate different training and test-time filtering configurations, including out-of-distribution testing on the MuPe-Diversidades dataset. SAMPA achieves competitive boundary-detection performance across settings, with the best models reaching F1=0.731 on the held-out test split and F1=0.796 on MuPe-Diversidades. Finally, through n-gram and acoustic-visual analyses, we show that our model follows morphosyntactic, semantic, and prosodic cues for detecting prosodic boundaries.
papers.summary: Automatic prosodic segmentation, which finds the boundaries between speech units, still relies mostly on rule-based or classical machine-learning methods for Brazilian Portuguese (BP). The authors fine-tune `Whisper large-v3` on manually segmented recordings from `NURC-SP` to build `SAMPA`, which transcribes BP speech and inserts explicit markers at terminal prosodic boundaries. The best models reach F1=0.731 on the held-out test split and **F1=0.796 on the out-of-distribution `MuPe-Diversidades` dataset**. N-gram and acoustic-visual analyses indicate that the model uses morphosyntactic, semantic, and prosodic cues to place boundaries.

papers.title: Can the Quantum Fisher Effective Dimension Judge a Hybrid Quantum Neural Network?
papers.abstract: Hybrid quantum neural networks (QNNs) pair a classical feature extractor with a variational quantum circuit, and the effective dimension of the circuit's quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) is widely used to assess such models. This scalar is often interpreted as an indicator of trainability or accuracy, although these readings are rarely tested under controlled conditions. We therefore investigate what it actually measures. We define the effective dimension as the participation ratio of the QFIM diagonal, which lies between one and the parameter count, and we evaluate it across two image datasets, four frozen backbones including a random-projection control, four circuit depths on eight qubits, and three seeds. During training, the effective dimension remains well below the parameter count, and its correlation with test accuracy ranges from -0.72 to +0.87, changing sign across seeds in half of the configurations. Increasing depth activates a larger share of the circuit directions, from 0.38 to 0.91 of the parameter count, while the initialization gradient variance remains between 1e-5 and 1e-4, so no barren plateau (BP) appears at eight qubits. At a fixed circuit, the four backbones share an initial effective dimension of 6 to 9, even though CIFAR-10 accuracy ranges from 23.14% to 86.44%. These results show that the effective dimension characterizes circuit geometry rather than model quality. We conclude with a practical protocol that assigns each diagnostic to the question it can answer.
papers.summary: Hybrid quantum neural networks (QNNs) combine a classical feature extractor with a variational quantum circuit, and the effective dimension of the circuit's quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) is often read as a sign of trainability or accuracy. The authors test that reading under controlled conditions across two image datasets, four frozen backbones (including a random-projection control), four circuit depths on eight qubits, and three seeds. The correlation between effective dimension and test accuracy ranges from -0.72 to +0.87 and flips sign across seeds in half of the configurations, and all four backbones start with an effective dimension of 6 to 9 even though their `CIFAR-10` accuracy ranges from 23.14% to 86.44%. They conclude that **the effective dimension describes circuit geometry rather than model quality**, and they propose a protocol that matches each diagnostic to the question it can actually answer.

papers.title: Anytime Contracts for AI Services
papers.abstract: AI services are prone to moral hazard, as model providers can silently route requests to cheaper, lower-quality models, and the inherent stochasticity of model outputs makes this degradation hard to detect. Contract theory addresses moral hazard by designing payment rules that reward high-quality outputs and prevent strategic overcharging. However, existing frameworks assume interactions of fixed duration, whereas AI services are typically consumed through subscriptions and pay-as-you-go APIs that users can terminate at any time based on observed performance. We show that this flexibility can break standard contracts, opening them up to abuse by either the providers or users. To address this, we extend contract theory to account for unknown exit rules. We formalize the problem as a Principal-Agent game, and show that budget-optimal contracts in this setting are proportional to anytime-valid hypothesis tests based on likelihood-ratio e-values. We give an efficient algorithm for computing anytime contracts and show how betting e-processes can be used to approximate them when the models are unknown. Finally, we evaluate our findings on synthetic data and data from deployed LLMs.
papers.summary: AI providers can quietly route requests to cheaper, lower-quality models, and because model outputs are stochastic, users find this degradation hard to detect. Contract theory handles this kind of moral hazard, but it assumes interactions of fixed length, whereas subscription and pay-as-you-go users can quit at any time based on what they observe; the authors show that this flexibility can break standard contracts. Modeling the problem as a Principal-Agent game with unknown exit rules, they prove that **budget-optimal contracts are proportional to anytime-valid hypothesis tests built on likelihood-ratio e-values**. They give an efficient algorithm for computing these contracts, approximate them with betting e-processes when the models are unknown, and evaluate the approach on synthetic data and data from deployed LLMs.

papers.title: LLM-Assisted Bi-Approximate CHC Solving
papers.abstract: Constrained Horn clause (CHC) solvers often struggle to discover deep counterexamples whose derivations may require extensive rule unfolding. Although large language models (LLMs) can propose long-range symbolic relations, prior work on formally checked LLM-assisted verification has mainly focused on generating inductive invariants and concrete traces. We exploit this broader capability through Derivation Power Under-approximations (DPUs). Each DPU is a solver-certified under-approximation of the relation induced by a multi-step CHC derivation. An LLM proposes each DPU with symbolic intermediate-state witnesses that enable SMT validation without introducing additional quantifiers. Validated DPUs can be composed and reused soundly. Building on this mechanism, our LLM-assisted framework HornCraft combines invariant generation for over-approximation with DPU generation for under-approximation in CHC solving. On 260 linear and nonlinear integer-arithmetic CHC-COMP benchmarks left unresolved by a 30-minute Spacer run, HornCraft returns certified verdicts for 228 instances. It certifies 42 instances as unsafe, compared with 22 when DPU construction and reuse are disabled.
papers.summary: Constrained Horn clause (CHC) solvers often fail to find deep counterexamples that require unfolding many rules. `HornCraft` has an LLM propose Derivation Power Under-approximations (DPUs), which are under-approximations of multi-step CHC derivations that include symbolic intermediate-state witnesses. These witnesses let an SMT solver validate each DPU without extra quantifiers, and validated DPUs can be composed and reused soundly. The framework pairs this under-approximation with LLM-generated invariants for over-approximation, and **returns certified verdicts for 228 of 260 `CHC-COMP` benchmarks** that a 30-minute `Spacer` run left unresolved. It certifies 42 instances as unsafe, compared with 22 when DPU construction and reuse are turned off.

papers.title: Web Agent Agentic Reinforcement Learning Decision Model Under Multi-Cost and Failure Risk
papers.abstract:
Intelligent agent interactions in real-world web environments are commonly constrained by request budgets, time delays, anti-crawling restrictions, and operational failure risks. Strategies solely optimizing task success rates often exhibit unusable phenomena such as "high success but high cost" or "low risk but conservative failure." This paper proposes a constrained agentic reinforcement learning model for web agents, unifying page access, search requests, and external API calls into a unified long-term decision-making framework with associated costs. It simultaneously incorporates cost budget constraints and tail risk control into the optimization objective: constructing a multidimensional cost vector comprising cumulative request count, total latency, and failure penalties to achieve budget compliance via Lagrange dual updates, while employing a CVaR risk term to suppress excessive exploration of high-failure-probability paths, thereby achieving an adaptive balance among "completion rate, cost, and risk."
  Experiments were conducted across 30-70 site/page templates and 800-1,500 end-to-end web tasks, including information extraction, price comparison, form submission, and cross-page navigation. Interaction sequences spanned 20-120 steps with tool scales of 30-200. Performance was benchmarked against unconstrained RL, budget-constrained RL, and rule-based/scripted web agents, quantifying task completion rates, cost-per-success, failure rates, and policy stability.
  Results demonstrate that at equivalent completion rates, our method reduces C-PS by 22%-31% and lowers failure rates by 18%-26% under high failure penalties. Under fixed budgets, task completion rates increase by 10%-16%, highlighting the necessity and effectiveness of constraint modeling for practical web agent deployment.
papers.summary: Web agents operate under request budgets, latency, anti-crawling limits, and the risk of failed operations, so optimizing only for task success can produce policies that succeed but cost too much, or that stay safe but fail. The authors frame page visits, search requests, and API calls as a single long-horizon reinforcement learning problem with a vector of costs (request count, latency, failure penalties). Lagrange dual updates enforce the budget, and a conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) term discourages exploring paths with high failure probability. Across 800–1,500 end-to-end tasks on 30–70 site templates, the method **cuts cost per success by 22%–31% at equal completion rates** and lowers failure rates by 18%–26% under high failure penalties, and it raises completion by 10%–16% under fixed budgets.

papers.title: I$^2$-Med: Interpretable Medical Inference through Visual-Guided Dynamic Logits Calibration
papers.abstract: Medical vision language models have demonstrated strong potential for medical image understanding and reasoning. However, their interpretability and reliability remain limited because medical vision language tasks require precise visual grounding and clinically coherent explanations. This is particularly challenging due to complex imaging patterns and scarce expert annotations. These challenges reduce the effectiveness of conventional reasoning methods and lead to visual hallucination, defined as the generation of text that is not grounded in the given visual input, which further limits their applicability in clinical practice. To mitigate these challenges, we propose an interpretable medical inference (I$^2$-Med) framework that enhances visual faithfulness during inference without additional training to improve reasoning and explanation faithfulness in medical vision language models. During text generation, I$^2$-Med uses a visual guidance module to check whether each candidate word is supported by the medical image and consistent with the current reasoning. Based on this guidance, the model's output scores are adjusted to favor visually grounded words, without changing the model parameters. Extensive experiments on the OmniMedVQA benchmark, covering eight medical imaging modalities and five clinical question types, demonstrate that our proposed I$^2$-Med framework generates more clinically meaningful and visually faithful reasoning chains and reduces visual hallucination under standard medical VQA evaluation metrics. The source code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/mtanveer1/l2-med}.
papers.summary: Medical vision-language models often produce visual hallucinations, meaning text that is not grounded in the image, which limits their use in clinical settings. `I^2-Med` addresses this at inference time with no extra training: during generation, a visual guidance module checks whether each candidate word is supported by the image and consistent with the reasoning so far. The model's output scores are then adjusted toward visually grounded words without changing its parameters. On `OmniMedVQA`, which covers eight imaging modalities and five clinical question types, the method **reduces visual hallucination** and produces more clinically meaningful and visually faithful reasoning chains.

papers.title: Modeling Human Behavior in the Prisoner's Dilemma with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: The Prisoner's Dilemma has long served as a foundational framework for studying human decision-making and cooperative outcomes across social scenarios, yet human behavior consistently deviates from predictions of fully rational economic theory. Previous works have studied human and LLM outcomes in the Prisoner's Dilemma; however, these studies have lacked at least one key feature: a memory component for LLM agents, accessible open-source models, or comparison against empirical human data. This project investigates whether open-source LLMs, TII Falcon 7B Instruct, Google Gemma 7B, Meta Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Microsoft Phi Mini MoE Instruct, and Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, can model human cooperation patterns in repeated Prisoner's Dilemma games, while examining how an LLM's knowledge that its opponent will be shuffled affects its decisions. Using a standardized prompting framework, we simulated interactions in two trial types: a fixed-partner setting where both agents retain memory, and a shuffled-partner setting where a memory-enabled agent, informed that its opponent changes across rounds, interacts with a memoryless agent. For each trial, we measured cooperation rates over 100 rounds and 10-round increments and compared them to human data from Montero-Porras et al. (2022). Under both frameworks, all LLMs differed from the human cooperation rate. Open-source LLMs generally over-cooperated relative to humans, particularly in the shuffled framework, where human cooperation averaged 28.5% while several models exceeded 80%. Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct showed deterministic tendencies, while Phi-mini-MoE-Instruct displayed greater variability and briefly approximated human rates. These findings suggest that LLMs have potential as behavioral simulation agents and provide a benchmark across two interaction environments, although open-source models are not yet reliable substitutes for human participants.
papers.summary: The authors test whether five small open-source LLMs (`Falcon 7B Instruct`, `Gemma 7B`, `Llama 3.1 8B Instruct`, `Phi Mini MoE Instruct`, and `Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct`) reproduce human cooperation patterns in the repeated Prisoner's Dilemma. They run 100-round games in two settings: a fixed-partner setting where both agents have memory, and a shuffled-partner setting where a memory-enabled agent knows its opponent changes each round. Results are compared against human data from Montero-Porras et al. (2022). Every model departed from human cooperation rates and most over-cooperated; **in the shuffled setting, humans cooperated 28.5% of the time while several models exceeded 80%**.

papers.title: PolyGraph: Plan-Buffered CUDA Graphs for Adaptive Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Adaptive speculative decoding changes the active batch size B and draft length d from one decode step to the next, whereas a CUDA Graph replays a fixed launch configuration. The resulting verification width M = B d forces serving systems to pre-capture many shapes, capture new ones on the serving path, or pad every step to the largest draft. We present PolyGraph, a plan-buffer mechanism for custom Triton kernels that avoids this choice. PolyGraph captures one maximum-grid graph and writes the active shape to GPU memory before each replay. Kernels skip tiles beyond that shape, while graph topology, allocations, layouts, pointers, and launch grids remain fixed; the update transfers only 28 bytes. On one NVIDIA H800, a trace-driven prototype with Qwen2.5-3B dimensions replaces 64 shape-specific graphs with one, matches the warmed baseline in observed step latency (17.7 vs. 17.8 ms P50), and reduces measured pre-serving graph-build time from 3,915 to 93 ms. Fixed-draft controls show that the benefit comes from avoiding padded payload: the P99 difference from MaxPad is negligible at zero padding waste but reaches an 18.7% reduction at 100% waste. Our evidence establishes a bounded work-shape mechanism for custom kernels, not a production serving system, and is limited to synthetic traces on one GPU.
papers.summary: Adaptive speculative decoding changes the batch size and draft length at every decode step, which clashes with CUDA Graphs because each graph replays one fixed launch configuration. Serving systems therefore pre-capture many graph shapes, capture new ones while serving, or pad every step to the largest draft. `PolyGraph` captures a single maximum-grid graph and writes the active shape to GPU memory (28 bytes) before each replay, and custom `Triton` kernels skip the tiles that fall outside that shape. In a trace-driven prototype with `Qwen2.5-3B` dimensions on one H800, **one graph replaces 64 shape-specific graphs** with matching median step latency (17.7 vs. 17.8 ms), and pre-serving graph-build time drops from 3,915 ms to 93 ms.

papers.title: Forecasting Patient Trajectories from the Electronic Health Records with Action-Conditioned World Models
papers.abstract: We introduce a predictive world model for electronic health records (EHR) that represents patient histories as action conditioned latent trajectories. Rather than modeling clinical events solely through autoregressive token prediction, our framework explicitly separates patient states from observed clinical actions and learns their evolution through a state and action conditioned transition operator. At its core is a state dependent linearization predictor that propagates local changes in latent patient state, enabling time resolved prediction, multi step rollout, and action conditioned simulation. Empirically, we show that generated latent trajectories preserve downstream predictive signal, temporal structure, and subgroup level statistical relationships present in encoder derived representations. We further decode free running rollouts into the original clinical feature space and evaluate future clinical measurements against observed values using task matched forecasting baselines, demonstrating that the learned dynamics retain predictive information beyond latent space agreement. Across binary classification and time to event tasks, EHR WM achieves competitive, though task dependent, performance relative to substantially larger EHR foundation models while using a 30x smaller parameter footprint. Finally, perturbing observed action sequences produces corresponding changes in generated trajectories, demonstrating the action sensitivity of the learned dynamics. Together, these results support world modeling as a complementary framework for learning explicit, time indexed representations of patient evolution from longitudinal EHR.
papers.summary: Instead of treating electronic health records (EHR) purely as tokens to predict autoregressively, the authors build a world model that separates latent patient states from observed clinical actions and learns how states evolve given those actions. A state-dependent linearization predictor propagates changes in the latent state, which supports time-resolved prediction, multi-step rollouts, and simulation of alternative action sequences. The generated trajectories preserve downstream predictive signal and temporal structure, and decoded rollouts forecast real clinical measurements. On classification and time-to-event tasks, the model is **competitive with much larger EHR foundation models while using a 30x smaller parameter footprint**, though results vary by task.

papers.title: Measuring the Influence of Modality-Specific Node Representations on Graphs
papers.abstract: Multimodal attributed graphs combine graph structure with node text and image representations in recommendation and multimedia analysis. Graph predictors propagate these representations across connected nodes, so one input can change predictions at its own and nearby nodes. Measuring this distributed response reveals which modality-specific inputs a trained model relies on and how predictor design changes that reliance. We study influence measurement for modality-specific node representations. Given an encoded graph, a trained predictor, a training split, and fixed candidate representations, the task outputs one influence score per candidate and separate text and image rankings. We score a candidate by replacing it with its modality's training-node mean and comparing the original and changed predictions. Existing feature attribution and data valuation generally target one output, training examples, whole nodes, or graph elements rather than prediction changes across graph nodes. Our empirical study shows that nearby-node responses contain information missed by source-only scores and simple proxies, while response magnitude alone does not identify which class changes support the task. Guided by these observations, we propose MoGI (Modality-specific Graph Influence). It propagates training labels to define task direction, reads the same replacement response for the favored class and full class distribution, and averages the resulting ranks. MoGI requires no predictor retraining or learned scoring parameters. Under a shared five-dataset, eight-predictor benchmark, it achieves the largest aggregate held-out loss increase against all five external methods at every tested ranking cutoff.
papers.summary: In graphs where nodes carry both text and image representations, changing one node's input can shift predictions at that node and at its neighbors, so measuring influence only at the source node misses part of the effect. The authors score each modality-specific input by replacing it with its modality's training-node mean and measuring how predictions change across the graph. They find that responses at nearby nodes carry information that source-only scores miss. Their method `MoGI` (Modality-specific Graph Influence) uses propagated training labels to define the task direction and needs no retraining or learned parameters; **on a five-dataset, eight-predictor benchmark it beats all five external methods at every ranking cutoff tested**.

papers.title: SAGE-CP: When Marginal Coverage Hides Route-Conditional Failures in Adaptive VLM Ensembles
papers.abstract: Adaptive VLM ensembles save computation by stopping early on easy images and escalating harder ones. Although a single conformal threshold can make the final predictor marginally valid, it can still fail severely along individual computational routes. We characterize this failure precisely: if a route has prevalence pi, marginal 1-alpha coverage allows its conditional coverage to fall to max{0, 1-alpha/pi}. To address this mismatch, we learn the router on development data, freeze all routing choices, and calibrate the returned score separately for early exits and escalated inputs. We call this pipeline SAGE-CP. Its calibration step applies Mondrian split conformal prediction to the operational groups created by the router. Under exchangeability, the resulting prediction sets achieve finite-sample coverage within each route. Across 10 benchmarks, 4 frozen VLMs, and 5 aligned splits, both global calibration and SAGE-CP achieve 0.900 marginal coverage at a 0.90 target, but their route behavior differs substantially. SAGE-CP raises mean worst-route coverage from 0.623 to 0.887 and reduces the mean route-coverage gap from 0.324 to 0.025, using the same routed scores and 1.177 source calls per image. The stronger guarantee increases the mean prediction-set size from 1.893 to 2.212; nevertheless, the sets remain smaller than those of the full ensemble (2.486) while requiring 70.6 percent fewer source calls. The route-level reliability persists across 6 fixed query fractions, while finer exit-depth groups demonstrate the need for additional calibration data on rare routes. Across 5 datasets, SAGE-CP also reduces measured batch-one latency by 58.8 to 63.4 percent and gross GPU energy by 55.7 to 57.5 percent relative to full inference. Thus, routing provides computational savings, while route-stratified calibration attaches coverage guarantees to the operational paths created by the router.
papers.summary: Adaptive vision-language model (VLM) ensembles save compute by exiting early on easy images and escalating hard ones, but a single global conformal threshold can hide severe failures on individual routes. The authors prove that marginal 1-alpha coverage only guarantees that a route with prevalence pi has conditional coverage of at least max{0, 1-alpha/pi}. `SAGE-CP` freezes the learned router and calibrates early exits and escalated inputs separately using Mondrian split conformal prediction. Across 10 benchmarks and 4 VLMs, it **raises mean worst-route coverage from 0.623 to 0.887** at the same 0.900 marginal coverage, while still using 70.6% fewer source calls than the full ensemble.

papers.title: GardenBench: A lightweight, daily evaluation of LLM capabilities
papers.abstract: We introduce GardenBench, a benchmark with 11 test suites that evaluate the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) across a range of tasks. By systematically prompting LLMs with various lightweight queries, we document day-to-day changes in model performance, including run costs and times, that other benchmarks miss. This allows us to compare the accuracy and features of responses across model providers and versions. We account for daily variations in model accuracy, capturing both model progress and degradation, for instance, when a model is changed post-deployment or when a new model is released. We base our evaluation on general-use tasks and make our results publicly accessible via a live dashboard, diversifying existing approaches to LLM testing. Our main contribution is an innovative, lightweight, and inexpensive benchmark, designed to be consumer-facing and for everyday tasks.
papers.summary: `GardenBench` is a lightweight, low-cost benchmark of 11 test suites that sends everyday queries to LLMs daily to track how their performance changes from one day to the next. Alongside accuracy, it records run costs and response times, so it can compare providers and versions and **detect both progress and degradation, such as when a deployed model is silently changed or a new one is released**. Results are published on a live public dashboard aimed at consumers.

papers.title: Composable Parametric Demographic Injection for Values Survey Simulation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as simulated respondents in computational social science, yet accurately reproducing population-specific heterogeneous response distributions remains challenging. Existing methods such as demographic prompting are sensitive to prompt design and increase inference overhead, while parameter-based methods struggle to reuse demographic information efficiently, limiting generalization to unseen combinations. In this regard, we propose PARADE, a composable PARAmetric DEmographic injection framework that represents each demographic attribute value with a reusable and composable LoRA module. Specifically, PARADE separates task-common survey capability from demographic-specific value shifts via a shared Task LoRA and attribute-level Demographic LoRAs, with composition calibration to reduce parameter interference. At inference time, target population models can be constructed on demand by recombining the relevant modules, including demographic combinations not observed during training. Extensive experiments on the World Values Survey and SocioBench across three backbone models show that PARADE achieves strong population-level distribution alignment while maintaining competitive predictive performance, reducing KL divergence by up to 52.8% relative to the strongest baseline.
papers.summary: Using LLMs as simulated survey respondents requires reproducing how answers are distributed within specific populations, but demographic prompting is sensitive to wording and parameter-based methods do not generalize well to unseen combinations of demographics. `PARADE` gives each demographic attribute value its own reusable `LoRA` module, keeps general survey-answering ability in a shared Task `LoRA`, and calibrates module composition to limit interference between them. Target populations, including demographic combinations never seen in training, are built at inference by recombining the relevant modules. On `World Values Survey` and `SocioBench` with three backbone models, it **reduces KL divergence by up to 52.8% relative to the strongest baseline**.

papers.title: Translating in style: An open-weight alternative to GPT-4 for culturally aligned machine translation
papers.abstract: Machine translation systems often preserve meaning but systematically flatten linguistic style, a failure that is most acute when translating into non-Western languages. The RASTA framework of Havaldar et al. (2025a) addresses this through retrieval-augmented stylistic alignment, but relies on GPT-4, a closed, proprietary model. We investigate whether an open-weight translation specialist, Hunyuan-MT-7B, can serve as an open-weight alternative. We evaluate three variants of the model, the base model, a LoRA supervised fine-tune, and a GRPO-steered policy. We do this across three style dimensions (formality, politeness, and intimacy) and twelve directed language pairs, measuring style alignment with the correlation-based metric $\mathcal{A}$. We find that fine-tuning does not reliably improve alignment: the three variants are statistically indistinguishable in aggregate. The open backbone does not match RASTA-GPT-4 overall, but the shortfall is concentrated in formality and largely closes for intimacy and Chinese directions, where the open model matches or surpasses GPT-4 on individual pairs. An accessible RASTA pipeline built on an open model is thus already viable for parts of the problem.
papers.summary: Machine translation often keeps meaning but flattens style, especially when translating into non-Western languages, and the `RASTA` retrieval-augmented style-alignment framework relies on the proprietary `GPT-4`. The authors test the open-weight `Hunyuan-MT-7B` as a replacement in three variants (base, `LoRA` fine-tuned, and `GRPO`-steered) across formality, politeness, and intimacy in twelve language directions. **Fine-tuning did not reliably help: the three variants were statistically indistinguishable in aggregate.** The open model trails `GPT-4` overall, but the gap is concentrated in formality and largely closes for intimacy and Chinese directions.

papers.title: DUET: Decoupled Upper- and Lower-Body Execution for Task-Agnostic Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.abstract: Changing a humanoid robot's manipulation policy should not require retraining the controller that maintains the robot's balance. This study introduces DUET, a decoupled execution framework that enables locomotion and manipulation controllers to operate simultaneously by combining their commands only at the robot interface. A reinforcement-learning locomotion policy controls the 12 leg joints and a waist yaw joint, tracking planar velocity, turning rate, and pelvis height from deep crouching to upright standing on a 23-degree-of-freedom Unitree G1. The 10 arm joints are excluded from the action space, while their positions and velocities are included only as observations, so that any compatible manipulation policy that generates arm-joint targets can control the upper body, and the locomotion policy keeps the lower body stable without requiring shared training or direct coordination. This study demonstrates the modular approach on hardware by pairing the same locomotion checkpoint with two different vision-language-action models, GR00T N1.7 and pi0.5. In simulation evaluation, the locomotion controller kept the robot's lower body stable with no falls while tracking the commanded planar velocity, yaw rate, and pelvis height with errors of 0.186 m/s, 0.142 rad/s, and 0.016 m, respectively. Ablation studies identify the upper-body pose curriculum as the dominant component, and removing this training step reduces episode survival from 20.0 to 7.4 seconds and increases the fall rate to 6.06 per environment minute. Robustness tests show no falls under pushes of up to 1.0 m/s within the trained payload range, and no falls at twice the payload limit for pushes below 0.7 m/s. These results show that a manipulation policy can be exchanged without retraining, restarting, or otherwise touching the layer that keeps the robot upright.
papers.summary: `DUET` lets a humanoid robot swap its manipulation policy without retraining the controller that keeps it balanced. A reinforcement-learning locomotion policy controls the legs and waist of a 23-degree-of-freedom `Unitree G1`, while it only observes the 10 arm joints, so any compatible manipulation policy can drive the upper body with no shared training. On hardware, the same locomotion checkpoint worked with two different vision-language-action models, `GR00T N1.7` and `pi0.5`. In simulation the controller had **no falls while tracking commanded velocity, turning rate, and pelvis height**, and ablations identify the upper-body pose curriculum as the most important training component.

papers.title: Context-Aware RGB-Thermal-Radar Obstacle Perception for Resource-Constrained ASVs
papers.abstract: Reliable obstacle perception is challenging for small autonomous surface vessels (ASVs): reflections and glare confound visible-light cameras, vessel motion shifts the apparent waterline, and darkness removes the dominant sensing modality altogether. Rather than treating multimodal fusion as a static accuracy gain, we propose a context-aware architecture that combines RGB and long-wave infrared (LWIR) imagery, frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) mmWave radar, and inertial context. A bearing-sector interface provides the navigation controller with calibrated obstacle probabilities, radar ranges, and sensor status. It also distinguishes sensor dropout from a valid observation with no detected obstacle. Using new multimodal lake recordings, we deployed the pipeline in a 24-leg closed-loop pilot under uncontrolled lake conditions (16 day, 4 dusk, and 4 night; 351 m), including night legs in which RGB was unusable and the vessel drove on LWIR and radar evidence alone. On eight held-out low-light recordings, the calibrated fusion model achieved average precision (AP) 0.869 and expected calibration error 0.108, compared with AP 0.673 for rule-based fusion, 0.620 for gated fusion, and 0.903 for RGB alone. Our results expose a central tradeoff: RGB ranks best when usable, whereas fusion preserves a navigation input when RGB fails. This work is a step toward perception that remains usable and degrades predictably across multi-day ASV missions.
papers.summary: Small autonomous surface vessels (ASVs) struggle with obstacle perception because of glare, a waterline that shifts as the boat moves, and darkness. The authors build a context-aware pipeline that fuses RGB and long-wave infrared (LWIR) cameras, FMCW mmWave radar, and inertial data, and that reports calibrated obstacle probabilities per bearing sector while distinguishing sensor dropout from genuinely empty water. In a 24-leg closed-loop lake pilot, the vessel navigated night legs on LWIR and radar alone. On low-light recordings, fusion reached an average precision (AP) of 0.869 against 0.903 for RGB alone, which shows the core tradeoff: **RGB ranks best when it is usable, but fusion keeps providing navigation input when RGB fails**.

papers.title: Latent Multimodal Memory Reasoning
papers.abstract: Long-term personalized agents are required to reason over distributed history across modalities and evolving dialogue states. While existing flat cross-modal methods compress visual evidence prematurely and struggle with temporally stale observations, they neglect the necessity to unify multimodal and cross-session evidence. Crucially, raw multimodal memories are inherently entangled and heterogeneous, making fine-grained visual grounding and cross-modal reasoning computationally prohibitive. To this end, we present latent multimodal memory reasoning, i.e., LMMR, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that shifts long-term multimodal memory organization into a continuous latent space. Specifically, (i) instead of converting images to text and relying on static retrieval, LMMR maps both textual hidden states and visual patch features into a shared Sparse Autoencoder concept space, establishing sparse activations as common semantic addresses to dynamically construct a turn-level multimodal memory graph. (ii) A graph encoder then aggregates cross-modal and temporal dependencies across the task-specific latent subgraph, injecting the graph readout as a continuous residual rollout into the generation backbone while retaining native visual tokens to preserve fine-grained details. Extensive experiments on nine Mem-Gallery tasks and twelve MemEye settings demonstrate that LMMR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in capturing complex multimodal dependencies while enabling faithful and grounded responses.
papers.summary: Long-term personalized agents have to reason over multimodal history spread across many sessions, and converting images to text for static retrieval discards fine visual detail. `LMMR` maps both text hidden states and visual patch features into a shared `Sparse Autoencoder` concept space, and uses the resulting sparse activations as common addresses for building a turn-level multimodal memory graph. A graph encoder aggregates cross-modal and temporal dependencies and injects its output into the generation backbone as a continuous residual, while keeping the native visual tokens. On nine `Mem-Gallery` tasks and twelve `MemEye` settings, it **outperforms state-of-the-art baselines** and gives more grounded responses.

papers.title: EMMA: Event-Driven Multimodal Memory System with Multi-Agent Retrieval
papers.abstract: Long video understanding requires reasoning over hours of content that far exceed the context window of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Existing approaches compress video into fixed-length clips, yet events are fragmented and unrelated content is merged, yielding noisy retrieval. To overcome this challenge, we propose EMMA, an Event-driven Multimodal Memory system with Multi-Agent retrieval, which organizes memory around semantic events in three stages: (1) Event segmentation: a dual-stream detector adaptively locates event boundaries by fusing visual semantic drift with spoken transitions, rather than fixed windows. (2) Memory construction: built on the detected events, a three-level hierarchy of raw video, clip-level memory, and event-level memory stores content at progressively higher semantic abstraction. (3) Memory retrieval: a multi-agent framework collaboratively queries this hierarchy through query decomposition, tiered search, evidence validation, and answer generation, narrowing evidence from coarse events to precise clips. Extensive experiments on three challenging benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements, showing the effectiveness of our event-aligned memory system. Code, prompt templates, and reproduction scripts are available at https://github.com/BAI-LAB/EMMA.
papers.summary: Multimodal LLMs cannot fit hours of video into their context windows, and splitting video into fixed-length clips fragments events and mixes unrelated content, which makes retrieval noisy. `EMMA` detects event boundaries by fusing visual semantic drift with spoken transitions, then stores the video in a three-level hierarchy of raw video, clip-level memory, and event-level memory. A multi-agent retrieval process decomposes each query, searches the hierarchy tier by tier, validates evidence, and narrows from coarse events to precise clips before answering. The system shows **substantial improvements on three long-video benchmarks**.

papers.title: Language-Forcing: Advancing Humanoid Loco-Manipulation via Semantic Alignment of Whole-Body World Action Models
papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict robot actions and future observations. However, their visual prediction objectives do not explicitly distinguish task-relevant transitions from incidental scene changes. For whole-body policies, this distinction matters because task progress depends on coordinated changes in body pose, contact, and object state. We introduce LANGUAGE-FORCING, a training strategy that uses language to emphasize task-relevant changes in the future visual representations of a whole-body WAM. Given paired current and ground- truth short-horizon future frames, a frozen vision-language model assesses task progress and predicts plausible subsequent state changes. We encode these descriptions with a frozen text encoder and align their embeddings with intermediate, action-conditioned future-visual features, complementing the original visual and action prediction objectives. All auxiliary components are used only during training, introducing no additional inference overhead. On HumanoidArena, LANGUAGE-FORCING achieves an average success rate of 79.17%, exceeding the strongest competing policy by 9.46 percentage points and the same WAM without language alignment by 10.77 percentage points. Across five real-world tasks, language alignment raises average success from 53.33% to 71.33% over the same WAM baseline.
papers.summary: World Action Models (WAMs) predict both robot actions and future observations, but their visual objectives treat task-relevant changes the same as incidental scene changes. This matters for humanoid whole-body control, where task progress depends on coordinated changes in body pose, contact, and object state. `Language-Forcing` addresses this at training time. A frozen vision-language model describes task progress and the state changes likely to follow, and a frozen text encoder embeds those descriptions so they can be aligned with the WAM's intermediate, action-conditioned future-visual features. None of these auxiliary parts are used at inference. On `HumanoidArena` the method reaches **79.17% average success, 9.46 points above the strongest competing policy**, and on five real-world tasks it raises success from 53.33% to 71.33% over the same WAM without language alignment.

papers.title: GeoForward: Geometry-Guided Cross-View Alignment for Feedforward 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract: Feedforward 3D reconstruction has largely followed an {appearance-driven paradigm}: multi-view images are encoded into visual representations, cross-view correspondence is implicitly inferred from learned features, and 3D primitives are subsequently predicted from these representations. However, calibrated cameras and sparse metric measurements already provide explicit constraints on where the same physical point should appear across views. We propose a novel paradigm, \textbf{Geometry-Conditioned Feedforward Reconstruction}, in which metric geometry establishes cross-view correspondence before the 3D representation is formed, while learned visual features refine rather than discover this correspondence. Based on this paradigm, we introduce \textbf{GeoForward}. Sparse LiDAR points are unprojected into 3D and analytically projected across calibrated cameras to provide metric correspondence anchors. A bounded continuous local search then refines these anchors using visual features, and the resulting geometry-conditioned representation is fused with global multi-view context from VGGT. The shared representation drives separate metric-depth and Gaussian-attribute prediction, establishing a direct path from explicit geometry to both Gaussian centers and spatial attributes. A sparse 3D refinement module subsequently improves local attribute compatibility while preserving the geometrically determined centers. For temporal reconstruction, endpoint Gaussians are composed using vehicle masks and motion priors. On nuScenes, GeoForward achieves the lowest cross-camera depth-consistency error and Chamfer distance among the compared methods while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality. These results demonstrate that explicitly conditioning correspondence formation on metric geometry provides an effective alternative to purely appearance-driven feedforward 3D reconstruction.
papers.summary: Feedforward 3D reconstruction usually infers correspondences between camera views from learned appearance features. `GeoForward` instead uses metric geometry to establish those correspondences before the 3D representation is built. Sparse LiDAR points are projected across calibrated cameras to serve as correspondence anchors, a bounded local search refines them with visual features, and the result is fused with global multi-view context from `VGGT`. The fused representation then predicts metric depth and 3D Gaussian attributes, and a sparse 3D refinement module improves local attributes while keeping the geometrically determined centers fixed. On `nuScenes` it achieves **the lowest cross-camera depth-consistency error and Chamfer distance** among the compared methods, with competitive reconstruction quality.

papers.title: InJePA: Intention-First Latent Planning with Coupled JEPA World Models for Visual Navigation
papers.abstract: Visual navigation requires goal directed planning informed by predictions of environment dynamics. Representative navigation world model methods propose complete action candidates before predicting consequences for selection or search updates. For each candidate, predictions primarily evaluate proposed actions rather than guide its stepwise construction. To this end, we propose InJepa, an intention first planning paradigm centered on latent states. A goal conditioned JEPA proposes latent intentions, and an action conditioned JEPA continually predicts future latent states. Both operate in a shared latent space to align their predictive representations. Within each candidate, predicted consequences feed into the next intention proposal and action inference, forming a closed loop of intention, action, and consequence. This extends the world model's role beyond evaluation to leading candidate construction through latent intentions. We evaluate InJepa through closed loop image goal navigation in Habitat MP3D. The results show effective multistep navigation through intention guided action generation and consequence feedback. Experiments across encoders further support applicability across visual representations. These findings support latent intentions as the central planning object and show that world models can directly guide plan construction through coordinated reasoning about intentions and consequences. Code is available at https://github.com/zhuxun132/InJepa.
papers.summary: Navigation world models typically propose complete action sequences first and only then predict their consequences to pick among them. `InJepa` reverses this with an intention-first planner that works on latent states. A goal-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (`JEPA`) proposes latent intentions, and an action-conditioned `JEPA` predicts the future latent states that follow. Because both share one latent space, each predicted consequence feeds the next intention and action, forming a closed loop. In closed-loop image-goal navigation in `Habitat MP3D`, the approach produces **effective multistep navigation guided by intentions and consequence feedback**, and it works across several visual encoders.

papers.title: EAGLE: Entropy-Aware Geometric Learning Enhancer for Partially Polygon-Supervised Object Localization
papers.abstract: Object detection is a critical application of computer vision, yet models trained uniformly on bounding boxes lack the geometric precision to be fully effective in inference settings, especially at high IoU thresholds. One common approach is the introduction of polygon-supervised localization, where a model is trained explicitly for localization but with access to polygon masks during training. Among such methods, partial polygon supervision is viable due to the higher annotation costs of developing fully supervised training datasets. However, this introduces a further challenge: in object classes of relatively low shape complexity, the addition of training masks and subsequent segmentation loss may obscure box localization, often worsening model performance despite access to deeper geometric information. To address the practical limitations of both full and partial polygon supervision, we introduce a mathematical framework for quantifying per-class geometric complexity by combining information theory and statistical shape analysis. With this framework, we develop Entropy-Aware Geometric Learning Enhancer (EAGLE), a lightweight, post-training model head that learns geometric information for the localization model, improving accuracy via edge refinement and localization rescoring using entropy-informed updates. Empirical analysis across MS COCO and Pascal SBD demonstrates the entropy framework meaningfully predicts shape reconstruction error and accuracy differences among mask-derived and standard box predictions, while the implemented EAGLE framework achieves consistent improvement on already SOTA detection frameworks (+0.9 mAP50-95 points on MS COCO) at minimal observed inference overhead.
papers.summary: Object detectors trained only on bounding boxes lose precision at high Intersection-over-Union (IoU) thresholds. Adding polygon-mask supervision can help, but for object classes with simple shapes the extra segmentation loss can actually make box localization worse. The authors build a framework that combines information theory and statistical shape analysis to quantify how geometrically complex each class is. On top of it they build `EAGLE`, a lightweight head added after training that refines box edges and rescores localizations using entropy-informed updates. On `MS COCO` and `Pascal SBD`, the complexity measure predicts shape-reconstruction error, and `EAGLE` adds **+0.9 mAP50-95 on `MS COCO`** to already state-of-the-art detectors with minimal inference overhead.

papers.title: Rethinking weakly supervised localization on chest radiographs: position nulls, protocol dependence, and PACE
papers.abstract: Weakly supervised localization on chest radiographs is reported as a single overlap accuracy, and those numbers are not comparable across papers. We measure what one contains. Against position-null controls that keep a readout's own box and move only its position, class activation mapping and its gradient-weighted variant beat the null on two to four of seven annotated findings on ChestX-ray14 and two of eight on CheXlocalize. The null is beatable: three board-certified radiologists clear it on four to seven. Three rarely stated choices each move a result by more than most reported method effects: the results regime, the extraction threshold, and the mask-to-box rule, whose cost is predicted by how fragmented the thresholded mask is. Predicted box area alone reverses a paired comparison. These measurements produced PACE, for \emph{population anomaly and class evidence}, which multiplies the finding identity from the label-trained head by the spatial evidence from a frozen radiograph backbone that never sees a pathology label. It is the case study that made the protocol dependence visible, and we report its costs beside its gain: in an exploratory matched-area analysis it improves strict-overlap accuracy on both corpora and beats a label-derived second map, but it is the least faithful of the three readouts to the classifier's causal map, its advantage depends on the box rule, and, this benchmark releasing no localization validation set, every design choice behind it was made on the boxes it is scored on. Its one clean transfer beats one baseline and loses to the other.
papers.summary: Weakly supervised localization on chest X-rays is usually reported as a single overlap accuracy that cannot be compared across papers. The authors test what that number actually measures by comparing methods against 'position-null' controls that keep a method's own box but move it elsewhere. **Class activation mapping and its gradient-weighted variant beat the null on only two to four of seven findings on `ChestX-ray14` and two of eight on `CheXlocalize`**, while three radiologists beat it on four to seven. The authors also show that rarely reported protocol choices (the results regime, the extraction threshold, and the rule for turning a mask into a box) each shift results by more than most reported method improvements. Their own method, `PACE`, gains in strict-overlap accuracy, but the authors flag its limits: it was tuned on the same boxes it is scored on, its advantage depends on the box rule, and its one clean transfer test beats one baseline and loses to the other.

papers.title: EgoVine: Post-Training with Branching Experience Compiled from Real-World Videos
papers.abstract: Real-world egocentric videos capture multi-step household procedures, but their recorded trajectories leave alternative actions and recovery from the learner's own mistakes largely unexplored. We introduce EgoVine, a post-training framework that turns a fixed demonstration set into interactive experience for long-horizon planning. EgoVine operates in executable symbolic environments compiled from real-world video annotations, where an agent must coordinate object manipulations under partial observation and account for delayed consequences. Restoring a decision state allows the learner to explore alternative actions and compare their eventual outcomes. Union jointly trains action generation and consequence prediction in one model, using the same executions to supervise candidate comparison and recovery. Verified repairs add recovery targets from failed attempts, while comparisons among sampled continuations guide policy updates. The updated planner then returns to the environments, with its own decisions and mistakes shaping the next round of experience. On a shared benchmark, EgoVine-1.5B achieves 81.8% success on Main planning tasks and 66.7% on longer task compositions, outperforming all evaluated Flash LLM baselines on both. EgoVine connects real demonstrations to an iterative learning process that trains compact planners on choices and futures beyond the recorded trajectories.
papers.summary: Egocentric videos of household procedures record only one trajectory, so they show neither alternative actions nor how to recover from mistakes. `EgoVine` compiles video annotations into executable symbolic environments where an agent must plan long-horizon object manipulations under partial observation. Because decision states can be restored, the learner can try alternative actions and compare their eventual outcomes. A single model is trained to both generate actions and predict their consequences, with verified repairs of failed attempts and comparisons between sampled continuations providing the training signal. The updated planner then collects new experience in further rounds. The compact `EgoVine-1.5B` reaches **81.8% success on main planning tasks and 66.7% on longer task compositions**, outperforming all evaluated Flash-tier large language model (LLM) baselines.

papers.title: When the Editing Intent Is Split: A Cross-Modal Jailbreak Attack for Large Image Editing Models
papers.abstract: Large image editing models increasingly infer editing intent from both textual and visual inputs, creating an underexplored safety risk when harmful intent is distributed across modalities. In this work, we formalize this split-intent vulnerability and propose the Split-Intent Jailbreak Attack (SIJA), which asymmetrically distributes an unsafe editing intent by specifying the editing referent in text while concealing the safety-critical action and specification through graphical visual semantics in an auxiliary cue. To systematically study this threat, we introduce the Split-Intent Image Editing Safety Benchmark (SI2ESBench) for evaluating image editing models under split-intent inputs. Extensive experiments on representative commercial and open-source models demonstrate that SIJA effectively compromises state-of-the-art image editing systems, achieving ASRs of 68.28% on GPT Image 2 and 91.38% on Qwen-Image-3.0-Pro. Our results expose a mismatch between multimodal editing and safety assessment: the distributed intent can be recovered to execute the requested transformation, yet its harmfulness often remains undetected by existing safeguards. To mitigate this vulnerability, we propose editing-intent reconstruction, a defense principle that explicitly evaluates the complete transformation implied by the joint multimodal context and substantially improves rejection of split-intent attacks. Our findings expose a cross-modal safety gap in modern image editing systems and highlight the need to assess the jointly inferred transformation rather than individual inputs in isolation. https://github.com/yexianmin/SIJA
papers.summary: Image editing models infer what to do from both text and images, which opens a risk when harmful intent is split across the two. The Split-Intent Jailbreak Attack (`SIJA`) names the target of the edit in text while hiding the unsafe action and its details in graphical cues inside an auxiliary image. The authors also release `SI2ESBench`, a benchmark for evaluating editing models under such split-intent inputs. The attack achieves **attack success rates of 68.28% on `GPT Image 2` and 91.38% on `Qwen-Image-3.0-Pro`**, because models can recover the combined edit while safeguards that check each input separately miss its harmfulness. As a defense, the authors propose editing-intent reconstruction, which judges the full transformation implied by all inputs together and substantially improves rejection of these attacks.

papers.title: UMI-WM: Interactive World Modeling for Bimanual Manipulation from Wrist Cameras
papers.abstract: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) pairs wrist-camera videos with camera trajectories and gripper openings, providing scalable, robot-free data for learning how bimanual actions change a shared scene. Existing interactive world models, however, typically rely on text or single-camera control and struggle to follow each arm's actions while maintaining consistency between the two wrist views. We introduce UMI-WM, an action-conditioned bimanual world model that jointly generates both wrist views from observation history, per-arm relative camera poses, and gripper widths, with cross-view consistency, action following, and visual fidelity. UMI-WM injects each arm's actions into its own wrist stream, while sparse hub tokens exchange scene information between the two streams. Camera-aware geometry conditioning and camera-guided noise further support per-view motion control and cross-view geometric exchange. We adapt the model for block-causal generation and distill the 30-step Teacher into a Student with four denoising steps. We train UMI-WM on self-collected open-world and in-studio UMI recordings combined with public manipulation data. To evaluate action following, we use an inverse dynamics model (IDM) to recover relative camera poses and gripper widths from generated videos, and introduce Bimanual Action Fidelity (BAF) to measure how closely these recovered actions match the conditioning actions. UMI-WM achieves the best results on all five reference-video fidelity metrics and the best or competitive performance on VBench and WorldArena. The Teacher and Student outperform all compared baselines in action following, while the four-step Student generates paired wrist videos 6.9 times faster than the Teacher.
papers.summary: `UMI-WM` is a world model for two-armed robot manipulation that generates both wrist-camera views from observation history, each arm's relative camera pose, and gripper widths. Its training data comes from the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI), which records wrist-camera video without a robot. Each arm's actions are injected into its own video stream, and sparse hub tokens exchange scene information between the two streams to keep them consistent. Camera-aware conditioning supports per-view motion control. A 30-step teacher model is distilled into a four-step causal student. To measure how well generated videos follow the commanded actions, the authors introduce Bimanual Action Fidelity (`BAF`), which uses an inverse dynamics model to recover actions from generated videos. `UMI-WM` leads on all five reference-video fidelity metrics and is best or competitive on `VBench` and `WorldArena`, and **the four-step student runs 6.9 times faster than the teacher**.

papers.title: SPIRIT: Sparse Physics-Informed Inverse Rendering for SAR Imaging
papers.abstract: Radio-frequency (RF) and wave-based imaging systems play a critical role in sensing under adverse conditions, but are fundamentally constrained by a trade-off between collection speed and spatial resolution. Reducing measurements to enable rapid collection of fragment geometric information across sensing dimensions, leading to highly non-injective inverse problems that destabilize conventional image-domain reconstruction and super-resolution methods. Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) exemplifies this challenge in sparse-aperture sampling. We introduce SPIRIT, a physics-informed inverse rendering framework for sparse-aperture SAR. Rather than enhancing formed images, SPIRIT reconstructs an explicit three-dimensional surface. By adopting an optimization strategy and explicitly modeling visibility, phase coherence, and wave propagation, SPIRIT aggregates distributed geometric features across sparse aperture views into a coherent reconstruction. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that SPIRIT recovers accurate geometry and signal under extreme sparsity, reducing data collection by over 90% while achieving low geometric and signal error and consistently outperforming baselines.
papers.summary: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) and other radio-frequency imaging systems trade collection speed against resolution. Sparse sampling speeds up collection but makes reconstruction ill-posed. `SPIRIT` is a physics-informed inverse rendering framework that, rather than enhancing formed images, reconstructs an explicit 3D surface by optimizing a model of visibility, phase coherence, and wave propagation across sparse aperture views. On synthetic and real data it recovers accurate geometry and signal under extreme sparsity, **reducing data collection by over 90%** while outperforming baselines.

papers.title: Your Self-Supervised Projection Head Captures Object Co-Occurrence Statistics
papers.abstract: Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) has achieved impressive success in learning semantic visual representations, yet the underlying principles driving this success remain underexplored. In this work, we hypothesize that common SSL pretext tasks implicitly model object co-occurrence statistics, a fundamental cue for visual learning. To test this, we curate three datasets of segmented objects from existing vision benchmarks using a state-of-the-art segmentation model. Through experiments across many SSL models, we reveal a hierarchical encoding of semantic information: while the visual backbone captures object categories, the projection head specializes in encoding co-occurrences between object categories. As a result, the projection head outperforms the backbone in aligning with human judgments of inter-category similarity. Furthermore, by controlling co-occurrence patterns during pre-training, we demonstrate that encoding object co-occurrences can significantly accelerate the emergence of category-level representations. Our findings uncover a previously hidden learning principle in SSL and suggest a path toward designing more effective pretext tasks by explicitly leveraging object co-occurrence structure.
papers.summary: The authors test whether common self-supervised learning (SSL) pretext tasks implicitly learn how often object categories appear together. They curate three datasets of segmented objects from existing benchmarks and probe many SSL models. They find a hierarchy: **the backbone encodes object categories, while the projection head specializes in encoding category co-occurrences**, which lets the head align better with human judgments of similarity between categories. Controlling co-occurrence patterns during pre-training also speeds up the emergence of category-level representations, which suggests pretext tasks could be designed to exploit co-occurrence structure explicitly.

papers.title: Announced Breaks Separate Conformal Reliability from Frequency Calibration
papers.abstract: An announced boundary reveals the partition before the first affected outcome, and a reset there serves one of two audits. The per-time audit reads conformal reliability, the expected distance of the threshold's coverage from nominal at miscoverage 0.1. The frequency audit reads frequency calibration, whether a closed window's error rate matched it. The reset rule, the post-boundary empirical quantile, attains the minimax per-time rate for independent scores. On bounded scores a recursion reset at the boundary attains a frequency gap of order one over the count when its floor adds a bounded total. At the 50th forecast after a large synthetic break, the reset rule's per-time gap stands below that of five adaptive methods, four from their authors' code, with every paired band below zero. After an electricity market reform, on 68 unseen scores, the band stands below zero against two, includes zero against two, adaptive conformal inference among them, and is a point at zero against one. After monetary policy decisions its pointwise band stands above zero against all five on 10 of the first 34 days. Of 9 announced boundaries one clears the smallest coverage difference its window detects, where every method's per-time gap at the 50th forecast exceeds the nominal miscoverage. Over the first 50 forecasts the reset recursion leads the frequency audit after every synthetic break.
papers.summary: When a structural break such as a policy change is announced in advance, a conformal predictor can reset at that boundary. The authors separate two ways of auditing such a reset: per-time conformal reliability, meaning how far coverage at each step deviates from the nominal level, and frequency calibration, meaning whether a window's overall error rate matches the target. They prove that resetting to the post-boundary empirical quantile attains the **minimax per-time rate for independent scores**, and that a recursion reset at the boundary achieves a frequency gap of order one over the number of observations on bounded scores. Empirically, the reset rule beats five adaptive methods after a large synthetic break. Results on an electricity market reform and on monetary policy decisions are mixed: it wins against some baselines, ties others including adaptive conformal inference, and on the monetary policy data trails all five on 10 of the first 34 days.

papers.title: Cross-Modal Forgetting and Transfer in Unified Multimodal Post-Training
papers.abstract: Unified multimodal models answer questions about images and also generate images with one shared set of weights. This creates a post-training risk that single-purpose models do not have: fine-tuning one capability can damage another that works in a different modality. We measure this cross-modal forgetting for LoRA post-training of Janus-Pro-7B. Every target is chosen by how poorly the base model already handles it, from a poetic register to a language it barely speaks, so that retention is tested against a real intervention; we then evaluate the capabilities we never trained, first after a single run and then after chaining three. A single run looks entirely safe: nothing we did not train degrades on four public benchmarks or in free-form English, even when the adapter cuts held-out Welsh perplexity by 76% with a relative weight change under 2%. That safety belongs to the run, not to the recipe. Chaining three runs destroys the capability learned one run earlier and raises general-text perplexity by one to two orders of magnitude above the never-adapted model, on the very measures that stayed flat before. The cause is in the objective, which constrains only the modality being trained and leaves the other head unconstrained: cutting the learning rate to one fifth does not prevent the collapse, while anchoring the other head removes the damage to the capabilities we never trained, at no cost to what is learned. What is learned also stays inside its own modality, with Welsh acquired from text closing only 3% of the English-Welsh gap in image generation.
papers.summary: Unified multimodal models share one set of weights for answering questions about images and for generating images, so fine-tuning one ability can damage another. The authors study this cross-modal forgetting for `LoRA` fine-tuning of `Janus-Pro-7B` on targets the base model handles poorly, such as Welsh. A single fine-tuning run appears safe, with no degradation on four untrained benchmarks. However, **chaining three runs erases the capability learned one run earlier and raises general-text perplexity by one to two orders of magnitude**. They trace the cause to an objective that constrains only the modality being trained. Lowering the learning rate does not prevent the collapse, while anchoring the other head removes the damage at no cost to what is learned. Learning also stays within its modality: Welsh learned from text closes only 3% of the English-Welsh gap in image generation.

papers.title: Vocabulary-Incomplete Unsupervised Vision-Language Model Adaptation
papers.abstract: In certain real-world scenarios, obtaining labeled data is excessively expensive, motivating increasing interest in adapting models without annotations. Vision-language models (VLMs) provide pseudo-labels for unlabeled images through image-text similarity, enabling adaptation without manual labeling. The previous unsupervised vision-language model adaption methods assume access to an adaptation vocabulary containing all class names. However, a complete vocabulary is difficult to construct in real-world scenarios, as unlabeled data may contain classes that are overlooked or fall outside the current task scope. Thus, we propose Vocabulary-Incomplete Unsupervised Vision-language model Adaptation (VI-UVA), where only a subset of class names are available during adaptation. The vocabulary incompleteness induces an adaptation bias toward provided classes, which degrades omitted-class recognition. To address this issue, we propose Label Space Reconstruction (LSR), which reconstructs a latent label space from the unlabeled data and incorporates it into prompt tuning, thereby extending adaptation beyond the incomplete vocabulary and mitigating the adaptation bias. Furthermore, we derive an omitted-class semantic discrepancy bound for LSR and identify the key factors affecting the bound. Extensive experiments across eight benchmarks demonstrate that LSR outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.
papers.summary: Unsupervised adaptation of vision-language models (VLMs) uses image-text similarity to pseudo-label unlabeled images, but existing methods assume a complete list of class names. The authors define Vocabulary-Incomplete Unsupervised Vision-language model Adaptation (`VI-UVA`), where only some class names are known, and show this biases adaptation against the omitted classes. Their method, Label Space Reconstruction (`LSR`), reconstructs a latent label space from the unlabeled data and incorporates it into prompt tuning. They also derive a bound on the semantic discrepancy for omitted classes and identify the factors that affect it. `LSR` **outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across eight benchmarks**.

papers.title: Doing Less with More: A First-Principles Exploration of the Suitability of Agentic Computing over Alternative Architectural Choices
papers.abstract:
There is growing interest in automating business activities with Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) due to latter's seeming ease of use. Never has it been easier, or costlier, to do less with more. However, little is known about when agents are preferable to established alternatives such as local computation, Representational State Transfer (REST), the Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP), and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), particularly when development speed, performance, and operational cost are considered. We investigate this question using a controlled mathematical task that compares seven methods on a benchmark of 1,000 arithmetic expressions where semantics of operator precedence has to be preserved. We ran this setup across a native Function Calling baseline (Python library), REST, SOAP and MCP microservice architectures, direct responses from large language models (LLMs) using a Groq cloud API and five locally deployed Ollama models, and agentic systems in which five local LLMs invoke MCP tools. The deterministic methods achieve 100% accuracy with negligible latency. Direct LLM evaluation achieves at most 92.9% accuracy at over 22,000x the latency of a native function call. With MCP tools, the best agent reaches 99.9% accuracy, but incurs nearly 1,000,000x the baseline latency. These results demonstrate that LLMs approaches are poorly suited for exact arithmetic evaluation and motivate an informed architectural decision framework (ADF) for choosing an architecture based on accuracy and throughput requirements. We recognize that an actual interaction with an agent may span both reasoning and linguistic tasks. Hence our recommendation is to explore multiple architectural choices (based on task type) rather than one-size-fits-all solution (LLMs).
  Code is available at - https://github.com/Ritvik-G/adf/
papers.summary: The authors ask when LLM agents are worth using instead of conventional architectures.
