They compare seven approaches on 1,000 arithmetic expressions that require correct operator precedence: native function calls, `REST`, `SOAP`, Model Context Protocol (`MCP`) microservices, direct answers from large language models (LLMs) via the `Groq` API and five local `Ollama` models, and local LLM agents calling `MCP` tools. The deterministic methods reach 100% accuracy with negligible latency. Direct LLM answers top out at 92.9% at over 22,000 times the latency of a native call. **The best `MCP` agent reaches 99.9% accuracy but at nearly 1,000,000 times the baseline latency.** The authors use these results to propose an architectural decision framework (`ADF`) that chooses an architecture by task type, accuracy, and throughput needs.

papers.title: Zero-Shot Tabular Learning via Hypergraph Reasoning with LLMs
papers.abstract: Tabular data are prevalent across diverse domains such as healthcare and finance. Zero-shot tabular learning aims to make predictions without labeled data. However, existing LLM-based approaches rely on row-wise prompting, resulting in high inference cost and limited use of inter-row dependencies. In this work, we propose TABHGR+, an efficient relation-aware zero-shot framework for tabular data that leverages LLM-generated rules to label and group rows. Specifically, based on column and task descriptions, we use LLMs to generate rules that assign weak labels to all rows. To refine these noisy weak labels, we construct a hypergraph by grouping semantically related rows using LLM-generated rules and perform hypergraph-based label propagation. Lastly, we further enhance the LLM-generated hypergraph for propagation, which is potentially sub-optimal, by assigning label-adaptive weights to hyperedges. By requiring only a constant number of LLM calls independent of dataset size, TABHGR+ substantially reduces inference cost while achieving higher classification accuracy than zero-shot and strong few-shot baselines.
papers.summary: Zero-shot classification of tabular data with large language models (LLMs) usually prompts the model once per row, which is expensive and ignores relationships between rows. `TabHGR+` instead has the LLM generate rules from column and task descriptions, then uses those rules to assign noisy weak labels to every row. It also uses the rules to group related rows into a hypergraph, refines the labels by propagating them through that hypergraph, and learns label-adaptive weights for the hyperedges. Because **the number of LLM calls is constant regardless of dataset size**, inference costs much less, and accuracy exceeds both zero-shot and strong few-shot baselines.

papers.title: SpinDoctor: Finding Innocuous Prompts for Biased Image Generation
papers.abstract: We introduce SpinDoctor, a method for discovering innocuous prompts for text-to-image models that result in images with a chosen target bias, while retaining the quality of the images and prompts. These prompts present a risk for user manipulation, in that a user who is given these seemingly unbiased prompts might be willing to use them and would receive biased images in return. Our method is flexible: it uses models in a black-box way only and the target image bias can easily be changed, and so our method can be applied with various motivations and in various scenarios. Our method shows some transferability between models-we saw the same bias emerge in 78.6% of cases-such that a victim who uses a prompt generated via our method using one model still likely receives a biased image from another model. In our experiments, a subset of which we corroborated with human evaluation, we were able to find an innocuous prompt that moved generated images in the direction of the desired bias in all but two of 304 experiments, with an average improvement of 34.8% and 33.5% on two open-source text-to-image models.
papers.summary: `SpinDoctor` uses only black-box access to text-to-image models to find innocent-looking prompts that nonetheless produce images with a chosen bias. This creates a manipulation risk for users who are handed such prompts. Across 304 experiments, it found a prompt that shifted images toward the target bias in all but two cases, with **average improvements of 34.8% and 33.5% on two open-source models**, and some results were confirmed by human evaluation. The prompts partly transfer between models, with the same bias appearing in 78.6% of cases.

papers.title: Improving Fake Profile Detection Through Multimodal Learning and Research-Guided Feature Integration
papers.abstract: Fake accounts continue to undermine online platforms, yet it remains unclear whether multimodal learning offers meaningful improvements over strong metadata baselines or graph-based approaches. In this work, we study bot detection by integrating textual, visual, and account metadata signals on the TwiBot-22 benchmark using a subsample of 30,000 users. We propose a multimodal framework combining pretrained textual (XLM-RoBERTa) and visual (CLIP) embeddings with structured account-level features such as follower counts, posting frequency, and account age, and evaluate multiple modality combinations using CatBoost alongside a Relational Graph Convolutional Network (R-GCN). Results show that metadata alone is highly predictive, while multimodal fusion yields only marginal and largely statistically insignificant gains. The graph-based model underperforms classical variants under the subsampled graph conditions of this study. Overall, our findings suggest that under practical constraints, feature quality and metadata richness matter more than fusion complexity.
papers.summary: The authors test whether multimodal learning beats strong metadata baselines for detecting bots, using a 30,000-user subsample of the `TwiBot-22` benchmark. They combine text embeddings from `XLM-RoBERTa`, image embeddings from `CLIP`, and account features such as follower counts, posting frequency, and account age. They evaluate these with `CatBoost` and with a Relational Graph Convolutional Network (`R-GCN`). **Metadata alone is highly predictive, and multimodal fusion adds only marginal, mostly statistically insignificant gains.** The graph model underperforms on the subsampled graph, which suggests that under practical constraints feature quality matters more than fusion complexity.

papers.title: miniTE: Diagnosing and Bridging the Execution Gap in Native NVFP4 Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Native NVFP4 promises to accelerate reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs), but achieving stable learning across separate training and sampling engines remains challenging. We show that matching model weights and numerical formats is insufficient to ensure consistent policy evaluation, highlighting the importance of cross-engine numerical execution. We introduce miniTE, a lightweight framework that combines execution diagnostics, cross-engine numerical alignment, and efficient native W4A4 (4-bit weights and activations) GEMM computation for LLM RL. It improves numerical execution consistency without modifying the RL objective, while reducing implementation overhead to realize the benefits of native low-bit computation. Long-horizon RL experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate stable training and benchmark performance close to BF16, outperforming naive Transformer Engine (TE) NVFP4 in evaluation quality. On single NVIDIA B300 GPU node, the optimized learner reaches 33,540 tokens/s, yielding 1.39x and 1.47x the throughput of BF16 and TE NVFP4, respectively, for complete learner updates. We released the framework, kernels, diagnostics, and training configurations to make native low-bit RL easier.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs) could run faster in the 4-bit `NVFP4` format, but training becomes unstable when the separate training and sampling engines evaluate the policy differently. The authors show that matching weights and number formats is not enough, because numerical execution itself must agree across engines. Their framework, `miniTE`, combines execution diagnostics, cross-engine numerical alignment, and efficient kernels with 4-bit weights and activations, without changing the RL objective. In long-horizon RL on `Qwen3-30B-A3B`, it trains stably with benchmark results close to `BF16`, beating naive Transformer Engine (`TE`) `NVFP4`. **On a single `B300` node the learner reaches 33,540 tokens/s, 1.39 times the throughput of `BF16` and 1.47 times that of `TE NVFP4`.**

papers.title: VERDICT: Visual Extraction-Result Decoder with Integrated Confidence and Traceable Evidence
papers.abstract: Enterprises run schema-guided structured field extraction on documents with frontier multimodal models, and accuracy keeps improving as new models and systems arrive. Two things have not kept pace: the evidence for each extracted value, meaning the location of the document it was read from, and how far to trust the value and that evidence. Neither is a component of most extraction systems today, so we build them as a framework that attaches to an existing extractor and leaves it untouched. We present VERDICT, a plug-in framework that uses a small Vision--Language Model (VLM) to ground/localize the evidence once per document over a fixed external extractor's output, then calibrates value and evidence confidence. Fine-tuning the VLM for evidence localization substantially improves visual evidence quality and, more importantly, expands VERDICT's selective-prediction operating range. At a strict confidence threshold $0.80$, VERDICT with the fine-tuned VLM gives usable precision--coverage trade-offs for both value and evidence confidence across the in-distribution and out of distribution datasets, whereas the frozen setting often collapses to little or no coverage. Running an open-weight VLM for localization rather than a closed API makes its internal states available to the calibrator, and they are worth more than output log-probabilities: in-distribution AUROC rises from $0.730$ to $0.914$ for value confidence and from $0.681$ to $0.906$ for evidence confidence. This advantage does not survive a distribution shift. We show that the signal is displaced rather than destroyed, and that labeling roughly $120$ fields from the target dataset takes evidence confidence from $0.641$ to $0.905$ on one dataset and from $0.675$ to $0.829$ on the other.
papers.summary: Enterprise document extraction with frontier multimodal models rarely reports where each value came from or how far to trust it. `VERDICT` is a plug-in framework that leaves an existing extractor untouched and uses a small vision-language model (VLM) to locate the evidence for each extracted value, then calibrates confidence for both the value and its evidence. Fine-tuning the VLM widens the range of usable precision-coverage trade-offs. Using an open-weight model exposes internal states that, in-distribution, **raise AUROC from 0.730 to 0.914 for value confidence and from 0.681 to 0.906 for evidence confidence**. This advantage disappears under distribution shift, but labeling about 120 fields from the target dataset recovers most of it.

papers.title: Organizing LLM Inference for Aggregate Predictions from Behavioral Data
papers.abstract: When using a large language model (LLM) to simulate a user population, how should we combine individual behavioral histories to predict the fraction of users who take a particular action? We study this question in e-commerce, predicting observed product-level conversion rates from browsing sessions without task-specific model training. We vary two design choices, each involving a bias-variance tradeoff. Summarizing a product's sessions before inference reduces cost but can discard predictive detail, adding bias, whereas predicting outcomes for individual sessions and averaging afterward preserves that detail but requires many calls to reduce variance. Evaluating products together in one prompt can help the model infer what is typical in the setting, reducing bias, but also makes each prediction depend on which other products appear alongside it, adding noise. We evaluate both choices across five LLMs and two datasets. Our main finding is that predictions from individual sessions outperform predictions from summaries when products are evaluated separately, but summaries lead when products are evaluated together. Comparative summaries achieve the highest Spearman correlation with observed rates in 12 of 15 settings, with no alternative significantly better. Comparison thus helps summaries far more than session predictions, overcoming the advantage of behavioral detail. We interpret this difference through a Bayesian model of the second tradeoff, which suggests that comparison helps more when the inputs in a prompt reveal more about differences across products, consistent with our results for four types of comparative context. Comparative summaries also incur a small fraction of the inference cost of the session methods. With the best model for each outcome, they attain 66-89% of the correlation of the best supervised benchmark trained on thousands of labeled products.
papers.summary: The authors study how to organize prompts when using large language models (LLMs) to predict the share of users who take an action, here product conversion rates from e-commerce browsing sessions. They vary two choices: summarizing sessions before inference versus predicting each session and averaging, and evaluating products one at a time versus together in one prompt. When products are evaluated separately, per-session predictions win. When products are evaluated together, summaries win, and **comparative summaries achieve the highest Spearman correlation in 12 of 15 settings** at a small fraction of the cost. A Bayesian model explains why comparison helps, and the best configurations reach 66-89% of the correlation of a supervised model trained on thousands of labeled products.

papers.title: Factorization-Guided Training and Inference for Diffusion-Drafted Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference through parallel verification of tokens proposed by a drafter. Diffusion drafters further parallelize proposal generation, but greater proposal capacity or higher mean accepted tokens (MAT) need not yield higher throughput. Because verification accepts only a consecutive prefix, early rejections can render later correct predictions ineffective, limiting MAT gains, while even higher MAT may not improve throughput if per-round latency increases. We introduce DScout, which uses two complementary factorizations to guide diffusion drafter training and inference for higher throughput. For training, DScout factorizes position-wise loss into inclusion, weighting, and prediction loss. This guides the design and combination of mixed-horizon training, intra-block unmasking, and acceptance-weighted loss to align supervision with prefix acceptance and improve MAT. For inference, DScout factorizes throughput as the ratio of MAT to per-round latency, guiding target-conditioning depth, drafter depth, and inference block size selection to identify a high-throughput configuration for each workload. Across six benchmarks, DScout achieves $3.84\times$ and $4.14\times$ mean speedups over autoregressive decoding on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, respectively, improving mean speedup over the state-of-the-art baseline by 9.1% and 7.1%. Across models and concurrency settings, our inference configuration policy provides up to 9.75% additional mean speedup over DScout's fixed configuration.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model inference by having a drafter propose tokens that the target model checks in parallel. Diffusion drafters propose a whole block of tokens at once, but because verification only accepts a consecutive prefix, a higher mean accepted tokens (MAT) count does not always mean higher throughput. `DScout` splits the training loss into inclusion, weighting, and prediction terms, and uses that split to combine mixed-horizon training, intra-block unmasking, and acceptance-weighted loss so that training targets prefix acceptance. At inference it treats throughput as MAT divided by per-round latency and uses that to choose target-conditioning depth, drafter depth, and block size for each workload, reaching **3.84x and 4.14x mean speedups over autoregressive decoding on `Qwen3-4B` and `Qwen3-8B`**, 9.1% and 7.1% better than the previous best baseline.

papers.title: Beyond Prediction: A Component-Level Study of Concept Recovery in In-Context Learning
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables language models to make accurate predictions from demonstrations, but prediction success alone does not reveal the extent to which the underlying concept has been recovered. Existing evaluations typically assess recovery at the level of the whole concept, making it difficult to identify which components are recovered and to separate model limitations from ambiguity in the demonstrations. We introduce a component-level framework for concept recovery that decomposes concepts into their defining components and uses controlled structural interventions to evaluate both component-level and whole-concept recovery under identifiable demonstrations. Across four instruction-tuned LLMs and three composition forms, we find that models often achieve high prediction accuracy despite poor whole-concept recovery, with systematic over-specification of relevant attributes and level constraints. Individual structural components are generally insufficient for whole-concept recovery, whereas jointly specifying complementary components, particularly relevant attributes and their level constraints, substantially improves recovery. However, this improvement is fragile: a single plausible but unnecessary level constraint can substantially disrupt recovery. Finally, joint supervision of recovery and implicit prediction substantially improves recovery while preserving prediction performance, with the learned capability transferring across composition forms. Overall, our component-level analysis provides a more diagnostic view of what models recover from demonstrations than the existing holistic view.
papers.summary: A model that predicts well from in-context learning (ICL) demonstrations may still not have recovered the concept behind them, and evaluations that score the whole concept cannot show which parts were missed. The authors break concepts into their defining components and apply controlled structural interventions so that each component's recovery can be measured under demonstrations that pin down a unique answer. Across four instruction-tuned LLMs, **models often reach high prediction accuracy while recovering the whole concept poorly**, typically by adding attributes and level constraints that are not needed. Specifying complementary components together helps but breaks easily, since one plausible extra constraint can derail recovery; training jointly on recovery and prediction improves recovery and transfers across composition forms.

papers.title: SECURE-AI: Multi-Signal Uncertainty Quantification for Trustworthy Acoustic Cough Detection
papers.abstract: Acoustic models for cough detection achieve high accuracy on curated benchmarks but fail silently in deployment, where speech, environmental noise, and audio unlike the training data induce confident misclassifications. In health monitoring, a confidently wrong prediction is worse than no answer at all. We present SECURE-AI (Self-aware Estimation of Cough Uncertainty for Reliable Evaluation of AI), a multi-signal uncertainty quantification framework that wraps a frozen MobileNetV3 cough classifier and estimates when its predictions should not be trusted, combining Monte Carlo Dropout, Temperature Scaling, and Mahalanobis distance in the embedding space. On a held-out split of 12,161 Coswara recordings, the probability-space methods are individually insufficient: Monte Carlo Dropout assigns lower uncertainty to incorrect than to correct predictions, and temperature scaling improves calibration but not discrimination. The strongest signal is embedding-space distance: Mahalanobis distance separates true positives from false positives (means 44.7 versus 63.4; Cohen's $d = 0.94$; AUROC 0.86) and, among predicted non-coughs, false negatives from true negatives (AUROC 0.82), so the same signal can flag both false alarms and missed coughs. At a descriptive operating point selected from labeled test data, retaining 90 percent of true-positive detections removes about two-thirds of false positives and raises precision from 59.9 to roughly 80 percent. A rejection threshold tuned on one split does not transfer to another (validation F1 of 82 percent falls to 34 percent on test), so we report threshold-independent AUROC as the main measure. An error taxonomy shows that failures are systematic, with most false positives related to speech. The pipeline runs on Raspberry Pi hardware costing 30 to 90 US dollars. Probabilistic calibration alone is thus inadequate for reliable cough detection.
papers.summary: Cough-detection models that score well on curated benchmarks make confident mistakes in deployment when they hear speech, noise, or unfamiliar audio. `SECURE-AI` wraps a frozen `MobileNetV3` cough classifier and estimates when its outputs should not be trusted, combining `Monte Carlo Dropout`, `Temperature Scaling`, and Mahalanobis distance in the embedding space. On 12,161 held-out `Coswara` recordings the probability-based signals fall short, while **embedding-space Mahalanobis distance separates true from false positives with AUROC 0.86** and also flags missed coughs. Rejection thresholds did not carry over between data splits, most false positives were linked to speech, and the pipeline runs on Raspberry Pi hardware costing 30 to 90 US dollars.

papers.title: Pack and Extract: An Effective Graph-Based Approach for Feature Selection
papers.abstract: Many molecular biology data sets contain thousands of features, such as genes in single-cell experiments or other omics data. Standard predictive models often perform poorly in such settings, as they tend to retain a large number of features and fail to adequately handle correlations among them. Combinatorial approaches, such as feature selection based on the Independent Dominating Set (IDS) model, have shown promising results, but appear to have been largely overlooked, possibly due to their high computational complexity. In this paper, we propose an improvement to IDS-based feature selection that (i) favors features exhibiting greater diversity and (ii) generalizes the notion of independent dominating set to a node packing model. The resulting formulation is used as an intermediate step within the feature selection process. We evaluate our approach on five genetic data sets and compare the results with those obtained using existing methods. Our experimental results demonstrate notable improvements in predictive accuracy over traditional models, as well as increased stability of the selected feature sets.
papers.summary: Omics datasets such as single-cell gene data contain thousands of correlated features, and standard predictive models handle them poorly. The authors extend feature selection based on the `Independent Dominating Set` (IDS) graph model by favoring more diverse features and generalizing the formulation to a node packing model, which serves as an intermediate step in the selection pipeline. On five genetic datasets the method **improves predictive accuracy over traditional models** and produces more stable sets of selected features.

papers.title: PeekKV: The First Content Token Already Knows Which Heads Matter
papers.abstract: The size of the KV cache grows linearly with context length, making it a major memory bottleneck in LLM serving. Motivated by recent progress in identifying the functional roles of attention heads, a growing body of work compresses the KV cache non-uniformly across heads. Existing methods either fix the important heads via offline profiling or select them using attention signals from the prefill stage. In both cases, however, accuracy fluctuates substantially across workloads. While investigating the cause of this instability, we find that the active heads shift between the prefill and decode stages even within a single input. Along the decode path, by contrast, the activehead composition remains stable across content tokens once format tokens are filtered out. Based on this observation, we propose PeekKV. PeekKV observes a single content token immediately after prefill - a one-token peek - to jointly obtain head-group scores and token-importance scores. Guided by these scores, PeekKV allocates KV cache budgets to head groups in proportion to their group scores and retains only the top-scoring tokens within each budget. PeekKV requires no offline profiling or training and thus applies directly to unseen workloads and new models. Across four public benchmarks, PeekKV achieves the highest accuracy in more than half of the per-model comparisons against state-of-the-art methods, and stays closest to the full-cache accuracy on RULER and LongBench. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, PeekKV retains 95.7% of the full-cache accuracy at a 10% memory budget on RULER with 16K contexts and 95.9% at a 1.5% budget on LongBench.
papers.summary: The KV cache grows linearly with context length, and methods that compress it unevenly across attention heads give unstable accuracy because they pick important heads by offline profiling or from prefill-stage attention. The authors find that the set of active heads changes between prefill and decode, but stays stable across content tokens during decoding once format tokens are filtered out. `PeekKV` looks at a single content token right after prefill to score both head groups and tokens, then splits the cache budget across head groups by score, with no profiling or training required. On `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` it **retains 95.7% of full-cache accuracy at a 10% memory budget on `RULER` with 16K contexts**, and 95.9% at a 1.5% budget on `LongBench`.

papers.title: Fast Construction of Inner Sphere Trees Using Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Collision detection for complex non-convex objects is a bottleneck in physics simulation, virtual reality, and robotics. Inner sphere trees (ISTs) answer proximity and penetration queries efficiently, but their greedy leaf-sphere construction is sequential and computationally expensive, which limits both large-scale preprocessing and runtime use. In this work, we present ML-IST, a machine-learning-based method that reformulates leaf-sphere generation as a single-shot set-prediction problem: a network predicts a fixed set of inscribed sphere candidates from multichannel voxel geometry, differentiable coverage feedback corrects the coarse prediction and fills residual gaps at finer scales, and a lightweight geometric projection enforces validity. Averaged over the test set, a single-GPU implementation of ML-IST reduces mean leaf-generation time by a factor of $2.0$--$2.6$ over single-core CPU construction across target capacities of 64--512 spheres, and qualitative results on complex models show multiscale sphere distributions that follow principal volumes and slender features. We further integrate ML-IST into the Jolt Physics and Bullet engines; in an alpha-puzzle benchmark it reaches 55.89~FPS, the highest among the compared representations (conventional IST, GImpact, and convex decomposition). These results support learned leaf generation as a practical component for fast, runtime construction of detailed collision representations.
papers.summary: Inner sphere trees (ISTs) answer collision and penetration queries for complex non-convex objects efficiently, but building their leaf spheres is a slow, sequential greedy process. `ML-IST` turns leaf-sphere generation into a single-shot set-prediction problem: a network predicts candidate inscribed spheres from voxel geometry, differentiable coverage feedback fills remaining gaps at finer scales, and a geometric projection keeps the result valid. On one GPU it cuts leaf-generation time by 2.0 to 2.6 times compared with single-core CPU construction. Integrated into the `Jolt Physics` and `Bullet` engines, it **reaches 55.89 FPS on an alpha-puzzle benchmark**, the highest among the compared collision representations.

papers.title: A Group-Aware Comparative Study of Classical Machine Learning and Deep Learning Methods for Sensor-Based Human Activity Recognition
papers.abstract: Human Activity Recognition (HAR) using wearable or smartphone inertial sensors is commonly evaluated with both classical machine learning and deep learning methods. However, reported performance can be strongly affected by sensor modality, dataset characteristics, and data-splitting strategy. This study presents a controlled comparative evaluation of four classical machine learning models and four deep learning models on two public HAR datasets, UCI-HAR and KU-HAR. Three sensor modalities were considered: accelerometer (ACC), gyroscope (GYRO), and their combination (ACC+GYRO). Classical machine learning models used handcrafted statistical features, while deep learning models operated directly on raw sensor sequences. The primary evaluation employed five-fold StratifiedGroupKFold cross-validation, with subject- or participant-level grouping to prevent group overlap between training and test folds. Macro-F1 was used as the primary performance metric. The results show that deep learning did not consistently outperform classical machine learning. On UCI-HAR, the evaluated deep learning models achieved slightly higher macro-F1 values, whereas on KU-HAR, LightGBM achieved 0.857 compared with 0.828 for the highest-performing evaluated deep learning model. Regarding sensor modality, the combined ACC+GYRO configuration generally outperformed ACC or GYRO alone on both datasets. The evaluation protocol also had a substantial effect: for CNNBiLSTMAttn with ACC+GYRO, random splitting increased macro-F1 by 0.033 on UCI-HAR and 0.093 on KU-HAR compared with grouped evaluation. These findings highlight the importance of model family, sensor modality, dataset characteristics, and group-aware evaluation when assessing sensor-based HAR systems.
papers.summary: Results for sensor-based Human Activity Recognition (HAR) depend heavily on sensor choice, dataset, and how data is split. The study compares four classical machine learning models on handcrafted features against four deep learning models on raw sequences, using `UCI-HAR` and `KU-HAR`, accelerometer and gyroscope inputs alone and combined, and subject-grouped five-fold cross-validation. Deep learning did not consistently win: it was slightly ahead on `UCI-HAR`, while `LightGBM` led on `KU-HAR` with macro-F1 of 0.857 against 0.828. Combining both sensors generally helped, and **random splitting inflated macro-F1 by up to 0.093 compared with subject-grouped evaluation**.

papers.title: ReTTT: Reflection-Driven Test-Time Training via Experience-Based Parametric Memory
papers.abstract: LLM agents accumulate valuable task-specific information through their actions, observations, and environmental feedback during multi-turn task execution. When effectively used, this information can help agents refine subsequent decisions and improve task performance. However, the learning value of an interaction depends on its context and subsequent feedback, making it challenging to extract reliable, actionable lessons and revise them as the task unfolds. In this paper, we introduce ReTTT, which enables experience-driven self-adaptation through test-time training on lessons constructed and continually revised within an episode. ReTTT lets the agent reflect on interaction feedback, maintain the resulting lessons in an explicit memory, and learn from them by updating an episode-local LoRA adapter while keeping the backbone frozen. The adapted model then performs both subsequent actions and reflection, coupling policy adaptation with the construction of future learning experience. We evaluate ReTTT on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SWE-bench Lite using two model families. ReTTT outperforms trajectory-based test-time training across all six model--benchmark settings, improving task success by up to 12.14 percentage points. A frozen-reflection comparison further shows a 7.14-point benefit from adapting the reflection policy, while trajectory analysis illustrates how adapted reflection derives more task-specific guidance from failed attempts. These findings suggest that learning to reflect on its own behavior can boost agents' performance on long-horizon tasks.
papers.summary: LLM agents gather useful feedback while working through multi-turn tasks, but turning it into reliable lessons that can be revised along the way is difficult. `ReTTT` has the agent reflect on feedback, store the resulting lessons in an explicit memory, and train an episode-local `LoRA` adapter on them while the backbone model stays frozen; the adapted model then handles both the next actions and the next reflections. On `ALFWorld`, `ScienceWorld`, and `SWE-bench Lite` with two model families, it beats trajectory-based test-time training in all six settings, **improving task success by up to 12.14 percentage points**. A comparison with a frozen reflection model attributes 7.14 points of that to adapting the reflection policy.

papers.title: TeleTwin: A Calibrated Digital Twin of Telegram Crisis Discourse as a Ground-Truth Testbed for Detecting LLM-Powered Information Operations
papers.abstract: Large language models make it cheap to run influence operations whose messages never repeat, yet real platforms offer almost no ground truth for testing whether coordination detectors can find them. The problem is sharpest on Telegram, which moderates little and spreads content through broadcast channels and forwarding rather than a follow graph. We introduce TeleTwin, an LLM-powered digital twin of a Telegram crisis-discourse ecosystem in which channels are agents, each instantiated from the history of a real channel, calibrated on 1.07 million messages from 195 public channels on the Israel-Gaza and Iran-Israel conflict (March-August 2025). On a held-out period containing the June 2025 Iran-Israel war, the twin tracks daily dynamics better than statistical baselines (correlation 0.86 against 0.64) and reacts to the war unprompted, but it over-focuses on the conflict, over-amplifies forwarding cascades, underestimates the shock and writes recognisably LLM-like text. We then inject LLM-written campaigns with known membership into the real data and into the twin. In real data, identical-text, co-URL and synchrony detectors fail once a campaign rewords, staggers or drops links; multilingual semantic similarity recovers loud campaigns, including cross-lingual ones, but not quiet ones, and its false positives fall unevenly across political perspectives. Inside the twin all detectors fail, because the simulated background is about 40 times more semantically homogeneous than the real one. Digital twins can supply ground truth for campaigns, but not, without calibrating their diversity, a realistic background for evaluating semantic detectors.
papers.summary: Influence operations written by LLMs never repeat their text, and real platforms provide almost no ground truth for testing whether detectors can find them, especially on lightly moderated Telegram. `TeleTwin` simulates a Telegram crisis-discourse ecosystem in which each channel is an LLM agent built from a real channel's history, calibrated on 1.07 million messages from 195 channels about the Israel-Gaza and Iran-Israel conflicts. The simulation tracks daily dynamics better than statistical baselines (correlation 0.86 against 0.64), but it over-amplifies forwarding and produces text that reads as LLM-written. Injected campaigns showed that identical-text, co-URL, and synchrony detectors fail once messages are reworded or staggered, and that semantic similarity catches only loud campaigns; **inside the twin every detector fails because the simulated background is about 40 times more semantically homogeneous than real data**.

papers.title: CrowdH-Edit: Reference-Guided Instruction-Based Synthetic Hajj Crowd Image Generation for Crowd Counting
papers.abstract: The scarcity of domain-specific annotated images remains a major limitation for developing computer-vision systems for Hajj crowd analysis. Existing crowd-counting datasets and unconstrained generative models do not capture Hajj-specific visual conditions, including sacred-site geometry, white-clothed pilgrim crowds, and indoor/outdoor illumination variation. This study presents CrowdH-Edit, a reference-guided, instruction-based framework for synthetic Hajj crowd-image generation. Real Hajj images provide structural references, while textual instructions guide changes in crowd conditions and illumination and help preserve the main scene layout. Stable Diffusion 2.1 and Stable Diffusion XL 1.0 with low-rank adaptation were evaluated as comparative baselines. Qwen Image Edit was used without additional training within a ComfyUI workflow and selected for final dataset construction. The workflow produced CrowdH-Edit, a cleaned pool of 6,122 synthetic images, from which 387 images were selected and annotated to construct CrowdH-Edit-Ann-387. Among the evaluated generation pipelines, Qwen Image Edit achieved the highest semantic-alignment score and the lowest distributional and perceptual distances. Downstream evaluation across five crowd-counting models showed that adding the annotated synthetic subset to real training data reduced mean absolute error for three models and root mean squared error for two. These findings indicate that reference-guided synthetic Hajj imagery can support crowd-counting training, although its benefits depend on the model and evaluation metric.
papers.summary: Few annotated images exist for Hajj crowd analysis, and general crowd datasets or unconstrained generative models do not reproduce its sacred-site geometry, white-clothed crowds, or lighting conditions. `CrowdH-Edit` edits real Hajj images according to text instructions that change crowd density and illumination while keeping the scene layout. `Qwen Image Edit`, used without extra training, outperformed `Stable Diffusion 2.1` and `Stable Diffusion XL 1.0` fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation, and produced 6,122 synthetic images, 387 of which were annotated. Adding these to real training data **lowered mean absolute error for three of five crowd-counting models**, so the benefit depends on the model and the metric.

papers.title: How Data Scales in Agentic Reinforcement Learning: Laws and Synthesis Strategies
papers.abstract: Pretraining scaling laws treat training data as a one-dimensional quantity: a token count. Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) inherits this scalar abstraction, but modern synthesis pipelines now generate \textit{tasks}, \textit{environments}, and \textit{trajectories} independently and at very different costs, turning data into a structured design space. This raises a question pretraining never had to answer: given a synthesis budget, \textit{which axis} should be scaled? We address this question end-to-end with three tightly coupled contributions. First, we decompose agentic data into three cardinality axes (task, environment, trajectory), plus a reward-density control variable, and fit per-axis scaling relations on different large language models (LLMs) across math+code, SWE, web, and UI/tool application domains. Across all model sizes, model families, domains, and RL algorithms (PPO and GRPO) we measured, the scaling exponents order as environment $>$ task $>$ trajectory. When environment diversity is decomposed into world and environment-structure diversity, its advantage is mainly driven by the former, while the latter is just comparable to the task diversity. Second, we use the fitted laws as a common ruler to price synthesis methods, capturing each method's efficiency as a per-axis discount factor and identifying critical synthetic-to-real ratios at which collapse begins; these ratios differ by an order of magnitude across axes. Third, we cast budget allocation as a constrained optimization under our laws and discounts, deriving a Chinchilla-style compute-optimal recipe and validating it at held-out scale. The empirical results demonstrate that following the recipe yields up to $1.7\times$ compute efficiency over the dominant ``scale-the-trajectories'' practice.
papers.summary: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) usually measures training data as one quantity, even though modern pipelines generate tasks, environments, and trajectories separately and at very different costs. The authors fit scaling laws along each of these axes across several LLMs, the math and code, software-engineering, web, and UI or tool domains, and both `PPO` and `GRPO`, and find that **scaling exponents consistently rank environment above task above trajectory**, with the environment advantage driven mainly by diversity of simulated worlds. They use the fitted laws to price synthesis methods and to find the synthetic-to-real ratios at which training collapses, then derive a Chinchilla-style budget allocation that gives up to 1.7 times better compute efficiency than the common practice of scaling trajectories.

papers.title: Parameter misspecification in physics-informed neural networks: A closed-form audit and its limits
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are trained to minimize the residual of a prescribed equation, so a low training loss does not indicate whether a coefficient in that equation was specified incorrectly. This study evaluates what can be inferred about the encoded parameter from the trained network alone. When the residual is linear in the parameter, written as $A - \nu B$, the least-squares estimate $\hat{\nu} = A^{\top}B/B^{\top}B$ is obtained from a single evaluation of the frozen network, without retraining or reference data. Its accuracy depends on how closely the network satisfies its own equation, quantified by a normalized residual $\rho$. Recovery error is associated with $\rho$ (log-log correlation 0.72 across 36 convection-diffusion networks), and empirical exponents of 0.63 to 1.20 across three equations decompose into one half plus a measurable angular term. For Burgers' equation, a single-model test based on a block-bootstrap standard error flagged 3 of 300 correctly specified networks (observed false-alarm rate 1%), all 2% misspecifications at a practical budget, and two thirds of 1% misspecifications after convergence. For the self-similar blowup rate of the C\'ordoba-C\'ordoba-Fontelos equation, where the rate also enters the architecture, the estimator recovers about half of the misspecification, whereas $\rho$ increases approximately quadratically and distinguishes a 0.2% error. When the incorrect rate enters both the equation and the architecture, errors of up to 2% were not detected at the precision reached. At practical budgets, the raw loss can be lower for the misspecified model, a scaling effect that $\rho$ does not share.
papers.summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) minimize the residual of a prescribed equation, so a low training loss cannot reveal whether a coefficient in that equation was set wrong. When the residual is linear in the parameter, a closed-form least-squares estimate computed from one pass of the frozen network recovers the encoded value, with accuracy governed by how well the network satisfies its own equation, measured as a normalized residual. On Burgers' equation a bootstrap-based test **detected every 2% misspecification at a practical training budget while flagging only 1% of correctly specified networks**. The audit weakens when the parameter also appears in the network architecture, as with the blowup rate of the Córdoba-Córdoba-Fontelos equation, where errors of up to 2% went undetected.

papers.title: DS-Net: A Dynamic Split Network for Edge-Cloud Collaborative Inference
papers.abstract: Collaborative inference serves as a critical methodology in edge intelligence. Existing collaborative inference methods operate by splitting the deep neural network (DNN) model between edge devices and cloud servers. However, these methods need to load different models for multiple split points when the communication or device changes, thus resulting in long switching times and substantial storage overhead on the edge side. To address this issue, we propose a Dynamic Split Network (DS-Net), which not only enables efficient split point switching but also enhances the collaborative speed and accuracy across various scenarios. Specifically, we design a dynamic switching framework that enables flexible selection among multiple split points within a single model, thereby reducing storage, memory, and switching overhead. To mitigate the feature distribution shifts and task-relevant information loss caused by dynamic splitting and high-ratio compression, we further propose a hierarchical compensation mechanism. Local alignment calibrates the decoded feature distribution at each split point, while task-specific global compensation restores task-relevant information at the global level. In addition, we incorporate sample-adaptive global compensation selection into split-point selection based on sample complexity and runtime resource conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that DS-Net reduces memory overhead by 74.6% and achieves millisecond-level switching latency. Moreover, under a 10 Mbps bandwidth constraint on the Nano platform, DS-Net outperforms state-of-the-art collaborative methods by achieving 1.2% higher accuracy on the COCO dataset, reducing latency by 42.5%, and improving throughput by a factor of 1.8$\times$.
papers.summary: Edge-cloud collaborative inference splits a deep neural network between a device and a server, but existing methods load a separate model for each split point, which is slow to switch and costly in storage. `DS-Net` supports multiple split points inside a single model and adds a hierarchical compensation mechanism that corrects feature-distribution shift at each split point and restores task-relevant information lost to heavy compression, choosing the split and compensation per sample based on its complexity and available resources. It **reduces memory overhead by 74.6% and switches split points in milliseconds**. Under a 10 Mbps bandwidth limit on a Jetson Nano, it improves `COCO` accuracy by 1.2% over prior methods, with 42.5% lower latency and 1.8 times the throughput.

papers.title: Compaction-Aware Reinforcement Learning For Ascend Triton Kernel Generation
papers.abstract: Automatically generating high-performance kernels with LLM-based agents promises substantial gains in development efficiency, but two obstacles remain. First, while increasing multi-turn interaction with execution environments is crucial for refining generation quality, continuous context accumulation rapidly exceeds the model's effective context window. Second, training long-horizon tasks via GRPO inherently incurs sparse rewards due to its reliance on terminal outcome evaluation, severely hindering step-level credit assignment; To address these obstacles, we propose ATRL (Ascend Triton Reinforcement Learning), a post-training method that refines GRPO into a compaction-aware, segment-level objective for long-horizon kernel generation. We also design a lightweight agent harness providing cascaded compilation, correctness, and profiling feedback, alongside an Ascend-specific knowledge base injected during agentic RL training and evaluation to compensate for the base model's missing platform expertise. Evaluations on NPUKernelBench and KernelBench, both executed on Ascend hardware, show that ATRL consistently surpasses all baselines, including GRPO, in both correctness and speedup.
papers.summary: LLM agents that write high-performance kernels improve with more rounds of execution feedback, but the growing context soon exceeds what the model can use, and outcome-only `GRPO` rewards give little signal about which steps helped. `ATRL` (Ascend Triton Reinforcement Learning) changes `GRPO` into a segment-level objective that accounts for context compaction over long-horizon kernel generation. It also adds an agent harness that returns compilation, correctness, and profiling feedback in sequence, plus an Ascend-specific knowledge base to fill gaps in the base model's platform knowledge. On `NPUKernelBench` and `KernelBench` running on Ascend hardware, **`ATRL` beats all baselines, including standard `GRPO`, in both correctness and speedup**.

papers.title: LatLM: Line-Parallel Language Models with Deferred Commitment
papers.abstract: Line-parallel language models advance multiple lines concurrently for substantial speedups. However, frameworks like the Line-Coupled Language Model (LCLM) enforce a fixed commitment schedule across lines. Because dependencies vary within text, a fixed schedule cannot hold back a line whose prerequisites remain uncomputed, forcing premature commitments and cascading reasoning errors. To address this limitation, we introduce the Lattice Language Model (LatLM), making commitment schedules an adaptive decoding-time choice. Text occupies a 2D lattice where eligible frontier tokens are scored each round; a policy commits confident candidates while deferring unready ones for extended context. One forward pass supervises entire sampled trajectories via 2D causal masking, while an append-only cache retains exact states. At 482M parameters, we establish two findings. (1) LatLM matches a data- and capacity-matched autoregressive model on held-out text when decoded sequentially, while its adaptive parallel decoder achieves near-autoregressive accuracy on independent-line tasks using 25--41% as many decoding rounds. (2) When cross-line dependencies cause LCLM's fixed schedule to fail, deferred commitment substantially improves accuracy while retaining parallelism where dependencies permit. On mixed dependency chains, LatLM achieves 96.5% accuracy versus LCLM's 78.5%, using fewer than half the decoding rounds of the autoregressive baseline.
papers.summary: Line-parallel language models generate several lines of text at once, but frameworks like the Line-Coupled Language Model (`LCLM`) commit tokens on a fixed schedule, forcing premature commitments when one line depends on content another has not yet produced. The Lattice Language Model (`LatLM`) places text on a 2D lattice and, at each round, commits confident frontier tokens while deferring ones that are not ready; training uses 2D causal masking, and an append-only cache keeps states exact. At 482M parameters it matches an autoregressive baseline when decoded sequentially and reaches near-autoregressive accuracy on independent-line tasks in 25 to 41% as many decoding rounds. On mixed dependency chains it **achieves 96.5% accuracy versus 78.5% for `LCLM`**, using fewer than half the autoregressive baseline's rounds.

papers.title: DISCERN: Identifiable Disease Evidence for Generalizable Medical Multimodal Learning
papers.abstract: Clinical multimodal models can learn enrollment shortcuts shared across modalities and fail on new cohorts. We model these data through a latent structural causal model: disease state and background factors generate physiology through shared mechanisms, while cohorts differ in selection and measurement. Holding acquisition fixed, we identify conditional disease evidence without observing disease-state labels or recovering the full causal model. In common Gaussian coordinates, cross-cohort state alignment and natural-parameter changes identify a minimal selection statistic; conditioning on it removes enrollment-dependent evidence and yields an identifiable reference posterior within the specified shift family. State-dependent interactions can carry evidence invisible to individual-modality posteriors, motivating joint, information-preserving representations. DISCERN combines an information-lattice encoder, a latent-state model, and an outcome head through joint training. Under reversed synthetic enrollment on known latent coordinates, conditioning raises state AUROC from 0.043 to 0.883 and from 0.265 to 0.825, while random conditioning does not. Exploratory cross-database mortality experiments between eICU and MIMIC-IV improve AUROC over matched empirical risk minimization by 0.036 and 0.035. Learned-coordinate diagnostics distinguish preservation of state information from identification of the coordinates required by the estimator.
papers.summary: Clinical multimodal models can learn shortcuts tied to how patients were enrolled and then fail on new cohorts. The authors model the data with a latent structural causal model and show that disease evidence can be identified, without disease labels, by conditioning on a minimal selection statistic that removes enrollment-dependent signal. `DISCERN` puts this into practice by jointly training an information-preserving encoder, a latent-state model, and an outcome head. Under reversed synthetic enrollment, **conditioning raises state AUROC from 0.043 to 0.883**, and in exploratory cross-database mortality prediction between `eICU` and `MIMIC-IV` it improves AUROC by about 0.035 over standard empirical risk minimization.

papers.title: Physics-Aware Self-Supervised Pretraining on Multi-Domain Raman Spectra
papers.abstract: Raman spectroscopy generates large volumes of unlabeled data that are difficult to exploit with conventional supervised learning. This work introduces a multi-domain self-supervised learning framework based on a masked autoencoder (MAE) for learning transferable Raman spectral representations from heterogeneous biological, chemical, forensic, and materials datasets. The proposed pretraining strategy incorporates physics-aware objectives by combining masked intensity reconstruction with a sparse Voigt-profile decoder that models spectral peak structure through differentiable peak centers, widths, and amplitudes. A denoising objective is further included to improve robustness to spectral corruption. The learned encoder is evaluated on substance classification, component identification, concentration estimation, and spectral denoising under linear probing, attention-based probing, end-to-end fine-tuning, and training from scratch. Experimental results show that self-supervised pretraining is most beneficial for challenging tasks with limited labeled data. Attention-based probing also reveals substantially more useful information in the frozen representation than linear probing, indicating that conventional linear evaluation may underestimate representation quality. In addition, the benefits of pretraining become more pronounced with increasing encoder capacity. Overall, the proposed framework demonstrates that physics-aware, multi-domain self-supervised pretraining can improve label efficiency, robustness, and transferability across diverse Raman spectroscopy tasks.
papers.summary: Raman spectroscopy produces large amounts of unlabeled data that supervised learning cannot easily use. The authors pretrain a masked autoencoder (MAE) on biological, chemical, forensic, and materials spectra, adding a sparse Voigt-profile decoder that models peak centers, widths, and amplitudes, plus a denoising objective. Evaluated on classification, component identification, concentration estimation, and denoising, **pretraining helps most on hard tasks with little labeled data**, and the benefit grows with encoder size. Attention-based probing extracts much more from the frozen representation than linear probing, which suggests linear evaluation underestimates representation quality.

papers.title: Same Space or Not: Benchmarking Spatial Intelligence Through Cross-View Contradictions
papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence, the capacity to represent and reason about physical space, underlies embodied perception and real-world visual understanding. Existing benchmarks probe it through spatial relations, perspective-taking, and mental modeling. What remains underexamined is whether a model can maintain a coherent scene representation across views, since pairwise comparison alone cannot reveal which view departs from the truth. We thus introduce Same Space or Not (SSoN), a benchmark of cross-view contradiction resolution comprising 1,000 questions from seven indoor scene sources and six categories of controlled 3D edits. Each question presents three views of an unchanged scene and one view of an edited variant. Models must identify the inconsistent view and explain the contradiction without a designated trusted reference or a marked target. Our pipeline iteratively translates human review into generation constraints. Automated checks and exhaustive human validation screen out both trivial visual shortcuts and questions lacking sufficient evidence for a unique answer. Humans achieve 83.3% accuracy, compared with 39.7% for the strongest vision-language models (VLMs), falling to 34.9% when a valid visual explanation is also required. We investigate prompting, camera information, and 3D reconstruction as interventions. On a 100-question intervention set with a 24% baseline, prompting and 3D reconstruction remain below 50% answer accuracy, except when ground-truth camera information is supplied, which reaches 61% answer accuracy but only 48% True solve accuracy. On a held-out 201-question test set, Qwen2.5-VL-7B achieves 21.89% accuracy, 33.33% after answer-only fine-tuning, and 41.79% after fine-tuning on both rationales and answers. These results identify cross-view contradiction resolution as a substantial weakness of current VLMs that can be partly addressed by targeted supervision.
papers.summary: Spatial-reasoning benchmarks rarely test whether a model keeps a consistent picture of a scene across different views. `SSoN` (Same Space or Not) contains 1,000 questions, each showing three views of an unchanged indoor scene and one view of a scene altered by a controlled 3D edit; the model must pick out the inconsistent view and explain the contradiction, with no trusted reference provided. **Humans reach 83.3% accuracy, while the strongest vision-language models (VLMs) reach 39.7%**, dropping to 34.9% when a valid explanation is also required. Prompting and 3D reconstruction stay below 50%, ground-truth camera information reaches 61%, and fine-tuning `Qwen2.5-VL-7B` on rationales and answers raises its held-out accuracy from 21.89% to 41.79%.

papers.title: UltraData-Code: From Raw Repositories to Algorithmically Dense and Task-Oriented Code Data
papers.abstract: Code generation has become a core capability of large language models (LLMs), and code data is central to the pre-training process that develops it. As obtaining public code of sufficient quality becomes more difficult, further progress cannot rely on corpus expansion alone. Tiered data management instead applies increasingly targeted processing to smaller data pools, producing data states suited to different training objectives. Following this perspective, we present UltraData-Code as four connected data states spanning repository archival at L0, standardized natural code at L1, algorithmic selection at L2, and task-oriented synthesis at L3. L0 preserves repository data and provenance for reprocessing, while L1 applies scalable filtering, normalization, and near-deduplication for broad pre-training. L2 selects high-quality algorithmically relevant files using language-adaptive relevance signals and quality constraints, yielding approximately 400B tokens of UltraData-Code-L2 across 11 programming languages for focused continual pre-training. L3 converts selected implementations into structured programming exercises, yielding approximately 150B tokens of UltraData-Code-L3 across the same 11 languages for task-oriented mid-training or supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Under controlled 10B-token continual pre-training of a 1B model, L2 improves pass@1 over L1 by 7.80 percentage points (pp) on EvalPlus and 5.13pp on MultiPL-E. Replacing half of the L2 training tokens with L3 yields a further gain of 8.42pp and 8.07pp on the two benchmarks, respectively. Both gains increase when the training budget scales to 100B tokens. We have released our datasets and classifiers to support further research on LLMs.
papers.summary: Good public code for pre-training is getting harder to find, so `UltraData-Code` applies increasingly targeted processing to smaller pools of data, in four tiers: archived repositories with provenance (L0), filtered and deduplicated code (L1), roughly 400B tokens of algorithmically relevant files across 11 languages (L2), and roughly 150B tokens of synthesized programming exercises (L3). In 10B-token continual pre-training of a 1B model, L2 improves pass@1 over L1 by 7.80 points on `EvalPlus` and 5.13 points on `MultiPL-E`. **Replacing half of the L2 tokens with L3 exercises adds a further 8.42 and 8.07 points**, and both gains grow at a 100B-token budget. The datasets and classifiers are publicly released.

papers.title: A Controlled LLM Workflow for Evidence-Grounded Diagnosis of Risk Score Differences
papers.abstract: We propose a controlled Large Language Model (LLM) workflow for explaining risk score differences using similar historical transactions. The workflow combines reference retrieval and contrastive SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) evidence with reference-based LLM reasoning and deterministic validation. Experiments on a test dataset show that the workflow produces more consistent, evidence-grounded and traceable diagnoses than the same LLM without structured workflow guidance.
papers.summary: Explaining why two transactions received different risk scores is difficult to make consistent and traceable. The proposed workflow retrieves similar historical transactions, computes contrastive SHapley Additive exPlanations (`SHAP`) evidence, has an LLM reason over these references, and checks the output with deterministic validation. On a test dataset, it **produces more consistent, evidence-grounded, and traceable diagnoses than the same LLM used without structured workflow guidance**.

papers.title: Geo-vision: Native-Resolution Geometry and Sampled Topology for Vehicle-Part Damage Classification
papers.abstract: Geo-vision classifies vehicle-part damage using a fixed representation combining appearance, multiscale geometry, orientation, and sampled digital topology. Connected components, holes, Euler characteristics, and spatial arrangement complement amplitude-sensitive pooling and a supervised tree classifier. We establish amplitude preservation, axial sign invariance, and conditional operator stability. Retrospective checkpoint evaluation on 55,303 crops from 4,916 source groups yields average precision 0.7577, exceeding 0.7458 for an ImageNet-pretrained frozen YOLO11n comparator on identical crops. The complete added structural block, comprising topology, occupancy, and component location, improves average precision by 0.00493 beyond appearance and geometry. Geo-vision uses no external encoder pretraining and has higher AP point estimates at every matched label budget. With approximately 25% fewer task labels, its AP point estimate exceeds full-data YOLO, although the adjusted interval includes zero. Complete serial CPU inference requires 26.98 ms per crop versus YOLO's 11.20 ms, with peak memory 185 versus 437 MiB. Independent external validation remains necessary.
papers.summary: Vehicle-part damage is classified with a fixed, hand-designed representation rather than a pretrained deep encoder. `Geo-vision` combines appearance features, multiscale geometry, orientation, and sampled digital topology (connected components, holes, Euler characteristics, and spatial arrangement), then feeds them to a supervised tree classifier, and the authors prove properties such as amplitude preservation and axial sign invariance. On 55,303 crops from 4,916 source groups it reaches **average precision 0.7577 versus 0.7458 for a frozen ImageNet-pretrained `YOLO11n`**, while using less peak memory (185 vs 437 MiB) but taking more than twice as long per crop on CPU. The authors note that the topology block adds only a small gain and that independent external validation is still needed.

papers.title: IMPULSE: Push First, Then Predict in V-JEPA 2 Feature Space
papers.abstract: Latent world models such as V-JEPA 2 forecast in the feature space of a video encoder, but one look at an object does not reveal how hard it is to rotate, how much it bounces or how much it slides. People find out by trying: a few pokes reveal how an object responds. IMPULSE, named after the impulse response it infers, gives a predictor in frozen V-JEPA 2 feature space the same ability. A Bayesian contact memory summarizes three short calibration pushes, a predicted object pose carries it into the predictor, and a lightweight random-Fourier pose head lets the predictor use the pose. On 512 fresh objects, in a pre-specified held-out confirmation with models sealed before the data existed, the memory lowers the 1-second feature-forecast error by 11.6-12.8% relative to the same predictor without experience, for all 8 training seeds, with a 95% seed-and-object interval excluding zero. The gain also holds for 128 objects with out-of-range physics (11.7-14.0%), and the full extension beats a plain predictor by 15.5-16.6%. An information-ladder argument, exact for ideal predictors, shows that physics reaches the features only through motion, so we measure how much the pathway lets pose help. On fresh objects, the Fourier head roughly triples the gain of a perfect memory over plain pose tokens (2.8-3.2x). Raw push measurements fed through the same pathway give a similar gain, so the Bayesian summary is not required; it condenses the trials into eight interpretable numbers. The gain is absent at contact onset and grows afterwards.
papers.summary: Latent world models such as `V-JEPA 2` forecast video in feature space, but a single view cannot reveal physical properties like friction, bounciness, or how hard an object is to rotate. `IMPULSE` gives a predictor in frozen `V-JEPA 2` feature space a short history of three calibration pushes: a Bayesian contact memory summarizes the pushes, a predicted object pose carries that summary into the predictor, and a lightweight random-Fourier pose head lets the predictor use it. In a pre-registered held-out test on 512 new objects, the memory **lowers 1-second feature-forecast error by 11.6-12.8%** across all 8 training seeds, and the gain holds for objects with out-of-range physics. Feeding in raw push measurements works about as well, so the Bayesian summary mainly serves to make the information interpretable.

papers.title: Spatio-Temporal Detection of Photovoltaic Systems on Industrial Building Rooftops Using Satellite Imagery and Machine Learning
papers.abstract: The global transition toward carbon-neutral energy systems is heavily dependent on the rapid deployment of solar photovoltaic (PV) infrastructure, yet the speed of this expansion has outpaced the ability of administrative registries to maintain accurate records. While high-resolution commercial imagery is often used for monitoring, its high cost and infrequent updates can create an information gap for grid operators, energy infrastructure developers and policymakers. This study addresses the lack of scalable monitoring for industrial-scale rooftop PV systems by developing a machine learning framework that utilizes open-access, multispectral Sentinel-2 satellite imagery. By integrating building geometries from OpenStreetMap with Sentinel-2 reflectance data, a Random Forest model was trained to identify the specific spectral signatures of PV modules. Moving beyond theoretical modeling, this work emphasizes practical implementation through the development of an interactive web-based prototype for on-demand site monitoring. The application enables users to retrieve up-to-date satellite observations and assess the presence of PV systems on industrial building rooftops. The tool incorporates quality metrics that inform users whether a prediction is supported by sufficient training data density or requires manual verification. This end-to-end framework demonstrates that open-source medium-resolution data can effectively bridge this monitoring gap.
papers.summary: Official registries have fallen behind the rapid growth of industrial rooftop solar photovoltaic (PV) installations, and high-resolution commercial imagery is expensive and updated infrequently. The authors combine building outlines from `OpenStreetMap` with open multispectral `Sentinel-2` reflectance data and train a `Random Forest` to recognize the spectral signature of PV modules. They package this as an interactive web prototype that pulls recent satellite observations on demand and flags predictions that have too little nearby training data and need manual checking. The authors conclude that **open medium-resolution imagery is sufficient for scalable rooftop PV monitoring**.

papers.title: Super-resolution as Spatial Downscaling: Coherence, Structure and Task Utility in Earth Observation
papers.abstract: Learned satellite super-resolution is commonly assessed by pixel fidelity and potential downlink savings, but these criteria do not establish whether the reconstructed field preserves spatial structure or supports reliable downstream analysis. We treat single-image super-resolution as a spatial downscaling problem and evaluate four lightweight networks, including our compact 0.36 million-parameter model, against interpolation using pixel metrics, directional variograms, spectral band correlation, codispersion and observation coherence. On 735 satellite tiles from 190 scenes, the networks differ by at most 0.03dB and outperform bicubic interpolation by $1.39-1.42$dB at $\times 2$. They recover about 30% of the spectral power above the observation's Nyquist frequency and, at $\times 4$, produce more isotropic fields than the reference (range anisotropy 0.59 against 0.49). Energy-based metrics can favour invented detail. Enforcing coherence reaches the quantisation limit, yet at least 99.7% of the remaining error lies in the observation operator's null space, which coherence cannot constrain. Under spatially blocked, paired evaluation with two backbones and a sharpening control, learned reconstruction changes land-use accuracy by $-1.0$ to $+3.1$ percentage points (significant in 7 of 24 comparisons) and building-change F1 by $-0.015$ to $+0.024$ (none significant) relative to bicubic interpolation, and amplifies spurious change between two observations of an unchanged scene by $1.3-1.5$ times where interpolation attenuates it. Full-resolution JPEG\,2000 matches or exceeds reduced-resolution transmission with reconstruction at every matched bitrate. Learned reconstruction is most useful when only low-resolution imagery is available, and its evaluation should combine pixel metrics with spatial structure, observation coherence and task-level tests under spatial validation.
papers.summary: Satellite super-resolution is usually judged by pixel fidelity, which says nothing about whether the output preserves spatial structure or helps downstream analysis. The authors treat it as spatial downscaling and evaluate four lightweight networks, including their own 0.36M-parameter model, against interpolation using variograms, spectral correlation, codispersion, and coherence with the original observation, on 735 tiles. The networks beat bicubic interpolation by about 1.4 dB, but in land-use classification and building-change detection the gains over bicubic are small and mostly not significant, and learned reconstruction **amplifies spurious change between two images of an unchanged scene by 1.3-1.5x**. Transmitting full-resolution `JPEG 2000` matches or beats sending reduced-resolution imagery for later reconstruction at every bitrate tested, so the authors recommend learned super-resolution mainly when only low-resolution data exists.

papers.title: REAP: Learning General Rearrangement Heuristics from Motion-Planner Feedback
papers.abstract: Robotic rearrangement tasks require planning sequences of actions that fulfill high-level specifications while also being geometrically feasible. Symbolic abstractions make the combinatorial structure of rearrangement tasks tractable, but they usually do not fully capture the geometric constraints that determine which actions a robot can actually realize. These constraints are hard to express in the symbolic model. We propose REAP (Rearrangement with Elicited Action Preconditions), a framework in which a relational graph neural network heuristic is learned over a simple symbolic abstraction. A motion planner serves as a supervisor that elicits the hidden geometric preconditions of the problem during training. Deployed with greedy best-first search, the learned heuristic generalizes out-of-distribution along object count, plan length, and object arrangement, and can be trained jointly on several domains. Compared to classical heuristic search and learning-based baselines, REAP solves more problems, requires roughly an order of magnitude fewer motion-planner queries than comparable methods, and the action it ranks first is geometrically feasible in 94% of sampled states, against 22% for a random choice.
papers.summary: Robotic rearrangement planning relies on symbolic abstractions that make the combinatorics tractable but miss geometric constraints on which actions a robot can actually perform. `REAP` (Rearrangement with Elicited Action Preconditions) learns a relational graph neural network heuristic over a simple symbolic model, with a motion planner acting as a supervisor during training to reveal hidden geometric preconditions. Used with greedy best-first search, the heuristic generalizes to more objects, longer plans, and new arrangements, and needs roughly an order of magnitude fewer motion-planner queries than comparable methods. **The action it ranks first is geometrically feasible in 94% of sampled states**, compared with 22% for a random choice.

papers.title: How Much Can We Prune? Exploring the Performance Limits of Visual Token Pruning
papers.abstract: Visual token pruning is increasingly used to reduce the memory and inference costs of vision-language models. Existing work has largely focused on designing method-specific selectors and demonstrating incremental improvements over prior methods at selected token budgets. It remains unclear whether the resulting performance reflects an inherent limit of visual token pruning or the limitations of current token-selection algorithms. We take a complementary perspective and ask: \emph{how well can visual token pruning perform when offline search cost is not the primary constraint?} We formulate pruning for general image understanding as selecting, under a fixed budget, one shared visual-token subset that supports a broad distribution of questions about an image. We approximate this utility with a finite auxiliary QA set generated by a frontier VLM and optimize a teacher-forced answer-probability objective with the evaluated model frozen. Motivated by the conceptual monotonicity and diminishing returns of adding visual evidence, we construct nested subsets greedily and introduce \emph{QA mini-batch greedy} (QA-MBG), which estimates token marginal gains from randomly sampled QA components at each step. Empirically, QA-MBG is both cheaper and more effective than full greedy. With one frontier-VLM call and approximately $0.5$ H100 GPU-hours per image, it produces a nested subset trajectory covering keep ratios up to $0.3$. Across Qwen3-VL-4B and Gemma~4 E4B on $900$ images from nine benchmarks, we find significant headroom over evaluated pruning baselines on held-out QA and image-grounded long-form generation, while the searched subsets substantially narrow the gap to full-token inference.
papers.summary: Visual token pruning cuts the memory and compute of vision-language models (VLMs), but it is unclear whether current results reflect an inherent limit of pruning or just weak token-selection algorithms. To estimate an upper bound, the authors use a frontier VLM to generate an auxiliary question set for each image and greedily search for one shared, nested token subset that maximizes answer probability for the frozen model. Their `QA mini-batch greedy` (`QA-MBG`) variant samples random question subsets at each step, which makes it both cheaper and better than full greedy search, at about 0.5 H100 GPU-hours per image. Across `Qwen3-VL-4B` and `Gemma 4 E4B` on 900 images from nine benchmarks, **the searched subsets show significant headroom over existing pruning methods** and substantially narrow the gap to full-token inference.

papers.title: FrameScout: Scouting Query-Relevant Frames for Long Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Long video understanding requires VideoLLMs to answer queries about videos spanning tens of minutes to hours, but such long videos produce far more visual tokens than current VideoLLMs can process. To address this issue, keyframe selectors are proposed to select the most query-relevant frames by computing the similarity between frame and query embeddings. Existing selectors either encode frames independently without temporal context or process chunks in isolation with ranking objectives that are difficult to optimize. To alleviate those limitations, we propose FrameScout with two core designs: (i) a streaming selector architecture that leverages a sliding-window KV cache and successor aggregation to produce temporally-contextualized frame embeddings; (ii) a frame-query contrastive objective that aligns frame and query embeddings in a shared space, directly training the selector to distinguish relevant frames from irrelevant ones. Extensive experiments on three long-video benchmarks and six base VideoLLMs demonstrate that FrameScout consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Hubert-1102/FrameScout.
papers.summary: Hour-long videos produce far more visual tokens than video LLMs can process, so keyframe selectors pick the frames most relevant to a query, but existing selectors either ignore temporal context or rely on ranking objectives that are hard to optimize. `FrameScout` uses a streaming selector with a sliding-window KV cache and successor aggregation to produce frame embeddings that carry temporal context. It is trained with a frame-query contrastive objective that teaches it to separate relevant frames from irrelevant ones. **It achieves state-of-the-art results across three long-video benchmarks and six base video LLMs.**

papers.title: LLM Evolutionary Search Strategies Should be Compared by Tokens
papers.abstract: LLM evolutionary search is currently evaluated by counting proposals (candidate programs). We demonstrate this metric hides the true cost of search, and redo the comparison using tokens. By replaying 600 logged runs across 5 tasks and 3 methods, we show that proposal costs vary wildly from 16k to 39k tokens. In equal-proposal comparisons, this silently grants some methods up to 1.9x the compute of others, and gives evolution roughly 6x the budget of independent sampling. When we match token budgets, giving sampling six times more attempts, and remove scorer exploits, the evolutionary advantage largely vanishes.
