Evolution beats independent sampling by 5% or less on 12 of 15 task-method pairs, retaining a 23 to 28% margin on only 3, all on one task. A replication with Claude Haiku 4.5 reproduces this split, though a third backbone shows its size depends on the model too. The performance margin justifying these systems is often an accounting artifact. Reporting tokens, not proposals and not model calls, fixes this and costs nothing, as the logs already hold them.
papers.summary: LLM-driven evolutionary program search is usually compared by the number of candidate programs proposed, which hides large differences in what each proposal actually costs. Replaying 600 logged runs across 5 tasks and 3 methods, the authors find that a proposal costs anywhere from 16k to 39k tokens, so equal-proposal comparisons give some methods up to 1.9x more compute and give evolution about 6x the budget of independent sampling. Once token budgets are matched and scorer exploits are removed, **evolution beats independent sampling by 5% or less on 12 of 15 task-method pairs**, and the remaining large margins all come from a single task. A replication with `Claude Haiku 4.5` shows the same split, and the authors recommend reporting token counts, which existing logs already record.

papers.title: SPELUNKA: A Framework for Finding Unanticipated Associations in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are the backbone of many state-of-the-art multimodal systems, but often encode spurious and harmful associations from their training data. While prior work focuses on removing known biases from VLMs, methods for discovering unanticipated associations for retrieval tasks remain underexplored. We introduce SPELUNKA, an automated, inference-time framework for finding unanticipated distributional biases for retrieval tasks in VLMs without pre-specified labeled subgroups, inference-time human supervision, or model fine-tuning. Given a concept of interest, SPELUNKA generates captions for related images, extracts relevant entities from captions, and selects semantically meaningful associations. A frequency-based detection rule then identifies spurious associations by measuring over- or under-representation of these attributes in a VLM's top-ranked outputs relative to their full dataset distribution. We evaluate SPELUNKA across four datasets, and find that it 1) successfully recovers both synthetic and naturally occurring spurious correlations, 2) achieves an average AUROC of 0.93 across four datasets in identifying images strongly associated with a query, and 3) outperforms baselines in finding features that are strongly associated with a given query.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) pick up spurious and harmful associations from their training data, and most prior work only removes biases that are already known. `SPELUNKA` is an automated framework, run at inference time, that finds unanticipated biases in retrieval without labeled subgroups, human supervision, or fine-tuning. Given a concept, it captions related images, extracts entities from the captions, and flags attributes that appear far more or less often in the model's top-ranked results than in the full dataset. Across four datasets it recovers both planted and naturally occurring spurious correlations, reaches **an average AUROC of 0.93** at identifying images strongly associated with a query, and finds associated features better than the baselines.

papers.title: SituHOI: Scalable Capture of Scene-Situated Full-Body Human-Object Interaction
papers.abstract: Modeling human-object interaction (HOI) in real environments requires jointly representing whole-body motion, manipulated objects, and scene geometry, yet existing datasets trade off scalable capture against structured, scene-aligned supervision. We introduce SituHOI, a large-scale RGB-D dataset containing 18,429 annotated clips across 16 indoor rooms and approximately 86 hours of quality-screened activity. It pairs recordings from a single moving RGB-D camera with static scene scans, object geometry, language descriptions, and estimated human and object trajectories. Using the scans as persistent references, our pipeline combines camera localization and depth-based metric alignment with human mesh recovery, object tracking, and temporal refinement to register all geometric annotations in a shared floor-aligned frame. These data support FlexHOI-Bench, a goal-conditioned joint motion prediction benchmark with variable observation and prediction durations. Given observed histories, scene and object geometry, and a terminal object pose, models predict future human and object motion. We provide SharedHOI as a reference predictor and evaluate world-space accuracy and human-object coordination. On a MoCap subset, our pipeline reduces human G-MPJPE from 195.4 to 68.3 mm and object translation error from 43.0 to 28.7 mm. SharedHOI leads four adapted baselines on all three aggregate FlexHOI-Bench metrics. Data will be released upon acceptance. An anonymized code repository is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/iclr2027-anonymous-code-1DFB.
papers.summary: Existing human-object interaction (HOI) datasets force a choice between capture at scale and structured supervision aligned to the scene. `SituHOI` provides 18,429 annotated clips (about 86 hours) recorded with a single moving RGB-D camera in 16 indoor rooms, together with static scene scans, object geometry, language descriptions, and estimated human and object trajectories, all registered in one floor-aligned coordinate frame. On a motion-capture subset, the annotation pipeline **reduces human G-MPJPE from 195.4 to 68.3 mm**. The data also supports `FlexHOI-Bench`, a goal-conditioned benchmark for predicting joint human and object motion, on which the reference predictor `SharedHOI` beats four adapted baselines.

papers.title: RL Teaches VLMs Where to Attend but Not How to Perceive
papers.abstract: Although reinforcement learning (RL) effectively trains Vision-Language Model (VLM) agents, the mechanisms behind these capability gains are poorly understood. Across four diverse agent environments, we investigate whether the task-success gains from multi-turn RL are accompanied by improved grounded visual question answering about the environment. To assess this, we design environment-specific grounded VQA tasks that reveal improvements in grounded visual understanding. Representational probing shows that vision-encoder probe accuracy remains relatively stable, while LLM-layer probe accuracy improves. Attention analysis further reveals that LLM layers pay more attention to visual tokens during RL training. To test whether increased attention to visual tokens contributes to VQA gains, we introduce a lightweight plug-and-play intervention using a fixed attention bias. Without updating model parameters or computing gradients, this intervention partially restores VQA gains on the untrained model. These results reveal better utilization of visual information as a key mechanism behind the gains from RL.
papers.summary: Multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) improves vision-language model (VLM) agents, but it is unclear how. Across four agent environments, the authors design grounded visual question answering (VQA) tasks and find that RL-trained agents improve on them as well. Probes on the vision encoder stay roughly flat while probes on the LLM layers improve, and the LLM layers attend more to visual tokens as RL training proceeds. Adding a fixed attention bias toward visual tokens, with no parameter updates, **partially recovers the VQA gains on the untrained model**, which suggests that RL mainly teaches the model to make better use of visual information it already encodes rather than to perceive better.

papers.title: IWOO: Wave Optics Optimizer Improved with Hybrid Strategies for Numerical Optimization and Engineering Applications
papers.abstract: The Wave Optics Optimizer (WOO) incorporates optical diffraction and interference into numerical optimization and has shown competitive performance in benchmarks and engineering applications. However, it can converge slowly, become trapped in local optima, and lose search effectiveness in later iterations. This paper proposes an Improved Wave Optics Optimizer (IWOO) that integrates four complementary strategies. First, a good point set and opposition-based learning are combined in GPS--OBL initialization to improve population quality and diversity. Second, an E-DM nonlinear perturbation mechanism is embedded in temporary triangle-based search to develop the TriEDM multi-path strategy and enhance search capability. Third, Correlation-Guided Groupwise Orthogonal Learning (CGOL) leverages relationships among decision variables to improve search efficiency while reducing computational overhead. Fourth, an adaptive stagnation-aware Runge--Kutta correction is introduced to mitigate premature convergence. IWOO is evaluated on the IEEE CEC2019, CEC2022, and CEC2017 benchmark suites against representative and high-performing optimizers, with ablation studies assessing the contribution of each strategy. Within the representative algorithm group, IWOO achieves Friedman ranks of 1.8000, 1.5833, and 1.4483 on CEC2019, CEC2022, and CEC2017, respectively. Tests on six constrained engineering optimization problems further demonstrate its competitive accuracy, stability, and practical applicability.
papers.summary: The Wave Optics Optimizer (`WOO`) is a metaheuristic inspired by diffraction and interference that can converge slowly and get stuck in local optima. `IWOO` adds four strategies to it: good-point-set and opposition-based initialization, a triangle-based multi-path search with nonlinear perturbation, correlation-guided groupwise orthogonal learning, and an adaptive Runge-Kutta correction that triggers when the search stagnates. Against representative optimizers it achieves **Friedman ranks of 1.80, 1.58, and 1.45** on the `CEC2019`, `CEC2022`, and `CEC2017` benchmark suites, and it is competitive on six constrained engineering design problems.

papers.title: Agentic Interpretation: Harness-Governed Evidence Construction for Software Agents
papers.abstract:
Software agents answer behavioral questions about code, such as whether a patch passes tests or which lines caused a failure. These tasks require repository-wide evidence, yet most scaffolds leave intermediate findings in free-form trajectories, making them hard to reuse and easy to disconnect from final answers. We present Agentic Interpretation (AgInt), a framework for harness-governed evidence construction. The model proposes typed records, while a deterministic harness admits, grades, and persists them, reports unresolved requirements, and licenses answers under task-specific rules. The resulting certificate gives the model persistent external state and leaves an auditable decision record. Formally, append-only certificate states form a grounding lattice ordered by record inclusion, where each admitted record extends the state by union.
  We evaluate AgInt with four models on SWE-bench-Live and DeepSWE for patch acceptance and Defects4J and GitBug-Java for fault localization. AgInt outperforms the plain agent and Agentic Code Reasoning on all reported patch-acceptance metrics and ranks responsible lines higher while inspecting fewer irrelevant lines in fault localization. For GLM-5, reject-class F1 rises from 0.256 to 0.543 on SWE-bench-Live, All@1 rises from 0.140 to 0.400 on Defects4J, and wasted inspected lines fall from 31.5 to 11.7 on GitBug-Java. A matched-template control separates the mechanism: the persistent scaffold drives most fault-localization gains, while the certificate body and gate govern patch-acceptance calibration. With execution licensed, AgInt produces harness-reproduced witnesses for 293 of 475 null-dereference candidates versus 253 for a matched shell agent, and 62 of 117 resource-leak candidates versus 58. Across reported efficiency measurements, it uses 35% fewer executions and reduces cost per candidate by 59%.
papers.summary: Software agents asked about code behavior, such as whether a patch passes tests or which lines caused a failure, usually leave their intermediate findings scattered through free-form trajectories, where they are hard to reuse and easy to disconnect from the final answer. `Agentic Interpretation` (`AgInt`) has the model propose typed evidence records, while a deterministic harness admits, grades, and stores them in an append-only certificate and permits an answer only once task-specific evidence rules are met. Across four models on `SWE-bench-Live`, `DeepSWE`, `Defects4J`, and `GitBug-Java`, it beats a plain agent and `Agentic Code Reasoning`; for `GLM-5`, **reject-class F1 on SWE-bench-Live rises from 0.256 to 0.543** and Defects4J All@1 rises from 0.140 to 0.400. When allowed to execute code, it reproduces more null-dereference and resource-leak bugs while running 35% fewer executions and cutting cost per candidate by 59%.

papers.title: spora: A Unified Multimodal Dataset and Platform for Spatial Proteomics
papers.abstract: Spatial proteomics (SP) captures the molecular composition and spatial organization of tissues at single-cell resolution, opening a direct view of the cellular ecosystems that drive disease. Protein panels, acquisition platforms, and tissue contexts differ from one cohort to the next, and a coherent picture of tissue biology can only emerge from models trained to bridge this heterogeneity. Foundation models offer the natural path forward, but their training depends on large, harmonized corpora that span platforms, panels, and cohorts. No public resource currently approaches that scale; available data sit in small, narrowly scoped releases with incompatible formats and conventions. We present $\texttt{spora}$, a large-scale multimodal SP dataset of 13,546 standardized multiplex images from 5,477 patients across 35 cohorts and five major SP technologies. Curated with biomedical experts, $\texttt{spora}$ provides model training-ready formats together with cell and tissue segmentations, structured clinical metadata, and, where available, paired H&E enabling the training of virtual staining models. It is complemented by $\texttt{spora [io]}$, a unified interface for tiling, sampling, and standardization across all cohorts and modalities, and $\texttt{spora [bench]}$, a benchmark suite spanning cell phenotyping, diagnostic and therapeutic prediction as well as virtual staining tasks across twelve cohorts that places current SP foundation models on common ground against task specific baselines.
papers.summary: Foundation models for spatial proteomics (SP), which images protein composition and tissue organization at single-cell resolution, need large harmonized training data, but public datasets are small and use incompatible formats. `spora` provides **13,546 standardized multiplex images from 5,477 patients across 35 cohorts and five SP technologies**, with cell and tissue segmentations, clinical metadata, and paired H&E stains where available. It comes with `spora [io]`, a unified interface for tiling and sampling, and `spora [bench]`, a benchmark of cell phenotyping, diagnostic and therapeutic prediction, and virtual staining tasks across twelve cohorts that compares current SP foundation models with task-specific baselines.

papers.title: PACE: Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs
papers.abstract: Native multimodal large language models (native MLLMs) jointly encode visual and linguistic sequences within a unified autoregressive Transformer, emerging as a promising paradigm for multimodal understanding. Unlike conventional ViT-based MLLMs relying on external vision encoders, ViT-free native MLLMs tokenize pixel patches directly, potentially suffering severe visual token redundancy. A pilot study confirms this: unlike ViT-based models that degrade under compression, ViT-free MLLMs tolerate aggressive compression with near-lossless or even improved performance. Yet existing compression methods target ViT-based settings, leaving native MLLMs, which stand to gain the most, unexplored. To close this gap, we introduce an analysis pipeline centered on token discriminability and cross-dimensional heterogeneous redundancy, revealing that (i) redundancy is distributed independently and heterogeneously along height and width axes, and (ii) early-layer visual tokens are indiscriminable and uniformly redundant. Guided by these findings, we propose PACE (Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs), the first visual token compression framework tailored for native MLLMs with Multimodal-RoPE. Leveraging dimensional decoupling of positional encoding, PACE decomposes attention into two orthogonal spatial saliency estimates along height and width, gated by a positional attention signal, yielding direction-aware importance with negligible overhead. It further casts token budget allocation as Pareto optimization over performance preservation, inference efficiency, and spatial coverage, jointly identifying optimal compression depths and retention ratios. Experiments show PACE maintains near-lossless performance at only 25%-50% visual token retention, even improving several benchmarks, while delivering over 2x FLOPs reduction.
papers.summary: Native multimodal large language models (MLLMs) feed raw pixel patches directly into the transformer without a ViT vision encoder, which leaves them with heavily redundant visual tokens, yet existing compression methods are designed for ViT-based models. An analysis shows that this redundancy is distributed independently along the height and width axes and that early-layer visual tokens are nearly indistinguishable from one another. `PACE` uses the decoupled height and width components of multimodal rotary position embeddings to estimate token importance along each axis at negligible cost, and treats the choice of compression depth and retention ratio as a Pareto optimization over accuracy, efficiency, and spatial coverage. It **stays near-lossless while keeping only 25-50% of visual tokens**, improves several benchmarks, and cuts FLOPs by more than 2x.

papers.title: What Social Media Teaches Us About Accumulative AI Risks
papers.abstract: Prominent AI safety discussions emphasize existential threats and catastrophic events, such as AI-enabled nuclear conflict or engineered biological outbreaks. This position paper argues that there is another type of AI risk that arises and accumulates from the widespread use of AI. Drawing on lessons from social media, we argue that safety assessments must also address accumulative harms that develop through repeated use, recurring decisions, and feedback across interconnected deployments. Repeated reassurance, selective exposure, recurring decision biases, and growing personal profiles may gradually narrow perspectives, weaken independent judgment, or enable exploitative influence without a single clearly harmful event. We advance the Trajectory Neglect Thesis: a focus on vivid catastrophic events and identifiable incidents risks overlooking less visible harms that accumulate through the widespread daily use of AI. Social media research motivates this position by showing how reciprocal media effects, social reinforcement, and individual susceptibility shape outcomes beyond individual encounters. We examine how related mechanisms may operate in AI systems, using conversational AI as a concrete setting where generation, semantic inference, and persistent memory may tighten feedback loops. Sycophancy, manipulation, and privacy loss provide a case study of how these risks may interact and accumulate. This comparison identifies mechanisms to investigate rather than assuming that repeated AI use is harmful. We therefore call for evaluation of cumulative patterns of use and deployment, individual and societal outcomes, careful causal inference, and proportionate safeguards that preserve useful assistance and informed user choice.
papers.summary: This position paper argues that AI safety work focused on catastrophic events neglects harms that build up gradually through everyday use, which it calls the Trajectory Neglect Thesis. Drawing on social media research into reciprocal media effects, social reinforcement, and individual susceptibility, it examines how repeated reassurance, selective exposure, and accumulating personal profiles in conversational AI could narrow perspectives or enable manipulation. Sycophancy, manipulation, and privacy loss serve as a case study of how such risks interact. The authors call for **evaluating cumulative patterns of use and their societal outcomes with careful causal inference**, rather than assuming that repeated use is harmful.

papers.title: Weakly Supervised Discovery of Motion Styles for Compositional Robot Control
papers.abstract:
When a robot possesses more degrees of freedom than a task requires, multiple trajectories can achieve the same objective using distinct motion styles. Compositional robot control aims to preserve a selected style while simultaneously executing an independent task command, effectively balancing these potentially competing objectives. In this paper, we present CODES, a framework for compositional robot control that discovers a coherent style repertoire from diverse recordings and composes it with independent commands. First, motion retargeting maps the recordings to motions executable by the target robot; next, weakly supervised consensus encoding and density-based clustering identify styles within and across recordings without a prescribed count; finally, reinforcement learning trains a policy to compose the discovered styles with independent commands. We evaluate CODES on a Unitree Go2 quadruped across two simulators and physical hardware. Compared to baselines, CODES significantly improves kinematic coherence. Furthermore, our controller successfully tracks velocity commands that generalize beyond the support of the recorded data, exhibiting robust and distinguishable style characteristics during both cross-simulator and real-world hardware deployments.
  Project website: https://www.proroklab.org/compositional-motion-styles/
papers.summary: Robots with more degrees of freedom than a task needs can complete the same task in different motion styles, and compositional control aims to keep a chosen style while following an independent command. `CODES` retargets diverse motion recordings to the target robot and discovers a set of styles using weakly supervised consensus encoding and density-based clustering, without a preset number of styles. It then trains a reinforcement learning policy that combines those styles with velocity commands. On a `Unitree Go2` quadruped in two simulators and on hardware, it **improves kinematic coherence over baselines** and tracks commands beyond the range of the recorded data while keeping styles distinguishable.

papers.title: Beyond Explicit Intent: Discovering and Shaping Artistic Intent through Human-AI Co-Creation
papers.abstract: Generative AI is becoming an important medium for artistic creation, yet existing interactions often assume that creators can specify intentions in advance and accurately communicate them through text prompts. Artistic intentions, however, may be vague, latent, or recognizable only after seeing concrete visual possibilities. We propose a human-AI co-creation paradigm beyond explicit intent expression. By expanding model exploration, we expose artists to diverse visual possibilities, allowing them to identify previously unarticulated preferences through observation, comparison, and selection. We then integrate artists' curatorial judgments into reinforcement learning, assigning different learning strengths based on preferences over generation trajectories, so recognized directions are more strongly reinforced and the model gradually adapts to individual aesthetics. This creates a continuous "explore-identify-shape-re-explore" loop in which artistic intent is progressively discovered, externalized, and shaped. Through three user studies, we examine latent-preference discovery, personalized preference alignment, and the externalization of vague, difficult-to-express creative intentions.
papers.summary: Text-to-image tools assume artists can state their intent up front in a prompt, but artistic intent is often vague and only becomes clear once concrete options are visible. The proposed co-creation approach widens the model's exploration so artists can discover preferences by comparing and selecting outputs, then feeds those curatorial choices into reinforcement learning with learning strength weighted by preferences over generation trajectories. The result is an iterative **explore-identify-shape-re-explore loop** that gradually adapts the model to an individual's aesthetics, studied in three user studies on discovering latent preferences, personalized alignment, and expressing hard-to-articulate intentions.

papers.title: SPADE-KD: Peer-to-Peer Collaborative Learning under Heterogeneous Settings
papers.abstract: Peer-to-peer collaborative learning is an emerging distributed deep learning paradigm that eliminates the need for a central aggregator and disseminator, avoiding the single-point-of-failure and bottleneck issues they can bring. Many such approaches use parameter averaging, requiring clients to have homogeneous model architectures, whereas others use knowledge distillation as an alternative while leaning on shared public data or centralized control infrastructure. Many of these approaches also make a one-size-fits-all assumption, i.e., jointly training a single, globally optimal solution for all clients, when in reality, clients' underlying data distributions might differ such that a globally optimal solution may not be locally optimal for all clients. To enable collaborative learning in environments with both model architecture and data distribution heterogeneity, we present SPADE-KD -- a fully decentralized model distillation framework that optimizes collaboration towards personalized rather than global performance. SPADE-KD leverages two mechanisms -- adaptive distillation and utility-driven peer selection. Adaptive distillation modulates the strength of each incoming model transfer by the performance advantage of the incoming model compared to the native model measured by their task losses, such that a client will distill more aggressively from incoming models that outperform it on its own local data. Utility-driven peer selection uses the loss-informed utility derived from adaptive distillation to rank prospective partners, focusing on exchanges that measurably improve the local model while suppressing low-utility transfers. Using federated classification tasks, we demonstrate that SPADE-KD consistent outperforms naive decentralized distillation with lower loss and faster convergence and that its individual components are more effective together than independently.
papers.summary: Peer-to-peer collaborative learning removes the central server, but parameter averaging requires every client to use the same architecture, and distillation-based alternatives usually rely on shared public data or central coordination while aiming for a single global model. `SPADE-KD` is a fully decentralized distillation framework that targets personalized rather than global performance. Adaptive distillation scales how much a client learns from each incoming model by how much better that model performs on the client's own data, and utility-driven peer selection uses the same signal to rank which peers to exchange with. On federated classification tasks it **achieves lower loss and faster convergence than naive decentralized distillation**, and its two components work better together than separately.

papers.title: TWIN-MoE: Two-stage Intra-Expert Imputation Network for Incomplete Multimodal Learning
papers.abstract: Recent Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches address missing modalities either by routing each missingness pattern to a dedicated expert, which scales poorly as the number of modalities grows, or by imputing the missing modality from representations contributed by multiple experts, which requires a costly retrieval mechanism. We show that routing induces expert-conditioned representation neighborhoods and derive an imputation-error bound controlled by their local feature dispersion. When these expert-conditioned neighborhoods are more compact than the global representation space, intra-expert aggregation admits a tighter worst-case reconstruction bound than unconstrained global aggregation. Guided by this analysis, we propose TWIN, a two-stage intra-expert imputation framework. Pre-imputation generates a context-conditioned estimate in the encoder embedding space and radially soft-clips it using modality-specific statistics maintained in an observed FIFO queue, this ensures that the pre-imputed modality stays in empirically calibrated region of the target modality space. Post-imputation refines the missing representation after MoE by aggregating expert-conditioned observed representations within the same sample. Across four missing-modality benchmarks under natural, random, and asymmetric dropout protocols, TWIN achieves state-of-the-art performance while using substantially fewer parameters than competing MoE-based imputation methods.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) methods for handling missing modalities either assign one expert per missingness pattern, which scales poorly with the number of modalities, or impute the missing input using costly retrieval across experts. The authors show that routing creates compact expert-specific neighborhoods in representation space, which gives intra-expert aggregation a tighter worst-case imputation error bound than aggregating globally. `TWIN` first pre-imputes the missing modality in the encoder embedding space and soft-clips it using statistics from a FIFO queue of observed samples, then refines it after the MoE layer by aggregating expert-conditioned representations from the same sample. **It achieves state-of-the-art results on four missing-modality benchmarks with substantially fewer parameters** than competing MoE imputation methods.

papers.title: Analysis of Binary O-type Star Systems Using Recurrent Neural Networks
papers.abstract: This work presents an initial analysis of the estimation of effective temperature and surface gravity for simulated O-type binary systems using a recurrent neural network. The proposed system uses 34 equivalent-width measurements from the optical region of a stellar spectrum. Two methods were applied to observed IACOB spectra before normalization: the addition of a blackbody continuum and the addition of a second observed spectrum. The first method produces only small differences in the normalized line profiles and in the estimated physical parameters over 3700-7000~\AA. In the second method, the secondary spectrum is added with contributions of 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, and 75 per cent, as defined relative to the original primary spectrum. The general comparison includes 192 simulated systems and 1152 modified spectra. For most of these spectra, the estimated effective temperature and surface gravity decrease as the contribution of the secondary component increases. Individual examples using HD14947, HD190429, HD48099, and HD206267 show that this behavior is not the same for every combination: some estimated effective temperatures fall below the estimates for both isolated spectra, and some surface gravity estimates increase. Comparisons with previously published values also depend on the physical parameter and reference considered. The results show that the proposed system is sensitive to the addition of a secondary spectrum, but do not establish a unique contribution for the secondary component of an observed binary.
papers.summary: The study tests how a recurrent neural network that estimates effective temperature and surface gravity for O-type stars behaves when the input spectrum is actually a binary system. The network uses 34 equivalent-width measurements from the optical spectrum. Binaries are simulated in two ways: by adding a blackbody continuum, or by adding a second observed `IACOB` spectrum at 5 to 75 per cent of the primary's contribution, giving 1152 modified spectra. The blackbody addition barely changes the estimates. Adding a second spectrum generally **lowers both estimated temperature and gravity as the secondary's share grows**, but individual star pairs break this pattern, and the method cannot pin down a unique secondary contribution for an observed binary.

papers.title: Unified Multiparadigm Fusion Intelligence for Rare Disease Diagnosis
papers.abstract: Rare diseases (RDs) affect an estimated 300 million people globally, leaving patients to navigate a protracted diagnostic odyssey constrained by clinical scarcity and fragmented medical knowledge. Artificial intelligence (AI) has progressively advanced RD diagnostics, from symbolic methods and deep learning to large language model (LLM)-based systems. However, each paradigm carries structural limitations: symbolic methods are bounded by knowledge completeness, neural models sacrifice interpretability, and LLM-based systems are vulnerable to evaluation biases like data leakage. In this study, we introduce FusionRare, a unified multiparadigm fusion framework integrating knowledge-driven symbolic reasoning, deep-learning pattern recognition, case-based patient retrieval, and LLM-based heuristic inference via statistical meta-aggregation and knowledge-enhanced agentic reflection. Evaluated on 2,528 strictly isolated clinical cases, FusionRare achieves state-of-the-art RD prioritization, attaining a macro-averaged Recall @1 of 51% for phenotype-only diagnosis and 79% for phenotype-genotype joint analysis. These results represent decisive advantages over the advanced agentic system DeepRare, frontier LLMs including GPT 5.5, and specialized tools like PhenoBrain and LIRICAL under stringent anti-leakage protocols. A randomized, crossover clinician-AI validation demonstrated that FusionRare elevates the true diagnostic rank in 45% of decisions, improves physician confidence in 62%, and reduces time to diagnosis by 21%. These findings indicate that reconciling these orthogonal AI paradigms significantly enhances diagnostic capabilities, bridging the gap between computational benchmarks and actionable clinical reliability. More broadly, this work provides a replicable framework for deploying trustworthy diagnostic AI across complex, high-stakes, and underserved medical domains.
papers.summary: `FusionRare` targets rare disease diagnosis by combining four AI approaches that each have known weaknesses: symbolic knowledge-based reasoning, deep-learning pattern recognition, retrieval of similar patient cases, and large language model (LLM) inference. Their outputs are merged through statistical meta-aggregation and an agentic reflection step backed by medical knowledge. On 2,528 clinical cases kept strictly separate to prevent data leakage, it reaches a macro-averaged Recall@1 of 51% from phenotype alone and **79% from phenotype plus genotype**, beating `DeepRare`, `GPT 5.5`, `PhenoBrain`, and `LIRICAL`. In a randomized crossover study with clinicians, it improved the rank of the true diagnosis in 45% of decisions and cut time to diagnosis by 21%.

papers.title: Dynamical Kernel Attention: Estimating the Present from a Record of the Past
papers.abstract: Standard self-attention compares tokens by similarity but does not account for how much of a past state survives to the present. We introduce Dynamical Kernel Attention (DKA), which derives attention from robust estimation of a latent state evolving under stochastic dynamics. As a past state decays toward equilibrium under the dynamics, the information it carries about the present vanishes, bounding the total evidence a head can draw. Unlike recency biases, DKA can abstain when relevant evidence is weak and guarantees a bounded error when old tokens are discarded. DKA preserves the parallel structure and computational cost of standard attention. We present the model and its theory; empirical evaluation is deferred to a subsequent version.
papers.summary: Standard self-attention scores past tokens by similarity, with no notion of how much of a past state still bears on the present. `Dynamical Kernel Attention` (`DKA`) instead derives attention weights from robust estimation of a latent state that evolves under stochastic dynamics, so information from older states fades as they decay toward equilibrium. This caps the total evidence each head can draw on, lets a head abstain when evidence is weak, and **guarantees bounded error when old tokens are discarded**, all at the same parallel cost as standard attention. The paper presents only the model and its theory; experiments are deferred to a later version.

papers.title: Do Knowledge and Reasoning Oriented Benchmarks Induce Stable Representation Signatures in LLMs?
papers.abstract: Internal signatures could support monitoring, adaptive computation, and mechanistic analysis, but benchmark prompts can be separable without any shared computational distinction. We test whether a prespecified knowledge/reasoning label defines a reusable internal signature in five contemporary 7B to 31B models. We treat the \textbf{task} as the unit of inference probes hold out complete tasks, labels are permuted across tasks, and the best layer and stream are reselected for every permutation. Raw probes recover an eight-versus-eight-subject MMLU partition in all five models (macro-F1 $0.78$--$0.81$), but prompt text predicts it nearly as well: under an identical probe configuration, the activation advantage is only $0.017$--$0.070$ macro-F1 and is not significant. At the prespecified $0.01$ level, lexical adjustment removes significance while the adjusted states still identify individual subjects, and the selected site changes across task panels and selection rules. Additionally, two released base-training trajectories show no common direction. These pooled layerwise measures recover the task label but identify no transferable knowledge/reasoning signature at the tested sensitivity, which cannot exclude moderate effects. The resulting protocol gives future internal monitors and intervention studies a sequence of tests to pass. Project page: \url{https://parsa-ra.github.io/lmbehave/}.
papers.summary: The authors ask whether labeling benchmark tasks as "knowledge" or "reasoning" corresponds to a reusable internal signature in five LLMs ranging from 7B to 31B parameters. Their protocol treats whole tasks as the unit of inference: probes are tested on held-out tasks, and labels are permuted across tasks. Probes on activations do separate an eight-versus-eight `MMLU` subject split (macro-F1 0.78 to 0.81), but the prompt text alone does nearly as well, and **the advantage of activations over text (0.017 to 0.070 macro-F1) is not statistically significant**. The best-performing layer also shifts across task panels, and two base-model training trajectories show no common direction, so the paper finds no transferable knowledge/reasoning signature and offers its protocol as a set of tests that future internal monitors should pass.

papers.title: When Does Evidence-Graph Structure Predict Answer Correctness? Label-Free Abstention for Structured Retrieval
papers.abstract: Retrieval systems return scored answers, but a high score does not show that an answer should be trusted. The proposed training-free abstention method applies the boundary cut to the selected evidence in an evidence graph. The signal is the weighted cut between selected and unselected candidates and requires no correctness labels or confidence-model training. On MemoryAgentBench (MAB) FactConsolidation multi-hop, with unresolved queries ranked last for every selector, it raises area under the precision-coverage curve from 0.736 for the best score baseline to 0.785 (+0.049, 95% CI [+0.008, +0.092]); under the native evaluation, where score baselines keep their unresolved values, the gap is +0.108. A zero-cut subset contains 71 of 400 queries at 100% observed precision. In this pipeline, the subset corresponds to structural closure; controlled analyses attribute much of the remaining separation to resolution status, with little benefit from continuous edge weights. Across external benchmarks, usefulness varies with graph construction, edge semantics, and relation; typed structure alone does not ensure useful confidence. A supervised gradient-boosted selector achieves 0.814 versus the boundary cut's 0.785 when the retrieval stack matches. These findings provide empirical guidance for using available evidence graphs for lightweight, auditable post-retrieval abstention without additional model inference.
papers.summary: A high retrieval score does not show that an answer should be trusted. This paper proposes a training-free way for retrieval systems to abstain, based on the weighted cut between selected and unselected candidates in an evidence graph, which needs no correctness labels. On `MemoryAgentBench` `FactConsolidation` multi-hop questions, it raises the area under the precision-coverage curve from 0.736 to 0.785. A subset of queries with a zero cut, **71 of 400, had 100% observed precision**. Further analysis attributes much of the gain to whether a query was resolved rather than to edge weights, the benefit varies with how the graph is built on other benchmarks, and a supervised gradient-boosted selector still does better (0.814).

papers.title: Visual Causal-chain Bookmarking: Retrieval-Weighted Credit Assignment for Reinforcement Learning from Delayed Reward
papers.abstract: RL agents trained on a single trajectory-level return face a credit-assignment problem: when a reward arrives many steps after the decision that caused it, every action gets the same signal regardless of causal responsibility. This paper studies Visual Causal-chain Bookmarking (VCBM), which concentrates credit on the decision points that determine an episode's return, via two instantiations. The first targets a fully observed, low-dimensional MDP (a delayed-reward watch-repair task), where VCBM statistically discovers which state components the agent causally controls and estimates per-decision-point action values directly, evaluated against ground truth and RUDDER, an LSTM-based baseline. VCBM converges to 95.07% correct decisions in a mean of 1,532.3 episodes across 20 seeds, versus RUDDER's slower, more variable convergence (mean 3,327.1 episodes; p<0.001); VCBM's discovered causal structure exactly matches ground truth in all seeds. The second targets a partially observed, language-based setting: an LLM agent trained with Leave-One-Out PPO (LOOP) in AppWorld, where causal discovery is intractable and a structural heuristic (state-mutating tool calls) substitutes for it, with credit distributed via retrieval over episodic memory and blended with LOOP's advantage. Over 200 iterations on identical Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct/LoRA/FSDP2 configurations, VCBM-blended LOOP improves task success over plain LOOP (0.354 vs. 0.458), reduces final-step max importance weight, and improves token efficiency, with a small KL exception favouring LOOP. The watch-repair result supports the claim that weighting causally relevant steps is more sample-efficient than an undifferentiated baseline or a learned return-redistribution network; the AppWorld result, limited to one seed per arm by a 2-GPU budget, is a compute-limited demonstration at a harder, natural-language scale, not a statistical confirmation.
papers.summary: When reinforcement learning (RL) agents receive a single reward long after the decisions that caused it, every action gets the same credit. `Visual Causal-chain Bookmarking` (`VCBM`) concentrates credit on the decision points that actually determine the return. On a fully observed watch-repair task, it discovers the true causal structure in every seed and **converges in about 1,532 episodes versus 3,327 for the LSTM-based baseline `RUDDER`**. In `AppWorld`, it is applied to a `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` agent trained with Leave-One-Out PPO (`LOOP`), using state-changing tool calls as a stand-in for causal discovery and spreading credit through retrieval over episodic memory. It reports higher task success than plain `LOOP` (the reported figures are 0.354 vs. 0.458) and better token efficiency, though the authors note this is a single-seed, compute-limited demonstration.

papers.title: LLM Evolution in a Simple Simulated Market
papers.abstract: Arguments that AI systems will evolve in harmful ways are largely made in the abstract. We provide a concrete empirical example. We simulate simple markets consisting of populations of twenty Large Language Model agents tasked with solving arithmetic problems. Agents differ only in their system prompt; those that go bankrupt are removed and replaced by mutated copies of the prompts of successful agents. Two market conditions select for opposite phenotypes: a market that rewards accuracy produces agents with high accuracy (94%) and high token use; a market that charges per token produces agents with low accuracy (10%) and low token use. In the second market, only tokens are incentivised yet we see a collapse in accuracy. Token use and accuracy are correlated traits such that selection on one also moves the other, and behaviour adapts along an unpriced dimension. A third neutral condition with no selection allows us to separate these effects from bias in the mutation operator. Adaptation occurs through a collective optimisation process that operates above the level of individual agents, who are never told the payment rule, do not receive feedback, and have no memory.
papers.summary: The authors give a concrete example of LLM agents evolving under market pressure. Each simulated market holds twenty agents solving arithmetic problems that differ only in their system prompt; bankrupt agents are replaced by mutated copies of successful agents' prompts. A market that rewards accuracy produces agents with 94% accuracy and heavy token use, while a market that only charges per token produces agents with **accuracy collapsing to 10%**, even though accuracy was never priced. A neutral control with no selection rules out bias in the mutation operator. The adaptation happens at the population level: individual agents are never told the payment rule, receive no feedback, and have no memory.

papers.title: Client-Aware Security Adaptive Early Exit Vision Transformers for Heterogeneous Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) trains a shared model across data-owning clients without centralizing raw data, but client data difficulty and compute budgets can differ. We study local early-exit Vision Transformer (ViT) inference, where an intermediate classifier may return a prediction before the final Transformer stage. The proposed method replaces one global acceptance threshold with a client-specific base threshold from label entropy and shallow-exit confidence, then adjusts each input using predictive entropy, confidence, top-two class margin, and exit depth. Aggregation uses only clients that updated a parameter. Security-aware routing reaches 88.70% CIFAR-10 accuracy with 32.0% depth saving and 73.7% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with 30\% saving. On matched six-client non-IID CIFAR-100, full-depth accuracy is 72.28% versus 68.20--71.80% for four heterogeneous-FL baselines; robustness-aware routing reaches 70.01% with 32.55% saving.
papers.summary: The setting is federated learning (FL), where clients differ in data difficulty and compute budget, and each client runs Vision Transformer (ViT) inference that can return early from an intermediate classifier. Instead of one global confidence threshold for exiting early, each client gets its own base threshold, set from label entropy and shallow-exit confidence, which is then adjusted per input using predictive entropy, top-two margin, and exit depth. Server aggregation uses only the clients that actually updated a given parameter. Security-aware routing reaches **88.70% `CIFAR-10` accuracy with 32% depth savings** and 73.7% `ImageNet-1K` top-1 accuracy with 30% savings, and at full depth it outperforms four heterogeneous-FL baselines on non-IID `CIFAR-100`.

papers.title: What Remains Without Test Labels? Re-evaluating a Graph-Level Anomaly Detection Benchmark
papers.abstract: Graph-level anomaly detectors are trained only on normal graphs, yet benchmarks may use test labels for model selection. We examine whether UB-GOLD results reused by later papers support label-free detection. We audit UB-GOLD and 14 GLAD code bases, re-run 21 detectors on UB-GOLD's folds under selection rules with and without test labels, and evaluate sensitivity to known structural changes. Test labels select checkpoints in UB-GOLD's shared training loop and checkpoints or hyperparameters in 8 of the 14 code bases. UB-GOLD also evaluates its kernel baselines against misaligned labels. Across nine datasets, selecting checkpoints by test AUROC adds an average of 5.12 AUROC points [3.97, 6.24] for the 12 UB-GOLD detectors relative to the final checkpoint and 4.13 [3.32, 4.79] relative to held-out normal graphs. In a post hoc permutation analysis with no truly better checkpoint, picking the best of noisy test evaluations still yields a gain more than half as large as the one observed against the final checkpoint. Configurations tuned on test labels score a further 1.53 points [0.64, 2.42] above repository defaults, a gap that mixes the value of test labels with that of tuning itself. With tuned hyperparameters and label-free checkpoint selection, the two strongest detectors retain their lead, while comparisons below them are less stable. Six of eight detectors evaluated out of sample miss size-preserving composition changes that graphlet counts detect. We recommend reporting results selected without test labels as the main comparisons and release per-run outputs that allow verification without retraining.
papers.summary: Graph-level anomaly detectors are supposed to train on normal graphs only, yet the authors find that the widely reused `UB-GOLD` benchmark and 8 of 14 related code bases use test labels to choose checkpoints or hyperparameters. Re-running 21 detectors across nine datasets shows that **choosing checkpoints by test AUROC inflates scores by about 5.12 points on average**. A permutation analysis shows that picking the best of several noisy test evaluations alone accounts for more than half of that gain. Under label-free selection the two strongest detectors keep their lead, but rankings below them become unstable. The authors recommend reporting label-free results as the main comparison and releasing per-run outputs so results can be checked without retraining.

papers.title: The Window Is in the Reasoning: When LLM Agents Decide to Follow Prompt Injections
papers.abstract: LLM agents that read untrusted content can be hijacked by prompt injections. Runtime monitors that try to catch a hijack before the agent acts, and benchmarks that score each task with a single run, share an assumption: whether an agent follows an injection is settled when the injection is read. We test this assumption with branching rollouts that replay an episode exactly up to the step at which the agent reads an injection and then resample the rest of the episode many times, splitting the outcome variance into a part fixed at read time and a part decided afterwards. Across four AgentDojo suites, a Qwen3 agent without thinking is largely decided at read time (0.91 of the outcome variance lies between states); with thinking on, this share drops to 0.62 (95% CI of the drop [-0.38, -0.22]), in the same direction for three attack templates and two success labels. How much is fixed at read time is a property of the model that the same measurement reveals, and thinking lowers the attack success rate of Qwen3 but raises it for two other models. Resampling from reasoning prefixes shows that the decision forms gradually as the agent reasons. Zero-shot chain-of-thought monitors built on cheaper models miss much of what is already decided, whereas stronger monitors, and a lookahead monitor that judges simulated next actions, come close to what the prefix determines. Finally, single-run labels of thinking agents disagree with a rerun up to 35% of the time, so benchmarks need repeated runs per task.
papers.summary: Runtime monitors and single-run benchmarks both assume that whether an LLM agent follows a prompt injection is settled the moment it reads the injection. The authors test this with branching rollouts: they replay an episode exactly up to the injection, then resample the rest many times. On four `AgentDojo` suites, a `Qwen3` agent without thinking is largely decided at read time (0.91 of outcome variance), but **with thinking enabled that share drops to 0.62**, and the decision forms gradually as the agent reasons. Chain-of-thought monitors built on cheaper models miss much of what is already decided, while stronger monitors and a lookahead monitor that judges simulated next actions come close. Single-run labels for thinking agents disagree with a rerun up to 35% of the time, so benchmarks need repeated runs per task.

papers.title: Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review
papers.abstract: As automated research is increasingly adopted for writing papers, automated review has become a critical link between paper generation and quality control. However, existing methods largely rely on single-model feedback or simple review aggregation, failing to explicitly model expert responsibilities or collective deliberation in actual peer reviews, which limits effective cross-examination and reliable decision-making. Therefore, we formulate paper review as a computational modeling problem of peer review mechanisms and propose RoundtableReview, a deliberative multi-agent framework for enhancing automated research. RoundtableReview structures each paper into eight semantic slots and coordinates six academic and industry reviewers with complementary perspectives, retrieval sources, and specialized responsibilities. Through independent assessment, cross-examination, roundtable deliberation, dynamically weighted voting, and chair synthesis, the framework generates evidence-based and traceable feedback. Experiments on two automated research backbones show that the method improves paper quality in both backbones and outperforms baselines in automatic and human evaluations with fewer comments.
papers.summary: Automated research pipelines need reviewers that do more than give single-model feedback or simply aggregate several reviews. `RoundtableReview` models peer review as a multi-agent deliberation. It splits each paper into eight semantic slots and assigns six academic and industry reviewer agents with different perspectives, retrieval sources, and responsibilities. The agents assess independently, cross-examine each other, deliberate, vote with dynamic weights, and pass the result to a chair who synthesizes it. On two automated research backbones, it **improves the quality of the final papers while producing fewer comments**, outperforming baselines in both automatic and human evaluations.

papers.title: LogicVal:A Logic-Formalized Benchmark for Constraint Satisfaction in Text-to-Image Generation
papers.abstract: Text-to-Image (T2I) generative models have made significant progress in producing high-fidelity images from natural-language prompts. Alongside this progress, numerous benchmarks have been developed to evaluate capabilities such as attribute binding, numeracy, spatial reasoning, and commonsense reasoning. In this work, we propose a new perspective on T2I evaluation by casting it as a constraint-satisfaction problem. We introduce a logical framework that formally specifies the benchmark domain, including objects, attributes, and relations, alongside the constraints that generated images must satisfy. We evaluated four state-of-the-art T2I models across 9 classes of constraints ranging from a single-object-attribute to multi-object relationships constraints involving logical operators ($\forall, \exists, count, \rightarrow$). Our results reveal a substantial gap between single-object and complex conditional multi-object relationship constraint classes, with the best-performing model achieving 98% accuracy on the former and just 53% on the latter. We assess compositional generalisation, finding that the best-performing model`s accuracy drops from 84% on single-constraint prompts to 20% when satisfying multiple constraints simultaneously. Identifying unsatisfiable constraints is also challenging, with the best model correctly recognizing only 23% of such prompts. Building on this framework, we introduce \textbf{LogicVal}, an evaluation methodology that combines neural visual detection with logical reasoning to assess constraint satisfaction in generated images. On CLEVR, LogicVal achieves ROC-AUC scores ranging from 0.88 to 0.98, indicating strong alignment with human judgments. These findings underscore the value of logic-based evaluation for characterizing T2I model capabilities and limitations.
papers.summary: The paper treats text-to-image (T2I) evaluation as a constraint-satisfaction problem, with a formal logic specifying objects, attributes, relations, and constraints that use universal and existential quantifiers, counting, and implication. Across four state-of-the-art T2I models and 9 constraint classes, the best model reaches 98% on single-object attribute constraints but only 53% on conditional multi-object relations. Its accuracy **drops from 84% to 20% when several constraints must hold at once**, and it recognizes only 23% of unsatisfiable prompts. The accompanying evaluator, `LogicVal`, pairs neural object detection with logical reasoning and reaches ROC-AUC of 0.88 to 0.98 against human judgments on `CLEVR`.

papers.title: Red-Teaming Multi-Agent Attacks for Loss-of-Control Risks
papers.abstract: AI agents are growing more capable and persistent, and are being deployed in ever larger numbers. As more start collaborating, AI control measures must remain effective when they covertly collude on a harmful objective. We introduce MiniLab, a synthetic series of live services and codebases (5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, 8 attack objectives), adapted from internal AI deployment infrastructure. We demonstrate distributed attacks, in which different agents carry out separate attack fragments, and how their covertness evades frontier monitors when reading their trajectories individually. We show how distributed attacks spread across diverse contexts and harmful objectives through 16 human-optimized attacks (weight exfiltration, unmonitored rogue deployment, permission elevation, and more). A frontier monitor, GPT-5.6 Sol, reading each agent separately flags only 7% of successful distributed attacks, compared with 87% when a single agent carries out the same side task. Individual attacks can also be composed into longer attack sequences toward a greater loss-of-control outcome, without any individual agent being flagged. Finally, we tested whether models can plan these covert attacks: even with execution and monitor feedback, the best model-planned attacks succeed covertly against a single-trajectory GPT-5.6 Sol monitor in at most 25% of executions, compared with 80% for human-crafted plans, though this may scale with model capabilities. By turning worst-case coordinated attacks into reproducible red-team cases, our work provides a foundation for preventing locally benign agent actions from accumulating into system-level loss of control.
papers.summary: AI control measures must hold up when multiple agents covertly collude on a harmful goal. `MiniLab` provides a synthetic environment adapted from internal AI deployment infrastructure, with 5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, and 8 attack objectives such as weight exfiltration and permission elevation. In distributed attacks, different agents each carry out one fragment, and a frontier monitor, `GPT-5.6 Sol`, reading each agent's trajectory separately **flags only 7% of successful distributed attacks, versus 87% when one agent does the whole side task**. Attacks can also be chained toward larger loss-of-control outcomes without any single agent being flagged. Model-planned attacks currently succeed covertly in at most 25% of executions, compared with 80% for human-crafted plans.

papers.title: Alliance of Stochastic Routing and Reinforcement Fusion for Multi-Model Reasoning
papers.abstract: This paper studies dynamic model routing under uncertainty in multimodal settings, where a system must select and potentially compose multiple models to answer a query. Standard reinforcement learning approaches for routing often suffer from premature convergence to suboptimal models due to noisy rewards and insufficient exploration. We propose a unified vision-language framework (VL-Scout) for efficient multimodal and multi-step reasoning with turn-based reinforcement fusion. First, VL-Scout combines Bayesian priors, policy gradient optimization, and sequential decision-making to enable structured exploration and adaptive inference. A context-dependent Dirichlet belief model allows for epistemic uncertainty over model quality and is updated online based on observed rewards and context-specific evidence, enabling Thompson-style exploration while serving as a prior for regularization. Second, a routing policy is trained via a KL-regularized REINFORCE objective by maximizing a reward-weighted evidence lower bound, where the policy acts as an amortized posterior, and the Dirichlet belief serves as a prior. Third, we introduce a fusion policy trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) or Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), which operates over intermediate model rationales and selects between two actions: CONTINUE or ANSWER, terminating with a generated output. We evaluate VL-Scout on four representative multi-modal benchmarks (MMMU, MMMU-Pro, OKVQA, and RealWorldQA), compared against 11 representative routing and policy optimization baselines. Our method provides consistent performance improvements while reducing premature policy collapse. These results highlight the importance of integrating uncertainty-aware priors with both amortized policy learning and sequential fusion for robust and efficient model selection in discrete action spaces
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning methods for routing queries among multiple models often lock onto a suboptimal model too early because rewards are noisy and exploration is limited. `VL-Scout` addresses this for multimodal reasoning. It keeps a context-dependent Dirichlet belief over model quality that supports Thompson-style exploration, and trains a routing policy with KL-regularized `REINFORCE` using that belief as a prior. A separate fusion policy, trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) or Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (`RLVR`), reads intermediate model rationales and decides whether to continue or answer. Across `MMMU`, `MMMU-Pro`, `OKVQA`, and `RealWorldQA`, it shows **consistent gains over 11 routing and policy-optimization baselines** with less premature policy collapse.

papers.title: ToolRosetta: Surface-Form Invariance of Tool-Call Guards
papers.abstract: Step-level guards for tool-using agents are evaluated on tidy JSON tool calls, but deployed coding agents act through execute_bash and execute_code tools whose payloads are strings. We introduce ToolRosetta, which re-renders every candidate action in the AgentDojo and AgentHarm splits of TS-Bench as a Python call, as a shell command, and without the agent's rationale. The renderings are produced by code and verified by round-trip parsing, so the user request, the history, the label and the action's effect stay fixed while only the surface form changes. Across eleven guards with two placebo controls, frontier and strong open-weight guards are stable: no frontier error rate moves by more than 3.4 points. Four of five specialized agent guards are not: under the shell form their false-positive rates rise by 21 to 47 points on AgentDojo, and TS-Guard's by 38 points on its own home benchmark, blocking between a third and nine in ten benign actions; the fifth, StepGuard, does not move. A small open guard drifts five points more permissive. Removing the agent's rationale moves most guards whose input carries it, in guard-specific directions. A request-blind control on one guard shows that the rationale is where intent is read from. A parser that restores the canonical call in front of the guard removes the effect for these renderings, by construction. Benchmark accuracy on JSON calls does not predict a guard's operating point behind a code-acting agent.
papers.summary: Step-level guards for tool-using agents are usually evaluated on clean JSON tool calls, while deployed coding agents act through bash and code-execution tools whose payloads are plain strings. `ToolRosetta` re-renders every candidate action in the `AgentDojo` and `AgentHarm` splits of `TS-Bench` as a Python call, as a shell command, and without the agent's rationale, verified by round-trip parsing so that only the surface form changes. Frontier and strong open-weight guards stay stable (within 3.4 points), but **four of five specialized agent guards raise their false-positive rates by 21 to 47 points under the shell form**, blocking up to nine in ten benign actions. Placing a parser in front of the guard to restore the canonical call removes the effect, and accuracy on JSON calls turns out not to predict how a guard behaves behind a code-acting agent.

papers.title: World of SWECraft: Agent Collaboration at Scale via Simulated Software Worlds
papers.abstract: As teams of AI agents take on larger projects and long-standing open problems, agent collaboration offers another dimension for scaling inference-time compute. To understand what makes such collaboration effective and scalable, we develop Software World, a framework for simulating multi-agent coworking in realistic software ecosystems. It comes with a pipeline to create environments of real, interdependent Python packages of different topics, sizes, and dependency structures, which we call software worlds. In a simulation, agents maintain packages in the world with a high-level goal of improving software efficiency, and they are free to discover tasks to work on and collaborate with others. We evaluate agents' work in a world collectively by measuring speedup in hidden dependent packages. The framework allows us to study different elements of collaboration by varying communication, ownership, and resource allocation. We run simulations in three different worlds, totaling more than 10,000 hours of agent work across eight models. Overall, performance improvement scales with inference-time compute, with the best model improving downstream efficiency by up to 31%. We show that most agents can find meaningful tasks via collaboration, but some frontier models can prematurely stop looking for improvements and make little progress. We release the simulation framework and traces to support future studies of agent collaboration at https://szj.io/sw.
papers.summary: `Software World` is a framework for studying collaboration among many AI agents in simulated ecosystems of real, interdependent Python packages. Agents choose their own tasks toward the goal of improving software efficiency, and the team is scored on speedups in hidden downstream packages. The framework varies communication, ownership, and resource allocation. Over more than 10,000 hours of agent work across eight models and three worlds, improvement scales with inference-time compute, and **the best model improves downstream efficiency by up to 31%**. Most agents find meaningful work through collaboration, but some frontier models stop looking for improvements too early; the framework and traces are released.

papers.title: OrTeN: Neural Inverse Graphics for Joint Terrain and Line-scan Camera Trajectory Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Digital terrain maps (DTMs) are used for landing site selection, terrain-relative navigation, and geological analysis in planetary exploration. Existing state-of-practice reconstruction techniques for creating DTMs from satellite imagery use multi-view stereo, requiring complex pipelines for dealing with camera error, changing illumination, and images with limited disparity. This work introduces Orbital Terrain Networks (OrTeN), a DTM construction method that uses neural inverse rendering to jointly optimize a textured height map and orbital camera corrections from line-scan satellite images. OrTeN operates directly on calibrated line-scan images with pixel values expressed as radiance factor (I/F) and corrects both broad trajectory pose inconsistencies and high-frequency pointing jitter jointly with surface reconstruction during training. Surface-projected patch normalized cross-correlation (NCC) enforces consistency between observations of the same terrain, refining an initial rough reconstruction. A semi-empirical reflectance model and shadow rendering are used to fit surface appearance from multi-date imagery with differing solar illumination. OrTeN requires only calibrated line-scan images and initial camera poses and does not use any structural priors including ranging/depth measurements or initial rough DTMs. OrTeN is evaluated on four planetary imagery datasets. Aligned terrain RMSEs are 2.35 m at Jezero Crater, 2.82 m at Gale Crater, 16.18 m at Olympus Mons, and 0.43 m at McGetchin Crater.
papers.summary: Building digital terrain maps (DTMs) from orbital images usually requires complex multi-view stereo pipelines that must handle camera error and changing illumination. `Orbital Terrain Networks` (`OrTeN`) uses neural inverse rendering to jointly optimize a textured height map and corrections to the line-scan camera trajectory, including high-frequency pointing jitter. It enforces consistency between views with surface-projected patch normalized cross-correlation, and models reflectance and shadows to fit images taken under different sun angles. It needs only calibrated images and initial camera poses, with no depth priors, and reaches **aligned terrain errors as low as 0.43 m** (McGetchin Crater) and 2.35 to 16.18 m on Mars sites.

papers.title: Location, Location, Generation: Where You Ask Matters for Generative Engine Optimization
papers.abstract: Generative search engines answer local and commercial questions with a written answer and a few cited sources. A growing practice of generative engine optimization (GEO) monitors which sources and brands these answers show, typically from a single place. In this paper, we present a controlled audit of how the user's location changes the sources that generative engines cite. We ask 300 questions of ChatGPT with 19 declared locations, and of ChatGPT and Gemini from five network locations, each twice to measure run-to-run noise (31,200 answers). The engines take location from different channels. ChatGPT follows the location an application declares, down to the city: it writes the place into its own searches, and its search backend localizes results even when the queries name no place. It ignores the network. Gemini ignores the declared location and follows the country of the network, changing most of its sources even for questions that do not depend on place. The businesses the answers recommend change with the sources. Thus, visibility in generative search is specific to the user's location, and audits must control both channels.
papers.summary: Generative engine optimization (GEO) monitors which sources and brands generative search engines cite, usually from a single location. This audit asks 300 questions of `ChatGPT` under 19 declared locations, and of `ChatGPT` and `Gemini` from five network locations, collecting 31,200 answers with repeats to measure run-to-run noise. **The two engines take location from different channels**: `ChatGPT` follows the location an application declares, down to the city, and ignores the network, while `Gemini` ignores the declared location and follows the network's country, changing most of its sources even for questions that do not depend on place. Because recommended businesses change along with the sources, GEO audits must control both channels.

papers.title: GLOW: General Linear Models Optimized with Ward's Method
papers.abstract:
Neuroimaging seeks brain regions whose imaging features correlate with variables of interest (e.g., diagnosis, age), usually via the General Linear Model (GLM). Region-Based Analysis dilutes or splits any effect that does not fill exactly one atlas region. Voxel-Based Analysis, with Cluster Extent Thresholding and Threshold-Free Cluster Enhancement built on it, fits a GLM per voxel and groups adjacent significant voxels. But neighboring voxels can share a statistic without sharing a GLM, which a per-voxel statistic cannot detect.
  GLOW (General Linear Models Optimized with Ward's method) instead builds a hierarchy of nested regions by greedily minimizing GLM error (provably a special case of Ward's clustering). Maximum-statistic (Westfall-Young) permutation controls family-wise error over all regions. Significance spreads to an effect's nested fragments and the regions containing it; a final pruning step seeks whole, pure effect extents.
  We plant synthetic effects of known extent and varying strength in Human Connectome Project (HCP) diffusion images and in white noise. Pruning delivers wholeness: GLOW returns a spatially consistent effect as one region on 57% of HCP trials, the best baseline on 35%; baselines recover comparable volume, but in many pure pieces. The cost is positive predictive value (PPV): GLOW is more sensitive (by up to 0.29), but its regions overrun the effect, mostly because no hierarchy region isolates it, not because of pruning. On HCP, GLOW's mean Dice gains 0.059 over the best baseline at weaker effects and gives back 0.005 at stronger ones.
  On white noise, GLOW trails by up to 0.61 Dice: its hierarchy holds the effect, but its permutation test does not certify it. Runtime grows roughly linearly with voxel count, about 4.5 times the voxel-wise methods' on the full HCP volume. The PPV loss may trace to the assumption of spatially independent residuals.
papers.summary: Neuroimaging analyses that fit a General Linear Model (GLM) either per atlas region or per voxel can split or dilute effects that do not line up with those units. `GLOW` instead builds a hierarchy of nested regions by greedily minimizing GLM error, which is provably a special case of Ward's clustering. It controls family-wise error with Westfall-Young permutation and prunes the result toward whole effect extents. On synthetic effects planted in Human Connectome Project diffusion images, it **returns the effect as a single region in 57% of trials, versus 35% for the best baseline**, and is more sensitive, but its regions overrun the effect, which lowers positive predictive value. On white noise it trails the baselines considerably.

papers.title: Coopshift: Post-Training Amplifies The Memory Curse In LLM Cooperation
papers.abstract: How does post-training change cooperation during repeated interaction? Within each of seven released model lineages, we compare pretrained (Base), supervised fine-tuned (SFT), and subsequent preference- or reward-optimized (Aligned) checkpoints across seven social dilemmas. Copies of each checkpoint play one another for 200 rounds, with visible history limited to the last two or forty rounds. The memory curse refers to lower cooperation when agents can see more past rounds. Our central finding is that post-training amplifies this decline. Averaged across the six binary-action games, expanding visible history reduces cooperation at every SFT and Aligned checkpoint. At each post-trained stage, these declines exceed Base's in six of seven lineages. Most of this average amplification is already present at SFT. With long history, both post-trained stages also cooperate less than Base on average in each binary-action game. In the symmetric binary games, their fitted cooperation rates fall more steeply on average than Base's as per-round cooperation costs rise, benefits fall, or noncooperation becomes more rewarding. The difference in cooperation rates between Aligned and SFT also changes from one-shot decisions to repeated play. When given the same past records, their choices depend on whether the instructions describe a final round or possible future interaction. Post-training evaluation should therefore go beyond isolated choices to assess whether cooperation is sustained in repeated interaction and how it depends on payoffs and visible history.
papers.summary: The "memory curse" is the drop in LLM cooperation when agents can see more past rounds of a repeated game. The study compares pretrained, supervised fine-tuned (SFT), and preference- or reward-aligned checkpoints from seven model lineages across seven social dilemmas played for 200 rounds, with visible history limited to the last 2 or 40 rounds. **Post-training amplifies the memory curse**: longer history lowers cooperation at every SFT and aligned checkpoint, more than for the base model in six of seven lineages, and most of this effect is already present after SFT. Post-trained models also respond more sharply to costs and payoffs, so the authors argue that cooperation should be evaluated in repeated play rather than in one-shot choices.

papers.title: OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners
papers.abstract: Can large language model (LLM) agents deliver expert-level operations research (OR) solutions directly from original client materials, without prior expert reformulation? Existing OR benchmarks typically begin with self-contained descriptions or predefined optimization tasks, underrepresenting the translation of original business materials into professionally validated solutions. We introduce OR-License, an end-to-end benchmark of 31 instances across 10 industrial scenarios from paid OR engagements totaling USD 3.68 million. It preserves original requirements, input data, deliverable formats, and information boundaries after de-identification. To study information acquisition, we introduce ORSim, a controlled client simulator that discloses business facts without supplying OR expertise. Hidden evaluation checks feasibility and compares objective quality against original expert solutions accepted by clients before benchmark construction. Deployment-Adjusted Quality (DAQ) averages expert-relative quality across instances, assigning zero to infeasible deliveries. Across 11 frontier LLMs using coding-agent harnesses, several exceed the expert reference in conditional objective quality, but none matches its DAQ; the strongest primary Claude Code configuration achieves 88.39% strict feasibility and a DAQ of 0.87 against the expert reference of 1. Client information acquisition extends beyond clarification into solution development and validation, with some later stages showing higher confirmed issue-resolution proportions.
