Trajectory analysis identifies formulation and implementation failures, while task-equalized research-chain completion rates range from 24% to 45% across models on evaluable tasks. These findings motivate sustained information-gap resolution, faithful problem formulation, and evidence-linked self-improvement for reliable long-horizon agents.
papers.summary: Operations research (OR) benchmarks usually start from clean, pre-formulated optimization problems. `OR-License` instead tests whether large language model (LLM) agents can go from raw client materials to a validated solution. It has 31 instances across 10 industrial scenarios, taken from paid engagements worth USD 3.68 million, and includes `ORSim`, a client simulator that reveals business facts but no OR expertise. Solutions are scored with Deployment-Adjusted Quality (DAQ), which compares objective quality against accepted expert solutions and gives zero to infeasible deliveries. Across 11 frontier LLMs running in coding-agent harnesses, some beat the expert on conditional objective quality, but none matched the expert overall: the best `Claude Code` configuration reached 88.39% strict feasibility and **a DAQ of 0.87 against the expert's 1.0**, with most failures coming from problem formulation and implementation.
papers.highlight_summary:
Existing operations research (OR) benchmarks usually hand LLMs a clean problem statement, so they skip the hard part of real consulting: turning messy client materials into a validated, deployable solution. `OR-License` tests that end-to-end process using 31 de-identified instances across 10 industries, taken from paid OR engagements worth **$3.68M** in total project value, and scores agents against the expert solutions the clients actually accepted.

- Agents get the original business brief and input files, and they can query `ORSim` throughout the task; `ORSim` is a client simulator where an LLM selects facts from a closed, expert-annotated catalog, and a deterministic controller enforces disclosure rules, so it supplies business facts but never OR expertise.
- Hidden verifiers check feasibility, and the headline metric, Deployment-Adjusted Quality (`DAQ`), averages expert-relative objective quality across instances while giving zero credit to infeasible deliveries, so the expert reference scores exactly 1.
- Across 11 frontier models running in the `Claude Code` harness, several beat the expert on the instances they solved feasibly (conditional quality up to **101%**), but none reaches the expert's `DAQ`; the best, `Grok 4.6`, hits **88.39% feasibility** and **86.55% DAQ**, and about **86%** of its gap to the expert comes from infeasible deliveries rather than weaker objective values.
- Trajectory analysis shows agents ask **86.7–98.3%** of their client questions before writing any solver code, even though later questions resolved issues more often (about **71%** for `Hy4 Preview` at the self-check stage, versus **10.6–37.0%** for early questions).
- Agents completed a full cycle of hypothesis, experiment and evidence-based revision in only **24–45%** of research opportunities, and most errors came from formulating the wrong problem (constraints, state transitions, objectives) rather than from implementation bugs, although the trajectory annotations are manual and the benchmark is small at 31 instances.

papers.title: Persistent Memory and Iterative Improvement in an LLM Agent for Chinese-Character Drawing
papers.abstract: Does persistent memory accumulated from previous attempts help an LLM agent solve new problems, and does memory design affect that benefit? We study programmatic Chinese-character drawing across five agent conditions attempting the same 668 items. Accumulated memory produces modest aggregate gains despite substantial growth in the memory stores: free-form notes improve first-attempt success by 4.6 percentage points, while a design combining free-form memory with reusable code improves it by 2.8 points. The two designs do not differ significantly overall, but the code bank shows a suggestive advantage on later, harder items. A separate post-hoc comparison finds a much larger improvement when the code-bank agent receives privileged, target-specific structural supervision. The agent can therefore exploit highly informative structural guidance, although the privileged per-item information does not establish what could have been learned from experience alone. These results suggest that memory design may affect where accumulated experience becomes useful, even when its average benefit is modest.
papers.summary: The question here is whether an LLM agent gets better at new problems when it keeps a persistent memory of earlier attempts, and whether the memory's design matters. Five agent conditions attempted the same 668 programmatic Chinese-character drawing tasks. Despite large growth in the memory stores, gains were modest: free-form notes raised first-attempt success by **4.6 percentage points**, and free-form memory plus a reusable code bank raised it by 2.8 points. The two designs did not differ significantly overall, though the code bank showed a suggestive edge on later, harder items. Giving the agent privileged, per-item structural supervision produced much larger gains.

papers.title: Does AI-Assisted Development Homogenize Software? An Empirical Study of Code Similarity, Quality, and Evolution
papers.abstract: AI-assisted software development is evolving from interactive LLM assistance toward agentic systems that autonomously perform software engineering tasks, yet the effects of this shift remain insufficiently understood. We present an empirical study of 50 long-lived Java and Python open-source projects across three eras: pre-LLM, potentially LLM-assisted, and detected agentic development. Using snapshots from Software Heritage, we examine code similarity, software quality, and software evolution. Similarity is measured semantically through embedding-based cosine similarity and syntactically through CodeBLEU*. Quality is assessed with SonarQube metrics covering maintainability, complexity, reliability, and security. Evolution is characterized by annualized growth rates of LOC, functions, classes, files, and statements, and by commit activity in the three months preceding each snapshot. Results show no consistent evidence of increased similarity as semantic and syntactic similarity decreased significantly in Java for both the LLM and agentic eras relative to the pre-LLM era, while Python showed no significant differences. Software quality remained largely stable, although the agentic era showed significantly lower code-smell and SQALE index densities. Structural growth was generally lower in the agentic era, particularly for files, whereas development activity increased moderately in Java, especially in commits and added lines. These findings challenge the assumption that LLM- and agent-assisted development necessarily homogenizes code, degrades quality, or accelerates growth.
papers.summary: The study asks whether AI-assisted and agentic development is making open-source code more uniform, worse in quality, or faster-growing. It examines 50 long-lived Java and Python projects across pre-LLM, potentially LLM-assisted, and detected agentic eras, using `Software Heritage` snapshots. Similarity is measured with embedding cosine similarity and `CodeBLEU*`, and quality with `SonarQube` metrics. **No consistent evidence of homogenization was found**: similarity actually fell significantly in Java and was unchanged in Python. Quality stayed largely stable, with lower code-smell and `SQALE` index densities in the agentic era, and structural growth was generally lower in that era even as Java commit activity rose.

papers.title: Cache2LoRA: Understanding and Improving Context Internalization
papers.abstract: Context-to-LoRA methods encode documents as low-rank parameter updates, allowing language models to answer without retaining the source text in their decoding context. How reliably do these updates preserve facts and support their use under different instructions? Controlled diagnosis of existing context-to-LoRA methods separates fact discrimination, target retention, and response adaptation. Competing sources influence answers, while target-only construction and memory-state optimization improve recovery at fixed update size. Recovering facts also does not ensure that answers follow response instructions. We introduce Cache2LoRA, which uses each query to aggregate evidence from a reusable frozen document cache before generating LoRA updates. Trainable encoding operates only on the query and memory-token suffix, and multi-style supervision teaches both evidence preservation and answer expression. Across 17 tasks, Cache2LoRA improves on existing context-to-LoRA methods and achieves macro F1 of 0.663, approaching full-context in-context learning at 0.671. For 32K documents and 256-token outputs at batch size 16, its decoding throughput is 5.9$\times$ that of full-context ICL. At matched memory size, generated LoRA preserves answer accuracy more reliably than the learned-KV variant under long, diverse intervening text and combines more effectively with retained document KV, yielding higher hybrid F1 and EM.
papers.summary: Context-to-LoRA methods compress a document into low-rank (LoRA) weight updates so a model can answer questions without keeping the source text in its context. A controlled diagnosis of existing methods shows that competing sources distort answers and that recovering a fact does not mean the answer follows response instructions. The proposed `Cache2LoRA` uses each query to gather evidence from a reusable frozen document cache before generating the LoRA update, and it is trained with multi-style supervision. Across 17 tasks it reaches a macro F1 of 0.663, close to full-context in-context learning (ICL) at 0.671, while delivering **5.9× the decoding throughput of full-context ICL** for 32K-token documents.

papers.title: Joint, Decoupled, or Agent: When Each Multimodal Alignment Paradigm Wins
papers.abstract: Jointly pretrained multimodal encoders are a common way to combine modalities, while alternatives integrate their information during downstream training or inference. When does each approach win? We compare three paradigms, instantiated with public checkpoints, across 16 paired datasets in five domains and multiple training-label budgets. JOINT trains a fusion head on frozen, jointly pretrained encoders. DECOUPLED trains a fusion head on frozen, independently pretrained encoders. AGENT gives a frozen LLM task instructions, labelled examples, available sample text, and supervised unimodal readouts. No paradigm dominates the complete 144 dataset-budget combinations: DECOUPLED wins 54, JOINT 44, and AGENT 46 by mean utility. ScienceQA, MELD, and MetMeme shift from AGENT to fusion as supervision increases. Between the fusion paradigms, JOINT leads on four of five QA datasets across all evaluated budgets, while higher unimodal 5-NN accuracy is associated with a relative shift toward DECOUPLED across eight classification datasets (Spearman $\rho=-0.67$). We test whether representation and task diagnostics predict these preferences on held-out datasets before fitting their candidate systems. A two-step cascade combines these diagnostics with task and budget metadata to select AGENT or fusion, then JOINT or DECOUPLED. Under leave-one-group-out evaluation, it selects the winner in 71.4% of cells versus 54.2% for metadata-only routing, with mean relative regret 0.028 versus 0.057. Using geometry, supervised representation diagnostics, and text-label matching together yields higher accuracy and lower regret than using any one of these sources with metadata. These results connect paradigm preferences to supervision budget, task format, and unimodal 5-NN accuracy. Target-task diagnostics thus support selecting among the three paradigms before candidate fitting.
papers.summary: Three ways of combining modalities are compared across 16 paired datasets in five domains and several label budgets: `JOINT` (a fusion head on jointly pretrained encoders), `DECOUPLED` (a fusion head on independently pretrained encoders), and `AGENT` (a frozen LLM given instructions, examples, and unimodal readouts). No paradigm dominates; across 144 dataset-budget combinations, `DECOUPLED` wins 54, `JOINT` 44, and `AGENT` 46, with some datasets shifting from `AGENT` to fusion as supervision grows. A two-step cascade uses representation and task diagnostics to pick the paradigm before any candidate system is fitted, and it **selects the winner in 71.4% of cases versus 54.2% for metadata-only routing**.

papers.title: BLANC: Adaptive Temporal Scheduling for Sign Language Production
papers.abstract: Sign language production (SLP) aims to synthesize expressive signing motion from written text. Modeling signing motion presents two key temporal challenges. First, fine-grained hand articulations demand higher temporal resolution than relatively slower body movements. Second, signing events unfold over variable durations, calling for adaptive temporal scheduling during generation. To address these challenges, we first introduce a Multi-Rate Vector Quantizer (MRVQ), an articulation-decoupled motion tokenizer that represents the body and both hands as separate discrete streams at distinct temporal resolutions. Building on this representation, we propose BLANC (BLock-wise Adaptive diffusioN with Articulatory Clock), a gloss-free SLP framework that generates variable-duration motion blocks causally while denoising tokens in parallel within each block. At its core, a Latent Articulatory Clock (LAC) learns temporal structure from multi-scale motion-derived partitions to predict block durations and sequence termination during generation. We further introduce inference-time body-conditioned hand refinement to improve coordination across articulators. Extensive experiments on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily demonstrate that BLANC achieves state-of-the-art performance in sign language production.
papers.summary: Sign language production (SLP) generates signing motion from text. It has to handle hand movements that are faster than body movements, and signing events whose durations vary. The authors introduce a Multi-Rate Vector Quantizer (`MRVQ`) that tokenizes the body and each hand as separate streams at different temporal resolutions. On top of it they build `BLANC`, a gloss-free framework that generates variable-length motion blocks causally while denoising tokens in parallel within each block. A Latent Articulatory Clock predicts block durations and when to stop, and an inference-time refinement step conditions the hands on the body. **`BLANC` reports state-of-the-art results** on `PHOENIX-2014T` and `CSL-Daily`.

papers.title: Interpretability of AI weather models via intermediate decoding
papers.abstract: AI weather prediction models are often regarded as black boxes. Despite their impressive skill, there is little understanding of how the input data is processed during inference to produce the forecast. This limitation arises from the use of high-dimensional latent representations in which individual dimensions are no longer directly interpretable in physical terms. To gain insight into how forecasts are constructed, we propose the method of intermediate decoding for AI weather models and apply it to GraphCast, Aurora and ArchesWeather. In this approach, latent states from intermediate depths are decoded back into meteorological fields. To do this, we use the decoder that has been trained to output the forecast at the end of processing. Since latent states at different depths do not share a consistent basis, we train affine transformations that align intermediate latent states with the decoder's expected input space. Applying this framework to the three models yields the following results. First, the skill of forecasts at intermediate stages of processing improves gradually through the processor layers. Second, bypassing all processor blocks shows that the encoder-decoder pair is not an identity mapping returning the input, but instead plays a significant role in the forecast construction. Third, by examining increments of individual processor blocks across model depth, we show that all three models progressively refine the forecast from coarse to finer spatial scales. Finally, we assess the physical consistency of the intermediate decoding forecasts and find that large scales remain physically balanced throughout processing, while small scales become more balanced with each additional processor block.
papers.summary: To look inside AI weather prediction models, the authors propose intermediate decoding: latent states from intermediate layers are passed through the model's own final decoder, using learned affine maps to align them with the decoder's expected input. Applied to `GraphCast`, `Aurora`, and `ArchesWeather`, the method shows forecast skill improving gradually through the processor layers. It also shows that the encoder-decoder pair is not an identity mapping and does real work in building the forecast. In all three models, **forecasts are refined progressively from coarse to fine spatial scales**, and large scales stay physically balanced throughout while small scales become more balanced with depth.

papers.title: Looped GNNs Beyond Fixed Depth: Graph Size Generalization and Parameter-Efficient Adaptation
papers.abstract: Generalizing from small graphs to larger ones can require computation beyond the depth of a neural model used during training. We study target tasks that admit a common local iterative computation and whose effective dependency radius grows with graph size. The central idea is to learn a local update rule through GNN pretraining, then repeatedly apply the same learned processor beyond the training depth to extend information reach on larger graphs without retraining. Calling such parameter-shared architecture a \emph{looped GNN}, we categorize six schemes for looped GNNs to separate the effects of depth extension, fine-tuning, and freeze-and-steer adaptation. Our analysis establishes fixed-depth information limits and sufficient conditions under which accurate iterative reuse overcomes them. To improve beyond unadapted reuse, we introduce \emph{Loop-Freeze-Steer} (LFS), which freezes the pretrained processor and learns a small controller to steer its repeated application, using much fewer trainable parameters than full fine-tuning. Our finite-sample analysis gives sufficient conditions for adaptation to improve performance on larger graphs. Experiments on synthetic tasks and chip placement evaluate depth extension and adaptation, highlighting LFS's accuracy--trainable-parameter trade-off for size generalization.
papers.summary: Some graph tasks need more message-passing steps on larger graphs than were used in training. This work studies looped graph neural networks (GNNs), which learn a local update rule and apply it repeatedly beyond the training depth. It sorts looped GNNs into six schemes and proves fixed-depth information limits, along with conditions under which iterative reuse overcomes them. It also introduces `Loop-Freeze-Steer` (`LFS`), which freezes the pretrained processor and trains a small controller to steer its repeated application. Experiments on synthetic tasks and chip placement show that **`LFS` trades off accuracy against far fewer trainable parameters than full fine-tuning** for size generalization.

papers.title: Graph-Regularized Synthetic Control for Stable Counterfactual Estimation under Donor Redundancy
papers.abstract: Synthetic control methods estimate counterfactual outcomes by weighting untreated donor units to match a treated unit before treatment. In recent applications, however, the donor pool can be large, highly correlated, and short in pre-treatment history, yielding many near-equivalent solutions with unstable and difficult-to-interpret donor weights. We propose Graph-Regularized Synthetic Control (Graph-SC), a convex estimator that augments the classical pre-treatment matching objective with a graph Laplacian penalty. The graph encodes similarity among donor trajectories, encouraging coherent weights over structurally related donors while preserving the transparency of synthetic controls. We provide theoretical results characterizing the bias-variance tradeoff induced by graph regularization and establish efficient convergence guarantees with an accelerated proximal gradient method. Across a controlled simulation under donor redundancy, the California Proposition 99 benchmark, and observational counterfactual analyses on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, Graph-SC improves weight stability, reduces sensitivity to redundant donor pools, and maintains competitive pre- and post-treatment accuracy relative to classical and regularized synthetic control baselines. Our results suggest that graph regularization is most valuable not as a universal accuracy booster, but as a principled mechanism for selecting stable and interpretable counterfactuals from near-equivalent synthetic controls with comparable pre-treatment fit.
papers.summary: Synthetic control estimates counterfactual outcomes by weighting untreated donor units, but large, highly correlated donor pools with short pre-treatment histories produce unstable, hard-to-interpret weights. `Graph-SC` adds a graph Laplacian penalty over donor-trajectory similarity to the classical convex matching objective, which encourages related donors to receive coherent weights. The authors characterize the resulting bias-variance tradeoff and give convergence guarantees for an accelerated proximal gradient solver. On simulations, the `California Proposition 99` benchmark, and the `Waymo Open Motion Dataset`, **`Graph-SC` improves weight stability while keeping accuracy competitive**, which the authors frame as a way to choose among near-equivalent fits rather than as an accuracy booster.

papers.title: Do LMs Know What Variables Do? Interpreting Code Representations via Variable Roles
papers.abstract: Variable roles describe recurring behaviors such as accumulation, traversal, and retaining the best candidate encountered. We use Sajaniemi's independently defined taxonomy to study which role distinctions can be recovered from large language models, how sparse autoencoders (SAEs) retain those distinctions, and whether associated directions support control of generation. We introduce static annotation rules for all eleven roles and a corpus of 126,926 natural-code files across five languages. Across five model-SAE systems, residual probes outperform individual SAE features and tested lexical baselines, with modest losses after neutral target renaming. Combining SAE features closes much of the single-feature gap, but probes on SAE reconstructions are less sensitive to role-changing edits reviewed by LLMs. High paired ranking accuracy coexists with frequent false positives at fixed thresholds. During generation, interventions often change role annotations at the cost of correctness; changes accompanied by passing tests show no clear aggregate advantage over random controls. The benchmark separates role-related recoverability, SAE fidelity, and correctness-preserving control through matched prediction, source edits, and generation interventions.
papers.summary: Using Sajaniemi's taxonomy of eleven variable roles (such as accumulator or most-wanted holder), the authors test whether language models internally represent what variables do. They build a corpus of 126,926 code files in five languages with static role annotations and probe five model and sparse autoencoder (SAE) systems. **Probes on the residual stream beat individual SAE features and lexical baselines**, and combining SAE features closes much of that gap. However, probes on SAE reconstructions are less sensitive to role-changing edits, and high ranking accuracy coexists with frequent false positives. Steering generation along role directions often changes role annotations but breaks correctness, with no clear advantage over random controls when tests pass.

papers.title: Prefix-Tuning for Arbitrary Output Sequences on Pretrained Transformers
papers.abstract: Prefix-tuning is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large language models (LLMs) that steers model outputs by prepending task-specific prefix representations to the input sequence. Despite its practical success, the theoretical understanding of the expressiveness of prefixes remains incomplete. In particular, the following question remains open: Given a pretrained autoregressive Transformer, for any input-output sequence pair $(\mathtt{x},\mathtt{y})$, does there always exist a prefix $\mathcal{S}$ such that prepending $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathtt{x}$ induces the model to generate the target output $\mathtt{y}$? In this work, we prove that under the assumption that $\mathtt{y}$ is in the range of the pretrained Transformer, such a prefix $\mathcal{S}$ exists and can be explicitly computed by solving multiple linear systems. We further show that this assumption is necessary, in the sense that such a prefix may not exist when the assumption fails, thereby providing a complete answer to the above question. Our analysis is constructive and the obtained theoretical results hold under fairly general assumptions on model architecture. Extensive experiments on GPT-2 and Qwen3-4B demonstrate that our algorithm produces prefixes with strong control over model outputs.
papers.summary: Prefix-tuning steers a frozen language model by prepending learned prefix representations, but how much it can express has not been fully understood. The authors prove that for a pretrained autoregressive Transformer, **a prefix producing any target output exists whenever that output lies in the model's range**. Such a prefix can be computed explicitly by solving multiple linear systems. They also show that the range condition is necessary, so the answer is complete, and that the result holds under fairly general architectural assumptions. Experiments on `GPT-2` and `Qwen3-4B` show the constructed prefixes give strong control over model outputs.

papers.title: On the Selectivity of Generative Models in Structure-Based Drug Design
papers.abstract: Designing small-molecule drugs that selectively bind to a target protein while avoiding unintended interactions with other proteins is essential for reducing side effects that contribute substantially to clinical attrition. Although structure-based drug design (SBDD) has advanced rapidly with deep learning, most generative models still optimize binding to a single target and disregard selectivity due to limited training data and unknown off-target interactions. Motivated by this gap, we introduce SELECTBENCH, a comprehensive benchmark assessing the selectivity of generative SBDD models. SELECTBENCH provides three curated evaluation tasks reflecting different real-world drug discovery scenarios: literature-based case studies, safety screening panels used in pharmaceutical development, and large-scale structure-based evaluation sets. We further introduce a suite of metrics to quantify selectivity and conduct a systematic evaluation of nine representative SBDD models, including methods explicitly trained for selectivity and widely-used inference-time guidance techniques. Our results show that even selectivity-trained models achieve only modest off-target discrimination and inference-time guidance provides limited gains, underscoring the need for method improvement. SELECTBENCH provides both a characterization of where current generative SBDD stands on selectivity and an open, extensible platform to accelerate progress. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/lovetaro/selectbench.
papers.summary: Generative models for structure-based drug design (SBDD) usually optimize binding to a single target and ignore selectivity, meaning avoidance of off-target proteins that cause side effects. `SELECTBENCH` provides three evaluation tasks (literature case studies, pharmaceutical safety screening panels, and large structure-based sets) along with metrics for quantifying selectivity. A systematic evaluation of nine SBDD models finds that **even models explicitly trained for selectivity achieve only modest off-target discrimination**, and that inference-time guidance adds little.

papers.title: Data-Driven Resource Aggregation for Scalable Digital Twin and Simulation Model Generation
papers.abstract: As industrial digitization accelerates, the use of digital twins has become widespread. However, modern manufacturing systems are highly dynamic and frequently reconfigured, making manual model development and updates increasingly difficult. Recent research on automated simulation model generation shows that historical data such as event logs can yield simulation models automatically. However, modeling every resource at full granularity leads to unnecessary complexity and computational cost. We propose a method for automatically selecting and aggregating resources to simplify simulation modeling. Our method uses ideas from inverse reinforcement learning to learn behavioral value representations of resources from production event logs. This process identifies and aggregates resources with similar functional contributions. Experiments on manufacturing systems, using throughput and system time as performance measures, demonstrate that value-based resource aggregation performs well when the goal is to substantially reduce complexity while preserving performance accuracy.
papers.summary: Automatically generating simulation models and digital twins from manufacturing event logs can produce overly complex models when every resource is modeled in full detail. The proposed method borrows ideas from inverse reinforcement learning to learn behavioral value representations of resources from production logs. It then aggregates resources that make similar functional contributions. In experiments on manufacturing systems, **value-based aggregation substantially reduces model complexity while preserving throughput and system-time accuracy**.

papers.title: Recording-Aware Evaluation of Multimodal OT Intrusion Detection
papers.abstract: Machine-learning-based intrusion detection systems (IDSs) for operational technology (OT) are commonly evaluated on benchmark datasets in which normal and attack data are collected in separate recordings. In such settings, high performance may reflect recording-associated differences as well as attack behavior. We introduce a recording-aware evaluation procedure that compares attack windows with background from the same recording, uses prior data for model fitting and calibration, tests temporal alignment against randomized event schedules, and reports event coverage together with alarm burden. On the ProvICS multimodal dataset, cyber modalities strongly distinguish the benign and attack recordings before the first labeled attack. Same-recording evaluation reverses the apparent modality ranking across all studied window sizes: the physical view becomes the strongest individual modality, while cyber-only fusion shows the largest difference between cross-recording and same-recording AUC, reaching 0.54. Operational analysis further shows that permissive event-overlap metrics can overstate detection when a small number of long alarm episodes cover multiple actions. An external analysis on HAI shows smaller and reference-dependent recording sensitivity. These findings show that cross-recording benchmark performance should be interpreted alongside same-recording, forward, temporal, and operational evaluations.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for machine-learning intrusion detection systems (IDSs) in operational technology (OT) often record normal and attack traffic separately, so high scores may reflect differences between recordings rather than detection of attack behavior. The authors propose a recording-aware evaluation that compares attack windows against background from the same recording and checks temporal alignment against randomized event schedules. It also reports event coverage alongside alarm burden. On the `ProvICS` multimodal dataset, **same-recording evaluation reverses the apparent modality ranking**: the physical view becomes the strongest modality, and cyber-only fusion shows an AUC gap of up to 0.54 between cross-recording and same-recording evaluation. A smaller, reference-dependent effect appears on `HAI`.

papers.title: Reducing double-dipping in single-cell topic models with three-way count splitting
papers.abstract: Topic models learn gene programs from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data, and the same counts are then used to test which genes and donors are associated with those programs. Count splitting is the standard remedy for this reuse, but it has not been tested when an encoder reads each cell's counts. On a 104,400-cell lupus cohort with 300 permuted null genes per run, naive tests rejected 36% of null gene-topic pairs at a nominal 5% level, and the usual two-way split rejected 38%, because the encoder sees the tested gene's own held-out count. Encoding topic usage on a separate third of the counts, with beta-binomial thinning, lowered this to 7.7% (6.7% for genes outside the model); for two other models, LDVAE and scETM, the rate was 7.0-7.3% (naive 51-59%). A label-free interferon program shifts in held-out counts in the lupus cohort and in a pre-specified COVID-19 cohort, and donor-level topic usage predicts disease (AUROC 0.96) beyond cell-type proportions (0.86 and 0.58 in the two cohorts). Calibration and prediction did not depend on the model. We do not claim better clustering, prediction or topic stability. Code, figures and result tables are public (MIT license; DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23307193).
papers.summary: Topic models for single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data find gene programs, and the same counts are then reused to test gene and donor associations. Standard two-way count splitting fails when an encoder reads each cell's counts, because the encoder sees the tested gene's held-out count. On a 104,400-cell lupus cohort, naive tests rejected 36% of null gene-topic pairs at a nominal 5% level, and two-way splitting rejected 38%. A three-way split with beta-binomial thinning brought this down to **7.7%**, with similar calibration for `LDVAE` and `scETM`. Donor-level topic usage also predicted disease with an AUROC of 0.96.

papers.title: The Weight of Teamwork: Does Communication Structure Help LLM Scientists Search for Scientific Laws?
papers.abstract: Team performance is often reported as one delivered score, even though that score is produced in two stages: a system generates candidate answers and a selection rule returns one of them. We use symbolic regression as an observable scientific-search setting and compare fixed-budget LLM teams that differ in peer visibility and update timing, evaluating both their frozen candidate archives and the expressions selected from those archives. Distributing the call budget across more independent trajectories produced the largest measured gain, improving mean held-out fitting score Q by 0.70 at the widest tested allocation. Under a common archive-wide selector, the implemented Ring policy reduced mean Q by 0.33 relative to Independent, while Star and Complete remained unresolved. Holding the generated archives fixed, changing the delivery rule changed the measured architecture gaps, including the sign of the Complete point estimate. These results support reporting candidate generation and final selection as separate endpoints. They do not identify a communication mechanism or a universally preferred topology; rather, they show that an architecture ranking is not identified by communication structure alone when the rule that returns the final answer is left unspecified.
papers.summary: Using symbolic regression as an observable setting for scientific search, the authors compare fixed-budget teams of LLM agents that differ in how much they see of each other's work and when they update. They separate how candidates are generated from how a final answer is selected. **Spreading the call budget across more independent trajectories gave the largest gain**, improving mean held-out fit by 0.70. A `Ring` communication topology reduced fit relative to independent agents, and results for `Star` and `Complete` topologies were inconclusive. Changing only the final selection rule, with the candidate archives held fixed, changed the measured gaps between team architectures and even flipped a sign. Topology rankings are therefore not identifiable unless the selection rule is specified.

papers.title: A Conditional No-Hair Theorem for Transformers: How Language Models Forget Their Prompt
papers.abstract: We ask how much an autoregressive transformer retains of its prompt after generating $t$ tokens. Consider two different prompts followed by the same continuation text, so that any difference in their hidden states comes from the prompt alone, and we find that the distance between their hidden states decays approximately as a power law $t^{-\alpha}$, where $\alpha=1$ is the rate at which a fixed prompt's share of uniform attention shrinks and smaller values mean longer memory. Trained models forget fast ($\alpha\approx0.55$--$0.7$), untrained ones slowly ($\alpha\approx0.2$--$0.5$). We prove that this offset is $O\big(P(\log t)^{L-1}/t\big)$ for a prompt of length $P$ and depth $L$. The bound holds for finite-depth pre-LN softmax transformers with bounded attention logits, under one additional condition: the pre-norm activations stay away from zero. The mechanism is geometric: the prompt's direct influence is diluted as the context grows, and \emph{relay} --- continuation tokens passing on what earlier tokens read from the prompt --- can only add logarithmic factors. This is what we call the \emph{conditional no-hair theorem}: given the text generated so far, the prompt's influence on the next token vanishes as $t$ grows, so any property of the prompt that survives, such as its language, must be carried by the text itself. An exactly solvable linear relay model shows that the bound cannot be improved and reproduces the rise of the local exponent towards $1$ seen in untrained networks. Cancelling the dilution with a logit bias stops the decay early in training and reverses it after, so dilution is necessary for the forgetting we measure; untrained networks and the solvable model show it is also sufficient.
papers.summary: The authors measure how much of its prompt an autoregressive transformer retains after generating t tokens. They feed two different prompts followed by the same continuation and track the distance between the resulting hidden states. That distance decays roughly as a power law, faster in trained models (exponent about 0.55 to 0.7) than in untrained ones. They prove a bound of **O(P(log t)^(L-1)/t)** for pre-LN softmax transformers under mild conditions, attributing the decay to the prompt's diluting share of attention, with relay through continuation tokens adding only logarithmic factors. They call this a conditional no-hair theorem: whatever prompt properties persist must be carried by the generated text itself, and cancelling the dilution with a logit bias confirms it is necessary for the observed forgetting.

papers.title: Inside the Loop: A Mechanistic Study of Weight-Tied Transformers on Depth-Bound Algorithmic Tasks
papers.abstract: Solving algorithmic tasks with many sequential steps typically requires scaling up transformer depth or chain-of-thought length, incurring unfavorable parameter and inference-compute costs, respectively. Looped transformers, which reuse one block of layers across many iterations, are poised to address this, since they scale effective depth without adding parameters or tokens. Yet, it remains unclear what each iteration is actually computing, or whether the loop merely simulates a deeper untied stack. Here, we study directed permutation traversal, in which a model follows $H$ hops from a starting node and reports the node it reaches, so every intermediate hop has a known ground truth. We find that a minimum effective depth is necessary to solve the task, beyond which the degree of weight tying becomes the determining factor. For instance, a looped transformer with a four-layer block iterated eight times solves the task in every seed, while an identically-trained untied transformer of the same effective depth never does, succeeding only with a lower learning rate or supervision of its intermediate layers. Probing and intervening on the residual stream, we find that the looped model advances through the intermediate nodes gradually, forming a staircase that adapts to its iteration budget, whereas the untied model, at that lower rate, exposes them only in its final layers. Taken together, our results recast looped transformers as iterative program learners, which allocate their iterations to successive steps of the algorithm and solve tasks that identically-trained untied models of the same effective depth do not. Code is available at https://github.com/magnus-sesodia/insidetheloop.
papers.summary: Looped transformers reuse one block of layers over many iterations to gain effective depth without adding parameters. This mechanistic study asks what each iteration computes, using multi-hop directed permutation traversal, where every intermediate hop has a known answer. Beyond a minimum effective depth, weight tying becomes decisive: **a four-layer block looped eight times solved the task in every seed, while an identically trained untied model of the same depth never did**. Probing shows the looped model advances through intermediate nodes in a staircase that adapts to its iteration budget, whereas the untied model, when trained at a lower learning rate, exposes them only in its final layers.

papers.title: Continual Test-Time Learning with Evolution Strategies
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly operate in open-ended environments, where they are expected to continually adapt to evolving tasks and distributions, often without access to external supervision. Existing continual learning approaches rely on external supervision, such as labeled data, demonstrations, or reward signals, which can be costly or unavailable in practice. Test-time adaptation removes this dependence by learning from self-generated supervision, but existing methods derive that supervision from the single policy being updated, so once the policy drifts, its own learning signal drifts with it, leading to policy collapse, degraded reasoning, and catastrophic forgetting. In this paper, we propose \textbf{Evolution Strategy Reinforcement Learning (ESRL)}, a continual test-time learning framework that draws its self-generated supervision from a population of policies instead of the single policy being trained. ESRL perturbs an anchor policy in parameter space to form a population of nearby policies, samples one trajectory from each, and aggregates their answers into label-free group-relative learning signals for the central student. The anchor is held fixed within each block and refreshed from the student at block boundaries, so the population stays centered on a stable yet current policy and continues to supply diverse and reliable supervision as the student moves. In single-task test-time adaptation across mathematical reasoning, general knowledge, and medical domains, ESRL improves average accuracy by up to 31.7% relative to the base model and 16.6% relative to the strongest test-time adaptation baseline. Notably, ESRL substantially reduces catastrophic forgetting and achieves the strongest final performance in continual learning.
papers.summary: Test-time adaptation lets LLMs learn without labels from self-generated supervision, but when that signal comes from the policy being updated, it drifts with the policy and leads to collapse and forgetting. Evolution Strategy Reinforcement Learning (`ESRL`) instead perturbs a fixed anchor policy in parameter space to form a population, samples one trajectory from each member, and aggregates their answers into label-free group-relative learning signals. The anchor is refreshed from the student at block boundaries. Across math reasoning, general knowledge, and medical domains, `ESRL` improves average accuracy by **up to 31.7% over the base model** and 16.6% over the strongest test-time adaptation baseline, and it substantially reduces catastrophic forgetting in continual learning.

papers.title: From Spectrograms to Shallow Speech SSL: Audio-Frontend Design for Generator-Disjoint and Low-Latency Audio--Visual Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: Video-mediated conversational systems rely on synchronized speech and facial video, making audio--visual input integrity important for reliable perception. We study audio-frontend design in a fixed MRDF (Modality-Regularization-based DeepFake)-based pipeline with AV-HuBERT visual processing and an MSCT (multi-scale cross-modal transformer) fusion encoder. We compare spectrogram-style log-filterbank features with frozen wav2vec~2.0 and WavLM representations, dual-SSL fusion, executed depth, and shallow-layer aggregation. Across three training runs, full wav2vec~2.0 improves mean macro AUROC from $84.19\%$ to $87.19\%$ on generator-disjoint MMDF. Six-layer execution further improves detection, and learned non-uniform aggregation adds $2.53$ percentage points, reaching $90.61\%$. Shallow execution reduces measured inference latency relative to full-depth wav2vec~2.0 across the tested input durations; first-second evaluation reaches $86.85\%$ macro AUROC. In a single-run comparison, dual-SSL concatenation outperforms either single stream, while one-way cross-attention yields lower detection performance and higher latency than concatenation. Layer-weight analysis shows greater emphasis on early speech layers, while removing the selector's visual input has little effect on detection performance.
papers.summary: Within a fixed `MRDF`-based audio-visual deepfake detector with `AV-HuBERT` visual processing and an `MSCT` fusion encoder, the authors compare audio front-ends: log-filterbank spectrograms and frozen `wav2vec 2.0` and `WavLM` self-supervised speech representations. On the generator-disjoint `MMDF` benchmark, full `wav2vec 2.0` raises mean macro AUROC from 84.19% to 87.19%. Running only six layers with learned non-uniform layer aggregation reaches **90.61%** while also cutting inference latency. Learned layer weights emphasize early speech layers, and evaluating only the first second of input still reaches 86.85%.

papers.title: Sequence-to-Sequence Neural Surrogate Modeling of Transient Responses in High-Speed Links with Variable Design Parameters
papers.abstract: This paper presents sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) neural surrogates for high-speed transient response modeling and signal integrity analysis in fixed and variable design parameter spaces. To identify the structural requirements for prediction accuracy, multiple neural architectures were evaluated with respect to different training strategies such as sample-based and unit interval-based, as well as input configurations such as TX-only and TX+RX. For fixed design parameters, feedforward neural networks achieve accuracy comparable to recurrent models while requiring lower computational cost, as the static mapping can be approximated by fully connected and non-sequential representations. Variable design parameters alter the electromagnetic characteristics of the interconnect, which creates parameter-dependent temporal dynamics that require sequence-aware architectures to resolve the evolving interactions within the transient response. The results based on a 14-dimensional variable design parameter scenario show that while autoregressive TX+RX feedback suffers from severe phase drift and error propagation under variable conditions, non-autoregressive TX-only inference leads to stability. To overcome the structural limitations of standard decoders, a recurrent Early Fusion LSTM is proposed, which injects design parameters at the initial encoding stage. This approach achieves superior prediction accuracy, with an RMSE of 31.0 mV and an R2 of 99.51% for transient waveform prediction, an RMSE of 30.7 mV and an R2 of 99.57% for eye-height prediction, and an RMSE of 19.5 ps and an R2 of 99.94% for eye-width prediction. These results demonstrate that neural seq2seq surrogates are accurate for transient response modeling and signal integrity analysis in complex variable design parameter spaces.
papers.summary: Neural sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) surrogates are used to predict transient waveforms and signal-integrity metrics in high-speed interconnects, so that slow electromagnetic simulation is not needed. Across several architectures, simple feedforward networks match recurrent models when design parameters are fixed. Once parameters vary, sequence-aware models become necessary, and autoregressive transmitter-plus-receiver (TX+RX) feedback suffers phase drift while non-autoregressive TX-only inference stays stable. A proposed `Early Fusion LSTM` injects the 14 design parameters at the encoding stage and reaches **an R² of 99.51% (31.0 mV RMSE) on transient waveforms**, with similarly high accuracy for eye-height and eye-width prediction.

papers.title: lepidoptera: A Domain-Agnostic Engine for Causal Simulation with Mixed Variable Types, Vine Copula Dependence, and Individual-Level Counterfactual Propagation
papers.abstract: lepidoptera is an open-source R and Python package for simulation from structural causal models with heterogeneous variable types. The package is built around a typed mechanism architecture, which separates the causal graph from the generating rule at each node and exposes each rule as an inspectable, serialisable object. A pre-built mechanism library covers all nine combinations of continuous, categorical, and ordinal parent and child types, removing the need for users to implement type-specific sampling from scratch. A vine copula mechanism estimates the full joint dependence structure from observed data using pair-copula constructions and the Rosenblatt conditional-simulation algorithm, supporting over twenty copula families. Individual-level counterfactual queries are supported through partial propagation, which freezes the random draws of unaffected nodes and replays only the downstream consequences of an intervention, thereby separating the individual treatment effect (ITE) estimand from the population-level average treatment effect (ATE) without additional model assumptions. An extension layer allows any pre-fitted predictive model to serve as a generative mechanism via a unified callable interface. Three worked illustrations spanning clinical trial planning, emergency-ward capacity analysis, and epidemiological mediation analysis demonstrate the package's scope.
papers.summary: `lepidoptera` is an open-source R and Python package for simulating data from structural causal models that mix continuous, categorical, and ordinal variables. Each node's generating rule is kept separate from the causal graph as an inspectable, serialisable object. A built-in library covers **all nine parent-child type combinations**, and a vine copula mechanism with over twenty copula families learns joint dependence from observed data. Individual-level counterfactuals use partial propagation, which freezes the random draws of unaffected nodes so the individual treatment effect (ITE) can be separated from the average treatment effect (ATE). Worked examples cover clinical trial planning, emergency-ward capacity, and epidemiological mediation analysis.

papers.title: Preservation and loss of algorithmic structure in experimental diffusion of joint-action norms
papers.abstract: Everyday norms of social interaction - e.g. norms of sharing space, taking turns, or queuing - are essential to large societies, offering structured procedures for common interactions. However, it remains unclear how the underlying algorithms of these implicit joint plans evolve as they diffuse through populations. Here we show that this process of diffusion can select against complex algorithms in the earliest stages. We conducted a large-scale study of experimental diffusion of novel social norms among human participants, leveraging advances in program synthesis to characterize the procedures people developed in independent populations. Inherited procedures became structurally simplified and lost during interactions between participants who inherited different variants of joint-action norms; however, opportunities for interactive repair offset this pressure, preserving complex algorithms despite misalignment. These results demonstrate that interactive reasoning mediates selective pressures on structural complexity during cultural evolution of procedural norms.
papers.summary: A large-scale human experiment studies how implicit procedures for joint action, such as turn-taking or sharing space, change as they pass through populations. Program synthesis is used to recover the underlying algorithms that participants developed. When participants who had inherited different variants of a norm interacted, the procedures were **structurally simplified or lost**, but chances for interactive repair offset this pressure and kept complex algorithms alive. The authors conclude that interactive reasoning shapes the selective pressure on complexity during the cultural evolution of procedural norms.

papers.title: Budgeted Bayesian Bandits for Future Utilization
papers.abstract: The multi-armed bandit problem models the trade-off between exploration and exploitation. In this paper, we study the variant where exploration has a hard budget and precedes exploitation. Prior guarantees include a 1/3 approximation by Guha and Munagala using Lagrangian duality, and a 4/27 approximation by Ma against a primal linear programming relaxation for a more general model. We show that the analyses of both algorithms are tight, even when their relaxations are asymptotically exact. We provide a different efficient algorithm that achieves a 0.43 approximation. We then provide an efficient algorithm whose guarantee approaches 1-e^{-1} approx 0.63 for bounded exchangeable reward observations in a non-vanishing regime, which is asymptotically tight against natural linear programming relaxations. The technique also gives certificates for stopping sequential model evaluation.
papers.summary: The setting is a Bayesian multi-armed bandit variant in which exploration has a hard budget and takes place entirely before exploitation. The authors show that existing guarantees, a 1/3 approximation via Lagrangian duality and a 4/27 approximation against a linear programming relaxation, are tight even when the relaxations are asymptotically exact. They give a new efficient algorithm with a 0.43 approximation, and another whose guarantee **approaches 1−1/e ≈ 0.63** for bounded exchangeable rewards, which is asymptotically tight against natural LP relaxations. The technique also yields certificates for deciding when to stop sequential model evaluation.

papers.title: CoDA: A Human-LM Collaborative Codebook Development Assistant for Domain-Specific Text Annotation
papers.abstract: We present CoDA, an open-source human-LM collaborative codebook development assistant that helps domain experts develop annotation guidelines for annotating new variables in unstructured text with language models. Existing language model annotation systems primarily focus on downstream classification performance, while assuming the availability of high-quality annotation guidelines, or codebooks. In practice, developing these codebooks is time-consuming and challenging, particularly for concepts that require expert knowledge. CoDA addresses this gap by collaborating with domain experts to iteratively develop codebooks through targeted review of incorrect language model predictions and incorporating expert feedback into the evolving codebook. We demonstrate CoDA on two real-world case studies: extracting health indicators from homelessness case management notes and classifying sentiment of wildlife trafficking posts on social media. Across both domains, CoDA produces codebooks that achieve downstream classification performance comparable to expert codebooks while reducing codebook development time from several weeks to two hours and requiring 5X fewer manually annotated examples. Applying CoDA to generate annotations at scale, we identified 2,410 case notes that contained health discussions or referrals and 10,196 social media posts expressing negative sentiment that may warrant investigation for potential wildlife trafficking. By accelerating codebook development, CoDA helps practitioners use language models to extract domain-specific insights from unstructured text at scale.
papers.summary: `CoDA` is an open-source assistant that helps domain experts write annotation guidelines (codebooks) for language-model-based labeling of unstructured text. Existing tools assume such guidelines already exist. `CoDA` instead builds them iteratively by surfacing incorrect model predictions for expert review and folding the feedback into the codebook. On homelessness case notes and wildlife-trafficking social media posts, its codebooks match the downstream performance of expert-written ones while **cutting development time from several weeks to two hours** and using 5x fewer manually annotated examples.

papers.title: TorchTPU - A Hybrid Eager/Compiled Architecture for Native PyTorch Execution on TPU
papers.abstract: TorchTPU is an open-source collaboration between Google and Meta that introduces a native and principled PyTorch backend for Google TPUs. It enables seamless out-of-the-box model execution and TPU migration while delivering industry-competitive inference and training performance through eager execution optimizations, torch.compile integration, and native hardware acceleration.
papers.summary: `TorchTPU` is an open-source PyTorch backend for Google TPUs, developed jointly by Google and Meta. It combines optimized eager execution with `torch.compile` integration and native hardware acceleration in a hybrid design. The goal is for existing PyTorch models to **run on TPUs out of the box** with competitive training and inference performance, without porting to another framework.

papers.title: Pronouncing Hard Words: Phoneme Adaptation of a Pretrained Conversational Text to Speech Model
papers.abstract: Voice agents built as cascaded automatic speech recognition (ASR)->large language model (LLM)-> text-to-speech (TTS) pipelines increasingly rely on conversational TTS: streaming, context conditioned models that adapt delivery to dialogue history. Such models are natural and expressive but offer little explicit control over how rare, trust-critical drug names are pronounced, because these entities are too infrequent, and their vocabulary too fast-growing, to be covered by any amount of pre-, mid-, or post-training. We retrofit phoneme controllability onto a pretrained conversational TTS model without any pre/mid-training, using an ARPAbet vocabulary exten-sion, continued phoneme-augmented supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and a training-free inference-time acoustic-biasing step. On a 7,500 clip clinical drug-pronunciation evaluation, our model raises strict Gemini-judged correctness from 54.6% (no phoneme augmentation) to 90.7%, outperforming every conversational and stateless TTS baseline on the automatic metric. Because no training stage sees a drug name, the entire evaluation is out-of-domain, so the gains reflect learned pronunciation rather than memorization. In a blinded, randomized human study, adult listeners judge 84% of our clips correct, versus 82% for the strongest baseline, with overlapping confidence intervals on a stratified subset. Across all 250 matched clips, Gemini agrees with the human majority on 84.8% of binary labels (k{appa}=0.57).
papers.summary: Voice agents built as speech-recognition, LLM, and text-to-speech (TTS) pipelines often use conversational TTS models that give little control over how rare terms such as drug names are pronounced. The authors add phoneme controllability to a pretrained conversational TTS model without further pre-training. They use an `ARPAbet` vocabulary extension, phoneme-augmented supervised fine-tuning, and a training-free acoustic-biasing step at inference time. On a 7,500-clip drug-pronunciation evaluation where no drug names appear in training, Gemini-judged correctness rises **from 54.6% to 90.7%**. In a blinded human study, listeners rated 84% of clips correct, versus 82% for the strongest baseline, with overlapping confidence intervals.

papers.title: Margin Certificates for Voting Classifiers under Mixing Dependence
papers.abstract: Margin bounds explain why weighted votes generalize after training error vanishes, but dependent observations require concentration arguments that keep the dependence model and failure budget explicit. We study stationary mixing streams without treating dependence as a formal substitution of an "effective sample size." For a finite base class, we combine independent-block Rademacher theory for stationary $\beta$-mixing processes with a clipped margin loss to obtain an explicit uniform voting-margin certificate, whose dependence penalty is set by the number of approximately independent blocks and the coupling budget $4(\mu-1)\beta(a)$. A black-box transfer theorem shows that any i.i.d. voting-margin guarantee remains valid on a regularly spaced subsequence, with only an additive $\beta$-mixing failure probability. For votes fixed independently of a stationary finite-state reversible Markov stream, spectral concentration gives the cleaner $\sqrt{t_{rel}/n}$ rate, and a sticky-refresh construction shows this exponent is unavoidable. The constant is statistic-specific: the effective sample size is $n/\tau_{int}(g)$, with $\tau_{int}(g) \le 2t_{rel}-1$. When the dependence scale is unknown, a batch-means Student-t interval is valid up to an explicit remainder vanishing in the number of batches, with width governed by $\tau_{int}(g)$ rather than the worst-case $t_{rel}$. Experiments show: the learned-vote certificate is nonvacuous once the block count is large; a two-timescale construction gives a batch-means interval 8.1x narrower than the worst-case interval at nominal coverage (0.945); block-bootstrap and batch-means intervals undercover under strong dependence while the certificate stays valid; and on real, ordered UCI HAR sensor data the dependence-agnostic certificate reaches 0.95 coverage where naive intervals reach only 0.38.
papers.summary: Margin-based generalization bounds for weighted voting classifiers are extended to dependent data from stationary mixing streams. The analysis tracks dependence explicitly rather than plugging in an "effective sample size." Using independent-block Rademacher theory for β-mixing processes, the authors derive explicit voting-margin certificates, a theorem that transfers any i.i.d. guarantee to regularly spaced subsequences, a provably unavoidable rate for reversible Markov streams, and a batch-means interval governed by the integrated autocorrelation time. Experiments show that block-bootstrap and batch-means intervals undercover under strong dependence while the certificate stays valid. On ordered `UCI HAR` sensor data the dependence-agnostic certificate **reaches 0.95 coverage versus 0.38 for naive intervals**.

papers.title: Model Capacity Frontier: A Development Framework for LLM-Supported Social Simulation
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly incorporated into agent-based models (ABMs) on the premise that richer, context-sensitive human behavior can improve empirical fidelity. However, LLM-supported ABMs introduce an open-ended design space in which subtle modeling and configuration choices, such as prompt design and environment coupling, can substantially alter outcomes. Developing LLM-supported ABMs to simulate human collective behavior therefore requires navigating configuration sensitivity while identifying the limitations of the current model architecture. In this paper, we introduce the \textit{Model Capacity Frontier} (MCF), a framework that characterizes the empirical performance attainable by a specified architecture across its admissible configurations. In multi-objective settings, this capacity is represented by an estimated Pareto frontier obtained through systematic configuration exploration. We demonstrate MCF in crowd simulation of university commencement events with approximately 12,000 agents, using empirical movement data on temporal occupancy, spatial distribution, and flow direction. We first characterize the capacity of a conventional crowd model and then evaluate successive LLM-supported architectural extensions. In the process, MCF reveals which dimensions of attainable performance expand and which remain limited, providing empirical targets for refinement and re-evaluation. Initial LLM integration improves flow direction but degrades temporal occupancy and spatial distribution; subsequent architectural refinement of the LLM layer improves temporal occupancy and recovers spatial performance, while retaining much of the earlier gain in flow direction. Our case study shows how MCF guides the systematic architectural development of LLM-supported ABMs in configuration-sensitive, open-ended design spaces.
papers.summary: Adding LLM agents to agent-based models (ABMs) of human behavior opens a large design space in which prompts and environment coupling can change outcomes substantially. The proposed `Model Capacity Frontier` (`MCF`) framework characterizes the best performance a given architecture can reach across its admissible configurations, estimated as a Pareto frontier from systematic configuration search. In a crowd simulation of about 12,000 agents at a university commencement, compared against real movement data, **initial LLM integration improved flow direction but degraded temporal occupancy and spatial distribution**. Later refinement of the LLM layer recovered those metrics while keeping much of the flow-direction gain.

papers.title: Prosodic Structure as a Critical Component in Phonemic Language Modelling at BabyLM Scale
papers.abstract: Human children learn language from continuous, prosodically structured speech long before they can read, yet almost all language models train on orthographic text. Building on previous phonemic BabyLM training (Goriely et al., 2024; arXiv:2410.22906), we ask whether supplying an estimate of the prosody infants exploit improves phonemic language modelling at BabyLM scale. We compare an orthographic baseline to three conditions forming a ladder of phonological richness. All conditions are trained as BERT MLMs at 10M and 100M words. Addressing the ecological validity of existing metrics in the small-data regime, we build a lexical decision task and two semantic organisation tasks. Our new lexical decision task offers improved insights into the distinction between wordlikeness, token familiarity, and lexicality as factors. Triphone phonotactic control and pseudo-log-likelihood scoring shows that these scores reflect phonotactic familiarity rather than wordhood: every model sits near or below chance on an adversarial inverted condition, revealing prior results of this kind as partly artefactual. On our new semantic tasks, a prosodically annotated phoneme stream gives the strongest taxonomic organisation at both the 10M and 100M word scales. Phonemic models with boundary structure are competitive with the orthographic baseline. These findings suggest that prosodic structure is a key component of phonemic language modelling in the small-data regime most analogous to infant learning.
papers.summary: The question is whether giving phonemic language models prosodic structure, the speech cues infants rely on, improves learning at BabyLM data scales. Orthographic and increasingly phonologically rich conditions are compared using `BERT`-style masked language models trained on 10M and 100M words. The authors also introduce a new lexical decision task and two semantic organisation tasks. With phonotactic controls, they show that existing lexicality scores mostly reflect phonotactic familiarity: every model sits near or below chance on an adversarial inverted condition. On the semantic tasks, **a prosodically annotated phoneme stream gives the strongest taxonomic organisation** at both scales.

papers.title: Self-Improving Video-to-Action Models
papers.abstract: Video generative models are an emerging tool for embodied agents: they can serve as scalable visual planners, generating videos that depict how to complete previously unseen tasks. However, executing these plans typically requires a video-to-action or "inverse dynamics" model trained on large, human-collected video-action datasets, severely limiting scalability. We introduce Mirror, a self-supervised approach that learns video-to-action mappings through environment interactions, without prior action data or hand-crafted rewards. Mirror learns by attempting to follow a visual plan by executing its best guess of the underlying actions in the environment. Mirror then trains on the resulting video-action pairs, incrementally self-improving and following the visual planner more closely. Across Atari, OGBench, and DeepMind Control, Mirror outperforms leading learning-from-observation methods with learned video plans, and achieves near-expert performance with oracle plans. On Minecraft BASALT, it outperforms methods with access to expert actions or hand-engineered task knowledge. In Minecraft survival, it is the first method to acquire an iron pickaxe through self-improvement alone, without rewards or expert action labels. In the offline setting, with expert action labels but no environment interaction, it sets a new state of the art in obtaining diamonds. Our results suggest that advances in video models can translate into increasingly capable agents without a corresponding need for hand-crafted rewards or large collections of expert action data.
papers.summary: Video generative models can act as visual planners for embodied agents, but executing their plans usually requires an inverse-dynamics model trained on large human-labeled video-action datasets. `Mirror` learns this video-to-action mapping through self-supervision, without action labels or rewards: it tries to follow a visual plan, then trains on the video-action pairs it produced, gradually tracking plans more closely. It beats learning-from-observation methods on `Atari`, `OGBench`, and `DeepMind Control`, and on `Minecraft BASALT` it beats methods that have expert actions. In `Minecraft` survival it is **the first method to obtain an iron pickaxe through self-improvement alone**.

papers.title: Multi-author style detection with stylistic embeddings
papers.abstract: We investigate the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) in multi-author style change detection. Using off-the-shelf LLMs or supervised fine-tuning solely within the target domain fails to yield effective features; for this reason, we propose cross-domain transfer learning with LLM-based embeddings fine-tuned for authorship verification. We fine-tune Mistral-7B embedding model and compare it with DeBERTa, used in the state-of-the-art (SOTA) systems in PAN-25 multi-author writing style analysis challenge. Results show that DeBERTa and Mistral excel in different user-generated text scenarios. We exploit this diversity by combining both embeddings, leading to more effective style change detection.
papers.summary: The task is multi-author style change detection: finding where the writer changes within a document. Off-the-shelf LLMs and in-domain fine-tuning both yield weak features. The authors instead fine-tune a `Mistral-7B` embedding model for authorship verification and transfer it across domains, comparing it against the `DeBERTa` models used by top systems in the `PAN-25` challenge. Each model does better on different kinds of user-generated text, and **combining both embeddings gives the most effective detection**.

papers.title: Bootstrap Stochastic Interpolant Tree for Inference-time Search Under Sparse Reward
papers.abstract: Tree-based samplers offer a compelling alternative for scalable inference-time search, bypassing the per-step reward and gradient dependencies that introduce systematic bias into SMC-style frameworks. Despite this advantage, contemporary tree samplers fail to achieve broad exploration. Their reliance on learned, DDPM-like transitions inherently couples neighbor states in a trajectory, thereby restricting child-parent feature divergence in the tree sampler. Consequently, these samplers suffer from restricted coverage of the target marginal distribution, severely hindering the exploration critical for efficient search under sparse reward. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a simple yet effective Bootstrap Stochastic Interpolant Tree (BSIT) sampler that decouples child node generation from explicit parent dependencies. By expanding the degrees of freedom during child node sampling, BSIT encourages diverse trajectory rollouts and unlocks broader path-space diversity-the exact catalyst needed for efficient exploration. Crucially, we show that BSIT's improved exploration accelerates convergence to the target distribution while achieving broader distributional coverage than samplers that rely on DDPM-like transitions for child-node generation, all without incurring additional function evaluations or reward feedback, thereby providing a highly efficient basis for rare target search. Extensive experiments across diverse search settings, including rare-species discovery and target-aligned molecule generation tasks, demonstrate BSIT's superior search efficiency over the baselines.
papers.summary: Tree-based samplers for inference-time search with generative models avoid the per-step reward and gradient bias of sequential Monte Carlo methods. However, their DDPM-style transitions tie child nodes closely to their parents, which limits exploration. The `Bootstrap Stochastic Interpolant Tree` (`BSIT`) sampler generates child nodes without explicit dependence on the parent, widening path-space diversity **with no extra function evaluations or reward queries**. The authors show it converges faster and covers the target distribution more broadly, and that it searches more efficiently on rare-species discovery and target-aligned molecule generation.

papers.title: Reasoning with Context Management and External Memory
papers.abstract: Reasoning models maintain information about the status of their reasoning process through in-context memory. Complex problems require larger context windows and memory requirements. In this scenario, context management without caching risks discarding useful information for reasoning. We propose RCMEM, an approach that extends context management with an external memory to maintain additional information without burdening the reasoning model with additional context. RCMEM significantly reduces computation time on problems that require repeated computation of intermediate steps, while achieving better performance on complex problems. We demonstrate our approach on a few mathematics problems using model sizes ranging from 0.4 to 25 million parameters, and GPT-2.
papers.summary: Reasoning models keep track of their progress in context, and context management that discards content can throw away information needed later. `RCMEM` adds an external memory alongside context management, so intermediate results can be stored and reused without enlarging the model's context. On mathematics problems, using models from 0.4M to 25M parameters as well as `GPT-2`, it **significantly reduces computation time on problems that repeat intermediate steps** while improving performance on complex problems.

papers.title: On Reparameterizing the Score Function
papers.abstract: Policy gradients for autoregressive sequence models differentiate each token's log-probability while holding the conditioning history fixed. This discards information about how earlier decisions shape later conditional distributions, creating a credit-assignment bottleneck when rewards are sparse. We introduce History-Reparameterized (HR) policy gradients, which replace the frozen prefix in the score function with a differentiable reparameterized or relaxed history, allowing gradients of downstream log-probabilities to propagate backward through the generated trajectory. The resulting history-pathwise term is generally biased when added directly, so we derive Optimal HR (OHR), a centered control-variate estimator with a closed-form coefficient that minimizes the trace of the gradient variance at the population level. The variance reduction is governed by temporal structure in the policy dynamics: random or weakly structured policies provide little benefit, while policies with learned sequential dependencies yield informative history-pathwise corrections. For discrete tokens, the choice of relaxation is crucial: embedding-level relaxation yields substantial variance reduction that grows with horizon, whereas straight-through Gumbel-Softmax yields essentially none in our diagnostics. We validate the method on a Gaussian linear Markov model, a sparse-reward T-maze with a recurrent policy, and an autoregressive Transformer model for small Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) instances.
papers.summary: Standard policy gradients for autoregressive models treat each token's conditioning history as fixed. This ignores how earlier choices shape later distributions and makes credit assignment hard under sparse rewards. History-Reparameterized (`HR`) policy gradients pass gradients back through a relaxed, differentiable history. `Optimal HR` (`OHR`) turns that extra term into a centered control variate with a closed-form, variance-minimizing coefficient. The variance reduction depends on learned temporal structure in the policy, and for discrete tokens **embedding-level relaxation gives large, horizon-growing variance reduction while straight-through Gumbel-Softmax gives essentially none**. Experiments cover a linear Gaussian model, a sparse-reward T-maze, and a Transformer solving small Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) instances.

papers.title: Agents' Last Doubt: Knowing When to Act and When to Step Back in Tool-Using Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using LLM agents repeatedly face decision points under uncertainty, choosing between autonomous action, additional information gathering, and human escalation. These decisions require balancing task success against interaction cost and the risk of irreversible errors. Learning to make these trade-offs is challenging because existing interaction trajectories record only the outcomes of actions taken, leaving the consequences of alternative actions unobserved. To address this gap, we construct a counterfactual dataset containing 3,115 action outcomes from 1,036 decision points in ToolSandbox. At each decision point, we execute each legal action and evaluate its downstream outcomes based on task completion, interaction cost, and irreversible errors. Using this dataset, we train SURE-Act, a controller that selects actions for a frozen backbone agent at inference time.
