Our benchmark and diagnostic protocol provide a basis for evaluating future optimizers on principle-level collapse. Our findings highlight the need for online collapse detection and better mechanisms for generating and maintaining alternative principles during optimization.
papers.summary: Optimizers driven by LLM feedback, used for evolutionary search, heuristic design, and scientific discovery, often stall after quick early gains. The authors identify principle-level search collapse, where the optimizer keeps producing distinct candidates but stays confined to a narrow set of design principles. They build a diagnostic benchmark covering molecular optimization, network sentinel-node selection, and GPU-kernel optimization; across 161 runs, **78.3% show evidence of collapse**. Common diversity fixes such as higher temperature, multiple LLMs, and web search help little, and giving the optimizer a better reference principle does not reliably lead it to use that principle.

papers.title: Inducing Fourier Geometry: A Smoothness Prior Imposes Approximate Translation Equivariance in Multimodal Stellar Embeddings
papers.abstract: Learned representations often contain geometric structure induced by symmetries in the underlying data. We ask whether a known continuous parameter space can instead be used to \emph{induce} such structure when the corresponding symmetry is only approximate. We introduce a graph-Laplacian smoothness prior that encourages representations to vary smoothly over a physical parameter space without specifying a representation geometry; in the continuum limit it selects Laplacian eigenfunctions and therefore predicts the Fourier-like geometry associated with translation symmetry. On multimodal stellar representations spanning six astronomical surveys, the prior induces Toeplitz Gram structure and sinusoidal modes along stellar parameters, including in modalities whose native representations lack this geometry, while modality-specific residuals preserve structure outside the imposed coordinates. Of the exact-symmetry predictions, stationarity in a recoverable warped coordinate survives; diagnostics assuming exact quantization or asymptotic rates do not. The prior also improves downstream linear-probe performance and label efficiency, suggesting a general strategy: where a meaningful continuous parameter space exists, its local geometry can serve as a data-informed prior.
papers.summary: The authors ask whether a known continuous parameter space can be used to induce geometric structure in learned representations when the underlying symmetry holds only approximately. They introduce a graph-Laplacian smoothness prior that encourages representations to vary smoothly over physical parameters; in the continuum limit it predicts the Fourier-like geometry associated with translation symmetry. Applied to multimodal stellar representations from six astronomical surveys, **the prior induces Toeplitz Gram structure and sinusoidal modes along stellar parameters**, even in modalities that lack this geometry natively, and it improves linear-probe accuracy and label efficiency.

papers.title: Constructive Universal Approximation by Infinite-Dimensional Neural Networks via Gaussian-Weighted Ridgelet Transform
papers.abstract: Neural networks whose inputs are functions, as in operator learning, are usually shown to be universal by existence arguments, either by reduction to finite-dimensional networks or by Stone--Weierstrass-type density; these prove that approximants exist but say little about how the parameters depend on the target. We take a constructive route. We extend the ridgelet transform, an integral transform related to the Fourier, Radon, and wavelet transforms, to continuous maps on a separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, replacing the Lebesgue measure that is unavailable in infinite dimensions by Gaussian weights with a homogeneous mixture on the direction space. The resulting transform has a Plancherel identity and reconstruction formulas incorporating the frame operator, the correction induced by the weights, and it assigns to each target an explicit coefficient measure, one for every admissible analysis filter. From these representations we obtain uniform approximation on compact sets for all continuous non-polynomial activations of polynomial growth, including ReLU, and, by Monte Carlo sampling of the coefficient, finite-width networks with a dimension-free $O(N^{-1/2})$ error in the width $N$ for globally Lipschitz activations and coefficients with finite variation and second moments. Explicit examples include Gaussian targets and neural-operator layers. A companion Lean~4 formalization provides machine-checked proofs, with its correspondence to the manuscript documented at https://shosonoda.github.io/lean-operator-ridgelet/ .
papers.summary: Proofs that neural networks taking functions as inputs, as in operator learning, are universal approximators usually show only that approximations exist, not how parameters relate to the target. The authors extend the ridgelet transform to continuous maps on a separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, replacing the Lebesgue measure, which is unavailable in infinite dimensions, with Gaussian weights. This yields a Plancherel identity and reconstruction formulas that assign each target an explicit coefficient measure, giving uniform approximation on compact sets for activations including `ReLU` and, through Monte Carlo sampling, finite-width networks with a **dimension-free O(N^-1/2) error in the width N**. A companion `Lean 4` formalization provides machine-checked proofs.

papers.title: Not Every User Says It All: Training Tool-Using Agents Beyond Ideal Simulated Users
papers.abstract: Tool-using agents are trained and evaluated almost exclusively with strong simulated users who state every detail clearly, yet real users are often weaker. We construct weak users by masking sentences of a simulated user's replies, holding the task and the user's knowledge fixed, and cross-evaluate agents trained with strong and weak users on tau2-bench and ToolWOZ. Weak users lower the success of every policy, and training with them does not help: no policy trained with weak users, through fixed masks, mixtures or a curriculum, serves weak users better than the strong-trained policy beyond run-to-run noise, and prompting the agent to ask more does not help either. We propose StaGPO (State-Grouped Policy Optimization): the agent writes what the task needs, what is missing and how it is being filled, and GRPO uses this state to compare turns of different rollouts that reach the same situation, assigning step-level credit. Within the standard recipe of a small SFT cold start followed by RL, StaGPO makes weak-user training useful: on ToolWOZ, the Qwen3.5-2B policy trained with weak users reaches 76.8% with weak users, the highest of any Qwen3.5-2B policy we trained, 4.8 points above GRPO and 2.8 above the strongest baseline; it is also 5.4 points above GRPO with strong users, and generalises to an unseen mask rate; trained with strong users instead, it serves weak users at least as well as GRPO trained with weak users. On tau2-bench it scores highest with weak users for both models, by a small margin for Qwen3.5-4B.
papers.summary: Tool-using agents are usually trained and evaluated with simulated users who state every detail clearly, but real users often leave things out. The authors simulate weaker users by masking sentences from simulated user replies and find that training with weak users, whether through fixed masks, mixtures, or a curriculum, does not help on `tau2-bench` or `ToolWOZ`. They propose `StaGPO` (State-Grouped Policy Optimization): the agent writes down what the task needs, what is missing, and how the gap is being filled, and `GRPO` uses this state to compare turns from different rollouts that reach the same situation, giving step-level credit. With `StaGPO`, **a `Qwen3.5-2B` policy trained with weak users reaches 76.8% on `ToolWOZ` with weak users**, 4.8 points above `GRPO`, and it also improves results with strong users.

papers.title: Predicting CVSS and CWE from CVE Descriptions with Fine-Tuned Small Language Models
papers.abstract: Until April 2026, the National Vulnerability Database labeled nearly every published Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entry with a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v3.1 vector, a severity tier, and a Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) weakness type. Now, NIST enriches only the high priority CVEs, leaving many newly published vulnerabilities unlabelled with the classifiers that security teams use for patch triage. In CVE enrichment, we predict the eight base components of CVSS v3.1 vector, base score, severity tier, and CWE from the vulnerability's textual description alone. To prevent leakage between near-duplicate descriptions, all systems are trained only on CVEs published in 2022 and 2023. Results are evaluated on all 36,325 usable 2024 CVEs in the pinned NVD snapshot. All scores are either directly predicted, or calculated from predicted vectors using the CVSS formula. A fine-tuned 3.8B-parameter model Phi-3.5-mini, trained with LoRA in 2.5 hours on a single Apple M5 Pro chip, achieves 69.9% accuracy on severity and 70.9% on CWE. It matches the official vector exactly for 48.8% of test CVEs, outperforming TF-IDF logistic regression by 2.8 to 4.7 points on all accuracy metrics based on zero-exclusion paired bootstrap intervals. When we evaluate the base model with a zero-shot prompt, it achieves 20.8% accuracy on severity in a sample of 2,000 CVEs. In this same sample, its stated scores match its own vector precisely for only 3.4% of CVEs. However, deriving scores from predicted vectors boosts the critical recall of TF-IDF logistic regression from 50.7% to 73.3% with no additional cost. And since the errors of the fine-tuned model and TF-IDF affect different CVEs, at least one system matches the correct severity tier for 75.8% of test CVEs.
papers.summary: Since April 2026 the National Vulnerability Database has enriched only high-priority Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) entries, leaving many without Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) vectors or Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) types. The authors predict these labels from vulnerability descriptions alone, training on CVEs from 2022 and 2023 and testing on 36,325 CVEs from 2024. `Phi-3.5-mini`, fine-tuned with `LoRA` in 2.5 hours on a single Apple M5 Pro chip, reaches **69.9% severity accuracy and 70.9% CWE accuracy** and outperforms a `TF-IDF` logistic regression baseline, while the zero-shot base model reaches only 20.8% severity accuracy. Computing scores from predicted vectors with the CVSS formula also raises the baseline's recall on critical vulnerabilities from 50.7% to 73.3%.

papers.title: Who Speaks, Who Authorizes, Who Acts? Understanding Trust Boundaries in Multi-Agent LLMs
papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems exchange messages before acting through tools, but message delivery, signing authority, and tool-side enforcement are separate trust boundaries. We represent them as communication, authorization, and execution structures, and use the authority cut to characterize the smallest independently compromised signer coalition that can construct a policy-valid false-claim proof under stated assumptions. Controlled paired hidden-state studies reveal four distinctions. First, no fixed-message routing contrast across four models meets the prespecified large-effect criterion; when relays rewrite messages, executed false-state action rates vary by model and route configuration. Second, presented source-identity cues do not uniformly increase protected-action selection across three models. Third, on invalid-proof cases, Nemotron and Llama request protected actions in 52.1% and 54.2% of trials, respectively, yet a deterministic tool gate commits none: request-level and commitment-level safety readouts diverge. Finally, a separate single-model authorization check shows that a false claim with a policy-valid compromised-signer proof can pass the gate, since proof validity is not factual truth. These findings motivate evaluating delivered information, qualified authorization, model proposals, and committed actions separately.
papers.summary: In multi-agent LLM systems, message delivery, signing authority, and tool-side enforcement are separate trust boundaries, which the authors model as communication, authorization, and execution structures. Using an "authority cut", they characterize the smallest coalition of compromised signers that can build a policy-valid proof for a false claim. In controlled studies, `Nemotron` and `Llama` request protected actions in 52.1% and 54.2% of invalid-proof trials, but **a deterministic tool gate commits none of them**, so safety measured at the request level and at the commitment level can diverge. A false claim backed by a valid proof from a compromised signer can still pass the gate, because a valid proof does not establish that the claim is true.

papers.title: Torch-DPhys: A Torch-Native, MOOSE-Compatible Framework for Differentiable Physics Simulation and Hybrid Machine Learning Integration
papers.abstract: We present Torch-DPhys, a Torch-native framework implemented in PyTorch for differentiable physics simulation and hybrid physics-machine learning. It implements selected thermal-hydraulic modeling concepts and discretizations from MOOSE's Thermal Hydraulics Module and the System Analysis Module (SAM), with a preliminary extension to continuum mechanics. Native tensor residuals support CPU and GPU execution, compilation of selected numerical kernels, and sparse direct linear solves. Sensitivities are obtained by differentiating executed numerical operations or through discrete adjoints of converged residual equations. Verification combines analytical solutions, reference-code comparisons, and derivative checks. Demonstrations cover plane-strain elasticity, one- and two-loop thermal-hydraulic transients, and an axisymmetric molten-salt fast reactor. For the reactor, comparison with SAM-Lite gives a maximum normalized field discrepancy of 1.13 x 10^-5 over 200 adaptive time steps, demonstrating agreement between the tested discrete implementations. Selected transient sensitivities are assessed using tangent-linear calculations and finite differences on fixed time schedules. Two applications illustrate the framework's connection between simulation and optimization. A residual-adjoint parameter-identification calculation recovers nominal pump head and heating power with relative errors below 0.06% from noiseless synthetic MOOSE observations. A separate three-loop plant demonstration uses solver-in-the-loop training of a predictive controller by differentiating trajectory-level objectives through the thermal-hydraulic simulation. These examples illustrate a foundation for gradient-based inference, control, and coupled physics-machine learning models in nuclear engineering.
papers.summary: `Torch-DPhys` is a `PyTorch` framework for differentiable physics simulation that implements thermal-hydraulic models from the `MOOSE` Thermal Hydraulics Module and the System Analysis Module (`SAM`), with CPU and GPU execution and sensitivities from automatic differentiation or discrete adjoints. On an axisymmetric molten-salt fast reactor, **it agrees with `SAM-Lite` to a maximum normalized field discrepancy of 1.13 × 10^-5** over 200 time steps. Demonstrations include recovering pump head and heating power with relative errors below 0.06% and training a predictive controller by differentiating through the thermal-hydraulic simulation.

papers.title: CME-SpectrumBench: Can LLMs Analyze Condensed Matter Spectral Data?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are presently well assessed by expert-level mathematics and physics benchmarks which focus on theoretical, symbolic reasoning. However, we lack experimental benchmarks that evaluate data analysis in frontier research problems, a capability that future domain-specific foundation models must have. To this end, we present CME-SpectrumBench, an expert-designed benchmark consisting of 190 questions that measures how reliably frontier LLMs analyze research-level spectral scientific data in condensed matter experiments (CME). Using simulated CME spectral data, we prompt models to identify structures from 2D intensity arrays in the face of noise and limited instrumental resolution, a test of dense context reasoning. Models are scored by how accurately their numerical answers approach the ground truth. Under direct query, scores generally pale in comparison to handwritten code due to clear failure modes: models can find simple features but struggle to trace patterns or compute derived quantities, and performance typically degrades with increased data resolution and noise/convolution levels. LLM performance becomes comparable to handwritten code by allowing tool use (access to a Python interpreter) with/without ReAct prompting, in effect mapping questions onto agentic code generation problems. Our findings show that frontier models can serve as research assistants by interfacing with data through code, but still face difficulties processing information directly from large datasets - a key barrier future foundation models must overcome. The code and data are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/jingene/CMESpectrumBench.
papers.summary: LLM science benchmarks mostly test theoretical, symbolic reasoning rather than analysis of experimental data. `CME-SpectrumBench` has 190 expert-designed questions asking frontier LLMs to find structures in simulated condensed matter experiment (CME) spectral data, given as noisy 2D intensity arrays with limited instrumental resolution. Queried directly, models find simple features but struggle to trace patterns or compute derived quantities, and they get worse as resolution and noise increase. **With access to a Python interpreter, with or without `ReAct` prompting, LLM performance becomes comparable to handwritten analysis code**, which effectively turns the task into agentic code generation.

papers.title: Muon Operates Beyond the Edge of Stability
papers.abstract: We study the Muon optimizer using sharpness and provide the first empirical evidence that the Flat Minima Hypothesis also applies to Muon. Further, we derive Muon's implicit preconditioner to analyze its potential Edge of Stability behavior. Experiments on CIFAR-10 show sharpness strongly correlates with generalization gap within each optimizer (Pearson $r = 0.45$-$0.69$, $p \leq 10^{-4}$), confirming the hypothesis holds for Muon similarly to Adam and SGD. However, Muon operates above the classical sharpness-based Adaptive Edge of Stability threshold that bounds diagonally-preconditioned optimizers like Adam and RMSprop, yet remains stable. Our findings suggest Muon operates in a fundamentally different regime than diagonally-adaptive methods. Defining the exact stability boundary for Muon remains an open question. All code is available at https://github.com/NikoCovic/DL-project.
papers.summary: The authors study the `Muon` optimizer through sharpness, a measure of loss curvature, and derive its implicit preconditioner to analyze edge-of-stability behavior. On `CIFAR-10`, sharpness correlates with generalization gap within each optimizer (Pearson r of 0.45 to 0.69), giving the first empirical evidence that the flat-minima hypothesis also holds for `Muon`. However, **`Muon` operates above the sharpness threshold that bounds diagonally preconditioned optimizers such as `Adam` and `RMSprop` while remaining stable**, which suggests it trains in a fundamentally different regime.

papers.title: Learning Administrative Boundary-Aware Location Encoders via Reverse Geocoding
papers.abstract: Location encoders learn compact representations of latitude--longitude coordinates for downstream geospatial prediction tasks. Existing approaches are pretrained using continuous or naturally occurring supervision, such as imagery, climate variables, or species distributions, and therefore do not explicitly capture administrative boundaries or place names, despite their strong influence on many real-world geospatial phenomena. We introduce, to our knowledge, the first method for learning administrative boundary-aware location encoders, using reverse-geocoded text as a self-supervised training signal. Our approach can be applied to existing location encoder architectures and consistently improves their downstream performance. We further introduce RevGeoRQ, a custom architecture tailored to reverse-geocoding supervision, which yields additional gains and exceeds contemporary location encoders on several downstream tasks. Finally, the use of human-interpretable reverse-geocoded strings and residual-quantized semantic IDs provides a more interpretable representation of geographic location than existing approaches. Code and model weights to be released soon.
papers.summary: Location encoders turn latitude–longitude coordinates into compact representations for geospatial prediction. Existing ones are pretrained on signals such as imagery, climate, or species data, so they ignore administrative boundaries and place names. The authors use reverse-geocoded text (the address strings returned for a coordinate) as a self-supervised training signal. Applied to existing encoder architectures, it **consistently improves downstream performance**. A purpose-built architecture, `RevGeoRQ`, beats contemporary location encoders on several tasks, and its residual-quantized semantic IDs make the learned representation more interpretable.

papers.title: RATION: Towards Quantitative Risk-Based Access Control for AI Agents
papers.abstract: AI agents increasingly interact with external environments to complete complex user tasks. These interactions can lead to unexpected behavior and expose agents to security threats such as indirect prompt injection. Current agent security systems largely protect agents by restricting their actions, which can result in a substantial security-utility trade-off for complex, open-ended tasks. To address this, we propose a quantitative risk-based approach to access control for AI agents that regulates measurable risks accumulated during task execution. As a concrete realization of this approach, we introduce RATION, a security framework that tracks measurable risks associated with agent actions and enforces quantitative constraints throughout execution. RATION first constructs a task-specific policy by combining explicit constraints derived from the user request with implicit risks calibrated from historical executions of similar tasks. During task execution, RATION continuously tracks the accumulated risks and applies different enforcement strategies depending on the type of risk. Extensive experiments on four security benchmarks show that RATION provides strong security while maintaining high task utility across diverse models and environments.
papers.summary: AI agents that interact with external environments are exposed to threats such as indirect prompt injection. Current defenses mostly restrict which actions an agent may take, which hurts usefulness on open-ended tasks. `RATION` instead measures the risk an agent accumulates during a task and enforces numeric limits on it. Each task gets a policy that combines explicit constraints taken from the user's request with implicit risks calibrated from past runs of similar tasks. Different enforcement strategies apply depending on the type of risk. Across four security benchmarks, the authors report **strong security while keeping high task utility** across diverse models and environments.

papers.title: Indirect Influences of Artificial Intelligence Advice on Complex Sepsis Treatment Decisions
papers.abstract: Sepsis is a major public health concern, and many sepsis patients die due to ineffective hemodynamic management. Artificial intelligence could support hemodynamic decisions, particularly in complex cases where conflicting information and comorbidities drive uncertainty and practice variation. However, these systems' real-world value depends on not just accuracy, but how they influence the quality of clinician decisions. We first retrospectively evaluated an AI system's recommendations in 6,928 sepsis patients, finding that they improved upon the original providers' decisions overall but had significantly worse performance in complex cases. We then conducted a pre-registered experiment with 228 US critical care physicians to test their use of this imperfect advice in six complex treatment decisions, using one of three advice types designed to vary reasoning autonomy. Participants given simple model recommendations overcame poor advice, choosing optimal treatments in 56.3% of decisions compared to 31.8% if they had always followed the recommendations. They also made significantly better decisions than those receiving a less prescriptive advice type (42.9%). Physicians selectively adapted and improved weak advice, likely because it prompted them to reconsider their assessment. Our findings suggest that improving sepsis care decisions with AI may require accounting for these indirect influences resulting from human-AI collaborative reasoning.
papers.summary: The authors study how AI advice on hemodynamic management in sepsis affects clinicians' decisions, not just how accurate the advice is. A retrospective check on 6,928 patients found the AI system's recommendations beat the original providers' decisions overall but did significantly worse in complex cases. In a pre-registered experiment, 228 US critical care physicians made six complex treatment decisions while receiving one of three advice types. Physicians given simple recommendations chose the optimal treatment **56.3% of the time, versus 31.8% if they had always followed the advice** and 42.9% for a less prescriptive advice type. This suggests weak advice prompted clinicians to reconsider their own assessments.

papers.title: Latent State Utilization in Probabilistic Circuits
papers.abstract: Probabilistic circuits (PCs) are generative models that support efficient probabilistic inference. Adding latent states to a PC increases its representational capacity, but yields diminishing gains in likelihood. We use mutual information to examine how the dependence represented by a trained PC changes with latent size. Experiments with Hidden Chow-Liu Trees (HCLTs) on ImageNet32 show that learned dependence grows slowly and remains well below both the latent-state upper bound and estimates of dependence in the data. To understand how learning uses these states, we examine how strongly each sample favors particular latent states and how broadly states are used across the dataset. Tracking these measurements during HCLT training distinguishes rapid early posterior concentration from the more gradual stabilization of sample-dependent state preferences. Early measurements also guide initialization selection in HCLTs and hidden Markov models (HMMs), as well as tree selection in HCLTs. The resulting choices improve the ultimate performance across the tested latent sizes, providing a practical benefit from our study of latent-state utilization.
papers.summary: Probabilistic circuits (PCs) are generative models that support efficient exact inference. Adding latent states increases their capacity but gives diminishing gains in likelihood. Using mutual information on `Hidden Chow-Liu Trees` (HCLTs) trained on `ImageNet32`, the authors find that **learned dependence grows slowly and stays well below both the theoretical upper bound and the dependence present in the data**. Tracking how strongly samples favor particular latent states during training shows a fast early concentration phase followed by slower stabilization. Measurements taken early in training also help choose initializations for HCLTs and hidden Markov models (HMMs), and tree structures for HCLTs, improving final performance.

papers.title: The Judge Can Debias Itself: Awareness and Self-Debiasing for Reliable LLM-as-a-Judge
papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge systems are increasingly employed for automated evaluation, yet remain susceptible to systematic biases that undermine their reliability. We demonstrate that the judge can effectively debias itself without additional training. We propose two lightweight strategies: bias-aware prompting, which explicitly alerts the judge to potential target biases prior to evaluation, and self-debiasing, in which the judge critiques the initial judgment for bias influence. To broaden the evaluation scope, we introduce three novel benchmarks--authority bias (fabricated citations), confidence bias (assertive phrasing), and formatting bias (structured presentation)--and evaluate across seven bias types in total. Across three frontier models, self-debiasing improves performance in 20 out of 21 model-bias combinations with gains up to 15 percentage points, while bias-aware prompting also yields consistent improvements. The recent fine-tuned external critic, however, does not generalize as reliably to the newly-introduced bias types (degradation observed in 5 out of 9 cases). Our findings demonstrate that prompting a judge to reason about bias, either preemptively or retrospectively, is a robust and generalizable approach for enhancing evaluation integrity.
papers.summary: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators suffer from systematic biases, and the authors show the judge can reduce them itself without extra training. They test two prompting strategies: bias-aware prompting, which warns the judge about a specific bias before it evaluates, and self-debiasing, where the judge critiques its own first judgment. They add three new benchmarks, for authority, confidence, and formatting bias, and evaluate seven bias types in total. Across three frontier models, **self-debiasing improves 20 of 21 model–bias combinations, with gains of up to 15 percentage points**. A recent fine-tuned external critic, by contrast, got worse in 5 of 9 cases on the new bias types.

papers.title: Morpheus-2.0: Multiscale Probabilistic Forecasting with Dual-Axis Attention
papers.abstract: A universal forecaster is trained once and applied everywhere, so it must serve tasks whose schemas, forecast horizons, and temporal resolutions all differ. The number of targets and covariates changes from dataset to dataset, horizons vary by orders of magnitude, and sampling rates range from seconds to years. Existing time-series foundation models address these only in part, since they isolate each series or visit the two grid relations in separate blocks, and they fix the horizon and resolution before training begins. We introduce Morpheus-2.0, a compact encoder-only foundation model that represents targets and covariates on a single variable-time grid. Its dual-axis attention runs both relations side by side in every layer, one across variables at a timestep and one across time within a variable; a learned gate weights the two per layer, and an axis-aware rotary encoding preserves both grid coordinates. The forecast length is sampled during training, so one set of weights spans short to long horizons at no additional inference cost. Morpheus-2.0 Multiscale extends the model to several temporal resolutions at once, weighting them according to the series being forecast. Across GIFT-Eval, which spans several domains and frequencies, the two models give complementary operating points: Morpheus-2.0 attains 0.685 relative MASE with 81M parameters, while the larger Morpheus-2.0 Multiscale attains 0.646 relative MASE and 0.455 relative CRPS, the lowest of any published system on both metrics.
papers.summary: A universal time-series forecaster must handle datasets with varying numbers of targets and covariates, horizons, and sampling rates. `Morpheus-2.0` is a compact encoder-only foundation model that places all variables on a single variable–time grid. In every layer, dual-axis attention runs across variables and across time in parallel, with a learned gate weighting the two. Forecast length is sampled during training, so one set of weights covers short and long horizons, and a `Multiscale` variant combines several temporal resolutions. On `GIFT-Eval`, the 81M-parameter model reaches 0.685 relative MASE (mean absolute scaled error). The Multiscale variant reaches **0.646 relative MASE and 0.455 relative CRPS (continuous ranked probability score), the lowest of any published system on both metrics**.

papers.title: Continuous Ontology Assurance through External Resources -- An Ontology Engineering Method with a Case Study in Software Language Engineering
papers.abstract: Domain ontologies require review against knowledge recorded in evolving external resources. We propose COATER, a method that manages executable review components called arrows. Each arrow compares a scoped part of an ontology with a relevant resource and reports support or challenges to its axioms. Challenges may prompt proposals for completion, correction, or restructuring and become tasks for human or agent-assisted triage. Per-axiom coverage summarizes the assessments. We illustrate COATER with the FSL ontology in software language engineering (SLE): arrows review language coverage, language conceptualization, and software-engineering activities. An LLM-assisted linkage exercise increases compliance with a defined Wikipedia-linkage policy from 405 to 600 of 600 entities. A structured catalogue of SLE resources organizes review opportunities.
papers.summary: `COATER` is a method for continuously reviewing a domain ontology against evolving external resources. It uses executable review components called arrows, each of which compares part of the ontology with a resource and reports whether its axioms are supported or challenged. Challenges become triage tasks for humans or agents, and per-axiom coverage summarizes the results. In a case study on the `FSL` ontology for software language engineering, an LLM-assisted linkage exercise raised compliance with a Wikipedia-linkage policy **from 405 to 600 of 600 entities**.

papers.title: VERAS: Verification-Guided Adaptive Search for Reliable Operations Research
papers.abstract: Advances in reasoning, coding, and tool use enable LLM agents to solve operations research (OR) problems through iterative problem modeling, program construction, and verification. Yet passing self-authored verification does not ensure that the solutions satisfy task constraints and meet optimization quality. This gap can arise from correlated specification errors, where the generated program and its checks share omissions or misinterpretations of task requirements, alongside incomplete verification coverage and ineffective optimization strategies. We propose VERAS, a verification-guided adaptive search harness for reliable OR that uses verification evidence to prioritize feasibility repair, constraint-coverage review, and solution-quality improvement. VERAS combines task-specific solution checkers with a separate verification agent to examine candidate solutions against the task requirements. It uses verification feedback to guide feasibility repair, additional constraint checking, and objective improvement, while candidate acceptance criteria screen revisions for deterioration in output validity or constraint satisfaction. On ORAgentBench, VERAS achieves a 42.99% pass rate, exceeding the reported 35.51% of Codex using the same LLM. Across two industrial-scale OR problems, VERAS reduces inter-datacenter peak bandwidth by 10.34% relative to native Codex and lowers annualized distribution network planning costs by 6.28% compared with expert-designed solutions. Code and evidence are available at https://github.com/holimario/VERAS.
papers.summary: LLM agents can solve operations research (OR) problems by modeling them, writing programs, and checking their own work. However, the program and its self-written checks often share the same misreading of the task. `VERAS` is a search harness that pairs task-specific solution checkers with a separate verification agent. It uses their feedback to prioritize fixing infeasible solutions, checking constraints that weren't covered, and improving the objective, and it rejects revisions that make solutions worse. On `ORAgentBench`, VERAS reaches a **42.99% pass rate versus 35.51% for `Codex` using the same LLM**. On two industrial problems, it cuts inter-datacenter peak bandwidth by 10.34% and network planning costs by 6.28% compared with expert-designed solutions.

papers.title: PAC Learning with Query Feedback
papers.abstract: We study realizable multiclass PAC learning with query feedback, where each training example provides a single binary response indicating whether its true label belongs to a chosen subset from a fixed query family. Our main contribution is the query dimension, a combinatorial parameter that captures both the structure of the hypothesis class and the ability of the available queries to distinguish labels. This parameter generalizes the bandit DS dimension, which it recovers under singleton queries. We establish a sample-complexity lower bound of $\Omega(D/\varepsilon)$ and an upper bound of $\widetilde{O}(D^2/\varepsilon)$, suppressing factors polylogarithmic in the number of labels and the failure probability. When the available queries can split every candidate set into two parts of comparable size, we improve the upper bound to $\widetilde{O}(D/\varepsilon)$, yielding a characterization up to logarithmic factors.
papers.summary: The authors study multiclass PAC (probably approximately correct) learning in a setting where each training example reveals only a yes/no answer to whether its true label falls in a chosen subset from a fixed query family. They introduce the query dimension, a combinatorial parameter that generalizes the bandit DS dimension, which it recovers when queries are single labels. They prove a lower bound of Ω(D/ε) samples and an upper bound of Õ(D²/ε). When queries can split every candidate set into two parts of comparable size, the upper bound improves to Õ(D/ε), giving **a characterization of sample complexity up to logarithmic factors**.

papers.title: Power-Law Correlations Without Apparent Temperature-Tuned Criticality in Fixed-Tree Hierarchical Languages
papers.abstract: Sampling temperature can substantially reshape autoregressive generation, but it is unclear when temperature changes in long-range correlations reflect a genuine phase transition rather than a smooth change in statistics. We study this question in a controlled analogue of temperature sampling: a finite-depth probabilistic context-free grammar on a fixed hierarchical tree, where exact next-token conditionals are computed by belief propagation and then rescaled by a softmax temperature before autoregressive sampling. We measure two-point mutual information between tokens as a function of separation. Across the tested temperatures and grammar ensembles, mutual information remains well described by a power-law envelope. Temperature changes the correlation magnitude and fitted exponent, but within the accessible system sizes we find no long-distance plateau characteristic of an ordered phase and no clear crossover to short-range exponential decay. An approximate mapping to an Ising model on a tree explains how exponential decay in tree distance becomes a power law in token distance, allowing power laws to persist without tuning to a special decoding temperature. This controlled baseline clarifies which temperature effects can arise from hierarchical structure alone, before adding training, approximation error, or neural architecture.
papers.summary: The authors ask whether changes in long-range correlations under different sampling temperatures reflect a genuine phase transition. They use a controlled setup: a probabilistic context-free grammar on a fixed hierarchical tree, with exact next-token probabilities computed by belief propagation and then rescaled by temperature. Mutual information between tokens follows a **power-law envelope across all tested temperatures**, with no sign of an ordered-phase plateau or a switch to exponential decay. An approximate mapping to an `Ising` model on a tree explains why exponential decay in tree distance becomes a power law in token distance, without tuning to a special temperature.

papers.title: Screening LLM Judges Without Ground Truth: A Preliminary Evaluation of an AI Dental Hygiene Coach
papers.abstract: Evaluating a fine-tuned coaching model with expert graders is slow and expensive, and an LLM judge cannot be trusted without ground truth. We present a staged pipeline that screens candidate LLM judges and student models before expert review, using explicit decision rules at each stage: judge output audit, similarity with hosted judges, bias checks, and decision robustness. We demonstrate it on an AI dental hygiene coach. The case study uses synthetic, clinically unvalidated training and reference data to demonstrate the operation of the pipeline, rather than to establish the clinical performance of the resulting models. Two fine-tuned small language models (Granite-4.1-8B and Qwen3-8B), each trained at three data sizes, were scored on seven metrics by five judges (three local, two hosted). Two local judges, Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it, were not distinguishable from the agreement between the hosted judges on six of seven metrics by rank correlation, and Qwen3.8-27B was the most similar to the hosted judges overall. No judge met our criterion for favoring its own model family or training-data source. The student comparison did not separate the two models on any metric under the pipeline's rule, so the choice of Granite-4.1-8B, which led in 29 of 35 judge-by-metric cells, is a lean that depends partly on truncated Qwen3-8B outputs. The pipeline also surfaced problems that raw scores hid, including the truncated outputs and hallucination flags from one hosted judge that no other judge corroborated. No dental hygiene expert has graded these responses, so the findings are preliminary and the pipeline's final stage, anchoring to expert judgement, is proposed but not performed.
papers.summary: Expert grading of fine-tuned models is slow and expensive, so the authors propose a staged pipeline to screen LLM judges and candidate models before expert review. The stages are an audit of judge outputs, similarity to hosted judges, bias checks, and decision robustness. They demonstrate it on an AI dental hygiene coach, using fine-tuned `Granite-4.1-8B` and `Qwen3-8B` models trained on synthetic data and scored by five judges. **Local judges `Qwen3.8-27B` and `Gemma-4-31B-it` were statistically indistinguishable from the hosted judges' mutual agreement on six of seven metrics**, and no judge favored its own model family. The pipeline also exposed problems that raw scores hid, such as truncated outputs, though no dental expert has yet graded the results.

papers.title: Uniform convergence at optimal rate and scale
papers.abstract: Uniform convergence asks how many random samples suffice for empirical averages to approximate expectations simultaneously over an entire class of functions. It is a central concept in probability and a foundation of statistical learning. For binary-valued classes, the Vapnik--Chervonenkis theorem characterizes uniform convergence by finiteness of the VC dimension. For dimension $d$, the sharp worst-case sample complexity for additive error $\varepsilon$ is of order $d/\varepsilon^2$. For real-valued functions, the analogous combinatorial parameter is the fat-shattering dimension, which depends on an approximation scale $\gamma$. The challenge is to achieve error $\gamma+\varepsilon$ with order $d/\varepsilon^2$ samples, matching the sample bound for binary classes, where $d$ is now the fat-shattering dimension at scale $\gamma$. Previous results achieved either the optimal scale or the optimal sample complexity, but not both. Our main result closes this gap, establishing the sharp sample complexity at the optimal scale. Along the way, we use several tools that may be of independent interest. The first concerns $\varepsilon$-nets with margin. A classical $\varepsilon$-net intersects every set of mass at least $\varepsilon$ in a prescribed family; we allow the net to intersect a slightly enlarged version of each such set. Remarkably, this relaxation permits bounds independent of the ambient dimension in natural geometric settings. Second, we derive improved covering bounds in both discrete and real-valued settings: we extend Haussler's covering lemma to partial concept classes and use this extension to obtain $\ell_2$ covers at the optimal scale for real-valued function classes. Third, we obtain a chaining bound at the optimal scale by aligning the covers so that successive approximations become increasingly close to one another.
papers.summary: Uniform convergence asks how many samples are needed for empirical averages to approximate expectations across a whole class of functions at once. For real-valued function classes, the relevant measure of complexity is the fat-shattering dimension at an approximation scale γ. Earlier results achieved either the optimal scale or the optimal sample complexity, but not both. The authors **establish the sharp d/ε² sample complexity at the optimal scale**, matching the binary case. New tools along the way include ε-nets with margin, an extension of Haussler's covering lemma to partial concept classes, and a chaining bound at the optimal scale.

papers.title: What Matters for NVFP4 Training? A Comparative Study of Low-Precision Pretraining Recipes
papers.abstract: Training large language models directly in 4-bit floating-point (FP) formats promises substantial improvements in throughput and energy efficiency. While some recipe design choices have been validated at scale, many promising approaches remain untested beyond small models and short token horizons, leaving open the question of which trends will hold. We present a systematic comparison of recent NVFP4 recipes at medium model scale, evaluating dense 8B and 30B-A3B MoE models trained for up to 1T tokens, with a focus on which ingredients are necessary for accuracy recovery. We propose a final recipe grounded in the principles behind established stable NVFP4 training at scale, incorporating state-of-the-art techniques such as unbiased gradient estimation with lower quantization error than stochastic rounding. To the best of our knowledge, this is the strongest FP4 training result demonstrated at this scale to date in loss gap to BF16. Through ablation studies, we find that: (i) each technique in the optimized recipe measurably improves loss trajectory, (ii) selective high-precision layers are necessary for recovering accuracy at scale, (iii) not all tensors in the backward pass benefit equally from de-biasing, leaving room to apply complementary error-reduction techniques to the remaining tensors.
papers.summary: Training large language models directly in 4-bit floating point promises large throughput and energy gains, but many proposed recipes have only been tested at small scale. The authors systematically compare recent `NVFP4` recipes on a dense 8B model and a 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts (MoE) model trained on up to 1T tokens. Their final recipe uses unbiased gradient estimation with lower quantization error than stochastic rounding and gives **the smallest loss gap to `BF16` of any FP4 training result at this scale to date**, according to the authors. Ablations show that every component helps and that some layers must stay in higher precision. Not all backward-pass tensors benefit equally from de-biasing.

papers.title: The Certification Exponent: Instance-Optimal Sequential Certification of Policy Improvement from History Dependent Logs
papers.abstract: Before a new policy replaces a deployed one, we often want a certificate, computed from logged episodes, that it is better. We ask how many episodes such a certificate needs when the logging policy is known but history-dependent, and the error probability must stay below $\delta$ in every environment consistent with the logs. The answer is an exponent $K^\star$: the smallest KL divergence from the logged law to a law with the same logged action probabilities under which the target does not improve. No sound certifier stops in fewer than $\log(1/\delta)/K^\star$ expected episodes, at any $\delta$, and whenever $0<K^\star<\infty$ a plug-in Kelly certifier attains this rate to first order as $\delta\to0$. Coverage, computed by one backward induction, decides whether certification is impossible ($K^\star=0$), possible at a finite rate, or possible in a constant number of episodes ($K^\star=\infty$). By convex duality, the optimal certificate bets on the importance-weighted advantage and also places fair bets on the logged actions, so doubly robust control variates act as hedges rather than estimators. As a consequence, no choice of off-policy estimator changes $K^\star$, a coverage ceiling explains the curse of memory, and structural assumptions can be priced in exponent units. A cushion certifier extends the approach to trees too large to enumerate. In experiments the plug-in's median stopping time is 1.13-1.43x the lower bound on memory tasks, 1.13-1.51x on Tiger ($H\le5$) and 1.17-1.64x on random trees. The best scalar betting baselines need up to 2.65x (memory) and 4.1x (Tiger) the plug-in's episodes; only on a few shallow random trees is a doubly robust bet faster, by at most 18%.
papers.summary: The authors ask how many logged episodes are needed to certify that a new policy beats a deployed one when the logging policy is known but depends on history. They show the answer is governed by an exponent K*, the smallest KL divergence (a measure of how different two probability distributions are) from the logged distribution to one where the target policy does not improve. **No sound certifier can stop in fewer than log(1/δ)/K* expected episodes**, and a plug-in Kelly-betting certifier attains this rate to first order. Convex duality shows that doubly robust control variates act as hedges rather than estimators, so the choice of off-policy estimator cannot change K*. In experiments, the plug-in certifier stops within 1.13–1.64× the lower bound and needs up to 4.1× fewer episodes than scalar betting baselines.

papers.title: Measuring the Task Value of Precision Upgrades in Closed-Loop Agents
papers.abstract: A low-precision agent can call its full-precision (BF16) model at selected decisions as a fallback. A learned precision router chooses where to call it from the disagreement between the two models and is judged by end-to-end success. An inserted BF16 action, however, can rescue a failing task or damage a succeeding one. We argue that a fallback's value is the number of tasks it saves minus the number it spoils, measured for the intervention that will actually run. From restored states, we run paired branches that cross which model supplies the current action with which model continues, separating replacement of one action, takeover of later execution, and both. On Qwen3 agents with simulated 4-bit weights in tau2-bench, replacing the first action where the two models differed in tool use changed many task outcomes, but rescues and damages nearly cancelled, and on held-out telecom tasks the action-only estimate was negative. Replacing both the action and the continuation had a positive net gain in two of five exploratory lower-bit stress settings. Two references changed outcomes at fixed bit width: replacing an action with that of a second 4-bit checkpoint changed about as many outcomes as replacing it with the BF16 action, and reordering tool-argument keys changed outcomes while the executed tool call stayed identical. At common states, the additional value of the BF16 action over that checkpoint remained unresolved. A frozen uncertainty trigger found more outcome changes than random selection, while its net benefit stayed within the range of random selection. We recommend evaluating each fallback by its signed task benefit under the intended continuation, against same-precision references, before attributing gains to more bits.
papers.summary: A quantized (low-precision) agent can fall back to its full-precision `BF16` model on selected decisions, but an inserted action can either rescue a failing task or spoil one that would have succeeded. The authors argue a fallback should be judged by tasks saved minus tasks spoiled. They measure this with paired runs from restored states that separate replacing a single action from handing over the rest of execution. On `Qwen3` agents with simulated 4-bit weights in `tau2-bench`, **rescues and damages from single-action replacement nearly cancelled, and the net effect was negative on held-out telecom tasks**. Swapping in another 4-bit checkpoint changed about as many outcomes as BF16 did, and merely reordering tool-argument keys also changed outcomes. The authors therefore recommend testing fallbacks against same-precision baselines before crediting gains to extra bits.

papers.title: Exact Risk Certificates for Pairwise-Judged Reranking
papers.abstract: Pairwise relevance judgments constrain both the loss numerator and the ideal-ranking denominator of nDCG. We characterize the exact worst-case loss of replacing a ranking with a fixed proposal. Binary gains attain this loss and provide an inspectable witness. Threshold verification reduces to at most $K+1$ maximum-closure problems. Our exposure-flow ablation isolates denominator coupling: on shared judge trajectories, exact verification saves 2.34 comparisons per TREC-DL development query and 1.98 per confirmation query at a budget of 32. Savings transfer to BEIR and a second proposer. Predictive gates achieve higher deployment gains, while certificates expose the worst gains still permitted by accepted comparisons.
papers.summary: Pairwise relevance judgments constrain both the loss and the ideal-ranking normalizer of nDCG (normalized discounted cumulative gain), a standard ranking metric. The authors characterize the exact worst-case loss of replacing a ranking with a proposed one and show that binary relevance gains achieve it. Checking whether the loss stays under a threshold reduces to at most K+1 maximum-closure problems. On `TREC-DL`, exact verification **saves about 2 pairwise comparisons per query at a budget of 32**, and the savings carry over to `BEIR` and a second proposer model.

papers.title: Blackbox Performance Analysis of LLM-based Network Control
papers.abstract: LLMs are becoming an indispensable part of network control systems due to their impressive reasoning. Before such LLM-enabled systems can be deployed, it is imperative to develop tools that can audit their performance on previously unseen inputs. However, auditing these systems is challenging due to the inherent opacity of LLMs. LENS is the first step towards black-box performance analysis of LLM-enabled network control systems. It uses novel methods to extend deep reinforcement learning to guide the search for performance gaps and inputs that make LLMs struggle. LENS finds large gaps for LLM-based traffic engineering and GPU allocation systems, and even matches existing white-box analyzers designed for hand-crafted TE heuristics.
papers.summary: LLMs are increasingly used in network control systems, and their opacity makes them hard to audit on unseen inputs. `LENS` is a black-box tool that extends deep reinforcement learning to search for inputs where LLM-based controllers perform poorly. It finds **large performance gaps in LLM-based traffic engineering and GPU allocation systems**. It also matches existing white-box analyzers built for hand-crafted traffic engineering heuristics.

papers.title: FlashRT-PAI: Fast Kernels Are Not Fast Pipelines for Physical AI Inference
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA), video-action (VA), and world action models (WAMs) form the backbone of modern physical AI systems, yet their real-time single-batch inference remains a defining bottleneck. Latency is dominated not by individual kernel computation, but by system-level overhead: thousands of short kernel launches, intermediate data movement across operator boundaries, and redundant recomputation across consecutive decisions. General-purpose graph compilers cannot address these costs, as they optimize individual calls in isolation and lack visibility into cross-call state semantics and global pipeline structure. We present FLASHRT-PAI, a low-latency inference engine built around model-hardware pipeline co-design rather than isolated kernel optimization. FLASHRT-PAI combines three core mechanisms: deep kernel fusion with launch overlap eliminates inter-operator boundaries and launch gaps; an execution contract formalizes the pipeline's stage DAG, update rates, and named buffers to enable cross-decision state reuse and selective refresh; and execution-state capsules enable fast snapshot, restore, and fork of persistent pipeline state. The system also supports drop-in acceleration of unmodified PyTorch models via parity- and latency-gated kernel replacement. Evaluation covers six policies on RTX 5090 and four on Jetson AGX Thor. At matched 16-bit precision, FLASHRT-PAI is 1.3-3.7x faster than official compiled paths. Combining pipeline co-design with reduced precision delivers 3.38-12.66x speedup over official eager implementations. In LIBERO-10, four-bit pi0.5 achieves 94.04% success on Thor and 93.32% on RTX 5090, compared with 92.4% for the measured official FP16 reference. FLASHRT-PAI is open source, distributed via Hugging Face Kernel Hub, and its opt-in pi0.5 kernels have been adopted into the LeRobot framework.
papers.summary: Real-time inference for vision-language-action (VLA), video-action, and world action models is limited mainly by system overhead rather than raw kernel compute. That overhead comes from thousands of short kernel launches, data movement between operators, and recomputation across consecutive decisions. `FlashRT-PAI` addresses it with deep kernel fusion, an execution contract that enables state reuse across decisions, and snapshot/restore of pipeline state. It also offers drop-in acceleration for unmodified `PyTorch` models. Across six policies on an RTX 5090 and four on a Jetson AGX Thor, it runs 1.3–3.7× faster than official compiled paths at 16-bit precision and **3.38–12.66× faster than official eager implementations when combined with reduced precision**. A 4-bit `pi0.5` reaches about 94% success on `LIBERO-10`, compared with 92.4% for the official FP16 reference.

papers.title: Koi: Evidence-Guided, Self-Calibrating Planning for Multi-Cloud, Heterogeneous LLM Inference Fleets
papers.abstract: Deploying a large language model (LLM) requires choosing the right accelerator, parallelization strategy, engine configuration, and replica count amongst ~140 other variables across clouds, regions, and markets. These decisions are intertwined, and the best cluster-wide plan continually changes as jobs contend for shared capacity on shifting workloads. We present Koi, a self-calibrating cluster planner for heterogeneous, multi-cloud fleets. Koi uses a Recursive Language Model (RLM) hierarchy to propose hypotheses and reason over deployment while deterministic components predict serving behavior, score candidates, and control placement. It represents inference behavior as a fixed causal graph linking decisions (e.g., accelerator, parallelism), runtime mediators (e.g., KV-cache pressure, communication overhead), and outcomes (e.g., latency, throughput). Each deployment strengthens or weakens scoped causal relationships, building a comprehensive playbook for inference that the planner employs to guide future decisions. Job-wise configurations are composed into cluster-wide plans and evaluated against serving objectives, resource constraints, SLO risks, and cost. Across benchmarks, Koi achieves 1.18x greater goodput than the strongest baseline while reducing $/token by 20% in a real heterogeneous cluster. Ablations isolate the contribution of Koi's architecture: a pure language model attains a composite score of 35.3, the same model equipped with Koi's deterministic tools reaches 51.6, and the full Koi planner reaches 70.8.
papers.summary: Deploying an LLM means jointly choosing accelerators, parallelization, engine settings, and replica counts across clouds, and the best cluster-wide plan shifts as workloads change. `Koi` is a self-calibrating planner in which a hierarchy of Recursive Language Models (RLMs) proposes and reasons about hypotheses. Deterministic components predict serving behavior, score candidate plans, and control placement. Every deployment updates a causal graph linking configuration choices to runtime factors and outcomes, building a reusable playbook. In a real heterogeneous cluster, Koi delivers **1.18× higher goodput than the strongest baseline and cuts cost per token by 20%**. Ablations show the full planner scores 70.8, versus 35.3 for a plain language model and 51.6 for that model with Koi's deterministic tools.

papers.title: DKnown-Jev: Fine-Tuning and Evaluation of a JEV-Style Model for Tasks Involving Normative Knowledge
papers.abstract: Tasks involving normative knowledge include concept interpretation, eligibility determination, procedure explanation, material requirements, and service-outcome assessment, all of which require rules and facts published, maintained, or recorded by authorized entities. Whether a candidate paragraph can answer a question therefore depends on applicability and answer completeness as well as topical relevance. We develop DKnown-Jev to classify the normative usability of candidate paragraphs into two classes. The 2B and 27B configurations are fine-tuned directly from the native Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.8-27B base models, respectively. The models combine question conditions, article metadata, and paragraph content, adopt the classes Answer Evidence (AE) and Non-answer Evidence (NE), and undergo domain adaptation using human-verified training data. Five configurations are evaluated on the same test set of 1,120 human-verified examples. DKnown-Jev 27B trained for one epoch achieves the highest accuracy of 98.75% and macro-F1 of 98.60%, exceeding Jev by 6.07 and 6.76 percentage points, respectively. DKnown-Jev 2B trained for one epoch achieves 92.86% accuracy and 92.18% macro-F1, the best aggregate results among the tested 2B configurations. Its gains over Jev are 0.18 and 0.33 percentage points on this test set, corresponding to only two additional correct predictions, which is insufficient to establish a stable advantage. The 27B one-epoch, 27B two-epoch, and 2B one-epoch configurations all exceed Jev on both metrics on this test set. Class-level analysis shows that the 27B two-epoch configuration has the highest AE recall, while the 27B one-epoch configuration has the highest NE recall. This study provides practical and empirical evidence for developing and applying candidate-scoring models to tasks involving normative knowledge.
papers.summary: `DKnown-Jev` classifies whether a candidate paragraph can actually answer a question that depends on normative knowledge, such as eligibility rules or administrative procedures, as opposed to merely being on-topic. 2B and 27B versions are fine-tuned from `Qwen3.5-2B` and `Qwen3.8-27B` on human-verified data, combining question conditions, article metadata, and paragraph content. On a 1,120-example test set, **the 27B one-epoch model reaches 98.75% accuracy and 98.60% macro-F1, about 6 points above the `Jev` baseline**. The 2B model's gain over Jev amounts to only two more correct predictions, which is too small to establish a stable advantage.

papers.title: Can Agents Keep Secrets They Were Never Told? Benchmarking Latent Privacy Risks Across Sessions with MemJoin
papers.abstract: To support sustained interactions and personalized assistance, agents use long-term memory to retain and combine user information across sessions. Reusing such memories can lead an agent to state a sensitive relation while completing an ordinary task that does not require it. The relation to protect and the combination of clues that reveal it may remain hidden at memory write time, when later records and tasks are still unknown. In this paper, we introduce MemJoin, a privacy benchmark of 288 synthetic analysis cases in which the complete history entails a sensitive relation, but every individual session is insufficient. We evaluate six memory systems with the same answer-generating model, alongside full-history and no-history controls. Each system writes and updates memories in session order and later retrieves context for an ordinary task, while target annotations remain with the evaluator. We separately check which target attribute values appear in stored records and retrieved context, and whether the final answer states the complete, person-linked relation. In a separate paired test on a prespecified subset, removing shared identifiers and other connecting clues can change complete-relation output while all checked target attribute values remain visible. These findings show why checking attribute visibility alone is insufficient to evaluate what records from different sessions reveal together.
papers.summary: Agents with long-term memory can combine details from separate sessions and end up stating a sensitive relation about a user during an ordinary task that never needed it. The risk is hard to catch when memories are written, because the relation and the clues that reveal it only come together later. `MemJoin` is a privacy benchmark of 288 synthetic cases in which the full history implies a sensitive relation but no single session does. It is used to evaluate six memory systems, plus full-history and no-history controls, by checking both which target attribute values show up in stored and retrieved context and whether the final answer states the complete, person-linked relation. In a paired test, removing shared identifiers and other connecting clues changed whether the complete relation was disclosed even though every checked attribute value stayed visible, showing that **checking attribute visibility alone cannot tell you what records from different sessions reveal together**.

papers.title: FlashMap: Flow Map Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose a block of tokens that the target model verifies in one parallel pass. Autoregressive drafters generate this block one token at a time, whereas block diffusion drafters such as DFlash generate it in one pass, making drafting faster. However, these diffusion drafters predict each token independently, ignoring dependencies between tokens in the block. We introduce FlashMap, a continuous flow drafter that conditions a flow map language model on the target model's hidden states and generates the whole block in one forward pass while capturing inter-token dependencies. On Qwen3-8B, FlashMap is faster than a matched DFlash baseline on every benchmark, with 7% higher average speedup and up to 6.1x lossless acceleration.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model (LLM) inference by having a small drafter propose a block of tokens that the target model checks in one parallel pass. Block diffusion drafters such as `DFlash` draft the whole block in one pass, but they predict each token independently and miss dependencies between tokens. `FlashMap` instead uses a continuous flow map language model, conditioned on the target model's hidden states, which generates the full block in one forward pass while still capturing those dependencies. On `Qwen3-8B` it beats a matched `DFlash` baseline on every benchmark, with 7% higher average speedup and **up to 6.1x lossless acceleration**.

papers.title: A Two-Stage Hybrid Framework for Inferring Air Trips from Mobile Location-based Service (LBS) Data under Incomplete Airport Sightings
papers.abstract: Mobile device location-based service (LBS) data provide large-scale spatiotemporal observations that can help airport planners understand air travelers' mobility patterns. However, airport sightings are often missing before or after flights, making strictly rule-based detection incomplete. This study develops a two-stage framework to infer U.S. domestic air trips from large-scale LBS data under incomplete airport sightings. Stage 1 uses heuristic rules to identify high-confidence air trips whose endpoints are observed at two distinct airports. Stage 2 addresses latent air trips with a probabilistic model that infers air routes using spatial proximity, temporal compatibility, and historical flight schedule information. Using January 2022 nationwide LBS data with nearly 10 million users and 131 million sightings, results are validated against T-100 Domestic Segment route benchmarks and a Stage 1 pseudo-ground-truth reference set. The framework increases air route coverage from 10.65% under Stage 1 to 50.60% and recovers nearly all top-1,000 benchmark routes. It improves Spearman rank correlation with T-100 route shares from 0.4490 to 0.7630 and reduces Jensen-Shannon divergence from 0.2808 to 0.2263. Stage 2 also recovers 92.2% of Stage 1 reference trips. This study formalizes three endpoint observation regimes for LBS-based air trip inference (airport-observed, semi-observed, and latent) and helps airport agencies identify domestic air travel patterns missed when airport sightings are incomplete.
papers.summary: Location data from mobile apps (location-based service, or LBS, data) could reveal how air travelers move, but devices often go unseen at the airport before or after a flight, so purely rule-based trip detection misses many trips. A two-stage framework first applies heuristic rules to find high-confidence trips seen at two different airports. It then uses a probabilistic model to infer hidden trips from spatial proximity, timing compatibility, and historical flight schedules. On January 2022 U.S. data covering nearly 10 million users, the method **raises air route coverage from 10.65% to 50.60%**, recovers nearly all of the top 1,000 benchmark routes, and improves Spearman rank correlation with `T-100` route shares from 0.449 to 0.763.

papers.title: WAQS: Weight Absorption for Quadratic Probing and Affine Steering
papers.abstract: Activation steering provides a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for controlling large language model behavior. Existing methods, however, often face a trade-off between efficiency and expressiveness: fixed steering vectors incur negligible inference overhead but cannot adapt to the current model input, whereas input-dependent nonlinear interventions provide greater flexibility at additional runtime cost. We introduce \textbf{WAQS} (\textbf{W}eight \textbf{A}bsorption for \textbf{Q}uadratic probing and affine \textbf{S}teering), a framework that obtains state-dependent steering, without additional inference-time computation. WAQS models a concept with a quadratic probe, whose gradient yields an affine, activation-dependent steering direction. We show that this affine intervention can be folded exactly into adjacent linear transformations through an offline weight update. Moreover, we prove that quadratic functions form the maximal class of smooth concept scores whose gradient-based interventions are affine and therefore exactly absorbable into linear layers. Under a Gaussian representation model, our formulation admits an interpretation as the difference of class-conditional Mahalanobis pulls and naturally generalizes linear discriminant and difference-in-means steering. To scale to high-dimensional representations, we introduce a low-rank parameterization of the quadratic term. Across truthfulness, refusal, and sycophancy steering tasks, quadratic steering matches or improves upon constant linear steering while preserving model utility, with the absorbed implementation introducing no additional inference-time operations. Our results suggest that quadratic probes provide a practical middle ground between static linear steering and computationally expensive dynamic nonlinear interventions.
papers.summary: Activation steering controls LLM behavior without fine-tuning. Fixed steering vectors add almost no cost but cannot adapt to the input, while input-dependent nonlinear interventions are more flexible but slow down inference. `WAQS` models a concept with a quadratic probe, whose gradient gives an affine steering direction that depends on the current activation, and that intervention can be folded exactly into neighboring linear layers through an offline weight update. The authors prove that quadratic functions are the largest class of smooth concept scores whose gradient-based interventions can be absorbed this way, and they show the method generalizes linear discriminant and difference-in-means steering. On truthfulness, refusal, and sycophancy tasks it matches or beats constant linear steering while preserving utility, with **no added inference-time operations**.

papers.title: Tactix: Towards a Programmable Strategy Interface for Flexible SAT Solving
papers.abstract: Modern SAT solvers combine a rich repertoire of proof rules with sophisticated strategies that determine when and how to apply them. Often, the internal implementations are tightly coupled to particular strategies, making it inconvenient to define new strategies without changing solver internals. We present Tactix, a proof-producing sequential CDCL solver that incorporates a wide range of techniques in state-of-the-art solvers with a clean separation of proof rules from solving strategies. This separation enables a public interface through which users can invoke particular techniques, observe their effects, and program a wide range of solving strategies. The default strategy of Tactix is programmable over this interface and outperforms state-of-the-art solvers on benchmarks from the 2024--2026 SAT Competitions. We also use the interface to develop novel strategies tailored to challenging benchmarks from two application domains, which led to performance gains over strong baselines. We intend Tactix to serve as an infrastructure for designing and evaluating novel solving strategies. Finally, we also present a self-study of the AI-assisted development process behind Tactix.
papers.summary: In modern SAT solvers, proof rules are usually tightly entangled with the strategies that decide when to apply them, so trying a new strategy means changing solver internals. `Tactix` is a proof-producing sequential conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) solver that separates proof rules from strategies and exposes a public interface for invoking techniques, observing their effects, and programming new strategies. Its default strategy, written against this interface, **outperforms state-of-the-art solvers on benchmarks from the 2024–2026 SAT Competitions**, and custom strategies built for two application domains beat strong baselines. The authors also include a self-study of the AI-assisted development process used to build the solver.

papers.title: Revisiting Smoothed Online Learning: Competitive Ratio, Dynamic Regret with Switching Cost, and Best of Both Worlds
papers.abstract: We revisit smoothed online learning and develop algorithms with improved competitive ratios, optimal dynamic regret with switching cost, and best-of-both-worlds guarantees. Surprisingly, minimizing the hitting cost alone is $\max(1,\frac{2}{\alpha})$-competitive for $\alpha$-polyhedral functions under the $\ell_2$-norm switching cost and $1+\frac{4}{\lambda}$-competitive for $\lambda$-quadratic growth functions under the squared $\ell_2$-norm switching cost, significantly improving existing guarantees. The polyhedral bound is tight for this naive algorithm, and we establish a matching lower bound for $\alpha\geq1$. For convex $\lambda$-quadratic growth hitting costs, minimizing a suitably weighted sum of hitting and squared $\ell_2$-norm switching costs yields a competitive ratio of $1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{\lambda}}$. For dynamic regret with the $\ell_2$-norm switching cost, we develop Smoothed Ader (SAder), which achieves the optimal $O(\sqrt{T(1+P_T)})$ rate in the standard online convex optimization setting, where $P_T$ is the comparator's path-length. Its lookahead version removes the bounded-gradient assumption, and a matching lower bound establishes optimality in this setting. Finally, for convex hitting costs on a bounded convex domain, we develop UDNP to aggregate any two experts in the lookahead setting under both switching costs. Its additional cumulative cost is at most $O(1)$ relative to the first expert and $O(\sqrt{T\log T})$ relative to the second, yielding best-of-both-worlds guarantees without bounded gradients.
papers.summary: Smoothed online learning is an online optimization setting in which each decision pays a hitting cost plus a cost for switching away from the previous decision; the authors revisit it and give improved guarantees. A key result is that **simply minimizing the hitting cost is max(1, 2/α)-competitive for α-polyhedral functions** under ℓ2 switching cost, with a tight matching lower bound for α ≥ 1, and similarly strong bounds hold for quadratic-growth functions. They also introduce `SAder`, which achieves the optimal O(√(T(1+P_T))) dynamic regret with switching cost, where P_T is the path length of the comparator sequence. A third method, `UDNP`, combines any two experts to give best-of-both-worlds guarantees without assuming bounded gradients.

papers.title: Beyond Next-Screen Prediction: The Decision Value of GUI World Models
papers.abstract: GUI world models are increasingly used to improve action selection by predicting the consequences of candidate actions, but it is unclear how much of the resulting gain comes from prediction itself rather than from the evaluator that interprets those predictions. We study this attribution problem through controlled interventions on GUI action selection. With candidates and predictions held fixed, lookahead gains can change with how the prediction is presented to the evaluator, so end-to-end gains cannot be attributed to prediction alone. We then introduce Direct Action Ranking (DAR), which learns from reference actions to score candidates without generating future screens, and compare it with a prediction-augmented variant under matched supervision. Predicted successors add no detectable ranking signal once evaluation is learned directly. Without retraining, DAR improves AndroidWorld task success by 5.8--16.4 points across three proposers, outperforms world-model lookahead, and transfers zero-shot to unseen apps, where every prediction-conditioned configuration falls below proposer confidence. These results suggest that GUI world models should be evaluated by their decision value, the incremental action-selection value of their predictions beyond a strong direct evaluator, rather than by prediction fidelity or end-to-end lookahead gain alone.
papers.summary: GUI world models predict what the screen will look like after a candidate action, and those predictions are used to pick better actions; the open question is how much of the gain comes from prediction itself versus from the evaluator reading the predictions.
