Controlled experiments show that, with candidates and predictions held fixed, lookahead gains change depending on how predictions are presented to the evaluator. `Direct Action Ranking` (`DAR`) learns to score candidate actions from reference actions without generating any future screens, and once evaluation is learned directly, predicted next screens add no detectable ranking signal. Without retraining, `DAR` **improves `AndroidWorld` task success by 5.8–16.4 points** across three action proposers, beats world-model lookahead, and transfers zero-shot to unseen apps.

papers.title: Defending Against Dormant Poisoning Attacks Across Language and Multimodal Agents
papers.abstract: Recent work shows that attackers can implant dormant malicious behaviors that remain hidden at release but emerge after benign fine-tuning. As foundation models are used as agents, whether dormant poisoning extends to harmful agent actions and multimodal settings remains unclear. We show two agentic risks: (1) harmful behaviors activated by benign fine-tuning can extend to unseen actions; (2) multiple harmful behaviors can coexist and be jointly activated by benign downstream fine-tuning. Existing defenses often rely on external safe responses, which are hard to obtain for agent actions, or a trusted clean reference model. We exploit a key property of dormant poisoning: the attacker must preserve safe behavior at release to conceal poisoning, and this behavior can serve as a safety reference. Leveraging this property, we automatically construct a Safety Buffer pairing harmful inputs with the released model's responses and benign versions generated by the same model to remove harmful intent. The Safety Buffer can replace external safe responses in existing defenses, but these defenses do not distinguish updates that weaken safety from those that preserve it, often increasing over-refusal or reducing utility. To address this limitation, we introduce LookAhead Defense, which previews benign fine-tuning updates using the Safety Buffer and penalizes only updates predicted to weaken safe behavior on harmful inputs or increase the likelihood of refusals on benign versions in the Safety Buffer. Across language models, language agents, and multimodal agents, LookAhead Defense reduces harmful behavior in agents from up to 93.9% to at most 14.2% and harmful responses in language models from up to 92.5% to at most 2.0% versus vanilla fine-tuning, while maintaining competitive utility and low over-refusal. It remains effective against other poisoning methods.
papers.summary: Dormant poisoning hides malicious behaviors in a released model that only appear after benign downstream fine-tuning. The authors show that in agents, these activated behaviors can extend to unseen harmful actions, and that several harmful behaviors can coexist and be activated together. Their defense relies on the fact that an attacker must keep the released model's behavior safe to hide the poisoning: they build a `Safety Buffer` from the released model's own responses to harmful inputs, paired with benign rewrites of those inputs. `LookAhead Defense` then previews each fine-tuning update and penalizes only updates predicted to weaken safety or increase over-refusal, **cutting harmful agent behavior from up to 93.9% to at most 14.2%** while keeping utility competitive.

papers.title: Train Locally, Learn Together: Distributed Multi-Agent Training via ADMM
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) can outperform individual language-model agents by combining specialized roles, diverse reasoning processes, and collaborative decision-making. However, collaborative MAS training is typically centralized, requiring a common trainer to aggregate role-local trajectories and learning signals and maintain model and optimization states. This motivates a distributed multi-agent learning paradigm in which agents improve system-level capabilities through role-local learning and decentralized communication, paving the way toward scalable, resilient, and self-organizing MAS. To this end, we introduce, to the best of our knowledge, the first optimization-grounded framework for distributed MAS training based on consensus alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). We formulate collaborative MAS learning as a consensus-constrained finite-sum optimization problem, naturally lending itself to distributed optimization via ADMM. The proposed approach alternates role-local learning with inter-agent consensus using distributed communication protocols such as ring all-reduce, enabling joint optimization while keeping each agent's data and training state local. We evaluate our framework on distributed safety alignment and general reasoning tasks. Under compromised-agent settings, ADMM can reduce HarmBench attack success rate (ASR) by up to 26.4%, while achieving reasoning gains comparable to centralized training. These results show that distributed MAS training retains the benefits of centralized joint optimization without requiring a centralized trainer.
papers.summary: Training LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) together usually needs a central trainer that gathers every agent's trajectories, learning signals, and optimizer state. The authors frame collaborative MAS learning as a consensus-constrained optimization problem and solve it with consensus alternating direction method of multipliers (`ADMM`), alternating local training for each role with inter-agent consensus over protocols such as ring all-reduce. Each agent's data and training state stay local. On safety alignment and general reasoning tasks, the approach **matches the reasoning gains of centralized training** and, when some agents are compromised, cuts `HarmBench` attack success rate by up to 26.4%.

papers.title: Learning from the Right Regions: Class-Conditioned Explanation Guidance for Medical Imaging
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks can achieve strong predictive performance in medical imaging while relying on regions unrelated to the predicted finding. Explanation-guided learning can address this problem, but multi-label classification introduces a key challenge: multiple abnormalities may coexist in an image, requiring each prediction to align with its corresponding spatial evidence. We propose a class-conditioned explanation-guided learning framework that constructs a separate explanation for each positive class and penalizes evidence outside its class-specific annotated regions. We instantiate the framework using Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) and evaluate it on 14 abnormalities using EfficientNet-B1, ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, and Swin-B. Explanation guidance substantially improves annotation alignment across all architectures: All-Saliency Precision increases from 0.140 to 0.625, 0.052 to 0.551, 0.060 to 0.403, and 0.095 to 0.570, respectively. These improvements are accompanied by smaller, architecture-dependent changes in classification performance. Our results show that class-conditioned explanation guidance can substantially improve where multi-label classifiers concentrate their explanatory evidence while largely preserving predictive performance.
papers.summary: Medical imaging classifiers can predict accurately while basing their decisions on image regions unrelated to the finding, and multi-label settings make this harder because several abnormalities can appear in the same image. The proposed framework builds a separate explanation for each positive class with Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (`Grad-CAM`) and penalizes evidence that falls outside that class's annotated regions. Across 14 abnormalities and four architectures (`EfficientNet-B1`, `ViT-B/16`, `ViT-B/32`, `Swin-B`), alignment with annotations improves sharply, for example **All-Saliency Precision rising from 0.140 to 0.625** on `EfficientNet-B1`. Classification performance changes only slightly, and the size of the change depends on the architecture.

papers.title: Is This Your Agent? Identity Watermarking for Agent Systems in Dynamic Environments
papers.abstract: Agent systems deployed in dynamic environments continuously update their memories, skills, and runtime configurations, leading to evolving trajectories and challenges for persistent identity authentication. Existing text and agent watermarking methods struggle to achieve stable watermark embedding under dynamic environments, while embedded watermarks may become difficult to recover due to environmental changes. This paper proposes DASMark, an identity watermarking framework for dynamic agent systems. DASMark introduces Action-Preserving Embedding (APE), which learns semantically similar but distinguishable decision-expression channels from diverse interaction trajectories to enable stable watermark embedding in dynamic systems. It further introduces Shift-Robust Recovery (SRR) to mitigate context-induced shifts and improve watermark recovery stability under dynamic environments. In dynamic settings, DASMark achieves 98.5% bit-decoding accuracy and maintains 95.2% accuracy under attack scenarios, while preserving task utility comparable to unwatermarked agents.
papers.summary: Agents deployed in changing environments keep updating their memories, skills, and configurations, which makes it hard to embed and later recover a watermark that proves an agent's identity. `DASMark` addresses this with `Action-Preserving Embedding`, which learns decision-expression channels that are semantically similar yet distinguishable from one another, drawn from diverse interaction trajectories. It adds `Shift-Robust Recovery` to counter context-induced drift when the watermark is read back. In dynamic settings it reaches **98.5% bit-decoding accuracy**, keeps 95.2% under attack, and preserves task utility comparable to unwatermarked agents.

papers.title: IF-MAP: Influence-Function-Inspired Agent Prioritization in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Improving every agent in an LLM-based multi-agent system can be prohibitively costly, making it important to identify which agent should be prioritized to achieve the greatest system-level gain with limited resources. Failure attribution can inform this decision, but an agent's responsibility for failures does not directly reveal the system-level gains achievable by improving it. We therefore introduce IF-MAP, an influence-function-inspired method for identifying agents with high potential for system-level improvement. For each agent, IF-MAP measures end-to-end loss changes under controlled semantic prompt perturbations, fits a regularized local response model in a low-dimensional prompt-embedding subspace, and uses the estimated response norm as a priority score. This black-box procedure requires no access to model parameters or gradients and produces agent priorities that can guide subsequent improvement effort. We evaluate IF-MAP across six multi-agent workflows spanning code generation, question answering, and mathematical reasoning, using the same priorities for prompt optimization and model upgrades. Optimizing the selected agents' prompts achieves a macro-average gain of 3.81 percentage points, compared with 1.85 for uniform agent selection. Across five target models, upgrading the selected agents yields macro-average gains of 7.62-16.42 percentage points, compared with 3.81-8.62 for uniform agent selection. Despite its probing overhead, IF-MAP reduces Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V3.2 token use by 74.2% and 35.2%, respectively, relative to optimizing every agent, and reduces target-model tokens by 63.6-64.9% relative to upgrading every agent. These results support the use of IF-MAP to identify promising agents and direct improvement effort toward greater end-to-end performance gains.
papers.summary: Improving every agent in an LLM multi-agent system is expensive, and knowing which agent caused a failure does not tell you which one would yield the biggest system-level gain if improved. `IF-MAP`, inspired by influence functions, applies controlled semantic perturbations to each agent's prompt, measures how end-to-end loss changes, fits a regularized local response model in a low-dimensional prompt-embedding space, and uses the size of that response as a priority score. The method is black-box and needs no access to parameters or gradients. Across six workflows spanning code generation, question answering, and math, optimizing the prompts of the selected agents yields **a 3.81-point macro-average gain versus 1.85 for uniform selection**, while using far fewer tokens than optimizing every agent.

papers.title: A decomposition-integration framework coupling singular spectrum analysis with a volatility-adaptive LSTM for stock price forecasting
papers.abstract: Financial time series exhibit multi-scale, high-noise, and non-stationary volatility dynamics. Decomposition--integration frameworks built on complete ensemble empirical mode decomposition with adaptive noise (CEEMDAN) have advanced this field, yet existing CEEMDAN hybrids remain unstable: high-frequency mode mixing contaminates downstream predictors, and the heterogeneous volatility of decomposed components is not matched by any volatility-adaptive mechanism. To address these gaps, this paper proposes CEEMDAN-SE-SSA-VMGL. CEEMDAN adaptively decomposes the original series, and sample-entropy-driven K-means clustering groups the intrinsic mode functions into high-, mid-, and low-frequency and residual components. Singular spectrum analysis (SSA) is then applied to the high-frequency group, whose singular-value decomposition of the trajectory matrix and principal-component reconstruction decouple intertwined pseudo-oscillatory modes and alleviate mode mixing. We further design a plug-and-play robust LSTM variant, the volatility-modulated GARCH-LSTM (VMGL), which embeds a differentiable GARCH(1,1) layer inside the LSTM cell as a risk gate; the estimated conditional volatility multiplicatively scales the forget-gate activation, letting memory decay adapt to the instantaneous volatility while remaining fully end-to-end trainable. Component predictions are linearly combined. On five US and Chinese financial series (CSI 300, CSI 500, AAPL, GOOGL, S&P 500), the proposed model is compared with eleven benchmark architectures, lowering the forecasting error by 9% to 24% relative to the best benchmark and by 60% to 70% relative to a standard LSTM. Diebold--Mariano and model-confidence-set (MCS) tests confirm the statistical significance and stability of the gains, spectral analyses verify the SSA denoising efficacy, and backtesting demonstrates the framework's economic utility.
papers.summary: Hybrid forecasters built on complete ensemble empirical mode decomposition with adaptive noise (`CEEMDAN`) are unstable for financial time series, because high-frequency mode mixing contaminates downstream predictors and no mechanism adapts to the differing volatility of each decomposed component. The proposed `CEEMDAN-SE-SSA-VMGL` model groups decomposed components by sample entropy and applies singular spectrum analysis (`SSA`) to the high-frequency group to reduce mode mixing. Each group is then forecast with `VMGL`, an LSTM variant whose forget gate is scaled by a differentiable `GARCH(1,1)` volatility estimate. On five U.S. and Chinese market series it **lowers forecasting error by 9–24% relative to the best of eleven benchmarks**, and statistical tests confirm the gains are significant.

papers.title: Bridging Exploration and Persona: Information-Directed Dueling for Test-Time Agent Personalization
papers.abstract: Effective test-time personalization requires LLM agents to adapt to query-dependent user preferences from lightweight interaction. We study persona selection with binary comparisons between candidate responses as the online signal. We present ID-TAP, a scalable, IDS-inspired neural dueling-bandit framework for large discrete persona spaces. ID-TAP combines a query-conditioned neural utility model with a lightweight Bradley-Terry explorer, and transfers comparison evidence across related queries through similarity-weighted warm starts. The neural model shares statistical strength across queries while preserving query-specific scores, and efficient BT updates score hypothetical challengers. Across seven user-conditioned generation benchmarks under reference- and model-based preference simulators, ID-TAP achieves the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated baselines within a fixed ten-round comparison budget. These results support information-directed challenger selection as an effective design for test-time persona adaptation.
papers.summary: LLM agents personalized at test time need to infer query-dependent user preferences from light interaction; here the signal is binary comparisons between candidate responses, used to choose among a large set of personas. `ID-TAP` is a neural dueling-bandit framework inspired by information-directed sampling (IDS). It pairs a query-conditioned neural utility model with a lightweight `Bradley-Terry` explorer and warm-starts new queries with comparison evidence from similar ones. Across seven user-conditioned generation benchmarks and two kinds of preference simulators, it achieves **the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated baselines within a ten-round comparison budget**.

papers.title: Learning volatility-adaptive forgetting via GARCH-modulated LSTM for stock price forecasting
papers.abstract: Stock price forecasting is hindered by the heteroscedastic nature of financial time series, in which turbulent and tranquil regimes alternate. Although the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network is widely used for this task, its gates are oblivious to such volatility variation, so memory retention remains fixed regardless of market conditions. A common remedy is to supply volatility estimates as an additional input feature, yet this leaves the internal memory dynamics untouched. Instead, volatility can serve as a direct regulatory signal over the gate activation itself. This paper presents the Gsigmoid-LSTM model, which embeds Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity (GARCH(1,1))-derived volatility estimates into the LSTM forgetting gate through the Gsigmoid activation function, a volatility-adaptive variant of the sigmoid that combines a volatility adjustment factor with slope regulation via a learnable parameter. The model thereby automatically prioritizes recent information during turbulent periods while preserving long-term dependencies in stable markets. In the engineering application of daily stock price forecasting, extensive experiments, including activation function comparisons, baseline evaluations, and ablation studies, demonstrate that this structural gating modification effectively improves forecasting accuracy and robustness. The proposed model significantly outperforms a feature-level fusion baseline carrying the same volatility signal on all five datasets, as confirmed by Diebold-Mariano tests with all p<0.01, attains the best average rank of 1.00 in the Friedman test across nine models, and achieves the lowest MSE and MAE on all five datasets.
papers.summary: Standard LSTM gates ignore whether markets are calm or turbulent, so memory retention stays fixed, and adding a volatility estimate as an extra input feature leaves the internal memory dynamics unchanged. `Gsigmoid-LSTM` instead feeds Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity (`GARCH(1,1)`) volatility estimates directly into the forget gate through `Gsigmoid`, a volatility-adjusted sigmoid with a learnable slope. The model therefore favors recent information in turbulent periods and keeps long-term dependencies in stable ones. On five daily stock datasets it **significantly outperforms a feature-fusion baseline that uses the same volatility signal (Diebold-Mariano p<0.01)** and achieves the lowest MSE and MAE among nine models.

papers.title: Trust the Edge, Doubt the Arrow: Auditing Validation Signals for Text-Mined Clinical Causal Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Clinical causal retrieval-augmented generation systems increasingly use knowledge graphs (KGs) mined from notes, yet extracted assertions remain candidates that require audit for patient-level EHR support and direction. We construct a directed candidate graph from 328,839 MIMIC-IV discharge summaries using LLM extraction and UMLS normalization, and evaluate three signals against SemMedDB: within-admission co-occurrence lift, cross-admission diagnosis-coding temporal precedence, and literature corroboration. Lift filters unsupported co-mentions and provides useful EHR support, but not causal proof. Coding order is a weak direction signal: among the 686 candidates where it commits, it reaches 54.2% agreement with SemMedDB, below the extractor's 69.4% on the same subset. Literature corroboration supplies independent direction evidence but covers only 30.4% of candidate relations. A MIMIC-III replication yields the same pattern: extractor direction remains stable (70.5%), whereas coding-order direction is near chance (50.9%). Thus, text-mined clinical causal candidate KGs are best treated as EHR-supported but direction-uncertain. In a leakage-controlled causal QA benchmark, lift-only retrieval achieves 35.7% accuracy; conservative causal demotion achieves 37.2% while reducing evidence-unsupported answers from 17.3% to 6.1% at fixed retrieval recall. We release code, aggregate summaries, and scripts to regenerate restricted outputs.
papers.summary: Clinical retrieval-augmented generation systems increasingly draw on causal knowledge graphs mined from clinical notes, but the extracted cause-and-effect links still need checking for patient-level support and for direction. The authors build a directed candidate graph from 328,839 `MIMIC-IV` discharge summaries using LLM extraction and `UMLS` normalization, then test three validation signals against `SemMedDB`: co-occurrence lift, the temporal order of diagnosis codes, and corroboration in the literature. Lift is useful for filtering unsupported links, but **coding order is a weak direction signal (54.2% agreement versus 69.4% for the extractor)**, and literature corroboration covers only 30.4% of relations; a `MIMIC-III` replication shows the same pattern. On a causal QA benchmark, conservatively demoting uncertain causal links cuts evidence-unsupported answers from 17.3% to 6.1%.

papers.title: MSCR: Jointly Balancing Utilization Across Modalities and Discovering Synergistic Information
papers.abstract: In multimodal learning, modality imbalance often lets one modality dominate optimization and keeps the model from fully exploiting cross-modal interactions. Balance-oriented methods such as the Multimodal Competition Regularizer (MCR) perform well by alleviating this imbalance during training. These dynamic balancing methods, however, mainly adjust modality contributions and do not consider how imbalance affects the formation of synergistic information during fusion. Synergy is a major source of multimodal advantage, because it is predictive gain that cannot be recovered from unimodal evidence alone. We propose the Multimodal Synergistic Competition Regularizer (MSCR), a fusion method that jointly promotes balanced modality utilization and the discovery of synergistic information. MSCR has two complementary objectives. An anti-dominance objective suppresses excessive unimodal influence and leaves room for synergistic information, and a synergy objective encourages the fused predictor to outperform a non-synergistic unimodal reference. An adaptive gate further concentrates the regularization on samples that need stronger collaborative modeling. Experiments on five benchmarks show that MSCR consistently improves performance over MCR and strengthens synergistic capability. It raises conditional recovery, the accuracy of the fused prediction on samples that the unimodal predictors misclassify, as well as the share of the model's output that InterSHAP attributes to cross-modal interactions. Its gain in conditional recovery persists when the fusion module is Transformer-based. Code is available at https://github.com/chenxinyu991-collab/MSCR.
papers.summary: In multimodal learning, one modality often dominates training, and existing balancing methods such as the Multimodal Competition Regularizer (`MCR`) adjust each modality's contribution without considering whether fusion is learning synergy, meaning predictive gains no single modality can provide. `MSCR` adds an anti-dominance objective that limits excessive influence from any single modality and a synergy objective that pushes the fused predictor to beat a non-synergistic unimodal reference. An adaptive gate focuses this regularization on the samples that need it most. On five benchmarks, `MSCR` **consistently improves over `MCR`** and raises both accuracy on samples that the unimodal predictors get wrong and the share of output that `InterSHAP` attributes to cross-modal interactions.

papers.title: Prototype-Guided Optimization of Quantum Data Embeddings with Linear Cost
papers.abstract: In supervised quantum machine learning with classical data, classification performance critically depends on the geometry induced by quantum data embedding. Existing data-adaptive approaches rely on pairwise fidelity evaluations between samples, which scale as $O(B^2)$ for $B$ samples and create a computational bottleneck in iterative embedding optimization. To address this issue, we propose a prototype-guided framework for efficient data-adaptive quantum embedding. Using class-prototype separation and sample-to-prototype compactness, we derive a measurable lower certificate for class-ensemble distinguishability and construct a prototype-based objective requiring only $O(B)$ fidelity evaluations. We integrate this objective into an end-to-end pipeline that combines task-specific quantum circuit architecture optimization with continuous refinement of the data-embedding parameters. Across five benchmark datasets with up to 20 qubits, our method retains competitive quantum kernel support vector machine (SVM) performance while reducing fidelity-evaluation cost, with particularly strong gains over budget-matched pairwise optimization on T-MNIST. Geometric analyses examine how the learned embeddings relate to kernel alignment and classification margins, revealing dataset-dependent benefits and limitations. We further derive a prototype-based classifier in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space that provides an explicit witness for the SVM objective and a low-cost proxy for model selection, and extend the framework to multiple prototypes for multimodal class structures.
papers.summary: In quantum machine learning on classical data, classification quality depends on how data is embedded into quantum states, and existing adaptive embedding methods need pairwise fidelity evaluations whose cost grows quadratically with the number of samples. The authors derive a measurable lower bound on how distinguishable the classes are, based on how far class prototypes are from each other and how close samples are to their own prototype. This yields an objective that **needs only a linear number of fidelity evaluations**, and they combine it with quantum circuit architecture search and refinement of the embedding parameters. On five datasets with up to 20 qubits, the method keeps quantum kernel support vector machine (SVM) accuracy competitive at lower cost, with particularly strong gains on `T-MNIST`.

papers.title: ZeroDSS: Semantic Segmentation from Class Names Alone
papers.abstract: Semantic segmentation depends heavily on real images with pixel-level annotations, making dense supervision a major obstacle to deployment in new domains. We study task-specific data-free semantic segmentation, where training uses generic pretrained generative priors but has access to no target-domain images, masks, or captions--only a predefined category set. We introduce Zero-Data Semantic Segmentation (ZeroDSS), a feedback-driven approach that treats synthetic supervision as an adaptively controllable training distribution rather than a direct surrogate for real data. ZeroDSS constructs a semantically structured prompt distribution through LLM-guided compositional generation and adaptive class rebalancing, then converts the prompts into image-mask pairs using diffusion attention. Its feedback-driven distribution refinement consists of a two-phase closed-loop training procedure with a single loop-back step. In Phase I, a segmenter is trained using confidence-weighted supervision and dual-scale consistency. In Phase II, model feedback is used to adaptively target underperforming categories and refine diffusion-derived masks using model predictions. After this refined initial training, a teacher-student framework is utilized in the final phase to iteratively improve the fused supervision and segmenter through exponential moving average (EMA) updates. Using synthetic training data only, ZeroDSS achieves 35.0% mIoU on MS COCO with DeepLabV3, and 66.3% and 63.5% mIoU on PASCAL VOC with DeepLabV3 and Mask2Former, respectively. These results show that explicitly constructing and iteratively refining the synthetic supervision distribution can substantially reduce the synthetic-to-real gap in dense prediction.
papers.summary: Semantic segmentation usually needs real images with pixel-level labels; this work asks how far a model can get given only a list of class names, with no images, masks, or captions from the target domain. `ZeroDSS` uses an LLM to compose a structured, class-balanced set of prompts, turns those prompts into image-mask pairs using diffusion model attention, and treats this synthetic data as a training distribution it can adjust. A closed training loop uses the segmenter's own feedback to target weak categories and refine the masks, followed by an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher-student phase. Trained only on synthetic data, it reaches **35.0% mIoU on `MS COCO`** with `DeepLabV3` and 66.3% mIoU on `PASCAL VOC`.

papers.title: Long Listening Thoughts: Eliciting Open Auditory Reasoning with Deliberative Perception and Cognitive Refinement
papers.abstract: We introduce Long Listening Thoughts (LLT), a framework for constructing post-training datasets that improves audio reasoning by pairing deliberate perceptual grounding with explicit cognitive behaviors. On audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks, large audio-language models (LALMs) are limited primarily by perceptual errors, yet existing post-training datasets rely on audio descriptions of limited diversity. Through a four-stage pipeline, LLT (1) builds multi-aspect dense audio descriptions spanning semantic, acoustic, and temporal information, (2) generates more challenging questions, (3) synthesizes incorrect reasoning traces, and (4) extends short reasoning traces into long ones via a thought-continuation strategy that elicits cognitive behaviors such as verification and backtracking. Using LLT, we synthesize 1.6M reasoning traces and train Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with a two-stage pipeline of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by direct preference optimization (DPO). This improves accuracy on MMAU Test-mini (71.5 to 78.2), MMAR (56.7 to 63.7), and MMSU (60.6 to 66.0).
papers.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) mostly fail audio reasoning benchmarks because of perception errors, and existing post-training data relies on audio descriptions with little diversity. `Long Listening Thoughts` (`LLT`) is a four-stage data pipeline that writes dense audio descriptions covering semantic, acoustic, and temporal detail, generates harder questions, synthesizes incorrect reasoning traces, and extends short traces into long ones that include verification and backtracking. The resulting 1.6M traces are used to train `Qwen2.5-Omni-7B` with supervised fine-tuning followed by direct preference optimization (DPO). Accuracy improves on `MMAU` Test-mini (**71.5 to 78.2**), `MMAR` (56.7 to 63.7), and `MMSU` (60.6 to 66.0).

papers.title: Ask Less, Ask Better: Allocating User Attention in Proactive LLM Agents with Interruption Budgets
papers.abstract: LLM agents can ask clarifying questions to complete tasks, but answering each question demands users' time and effort. Existing evaluations typically measure this burden by counting questions, treating necessary and avoidable questions equally. We propose an evaluation protocol that distinguishes how often agents ask from how well they ask. An interruption budget limits the number of questions, while a user-attention cost charges extra for questions that are hard to read or not worth asking, as rated by a human-validated LLM judge. Beyond question counts, this cost captures perceived effort: on conversation pairs with the same number of questions, human annotators agreed with the cost on which conversation required more effort 75% of the time. Across eight LLMs and four customer-service domains, limiting agents to one to three questions reduces user-attention cost by 36-73% while keeping 86-94% of the task reward they earn with unlimited questions. At the same budget, reviewing each question against the memory of users' earlier answers cuts attention cost by another 13% with little reward loss and yields more valuable questions. Models also differ sharply in how well they ask: at the same user-attention cost, the most efficient models gain more than twice as much reward from their questions as the others. These results show that asking less and asking better are distinct goals, and that evaluations of proactive agents should measure both.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can ask users clarifying questions, but current evaluations mostly just count those questions, so a necessary question costs the same as an avoidable one. The authors propose an evaluation that pairs an interruption budget (a cap on questions) with a user-attention cost, which a human-validated LLM judge assigns to penalize questions that are hard to read or not worth asking. Human annotators agreed with this cost 75% of the time when comparing conversations that had the same number of questions. Across eight LLMs and four customer-service domains, limiting agents to one to three questions **cuts user-attention cost by 36-73% while keeping 86-94% of the task reward**. Checking each question against the user's earlier answers lowers cost by a further 13%, and the most efficient models get more than twice as much reward from their questions as others at the same cost.

papers.title: Cross-Dimension and Cross-Modality Relational Tensor Representation Learning for Multimodal Health Data Modeling
papers.abstract: Multimodal health data integrate information from heterogeneous clinical sources, creating substantial opportunities for data-driven decision support. Realizing these opportunities, however, requires effectively modeling complex dependencies that arise both within individual modalities and across modalities. This paper proposes Relational Tensor Representation (RTR), a unified framework that jointly learns dimension-specific tensor representations and cross-dimensional and cross-modality relationships. RTR introduces learnable relational bridge matrices that maintain relational information while preserving the structural identities of tensor dimensions and modalities. A structured fusion mechanism further integrates factor-level and relationship-level information into compact representations for downstream prediction. Experiments on simulated data and two multimodal neurophysiological datasets, covering emotion recognition and brain activity classification, demonstrate that RTR consistently outperforms representative tensor learning, multimodal fusion, and Transformer-based baselines. These results highlight the value of explicitly modeling cross-dimensional and cross-modality relationships for learning informative representations from heterogeneous multimodal tensor data. The source code is planned for public release to support reproducibility and future research.
papers.summary: Multimodal health data combines several clinical sources, and modeling it well means capturing dependencies both within each data source and across sources. `Relational Tensor Representation` (`RTR`) learns a separate tensor representation for each dimension, plus learnable relational bridge matrices that link dimensions and modalities while keeping each one's identity intact. A structured fusion step then merges factor-level and relationship-level information into compact features for prediction. On simulated data and two neurophysiological datasets, one for emotion recognition and one for brain activity classification, **`RTR` consistently outperforms tensor learning, multimodal fusion, and Transformer baselines**.

papers.title: Toward a Universal Local Speech Feature Extractor Through Distillation
papers.abstract: Self-supervised speech models commonly consist of a set of convolutional neural network (CNN) layers used as a local feature extractor, followed by transformer layers. The CNN layers are computationally demanding, and are also similar across models and resemble the much simpler mel spectral features. We hypothesize that the CNN layers can be replaced by a simple, universal model. To test this hypothesis, we learn a two-layer feature extractor via distillation from one or more teacher models (HuBERT, data2vec, and WavLM). Experiments on SUPERB(-SG) benchmark tasks show that our model largely retains the performance of the teacher models and can also be used in an unseen model (wav2vec 2.0). Our feature extractor requires only 3% of the MACs of the CNNs, resulting in a $>$20% overall inference runtime reduction.
papers.summary: Self-supervised speech models usually start with a stack of convolutional neural network (CNN) layers that extract local features. These layers are expensive to run, look similar across models, and resemble simple mel spectral features. The authors replace them with a two-layer feature extractor distilled from one or more teachers (`HuBERT`, `data2vec`, `WavLM`). On `SUPERB` and `SUPERB-SG` tasks, the extractor largely keeps the teachers' performance and also works when plugged into a model it was not distilled from (`wav2vec 2.0`). It needs **only 3% of the CNN's multiply-accumulate operations, which reduces total inference runtime by more than 20%**.

papers.title: Margin-Based Generalization for Quantum Machine Learning with Classical Data Encoding
papers.abstract: Understanding generalization is essential for assessing the practical viability of quantum machine learning. In many applications, quantum models operate on classical data that must first be encoded into quantum states, making the encoding part of the effective hypothesis class. We develop a margin-based generalization framework for this setting, covering both fixed and trainable quantum data encodings. For fixed encodings, the existing margin bound transfers unchanged. For trainable encodings, we derive a bound using a two-scale covering argument that combines the original margin-dependent term with an additive encoding-capacity term of order $\tilde O(\sqrt{L/m})$, where $L$ is the number of trainable encoding parameters and $m$ is the training-sample size. Across 19,440 simulated training runs spanning various image datasets, circuit architectures, and optimization settings, the inverse margin performs best among five baseline and two bound-derived complexity measures under conditional-independence and 90th-percentile sign-error criteria, within bootstrap uncertainty. These results provide a unified margin-based view of generalization in quantum machine learning with classical data.
papers.summary: When quantum machine learning models work on classical data, the step that encodes that data into quantum states becomes part of what the model learns, which complicates generalization theory. The authors develop margin-based generalization bounds for this setting. For fixed encodings, the existing margin bound carries over unchanged. For trainable encodings, a two-scale covering argument adds an encoding-capacity term of order **√(L/m)**, where L is the number of trainable encoding parameters and m is the number of training samples. Across 19,440 simulated training runs, the inverse margin predicts generalization better than five baseline measures and two measures derived from the bounds.

papers.title: When Opposite Premises Translate Identically: A Source-Conditioned Diagnostic for Multilingual Commonsense Items
papers.abstract: Multilingual reasoning comparisons depend on translated premises preserving the relations in their English sources. Automatic translation scores can rank source-target pairs, but an acceptance decision alone cannot certify a counterfactual benchmark field. We test a source-contrast diagnostic for ACCORD premises: reverse the English polarity, translate both arms independently, count identical target outputs, and score each arm against its own source. Across 71 matched question identities at two containing-item depths, five target languages, and three translation checkpoints, Swahili has 63, 113, and 67 exact collisions among 710 pairs per checkpoint. At a human-reference-calibrated threshold, round-trip NLI passes both arms of 3 of the 113 NLLB-3.3B collisions, while LaBSE passes 78. Each collision proves at least one unfaithful translation, but does not identify its arm. These controlled measurements do not establish screening accuracy on spontaneous translation errors or a language-by-hop reasoning effect; the study has no native equivalence labels or answer-model evaluation.
papers.summary: Comparisons of multilingual reasoning depend on translated premises keeping the meaning of their English sources, yet automatic translation-quality scores cannot certify that a counterfactual premise survived translation. The proposed diagnostic reverses the polarity of each English `ACCORD` premise, translates both versions independently, and counts cases where the two opposite premises come out identical in the target language. Swahili produced 63 to 113 such collisions out of 710 pairs, depending on the translation model. On the 113 collisions from `NLLB-3.3B`, **round-trip natural language inference (NLI) passed both versions in only 3 cases, while `LaBSE` passed 78**, showing that common quality filters can miss these errors. The authors note that the study has no native-speaker labels and does not evaluate answer models.

papers.title: Transport What Shares the Conduction Pathway: Normal-Anchored SPD Geometric Transport for Source-Free Patient Adaptation of Holter and Patch ECG
papers.abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) beat classifiers lose accuracy on new patients and devices, and source-free adaptation methods that assume class-balanced target batches fail on real recordings, whose label-free prefix is 87.9--98.6% normal beats. We propose Normal-Anchored Geometric Transport (NAGT, GA_NS), which estimates a closed-form symmetric positive-definite congruence map from label-free normal anchors in the first 5 min of each recording and applies it only to the normal and supraventricular prototypes, keeping the ventricular and fusion prototypes fixed. The score offsets and decision rules were set on MIT-BIH only; the rate-invariant RR head (relA) was adopted after the development databases (INCART, SVDB) had been opened; the frozen model was then evaluated once on Icentia11k chest-patch recordings under a pre-registered protocol. In 493 patients (973 recordings, 3,615,388 evaluated beats), NAGT reached an arrhythmia macro-$F_1$ $J = \frac{1}{2}(\text{S-}F_1 + \text{V-}F_1) = 48.7\%$ [95% CI 42.1, 54.7] versus 34.5% without adaptation ($\Delta J = +14.1$ [+8.6, +19.3] pp; 59.8% versus 43.9% in non-AF) and outperformed all five Holm-adjusted comparators, including AdaBN, Tent and T3A. In the 75-patient test subgroup of the historical split (73 analyzed), the gain was not significant (+6.1 [-8.5, +23.4] pp). Adaptation takes a median of 5.8 ms per record without back-propagation.
papers.summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) beat classifiers lose accuracy on new patients and devices. Existing source-free adaptation methods assume class-balanced data, while real recordings start with 87.9-98.6% normal beats. `Normal-Anchored Geometric Transport` (`NAGT`) computes a closed-form symmetric positive-definite congruence map from unlabeled normal beats in the first five minutes of a recording, then applies it only to the normal and supraventricular class prototypes. In a pre-registered one-time evaluation on 493 patients from the `Icentia11k` chest-patch dataset, it **raised arrhythmia macro-F1 from 34.5% to 48.7%**, beating `AdaBN`, `Tent`, and `T3A`. The gain was not significant on a smaller historical test split, and adaptation takes about 5.8 ms per recording without back-propagation.

papers.title: Transformers as Adaptive Kernel Learners across Tasks for In-Context Learning
papers.abstract: Transformers have emerged as a dominant architecture in modern machine learning, with in-context learning (ICL) enabling models to adapt to new tasks by conditioning on prompts, without any parameter updates. To understand the attention mechanism in transformer blocks, a growing line of theoretical work interprets ICL through the lens of classical statistical estimators. Recent works have established a connection between the attention mechanism and kernel methods, while the kernel function is usually assumed to be fixed. In practice, the query and key matrices in the attention mechanism are trained, which allows the attention mechanism to serve as an adaptive kernel method. In this work, we demonstrate that transformers can act as adaptive anisotropic kernel learners. Specifically, we study ICL for low-rank linear and multi-index nonlinear regressions, and conduct numerical simulations to show that the learned attention scores closely resemble the oracle kernels for these function classes. We then develop a general framework to analyze the generalization error of ICL by connecting transformers to the oracle kernel estimator for each function class. Our theory gives an explicit and constructive implementation of the oracle kernel estimators for these function classes using a wide and shallow transformer architecture, illustrating how the prediction is carried out by the interaction between the query token and the context tokens. Our work complements existing studies by providing numerical and theoretical evidence of how the attention mechanism adapts to anisotropic kernels in both linear and nonlinear settings.
papers.summary: Theoretical work often links attention in transformers to kernel methods, but it usually assumes a fixed kernel, even though the query and key matrices are trained. Studying in-context learning (ICL) on low-rank linear and multi-index nonlinear regression, the authors show in simulations that **learned attention scores closely match the oracle anisotropic kernels** for these function classes. They develop a framework that bounds ICL generalization error by relating transformers to these oracle kernel estimators. They also give an explicit construction that implements the estimators with a wide, shallow transformer.

papers.title: Near-Optimal Regret for Semi-Bandit Learning of Monotone Stochastic Problems
papers.abstract: We consider the task of learning an (approximately) optimal policy for stochastic optimization problems where the true distributions are unknown. In each period, the algorithm plays a policy for the stochastic problem and observes semi-bandit feedback, i.e., it only receives new samples from the random variables that were selected by the policy. We obtain an algorithm that works for a large class of ``monotone'' stochastic problems, including prophet inequality, Pandora's box, series testing, stochastic knapsack and stochastic matching. We obtain $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{nkT})$ regret for ``weakly'' monotone problems and $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{nT})$ regret for ``strongly'' monotone problems, where $T$ is the number of periods, $n$ is the problem dimension (number of random variables) and $k$ is the maximum support size of any random variable. This improves over previous regret bounds by a $\sqrt{n}$ factor. In fact, our dependence on $n$ and $T$ is the best-possible due the $\Omega(\sqrt{nT})$ lower bound for multi-armed-bandits. Our main technique is the use of Hellinger distance in bounding the ``error'' between the true and learned distributions, and the use of a constant-factor chain rule for the Hellinger distance of dependent random variables.
papers.summary: The setting is learning near-optimal policies for stochastic optimization problems with unknown distributions, under semi-bandit feedback, where the learner only observes samples of the random variables its policy chose. The algorithm covers a broad class of "monotone" problems, including prophet inequality, Pandora's box, stochastic knapsack, and stochastic matching. It achieves **Õ(√(nT)) regret for strongly monotone problems**, and Õ(√(nkT)) for weakly monotone ones. This improves prior bounds by a √n factor and matches the multi-armed bandit lower bound in n and T. The main tools are Hellinger-distance error bounds and a constant-factor chain rule for the Hellinger distance of dependent variables.

papers.title: Do 3D Large Language Models Really Use 3D Evidence?
papers.abstract: Recent 3D Large Language Models (3D-LLMs) have shown strong performance on scene question answering with extensive post-training. Yet, existing benchmarks rarely evaluate how 3D-LLMs respond to referential ambiguity, insufficient scene evidence, or false presuppositions, obscuring whether their responses are grounded in 3D evidence. In this work, we introduce UNICORNS, a benchmark for evaluating the reliability of 3D-LLM responses across four evidence conditions. UNICORNS contains 11,387 questions across 557 ScanNet scans, covering eight challenge categories alongside answerable controls. A response passes only if it satisfies the required response behavior and contains no scene claim unsupported by the available evidence. Evaluation of six open-sourced 3D-LLMs reveals a pronounced performance gap: even the strongest zero-shot model achieves 61.22% accuracy on answerable controls, but only 40.94% across the eight challenge categories. To address this gap, we further propose HORN, an obligation-aware post-training method combining group-relative task rewards, leaf-conditioned obligation rewards, and supervised control replay. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HORN reaches $75.1 \pm 1.0\%$ across the challenge categories and $77.2 \pm 0.8\%$ overall, outperforming all baselines without degrading answerable-control accuracy. Our findings enable a systematic evaluation and improvement of evidence-grounded 3D reasoning for 3D-LLMs (code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/unicorns-6B38/).
papers.summary: 3D large language models (3D-LLMs) score well on scene question answering, but benchmarks rarely test whether their answers actually rest on 3D evidence. `UNICORNS` is a benchmark of 11,387 questions over 557 `ScanNet` scans covering referential ambiguity, insufficient evidence, and false presuppositions, with answerable questions as controls. A response passes only if it behaves as required and makes no unsupported scene claims. The strongest of six open 3D-LLMs scores 61.22% on the controls but only 40.94% on the challenge categories. The proposed post-training method `HORN` combines group-relative task rewards, obligation rewards, and replay of supervised control examples, **raising challenge-category accuracy to 75.1%** without hurting accuracy on answerable questions.

papers.title: HumanSkill-4D: Training-Free Language Querying of Animatable Gaussian Avatars in Space and Time
papers.abstract: We introduce avatar referring segmentation, which selects regions of animatable Gaussian avatars from language queries. A query can also specify a pose or motion to select matching intervals. This lets users interact with avatars for local editing and motion inspection. However, making these selections with existing language Gaussian splatting methods poses two challenges: adjacent parts and garments are hard to separate and may be referred to indirectly (region ambiguity), while fine-grained motions can look alike in RGB (motion ambiguity). We address these challenges with HumanSkill-4D, a training-free framework that shares a multimodal large language model (MLLM) and geometric operators across avatars. For each avatar, a semantic memory links body-part and garment categories to persistent Gaussian regions and appearance descriptions. The MLLM uses category names and descriptions to select categories by appearance, relation, or function. To find matching intervals, it composes operators into programs that check query conditions on driving joint trajectories stored in a motion memory. These category choices and operator outputs make selections traceable, while composing or adding operators supports new motion conditions. To evaluate this task, we introduce three human-annotated benchmarks and show that HumanSkill-4D outperforms the baselines in part segmentation and 3D and 4D referring segmentation, with compact memories and only minutes of setup per avatar.
papers.summary: Avatar referring segmentation is a new task: selecting regions of animatable Gaussian-splatting avatars from language queries, optionally restricted to the time intervals where a described pose or motion occurs. `HumanSkill-4D` is a training-free framework in which a multimodal large language model (MLLM) chooses body-part and garment categories from a per-avatar semantic memory. To find matching time intervals, it composes geometric operators into programs that run over joint trajectories stored in a motion memory. On three new human-annotated benchmarks, **it outperforms baselines on part segmentation and on 3D and 4D referring segmentation**, with only minutes of setup per avatar.

papers.title: Hippo: Training-Free Agent Self-Evolution via Hippocampal Replay
papers.abstract: Motivated by recursive self-improvement (RSI), we study how LLM agents can learn through external memory without updating model parameters. Extracting useful experience from a single attempt is difficult: flawed reasoning can produce success, while poor execution can obscure a sound strategy. Preserving its value over time is also difficult: our accumulation baseline without consolidation initially improves but eventually performs below a no-memory baseline. Our key idea is to compare attempts at the same task to identify reusable decisions and refine when they apply. We introduce Hippo, a memory framework inspired by selective hippocampal encoding and replay that learns from these comparisons when shortcomings are diagnosed. It compares the resulting experience with existing memory to merge overlaps and resolve conflicts through explicit applicability conditions. This allows prior guidance to be revised without storing every lesson as a separate entry. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified, WebArena, and Mind2Web show performance gains in all three settings and substantially fewer retained experiences than the accumulation baseline. The gains extend across the evaluated base models of varying capabilities, indicating that memory-based adaptation remains useful even for highly capable models.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can improve through external memory without weight updates, but simply accumulating experience from single attempts eventually **performs worse than using no memory at all**. Inspired by hippocampal replay, `Hippo` compares multiple attempts at the same task to find reusable decisions and refine when they apply. It then consolidates the new experience with existing memory by merging overlaps and resolving conflicts through explicit applicability conditions. On `SWE-bench Verified`, `WebArena`, and `Mind2Web`, `Hippo` improves performance while retaining far fewer experiences than the accumulation baseline, and the gains hold across base models of varying strength.

papers.title: MELD: Recursive Self-Improvement via Hierarchical Coordination for Multi-Agent Scientific Discovery
papers.abstract: Multi-agent scientific discovery with large language models raises a coupled learning problem: research assignments determine both which experiments are pursued and the experiences from which agents adapt. We introduce MELD, a unified hierarchical test-time training framework that jointly adapts a team-level Coordinator policy and agent-level individual Scientist policies within a single discovery process. The Coordinator generates a joint portfolio of search branches and research directives over a shared derivation tree, while Scientists develop hypotheses and execution plans implemented by a shared frozen Executor. Both levels receive alternating GRPO-style parameter updates under a shared smooth best-of-budget objective, allowing team organization and individual research behavior to co-evolve in a recursive self-improvement loop. Our analysis establishes objective alignment for the hierarchy, characterizes conditions for coordination gains over independent parallel discovery and the first-order benefit of private adaptation, and derives a finite-budget regret bound for adapted models. On 22 MLGym and MLE-bench tasks, MELD is best on 20 of them and achieves the highest aggregate normalized scores on MLGym, using a 4B backbone for coordination and research. Most baselines use proprietary Scientists, and all systems share one frozen Executor.
papers.summary: In multi-agent scientific discovery, the way research is assigned decides both which experiments get run and what each agent learns from. `MELD` jointly trains a team-level Coordinator, which allocates search branches and research directives over a shared derivation tree, and individual Scientist agents that propose hypotheses and plans for a shared frozen Executor. Both levels receive alternating `GRPO`-style updates toward a shared best-of-budget objective, backed by analysis of objective alignment, coordination gains, and a finite-budget regret bound. Using a 4B-parameter backbone, **`MELD` is best on 20 of 22 `MLGym` and `MLE-bench` tasks**, even though most baselines use proprietary models as Scientists.

papers.title: Tree Plurality Veto: Voting in Few Rounds with Efficient Communication and Low Metric Distortion
papers.abstract:
We consider the metric distortion framework for voting, where $n$ voters and $m$ candidates are embedded in an unknown metric space. A voting rule selects a candidate using only voters' ordinal preferences, and its distortion is the worst-case ratio between the social cost of the selected candidate and the minimum social cost. We study how round complexity trades off against total communication in deterministic voting protocols with low distortion. Deterministic rules can achieve the optimal distortion of $3$ in one round by eliciting complete rankings using $\Theta(nm\log m)$ bits, while a direct sequential implementation of PluralityVeto achieves the same distortion using only $O(n\log m)$ bits but requires $\Theta(n)$ rounds.
  Our main result is TreePluralityVeto, a deterministic voting protocol that, for every $r\ge 2$, achieves distortion at most $2r-1$ using at most $r$ rounds and $O(n\log m+n s^{1/(r-1)}\log s)$ bits of total communication, where $s = \min\{n, m\}$. The protocol runs PluralityVeto on a hierarchical partition of the voters, collecting restricted rankings in parallel at each level. The branching factor controls the tradeoff between rounds and communication, and a matching-based analysis shows that each level increases the distortion bound by at most $2$.
papers.summary: In metric-distortion voting, deterministic rules can reach the optimal distortion of 3 either in one round with full rankings, which uses a lot of communication, or with little communication over Θ(n) sequential rounds. `TreePluralityVeto` runs the `PluralityVeto` rule over a hierarchical partition of voters, collecting restricted rankings in parallel at each level. For any r ≥ 2, it achieves **distortion at most 2r−1 in r rounds**, using O(n log m + n·s^(1/(r−1)) log s) bits, where s = min(n, m). The tree's branching factor controls the trade-off between rounds and communication.

papers.title: Generative Retrieval for Reverse Target Fishing with a Proteome-Scale Benchmark
papers.abstract: Reverse target fishing identifies protein targets for a query molecule and is central to drug discovery and repurposing. Discriminative approaches adapted from virtual screening face sparse, long-tailed associations and missing-not-at-random measurements: treating unrecorded pairs as negatives can suppress genuine targets. We reformulate the task as generative retrieval and introduce GenFish. Residual vector quantization converts frozen protein language model features into shared semantic identifiers. Given a molecular fingerprint, GenFish autoregressively models codes conditioned on the query and preceding code, ranking proteins by identifier likelihood without explicitly labeling unrecorded pairs as negatives. We introduce ProTargetBench, the first proteome-scale benchmark for reverse target fishing to jointly support measured-panel discrimination and full-catalogue recovery of experimentally recorded positives. Covering 20,431 UniProt-reviewed human proteins, it integrates curated bioactivity evidence and distinguishes experimental inactivity from unmeasured associations. On 198 held-out molecules, GenFish achieves higher mean performance across all three full-catalogue retrieval metrics than four discriminative neural baselines and three non-neural baselines, including ligand-based methods. A controlled positive-hiding experiment shows that targeted removal of false-negative competition improves contrastive retrieval beyond matched random masking; GenFish remains stronger under the same incomplete supervision. Pfam alignment indicates that the semantic identifiers capture biologically meaningful relationships among proteins. These results establish generative retrieval as a principled paradigm for reverse target fishing under incomplete bioactivity records.
papers.summary: Reverse target fishing means finding the protein targets of a given molecule. Discriminative methods struggle with it because untested molecule-protein pairs are treated as negatives, which can suppress real targets. `GenFish` recasts the task as generative retrieval: it quantizes protein language model features into semantic identifiers and, given a molecular fingerprint, generates those identifiers autoregressively to rank proteins, without labeling unrecorded pairs as negatives. The authors also release `ProTargetBench`, a benchmark covering 20,431 human proteins that separates experimentally inactive pairs from unmeasured ones. On 198 held-out molecules, **`GenFish` beats seven neural and non-neural baselines on all three full-catalogue retrieval metrics**.

papers.title: Measuring Empowerment from Offline Data for Intrinsically Motivated Exploration
papers.abstract: Large, unlabeled datasets of prior experience have become increasingly available for agentic tasks in domains such as robotics and coding. A common recipe for these tasks is to train a policy using the prior data, and then further improve it with online rollouts. But while much work has studied how to use both the offline and online data for policy extraction, far less work has been done to understand how the prior data can be used to efficiently \textit{explore} during the online learning phase. Previous work has attempted to formalize this idea by defining the \textit{empowerment}, a measure of how many future states an agent can realize; states with higher empowerment require more exploration as there are more futures to explore. However, existing methods for estimating empowerment require online policy rollouts in the environment. We propose the first method for estimating empowerment from unlabeled prior data, without any environment interaction. By jointly learning an empowerment-maximizing policy together with its discounted state-occupancy measure, our estimator can be trained on unlabeled trajectories generated from any unknown policy. We demonstrate that our empowerment estimator qualitatively gives intuitive empowerment measures and show that the pretrained estimator can be used to improve exploration in the online goal-conditioned reinforcement learning setting. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/ishirgarg/offline-empowerment}.
papers.summary: Agents are often pretrained on large unlabeled datasets and then improved with online rollouts, but little work uses that prior data to guide exploration. Empowerment measures how many future states an agent can reach and can serve as an exploration signal, but existing estimators need online interaction with the environment. The authors present **the first method for estimating empowerment purely from unlabeled offline trajectories**. It jointly learns an empowerment-maximizing policy and that policy's discounted state-occupancy measure. The pretrained estimator gives intuitive empowerment values and improves exploration in online goal-conditioned reinforcement learning.

papers.title: Learning to Compose: Recursive Self-Improvement of Shared Executable Stacks for Zero-Shot Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: Individually competent robot skills can fail when composed: tools may lack a required capability, completion signals may misrepresent physical progress, and one skill may leave a state that violates its successor's prerequisites. We introduce Recursia, a recursive self-improvement framework that treats the shared executable stack, rather than individual task programs, as the persistent unit of improvement. The stack integrates tools, skills with execution contracts, handoffs, and verifiers. Source-side execution traces guide failure attribution and the generation of missing tools or repairs to existing shared components. Generality checks, mechanism tests, and paired selection and regression gates determine which changes become the next parent. The resulting stack is frozen and reused through declarative task adapters, allowing source-derived changes to support new compositions without target-side code repair. Experiments cover LIBERO-Pro Long simulation and a physical Franka FR3 equipped with a Franka Hand. In simulation, Recursia improves success over ASPIRE by 5.8 percentage points under Pos perturbations and 15.1 points under Task perturbations. Across three physical compositional target tasks, it improves mean success over the Skill Document Only baseline by 40 percentage points. Analyses of constituent execution, candidate rejection, and inference drivers distinguish local mechanism improvements from complete task success and characterize the cost of feedback-conditioned orchestration. These results examine shared executable interfaces as a concrete mechanism for compositional transfer in robot programming.
papers.summary: Robot skills that work on their own often fail when chained together, because of missing tool capabilities, misleading completion signals, or states that break the next skill's prerequisites. `Recursia` treats the shared executable stack of tools, skills with execution contracts, handoffs, and verifiers as the thing to improve recursively. It uses execution traces to attribute failures and generate new tools or repairs, and accepts a change only after it passes generality, mechanism, and regression gates. The frozen stack transfers to new task compositions through declarative adapters, without fixing code for each new task. It beats `ASPIRE` by 5.8 to 15.1 points on `LIBERO-Pro` Long, and **improves mean success by 40 percentage points** over a documentation-only baseline on three physical tasks with a Franka FR3 arm.

papers.title: SENTRY: A Streaming Edge Network Trust Engine for Real-Time Audio Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: Real-time voice cloning has enabled large-scale streaming deepfake and vishing attacks, while existing Network Detection and Response (NDR) solutions rely on GPU-based post-processing that requires buffered audio and generalizes poorly to unseen speech synthesis models. This paper presents SENTRY, a hardware-oriented, streaming trust engine for inline deepfake detection at the network edge. SENTRY employs an integer lifting-wavelet front end together with a bank of multiplier-free transforms, including wavelet-packet envelopes, Walsh-Hadamard sequency profiles, waveform micro-statistics, and long-term spectral features, designed so that acoustic analysis needs only integer add, shift, compare and bitwise operations. A supervised gradient-boosted tree classifier is combined with an unsupervised Mahalanobis out-of-distribution detector trained solely on authentic speech, and their outputs are fused by a lightweight logistic layer to produce graduated LOG, CHALLENGE, or DROP actions. Under a closed-set protocol, SENTRY reaches 98.75% accuracy at a 1.25% equal-error rate (EER) on WaveFake, with perfect separation of HiFi-GAN and WaveGlow; its supervised track alone achieves an AUC of 0.9994 (fused: 0.9993). On ASVspoof 2019 LA (attacks A01-A06) over an 8 kHz mu-law telephony channel, it reaches 94.75% accuracy at a 5.05% EER, with a supervised-track AUC of 0.9948 (fused: 0.9884) and per-attack EERs below 7%. In our prototype, the feature front end runs as bit-exact integer code on one Arm Cortex-A53 core, and the classifier and fusion stage are synthesized for a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC using no DSP slices, returning a decision 220 ns after a feature vector is ready. These results indicate that deepfake screening can be placed inline without GPUs or floating-point hardware; generalization to unseen generators is left to future work.
papers.summary: Real-time voice cloning enables streaming deepfake and voice-phishing attacks, while existing network detection tools rely on GPU post-processing of buffered audio. `SENTRY` is a streaming detector for the network edge that extracts features using only integer add, shift, compare, and bitwise operations. These include a lifting-wavelet front end, Walsh-Hadamard profiles, and spectral statistics. A gradient-boosted tree classifier and an out-of-distribution detector trained only on real speech are fused to choose LOG, CHALLENGE, or DROP actions. It reaches 98.75% accuracy on `WaveFake` and 94.75% on `ASVspoof 2019 LA` over telephone-quality audio, **returning a decision 220 ns after features are ready** on an FPGA without DSP slices, though generalization to unseen speech generators is left untested.

papers.title: Which Long Documents Matter? A Controlled Study of Data Selection for Context Extension
papers.abstract: Natural long documents are widely used for context extension, but which selection pipelines are effective remains unclear. We conduct a controlled comparison on Qwen2.5-3B at 128K under matched 6B-token continued-training budgets. Random sampling of natural long documents (random-long) outperforms repacking at longer evaluation lengths. Within the same candidate pool, selecting documents with high LongPPL key-token density yields further gains, unlike the evaluated generic-quality and LLM-judge selectors. We introduce truncLongPPL to reduce scoring cost by computing key-token density over a truncated prefix. At 128K, scoring the first half of the reference span yields downstream performance close to full-span scoring with a measured $2.28\times$ end-to-end scoring speedup. Across three training seeds, truncLongPPL achieves the highest mean scores among evaluated pipelines, exceeding random-long by 4.54 points on validation HELMET and 3.28 on held-out RULER, with gains most consistent in retrieval. At a 256K target context, it gains 2.82 average RULER points over random-long on Qwen2.5-3B. In short/long mixed training across Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen3-8B, and OLMo~3-7B, it gains 1.47--7.31 average RULER points over random-long mixing, with seven-task short-context averages within 0.23 points of the corresponding baselines. After supervised fine-tuning (SFT), Qwen3-8B and OLMo~3-7B models trained with selected long documents outperform their random-long counterparts by 1.13--1.67 points on LongBench v2 and 0.62--1.44 points on MRCR.
papers.summary: Natural long documents are widely used to extend a model's context window, but it is unclear which ways of selecting them work best. In controlled experiments on `Qwen2.5-3B` at 128K tokens with matched 6B-token training budgets, randomly sampling naturally long documents beats repacking shorter ones, and selecting documents with a high density of `LongPPL` key tokens helps further. Generic quality filters and LLM-judge selectors did not show this gain. The proposed `truncLongPPL` scores only a truncated prefix of each document for a 2.28× scoring speedup and **beats random selection by 4.54 points on `HELMET` and 3.28 on `RULER`**. Gains carry over to 256K context, to mixed short and long training on `Qwen3-8B` and `OLMo 3-7B`, and through supervised fine-tuning, with short-context performance essentially unchanged.

papers.title: Pluralistic Alignment in Language Models: Objectives, Human References, and Preference Representations
papers.abstract: Pluralistic alignment aims to represent meaningful variation in human preferences rather than collapse heterogeneous judgments into a single target. Yet existing work often mixes three distinct questions: what pluralistic behavior a model should exhibit, whose preferences define the reference, and what evidence is sufficient to demonstrate success. We organize the literature around a two-layer taxonomy. Layer 1 distinguishes representing a range of human-supported viewpoints (Overton Pluralism), adapting faithfully to a specified perspective or preference condition (Steerable Pluralism), and matching the response distribution observed in a target population (Distributional Pluralism). Layer 2 distinguishes aggregate populations, countries and regions, and subgroups as human references. Preference representation, implementation mechanism, modality, and evidence quality are treated as cross-cutting design choices rather than additional forms of pluralism. We synthesize a protocol-bounded corpus of 70 works on pluralistic alignment and neighboring areas, using the objective-by-human-reference matrix to map existing approaches and identify underexplored combinations. The coded literature concentrates on Steerable Pluralism and Distributional Pluralism, while eligible Overton Pluralism work appears only at the aggregate-population level under our stated protocol. We then connect each objective to the evidence needed to support it, including perspective validity, conditional fidelity, distributional fidelity, support preservation, and uncertainty in subgroup estimates. Together, the taxonomy and evaluation framework clarify what current methods establish, where their claims exceed their evidence, and how future systems can represent disagreement without mistaking variation for faithful representation.
papers.summary: Work on pluralistic alignment, which aims for models that represent varied human preferences instead of a single averaged target, often blurs three questions: what behavior is wanted, whose preferences serve as the reference, and what evidence shows success. This survey of 70 works organizes the field by objective (`Overton`, `Steerable`, and `Distributional` pluralism) and by human reference (aggregate populations, countries and regions, or subgroups). Mapping the literature onto this grid shows that **work concentrates on steerable and distributional pluralism, with Overton pluralism studied only at the aggregate-population level**. The authors connect each objective to the evidence needed to support it, such as conditional fidelity, distributional fidelity, and uncertainty in subgroup estimates, and point out where current claims go beyond that evidence.

papers.title: Ben-Misandry: A Bengali Dataset and Late-Fusion Transformer Framework for Detecting Anti-Male Gender Hate
papers.abstract: Gender based hate speech research in Bengali has focused almost exclusively on misogyny, leaving anti male hate, or misandry, entirely unstudied for this language and creating a systematic blind spot in moderation systems trained to catch attacks on women but not on men. We introduce Ben-Misandry, the first Bengali misandry detection dataset: 5,000 comments across six taxonomy classes, including a novel category for mocking male emotional vulnerability with no direct analogue in existing misogyny taxonomies. The corpus is taxonomy-controlled synthetic data generated with GPT-4.1, spot-checked by four human reviewers on a 500-comment sample who confirmed the large majority of assigned labels; a full inter-annotator- agreement study is left to future work. We benchmark it with a classical pipeline (seven classifiers over four text representations) and a transformer pipeline (BanglaBERT, XLM-RoBERTa, and two fusion strategies). The best classical model, a linear SVM over character-level TF-IDF, reaches 91.8% accuracy; a late fusion ensemble averaging BanglaBERT and XLM-RoBERTa softmax outputs reaches 96.6% accuracy and macro ROC-AUC above 99%, nominally ahead of every single model and early fusion, though we have not run significance testing to confirm these margins are meaningful. We relate this to classifier combination theory, under which averaging encoders with decorrelated errors is expected to reduce variance, and corroborate the decision boundary with Shapley explanations that recover the same class- discriminative vocabulary found in our exploratory analysis, while noting this cannot rule out the model partly keying on synthetic-generation artifacts. Our results indicate misandry detection in Bengali is feasible and measurable on this synthetic corpus, offered as an initial public resource pending validation on real-world data.
papers.summary: Bengali hate-speech research has focused on misogyny and left anti-male hate (misandry) unstudied. `Ben-Misandry` is a dataset of 5,000 synthetic comments in six classes, generated with `GPT-4.1` and spot-checked by human reviewers on a 500-comment sample. A late-fusion ensemble that averages the outputs of `BanglaBERT` and `XLM-RoBERTa` reaches **96.6% accuracy**, compared with 91.8% for the best classical model, a linear support vector machine (SVM) over character-level features. The authors note that they ran no significance tests and that the models may partly rely on artifacts of synthetic generation.

papers.title: Private Evaluation of High-Dimensional Functions
papers.abstract:
We study differentially private black-box evaluation of arbitrary high-dimensional functions. Given a dataset $S$ and query access to a function $f$---whose sensitivity may be unknown or unbounded---the goal is to privately output an approximation to $f(S)$. The black-box evaluator can only query the value of $f$ over a down neighborhood of $S$ (i.e., those subsets of $S$ that are obtained by removing a bounded number of elements from $S$). We design generic black-box evaluators for both pure and approximate differential privacy through a reduction to high-dimensional private quasi-concave optimization (QCO).
