  Our black-box evaluator enjoys a geometric notion of utility. Consider the vectors obtained by applying $f$ on sets in a down neighborhood of $S$. With high probability, the evaluator's output is guaranteed to be in the convex hull of these vectors.
  Our work generalizes the result of Linder et al. [LRSS25] for real-valued function evaluation to high dimensions. It also recovers the private center-point guarantees of Beimel et al. [BMNS19], with an explicit additive approximation to maximum Tukey depth. We also apply our evaluators to user-level quasi-concave and convex optimization, showing how they can improve upon the sample-and-aggregate baseline of Nissim et al. [NRS07] by replacing the multiplicative data overhead with an additive overhead.
  Finally, we show that our formulation of high dimensional black-box evaluation and high dimensional private QCO are equivalent up to a factor of the dimension: the hardest private evaluation instances already arise from the cases that $f$ is a (non-private) quasi-concave optimizer.
papers.summary: The goal is to privately approximate the value of an arbitrary high-dimensional function on a dataset when the function's sensitivity may be unknown or unbounded, using only queries on subsets formed by removing a bounded number of elements. The authors build generic black-box evaluators for both pure and approximate differential privacy by reducing the problem to high-dimensional private quasi-concave optimization (`QCO`). The main guarantee is geometric: **with high probability the output lies in the convex hull of the function's values on that down neighborhood**. The framework extends earlier real-valued results to high dimensions and recovers known private center-point guarantees. For user-level optimization it replaces the multiplicative data overhead of `sample-and-aggregate` with an additive one, and the authors show that private evaluation and private `QCO` are equivalent up to a factor of the dimension.

papers.title: Beyond Recall Saturation: Scaling Hard-Negative Reranker Training for Industrial Legal Retrieval
papers.abstract: Industrial retrieval systems often improve quality by enlarging embedding candidate pools or adopting complex training pipelines. We show that, under a sufficiently large but practical candidate pool, embedding recall exhibits diminishing returns, motivating a closer examination of reranker quality. On Chinese legal retrieval benchmarks, embedding top-300 reaches a high-recall operating region, while relevant evidence may still be ranked below the output cutoff. We compare hard-negative strategies for reranker training, including embedding-mined, self-mined, and dynamic-negative variants, under aligned retrieval protocols that evaluate reranking after candidate retrieval. Among the evaluated staged configurations, an embedding-to-self-mined pipeline provides a favorable trade-off; additional dynamic stages do not improve all held-out metrics. The selected pipeline scales from a 0.6B to a 4B reranker. Relative to the native 4B reranker, the trained 4B Stage2 model improves reported metrics on the STARD and CSAID benchmarks and on an internal development set, and is preferred in 72.4\% of non-tied comparisons on 410 de-identified, reconstructed internal operational-query inputs in a latency-sensitive offline preference evaluation. These results support evaluating the retrieval and reranking stages separately when selecting an optimization target for industrial retrieval systems.
papers.summary: On Chinese legal retrieval, the authors show that once the embedding candidate pool is large enough (top-300), recall gains level off, so the reranker becomes the main bottleneck. They compare hard-negative mining strategies for reranker training (embedding-mined, self-mined, and dynamic negatives) under protocols that evaluate reranking separately from retrieval. A staged embedding-to-self-mined pipeline gave the best trade-off and scaled from a 0.6B to a 4B reranker. The trained 4B model improved on the `STARD` and `CSAID` benchmarks and an internal set, and was **preferred in 72.4% of non-tied comparisons** on real operational queries.

papers.title: Write Once, Check Many: Reusable Ledgers for Post-Hoc Policy Compliance Auditing of Agent Trajectories
papers.abstract: Auditing LLM agents against policies is critical to ensure safety but requires rereading long trajectories once per policy. Can we instead record each trajectory once and reuse that record for policies not known in advance? We propose write once, check many, a framework in which a writer model converts each agent trajectory into a policy-independent ledger of the agent's actions and outcomes. A reader then checks each new policy against the ledger alone, without access to the original trajectory. On 900 trajectories from SHADE-Arena, $\tau$-bench, and $\tau^2$-bench, we show that a 12B reader of narrative ledgers can either match or in fact achieve higher AUC than the same 12B model reading full trajectories. On SHADE-Arena policies that combine several facts, our approach outperforms a 31B model reading the trajectory (.777 vs. .713 AUC). When checking eight SHADE-Arena policies separately, ledgers use about $5\times$ fewer tokens, including the cost of writing them. A deeper analysis shows that rule-based extraction performs better on some single-action policies, and ledgers can miss evidence in long tool outputs and message contents. Our results suggest that reusable, policy-independent records can make retrospective agent auditing more efficient and effective, and highlight important considerations in ledger design.
papers.summary: Checking LLM agent trajectories against policies usually means rereading each long trajectory once per policy. The proposed `write once, check many` framework has a writer model turn each trajectory into a policy-independent ledger of the agent's actions and outcomes, and a reader then checks any new policy against the ledger alone. Across 900 trajectories from `SHADE-Arena`, `τ-bench`, and `τ²-bench`, a 12B reader of narrative ledgers matched or beat the same model reading full trajectories. On multi-fact policies it outperformed a 31B model reading the raw trajectory (.777 vs. .713 AUC), and it used **about 5× fewer tokens when checking eight policies**, including the cost of writing the ledgers. The analysis also finds that rule-based extraction does better on some single-action policies and that ledgers can miss evidence buried in long tool outputs.

papers.title: Modeling Discourse Profiles in Climate Misinformation Discourse
papers.abstract: Prior work on climate misinformation detection typically classifies individual comments or claims using text alone. This framing overlooks a key property of online climate discourse: misinformation is often produced, reinforced, and sustained through recurring rhetorical patterns that reappear across comments and threads. Using a large-scale TikTok climate discourse dataset, we construct discourse profiles by clustering climate-related comments into recurring rhetorical patterns. We then incorporate these profiles into fine-grained climate misinformation classifiers using a late-fusion architecture. Under video-disjoint evaluation across three training seeds, discourse-profile-aware models significantly improve macro-F1 over text-only baselines for bag-of-words, TF-IDF, and MPNet representations. RoBERTa-large exhibits a positive mean improvement but substantially greater variability, and the difference is not statistically significant. Beyond classification, our results show discourse profiles shape misinformation reception and propagation. Discourse-profile-conditioned language model agents exhibit misinformation acceptance patterns aligned with profile-level misinformation prevalence in ClimateDisc, and the relationship between misinformation prevalence and engagement persistence differs across dominant discourse profiles.
papers.summary: Climate misinformation detection usually classifies single comments, which ignores the recurring rhetorical patterns that sustain misinformation across threads. Using a large TikTok climate discourse dataset (`ClimateDisc`), the authors cluster comments into discourse profiles and add them to fine-grained classifiers through late fusion. In video-disjoint evaluation, **profile-aware models significantly improve macro-F1 over text-only baselines** for bag-of-words, `TF-IDF`, and `MPNet` representations, while the gain for `RoBERTa-large` is not statistically significant. Language model agents conditioned on a profile also show misinformation acceptance patterns that track that profile's misinformation prevalence.

papers.title: Vocal-Tract Acoustics, Aerodynamics, and Overlap-and-Add Synthesis in DYNARTmo
papers.abstract: This paper presents the acoustic and aerodynamic extension of DYNARTmo, a dynamic articulatory model for visualizing and synthesizing speech production. Gestural control trajectories determine vocal-tract geometry, which is converted into an acoustic tube with nasal branching and effective lateral passages. A lumped aerodynamic network relates prescribed glottal motion and pulmonary pressure to airflow and supraglottal pressure storage. Phonatory excitation, oral friction, and glottal aspiration are synthesized as separate contributions. Frame-specific acoustic responses are combined by overlap-and-add, preserving response tails beyond individual control frames. Three German words, ``Tasse'', ``Muse'', and ``Lade'', illustrate the coordination of articulation, pressure, flow, and acoustic sources across vowels, nasals, laterals, fricatives, and plosives. The implementation has been optimized by the author primarily for sound recognizability; independent perceptual evaluation remains outstanding, and fricative-noise naturalness requires further refinement. The model provides an inspectable, articulatorily controlled production plant for future neural simulations of babbling, imitation, and early word acquisition. Further work will improve acoustic realism, reduce empirical source corrections, and extend the sensory information available to developmental learning models.
papers.summary: This work adds acoustics and aerodynamics to `DYNARTmo`, a dynamic articulatory model for visualizing and synthesizing speech. Gestural trajectories set the vocal-tract geometry, which is converted into an acoustic tube with nasal and lateral branches, and a lumped aerodynamic network links glottal motion and lung pressure to airflow. Phonation, friction, and aspiration sources are synthesized separately, and frame responses are combined by **overlap-and-add so that response tails carry across control frames**. Three German words demonstrate the system, though no independent perceptual evaluation has been done yet and fricative naturalness still needs work.

papers.title: VBO-MI: A Differentiable Black-Box Optimization Framework via Variational Mutual Information Estimation
papers.abstract: Many real-world tasks require optimizing expensive black-box functions accessible only through noisy evaluations, a setting commonly addressed with Bayesian optimization. While Gaussian processes(GPs) and Bayesian neural networks have driven significant progress, GP-based methods scale cubically with observations, and BNN-based approaches remain burdened by expensive posterior sampling such as Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, and inner-loop acquisition optimization in high-dimensional setting. In this work, we propose VBO-MI, a fully gradient-based BO framework that requires no assumptions on a Gaussian prior or a variational posterior family over $f$. While our framework uses gradient-based updates to train the internal action and information-estimation networks, it treats the objective function $f$ as a strict black box, requiring only zeroth-order evaluations. To enable end-to-end gradient flow, we employ an actor-critic architecture consisting of an action-net to navigate the input space and a variational critic to estimate a surrogate information signal for exploration. Additionally, we design a lightweight surrogate that approximates the objective from observed data using a replay buffer, which reduces the total required real function queries to one batch per iteration. We provide theoretical analysis for our framework, establishing convergence of its training objective and surrogate estimator, and showing, that near-optimal solutions exist. We evaluate our method on a diverse suite of benchmarks, including high-dimensional synthetic function and complex real-world tasks such as Rover Trajectory planning optimization, the Lunar Lander, and Pest Control problems. Our experiments demonstrate that VBO-MI provides the same or superior optimization performance over the various baselines.
papers.summary: Bayesian optimization of expensive black-box functions usually relies on Gaussian processes, which scale cubically with the number of observations, or on Bayesian neural networks, which need costly posterior sampling. `VBO-MI` is a fully gradient-based alternative: an actor-critic setup in which an action network explores the input space and a variational critic estimates a mutual-information signal for exploration, while the objective is only ever evaluated as a black box. A lightweight surrogate trained from a replay buffer cuts real function queries to one batch per iteration, and the authors prove convergence of the training objective and surrogate. On high-dimensional synthetic functions and tasks such as `Rover` trajectory planning, `Lunar Lander`, and `Pest Control`, it **matches or beats the baselines**.

papers.title: Backend-Frontend Converter: Component-Based Conversion of .NET Computational Models to TypeScript
papers.abstract: Computational models developed in .NET often need to run locally within web applications. We present Backend--Frontend Converter, an architecture for generating TypeScript implementations of component-based models. The converter maps components, connections, aliases, and formula trees to model-specific TypeScript code. Reusable runtime libraries provide numerical integration, data access, and state handling. We evaluate stored generated implementations through four orbital scenarios and a recorded trading-strategy comparison. Orbital calculations execute in a browser and are paired with C\# results by crossing event and timestamp; trading outputs are aligned by date. Analytic scheduler tests and deliberately perturbed outputs assess the validation procedure. Each orbital scenario produces 91 paired events with identical timestamps. Position and velocity differences remain below $(10^{-6}\)~km$ and $(10^{-9}\)~km/s$. All 20 analytic scheduler checks pass, and the comparator detects each of three prescribed state and time perturbations. The trading comparison contains 501 aligned daily records with matching indicator values, positions, and order events. The evaluated implementations preserve the compared outputs across the C#/TypeScript boundary. Component-specific generation and reusable execution libraries provide a practical route from supported .NET computational models to TypeScript applications.
papers.summary: Computational models written in .NET often need to run locally inside web applications. The `Backend-Frontend Converter` generates model-specific TypeScript from component-based .NET models by mapping components, connections, aliases, and formula trees, and it relies on reusable runtime libraries for numerical integration, data access, and state handling. In four orbital scenarios, browser results matched C# with **position differences below 10⁻⁶ km and velocity differences below 10⁻⁹ km/s**. A 501-day trading-strategy comparison produced matching indicators, positions, and orders, and the validation procedure caught every deliberately injected perturbation.

papers.title: ConCI: A Controlled Counterfactual Benchmark for Contextual Integrity in LLMs
papers.abstract: Contextual integrity (CI) holds that the appropriateness of sharing personal information depends on the context of the information flow, not on the information alone. However, existing CI benchmarks often use independent scenarios that vary multiple CI parameters simultaneously and are dominated by inappropriate flows, making it unclear whether correct predictions reflect sensitivity to context or a general refusal tendency. We present ConCI, a controlled-counterfactual benchmark in which an anchor flow is paired with two counterfactuals that each modify a single CI parameter. The resulting triplet is scored jointly, with credit given only when all three flows are judged correctly. Built from six existing benchmarks, ConCI contains 1,592 flows in 556 triplets, is approximately label-balanced, and is validated by seven human annotators per flow. Across seven LLMs, many correct anchor predictions fail on at least one counterfactual, and even the strongest model errs on about a fifth of triplets. Furthermore, models perform near ceiling on inappropriate flows but weaker on appropriate ones, often continuing to judge a flow inappropriate even when a contextual change should make it appropriate. Larger models narrow this bias toward non-disclosure but do not eliminate it, and reasoning yields only modest gains.
papers.summary: Contextual integrity (CI) holds that whether sharing personal information is appropriate depends on the context of the flow. Existing CI benchmarks change many parameters at once and are dominated by inappropriate flows, so it is hard to tell whether models are reading context or simply refusing. `ConCI` pairs each anchor flow with two counterfactuals that each change a single CI parameter and gives credit only when all three are judged correctly. It contains 1,592 human-validated, roughly label-balanced flows. Across seven LLMs, many correct anchor predictions fail on a counterfactual and **even the strongest model gets about a fifth of triplets wrong**. Models do well on inappropriate flows but keep refusing when a change in context should make sharing acceptable, a bias that larger models and reasoning reduce but do not remove.

papers.title: CoTs remain monitorable when being unfaithful requires computation: Replicating and Extending the Necessity Effect Across Eleven Models
papers.abstract: While a LLM's chain of thought (CoT) is a promising approach to interpreting model outputs, prior work shows CoT's content does not always accurately reflect the reasoning process. Emmons et al. (2025) finds that models can follow a question hint without revealing so in its chain of thought, but when the hint is sufficiently complex the computation is forced into the CoT. This claim, however, has only been tested on Gemini models, and the datasets and code is closed source. We replicate their proxy task across eleven models from six families and find the necessity effect generalizes. Every model follows simple cues above a no-hint baseline, while concealed complex-cue following falls back near baseline for most models. We also extend the study from Emmons et al. (2025) to measure CoT-necessity and unfaithfulness across five cue families (four of them new) and three difficulty levels. The relationship between when CoT is necessary and unfaithfulness is task-specific and model-specific. For some hint types, models often verbalize their hint-following behavior even when the hint can be decoded in a single forward pass. These results support the case for CoT monitoring when unsafe behavior requires non-trivial computation, and that properties of CoT unfaithfulness are sensitive to model and setting.
papers.summary: Prior work on `Gemini` models found that models can secretly follow simple hints without mentioning them in their chain of thought (CoT), but complex hints force the computation into the visible CoT, which supports CoT monitoring. This study replicates that proxy task across eleven models from six families and confirms that **the necessity effect generalizes**: every model follows simple cues above baseline, while concealed following of complex cues falls back to near baseline for most models. It also adds four new cue families and three difficulty levels, and finds that the link between CoT necessity and unfaithfulness depends on both task and model. In some cases models even verbalize hints they could have decoded in a single forward pass.

papers.title: TideKV: Delayed KV Eviction via Layer-Wise Chunked Prefill for Memory-Efficient Long-Context LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) inference is important for modern intelligent applications but remains constrained by peak memory during prompt prefill. Existing KV cache compression reduces decoding memory but typically requires full-prompt prefill to preserve global context, retaining a high construction peak. Online chunk-level eviction lowers memory earlier but selects before each layer has observed the complete prompt, potentially degrading cache construction and decoding. We present TideKV, an on-GPU cache-construction architecture using layer-major delayed eviction. TideKV processes all prompt chunks within each Transformer layer, retains full-prompt KV only for the active layer, and evicts at layer end. This schedule preserves full-prompt-aware selection while reducing activation and temporary memory. Experiments across multiple computing platforms show that TideKV preserves the inference quality and final cache size of the evaluated compression methods. At 64K on A100, it reduces the construction-time transient footprint by 83.89%. On RTX 4090, it increases time to first token by only 1.06% at 64K and enables 128K prefill. TideKV also completes 128K on Jetson, whereas matched post-prefill compression runs out of memory on both resource-constrained platforms. These results show that delayed layer-end eviction substantially expands feasible context lengths without sacrificing cache utility.
papers.summary: Long-context LLM inference is limited by peak memory during prompt prefill. KV cache compression usually needs the full prompt prefilled first, and online chunk-level eviction makes its choices before each layer has seen the whole prompt. `TideKV` uses a layer-major schedule instead: it processes all prompt chunks within one Transformer layer, keeps full-prompt KV only for the active layer, and evicts at the end of that layer, so selection still sees the full prompt. It preserves the quality and final cache size of the compression methods tested, **reduces transient construction memory by 83.89% at 64K on A100**, adds only 1.06% to time to first token on an RTX 4090, and enables 128K prefill on RTX 4090 and Jetson, where matched post-prefill compression runs out of memory.

papers.title: HiPPO Functional Memory: Coordinate-Queryable Attention for Irregular Time Series
papers.abstract: Irregular time series require models to answer temporal queries at arbitrary coordinates, yet existing approaches typically retain observation-dependent representations that must be repeatedly resolved for each query. We introduce HiPPO Functional Memory (HiPPO-FM), a functional-memory attention operator that compiles an irregular history into a reusable coordinate-addressable state. Instead of storing observation-indexed tokens or latent trajectories, HiPPO-FM writes observations into a fixed-rank functional space and performs direct coordinate evaluation through matched functional geometry. Kernel-smoothed HiPPO coordinates and Gram-based readout define a shared write/read mechanism, while observed-support self-attention enables content-dependent representations before compression. We characterize the induced finite-dimensional query space and derive an error decomposition separating functional geometry approximation from learned-memory mismatch. Across continuous-coordinate reconstruction, irregular representation learning, real-world extrapolation, and event-sequence prediction, HiPPO-FM consistently improves strong irregular time-series baselines, achieving strong reconstruction accuracy on Spiral, competitive performance across 20 UEA datasets, improved real-world extrapolation, and superior results on several irregular event benchmarks. After encoding, the compact functional state can be reused across different query sets without reprocessing the observation history.
papers.summary: Models for irregularly sampled time series must answer queries at arbitrary time coordinates, but existing methods keep observation-dependent representations that have to be re-resolved for every query. `HiPPO-FM` is an attention operator that writes observations into a fixed-rank functional space built on kernel-smoothed `HiPPO` coordinates and reads values back at any coordinate through a Gram-based readout. Self-attention over the observed points runs before compression, and the authors derive an error decomposition for the approach. It improves on strong baselines in reconstruction (`Spiral`), classification (20 `UEA` datasets), extrapolation, and event prediction, and **the compact state can be reused across query sets without reprocessing the history**.

papers.title: GazeAct: A Human-Gaze-Annotated Manipulation Dataset for Attention-Regularized Policies
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies must ground language instructions in the right objects, contact points, and target locations for reliable manipulation. Human gaze provides a natural signal for this grounding, but existing robot datasets rarely pair real human gaze with the multi-camera observations used by modern policies. We introduce GazeAct, a gaze-equipped real-robot manipulation dataset and training framework for multi-view VLA policies. Using screen-based teleoperation, we record gaze directly on the robot camera feed viewed by the operator, yielding 12000 demonstrations across 40 tasks and five domains with 300 Hz gaze synchronized with images, proprioception, and actions. We transfer gaze from the operator-selected view to the remaining synchronized cameras, producing spatially consistent targets across the policy's visual inputs. We then use these gaze-derived targets to regularize language-conditioned visual attention during training while keeping inference gaze-free. Across 18 real-world tasks, our method improves average success from 48.1% to 58.6%, with gains up to 25 percentage points. Ablations show that gaze works best as soft supervision and that real human gaze provides stronger attention targets than generic attention-shaping priors. The gains transfer to LIBERO-Spatial (57.9% to 69.6%) and different VLA backbones.These results show that gaze collected in the robot observation space can provide effective training-time targets for improving visual grounding in VLA manipulation.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies need to ground instructions in the right objects and locations, and human gaze is a natural signal for that, but robot datasets rarely include it. `GazeAct` records operator gaze directly on the robot camera feed during screen-based teleoperation, producing 12,000 demonstrations across 40 tasks with 300 Hz gaze, which is then transferred to the other camera views. The gaze targets regularize the policy's language-conditioned visual attention during training only, so inference needs no gaze. Across 18 real-world tasks, **average success rises from 48.1% to 58.6%**, and the gains carry over to `LIBERO-Spatial` (57.9% to 69.6%) and to other VLA backbones.

papers.title: BEM: Learning Bregman Divergences for Concept Erasure in Flow Matching Models
papers.abstract: Concept erasure removes harmful, private, or copyrighted concepts from text-to-image models while preserving their other abilities. Leading models such as FLUX and Stable Diffusion 3 are trained with flow matching, and erasure methods for them fine-tune the model toward a guided teacher's velocities under a Euclidean loss. Yet the squared distance is only one member of a larger family: Bregman divergences are exactly the losses under which flow matching recovers the correct velocity field, and each member shapes differently what is erased and what is preserved. We introduce BEM (Bregman erasure matching), which is, to our knowledge, the first to learn this divergence through bi-level optimization, so that the fine-tuned model forgets the concept on unseen prompts while its unrelated generations stay unchanged. In the experiments we target the suppression of nudity, violence, real identities, and copyrighted characters. Under the evaluation protocol of GEM, BEM removes more of the concept than GEM on most settings, cutting the unsafe rate on bloody gore from 53.9% to 14.4% and the FID on nudity from 8.64 to 6.64, while retention holds on some concepts and degrades on others.
papers.summary: Concept erasure methods for flow-matching text-to-image models such as `FLUX` and `Stable Diffusion 3` fine-tune toward a guided teacher's velocities under a squared Euclidean loss. The authors note that any Bregman divergence recovers the correct velocity field in flow matching, and that each choice shapes differently what is forgotten and what is kept. `BEM` (Bregman erasure matching) learns this divergence through bi-level optimization, aiming to erase the concept on unseen prompts while leaving unrelated generations unchanged. Under the `GEM` protocol it erases more than `GEM` in most settings, **cutting the unsafe rate on bloody gore from 53.9% to 14.4%**, though retention of unrelated content holds for some concepts and degrades for others.

papers.title: Denoising Implicit Variational Inference
papers.abstract: Semi-implicit variational inference (SIVI) expands the representational capacity of variational families, but optimizing the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) remains challenging because the marginal score of the semi-implicit distribution is generally intractable. Unbiased Implicit Variational Inference (UIVI) and related methods address this difficulty through reparameterized ELBO gradients, but existing approaches estimate the required score indirectly through reverse-conditional sampling or approximation, which can be computationally costly and unstable. We propose Denoising Implicit Variational Inference (DIVI), which learns the marginal score directly via denoising score matching. The learned score is used as a plug-in estimator in the pathwise ELBO gradient, replacing inner reverse-conditional sampling with a score-network evaluation. We analyze DIVI as inexact stochastic gradient ascent and show, under stated assumptions, that the averaged stationarity measure is controlled by the usual optimization term and the average score-matching error. Empirically, we evaluate DIVI on both synthetic distributions and a variety of real-data Bayesian inference tasks. The results show that DIVI improves over the current UIVI baselines while reducing the cost of ELBO-gradient estimation.
papers.summary: Semi-implicit variational inference (SIVI) gives richer variational families, but optimizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is hard because the marginal score is intractable. Existing methods such as `UIVI` estimate it through costly and unstable reverse-conditional sampling. `DIVI` instead learns the marginal score directly with denoising score matching and plugs it into the pathwise ELBO gradient. The authors analyze the method as inexact stochastic gradient ascent with error controlled by the score-matching error, and show empirically that it **improves over `UIVI` baselines while lowering the cost of gradient estimation**.

papers.title: What "Form'' of Uncertainty Does Conformal Prediction Quantify?
papers.abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) is a post-hoc calibration method that returns prediction sets with distribution-free coverage guarantees, and the size of the output set is often interpreted as a notion of uncertainty. We show that the difference in set size between full and split CP is directly connected to Bayesian posterior variance, which is the epistemic uncertainty of the model. Essentially, this difference in set size is an aggregation of two opposite effects: (1) better model accuracy and therefore smaller set size achieved by training over extra calibration points, and (2) the "formability" of the model at test point towards every possible label. The latter effect vanishes with stronger models or more calibration data (as epistemic uncertainty is known for that behavior). It turns out that the model's formability itself (without the quantization effect of prediction sets, and through estimating the posterior variance) is a useful tool to quantify the epistemic uncertainty. In our empirical evaluation it performs on par with the state of the art in many setups.
papers.summary: The size of a conformal prediction (CP) set is often read as a measure of uncertainty, but it is unclear what kind of uncertainty it captures. The authors show that **the difference in set size between full and split CP is directly tied to the Bayesian posterior variance**, that is, the model's epistemic uncertainty. That difference combines two opposing effects: higher accuracy from training on the extra calibration points, and the model's formability at the test point toward every possible label. Estimating formability directly turns out to be a useful epistemic uncertainty measure that performs on par with the state of the art in many setups.

papers.title: TopoCompile: Molecular Generation with Exact Global Count Constraints
papers.abstract: Molecular generation designs novel molecules with desired structures and properties. Global count constraints specify molecular size, elemental composition, and ring content without prescribing detailed structure. Property-conditioned generators steer generation toward such targets but do not guarantee exact satisfaction. We introduce TopoCompile, which combines an autoregressive component-tree generator with a dynamic-programming compiler for supported component-additive integer counts. TopoCompile represents molecules as trees of intact ring systems and individual atoms, making each supported count additive over components. At each step, an autoregressive Transformer scores component and attachment actions, while the compiler masks actions with no target-satisfying completion. Within the fixed component vocabulary and typed attachment rules, constrained decoding guarantees exact equality for supported non-negative, component-additive integer counts. Applied at inference time, these checks let the same trained generator support different targets and count combinations without retraining. Across four benchmarks, TopoCompile achieves 100% Exact-valid yield for Common and Rare four-count target groups; the strongest baseline within each dataset reaches 44.9% or less on Rare targets. In unconditional generation, it achieves the highest validity or valid-unique-novel (V.U.N.) among the compared methods across all four benchmark datasets.
papers.summary: Property-conditioned molecular generators steer toward targets like molecular size, elemental composition, or ring counts but do not guarantee them exactly. `TopoCompile` represents molecules as trees of intact ring systems and individual atoms, so that these counts add up over components. An autoregressive Transformer scores each generation step, and a dynamic-programming compiler masks any action that cannot lead to a completion meeting the targets. This guarantees exact satisfaction at inference time without retraining, giving **100% exact-valid yield on common and rare four-count targets**, where the strongest baselines reach 44.9% or less on rare targets. It also achieves the best validity or valid-unique-novel scores in unconditional generation across four benchmarks.

papers.title: ProbePO: Sparse Probes, Redistributed Credit for Critic-Free LLM Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards assigns one terminal reward to an entire reasoning trajectory, obscuring how individual reasoning steps contributed to the outcome. GRPO broadcasts a group-normalized advantage to every response token, while finer-grained approaches often rely on dense auxiliary rollouts or branching schemes that can also alter the data used for policy updates. We cast the missing middle as budgeted measurement: with a limited rollout budget, which partial solutions should be evaluated, and how should their value estimates refine credit? ProbePO selects partial-solution states with a reward-free uncertainty score and estimates their expected verifier rewards under a capped continuation budget. ProbePO redistributes, rather than replaces, GRPO's trajectory-level advantage across tokens while preserving each trajectory's mean token-level advantage; probe continuations serve only as measurements. Across three DeepSeekMath and Qwen-family models spanning 1.5B-7B parameters, ProbePO consistently outperforms GRPO and achieves the highest accuracy among the four evaluated methods in 16 of 18 model-benchmark comparisons. Against dense-probing VinePPO on DeepSeekMath-7B, ProbePO achieves higher accuracy on all six benchmarks with 76% less end-to-end training time.

papers.title: $M^2Net$: Unifying Scale-Specific Structures and Prototype Decomposition for Spatial-Temporal Forecasting
papers.abstract: Spatial-temporal forecasting is pivotal for intelligent urban management yet remains challenging due to the intricate coupling of spatial dynamics and temporal non-stationarity. Existing approaches, while effective, often overlook two fundamental characteristics of real-world data: (1) Granularity-dependence, where dominant spatial correlations shift significantly across different time scales, and (2) Signal entanglement, where global common patterns are inextricably mixed with node-specific disturbances. In this paper, we propose a novel framework named $M^2Net$ (Multi-Scale Masked attention and Prototype network) to unify scale-specific structural learning and semantic decomposition. First, to capture the evolution of spatial dependencies, we introduce a Multi-Scale Masked attention mechanism. By downsampling temporal features into multiple resolutions, we dynamically generate scale-adaptive spatial masks, allowing the model to distinguish between micro-scale physical neighbors and macro-scale functional correlations. Second, to disentangle unique variations from shared trends, we propose a Prototype Residual Learning module. It retrieves global common patterns from a momentum-updated prototype bank and subtracts them from node representations, explicitly forcing the network to model the residual unique deviations. By integrating these two orthogonal views, i.e., structural multiscaling and semantic decomposition, our approach effectively isolates valid spatial-temporal signals from noise. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that $M^2Net$ outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on extensive empirical verifications.

papers.title: Axiomatic World Modeling for Physics Reasoning
papers.abstract: Recent research-level physics-reasoning benchmarks for LLMs reveal a failure mode that lies not in knowledge or execution, but in modeling the world being reasoned about. Models often silently alter given quantities, fabricate laws, or inject unstated assumptions to force a problem into familiar patterns, and then reason inside this corrupted world. We define this premise-level divergence as modeling drift: the gap between a model's internal axiomatic world model (AWM) and the true physical world specified in the problem. Although RLVR and PRM have yielded substantial gains in mathematics and code, their reward shapes do not directly supervise world modeling in axiomatic domains such as physics. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Axiomatic World Modeling (RLAWM), which optimizes the policy by penalizing divergence between its inferred axiomatic world model and the true physics world. RLAWM probes physics reasoning at two hierarchical levels (modeling and solving), each scored by a physically grounded reward. The modeling reward targets abstract knowledge formulation, evaluating whether the model captures the true axiomatic world before attempting calculation. The solving reward targets instantiated knowledge reasoning, checking whether the model's concrete derivation remains consistent with the axiomatic world. This two-level structure separates what world the model believes it is reasoning in from how it reasons within that world. The framework operates exclusively during training, with no extra cost during inference. RLAWM improves performance by up to +12.2 points on PhysReason and +5.2 on PHYSICS over the baseline. It also generalizes zero-shot across difficulty, source, and domain, with a 2.45x gain and +10 points over the strongest baseline on olympiad-level physics and math.

papers.title: HABIT-Bench: Evaluating Habit Induction from Longitudinal Weak Evidence in Agent Memory
papers.abstract: In long-term interactions with large language model (LLM) agents, users reveal habits through their choices and actions. These habits capture implicit user information that agents must infer across conversations. However, individual observations may provide only partial evidence about a habit or when it applies. Retaining past interactions alone does not ensure that agents can infer habits and apply them appropriately. We introduce HABIT-Bench to evaluate how well agent memory systems infer habits from weak evidence and apply them to later requests. We construct synthetic user histories from task-oriented dialogue data and controlled habit graphs. The histories span hundreds of sessions across food, finance, software, and travel. Four-choice tasks assess agents' ability to infer user habits and apply them appropriately. They include temporary exceptions, changes in habits, and suggestions that users have not accepted. Sampled tasks undergo independent human review. We evaluate eight memory methods with Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.3-Flash. The best-performing memory method achieves 33.61\% macro accuracy across the four domains. Performance remains limited even when annotated evidence is supplied directly. These results expose a persistent gap between access to past interactions and the ability to infer and appropriately use user habits.

papers.title: Comparing Sparsified MLPs and Transcoders: Many Transcoder Features Are Neurons in Disguise
papers.abstract:
MLP neurons in transformer language models are widely understood to be polysemantic, motivating transcoders - sparse, learned approximations of MLP layers - as interpretable replacement models for mechanistic analysis. However, recent work shows that MLP neurons can be used to recover sparse, interpretable circuits (Arora et al. 2026, Ye et al. 2025), raising the question of whether transcoders are necessary for circuit analysis.
  We define neuron features as transcoder features whose weights are strongly aligned with individual MLP neurons, and show that they account for a substantial fraction of active features in late layers across 13 open-source transcoders. Only neuron features have a stable correspondence with something in the underlying MLP: other features vary more between training runs, do not match the MLP's Jacobian, and change less significantly from their random initialization. Our findings reframe MLP neurons as a stronger basis for interpretability than commonly assumed, and call for better methods of attributing the non-neuron structure that is used by the model.
papers.summary: Transcoders are sparse, learned stand-ins for transformer MLP layers. They are used in mechanistic interpretability because individual MLP neurons are thought to be polysemantic, yet recent work recovers interpretable circuits directly from neurons. The authors define "neuron features" as transcoder features whose weights closely align with a single MLP neuron, and they find these make up a substantial share of active features in late layers across 13 open-source transcoders. **Only neuron features correspond stably to something in the underlying MLP**: the other features vary more between training runs, do not match the MLP's Jacobian, and move less from their random initialization. The authors argue that MLP neurons are a stronger interpretability basis than commonly assumed and that better methods are needed to attribute the remaining non-neuron structure.

papers.title: Reconstruction of Unobserved Core Electron Density in Tokamak Plasmas with a Neural Operator Transport Surrogate and Uncertainty Quantification
papers.abstract: Real-time control of tokamak plasmas requires the electron density profile. However, in a reactor-relevant device, diagnostic port access is limited and the profile can be observed only partially. In the present work we reconstruct the density profile by inferring the coefficients of a physics-based one-dimensional particle transport equation, using a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) surrogate of the transport solver as a fast differentiable forward model. The surrogate enables realtime-compatible gradient-based reconstruction and uncertainty quantification from the reflectometry and interferometry measurements. We compare four uncertainty quantification methods - multi-seed ensembles, the Laplace approximation, Metropolis-Hastings, and a Gaussian method independent of the reconstruction fit. The resulting uncertainty is scored with CRPS and coverage calibration, separately on the observed and unobserved regions. We further demonstrate advantage of our approach over standard analytical function fit on synthetic and experimental DIII-D discharges.
papers.summary: Real-time tokamak control needs the electron density profile, but reactor-relevant devices allow only limited diagnostic access, so the core of the profile often goes unobserved. The authors reconstruct the full profile by inferring the coefficients of a one-dimensional physics-based particle transport equation. They use a `Fourier Neural Operator` (`FNO`) surrogate of the transport solver as a fast, differentiable forward model, fitted to reflectometry and interferometry measurements. Four uncertainty quantification methods (multi-seed ensembles, the `Laplace approximation`, `Metropolis-Hastings`, and a fit-independent Gaussian method) are scored with `CRPS` and coverage calibration separately on observed and unobserved regions. On synthetic and experimental `DIII-D` discharges, **the approach outperforms standard analytical function fits**.

papers.title: Rethinking EEG Spatial Super-Resolution as Dynamic State Decomposition and Filtering
papers.abstract: EEG spatial super-resolution aims to recover high-density neural signals from sparse electrode observations. Existing methods have achieved substantial progress through spatial modeling, generative reconstruction, and temporal representation learning. However, the current EEG state contains two different sources of information: predictable evolution inherited from preceding states and newly emerging changes revealed by the current observation. Most approaches typically do not model these two components explicitly. In this work, we formulate streaming EEG spatial super-resolution as a sequential state filtering problem and propose Dynamic State Filtering (DSF). Rather than relying on a single temporal reconstruction pathway, DSF combines a history-aware dynamical branch with an innovation-filtering branch that explicitly decomposes waveform-state estimation into prediction and observation-driven correction. To infer how spatially incomplete innovations should affect missing locations, DSF routes the observed innovations across electrodes through a mask-constrained, topology-aware transition operator and incorporates them through uncertainty-aware state correction. The two complementary estimates are finally fused to reconstruct the dense EEG signal. Experiments on SEED, SEED-IV and BCI2000 demonstrate that DSF improves reconstruction fidelity and downstream utility while maintaining robustness under dynamically changing and unreliable sparse observations.
papers.summary: EEG spatial super-resolution recovers high-density brain signals from a sparse set of electrodes. The authors frame the streaming version as a sequential state-filtering problem. Their method, `Dynamic State Filtering` (`DSF`), splits estimation into a history-aware branch that predicts how the signal evolves and an innovation-filtering branch that corrects with new observations. Observed innovations are spread to missing electrodes through a mask-constrained, topology-aware transition operator with uncertainty-aware correction, and the two estimates are then fused. On `SEED`, `SEED-IV`, and `BCI2000`, `DSF` **improves reconstruction fidelity and downstream utility** and stays robust when sparse observations change dynamically or are unreliable.

papers.title: Contrastive Hypergraph Source-free Domain Adaptive Object Detection in Adverse Weather Conditions--Extended Version
papers.abstract: Adverse weather conditions such as fog, rain, snow, and low illumination introduce structured visibility degradations that severely impair object detectors trained on clear-weather data. When source data are inaccessible due to privacy or trans- mission constraints, source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) becomes necessary. However, existing SFDA methods based on pairwise contrastive learning struggle to capture high-order semantics and often suffer from agreement collapse under severe corruption. We propose REUNION, a hypergraph-guided SFDA framework for object detection in adverse weather conditions. REUNION constructs a contrastive hypergraph over target-domain object proposals, encoding high-order relations through intra-image context, weather-aware grouping, prototype-based semantic anchors, and uncertainty-aware connections between reliable and low-confidence instances. To effectively exploit these structured relations, we introduce a group-wise Hyper-InfoNCE objective that optimizes representations at the hyperedge level, enabling semantic information to propagate from confident proposals to corrupted or low-contrast instances. Experiments with diverse benchmarks demonstrate that REUNION effectively mitigates domain shifts and achieves state-of-the-art performance in SFDA settings.
papers.summary: Object detectors trained on clear-weather data degrade badly in fog, rain, snow, and low light. When the original training data cannot be accessed, adaptation must be source-free (source-free domain adaptation, or SFDA), and existing pairwise contrastive SFDA methods miss higher-order relations and can suffer agreement collapse under heavy corruption. `REUNION` builds a contrastive hypergraph over target-domain object proposals that links them by intra-image context, weather-aware grouping, prototype anchors, and uncertainty-aware connections between confident and low-confidence instances. A group-wise `Hyper-InfoNCE` loss optimizes representations at the hyperedge level so that semantic information flows from confident proposals to corrupted ones, and the method **achieves state-of-the-art SFDA detection performance** across several adverse-weather benchmarks.

papers.title: Structured Latent Dynamics for Long-Horizon Embodied World Models
papers.abstract: Reliable long-horizon prediction remains a central challenge for embodied world models. Although recent generative models can synthesize visually plausible action-conditioned futures, their latent dynamics are typically learned through unconstrained transition modules, which may gradually deviate from coherent physical evolution as predictions are recursively rolled forward. We investigate whether explicitly structuring latent state evolution can improve the stability and utility of such imagined trajectories. To this end, we introduce HWM, a structured dynamics framework that represents backbone latents in a learned phase space consisting of generalized coordinates and momenta. Future states are propagated through dissipative Hamiltonian dynamics and mapped back to the original latent representation through a learnable inverse interface. The resulting formulation can be integrated into existing world-model architectures without redesigning their perception or decoding components, while multi-step transition supervision encourages the structured rollout to remain aligned with the latent trajectories induced by real observations. Controlled simulation experiments show that HWM produces more accurate estimates of velocity, acceleration, and jerk and substantially reduces long-horizon energy drift relative to unstructured latent dynamics. We further evaluate the approach across three distinct embodied world-model settings, covering single-arm multi-view prediction with Ctrl-World, dual-arm single-view prediction with EVAC, and task-oriented single-arm prediction with Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B. On RoboCasa, incorporating HWM into Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B yields a 2.7% relative improvement in task success. On real-world AgiBot World trajectories, it improves nDTW by 9.7% with Ctrl-World and Logic by 8.4% with EVAC.
papers.summary: Generative embodied world models can produce plausible action-conditioned futures, but their unconstrained latent transition modules tend to drift away from coherent physics over long rollouts. `HWM` maps backbone latents into a learned phase space of generalized coordinates and momenta, advances them with dissipative Hamiltonian dynamics, and maps them back through a learnable inverse interface, so it can be added to existing architectures without changing their perception or decoding components. In controlled simulations, it estimates velocity, acceleration, and jerk more accurately and substantially reduces long-horizon energy drift. Added to `Ctrl-World`, `EVAC`, and `Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B`, it raises task success on `RoboCasa` by 2.7% (relative) and **improves nDTW by 9.7% on real `AgiBot World` trajectories** with `Ctrl-World`.

papers.title: From Score to Diagnosis: Search-Independent Post-Diagnosis for Symbolic Regression
papers.abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) solvers employ diverse search mechanisms, yet most rely on the same low-information scalar fitness. Such scores provide little guidance on why a skeleton fails or how it should be revised. Recent methods develop new methods to address this bottleneck. Their enhanced feedback mechanisms are tightly coupled to their search processes and are difficult to reuse across diverse SR solvers. Instead, we ask whether a shared feedback mechanism can further improve diverse solvers facing the same bottleneck. To this end, we propose PostDiag, a search-independent feedback mechanism, which can be shared to different SR solvers. PostDiag introduces Patch-wise Feature Profiling (PFP) to capture local behavior through patch-wise features of level, trend, and roughness. Based on PFP, PostDiag quantifies Skeleton Expressiveness Risk by comparing the fitted candidate with the observations, and Skeleton Stability Risk by measuring variability of behavior after bootstrap refitting. The Diagnostic Risk Plane (DRP) combines two risks to determine whether a skeleton should be preserved, repaired, simplified, or rewritten, while the patch-wise discrepancies provide evidence for the intervention. An LLM editor then performs the diagnosis-guided intervention, and the validated revision is returned to the original solver through a lightweight adapter. Experiments across multiple LLM-based and GP-based SR solvers show that PostDiag consistently improves accuracy and accelerates convergence.
papers.summary: Symbolic regression (SR) solvers search for equations in different ways, but most are guided by the same uninformative scalar fitness score, and existing richer feedback schemes are tied to specific search procedures. `PostDiag` is a solver-independent diagnosis layer. Its `Patch-wise Feature Profiling` describes local level, trend, and roughness, and from these it computes an expressiveness risk (fit versus observations) and a stability risk (variability under bootstrap refitting). A `Diagnostic Risk Plane` combines the two risks to decide whether a candidate skeleton should be kept, repaired, simplified, or rewritten, an LLM editor carries out the change, and an adapter returns the validated revision to the original solver. Across multiple LLM-based and genetic-programming SR solvers, **`PostDiag` consistently improves accuracy and speeds convergence**.

papers.title: A Multi-Step Inertial ADMM Algorithm for Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning has recently emerged as an important paradigm for large-scale distributed model training, which can be naturally formulated as a class of distributed learning problems. The alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is a widely used approach for solving such problems. However, its practical performance is often hindered by significant communication overhead and system heterogeneity. In this paper, we propose a multi-step inertial ADMM algorithm, called MiFedADMM, for federated learning. The proposed method leverages multiple historical iterates on the server side to construct a higher-order extrapolation after each aggregation to accelerate the convergence behavior. Under mild assumptions, we establish convergence results for the single-step variant of the proposed method and derive an O(1/K) convergence rate. Numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and improved performance of the proposed method compared with existing approaches.
papers.summary: The alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is widely used for federated learning, but communication overhead and system heterogeneity limit how well it works in practice. `MiFedADMM` speeds convergence by having the server extrapolate from several historical iterates after each aggregation step, a multi-step inertial scheme. The authors prove convergence for the single-step variant with **an O(1/K) convergence rate**, and experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show it outperforms existing approaches.

papers.title: Write Once, Query Many: Evolving Compact Reusable Memory for Long Videos
papers.abstract: Long videos often exceed the context capacity of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), while agentic search repeats costly video processing and grounding for each query. Reusable memory can amortize this cost, but must preserve information for questions unknown during construction. We propose Video-EMem, an evolvable video memory harness built on time-anchored perceptual observations. This representation combines compact free-form text with sparse images to preserve semantic content and complementary visual details across temporal scales, supporting temporal navigation without a fixed semantic schema. A Writer encodes each video once by consolidating overlapping multiscale observations, and a Reader retrieves and organizes evidence solely from the resulting memory. With the underlying models frozen, we evolve their workflows and operators using distinct feedback: query-independent source fidelity and coverage for the Writer, and QA failures in evidence localization and utilization for the Reader. Experiments support this separation for generalization beyond development queries, with our evolution strategy improving average accuracy by 7.2% over the unevolved harness. While reducing storage by about 99.86% on average relative to raw videos, Video-EMem improves Qwen3-VL-30B by an average of 2.6% across three long-video QA benchmarks over direct input of 2,048 frames. Using the same o3 answer model as the state-of-the-art agentic method, it improves average accuracy by 2.5% with lower per-query latency.
papers.summary: Long videos exceed the context window of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), and agentic search pipelines reprocess the video for every query. `Video-EMem` encodes each video once into a reusable memory of time-anchored observations, stored as compact free-form text plus sparse images. A Writer builds this memory and a Reader answers questions from it alone, and with the models kept frozen, the workflows of both are evolved using separate feedback signals (source fidelity and coverage for the Writer, QA failures for the Reader). Evolution improves accuracy by 7.2% over the unevolved harness. While **cutting storage by about 99.86% relative to raw video**, the system improves `Qwen3-VL-30B` by 2.6% over direct 2,048-frame input and beats the state-of-the-art agentic method by 2.5% with the same `o3` answer model at lower per-query latency.

papers.title: Accelerating Finite-Sum Bilevel Optimization with Fully First-Order Oracles
papers.abstract: We study nonconvex--strongly-convex bilevel optimization with finite-sum objectives and fully first-order oracles. We propose Sampled Implicit Corrections for Bilevel Optimization (SICBO), which combines a penalty approximation with variance-reduced corrections for the lower-level variables. Under componentwise lower strong convexity, SICBO finds a point $x$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi(x)\|^2\le\varepsilon^2$ within $\tilde{O}(N+\sqrt{N}\kappa^{7/2}\varepsilon^{-2})$ component-gradient calls, where $N$ is the total number of components and $\kappa$ is the normalized lower-level condition number. The bound achieves square-root finite-sum dependence using only gradients and preserves the best known deterministic fully first-order condition-number exponent for smooth problems. Our improvement follows from a curvature-dependent bound for nonlinear correction errors, which permits epochs of length $\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N/\kappa})$ with batches of size $\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N\kappa})$. A single-level reduction shows that the dependence on $N$ and $\varepsilon$ is optimal up to logarithmic factors for fixed $\kappa$.
papers.summary: This work addresses nonconvex–strongly-convex bilevel optimization with finite-sum objectives when only gradients are available (no Hessian computations). `Sampled Implicit Corrections for Bilevel Optimization` (`SICBO`) combines a penalty approximation with variance-reduced corrections for the lower-level variables. It reaches an ε-stationary point in Õ(N + √N κ^{7/2} ε^{-2}) component-gradient calls, which achieves square-root dependence on the number of components while keeping the best known condition-number exponent for fully first-order methods. A single-level reduction shows that **the dependence on N and ε is optimal up to logarithmic factors** for fixed κ.

papers.title: EGIP: An Evidence-Grounded Interaction Protocol for Clinical Agents
papers.abstract: Interactive clinical agents acquire evidence through patient dialogue and diagnostic examinations, yet their performance also depends on how the interaction environment exposes information, available actions, and examination results. When these conditions are implicit or inconsistently controlled, final-answer accuracy can conflate diagnostic reasoning with the effects of the interaction protocol. We propose the \textbf{E}vidence-\textbf{G}rounded \textbf{I}nteraction \textbf{P}rotocol (EGIP), which enforces role-specific information boundaries, exposes diagnostic actions without revealing their results, retrieves examination results from stored clinical records, and organizes acquired evidence for final decision-making. By separating evidence acquisition from terminal prediction, EGIP enables different decision strategies to operate on the same observations. We evaluate EGIP across two clinical-agent frameworks, five datasets, and six language models. EGIP improves diagnostic accuracy over native baselines across all primary comparisons. A clinician review further shows that the proportion of automatically scored correct responses jointly judged evidence-supported rises from 10.20\% to 36.55\%. These findings support the effectiveness of EGIP as a unified interaction protocol for improving clinical-agent performance through controlled evidence access and acquisition.
papers.summary: Interactive clinical agents gather evidence through patient dialogue and diagnostic tests, but final-answer accuracy can mix up diagnostic reasoning with quirks of how the environment exposes information. The `Evidence-Grounded Interaction Protocol` (`EGIP`) enforces role-specific information boundaries, lists diagnostic actions without revealing their results, pulls examination results from stored clinical records, and organizes the gathered evidence for a separate final decision step. Across two clinical-agent frameworks, five datasets, and six language models, `EGIP` improves diagnostic accuracy over native baselines in every primary comparison. In a clinician review, **the share of correct answers also judged evidence-supported rose from 10.20% to 36.55%**.

papers.title: Theory-Guided Instance-Dependent Early Stopping via Second-Order Loss Dynamics
papers.abstract: Instance-dependent early stopping (IES) reduces training computation by skipping backpropagation for examples whose losses have stabilized, but the second-order loss-difference criterion used by IES lacks a theoretical justification. We develop Theory-Guided Instance-Dependent Early Stopping (TG-IES), which analyzes this criterion under explicit assumptions and derives a noise-calibrated mastery threshold and a conditional stability bound for instance exclusion. We show that second-order differencing has a favorable bias-variance trade-off over first- and third-order differences in a specific signal-to-noise regime, and that its signal contains both gradient-drift and curvature terms. TG-IES derives its stopping threshold and patience from training-run statistics rather than using the manually selected threshold of IES. Across CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, TG-IES saves 53-58% of backpropagation instances in its main convolutional settings while keeping accuracy within 0.1-0.9 percentage points of full training; in the primary ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 setting, this corresponds to 35.7% FLOP-normalized savings. The method also transfers to ViT-Tiny, where it achieves smaller savings and incurs a modest accuracy cost. These results provide a theoretical basis for second-order instance-dependent early stopping and show that theory-guided calibration can substantially reduce training computation under the assumptions and experimental settings studied.
papers.summary: Instance-dependent early stopping (IES) saves training compute by skipping backpropagation for examples whose loss has stabilized, but its second-order loss-difference criterion has lacked theoretical grounding. `TG-IES` analyzes the criterion under explicit assumptions. It shows that second-order differencing has a favorable bias-variance trade-off in a specific signal-to-noise regime, and it derives the stopping threshold and patience from training-run statistics rather than tuning them by hand. On `CIFAR-10` and `CIFAR-100`, it **skips 53–58% of backpropagation instances while keeping accuracy within 0.1–0.9 points of full training**, which corresponds to 35.7% FLOP-normalized savings for `ResNet-18` on `CIFAR-10`. Savings are smaller and accuracy drops modestly on `ViT-Tiny`.

papers.title: When Code Becomes an LLM Call: An Empirical Study of Call-Site Contracts in Agentic Systems
papers.abstract: Software quality has long rested on specifications that state what code must do, and on testing and verification that check that the code does it. Agentic systems change this foundation: they replace parts of their logic, such as choosing the next tool, judging whether an action is allowed, or writing code to run, with calls to a large language model (LLM). The program still relies on what this logic must guarantee, but the model's behavior is not fixed by code, varies across runs, and can be steered by its input. The guarantee must therefore come from the program around each LLM call site, as a contract of pre-conditions, prompt constraints, and post-conditions. We present an empirical study of these contracts in 496 LLM call sites of 40 popular open-source agentic systems (13.4 MLOC, four languages). Using a multi-agent pipeline validated by 17,428 human judgments, we trace where every model output flows, derive an expected contract for each call site without access to its code, and compare it with the contract that the code implements. We find that 48% of LLM outputs reach control flow or execution, and 73% of these never reach a person. Programs enforce 78% of their constraints in code, but in the prompt, 67% of the constraints are only requested from the model. Although 82% of call sites are checked before and after the call, 63% of the expected constraints are unmet and only 5.3% of call sites satisfy their whole contract; ten recurring patterns explain 99% of the gaps. 38 mechanisms behind these gaps trigger at runtime, and a small code fix that enforces the expected constraint stops all 38. Our results show that the presence of checks says little about their adequacy, and we derive implications for agent developers, framework maintainers, and researchers.
papers.summary: Agentic systems hand parts of their program logic, such as picking tools, approving actions, or writing code to run, to LLM calls whose behavior is not fixed by code. Any guarantees therefore have to come from a contract of pre-conditions, prompt constraints, and post-conditions around each call site. The authors study 496 LLM call sites in 40 popular open-source agentic systems (13.4 million lines of code), using a multi-agent pipeline validated against 17,428 human judgments to compare the contract each call site should have with what its code enforces. They find that 48% of LLM outputs reach control flow or execution and 73% of those never reach a person, and that although 82% of call sites have checks, **only 5.3% satisfy their full expected contract**. Ten recurring patterns explain 99% of the gaps, and a small code fix that enforces the expected constraint stopped all 38 gap mechanisms that trigger at runtime.

papers.title: CARVS: A Congestion-Aware Algorithm for Online Multi-Agent Pickup-and-Delivery in Human-Collaborative Warehouses
papers.abstract: Intelligent warehouse systems have transformed logistics by integrating robots with minimal infrastructure changes, boosting efficiency and optimizing workflows compared to traditional human-only operations. However, human-robot collaboration introduces new challenges, particularly due to human uncertainty, which leads to dynamic interactions and unpredictable behavior. To address these complexities, this paper presents the Multi-Agent Pickup-and-Delivery with Human Collaboration (MAPDwHC) problem, an extension of the Multi-Agent Pickup-and-Delivery (MAPD) problem that incorporates human unpredictability. This problem adds key constraints, such as dynamic obstacles caused by robots temporarily blocking paths when interacting with humans, and the need for real-time responsiveness. We formalize the MAPDwHC problem with additional constraints and properties. Based on this problem setting, we propose the CARVS algorithm, which improves task assignment and path planning by integrating task swapping, validation checks, and random initialization. CARVS reduces congestion, enhances adaptability to human-robot interactions, and ensures real-time responsiveness. Simulation results show that CARVS significantly reduces timeouts of path planning in large-scale scenarios where traditional MAPD algorithms fail, improving both efficiency and scalability.
papers.summary: Warehouses that mix robots and human workers face unpredictable dynamics, such as robots temporarily blocking aisles while interacting with people. The authors formalize this as `Multi-Agent Pickup-and-Delivery with Human Collaboration` (`MAPDwHC`), an extension of the standard pickup-and-delivery problem with dynamic obstacles and real-time requirements. Their `CARVS` algorithm improves task assignment and path planning through task swapping, validation checks, and random initialization. In large-scale simulations where traditional pickup-and-delivery algorithms fail, `CARVS` **significantly reduces path-planning timeouts** and improves efficiency and scalability.

papers.title: From Stories to Features: Scaling Concept Vectors for AI Alignment & Interpretability
papers.abstract: We study feature vectors: directions in a language model's activation space that correspond to human-interpretable concepts, such as honesty or deception. Existing unsupervised methods like sparse autoencoders attempt to recover the whole feature space, often at the cost of feature quality and interpretability. We take a more pragmatic route: focusing on concepts relevant to AI safety and alignment, we generate synthetic concept-antagonist story pairs and use the difference of their mean model activations as a feature vector. We scale this approach to 1,036 alignment-relevant concepts using 2M synthetic stories across multiple languages and genres, which we publicly release. Across six models from three model families, our feature vectors reliably generalize to detecting their corresponding concepts in chat dialogues and web text. They form an interpretable geometry shared across models and can causally steer model behavior when injected into activations. We further use these features to analyze model representations during jailbreak attacks, mathematical and agentic reasoning. Our targeted feature construction thus offers a scalable route to studying concepts in language models, potentially extending to millions of features across arbitrary domains.
papers.summary: Instead of recovering a model's entire feature space with sparse autoencoders, the authors build targeted feature vectors for safety-relevant concepts such as honesty or deception. Each vector is the difference in mean activations between synthetic stories that express a concept and stories that express its opposite. They scale this to **1,036 alignment-relevant concepts using 2M synthetic multilingual stories**, which they publicly release. Across six models from three families, the vectors detect their concepts in chat dialogues and web text, form an interpretable geometry shared across models, and steer model behavior when injected into activations. The authors also use them to analyze model representations during jailbreak attacks and during mathematical and agentic reasoning.

papers.title: No-Regret Revenue Maximization in Sequential Market Making Under Inventory Constraints
papers.abstract: Market makers keep trading efficient by setting bid and ask prices for buyers and sellers. In sequential market making, trades happen independently based on price thresholds, requiring the market maker to maintain balanced, low-risk inventory over T rounds. This paper studies how to maximize revenue with unknown buyer and seller valuations using regret minimization. When the market maker only sees trade success or failure, an algorithm achieves regret and inventory bounds proportional to T to the power of 2/3. When full order book data is available for failed trades, regret and inventory limits improve significantly to the square root of T. We also establish a fundamental trade-off via a lower bound, by proving that tighter round-by-round inventory limits strictly force higher minimum regret.
papers.summary: A market maker posts bid and ask prices over T rounds without knowing buyers' and sellers' valuations, and must keep its inventory balanced while maximizing revenue. Framed as regret minimization, the problem admits an algorithm with regret and inventory bounds of order T^{2/3} when the market maker sees only whether each trade succeeded. With full order-book data on failed trades, both bounds improve to √T. A lower bound shows that **tighter per-round inventory limits strictly force higher minimum regret**.

papers.title: Representations Have Trajectories: Characterizing Temporal Representation Dynamics in Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that deep neural networks exhibit an implicit low-rank simplicity bias. In this paper, we investigate the questions that naturally arise from this observation. What are the temporal consequences of low-rank simplicity bias during optimization? How does representation geometry evolve throughout optimization rather than only at convergence? Do different neural architectures exhibit distinct geometric optimization behaviors? To answer these questions, we conduct a large-scale empirical study tracking representational geometry throughout training. We find that neural networks follow three recurring geometric trajectories: persistent high-rank, collapse-and-recovery, and persistent low-rank. We further identify Destructive Representation Collapse (DRC) as a pathological regime in which representations collapse to rank-one and fail to recover, leading to a sustained loss of representational capacity. While collapse-and-recovery is consistently associated with successful optimization in controlled settings, experiments on real-world models show that the relationship between geometric trajectories and optimization outcomes is configuration dependent. Overall, our findings suggest that representation geometry evolves dynamically during training and provide a new perspective on how deep neural networks learn.
papers.summary: Building on evidence that deep networks have an implicit bias toward low-rank representations, a large-scale empirical study tracks how representation geometry changes over the course of training rather than only at convergence. Networks follow three recurring trajectories: persistent high-rank, collapse-and-recovery, and persistent low-rank. The authors also identify `Destructive Representation Collapse` (`DRC`), a pathological regime in which **representations collapse to rank one and never recover**, permanently losing capacity. Collapse-and-recovery is consistently associated with successful optimization in controlled settings, but in real-world models the link between trajectory and outcome depends on the configuration.

papers.title: ASR Personalization in Pathological Voice: Accuracy, Efficiency, and Duration Effects
papers.abstract: Automatic Speech recognition (ASR) struggles with Pathological speech due to persistent speaker-specific mismatch. In clinical and accessibility scenarios, only limited target-speaker data is typically available, making full model retraining impractical. We present a component-level analysis of LoRA adaptation in Whisper, investigating how adapter placement interacts with the model size, training efficiency and utterance-duration in single-speaker settings. Our experimental comparative study shows that while scaling reduces errors, it does not eliminate mismatch. Furthermore, the full attention LoRa provides the most reliable accuracy, and the best time--accuracy trade-off. Improvements vary across utterance length, with medium-length recordings benefiting the most, while short and long utterances remain challenging. These findings highlight the importance of adaptation placement and duration-dependent evaluation, under challenging, data-scarce personalization scenarios.
papers.summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) performs poorly on pathological speech, and typically only a little data from the target speaker is available, which rules out full retraining. The authors run a component-level analysis of `LoRA` adapters in `Whisper` for single-speaker personalization, varying adapter placement, model size, training efficiency, and utterance duration.
