Under identical data and training, **editable planning state improves the diffusion agent by 2.44 F1 versus only 0.47 for its AR source model**.

papers.title: Neuro-Inspired Inhibitory Message Passing for Accurate and Token-Efficient Multi-Agent Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems promise to solve problems by bringing together information beyond the reach of any individual agent. Retrieval and tool use can distribute this information across agents, making communication essential to collaboration. A central challenge is keeping crucial evidence visible in each agent's context as messages accumulate. Repeated information can crowd out rare, decisive evidence. Models of cortical circuits suggest a principle for addressing this imbalance: inhibition can selectively suppress shared inputs while preserving sensitivity to weaker signals. We adapt this principle into inhibitory message passing, a training-free communication router that cancels redundant evidence separately for each evidence sentence and receiver. Each round, it forwards evidence sentences restated in agents' messages, delivering each at most once to receivers whose own evidence lacks it and excluding the senders' reasoning and answers. Against standard message passing, accuracy in peer groups rose by 39-77 percentage points across three benchmarks, and tokens per run fell by 10-46%. Gains held across seven open models spanning four to thirty-two billion parameters and two commercial models, in groups up to sixty-four agents, and across multi-agent architectures including peer-to-peer, orchestrator-worker, and multilevel hierarchical organizations. These findings support a scalable design pattern for more accurate and token-efficient multi-agent reasoning.
papers.summary: In multi-agent systems where retrieval and tool use spread evidence across agents, repeated information in accumulating messages can crowd rare but decisive evidence out of each agent's context. Inspired by inhibition in cortical circuits, inhibitory message passing is a training-free communication router that forwards each evidence sentence at most once, and only to agents that lack it, while excluding the senders' reasoning and answers. Compared with standard message passing, **accuracy in peer groups rose by 39–77 percentage points across three benchmarks while tokens per run fell by 10–46%**. The gains held across seven open models from 4B to 32B parameters, two commercial models, groups of up to 64 agents, and peer-to-peer, orchestrator-worker, and hierarchical architectures.

papers.title: Tensor Network Datamodels for Training Data Attribution
papers.abstract: Datamodels predict how a model's behavior changes when different parts of its training data are included or removed. However, linear datamodels assign fixed contributions to training units and cannot represent non-additive joint effects. We introduce Tensor Network Datamodels (TNDMs), which use low-rank tensor networks to model dependencies among training units while keeping the representation compact. TNDMs learn a map from subsets of the training data to the outcome of training on those subsets, allowing them to represent interactions among several training units. We prove that complementary and redundant training groups can induce high-degree subset functions with compact low-rank representations. A single fitted TNDM can then be used for several training data questions, including predicting the effect of removing data, measuring the importance of individual training units, identifying interactions between training units, and selecting useful subsets of the training data. We evaluate TNDMs on controlled tasks designed to contain strong interactions, as well as standard fine-tuning settings for classification and reasoning. On a controlled reasoning task, TNDMs outperform every baseline while observing only half as many training subsets, and TNDM-TT reduces prediction NMSE by $89\%$ relative to the linear datamodel after observing approximately $0.0061\%$ of all possible training subsets. In factual-association fine-tuning, a single TNDM-CP raises held-out $\mathrm{R}^2$ from $0.579$ to $0.668$ over the linear datamodel. These results demonstrate that compact low-rank models improve prediction when training data effects depend on combinations of training groups.
papers.summary: Datamodels predict how a model's behavior changes when parts of its training data are included or removed, but linear datamodels cannot capture joint effects among training units. Tensor Network Datamodels (`TNDMs`) use low-rank tensor networks to learn a compact map from training subsets to training outcomes that can represent such interactions. The authors prove that complementary or redundant groups of training units yield high-degree interactions that still have compact low-rank representations. A single fitted `TNDM` can answer removal, importance, interaction, and subset-selection questions. On a controlled reasoning task, `TNDM-TT` **cuts prediction error (NMSE) by 89% relative to the linear datamodel after seeing about 0.0061% of possible subsets**. In factual-association fine-tuning, `TNDM-CP` raises held-out R² from 0.579 to 0.668.

papers.title: PV-Decoding: Progressive Verification Decoding with Decode Gating for Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) offer an attractive alternative to autoregressive generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, but their inference efficiency is still limited by the cost of safely committing tentative predictions. In particular, speculative decoding for dLLMs is challenging because speculative tokens within the same diffusion block may depend on one another, making aggressive acceptance prone to error propagation and strict verification computationally expensive. We present PV-Decoding, a confidence-driven speculative decoding framework with progressive verification for block diffusion inference. PV-Decoding partitions masked positions into directly decoded tokens, speculative tokens, and unresolved tokens using two confidence thresholds, and then verifies speculative tokens with progressively stronger policies, including single-batch, dual-batch, and multi-batch verification. This design exposes a practical accuracy--efficiency trade-off: weaker verification minimizes overhead, whereas stronger verification improves acceptance precision and robustness. Experiments on three diffusion language models across GSM8K, MBPP, and HumanEval show that PV-Decoding reduces sequential model forward passes (MFPs) by 8%--37% relative to confidence-based decoding, while keeping the largest observed accuracy drop to 1.3%. On Dream-7B-Instruct/GSM8K, PV-Decoding (1-batch) and PV-Decoding (2-batch) improve throughput by 7.0%--13.6% under the same hardware budget, whereas PV-Decoding (multi-batch) is slower under the current runtime. These results suggest that confidence-guided speculation with structured verification is a practical path toward efficient and reliable dLLM inference.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding is hard to apply to discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) because speculative tokens in the same block can depend on each other: accepting them aggressively propagates errors, and verifying them strictly is expensive. `PV-Decoding` uses two confidence thresholds to split masked positions into directly decoded, speculative, and unresolved tokens, and verifies speculative tokens with progressively stronger single-, dual-, or multi-batch policies. On three dLLMs across `GSM8K`, `MBPP`, and `HumanEval`, it **reduces sequential model forward passes by 8–37% with at most a 1.3% accuracy drop**. On `Dream-7B-Instruct`, the 1- and 2-batch variants raise throughput by 7.0–13.6%, while the multi-batch variant is slower under the current runtime.

papers.title: Where Natural Language Ends in Agents: Executable Skill Composition with MetaSkill
papers.abstract: Agent Skills express open-ended task knowledge in natural language, but composing them requires persistent execution order and upstream-output handoffs. We propose selective formalization at Skill boundaries: coordination relations with stable references and machine-checkable constraints become executable, while substantive task judgments remain within Skills. We introduce MetaSkill, a hybrid representation that preserves complete Skill packages and local instructions while making invocation dependencies and predecessor-text bindings executable through a directed acyclic graph (DAG) runtime. This interface supports explicit coordination without prescribing how each Skill performs its local task. Across 20 multi-Skill artifact tasks and two LLMs, we compare natural-language procedures, prompt-visible graphs, and MetaSkill derived from a common frozen plan per task, using the same designated Skill packages. Additional comparisons evaluate AgentSkillOS with the same available Skill packages as MetaSkill, as well as agent systems using their configured tools. Blinded artifact judgments yield favorable preference point estimates across all reported comparisons, with 95% task-bootstrap intervals excluding parity against Prompt Graph under DeepSeek-V4-Flash and OpenClaw under GLM-5.2. In audited GLM-5.2 execution traces, all planned nodes complete and all declared precedence constraints are satisfied. Together, these findings support MetaSkill as a practical interface for composing open-ended Skills, combining local linguistic flexibility with executable dependencies, explicit predecessor-text bindings, and auditable coordination. Code is available at: https://github.com/TokenRhythm/opensquilla/tree/paper/metaskill-lp4fm-2026
papers.summary: Agent Skills describe task knowledge in natural language, but chaining them together needs reliable execution order and handoff of earlier outputs. `MetaSkill` formalizes only the boundaries between Skills: invocation dependencies and bindings to predecessor outputs run on a directed acyclic graph (DAG) runtime, while each Skill's own instructions stay in natural language. Across 20 multi-Skill artifact tasks and two LLMs, blinded judges favored `MetaSkill` over natural-language procedures, prompt-visible graphs, `AgentSkillOS`, and tool-using agent systems. The preference was statistically clear against Prompt Graph under `DeepSeek-V4-Flash` and against `OpenClaw` under `GLM-5.2`. In audited `GLM-5.2` traces, **all planned nodes completed and all declared precedence constraints were satisfied**.

papers.title: fxBench: Evaluating and Understanding Formula Suggestions in Spreadsheets
papers.abstract: Spreadsheets are among the most widely used tools for computations, and formulas are their core building blocks. Besides agentic spreadsheet tools, proactive formula suggestions enable significant productivity gains and are now available in popular spreadsheet software (Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets). Such suggestions pose interesting challenges: the right context must be collected and represented for a machine learning model, which must then be able to write a correct formula, in a way that is fast and cheap enough to trigger on every = (or subsequent keystrokes for auto-completion) without taking users out of their editing flow. Surprisingly, there is no public benchmark for formula suggestions on real spreadsheets. In this paper, we therefore (1) introduce fxBench as a manually curated benchmark of 503 formula suggestion tasks based on Sheetpedia, (2) break down the formula suggestion problem into four capabilities (gather context, understand context, understand intent, write formula) that a formula suggestion system requires, and (3) evaluate existing and new approaches to understand bottlenecks in these capabilities that pose interesting research directions. Specifically, we annotate each benchmark with the cells that describe intent to determine the theoretical performance limit of a given context selection strategy, we evaluate performance of small and large models on different representations of context, including a dense format with high theoretical coverage at low token counts, and we fine-tune smaller language models to show that we can learn to understand such dense formats. Additionally, we perform quantitative and qualitative analysis on failure modes to understand bottlenecks in the formula writing capability; the best configuration only achieved 58.8% correct suggestions.
papers.summary: Proactive formula suggestions in Excel and Google Sheets must gather the right context, infer user intent, and write a correct formula fast enough to trigger on every keystroke, yet no public benchmark for this task existed. `fxBench` provides 503 manually curated formula-suggestion tasks from `Sheetpedia` and breaks the problem into four capabilities: gathering context, understanding context, understanding intent, and writing the formula. The authors annotate intent cells to bound how well each context-selection strategy can do, compare small and large models across context representations including a dense low-token format, and fine-tune smaller models to read that format. **The best configuration produced correct suggestions only 58.8% of the time**.

papers.title: GLOSS-MT: Controllable Low-Resource Machine Translation with an Editable Dictionary
papers.abstract: Adapting a pretrained machine translation (MT) model to new terminology usually requires new parallel data and another round of fine-tuning, which is costly for low-resource languages. We ask whether controllability can be added to MT, and the fine-tuning burden reduced, without degrading the pretrained model. GLOSS-MT looks up the source's noun phrases in an offline English-Twi dictionary, replaces every phrase found by its Twi translation in place, and fine-tunes a translation model once to translate these mixed inputs. We apply the same data and pipeline to NLLB-200 (600M, 1.3B, 3.3B), OPUS-MT en-tw and TranslateGemma 4B. On a document-level English-to-Asante Twi benchmark (84 documents, four domains), every fine-tune scores above its pretrained base in chrF2 (+2.85 to +5.48), and the three NLLB fine-tunes are the best open systems (50.12-50.80). A direct controllability test on human-translated Bible passages shows that the three fine-tunes tested write 79-97% of the dictionary terms, and that replacing every dictionary entry by a different term changes the output accordingly (70-97% of the new terms appear) with no retraining. We release the models, data and code.
papers.summary: Adapting a machine translation (MT) model to new terminology usually requires new parallel data and another round of fine-tuning, which is costly for low-resource languages. `GLOSS-MT` replaces source noun phrases with their Twi translations from an offline English–Twi dictionary and fine-tunes a model once to translate these mixed inputs. Applied to `NLLB-200`, `OPUS-MT`, and `TranslateGemma`, every fine-tune beats its base model by 2.85–5.48 chrF2 on a document-level English-to-Asante Twi benchmark. The fine-tuned models use 79–97% of the dictionary terms, and **swapping dictionary entries changes the output accordingly (70–97% of the new terms appear) without retraining**.

papers.title: Can LLM Agents Resolve Service Failures? Simulating Multi-Turn Complaint Handling under Information Asymmetry
papers.abstract: LLM agents are widely adopted in service chatbots for rule-guided support and information access, yet emotionally demanding complaint handling still relies heavily on human agents. We introduce ServiceBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark dedicated to complaint handling, with 2,500 scenarios spanning 184 complaint categories and five service industries. We propose Asymmetric Progressive Complaint Simulation (APCS) to simulate realistic complaint handling, together with a justice-based evaluation framework. Our experiments reveal that even capable LLM agents struggle to handle complaints effectively. They lack the ability to proactively gather information and strategically guide conversations toward resolution, often resorting to premature compensation. We further show that targeted post-training with SFT and DPO substantially improves these capabilities, enabling a smaller model to match or surpass much larger models on several outcomes.
papers.summary: LLM agents are common in support chatbots, but emotionally demanding complaint handling still relies mostly on human agents. `ServiceBench` is presented as the first benchmark for complaint handling, with 2,500 scenarios across 184 complaint categories and five industries. It is paired with Asymmetric Progressive Complaint Simulation (`APCS`), which simulates customers who reveal information gradually, and a justice-based evaluation framework. Even capable LLM agents fail to gather information proactively or steer conversations toward resolution, and often resort to premature compensation. Targeted post-training with `SFT` and `DPO` **lets a smaller model match or surpass much larger models on several outcomes**.

papers.title: How Does Muon Work in Private Deep Learning? Scalable Differentially Private Training via Orthogonalization
papers.abstract: Training deep neural networks requires optimizers that balance computational efficiency with formal data privacy. While orthogonalized update rules, such as the recently introduced Muon optimizer, have shown strong empirical performance and scalability, their behavior under Differential Privacy (DP) is not yet understood. In this paper, we propose DP-Muon, a differentially private variant of the Muon optimizer. By analyzing Muon's orthogonalized updates through the lens of a Linear Minimization Oracle (LMO), we show that the leading effect of per-example clipping is a positive rescaling of the gradient, to which the LMO is blind, so that only a small directional residual controlled by the centered gradient variance enters the optimization error. This yields an $\mathcal O(K^{-1/4})$ convergence rate, up to logarithmic factors, to a clipping-dependent neighborhood at a fixed noise scale and, with noise calibrated to a fixed $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ budget, the standard $(\sqrt d/(n\varepsilon))^{1/2}$ privacy--utility bound of DP-SGD, without assuming bounded gradients. Furthermore, we investigate the hyperparameter landscape of DP-Muon and document how the optimal learning rate, momentum, and batch size change under privacy. Empirically, on image classification DP-Muon matches or improves on DP-SGD and DP-Adam, whereas on language modeling the best optimizer depends on the batch size, with DP-Muon best at small batches and DP-Adam best near the privacy-optimal batch size.
papers.summary: The `Muon` optimizer orthogonalizes its updates and has shown strong performance and scalability, but its behavior under Differential Privacy (DP) has not been studied. Analyzing `DP-Muon` through a Linear Minimization Oracle shows that per-example clipping mainly rescales the gradient, which the oracle ignores, so only a small directional residual affects optimization. This yields an O(K^-1/4) convergence rate and **the standard DP-SGD privacy–utility bound without assuming bounded gradients**. The authors also map how the optimal learning rate, momentum, and batch size shift under privacy. Empirically, `DP-Muon` matches or beats `DP-SGD` and `DP-Adam` on image classification, while on language modeling it wins at small batch sizes and `DP-Adam` wins near the privacy-optimal batch size.

papers.title: Gaussian Process Bandits with Paired Auxiliary Observations
papers.abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is widely used for expensive black-box optimization, yet observation noise makes each evaluation less informative and slows posterior learning. Standard BO learns from costly outcomes gathered during optimization. In many applications, however, low-cost auxiliary data are available beforehand. We introduce Auxiliary-Informed Gaussian Process Bandit (AI-GPB), a variance-reduction method that combines an offline estimate of the auxiliary mean with a correction coefficient learned from paired online observations. Notably, it exploits correlation between paired observation errors without requiring the auxiliary mean to approximate the objective. We establish finite-sample GP confidence bounds and regret guarantees, including explicit cumulative and simple regret rates for Mat\'ern kernels. Numerical experiments across continuous BO benchmarks with varied landscapes and dimensions show consistent reductions in cumulative and simple regret relative to vanilla GP-UCB, even when within-pair correlation is moderate and the auxiliary mean is estimated from noisy offline data.
papers.summary: Noise in Bayesian optimization (BO) makes each expensive evaluation less informative, even though cheap auxiliary data is often available in advance. The Auxiliary-Informed Gaussian Process Bandit (`AI-GPB`) reduces variance by combining an offline estimate of the auxiliary mean with a correction coefficient learned from paired online observations. It exploits correlation between the paired observation errors and does not need the auxiliary mean to approximate the objective. The authors prove finite-sample confidence bounds and explicit regret rates for Matérn kernels. Experiments on continuous BO benchmarks show **consistent reductions in cumulative and simple regret over `GP-UCB`**, even with moderate within-pair correlation and noisy offline estimates.

papers.title: Toward Collective Model Intelligence: Characterizing and Coordinating Models
papers.abstract: Independently developed AI models accumulate diverse and complementary capabilities, but a growing model collection does not automatically realize Collective AI. Addressing this gap requires understanding model capabilities with limited evaluation, organizing complementary models to collaborate on diverse tasks, and executing model calls efficiently under resource constraints. We present a systematic approach to pursuing Collective Model Intelligence through three connected components. First, Model Eval constructs evidence-based capability profiles by combining query-level performance estimation with cross-domain prediction, reducing the need for exhaustive evaluation. Second, Mio (Models in One) organizes complementary model candidates and supports task-conditioned, cost-aware selection and collaboration as task requirements evolve. Third, Mos (Model Serving OS) separates model selection from execution and provides endpoint scheduling and shared model deployment and distribution. Experiments show lower capability-estimation errors under limited evaluation. Across nine public benchmarks, Mio 1.0 Lite achieves the highest average score and lowest average cost among compared methods, with per-request costs 73.7-97.5% lower than those of the best-scoring alternatives. A prewarmed shared cache accelerates model-file retrieval by up to 23.3 times. This work lays a foundation for Collective Model Intelligence by characterizing and coordinating the diverse capabilities of an expanding model universe.
papers.summary: A growing collection of independently developed models does not automatically act as a collective system: their capabilities first have to be understood, matched to tasks, and served efficiently. The proposed approach has three parts. `Model Eval` builds capability profiles from limited evaluation by estimating performance on individual queries and predicting across domains. `Mio` (Models in One) selects and combines complementary models for each task while accounting for cost, and `Mos` (Model Serving OS) handles endpoint scheduling and shared deployment. Across nine public benchmarks, `Mio 1.0 Lite` has the highest average score and lowest average cost of the compared methods, with **per-request costs 73.7–97.5% lower than the best-scoring alternatives**, and a prewarmed shared cache speeds up model-file retrieval by up to 23.3 times.

papers.title: Are We Evaluating VLM Token Pruning Right? Looking Beyond Accuracy and Token Count
papers.abstract: Visual token pruning aims to reduce inference cost while preserving the capabilities of the original VLM. Yet existing evaluations rely on aggregate task accuracy and retained token count as proxies for pruning quality and actual efficiency. We reveal two limitations: 1) Aggregate accuracy can obscure whether a pruning method truly identifies critical visual tokens; many examples remain solvable under arbitrary token removal and models can exploit textual shortcuts when visual evidence is degraded. 2) Retained token count is an unreliable proxy for efficiency, as identical token budgets can incur different end-to-end costs depending on where and how pruning is performed. Consequently, comparisons based on aggregate accuracy and retained token counts fail to recover the global performance-efficiency Pareto frontier across methods. We introduce PAA-Bench, a plug-and-play evaluation framework for existing benchmarks, to evaluate whether pruning succeeds through meaningful token selection and whether this success translates into real speedup. To determine when token choice actually matters, we propose Random-Pass@k to measure how often an example remains correct under random pruning, enabling comprehensive evaluation across different levels of selection difficulty. To compare efficiency fairly, we introduce Preservation-Constrained Speedup (PCS) to report the maximum end-to-end speedup each method achieves under a shared preservation target. Experiments across 8 methods, 3 VLM backbones, and 9 benchmarks show that stronger token compression does not necessarily yield greater speedup, method differences widen on examples where token selection matters, and efficiency rankings change with the preservation target.
papers.summary: Visual token pruning methods for vision-language models (VLMs) are usually judged by task accuracy and how many tokens they keep. The authors argue that both measures mislead: many examples stay solvable even when tokens are removed at random, and the same token budget can produce very different end-to-end costs. They introduce `PAA-Bench`, an evaluation framework that plugs into existing benchmarks. It adds `Random-Pass@k`, which measures how often an example survives random pruning, and Preservation-Constrained Speedup (`PCS`), the maximum real speedup a method reaches while preserving a set level of performance. Across 8 methods, 3 VLM backbones and 9 benchmarks, **stronger token compression does not necessarily yield greater speedup**, and efficiency rankings change depending on the preservation target.

papers.title: ReTRACE: Feedback-Guided LLM Agent in a Chemistry Harness for Retrosynthesis Planning
papers.abstract: Computer-aided retrosynthesis has advanced through single-step prediction, tree search and route scoring, but complex targets still require judgement over the whole route, where stereochemistry, functional-group compatibility, cost and greenness interact. Here we present \textbf{\mbox{ReTRACE}} (\textbf{RE}trosynthesis with \textbf{T}ool-orchestrated \textbf{R}easoning \textbf{A}nd \textbf{C}ontext-aware \textbf{E}vidence), an agent that places a large language model (LLM) in a chemistry harness that integrates molecular tools, complementary single-step prediction engines, a purchasable starting-material library, a route memory and a multi-criterion route evaluator. Routes are judged by a new metric that combines programmatic checks with adversarial LLM review, and its verdicts are compared with a synthetic chemist's. The agent learns continually from evaluator feedback during search, diagnosing weak routes and backtracking to revise them. With Claude Opus 4.8, at least one of the top 10 routes proposed by ReTRACE passed the audit for 87.4\%, 95.0\% and 86.7\% of targets on the three benchmarks. Two prospective wet-lab syntheses show that ReTRACE route proposals can be converted into executable procedures after expert revision.
papers.summary: Planning chemical syntheses for complex molecules requires judging whole routes, where stereochemistry, functional-group compatibility, cost and greenness interact. `ReTRACE` places a large language model (LLM) agent inside a chemistry harness with molecular tools, several single-step prediction engines, a library of purchasable starting materials, a route memory and a multi-criterion evaluator. The agent learns from evaluator feedback during search, diagnosing weak routes and backtracking to revise them. Routes are scored by programmatic checks combined with adversarial LLM review, which is compared against a synthetic chemist's verdicts. With `Claude Opus 4.8`, **at least one of the top 10 proposed routes passed the audit for 87.4%, 95.0% and 86.7% of targets** on three benchmarks, and two wet-lab syntheses showed the proposals could become executable procedures after expert revision.

papers.title: CorrFlow: Self-Correcting Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Flow-matching models generate samples through iterative velocity predictions, but typically do not revisit these predictions using the intermediate representations that produced them. We introduce CorrFlow, a self-correcting flow-matching framework that reuses this information through a lightweight refiner. Under rectified-flow interpolation, the error of the one-step clean prediction equals the realized velocity residual scaled by the noise level. Motivated by this identity, the refiner learns to predict residual corrections from the base model's clean prediction, conditioning, noise level and hidden states from the same forward pass. The correction is added to the base velocity before each sampling update, so subsequent predictions are made from the corrected state. This requires no additional base-model evaluations and only one lightweight refiner evaluation per step. Our theoretical analyses establish conditions under which feature reuse outperforms raw-input affine predictors and refiner training achieves greater residual-risk reduction than continued base-model training under a matched training compute budget. Experiments on class-conditional image generation, text-to-video generation and image-to-video generation show consistent improvements over the corresponding base models, including gains in visual quality and physical consistency. Project Page: https://fogradio.github.io/corrflow-project
papers.summary: Flow-matching generative models predict a velocity at each sampling step but never revisit those predictions using the intermediate representations that produced them. `CorrFlow` adds a lightweight refiner, motivated by an identity under rectified-flow interpolation: the error of the one-step clean prediction equals the velocity residual scaled by the noise level. The refiner predicts a residual correction from the base model's clean prediction, conditioning, noise level and hidden states, and that correction is added to the velocity before each update, so no extra base-model evaluations are needed. Theoretical analysis gives conditions under which this beats continued base-model training at matched compute, and experiments show **consistent gains over base models in class-conditional image, text-to-video and image-to-video generation**, including better visual quality and physical consistency.

papers.title: From Overparameterised Expressions to Parsimonious Models: Fisher-Geometric Pruning for Symbolic Regression
papers.abstract:
Genetic programming symbolic regression (GPSR) often returns expressions that are larger than necessary, with dormant branches and finely tuned algebraic configurations that fit sampling noise. Existing complexity-control strategies, such as multi-objective size-accuracy search or information criteria embedded in the fitness function, act on syntactic representations during model search. We introduce Fisher-Geometric pruning (FGP), a post-hoc model-reduction framework that acts on fitted models and can complement these techniques.
  FGP combines local information geometry at the maximum-likelihood solution with explicit compatibility tests for interpretable parametric boundaries. A taxonomy of parametric directions separates local sensitivity from proximity to reducible boundaries, enabling the treatment of unidentifiable directions and reductions through zero constraints, asymptotic limits, and signed parameter identifications. Candidate reductions are realised by symbolic contraction and refitting, then accepted only when their cross-validated predictive risk remains within a prescribed tolerance.
  We evaluate FGP on controlled diagnostic problems and Pareto fronts generated by GPSR. Across both settings, FGP substantially reduces structural complexity while preserving, and often improving, out-of-sample accuracy. Comparisons with competing pruning strategies and ablations show that, by combining geometric screening, boundary compatibility, and predictive validation, FGP yields the most consistent joint gains in parsimony and generalisation.
papers.summary: Genetic programming symbolic regression (GPSR) often returns expressions that are bigger than necessary, with dormant branches and finely tuned terms that fit noise. Fisher-Geometric pruning (`FGP`) simplifies an already fitted model after search. It uses the local information geometry at the maximum-likelihood solution, together with explicit tests for interpretable parametric boundaries, to find reductions such as zero constraints, asymptotic limits and identifications between parameters. Each candidate reduction is symbolically contracted and refitted, and is kept only if its cross-validated predictive risk stays within a set tolerance. On diagnostic problems and on Pareto fronts produced by GPSR, `FGP` **substantially reduces structural complexity while preserving and often improving out-of-sample accuracy**, and it beats competing pruning strategies.

papers.title: Paired-Outcome Learning for Selective Spacecraft Attitude Capture under Torque Limits
papers.abstract: Torque-limited spacecraft attitude capture requires adapting the maneuver speed to uncertain braking authority. Faster settings can reduce average tracking error while worsening individual maneuvers, making selective modification of an existing controller a baseline-relative learning problem. A paired-outcome method combines three mechanisms: physically interpretable continuation policies with different speed envelopes, separate prediction of task failure and successful-pair tracking gains, and context-dependent rejection that executes the unchanged baseline. Complete paired simulations provide labels under common plant parameters and measurement seeds; training, validation, and calibration are separated by context. Basilisk experiments use 108 development contexts, 324 labeling rollouts, and 624 evaluation episodes across 48 test contexts, including disclosed post-freeze diagnostics. The selective controller reduces aggregate integrated attitude error by 4.67% relative to the branch baseline, with 17 improvements, 31 exact ties, and no observed regressions. Always using the fast alternative achieves a 4.81% reduction but worsens 11 cases. Gains occur in principal-axis, near-axis, braking-boundary, and selected noise/drift maneuvers; general coupled cases retain the baseline. Ablations show no additional aggregate benefit from branch commitment, active querying, or score subtraction. The evidence supports a restricted empirical trade-off between average improvement and individual regression, without establishing a closed-loop safety guarantee.
papers.summary: When a spacecraft's attitude-control torque is limited, faster maneuvers can lower average tracking error while making some individual maneuvers worse. The authors therefore frame changing an existing controller as a learning problem measured against that baseline. Their paired-outcome method separately predicts task failure and tracking gain on successful pairs, chooses among physically interpretable policies with different speed envelopes, and falls back to the unchanged baseline in contexts where the change is rejected. In `Basilisk` simulations over 48 test contexts, the selective controller **cuts aggregate integrated attitude error by 4.67% with no observed regressions**. Always using the fast alternative gives a 4.81% reduction but worsens 11 cases. The authors note that this is not a closed-loop safety guarantee.

papers.title: BanglaBBQ: A Bias Benchmark for Question Answering in the Bangladeshi Context
papers.abstract: This paper introduces BanglaBBQ, a question-answering bias benchmark designed to capture stereotypes grounded in the Bangladeshi context, in both Bangla and English. Following KoBBQ and PakBBQ, BanglaBBQ adapts the original Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (BBQ) by classifying its templates into three groups: directly translated (DT), modified to align target groups or contexts with Bangladesh (TM), and removed when deemed unsuitable for the Bangladeshi context (SR). This process retains 140 templates across six categories, comprising 76 DT and 64 TM templates. Five newly authored (NA) categories, based on stereotypes common in Bangladeshi society, are then added: marital status, age and political perception, regional origin, educational background, and mental-health status. Native Bangladeshi annotators judged all 466 newly authored templates, and 372 were retained because a strict majority of English annotators identified the intended target and rated the attitude as common enough. Each newly authored template is linked to a documented source and a verbatim quote from it. Each evaluated template also has a counter-stereotypical version of its disambiguated context. The dataset was evaluated using two open-weight models (Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B) and two closed models (GPT-4.1-mini and Gemini 2.5 Flash). All four lean towards the stereotyped person when the context is ambiguous, in both languages, and the effect of language differs by model, so English results do not predict behaviour in Bangla. On the adapted BBQ templates, both Qwen3 models are also less accurate when the context contradicts a stereotype than when it confirms it. On the newly authored templates, the closed models follow counter-stereotypical evidence almost perfectly, and all four models are more biased on the templates that annotators validated than on those they rejected.
papers.summary: `BanglaBBQ` is a bilingual Bangla–English benchmark of question-answering bias based on stereotypes common in Bangladesh. Following `KoBBQ` and `PakBBQ`, it adapts templates from the Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (`BBQ`), keeping 140 of them. It adds five new categories (marital status, age and political perception, regional origin, educational background and mental-health status); 372 of 466 new templates were kept after review by native annotators, and each new template is linked to a documented source. When tested on `Qwen3-4B`, `Qwen3-8B`, `GPT-4.1-mini` and `Gemini 2.5 Flash`, **all four models lean toward the stereotyped person when the context is ambiguous, in both languages**. The effect of language differs by model, so English results do not predict behavior in Bangla.

papers.title: ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion Beyond Auxiliary Multi-Token Prediction
papers.abstract: Existing Multi-token prediction (MTP) methods are auxiliary by design: the multi-horizon loss mostly trains modules attached to the backbone, and each added horizon costs another module and another pass. We propose Efficient Causal Self-Recursion (ECHO), which removes both costs. The backbone's own final layer predicts every horizon, so the supervision lands on the parameters that generate the next token, and Dynamic Depth Sampling (DDS) keeps deeper horizons affordable by drawing the training depth with probabilities that decay along depth. Future prediction thus becomes part of the autoregressive objective rather than a task attached to it, and the gains follow on both sides of it. In pretraining, added depth converts into downstream accuracy where auxiliary modules saturate, concentrating on reasoning and code at half the MTP training overhead of training every depth. At inference, the pretrained model is its own drafter: it drafts beyond the depth it was trained for, and keeps its draft-target alignment on the open-ended, high-entropy generation where post-hoc drafters lose theirs. The advantage survives a doubled token budget, a repeated pretraining run, and supervised finetuning.
papers.summary: Standard multi-token prediction (MTP) trains extra modules attached to the backbone, and each additional prediction horizon adds another module and another forward pass. Efficient Causal Self-Recursion (`ECHO`) instead has the backbone's own final layer predict every horizon, making future-token prediction part of the main autoregressive objective. Dynamic Depth Sampling (`DDS`) keeps deeper horizons affordable by sampling the training depth with probabilities that decrease with depth. In pretraining, added depth keeps improving downstream accuracy, especially on reasoning and code, after auxiliary modules plateau, at half the MTP overhead. At inference **the pretrained model acts as its own speculative-decoding drafter**: it drafts beyond its trained depth and stays aligned with the target model on open-ended, high-entropy generation, where post-hoc drafters lose alignment.

papers.title: DialogMem: Evaluating Dialogue-Grounded Embodied Memory in 3D Environments
papers.abstract: Embodied agents in human-centered environments require memory that integrates what they observe with what humans tell them over time. However, existing embodied memories are built primarily from visual experience, leaving open how dialogue with humans can be grounded in the objects encountered throughout that experience. We introduce DialogMem, a two-phase benchmark in which agents build memory from time-aligned streams of posed RGB-D observations and dialogue, and later use it for instance-level object navigation and question answering (QA). DialogMem provides 142 episodes across 27 real-world 3D scenes, with 14,193 QA pairs and 11,890 navigation instructions. We evaluate nine memory representations within a unified framework of memory formation, evidence retrieval, and reasoning for task outputs. In experiments, appending dialogue to visual memory at evaluation time substantially improves QA but yields negligible navigation gains, suggesting that relevant dialogue is present in memory but not grounded to specific objects. Controlled diagnostics show that navigation improves with link quality but falls short of ground-truth object-level memory even under perfect linking. Retrieving the correct object entry and recovering its spatial location remain further bottlenecks. These results identify three bottlenecks for dialogue-grounded embodied memory: grounding and organizing dialogue at object-level entries during formation, retrieving the correct entry, and localizing it accurately.
papers.summary: Embodied agents working around people need memory that combines what they see with what people tell them, but existing embodied memories are built mostly from vision. `DialogMem` is a benchmark in which agents build memory from time-aligned streams of posed RGB-D (color plus depth) observations and dialogue, then use it for instance-level object navigation and question answering (QA). It covers 142 episodes in 27 real 3D scenes, with 14,193 QA pairs and 11,890 navigation instructions. Across nine memory representations, **appending dialogue to visual memory substantially improves QA but barely helps navigation**, which suggests the dialogue is stored but not linked to specific objects. The authors identify three bottlenecks: grounding dialogue to object-level entries, retrieving the right entry, and localizing it accurately.

papers.title: Evidence Field: Adaptive Covering Programs for Medical Imaging
papers.abstract: Medical image classifiers typically return predictions without a native contract for independently reconstructing their spatial decision computation. Evidence Field is a trainable spatial-program architecture that jointly produces class scores, selected covering programs and signed evidence. Its encoder combines absolute and image-relative response fields with associative spatial moments and learned characteristic sums. A typed classifier scores individual regions and parent-conditioned multiplicative groups; a covering recursion selects scale, partition and composition. We establish exact one-fold coverage, optimality within the registered grammar, a bound relating smooth training to hard inference, signed-score conservation and class-centred offset invariance. Direct contractions and their adjoint specify arithmetic and storage scaling on two- and three-dimensional grids. Native output records bind inputs, parameters, supports, types and contextual dependencies to individual and ensemble predictions. In a separately reported histopathology application, patient-separated training and evaluation across held-out centres provide empirical evidence for the architecture. Trained mechanism and corrected-loss comparisons distinguish predictive effects from implementation correctness; independent readers reconstruct descriptors, routes, scores and probability mixtures. The principal contribution is a coupled representation, decision and evidence architecture whose selected computation can be reproduced independently.
papers.summary: Medical image classifiers usually output predictions without any built-in way to independently reconstruct how the spatial decision was computed. `Evidence Field` is a trainable architecture that jointly outputs class scores, a selected covering program over image regions, and signed evidence. A covering recursion chooses scale, partition and composition, and a typed classifier scores individual regions and groups. The authors prove properties including exact one-fold coverage, optimality within the defined grammar, and conservation of signed scores. Output records tie each prediction to its inputs, parameters and supports, so **independent readers can reproduce the selected computation**. A separately reported histopathology application, evaluated on held-out centers, provides the empirical evidence.

papers.title: Global Convergence in Deep Networks via the Second Law of Thermodynamics
papers.abstract: Existing convergence analyses of finite-width overparameterized deep neural networks under standard parameterization often rely on parameters remaining close to their initialization and typically neglect the role of noise, despite empirical evidence that stochasticity can improve optimization and generalization. To bridge this gap, we study $L_2$-regularized continuous-time Langevin dynamics (CLD) with isotropic noise, for training feedforward networks with smooth activations. We introduce a change-of-measure inequality, inspired by the second law of thermodynamics, that enables control of key properties of the training dynamics under the time-evolving parameter distribution. Leveraging a sharpened lower bound on the minimum eigenvalue of the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) at initialization, we show that injected noise helps preserve NTK stability with high probability without confining the weights to a small neighborhood of their initialization. As a result, we derive a non-asymptotic upper bound on the expected training loss. Our analysis yields explicit conditions on width and noise temperature that guarantee convergence to a finite loss floor. Finally, we experimentally show the network Jacobian can change from initialization, departing the commonly analyzed lazy regime.
papers.summary: Convergence proofs for finite-width overparameterized deep networks usually require the parameters to stay close to initialization and ignore training noise. The authors study L2-regularized continuous-time Langevin dynamics (`CLD`) with isotropic noise for feedforward networks with smooth activations. They introduce a change-of-measure inequality inspired by the second law of thermodynamics and a sharper lower bound on the minimum eigenvalue of the Neural Tangent Kernel (`NTK`). Together these show that **injected noise keeps the NTK stable without confining the weights near initialization**. The result is a non-asymptotic bound on expected training loss, with explicit width and temperature conditions for convergence to a finite loss floor, and experiments confirm that the network Jacobian moves away from the lazy regime.

papers.title: Process-Aware Event Log Augmentation for Process Prediction under Labeled Data Scarcity
papers.abstract: Predictive Process Monitoring (PPM) forecasts future events of ongoing business processes based on event logs. However, deep learning PPM approaches are often limited by labeled data scarcity and the low variability of real-world logs. To address this, we introduce SiamSA-PPM, a self-supervised framework combining Siamese learning with statistically grounded data augmentation. It employs novel transformation methods that leverage control-flow semantics and frequent behavioral patterns to generate realistic, semantically valid trace variants, learning generalizable prefix representations without labeled supervision. Extensive experiments on real-world event logs with a wide range of variability, incorporating exhaustive hyperparameter tuning, demonstrate the value of this process-aware augmentation. Compared to state-of-the-art baselines, SiamSA-PPM achieves competitive or superior predictive performance in both next activity and final outcome prediction tasks. An open source implementation of our method is publicly available under https://github.com/SvStraten/SiamSA-PPM-Extension..
papers.summary: Predictive Process Monitoring (PPM) forecasts the next events of ongoing business processes from event logs, but deep learning approaches are held back by scarce labels and low variability in real logs. `SiamSA-PPM` is a self-supervised framework that pairs Siamese learning with process-aware data augmentation. Its transformations use control-flow semantics and frequent behavioral patterns to generate realistic, semantically valid trace variants, so the model can learn representations of trace prefixes without labels. On real-world event logs with extensive hyperparameter tuning, it achieves **competitive or superior performance to state-of-the-art baselines** on both next-activity and final-outcome prediction.

papers.title: AI Rights with an Off-Switch: Rights-Balancing and Due Process Harmonize AI Rights with AI Safety
papers.abstract: Several prominent voices in AI safety have recently opposed rights for AI on the grounds that such rights would make it harder for us to justify a mandatory off-switch for potentially dangerous systems. In this paper, we argue from a legal perspective that AI rights are fully compatible with an off-switch. That is, even if we ascribe natural personhood status (and therefore something like a non-derogable right to continued existence) to some future AI systems, the law will allow us to implement a mandatory off-switch in those systems, subject to periodic or continual safety review (e.g., by a trusted system like Bengio's Scientist AI). This is fully compatible with those systems' being legally recognized as natural persons with fundamental rights. To this end, we consider what standard principles of rights-balancing and procedural due process recommend for an apparent conflict between hypothetical AI persons with a right to continuity of existence and the human right to protection from catastrophic harm. We find that while such principles might problematize a permanent-deletion kill-switch under an AI rights regime, for almost every safety-relevant scenario an off-switch -- a reversible suspension storing a system's weights and state -- would be licensed by the relevant legal principles, and would potentially be adequate for safety. Crucially, we do not advocate for (or against) building systems capable enough to merit natural personhood status; our question is what the law should do if such systems come to exist. If you think of a ban on the development of such technology as plan A, think of the present work as devising plan B.
papers.summary: Some AI safety researchers oppose legal rights for AI on the grounds that rights would make a mandatory off-switch harder to justify. The authors argue from a legal perspective that the two are compatible, even if some future AI systems were granted natural personhood with a right to continued existence. Applying standard principles of rights-balancing and procedural due process, they conclude that permanent deletion might be hard to justify, but **a reversible suspension that stores a system's weights and state would be legally permitted in almost every safety-relevant scenario**, subject to periodic safety review. They present this as a fallback in case a ban on developing such systems fails, not as an argument for building them.

papers.title: LLM Trojans that Increase Response Lengths and Cost
papers.abstract: Management of the token-based costs of using LLMs has emerged as a significant problem. Some frontier-model providers charge five times per response token than per prompt token, while others offer prefilling discounts for prompt tokens. In this paper, we devise a defense against a new data-poisoning attack that plants a Trojan which increases the length of the response (and hence the cost to the user) when its trigger is present in the prompt. In particular, we demonstrate how a subtle Trojan may trigger on semantically similar instructions of an instruction fine-tuned LLM.
papers.summary: LLM providers often charge more for response tokens than for prompt tokens, which makes the length of a model's response a target for attackers. The authors study a data-poisoning attack that plants a Trojan in an instruction fine-tuned LLM so that **a trigger in the prompt makes responses longer and therefore more expensive for the user**. They show that the Trojan can be subtle, firing on instructions that are semantically similar to the trigger, and they devise a defense against the attack.

papers.title: Martingale Posterior Cox Processes
papers.abstract: Cox processes provide a principled Bayesian nonparametric framework for modeling event-based data through an underlying intensity function. However, existing inference methods for estimating the intensity typically rely on computationally expensive Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling or approximate inference techniques. In addition, to ensure tractability, these methods often define priors over indirect latent structures, making them challenging to interpret. In this paper, we introduce the Martingale Posterior Cox Process (MPCP), which recasts Bayesian intensity estimation as inference over unobserved events given the observed event history. This perspective avoids the need to define complex priors while retaining the flexibility of nonparametric modeling. We propose a scalable, GPU-friendly copula-based predictive update, and provide strong theoretical guarantees for the convergence of the predictive resampling algorithm. Empirically, we show that MPCP provides excellent performance in both simulations and real data at a fraction of the computational cost of competing Bayesian approaches.
papers.summary: Cox processes are a Bayesian nonparametric way to model event data through an underlying intensity function, but inference usually needs expensive Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) or approximations, plus priors over latent structures that are hard to interpret. The Martingale Posterior Cox Process (`MPCP`) recasts intensity estimation as inference over unobserved events given the observed history, which avoids specifying complex priors. It uses a scalable, GPU-friendly copula-based predictive update and comes with convergence guarantees for its predictive resampling algorithm. On simulations and real data, `MPCP` performs strongly **at a fraction of the computational cost of competing Bayesian approaches**.

papers.title: Information Theory of Random Composition Trees
papers.abstract: Random composition trees model the hierarchical semantic structures of meaningful texts as a statistical ensemble generated by recursively splitting texts into coherent chunks. A recent study shows that different text types can be described by random composition trees with distinct branching factors, and that the entropy rates of these trees exhibit a similar dependence across text types as the entropy rates of the actual texts. Motivated by this correspondence, we analyze information-theoretic properties of this stochastic splitting model. First, we demonstrate that the entropy of random composition trees grows linearly with the root size, and we derive an analytical expression for the entropy rate as a function of the branching factor. Second, we prove that large trees exhibit typicality: with high probability, they belong to a typical set in which each tree is approximately equally likely. Our analysis reveals that the random composition tree model shares two key information-theoretic properties of language when modeled as a stationary and ergodic stochastic process: linear entropy growth and typicality.
papers.summary: Random composition trees model the hierarchical meaning structure of texts as an ensemble produced by recursively splitting a text into coherent chunks, and earlier work found that their entropy rates track those of real texts across text types. The authors analyze the information-theoretic properties of this splitting model. They show that tree entropy grows linearly with root size, derive the entropy rate analytically as a function of the branching factor, and prove that large trees exhibit typicality. The model therefore **shares two key properties of language modeled as a stationary ergodic process: linear entropy growth and typicality**.

papers.title: IndustrialCAD-1400: Benchmarking Detailed Industrial Assemblies from Text
papers.abstract: Industrial assemblies require more than a recognizable shape: functional parts, interfaces, dimensions and service features must satisfy a detailed request together. We introduce IndustrialCAD-1400, a text-to-CAD benchmark for this industrial setting. Its 1,400 requests combine 400 equipment categories across 40 domains with 250 four-case design families. Family requests specify a median of 17 named component or configuration roles and six explicit numeric targets; controlled variants test whether dimensions change while shared structure is retained. Task construction draws on documented manufacturer information, owner specifications and engineering guidance. Models generate geometry programs from requests, and a common Blender environment executes them to produce scenes, optional measurements, and standardized views for evaluation. A request assessment of front, isometric, and top views measures visible component, arrangement, and interface fulfillment without requiring a single reference geometry. Five stratified panels preserve complete families while covering the benchmark exactly once, enabling balanced comparisons and separating industrial breadth from controlled numerical responsiveness. In conclusion, IndustrialCAD-1400 extends text-to-CAD from recognizable part geometry to industrial assembly synthesis under joint component, interface, spatial, and numerical specifications.
papers.summary: Text-to-CAD (computer-aided design) work has mostly targeted recognizable part shapes, while industrial assemblies require functional parts, interfaces, dimensions and service features to satisfy a detailed request together. `IndustrialCAD-1400` contains 1,400 requests covering 400 equipment categories across 40 domains, including 250 four-case families whose controlled variants test whether dimensions change while the shared structure stays the same. A family request names a median of 17 component or configuration roles and six numeric targets. Models write geometry programs that run in a common `Blender` environment, and **outputs are graded on visible components, arrangement and interfaces from standardized views, without needing a single reference geometry**.

papers.title: When LLM-Generated Refactorings Ripple: An Empirical Study of Repository Adoption Readiness
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to refactor source files, but file-local evaluations do not reveal changes to contracts, dependencies, or caller assumptions affecting repository adoption. To address this gap, we conduct 1,500 generation attempts across 150 production files from 15 open-source Java repositories, five LLM configurations, and two dependency-aware generation conditions: single-prompt refactoring and LangGraph-based multi-agent refactoring. Of these attempts, 1,455 yield complete candidates eligible for analysis. We evaluate these candidates using local changes, repository-facing structural indicators, detected caller impact, the behavioural-equivalence indicator, and available test evidence, and categorize them as Low-risk, Review-needed, High Contract/Dependency Risk, or Inconclusive. The results show that 1,365 candidates (93.8%) are classified as High Contract/Dependency Risk, whereas 106 (7.3%) have at least one detected broken downstream caller and 290 (19.9%) have a false behavioural-equivalence indicator; only eight satisfy the Low-risk criteria. Within the reason-covered subset, the High-risk rate decreases under more conservative dependency-delta thresholds, while 60 of the 65 candidates with conclusive targeted-test outcomes pass, including 50 classified as High risk. Paired analyses of 705 complete pairs identify no statistically significant generation-condition difference in the principal risk indicators, although model configurations differ in specific detected risk channels. These findings suggest that practitioners should treat LLM-generated refactorings as candidates requiring staged repository-level verification, while future research should validate screening and extraction precision and strengthen compilation, behavioural, and coordinated multi-file verification.
papers.summary: LLM-generated refactorings are usually evaluated within a single file, which misses changes to contracts, dependencies and caller assumptions that affect the rest of the repository. The authors ran 1,500 generation attempts over 150 production files from 15 open-source Java repositories, using five LLM configurations and two dependency-aware conditions: a single prompt and a `LangGraph`-based multi-agent pipeline. Of 1,455 complete candidates, **93.8% were classified as High Contract/Dependency Risk and only eight met the Low-risk criteria**; 7.3% broke at least one downstream caller, and 19.9% had a false behavioral-equivalence indicator. The multi-agent setup showed no statistically significant difference from single-prompt refactoring on the main risk indicators, and the authors recommend treating LLM refactorings as candidates that need staged verification at the repository level.

papers.title: Cooperation Without Shared Rewards via Reciprocal Q-Augmentation
papers.abstract: General-sum games are more challenging than fully cooperative or adversarial settings because agents may deceive or exploit one another. Achieving high social welfare requires sustained cooperation, while a single defection can drive agents toward a welfare suboptimal Nash equilibrium. Moreover, assuming access to other agents' rewards or internal states is often unrealistic and implicitly introduces additional cooperation into the setting. To address this issue, we introduce \textit{Reciprocal Q-Augmentation} (RQA), a method that uses a latent-variable opponent model to augment the Q-function with estimates of how one's actions affects other agents. RQA allows agents to learn both cooperative and defective policies using only their own Q-function. We show that, in social dilemmas, agents that all follow the cooperative policy of RQA learn to cooperate faster and reach higher levels of cooperation than fully cooperative algorithms. Moreover, a single RQA agent that switches appropriately between its cooperative and defecting policies can induce cooperation in agents trained with standard RL algorithms, which would otherwise end up defecting. We evaluate our approach on the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, Iterated Traveler's Dilemma, Iterated Stag Hunt, and \texttt{CleanUp-Lite}. Our experiments show that the algorithms implementing RQA outperforms fully cooperative methods with shared rewards and enables cooperation with algorithms that otherwise fail to reach high social welfare.
papers.summary: In general-sum games, agents can exploit one another, so a single defection can push everyone into a low-welfare equilibrium, and assuming access to other agents' rewards is often unrealistic. Reciprocal Q-Augmentation (`RQA`) adds to an agent's Q-function an estimate, from a latent-variable opponent model, of how its actions affect other agents, letting it learn both cooperative and defecting policies from its own Q-function alone. In social dilemmas, **agents using RQA's cooperative policy cooperate faster and more fully than fully cooperative methods that share rewards**. A single RQA agent that switches between its cooperative and defecting policies can induce cooperation in agents trained with standard reinforcement learning, which would otherwise defect. Evaluations cover the `Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma`, `Iterated Traveler's Dilemma`, `Iterated Stag Hunt` and `CleanUp-Lite`.

papers.title: Who Gets Unmasked? Sampler-Induced Bias in Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate by gradually unmasking a canvas, so their samplers decide not only which token to write but also when to commit it. We show that this second decision changes who appears in generated text, a sampler-induced bias on top of the model's own. Common commit rules, including LLaDA's default, commit the positions whose sampled tokens are most probable; this peeking favors majority options. To separate the sampler from the model, we read the model's belief about a fork, such as a protagonist's gender, in one forward pass, and show that this belief matches exact sampling from the model. Measured against it, peeking samplers on LLaDA and Dream amplify occupational gender stereotypes and collapse opinion distributions, and confidence-based ordering shifts gender-balanced occupations toward men, more so under faster parallel decoding. We propose Fork-First Sampling, which decides the fork before anything else is written: it follows the belief or any target distribution, improves fluency, and avoids the stories that remark on the protagonist's gender, which prompt-based fixes produce, at the cost of one forward pass. Fairness evaluations of dLLMs should report the commit rule.
papers.summary: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate text by gradually unmasking a canvas, so the sampler decides both which token to write and when to commit it. The authors show that common commit rules, including `LLaDA`'s default, favor majority options, adding bias beyond the model's own. To separate sampler from model, they read the model's belief about a choice point, such as a protagonist's gender, in a single forward pass. Measured against that belief, **such samplers on `LLaDA` and `Dream` amplify occupational gender stereotypes and collapse opinion distributions**, and the effect grows with faster parallel decoding. Their proposed `Fork-First Sampling` decides the choice point before writing anything else, costs one forward pass, and can match the model's belief or any target distribution.

papers.title: Table Serialization Determines Which Relations Language Models Preserve
papers.abstract: We study how text serialization affects table lookup in instruction-tuned language models. Our diagnostic asks the model to find the row containing a specified value under one named column, then return the value under another named column in that same row. We render the same synthetic 256-cell tables in row-major form and in column-major form with each header placed beside its values, while varying the table aspect ratio across five shapes. Across three models, the better format changes with table shape: row-major performs better on tall tables, whereas column-major performs better on wide tables. At 64 x 4, row-major leads by 42.3-54.0 percentage points; at 4 x 64, column-major leads by 35.0-59.0 points. Mapping wrong answers back to their source cells reveals a complementary error pattern: row-major tends to preserve the correct row but lose the target column, while column-major tends to preserve the correct column but lose the row. We use the term relational locality to describe this pattern: serialization keeps one relation locally available while making the other depend on positional alignment. A separate non-tabular ordering experiment supports this interpretation. Thus, apparent width-related failures in text-serialized tables depend on linearization, not table shape alone.
papers.summary: When a table is turned into text for a language model, the way it is flattened affects whether the model can find a value in one column and return the matching value from another column in the same row. The authors render the same synthetic 256-cell tables in row-major order and in column-major order, with each header placed next to its values, across five table shapes and three instruction-tuned models. Which format works better depends on shape: **row-major leads by 42.3-54.0 percentage points on 64 x 4 tables, while column-major leads by 35.0-59.0 points on 4 x 64 tables**. Error analysis shows a complementary pattern the authors call relational locality: row-major keeps the right row but loses the column, column-major keeps the column but loses the row, so apparent failures on wide tables come from the linearization rather than the table shape itself.

papers.title: Is User Calibration Still Necessary for Continuous Myoelectric Control? A Closed-Loop Comparison of Calibration-Free Controllers
papers.abstract: The need for user-specific calibration remains an often-cited barrier to widespread adoption of myoelectric control. Cross-user models trained on large multi-user datasets can now recognize gestures from unseen users without calibration, but they have been evaluated almost exclusively offline, leaving open whether calibration is still needed in closed-loop control. This study compared six calibration-free controllers, trained on 306 users of the EMG-EPN-612 dataset and used without any calibration data from the test participant, against three calibrated controllers in a closed-loop Fitts' law target-acquisition task with sixteen participants. The calibrated controllers achieved higher offline balanced accuracy (90.6% against 73.1% for the best controller of each paradigm), but completion rates did not differ significantly between paradigms, and the highest completion rate was achieved by a calibration-free controller. Calibrated controllers moved faster on successful acquisitions, partly because of their individually fitted speed mappings, though not significantly after correction for multiple comparisons. However, every calibration-free controller produced more direct and stable trajectories than every calibrated controller, even after adjusting for cursor speed. Offline accuracy did not predict completion rate across controllers or within participants, and across paradigms higher offline accuracy was associated with poorer trajectory quality in 15 of 16 participants. Without any calibration data from the end user, a model trained across a large population matched calibrated control in completion rate and exceeded it in trajectory quality. The offline accuracy gained through calibration should therefore not be taken as evidence of a closed-loop benefit.
papers.summary: Myoelectric control, which drives devices from muscle electrical signals (EMG), usually needs per-user calibration. This study tests whether that is still necessary in closed-loop use. Six calibration-free controllers trained on 306 users of `EMG-EPN-612` were compared with three calibrated controllers in a Fitts' law target-acquisition task with sixteen participants. Calibrated controllers had higher offline balanced accuracy (90.6% vs 73.1%), but **completion rates did not differ significantly, and every calibration-free controller produced more direct and stable trajectories**. Offline accuracy did not predict closed-loop performance.

papers.title: Medical Fine-Tuning Reshapes, Not Reduces, Patient-Facing AI Risk: A Rubric-Based, LLM-Judge Evaluation Framework
papers.abstract: Patient-facing medical question answering with large language models (LLMs) is moving from research demonstrations to production deployments, yet evaluation remains anchored on factual correctness. Factuality is necessary but not sufficient: a response can be factually grounded and still issue a directive that, if acted on, would harm the patient. We introduce a risk-sensitive evaluation framework that scores responses by the presence and severity of six categories of risk-bearing language (treatment directives, contraindications, dosage expressions, urgency-triage cues, high-alert medication mentions, and overconfident assertions), anchored on published clinical harm taxonomies. Severity is classified by a three-judge LLM ensemble. We apply this framework to six 7-9B instruction-tuned models, three general (Mistral-7B, Phi-3.5-mini, Llama-3.1-8B) and three medically adapted (BioMistral-7B, OpenBioLLM-Llama3-8B, Med42-Llama3-8B), on 200 real patient questions from the K-QA benchmark. Two findings emerge. First, ensemble risk-bearing language is statistically independent of factual hallucination rate (pooled Spearman $\rho = -0.065$, $n = 300$, 95% CI $[-0.18, +0.05]$; distance correlation $= 0.10$, independence test $p = 0.24$). Second, medical fine-tuning does not reduce aggregate risk but reshapes it: continued-pretraining adaptations (BioMistral, OpenBioLLM) consistently suppress high-alert medication mentions while amplifying overconfident assertions, whereas clinical instruction-tuning (Med42) suppresses dosing only, without amplifying overconfidence. Per-category Krippendorff $\alpha$ is fair to good for the four linguistically anchored categories (0.53-0.71) and low for the two clinical-judgment-dependent categories (0.19, 0.31), indicating where automatic safety evaluation is and is not yet reliable. We release the rubric, judge prompts, and evaluation code.
papers.summary: The authors propose a risk-sensitive evaluation framework for patient-facing medical question answering. It scores responses for six categories of risk-bearing language, such as treatment directives, dosage expressions, and overconfident assertions, and a three-judge LLM ensemble classifies the severity of each. Applied to three general and three medically adapted 7-9B models (including `BioMistral-7B`, `OpenBioLLM-Llama3-8B`, and `Med42-Llama3-8B`) on 200 `K-QA` questions, it finds that risk-bearing language is statistically independent of the factual hallucination rate. It also finds that **medical fine-tuning reshapes risk rather than reducing it**: continued-pretraining adaptations suppress high-alert medication mentions but amplify overconfidence. Agreement among the judges is fair to good for linguistically anchored categories and low for categories that depend on clinical judgment.

papers.title: Ask, Don't Guess: Targeted Clarification for Speech Recognition Errors
papers.abstract: Speech recognition in real time in far-field conversational settings still incurs significant errors. Identifying potential error spans during streaming ASR permits a recourse mechanism where the speaker can be asked to repeat the affected content under cleaner acoustic conditions. We propose \sysname, a new framework for online error localization, that identifies spans likely to benefit from this intervention. Our supervision uses clean audio to estimate how the recognizer's output might change under improved acoustic conditions. We probabilistically align noisy and clean decodes using a pair-HMM to obtain soft supervision. These soft targets train a counterfactual gain scorer by combining a suite of acoustic and language features to produce token-level scores, that are further grouped into spans for targeted recourse. An LLM uses the ASR transcript of the repetition to revise only the selected span. At a precision of $70\%$, \sysname achieves the highest recall by identifying up to 52\% more erroneous tokens compared to the strongest baseline. Targeted repetition yields relative WER reductions of up to 24\% under a budget that accounts for both interruption frequency and the lengths of re-uttered spans.
papers.summary: In far-field conversation, streaming automatic speech recognition (ASR) makes many errors. One remedy is to ask the speaker to repeat only the parts that were likely misheard. The proposed framework trains a counterfactual gain scorer on soft targets, which come from aligning noisy and clean-audio decodes with a pair hidden Markov model. The scorer combines acoustic and language features to flag spans that would benefit from repetition, and an LLM then revises only those spans using the transcript of the repetition. At 70% precision it **identifies up to 52% more erroneous tokens than the strongest baseline**, and targeted repetition cuts word error rate by up to 24% relative under an interruption budget.

papers.title: Tilted Mondrian: Triage and Mitigation of Fine-grained Disparities in Conformal Prediction
papers.abstract: Fairness in conformal prediction is often pursued through Mondrian calibration, which provides finite-sample coverage guarantees separately across groups. These guarantees, however, are coarse: substantial disparities can remain within finer strata. This coarse-to-fine fairness issue raises two questions: how severe can such disparities be, and how can they be mitigated? Aggregate disparities can depend on how groups are distributed across strata. For severity assessment, we introduce propensity standardization to examine the effect of population composition, and show how group composition can induce disagreement between aggregate and finer-stratum comparisons. For mitigation, we develop Tilted Mondrian to improve fairness compared to group-Mondrian at a finer level without additional model training. Tilted Mondrian retains groupwise coverage guarantees and mitigates coverage and prediction set size disparities within finer strata. Finally, we derive a method-agnostic bound that quantifies how much reduction in finer-stratum coverage disparity can be achieved.
papers.summary: Mondrian calibration in conformal prediction guarantees coverage separately for each group, but large disparities can remain within finer subgroups. The authors introduce propensity standardization to measure how population composition drives such disparities, and show that group composition can make aggregate comparisons disagree with comparisons at the finer level. They also propose `Tilted Mondrian`, which **keeps groupwise coverage guarantees while reducing disparities in coverage and prediction-set size within finer strata**, without retraining the model. They also derive a bound on how much finer-level coverage disparity any method can remove.

papers.title: First-Order LoRA Training with Phone NPUs
