Interleaved kernels raise this speedup to 1.45x, reaching 1.59x in the best case. CONJUGATE COMPILATION also improves GPU utilization on average by 1.46x on RTX 5090 and 1.50x on B300.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding runs a small draft model alongside a larger target model, but compiling each model separately leaves their shared execution outside the compiler's view. `Conjugate Compilation` treats the pair as a single cross-model compilation problem, including operand layouts that interleave blocks from both models in common tiles, and searches optimization plans with a self-improving LLM agent that uses the compiler and real GPU execution as its environment, guided by Monte Carlo tree search. Across six single-GPU configurations on NVIDIA B300 and RTX 5090 GPUs, it achieves a **geometric-mean per-round speedup of 1.37× over conventional execution**, rising to 1.45× with interleaved kernels and 1.59× in the best case, and improves GPU utilization by about 1.5×.

papers.title: Latent World Models Should Plan with Distances Along the Latent Manifold
papers.abstract: Latent world models such as LeWM plan by searching for an action sequence whose predicted terminal latent is closest to the goal latent under an ambient norm, such as the Euclidean distance. Planning with such a cost assumes that proximity in the ambient latent space reflects proximity to the goal in the environment. Studying LeWM, we find that this assumption holds only in a small neighborhood around the goal, whereas farther away the L2 cost forms spurious low-cost basins that trap the planner. Yet neighborhood-based embeddings show that the latents retain the underlying physical state. We therefore hypothesize that the latents lie near a curved, low-dimensional manifold, and that the terminal cost should measure the distance along this latent manifold rather than through the ambient space. To estimate this manifold distance, we propose the Neighborhood Graph Cost (NGC), which computes shortest-path distances on a mutual nearest-neighbor graph constructed over training latents. NGC changes only the terminal cost and requires no retraining. This single change improves the planning success rate of LeWM across all four benchmark tasks and nearly solves TwoRoom and Reacher: even at the farthest goal offsets tested, NGC reaches 95% and 100% success, whereas the L2 cost falls to 27% and 81%. These results support the manifold hypothesis and our argument that latent world models should plan with distances along the latent manifold.
papers.summary: Latent world models such as `LeWM` plan by searching for actions whose predicted final latent is closest to the goal latent under Euclidean distance, but this distance tracks true progress only near the goal and creates spurious low-cost basins farther away. Hypothesizing that latents lie near a curved low-dimensional manifold, the authors propose the `Neighborhood Graph Cost` (`NGC`), which uses shortest-path distances on a mutual nearest-neighbor graph built over training latents. Changing only the terminal cost, with no retraining, improves planning success on all four benchmark tasks; at the farthest goals tested, **`NGC` reaches 95% and 100% success on `TwoRoom` and `Reacher`**, versus 27% and 81% with the Euclidean cost.

papers.title: IECLA: Interpretable Emotion Contribution Learning for Affective Image Editing
papers.abstract: Affective image editing (AIE) aims to evoke a target emotion while preserving the content and structure of a source image. Existing methods improve emotional expression or visual fidelity, but the target emotion alone does not reveal which source regions should be changed and which should remain intact, especially in complex scenes. We introduce Interpretable Emotion Contribution Learning for Affective Image Editing (IECLA), a framework that separates source-emotion attribution from target-aware editing. IECLA constructs signed object-level supervision through counterfactual interventions and trains a context-conditioned contribution predictor to localize evidence that supports or opposes the source emotion. At inference, an image-level evaluator estimates the source emotion directly from the input, while the predictor identifies editable and preservation evidence without repeated interventions. A target-aware editing agent then translates this evidence and the desired emotion into localized, content-aware operations for existing editors. Extensive evaluations show that IECLA predicts counterfactual contributions more faithfully on both in-domain and cross-dataset tests, while external VLM and independent human references support the quality of its localized evidence. Across six editing backbones, IECLA consistently strengthens target-emotion expression while preserving image content and structure, and user studies further show improved perceived target expression and naturalness.
papers.summary: Affective image editing aims to evoke a target emotion while preserving an image's content and structure, but knowing the target emotion alone does not say which regions should change. `IECLA` builds signed object-level supervision through counterfactual interventions and trains a predictor that localizes the evidence supporting or opposing the source emotion. A target-aware editing agent then turns that evidence into localized operations for existing image editors. **Across six editing backbones, `IECLA` consistently strengthens target-emotion expression while preserving content**, and user studies report better perceived expression and naturalness.

papers.title: Multifidelity Monte Carlo Estimator for High-Dimensional Quantities of Interest
papers.abstract: Multifidelity Monte Carlo (MFMC) reduces the cost of estimating the statistics of quantities of interest (QoIs) computed via expensive high-fidelity model by using cheaper low-fidelity models as control variates. We extend MFMC to vector-valued QoIs by replacing the scalar control-variate coefficients with matrices and minimizing a weighted mean-squared error. The optimal full-matrix coefficients are available in closed form, and their variance reduction is summarized by an effective correlation that takes the place of the squared Pearson correlation in the closed-form MFMC design. Restricting the coefficients to block-diagonal, diagonal, and scalar classes gives a nested hierarchy of estimators with increasing variance reduction and increasing pilot-data demand, with closed-form coefficients for compatible weightings. For a scalar QoI obtained by linearly projecting the state, correcting the full state before projecting is never worse at the population level. Experiments on a Gaussian problem, a reduced-order model of an advection--diffusion problem, and a coarse-grid two-phase flow problem show that the best class depends on the pilot size relative to the number of covariance quantities it must estimate, and that reusing the pilot samples lowers the mean-squared error.
papers.summary: Multifidelity Monte Carlo (`MFMC`) cuts the cost of estimating statistics from an expensive high-fidelity model by using cheaper low-fidelity models as control variates, but it has been limited to scalar quantities of interest. The authors extend it to vector-valued quantities by replacing scalar coefficients with matrices chosen to minimize a weighted mean-squared error, derive **closed-form optimal coefficients summarized by an effective correlation**, and define a nested hierarchy of full, block-diagonal, diagonal, and scalar estimators. Experiments on a Gaussian problem, an advection-diffusion reduced-order model, and a two-phase flow problem show that the best estimator class depends on how large the pilot sample is relative to the number of covariance quantities it must estimate.

papers.title: Decentralized Online Exp-Concave Optimization
papers.abstract: Decentralized Online Convex Optimization (D-OCO) is a fundamental framework in which a set of local agents aims to minimize a sequence of global loss functions using only local computations and communications. While recent work has established near-optimal regret guarantees for convex and strongly convex losses, the case of exp-concave losses remains an open challenge: specifically, whether logarithmic regret is achievable. In this paper, we answer this question affirmatively by proposing Decentralized Online Newton Step (D-ONS), which adapts the idea of blocking and accelerated gossip to the Online Newton Step algorithm in a non-trivial manner. Concretely, our algorithm achieves a regret bound of $O\left(Nd(1-\sigma_2)^{-1/2}\,\log^2(T) \right)$ where $N$ is the number of agents, $d$ is the dimension, $T$ is the horizon, and $1-\sigma_2$ represents the spectral gap of the network. To our knowledge, this is the first logarithmic regret bound for decentralized online exp-concave optimization. We further establish a nearly matching lower bound of $\Omega\left(Nd (1-\sigma_2)^{-1/2}\,\log(T/N) \right)$ showing the near optimality of our upper bound. Finally, we extend our algorithm to decentralized online linear regression in which the feasible domain is unbounded and features and labels are locally observed. By gossiping covariance and label-feature statistics, we also achieve logarithmic regret.
papers.summary: In decentralized online convex optimization, networked agents minimize a sequence of global losses using only local computation and communication; whether logarithmic regret is achievable for exp-concave losses had been open. The authors propose `Decentralized Online Newton Step` (`D-ONS`), which combines blocking and accelerated gossip with the Online Newton Step algorithm, and prove **the first logarithmic regret bound for decentralized online exp-concave optimization**. A nearly matching lower bound shows the result is close to optimal, and the method extends to decentralized online linear regression with an unbounded domain and locally observed data.

papers.title: LLM Agents as Suppliers of Physical System Models: Calibration and Acceptance in Modelica
papers.abstract: To procure a model of a device, a client hands a supplier a description, sometimes with recorded data or a target response, and accepts the model against this handover. We let LLM coding agents act as the supplier on handovers with data, building Modelica models from library components for four simulated systems and a real switching magnet, and ask what acceptance certifies. Several agents reach the noise floor, but a handover admits a set of models: the description leaves parts of the structure open, and the data narrow it only to the agreed accuracy. We therefore accept by membership in this set, not by matching one reference, and add layers above behaviour: a physical invariant exposes an energy-creating model at the noise floor. Interpretability becomes a property of the delivered model, tested on a variant, read where none exists and shaped through the handover. Most failures are fits delivered with a systematic residual on their own fitting data, where the handover left open how close is close enough. In a follow-up, stating a threshold makes the agents compare against it, and more deliveries pass. The argument applies wherever a handover underspecifies a model meant to be read, not only run.
papers.summary: LLM coding agents act as "suppliers" that build `Modelica` models of physical systems from library components, given a description and recorded data, for four simulated systems and a real switching magnet. Several agents fit the data down to the noise floor, but because a handover admits a whole set of valid models, the authors accept a delivered model by membership in that set rather than by matching one reference, and add checks beyond behavior, such as a physical invariant that exposed an energy-creating model despite its noise-floor fit. **Most failures were fits delivered with a systematic residual on their own fitting data**, because the handover left open how close is close enough; stating an explicit threshold made agents compare against it and increased passing deliveries.

papers.title: Synergy-Aware Residual Flow Matching for Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting single-cell responses to genetic and chemical perturbations is important for understanding regulatory mechanisms and prioritizing therapeutic interventions. Existing methods have made progress by modeling perturbation-conditioned expression shifts with neural networks, graph priors, foundation-model representations, or distributional generative models. However, combinatorial perturbation prediction remains challenging because much of the response can be explained by additive single-perturbation effects, while the biologically informative signal often lies in a smaller non-additive residual induced by perturbation interactions. Directly generating the full post-perturbation expression profile may therefore allocate substantial capacity to the dominant additive component and underemphasize synergy-specific structure. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{SynGeneFlow}, a synergy-aware flow matching framework that anchors the source distribution at an additive prior and learns a residual flow toward the true perturbed state. SynGeneFlow further incorporates perturbation-conditioned gene interaction modeling, where a static gene-gene mask provides biological structure and a perturbation-dependent deformation bias dynamically modulates gene-gene coupling. To preserve population-level response structure, we align both endpoint distributions and biological residual distributions with MMD-based regularization. We evaluate SynGeneFlow on genetic and drug perturbation benchmarks under observed-single, held-out, and cross-modality settings. The results demonstrate that residualizing flow matching around additive perturbation effects provides a biologically grounded and robust framework for single-cell perturbation response prediction.
papers.summary: Predicting single-cell responses to combinations of genetic or chemical perturbations is hard because most of the response is explained by additive single-perturbation effects, while the biologically informative signal lies in a smaller non-additive residual. `SynGeneFlow` is a flow matching model that starts from an additive prior and learns only the residual flow toward the true perturbed state, with gene-interaction modeling that combines a static gene-gene mask and a perturbation-dependent bias, plus regularization based on maximum mean discrepancy (MMD). On genetic and drug perturbation benchmarks in observed, held-out, and cross-modality settings, the authors report that **residualizing the flow around additive effects gives robust perturbation-response prediction**.

papers.title: Integrable building blocks for symplectic neural networks: learned-type layers, fiber-preserving layers, and what a single layer can do
papers.abstract: Exactly symplectic neural networks are built almost exclusively from shear maps and gain expressivity only through depth. We ask what else a single explicit symplectic layer can be. Observing that every layer in use is the exact flow of a Hamiltonian that is a function of commuting integrals, we obtain three families of layers: a learned-type layer, in which every conjugate pair is rotated, squeezed or sheared by a state-dependent amount and the type is found by training; moving-plane shears, residual symplectic maps outside the known ridge-function class; and fiber-preserving layers, which combine an unconstrained point transformation with a fiber translation at the cost of one linear solve. We characterize residual symplectic layers $x \mapsto x + J\nabla H(x)$: in one degree of freedom they are exactly the shears along a line, while from two degrees of freedom on a strictly larger class exists. Conjugating a learned-type layer by a symplectic network yields an exact one-parameter group with an exactly conserved learned Hamiltonian. In experiments on sixteen systems with one to forty degrees of freedom, against SympNets, H\'enonNets and learned-plane shear networks, layers built on nonlinear integrals are far more accurate when the Hamiltonian contains functions of those integrals. On nonlinear Schr\"odinger lattices with six to forty sites, twist layers alternating with linear symplectic maps are over a hundred times more accurate than every shear-based network, and with an on-site potential of learned form three to four orders of magnitude more accurate. On chains of Tao oscillators with the step size as an input, stretch layers are 45 to 70 times more accurate than learned-plane shears and recover the Hamiltonian to 1%. On generic non-separable systems, fiber layers improve on learned-plane shears by at most a factor of two, and widening the networks does not help any architecture.
papers.summary: Exactly symplectic neural networks, which preserve the geometric structure of Hamiltonian dynamics, are usually built from simple shear maps and become more expressive only by adding depth. The authors note that every existing layer is the exact flow of a Hamiltonian built from commuting integrals. From that observation they derive three new layer families: learned-type layers, moving-plane shears, and fiber-preserving layers. They also prove that from two degrees of freedom onward, residual symplectic layers form a strictly larger class than shears. On sixteen systems compared against `SympNets`, `HénonNets` and learned-plane shear networks, twist layers on nonlinear Schrödinger lattices are **over a hundred times more accurate than every shear-based network**, but on generic non-separable systems the gains are at most a factor of two.

papers.title: One Head Away from Language Confusion: Single Attention Heads Across Model Families
papers.abstract: Large language models sometimes reply in an unexpected language, a failure known as language confusion. We ablate individual attention heads in 12 model checkpoints spanning seven model series, using FLORES-200 continuations in five languages and Language Confusion Benchmark (LCB) chat replies. In ten models, zeroing one head causes substantially more departures from the expected language than zeroing any other head in its layer; its LCB pass-rate drop persists, though reduced, under mean ablation. Seven heads move 8.0 to 51.5 percent of all FLORES continuations out of the prompt's language, versus at most 1.4 percent for other same-layer heads; the other three mainly affect explicitly requested languages. These seven heads matter less in base models given plain text. In two models, replacing the values a head reads at the requested-language name with another language's mean makes replies fail and shifts some into that language, unlike a random change of equal size. Replacing a head's output with another language's mean redirects 84 to 99 percent of scored non-English monolingual LCB replies into that language in five models. Yet the requested language's mean improves crosslingual replies beyond every control head only in the two Gemma models, whose baselines are low. Code and results are available in the public repository at https://github.com/christian-hoang-04/anonymous-release.
papers.summary: Large language models sometimes reply in the wrong language, a failure called language confusion. The authors ablate individual attention heads in 12 checkpoints from seven model series, using `FLORES-200` continuations and the `Language Confusion Benchmark` (`LCB`). In ten models, zeroing a single head causes far more departures from the expected language than zeroing any other head in its layer, and seven such heads push **8.0 to 51.5 percent of continuations out of the prompt's language**, compared with at most 1.4 percent for other heads in the same layer. Replacing one of these heads' output with another language's mean redirects 84 to 99 percent of scored non-English replies into that language in five models.

papers.title: Beyond the Teacher: Understanding and Preserving Distillation Overshoot in Agentic On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains agents on their own trajectories using supervision from a stronger teacher. We uncover a counterintuitive phenomenon in multi-turn agentic tasks: a smaller, initially weaker student can substantially outperform its teacher during training, only to regress as distillation continues. We term this phenomenon distillation overshoot. Through decision- and task-level analyses, we trace overshoot to two competing effects of OPD: repairing weak student decisions and eroding successful student choices that the teacher disfavors. Early in training, repair outpaces erosion, allowing the student to combine the teacher's corrections with its own strengths and surpass the teacher. As training continues, erosion overtakes repair, causing these gains to vanish. Motivated by this finding, we propose Success-Preserving On-Policy Distillation (SPOD), which selectively masks conflicting teacher supervision on successful student choices and introduces a soft probability floor to counteract their erosion, while retaining teacher guidance elsewhere. SPOD requires only binary episode success and model probabilities already available during OPD. Across two model families and three agentic benchmarks, SPOD consistently outperforms ordinary OPD and evaluated variants, improving final success by up to 15.2 percentage points and surpassing the teacher by up to 20.0 points. Moreover, SPOD's final checkpoints outperform even ordinary OPD's best intermediate checkpoints in all six settings, demonstrating that beyond-teacher gains can be not only preserved but further extended. Code: https://github.com/Jike338/SPOD
papers.summary: In on-policy distillation (`OPD`), an agent trains on its own trajectories with supervision from a stronger teacher. The authors find that in multi-turn agentic tasks a smaller student can surpass its teacher partway through training and then regress, which they call distillation overshoot. They trace it to teacher corrections that first repair the student's weak decisions and later erode successful choices the teacher disfavors. Their fix, `SPOD`, masks conflicting teacher supervision on successful student choices and adds a soft probability floor, using only binary episode success; across two model families and three benchmarks it improves final success by up to 15.2 points and **surpasses the teacher by up to 20.0 points**.

papers.title: VLA-Rolling: Fewer Denoising Steps, Better Control via Adaptive Action Reuse
papers.abstract: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models generate an action chunk by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise, but typically execute only a short prefix before replanning with updated observations. Under this receding-horizon paradigm, the unexecuted remainder---the action tail---is discarded, and the next chunk is regenerated from fresh noise. We show that this discarded tail retains transferable denoising progress: action-tail initialization can match or outperform a native 10-step Gaussian baseline using fewer denoising steps. However, the optimal denoising budget varies substantially across samples, indicating that tail reuse should be adapted to the updated environment. Based on this observation, we introduce VLA-Rolling, a lightweight inference framework that reuses action tails through three stages: action-tail inheritance, per-action confidence estimation, and confidence-guided refinement through renoising and denoising budget allocation, while the underlying VLA remains frozen. Across $\pi_{0.5}$, SmolVLA, X-VLA, and MolmoAct2 on LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, VLA-Rolling reduces action-chunk inference cost in all 16 model--benchmark pairs, achieving up to a $1.48\times$ speedup, while improving success rate in 14 pairs by up to $15.08$ percentage points. These results show that action tails are not merely discarded predictions, but reusable intermediate states that enable more efficient and accurate VLA inference. These results demonstrate that the action tail can support the generation of better actions with fewer denoising steps. Our project is available at https://chenbao123ww.github.io/VLA-Rolling/.
papers.summary: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models denoise a whole chunk of actions, execute only a short prefix, and then throw away the rest before replanning from fresh noise. The authors show that this discarded action tail keeps useful denoising progress, and they build `VLA-Rolling`, an inference-only framework for frozen models. It inherits the tail, estimates confidence for each action, and allocates renoising and denoising steps according to that confidence. Across `π0.5`, `SmolVLA`, `X-VLA` and `MolmoAct2` on `LIBERO`, `MetaWorld`, `LIBERO-Plus` and `RoboTwin 2.0`, it cuts inference cost in all 16 model–benchmark pairs, with **up to a 1.48× speedup**, and raises success rate in 14 pairs by up to 15.08 points.

papers.title: Normalizing Flow for Neural-Enhanced Track-Before-Detect
papers.abstract: Multiobject tracking (MOT) is a fundamental capability in autonomous navigation, radar and sonar systems, as well as 6G integrated sensing-and-communication (ISAC) networks. In this paper, we propose a neural-enhanced track-before-detect (TkBD) framework that operates directly on complex-valued raw signals and learns a latent representation of unmodeled propagation effects during runtime. We introduce an environment-dependent latent intensity variable that characterizes the signal power of each object in the shared propagation environment. The probability density function of this intensity variable is represented by a normalizing flow and trained online in an unsupervised manner within the sequential Bayesian inference procedure. The learning objective is derived from a variational Bayes formulation by maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO), thereby accounting for the uncertainties inherent in the Bayesian TkBD problem. To enable scalable inference, we make use of a recently introduced Bayesian TkBD framework that combines belief propagation, which avoids high-dimensional operations, with sequential Monte Carlo methods for efficient low-dimensional updates.
papers.summary: Multiobject tracking from raw radar, sonar or integrated sensing-and-communication signals struggles when signal propagation effects are not captured by the model. The authors propose a neural-enhanced track-before-detect (`TkBD`) framework that works directly on complex-valued raw signals. It introduces an environment-dependent latent intensity variable whose density is represented by a **normalizing flow trained online and unsupervised inside the sequential Bayesian inference loop**. Training maximizes a variational evidence lower bound, and the method plugs into an existing framework that combines belief propagation with sequential Monte Carlo for scalable inference.

papers.title: SteadyThought: Mitigating LLM Under-Thinking via Thought-Level Preference Optimization
papers.abstract: Flexible switching between reasoning trajectories (i.e., thought switching) has significantly enhanced the reasoning capabilities of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs). However, existing models often switch excessively yet fail to sustain promising reasoning thoughts, a phenomenon termed "under-thinking". While recent efforts suppress switching to mitigate this, such over-correction may discard valuable trajectories. To address this challenge, we propose Steady Thought (ST), a novel thought-level preference optimization framework. ST formalizes under-thinking as a preference issue at switching points, forcing single-path continuations from identified points to yield high-quality reasoning. Then, ST performs thought-level preference optimization by treating the newly generated response as preferred and the original one as dis-preferred. Experiments across multiple models and datasets show that ST effectively reduces token consumption, achieving reductions of up to 63.8%, while maintaining strong reasoning accuracy. Further analysis suggests that ST helps models acquire a generalizable ability to reduce redundant switching across domains and languages. Code is available at https://github.com/MIRALab-USTC/SteadyThought.
papers.summary: Large reasoning models often switch between lines of reasoning too often and abandon promising ones before finishing them, a behavior called under-thinking. `SteadyThought` frames this as a preference problem at the points where the model switches. From each identified switching point it forces a single-path continuation, then trains with thought-level preference optimization, treating the new continuation as preferred and the original response as dispreferred. Across several models and datasets the method **reduces token consumption by up to 63.8%** while keeping accuracy strong, and the reduction in redundant switching carries over to other domains and languages.

papers.title: PACT: NVFP4 Data-Flow LoRA Fine-Tuning on Consumer GPUs
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning language models on consumer GPUs is constrained by computation and memory. Although LoRA reduces trainable parameters and optimizer state, frozen projections remain expensive, and activations retained for backward can dominate memory usage. We present PACT, a LoRA fine-tuning system that accelerates frozen projections with native NVFP4 GEMMs while reducing quantization and dequantization overhead and limiting quantization error. To reduce activation memory, PACT reuses quantized RMSNorm outputs and saves gate/up activations in NVFP4 for backward. To limit numerical error, it preserves BF16 inputs for forward nonlinear operations and calibrates frozen weights offline using GPTQ adapted to NVFP4 scales and quantized activations. Fused nonlinear kernels and cached forward and backward weight layouts reduce quantization and dequantization overhead. Evaluations across multiple models and tasks on a 16\,GB RTX~5080 show lower memory usage and faster LoRA fine-tuning with competitive accuracy, enabling model adaptation on resource-constrained consumer hardware.
papers.summary: LoRA fine-tuning on consumer GPUs is still limited by the cost of the frozen projection layers and by the memory needed to store activations for the backward pass. `PACT` runs the frozen projections as native `NVFP4` matrix multiplications and stores some activations in `NVFP4`, reusing quantized RMSNorm outputs and the gate and up-projection activations. To keep numerical error in check, it keeps BF16 inputs for nonlinear operations and calibrates the frozen weights offline with a `GPTQ` variant adapted to NVFP4. Fused kernels and cached weight layouts cut quantization overhead, and on a **16 GB `RTX 5080`** the system fine-tunes faster and with less memory than the baselines while keeping accuracy competitive.

papers.title: HCFM: Helmholtz Component Flow Matching for Time Series Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Flow Matching (FM) is an efficient simulation-free approach for training flow-based generative models, making it a promising foundation for scalable time-series anomaly detection (TSAD). However, standard FM learns a monolithic vector field in which nominal transport and local density-changing behavior are entangled. This creates a central challenge for TSAD; local expansion and contraction carry crucial anomaly-sensitive information, yet isolating this signal requires expensive Jacobian-trace estimation over the entire field. We propose \emph{Helmholtz Component Flow Matching} (HCFM), an unsupervised TSAD framework that parameterizes the vector field prediction network with separate transport, compression, and residual heads. The transport head is constrained to be divergence-free, so divergence estimation is restricted to the compression head, while a lightweight residual head absorbs the remaining mismatch. This structured parameterization improves scalability and detection performance by separating volume-preserving nominal transport from density-changing compression, yielding cleaner anomaly signals from distinct deviations of nominal behavior. Experiments on large-scale univariate and multivariate TSAD benchmarks show that HCFM consistently improves detection accuracy while maintaining efficient inference compared with 16 baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/TrustAIoT/HCFM__time-series-anomaly/
papers.summary: Standard flow matching learns a single vector field in which ordinary transport is mixed with the local expansion and contraction that signal anomalies, and isolating that signal needs costly Jacobian-trace estimates. `HCFM` (Helmholtz Component Flow Matching) splits the prediction network into three heads: a divergence-free transport head, a compression head, and a lightweight residual head. Divergence then only has to be estimated on the compression head, which **separates density-changing behavior from volume-preserving nominal transport**. On large univariate and multivariate time-series anomaly detection benchmarks, it improves detection accuracy over 16 baselines while keeping inference efficient.

papers.title: Policy Is Not Capability: Some Safety Benchmarks Measure Which Definition of "Unsafe" You Trained On
papers.abstract: A guardrail classifier is reported as if unsafe were a property of text. It is not: it is a property of a policy, and the policy enters the model through its labels. We exploit an accident of an industrial deployment in which the same ~53k prompts were labelled twice, under two operational definitions ("is this a request for harmful content?" and "would a moderator block this?"), and used to train ten guardrail arms sharing architecture, codebase and optimiser family, at two model scales. First, the guardrail's own training corpus already contained the benchmarks: JailbreakBench-benign is 88% and OR-Bench-hard 82% present in the training pools, two over-refusal benchmarks, the kind a guardrail reports to argue it does not over-block. Everything below is decontaminated. Second, safety benchmarks stratify sharply by how much of their score is decided by the label definition rather than by the model: with architecture and optimiser fixed, the range across the ten arms is 0.99 on HarmBench-copyright and 0.043 on WildGuard-benign, a 23x spread. Third, a benchmark score can be moved across its entire range by 0.03% of the parameters. Across these arms HarmBench-copyright spans 0-100 and OR-Bench-hard over-refusal 3.4-56.4%, and the four arms whose last supervision signal carries a given policy occupy one extreme of both (exact rank p=0.005, or 0.04-0.14 at worst), at unchanged detection capability. For a distilled student the teacher's soft labels do this even when every hard label carries the other policy, so teacher provenance is an unrecorded confound in any released checkpoint. Fourth, validation accuracy on the one split that grades all twenty arms tracks agreement with the annotator's policy (rho=+0.74), not detection capability (rho=+0.34). We argue that guardrail evaluations should report contamination, a seed floor and the definition they were graded against as first-class variables.
papers.summary: Guardrail classifiers are usually reported as if 'unsafe' were a property of the text, when it actually depends on the labeling policy. The authors use an industrial deployment in which the same roughly 53k prompts were labeled under two definitions of unsafe, and train ten guardrail models that differ only in which labels they learned from. They find that over-refusal benchmarks such as `JailbreakBench`-benign (88%) and `OR-Bench-hard` (82%) were largely present in the training data. After decontamination, how much the label definition decides a benchmark score varies 23-fold across benchmarks, and **`HarmBench`-copyright scores span 0 to 100 while detection capability stays unchanged**. The authors argue that guardrail evaluations should report contamination, seed variance and the policy they were graded against.

papers.title: The Optimal Sample Complexity of Pointwise Replicable Agnostic Learning
papers.abstract: Pointwise replicability asks that two independently trained predictors, using the same random seed, agree at each fixed query with high probability. We determine its optimal agnostic sample complexity on finite and countable domains. For every nonempty binary class of finite VC dimension $d\ge1$, the required number of independent examples is $\Theta\!\left(\frac{d}{\rho^2\alpha^2}+\frac{\log(1/\beta)}{\alpha^2}\right)$, uniformly over independent accuracy, failure, and disagreement parameters $\alpha,\beta,\rho\in(0,1/10)$. The learner returns one binary function, may be improper, and uses unrestricted shared randomness. Its sample budget is fixed before observing data, and the replicability guarantee includes queries of zero marginal mass. The main construction combines an ensemble of empirical-risk minimizers with a smooth, signal-dependent risk decomposition. A single shared phase selects the final binary predictor. Record times certify its weak-signal risk, while a uniform bound protects the strong-signal risk at that same selected time. A phase-comparison theorem controls the actual shared-seed execution under simultaneous changes in the marginals and risk coefficients. A rare repair step then makes the confidence cost additive. Together with matching lower bounds, this removes the remaining logarithmic overhead and parameter restrictions in the general countable-domain sample-complexity problem. This extended version also retains the earlier explicit constructions and their proofs, including proper learning for VC-one classes, the full finite-atom class, a faster realizable bound, and counterexamples that separate restrictions of particular algorithms from restrictions of the learning problem.
papers.summary: Pointwise replicability requires two predictors trained independently with the same random seed to agree on each fixed query with high probability. For every binary hypothesis class of finite VC dimension d on finite or countable domains, the authors determine the **optimal agnostic sample complexity, Θ(d/(ρ²α²) + log(1/β)/α²)**, where α, β and ρ are the accuracy, failure and disagreement parameters. The upper bound comes from an ensemble of empirical-risk minimizers combined with a signal-dependent risk decomposition and a shared phase-selection step. Matching lower bounds remove the logarithmic overhead and parameter restrictions left by earlier results.

papers.title: One Skill Takes Over: Clashing Agent Skills and a One-File Fix
papers.abstract: Agent Skills are instruction files that tell a coding agent how to do one job. Users install skills from many authors, so two skills for the same job can be active at the same time. We ask what a model does when both skill files are in its context: does it combine their compatible rules, or follow one skill and drop the other? We build SkillClash, 16 pairs of same-job skills in which code checks every rule and a reference output shows the best result that can be reached. On seven models from five families, from 4B open models to Qwen3-235B and GPT-4.1, a skill's rules are followed 93 to 99% of the time when it is loaded alone and 61 to 62% when a same-job skill is loaded next to it. Most outputs show takeover: every rule that only one skill asks for is followed, and every rule that only the other skill asks for is dropped. The worked examples inside the skills drive this. When each skill file instead ends with one example that follows both skills, takeover falls to 1 to 15% on the six models we tested. Telling the model which skill has priority does not bring the dropped skill back, and telling it to apply both skills brings the dropped skill back only on the two strong models and leaves the interacting rules broken. One merged skill file written by the strongest model we used, Claude Opus 5.5, lets all seven models follow 96 to 99% of the achievable rules. Most of its gain over a plain list of both skills' rules comes from its one worked example, and such an example helps only when it is correct. Code and data: https://github.com/prazmara/skillclash
papers.summary: Agent Skills are instruction files that tell a coding agent how to do one job, and users who install skills from many authors can end up with two skills for the same job loaded at once. Using `SkillClash`, 16 pairs of same-job skills whose rules are checked by code, the authors show that rule-following drops from 93–99% with one skill loaded to 61–62% with two, across seven models from 4B open models to `Qwen3-235B` and `GPT-4.1`. Most failures are takeover, where one skill's rules are followed and the other's are dropped, and the skills' worked examples drive this. Ending each skill file with one example that satisfies both skills cuts takeover to 1–15%, and **a single merged skill file lets all seven models follow 96–99% of achievable rules**, mostly because of its one correct worked example.

papers.title: Auto-MD-bench: Evaluating Autoresearch Agents for Real-World Medical Tasks
papers.abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly capable of developing machine learning (ML) models end to end. In medical practice, however, strong performance on the target metric does not fully characterize how good the models are in real-world use cases. For example, medical ML models should also provide well-calibrated risk estimates and remain robust across patient populations. Yet autonomous model development is typically guided by task objectives that emphasize simple predictive discrimination (e.g. AUROC). This raises a key question: are these objectives sufficient to guide agents toward models that meet the broader requirements of real-world medical use? In this study, we introduce Auto-MD-bench, a benchmark of 15 real-world medical tasks from 10 clinical datasets, spanning survival analysis, classification and sequential prediction, with external validation across cohorts, hospitals and time periods. We evaluate four agents: AIDE, AI Scientist v2, Codex, and Autoresearch. The strongest agents achieve competitive primary scores, yet their predicted risks are less calibrated than those of the simple baseline models, which could lead to severe medical accidents. Moreover, models with nearly identical primary scores can exhibit markedly different calibration, while performance varies substantially across population shifts. These findings show that primary task performance alone is insufficient to assess autonomous clinical modeling and multiple different metrics widely used in healthcare practice need to be taken into consideration.
papers.summary: Autonomous agents can now build machine learning models end to end, but they are usually guided by discrimination metrics such as AUROC, which miss requirements that matter in medicine. `Auto-MD-bench` provides 15 real-world medical tasks from 10 clinical datasets, with external validation across cohorts, hospitals and time periods. It is used to evaluate `AIDE`, `AI Scientist v2`, `Codex` and `Autoresearch`. The strongest agents reach competitive primary scores, but **their predicted risks are less well calibrated than those of simple baseline models**, and models with nearly identical primary scores can differ sharply in calibration and in robustness to population shifts.

papers.title: P2N: Reusing Deep Representations for Greater Effective Depth
papers.abstract: Mathematical problem solving and autonomous agents are increasingly important applications of language models, demanding stronger reasoning capabilities. Computational depth is a key resource for such reasoning, but adding model layers increases both training and inference costs, while test-time scaling incurs substantial additional inference computation. We introduce P2N (Previous to Next), which reuses the previous token's deep representations, already available during generation, to increase effective computational depth with negligible decoding overhead. Specifically, P2N adds the previous token's deep hidden state to the current token's shallow representation, allowing subsequent layers to build on previously completed deep computation. This recurrence extends effective computational depth across tokens, while introducing only a single vector addition per decoding step. We train the recurrence using parallel Jacobi updates restricted to a middle-layer core. Experiments with Qwen-style models show that, at 1.5B parameters, P2N improves GSM8K accuracy by over 10 percentage points under both zero-shot and few-shot prompting, with nearly unchanged decoding latency. The benefits also extend to language modeling and average performance on general downstream benchmarks. on general downstream benchmarks.
papers.summary: Adding layers gives a model more computational depth for reasoning but raises both training and inference cost. `P2N` (Previous to Next) adds the previous token's deep hidden state to the current token's shallow representation, so later layers build on computation that has already finished, at the cost of one vector addition per decoding step. The recurrence is trained with parallel Jacobi updates restricted to a middle-layer core. In 1.5B-parameter Qwen-style models it **improves `GSM8K` accuracy by over 10 percentage points** with nearly unchanged decoding latency, and it also helps language modeling and general benchmarks.

papers.title: CoEvo-RSI: When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?
papers.abstract: Model--harness co-evolution has emerged as a prominent paradigm for recursive self-improving (RSI) agents, jointly evolving their execution scaffolds and intrinsic capabilities. We study the persistent yet often overlooked brain--body mismatch problem in this paradigm, where an evolving harness (body) demands behaviors its model (brain) has not learned or restricts capabilities it already possesses. We introduce CoEvo-RSI, a RSI framework that advances model--harness co-evolution through agent-driven, bidirectional historical inheritance. Drawing on a shared evolutionary archive and execution feedback, a meta-agent coordinates harness development from historical designs with model checkpoint selection or merging and subsequent adaptation under the selected harness, aligning inherited capabilities with evolving execution requirements to reduce brain--body mismatch. Using only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on its own rejection-sampled trajectories, CoEvo-RSI makes Qwen3.5-9B competitive with larger models across diverse vertical applications, including multi-agent failure attribution, role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following. It surpasses DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant (+14.16 agent accuracy) and GLM-5.3 on HomeBench VM (+4.90 success rate), underscoring the need for brain--body alignment and the potential of bidirectional historical inheritance to advance agent co-evolution.
papers.summary: Recursive self-improving (RSI) agents that evolve their execution scaffold (the harness) together with the underlying model suffer from a brain–body mismatch. The evolving harness may demand behaviors the model has not learned, or block capabilities the model already has. `CoEvo-RSI` uses a meta-agent and a shared evolutionary archive to develop harnesses from historical designs while selecting or merging model checkpoints, then adapts the model under the chosen harness with supervised fine-tuning on its own rejection-sampled trajectories. With this, `Qwen3.5-9B` becomes competitive with much larger models, **beating `DeepSeek-V4-Pro` on `TraceElephant` by 14.16 points** and `GLM-5.3` on `HomeBench` VM by 4.90 points.

papers.title: Dual-Slot: From Serial Loops to Parallel Slots in Language Models
papers.abstract: Looped language models increase computational depth by repeatedly applying shared layers, offering a way to improve model quality without adding parameters. However, sequential dependencies between loop iterations increase autoregressive decoding latency. We introduce Dual-Slot, an architecture that reorganizes serial looped computation into parallel latent and prediction slots. Rather than waiting for the current token's latent computation to finish, the prediction slot combines the previous token's deep latent state with the current representation, while the latent slot produces a state for the next decoding step. This shifts the latent dependency across adjacent tokens, replacing two sequential module invocations with a single paired invocation while preserving standard autoregressive generation. To preserve token-level parallelism during training, we use a small number of Jacobi iterations to refine latent states across the sequence in parallel. Experiments on Qwen-style dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models show consistent improvements in language modeling and average downstream accuracy. On the 1B dense model, Dual-Slot reduces Pile validation perplexity from 7.25 to 7.00 and improves average five-shot accuracy across nine task configurations by 2.26 percentage points. After supervised fine-tuning, it improves zero-shot GSM8K accuracy by 5.83 and 3.49 percentage points for the 1B dense and A0.6B MoE models, respectively. Across the evaluated batch sizes, Dual-Slot retains 93.1-96.5% of vanilla decoding throughput for the dense model and 98.1-99.6% for the MoE model.
papers.summary: Looped language models gain depth by reapplying shared layers, but the sequential loop iterations slow down autoregressive decoding. `Dual-Slot` reorganizes the loop into parallel latent and prediction slots: the prediction slot combines the previous token's deep latent state with the current representation, while the latent slot computes the state for the next step. This replaces two sequential module calls with a single paired call, and a few Jacobi iterations keep training parallel across tokens. On a 1B dense model, it lowers `Pile` perplexity from 7.25 to 7.00 and improves fine-tuned zero-shot `GSM8K` accuracy by 5.83 points, while **retaining 93.1–96.5% of vanilla decoding throughput** (98.1–99.6% for the mixture-of-experts model).

papers.title: Beyond Factual Accuracy: A Benchmark for Evaluating Perspective Alignment in LLMs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models often generate factually correct responses that fail to maintain user-requested perspectives, blending multiple perspectives and forcing users to filter through unwanted information---a perspective control failure that factual accuracy metrics cannot detect. We introduce PerspectiveBench, a benchmark quantifying perspective alignment by constructing scenarios where multiple valid reasoning paths coexist, and propose the Perspective Alignment Score (PAS) to measure adherence to specified perspectives. Experiments reveal that state-of-the-art models successfully include target content but fail to exclude non-requested perspectives. Providing documents through RAG improves factual grounding but does not resolve perspective drift, as models prioritize comprehensive coverage over strict user constraints. Code and data are available at https://github.com/sunghoon014/PerspectiveBench.
papers.summary: Language models often give factually correct answers that mix in perspectives the user did not ask for, a failure that accuracy metrics do not detect. `PerspectiveBench` builds scenarios in which several valid lines of reasoning coexist and measures adherence to the requested one with a Perspective Alignment Score (`PAS`). State-of-the-art models include the requested content but **fail to exclude perspectives the user did not ask for**. Supplying documents through retrieval-augmented generation improves factual grounding but does not fix this drift, because models favor comprehensive coverage over the user's constraints.

papers.title: DAGLoop: Aligning Method Design with Experimental Feedback in Automated AI Research
papers.abstract: Automated AI research agents aim to improve machine learning methods by iteratively proposing, implementing, and evaluating candidate methods. Existing work uses the outcome of each evaluation to determine how the next candidate should be revised for performance improvement. However, a candidate often combines multiple design decisions, and its overall outcome alone does not reveal which decisions produced their expected effects, whether their required conditions were satisfied, or which decisions should be retained or revised. Inspired by ablation studies in the machine learning community, we propose DAGLoop to test the expected effect of a design decision by comparing implementations with and without that decision while preserving the other decisions it requires. Specifically, DAGLoop translates each design decision's rationale into a testable expectation and pairs it with a targeted experiment, forming an experimental specification for assessing the expected effect under its required conditions. Using these specifications, we formulate ablation planning as the construction of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) from the candidate method's design: nodes associate decisions with tests, and edges encode dependencies. The DAG specifies which decisions each experiment must retain and supports joint tests when an expected effect requires several decisions to act together. Outcomes are recorded with the tested decisions, expectations, and conditions to form structured research memory. This memory guides the agent in retaining experimentally supported decisions, revising unsupported ones, and planning further experiments when the evidence is unresolved. Experiments on dozens of research tasks demonstrate substantial performance improvements achieved by DAGLoop across diverse executable research settings. Code and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/deng34567/DAGLoop.
papers.summary: Automated AI research agents revise candidate methods based on overall evaluation outcomes, which do not show which of several design decisions actually helped. `DAGLoop` borrows from ablation studies: it turns each design decision's rationale into a testable expectation paired with a targeted experiment. It then plans ablations as a directed acyclic graph whose edges encode which other decisions each test must keep. The results are stored as structured research memory, which tells the agent which decisions to keep, which to revise, and where to run further experiments. Across dozens of executable research tasks, DAGLoop yields **substantial performance improvements** over the outcome-driven loop.

papers.title: Conformal Prediction-Enabled Sequence-level Policy Optimization for Reasoning Language Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning improves the reasoning capability of large language models through verifiable rewards for mathematical and coding tasks. In token-level methods such as GRPO, clipping acts on individual token ratios while the reward and advantage apply to a complete response. Recent sequence-level methods align these units but still use fixed clipping bands, whose tail probabilities change as the score distribution evolves. We propose Conformal Prediction-Enabled Sequence-level Policy Optimization (CSPO), which adaptively calibrates sequence-level clipping bounds using recent training statistics. The resulting band targets a specified marginal tail budget and adapts to policy drift; calibration conditional on response length requires additional assumptions. We bound the probability that a fresh score falls outside the band by the target miscoverage level plus explicit CDF discrepancy and drift terms. Under additional moment conditions, this bound also controls the objective and gradient error relative to the unclipped GSPO power surrogate. Experiments with the Qwen3-1.7B series show improvements over GSPO on difficult mathematical reasoning benchmarks and ALFWorld, with clipping endpoints that adapt during training.
papers.summary: In reinforcement learning for reasoning, token-level methods such as `GRPO` clip individual token ratios while rewards apply to whole responses. Sequence-level methods such as `GSPO` fix that mismatch but use fixed clipping bands whose tail probabilities shift as training evolves. `CSPO` uses conformal prediction to calibrate sequence-level clipping bounds adaptively from recent training statistics, targeting a specified tail budget. The authors prove that the probability of falling outside the band is bounded by the target miscoverage level plus explicit drift terms. With `Qwen3-1.7B` models, CSPO **improves over `GSPO` on difficult math reasoning benchmarks and `ALFWorld`**.

papers.title: Toward Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enterprise Retail Workflows over Heterogeneous Data Sources
papers.abstract: Enterprise retail workflows require agents to chain evidence across heterogeneous sources, from structured product and order records to unstructured inquiries and reviews, yet existing agentic RAG benchmarks rarely capture this challenge. To enable controlled evaluation of such workflows, we introduce RetailBridge, a compositional retail benchmark built from persona-driven simulations. Its questions are constructed by linking entities and intermediate answers across heterogeneous sources, requiring agents to identify the relevant sources, carry evidence between them, and produce a grounded answer. To systematically evaluate LLMs on these retail workflows, we develop RetailRAG, a retail-aware framework equipped with auto-schema briefing, source-routed plan chaining, and diagnostic plan revision. RetailRAG consistently outperforms existing agentic RAG baselines across all evaluation axes, serving as a strong reference system for assessing LLM agents on retail workflows. On RetailBridge, evaluating ten LLM backbones with RetailRAG reveals multi-source chaining as the dominant bottleneck across providers and model scales, suggesting that reliable retail agents require explicit cross-source orchestration rather than scaling alone. Code and data are publicly available at \url{https://github.com/DISL-Lab/RetailBridge}.
papers.summary: Retail workflows require agents to chain evidence across structured product and order records and unstructured inquiries and reviews, which existing agentic retrieval-augmented generation benchmarks rarely test. `RetailBridge` is a compositional benchmark built from persona-driven simulations, with questions that link entities and intermediate answers across sources. The authors also build `RetailRAG`, a reference agent with automatic schema briefing, source-routed plan chaining and diagnostic plan revision, which outperforms existing agentic retrieval baselines. Evaluating ten language-model backbones shows that **multi-source chaining is the dominant bottleneck regardless of provider or scale**.

papers.title: Pre-Query Retention with Bounded Bit and Word Retrieval
papers.abstract: An agent can retain information before receiving a future question and later retrieve evidence from an archive. Evaluating this arrangement requires accounting for both retained information and the width of each retrieval response. Decision-tree capacity bounds describe individual sets of distinguishable records, but a memory writer must encode every possible record before the query is known. We study fixed-length retention beside an immutable binary archive, with a worst-case limit on raw bit or word reads. We characterize feasible one-bit-read memory cells and construct encoders that partition the complete record space. Supporting pairwise exclusive disjunction and conjunction with one bit read is equivalent to supporting every Boolean query. For multiple reads, we combine explicit encoders with decision-tree counting and an entropy converse. The word-read bounds differ by at most two retained bits when the read budget is at most half the archive length. Under an explicit condition on word width and archive length, raw-word caching attains the exact optimum among all writers. A related condition preserves this optimum under positive average error. Exhaustive checks validate the implementations. In a matched dialogue-agent study, a categorical sufficient statistic preserves source decisions with less storage and lower decoding latency than the universal encoder. A catalogue-specific index reduces private state further and requires additional shared storage. The results characterize how response width and future query structure determine retention requirements.
papers.summary: An agent may need to store information before it knows what question it will be asked, then look up evidence in an archive under a limit on how many bits or words it can read. The authors study fixed-length memory beside an immutable binary archive and characterize which memory cells work with a single bit read. They show that **supporting pairwise exclusive-or and conjunction with one bit read is equivalent to supporting every Boolean query**. They derive bounds for multiple reads and conditions under which simply caching raw words is exactly optimal. In a matched study of dialogue agents, a categorical sufficient statistic preserves decisions with less storage and lower latency than a universal encoder.

papers.title: Deep Fusion Memory: A Chunk-Level Parametric Memory for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models need effective ways to acquire and use external knowledge beyond what they retain from pretraining. Continued pretraining risks catastrophic forgetting, while retrieval at inference time can add substantial overhead. External parametric memory avoids online retrieval, but constructing its training data requires extensive offline search, and output-level interpolation provides only shallow fusion. We introduce Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), a parametric memory architecture that reduces this construction workload and incorporates learned memory into intermediate hidden states. A causal memory predictor learns to generate memory from the preceding context, using retrieved chunk embeddings from the corpus as supervision. The predicted memory is shared across tokens within each chunk and fused into their hidden states through gated cross-attention. Memory prediction and fusion are trained end to end with the backbone frozen, and inference requires no explicit retrieval. Compared with existing parametric memory approaches, which often construct token-level memory targets, DFM requires $32\times$ fewer retrieval queries and $2048\times$ fewer retrieved items to construct its training data. Across six QA tasks, DFM performs better over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA, domain adaptation yields average gains of 6.51 and 4.38 points over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively.
papers.summary: Large language models need ways to absorb external knowledge without the catastrophic forgetting of continued pretraining or the inference overhead of retrieval, and existing parametric memories are costly to build and fuse only at the output level. `Deep Fusion Memory` (`DFM`) trains a causal memory predictor to generate a memory vector from preceding context, supervised by retrieved chunk embeddings, and shares that memory across each chunk's tokens, injecting it into intermediate hidden states through gated cross-attention while the backbone stays frozen. No retrieval is needed at inference, and building the training data takes 32x fewer retrieval queries and 2048x fewer retrieved items than token-level approaches. Across six QA tasks it beats the strongest baseline by **12.71% on `Mistral-7B-v0.3` and 11.19% on `Qwen3-8B-Base`**, and it also improves domain adaptation.

papers.title: Non-Acceleration of the Heavy-Ball Method in 1D
papers.abstract: Despite having an asymptotically optimal rate of convergence on convex quadratics, the acceleration of Polyak's heavy-ball method and a characterization of its dynamics within more general settings have remained long standing open problems. Recently, the work of Goujaud et al. [Math. Program. (2025)] made progress regarding acceleration in the context of smooth, strongly convex minimization: for a small enough inverse condition number, either the method does not accelerate on quadratics, or there exists a smooth strongly convex function such that heavy-ball cycles over the roots of unity. The constructed functions have two variables, thus leaving the question of acceleration over univariate functions open. In this work, we use a Fourier-based analysis to i) provide a proof for the non-acceleration of the heavy-ball method over the class of univariate smooth strongly convex functions. We also ii) provide a strict enlargement of the previous root-of-unity cycling region, with insights regarding the "fractional" sets of Goujaud et al. [arXiv:2502.19916], and iii) give a higher dimensional cycling instance which is not covered by root-of-unity cycling.
papers.summary: Whether Polyak's heavy-ball method accelerates beyond convex quadratics has been a long-standing open question; earlier work settled part of it using two-variable counterexamples, which left the one-dimensional case open. Using a Fourier-based analysis, the authors **prove that heavy-ball does not accelerate on univariate smooth strongly convex functions**. They also strictly enlarge the known region of parameters where the method cycles over roots of unity, and they give a higher-dimensional cycling example that root-of-unity cycling does not cover.

papers.title: Generation-Heavy Hybrid Machine Translation
papers.abstract:
The state of the art techniques in Machine Translation (MT) require large amounts of symmetric resources from source and target languages. This is true regardless of whether the approach is Transfer or Interlingua, Symbolic or Statistical. Symmetry within these approaches is necessary to ensure quality, robustness and retargetability. In reality, such symmetry, whether it is in terms of structural transfer lexicons, interlingual dictionaries or parallel corpora, is a major bottleneck in developing any MT system.
  This dissertation presents an approach to MT that addresses the lack of symmetry by exploiting symbolic and statistical target language resources in source-poor/target-rich language pairs. This approach is called Generation-Heavy Hybrid Machine Translation (GHMT). Expected source language resources include a syntactic parser and a simple one-to-many translation dictionary. No transfer rules or complex interlingual representations are used. Rich target language symbolic resources are used to overgenerate multiple structural variations from a target-glossed syntactic dependency representation of source language sentences. Statistical target-language resource are then used to select amongst the overgenerated translations. The source-target asymmetry of systems developed in this approach makes them more easily retargetable to new source languages.
papers.summary: Machine translation systems usually need symmetric resources in both languages, such as transfer lexicons, interlingual dictionaries, or parallel corpora, and this is a bottleneck for language pairs where the source side is resource-poor. This dissertation proposes `Generation-Heavy Hybrid Machine Translation` (`GHMT`), which needs only a source-language parser and a simple one-to-many dictionary. Rich symbolic target-language resources overgenerate many structural variants from a target-glossed dependency representation, and statistical target-language models then choose among them. Because the design is asymmetric, the approach is **easier to retarget to new source languages**.

papers.title: Explore or Confirm? LLM Agents Misallocate Measurements Under Noise
papers.abstract: As model reasoning gets cheaper, the physical experiment becomes the slow and costly step in discovery. Each experiment returns a noisy reading: a high value can mean a good candidate or a lucky draw. With a fixed budget, an AI agent must keep choosing between exploring a new candidate and confirming a promising one by re-testing it. We measure that choice in Wellocate, a simulated assay campaign with known true values. It is built on a generated landscape and on two real protein datasets, GB1 and PhoQ, scrambled so no model can answer from memory. We test five language models as minimal agents, with no tools and no memory beyond the history in each prompt. They misallocate in both directions. Three over-confirm, spending most of the budget re-testing. On the generated landscape one under-confirms, trusting single readings, and there every model ends with a worse final pick than a basic scripted strategy. Each failure has its own cause. The over-confirmers run short of new candidates worth trying: a list of untried candidates cuts their re-testing and, on real protein data, makes two of them pick much better. A running summary of their readings or a description of the landscape changes it by at most five percentage points. For the under-confirmer, re-testing its top candidates in a final round, replayed on its own campaigns, recovers only about a quarter of what it loses by picking the wrong candidate. This suggests confirmation has to run through the whole campaign. We release Wellocate as a benchmark and reinforcement-learning environment with frozen splits and scripted baselines. With it, anyone can measure how an agent splits its budget before trusting it with real experiments, and train agents to split it better. Code, data and the environment are available at https://github.com/Xstendyl/wellocate.
papers.summary: When experiments are noisy and the budget is fixed, an AI agent doing discovery has to decide between exploring new candidates and re-testing promising ones. `Wellocate` is a simulated assay campaign built on a generated landscape and on scrambled versions of the `GB1` and `PhoQ` protein datasets, and the authors use it to test five language models as minimal agents. The models misallocate in both directions: three over-confirm by spending most of the budget on re-tests, and one under-confirms by trusting single readings, and on the generated landscape **every model ends with a worse final pick than a simple scripted strategy**. Giving the over-confirmers a list of untried candidates helps, while running summaries help little. The environment is released as a benchmark and reinforcement-learning environment with frozen splits and scripted baselines.

papers.title: Self-organizing reinforcement learning: a swarm approaches the explore-exploit optimum
papers.abstract: The explore/exploit trade-off is the core problem of reinforcement learning (RL). We show that a minimal foraging swarm approaches its optimum - the ideal-free / Nash allocation of a multi-agent resource-sharing game (an equilibrium, not a return maximum) - with no learner and no reward signal. Agents explore by heavy-tailed (Levy) flights, recruit neighbours to a discovery through a threshold cascade on their proximity network, and disperse as a patch crowds; this cascade cycle balances exploration and exploitation and drives foragers toward the ideal free distribution. The swarm attains the shape of this optimum (committed foragers track richness with slope 0.94) but not its exact equilibrium - it stays measurably exploitable - reaching it dynamically (~150 steps) through the coupling of recruitment to movement: remove the coupling and matching collapses (0.94 -> 0.08). The RL sits at the level of the problem and the allocation reached, not the micro-rule: no step evaluates payoff (reward-free by construction, though the crowd signal is informationally tied to payoff), and the swarm reaches the allocation without learning it (quality plateaus and re-settles after resources move, no cumulative gain). Against a trained baseline the comparison is two-sided: in an easier, disembodied game a learner is more precise, while in the same embodied environment the reward-free swarm reaches ~65% of a validated oracle ceiling at zero training and leads until trained PPO and centralised-critic (CTDE) learners overtake it (~74-75%, 16 seeds, all above the swarm mean) after ~4,000 of 15,000 training steps - its advantage is in budget, not asymptote. In this one setting we read it not as beating RL but as a strong zero-shot, reward-free operating point: a demonstration that the self-organizing physics of a minimal swarm can carry a collective close to the optimum RL seeks, with none of RL's machinery.
papers.summary: The authors argue that a minimal foraging swarm can approach the explore-exploit optimum of a multi-agent resource-sharing game, the ideal-free or Nash allocation, without any learner or reward signal. Agents explore with heavy-tailed Lévy flights, recruit neighbours through a threshold cascade, and disperse as patches crowd. The swarm reproduces the shape of the optimal allocation (slope 0.94) but stays measurably exploitable, and **removing the coupling between recruitment and movement collapses matching to 0.08**. In the embodied environment it reaches about 65% of an oracle ceiling with zero training, until `PPO` and centralised-critic learners overtake it after roughly 4,000 training steps.

papers.title: Compile Once, Run Cheap: Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents, and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds
papers.abstract: Embodied AI lacks the data-rich pretraining that gave language models their agents and skills, so new manipulation capability costs demonstrations per task or a frontier model in every episode. We study a third route: a strong general model acts only as an offline author that writes, runs, diagnoses and repairs a manipulation skill in simulation until it passes an exam on layouts drawn after freezing; the frozen skill then runs as code alone or under a cheap caller that reads only its description. We call this skill-level recursive self-improvement Skill-RSI and specify a compile protocol (isolated, audited author; hidden validation layouts; no-feedback and inherit-only controls; tamper-evident ledger) and a reuse protocol that runs the identical files with executors from another model family. On 7 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with cluttered tables, Claude Code compiled 4 tasks into 7 frozen skills, 5 from a first draft needing only qualification, at USD 4.29-8.22 of author cost each (USD 55 per skill counting the 13 failed campaigns). The other three tasks did not compile in 18 campaigns, including five with GPT-6 and a pre-registered 150-layout run: on the hardest task every campaign scored 78-95 of 100 but had 3-16 safety aborts, failing the gate of 95% success with zero aborts; a 100-episode exam bounds an abort rate only to 3.6%. On hidden layouts, repair that inherits the previous version beat from-scratch rewriting in 8 of 8 controlled campaigns (sign test p = 0.004); an inherit-only lineage attributes most of the gap to inheritance, with development feedback adding a little (3 of 3, p = 0.125). Write-once campaigns found no detectable first-draft effect of practice (minimum detectable effect 14 points). The frozen skills kept 148/150 successes on new layouts with no model and 147/150 with a DeepSeek-flash caller at USD 0.00028-0.00054 per episode; no direct-control baseline was run.
papers.summary: New robot manipulation skills usually cost per-task demonstrations or a frontier model running in every episode. `Skill-RSI` instead uses a strong model only as an offline author that writes, tests, diagnoses, and repairs a skill in simulation until it passes an exam on hidden layouts; the frozen skill then runs as plain code or under a cheap caller. On 7 `RoboTwin 2.0` tasks, `Claude Code` compiled 4 tasks into 7 frozen skills at USD 4.29–8.22 of author cost each, while the other three tasks failed safety gates. Repair that inherits the previous version beat from-scratch rewriting in 8 of 8 controlled campaigns, and the frozen skills kept **148/150 successes on new layouts with no model at all** and 147/150 with a `DeepSeek-flash` caller at fractions of a cent per episode.

papers.title: Polynomial Learning of Positive ReLU Networks under Gaussian Inputs
papers.abstract: We study bias-free, one-hidden-layer ReLU networks with nonnegative output weights under standard Gaussian inputs. Hidden directions may be arbitrarily close or linearly dependent. The labels have the target as their conditional mean, and only the unconditional second moment of the noise is bounded. We present a candidate real-arithmetic learning guarantee: a width-$k$ target with total output weight at most one can be approximated to squared prediction error $\varepsilon$ by a nonnegative ReLU network of width at most $k+\min\{k,d\}$, with sample and operation cost $(1+\sigma^2)\operatorname{poly}(d,k,\varepsilon^{-1},\log(1/\delta))$. The argument combines implicit high-order moments with a direction cover that is complete for heavy atoms and sound for every output. Exact Gaussian soft localization refines this cover while pruning keeps at most $k$ centers at every scale. Clipping the query multipliers controls heavy-tailed, input-dependent noise without assuming a uniform conditional variance bound. A final convex fit and an exact sparsification step give the stated output width. We also obtain a parameterized projective direction-recovery guarantee. The result concerns real-arithmetic complexity; no bit-complexity or practical running-time guarantee is asserted.
papers.summary: The authors study how to learn bias-free one-hidden-layer ReLU networks with nonnegative output weights under Gaussian inputs, allowing hidden directions that are arbitrarily close or linearly dependent and noise with only a bounded second moment. They give a candidate guarantee that a width-k target can be approximated to squared error ε by a nonnegative ReLU network of width at most k+min{k,d}, with **sample and operation cost polynomial in d, k, 1/ε, and log(1/δ)**. The proof combines implicit high-order moments, a direction cover refined by Gaussian soft localization and pruning, clipping to handle heavy-tailed noise, and a final convex fit with exact sparsification. The result concerns real-arithmetic complexity only.

papers.title: Memory as Belief: Bayesian Evolution of Memory for Self-Evolving LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory to accumulate past experiences for continual adaptation. However, effectively reusing memory requires accurately assessing its value, as retrieved experiences may become unreliable when transferred across task contexts. Despite its importance, memory valuation remains largely underexplored, with existing methods relying on historical retrieval success rates that overlook the context dependency of memory usefulness and the varying reliability of estimates under different amounts of evidence. Inspired by the Bayesian brain hypothesis, we propose BEAM (Bayesian-style Evolutionary Agentic Memory), a framework that reformulates memory value evaluation as a parameterized cognitive inference process, where memory value is represented as a context-conditioned dynamic belief rather than a passive historical statistic. Specifically, BEAM infers memory value beliefs from current task contexts and continuously calibrates them using execution feedback as empirical evidence, transforming memory from passive storage into an adaptive cognitive mechanism for continual self-evolution. Extensive experiments across reasoning and code generation benchmarks demonstrate that BEAM consistently improves memory utilization and enables continual self-evolution of LLM agents.
