papers.summary: LLM agents that reuse stored experiences need to judge how valuable each memory is, but existing methods rely on historical retrieval success rates that ignore context and evidence strength. `BEAM` (`Bayesian-style Evolutionary Agentic Memory`), inspired by the Bayesian brain hypothesis, treats memory value as a **context-conditioned belief that is inferred from the current task and calibrated with execution feedback**. Experiments on reasoning and code generation benchmarks show that it consistently improves memory utilization and supports continual self-evolution of agents.

papers.title: ClinSDT: LLM-Encoded Clinical Semantic Guidance for Sepsis Treatment via Decision Transformer
papers.abstract: Offline sepsis treatment aims to learn treatment policies from retrospective ICU trajectories. Decision Transformer-based methods provide a natural sequence modeling framework for this task, but they mainly rely on raw physiological states and historical clinician actions. Such raw trajectory tokens may not explicitly capture clinical semantics that clinicians use in practice, such as patient severity, recent treatment response, and current risk priorities. To address this limitation, we propose ClinSDT, an LLM-assisted Decision Transformer framework for offline sepsis treatment. ClinSDT uses a frozen LLM as a semantic bridge rather than a treatment decision maker. It constructs three clinical semantic views from ICU trajectories, namely Profile, Context, and Advisory, and inserts their encoded representations as independent tokens into a Decision Transformer policy. To support policy refinement and rollout, ClinSDT further trains a Treatment-Response Forecaster to estimate the next physiological state, SAPS-II change, and predictive uncertainty from state-action inputs. In the second training stage, the forecaster screens local counterfactual treatment candidates, and only low-uncertainty candidates with lower predicted SAPS-II increase are distilled into the policy after semantic regeneration. During inference, ClinSDT performs closed-loop treatment rollout by refreshing semantic inputs from the currently available patient state. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV show that ClinSDT achieves consistent relative improvements over representative imitation learning, offline reinforcement learning, and Decision Transformer baselines under the same rollout protocol. Code and data are available at https://github.com/KAG778/ClinSDT.
papers.summary: Decision Transformer approaches to offline sepsis treatment work from raw physiological states and clinician actions, and so miss clinical semantics such as severity and treatment response. `ClinSDT` uses a frozen LLM to encode three semantic views (Profile, Context, and Advisory) as extra tokens in a Decision Transformer policy, and it trains a Treatment-Response Forecaster that predicts the next state, the change in `SAPS-II` severity score, and uncertainty. The forecaster screens counterfactual treatment candidates, and only low-uncertainty improvements are distilled back into the policy. On `MIMIC-III` and `MIMIC-IV` it shows **consistent relative improvements over imitation learning, offline RL, and Decision Transformer baselines**.

papers.title: Behave Like Experts: Fusing Data with Semantic Knowledge for Effective and Efficient Semantic Map Construction
papers.abstract: Semantic map models (SMMs) construct a graph that reflects conceptual similarity by comparing cross-lingual form-meaning mappings. Experts build such models not only by obeying the data constraint, i.e., the connectivity hypothesis, which states that conceptual nodes belonging to the same form must be connected, but also by incorporating their prior semantic knowledge. Current automatic methods ignore this knowledge, which harms both accuracy and efficiency by enlarging the search space of candidate graphs. In this paper, we fuse the distributional semantic knowledge hidden in the internal representations of language models into a top-down, data-driven algorithm. This expert-like behavior re-sorts the candidates in a huge search space, guided by conceptual semantics similarity. Experiments on a self-collected benchmark of 10 datasets and comprehensive metrics show that our method builds SMMs both effectively and efficiently.
papers.summary: Semantic map models are graphs of conceptual similarity built from cross-lingual form-meaning mappings. Experts build them using both the connectivity hypothesis and prior semantic knowledge, whereas automatic methods ignore that knowledge and search a needlessly large space of candidate graphs. The authors fuse distributional semantic knowledge from language model representations into a top-down, data-driven algorithm that re-ranks candidates by conceptual similarity. On a self-collected benchmark of 10 datasets, the method **builds semantic maps both more accurately and more efficiently**.

papers.title: Memories That Outlive Their Reasons: Dependency-Tethered Memory for Tool-Using LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Agents now act on the Web, publishing packages, models and datasets through registry APIs, and remembering past verifications spares them the work. But a verdict rests on premises. When a signing key is revoked, everything built on it stops passing, yet the advisory names only the key, and the old verdicts of its dependents may never share a retrieval window with it. This non-locality of invalidation turns memory into a liability: in long simulated chats, an agent reading a memory of atomic facts publishes 62% of the objects whose failure lies upstream, each backed by a record that was true when written. Yet derivation is local even when invalidation is not. Tether records, at write time, the exact versions each verdict derives from, and at read time withdraws any verdict whose support has failed anywhere in the store; the agent reads the same fields as before. On Fallout, a generator of versioned worlds with hypothesis-blind simulated histories shared by every memory, Tether publishes 0.3% of upstream-failing objects across three domains when relations are stated with their verdicts, with 37% fewer verification calls than checking everything. A-Mem and Graphiti re-verify most candidates (0.83-0.86 checks per candidate), which limits their savings, yet publish 9% of upstream-failing objects; Mem0 relies on memory more and publishes 42%. Flushing every verdict on any failure is as safe as Tether but costs 32% more checks. The gain over fact memory holds with three open-weight backbones and against a whole-store window. These gains depend on capturing dependencies: when relations arrive in sessions apart from their verdicts, Tether's downstream unsafe publication rate rises to 9.4-22.1%, and a weak writer that misses edges loses safety in the same way.
papers.summary: Tool-using agents that cache past verification verdicts can publish unsafe objects when an upstream premise, such as a revoked signing key, is invalidated, because the advisory never surfaces alongside the dependent verdicts; in simulation, an agent with atomic-fact memory publishes 62% of upstream-failing objects. `Tether` records at write time the exact versions each verdict depends on, and at read time withdraws any verdict whose support has failed anywhere in the store. On the `Fallout` generator of versioned worlds it **publishes only 0.3% of upstream-failing objects with 37% fewer verification calls than checking everything**, compared with 9% for `A-Mem` and `Graphiti` and 42% for `Mem0`. Safety degrades when dependency relations arrive in separate sessions or the writer misses edges.

papers.title: Trackable Skill Library Lifecycle Management for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Skill-augmented agentic RL has emerged as an effective approach to improving LLM agents on long-horizon tasks. Despite this progress, individual skills may follow distinct trajectories as the policy evolves, with some becoming redundant after the model internalizes their capabilities, others remaining valuable as external scaffolding, and still others turning harmful. However, existing skill library systems fail to identify each skill's true contribution due to free-riding among co-retrieved skills, difficulty confounding across tasks, and the absence of skill-specific counterfactual evidence, which prevents reliable skill lifecycle management. We propose TrackRL, an agentic RL framework where skill tracking drives skill library full lifecycle management. Specifically, within each GRPO group, we turn grouped sampling into online randomized controlled experiments. Independent random injection and within-group contrasts on the same task isolate each skill's true contribution, and reliability-weighted aggregation accumulates evidence across groups. As evidence accumulates, we continuously track skill utility, which measures the skill's causal contribution as external scaffolding, and model mastery, which reflects how far the corresponding capability has been internalized. Along this line, we formulate skill lifecycle management as an evidence-gated state-transition process that governs each skill from generation and admission through protected incubation to retention, retirement, or removal, while a soft capacity bound controls library growth. Experiments show that TrackRL outperforms recent skill-augmented RL baselines in both library-assisted and skill-free evaluation, with further analyses revealing how skill value shifts during policy learning and how evidence-driven state transitions shape skill library evolution. Our code is available at https://github.com/xizhu1022/TrackRL.
papers.summary: In skill-augmented agentic RL, individual skills can become redundant, stay useful, or turn harmful as the policy learns, but existing libraries cannot isolate each skill's contribution because co-retrieved skills free-ride on each other. `TrackRL` turns each `GRPO` sampling group into an **online randomized controlled experiment, randomly injecting skills and contrasting outcomes on the same task** to estimate each skill's causal utility and how far the model has internalized it. Those estimates drive an evidence-gated lifecycle that admits, incubates, retains, retires, or removes skills under a soft capacity bound. It outperforms recent skill-augmented RL baselines in both library-assisted and skill-free evaluation.

papers.title: MemBubble: Benchmarking How Agent Memory Shapes LLM Response Diversity
papers.abstract: Memory serves as the core component of LLM-based agents, enabling personalized responses via extracting and using user preferences from past interactions. However, its use may reduce response diversity, thereby narrowing the range of information available to users. Existing evaluations rely largely on synthetic interactions and cover few memory systems, leaving the effects of memory on response diversity insufficiently evaluated in real-world scenarios. We introduce MemBubble, a benchmark of 1000 instances built on preferences extracted from real user-assistant conversations. To measure the extent to which memory concentrates response distributions, we construct test queries in scenarios distinct from user preferences while preserving topical relevance through shared preference categories. Across multiple LLMs and memory mechanisms, entropy decreases by 34.7% on average compared with directly providing the full interaction history, highlighting the important role of memory processing in diversity loss. We also explore simple user-side interventions and changes in information availability but find that these do not effectively close the diversity gap. Our findings highlight the need to consider preserving diversity and user access to information alongside improvements in personalization when designing and using agent memory systems.
papers.summary: Agent memory personalizes responses from past interactions, but it may also narrow the range of information users see. `MemBubble` is a benchmark of 1,000 instances built from preferences extracted from real user-assistant conversations, with test queries set in scenarios distinct from those preferences but topically related. Across multiple LLMs and memory mechanisms, **response entropy drops by 34.7% on average compared with providing the full interaction history**, which points to memory processing as a source of diversity loss. Simple user-side interventions did not close the gap.

papers.title: Decision-Target Reversal under Informative Label Missingness
papers.abstract: Informative label missingness can improve classification efficiency because the pattern of label availability may itself contain information about the discriminant structure. We show that this advantage need not persist across deployment objectives: with the data-generating model and statistical experiments held fixed, informative partial classification can be favourable under one loss and unfavourable under another. We call this phenomenon decision-target reversal. For binary Gaussian discrimination, we derive a local cost-sensitive excess-risk expansion and, in one dimension, obtain explicit critical cost ratios at which the first-order risk ordering reverses. We show that the required covariance geometry arises under finite uncertainty-dependent missingness mechanisms with a fixed marginal missing-label proportion. We then extend the analysis to multiclass finite-action problems through loss-specific active-boundary curvature, yielding a general decision-target frontier. Monte Carlo experiments illustrate the predicted reversals, and a descriptive gastrointestinal-lesion application with agreement-defined label availability illustrates sensitivity to deployment costs. The results show that favourable informative missingness is a property of the statistical experiment relative to the deployment decision, rather than of the experiment alone.
papers.summary: Informative label missingness, where the pattern of which labels are available carries signal, can make classification more efficient. The authors show this advantage can flip depending on the deployment loss, a phenomenon they call decision-target reversal: **with the data and experiment held fixed, informative partial labelling can help under one loss and hurt under another**. For binary Gaussian discrimination they derive cost-sensitive excess-risk expansions with explicit critical cost ratios, then extend the analysis to multiclass problems. Monte Carlo experiments and a gastrointestinal-lesion example illustrate the predicted reversals.

papers.title: Many Repairs, One Direction: Steering Code Models Toward Safer Cryptographic API Use
papers.abstract: Cryptographic API misuse in large language model-generated code can compromise software security. While many existing approaches improve code security by modifying model parameters or inputs, how representation changes associated with different cryptographic API repairs can support a shared intervention for safer code generation remains underexplored. To investigate this, we construct 48,000 matched program pairs across four programming languages and ten cryptographic API misuse categories. Each pair changes a specified API decision while preserving the programming task. Subtracting the misuse program's internal representation from its secure counterpart's gives a repair vector. Across five models, comparisons of mean repair vectors reveal stronger organization by misuse category than by language. These category-specific patterns also support a shared intervention. We introduce CrypSteer, which extracts a shared direction by normalizing repair differences and selecting a principal component aligned with repairs across misuse categories. With model weights fixed, adding one shared direction per model to its internal activations during generation improves aggregate target security rates by 5.28--15.00 percentage points over unsteered generation across languages and misuse categories. These findings connect the shared structure of cryptographic repair representations to a reusable intervention for safer code generation.
papers.summary: LLM-generated code often misuses cryptographic APIs. The authors build 48,000 matched program pairs across four languages and ten misuse categories, and they compute repair vectors as the difference between the internal representations of the secure and insecure versions. Across five models these vectors cluster more by misuse category than by language, and `CrypSteer` extracts a single shared principal direction aligned with repairs across categories. With weights frozen, adding that one direction to activations during generation **raises target security rates by 5.28–15.00 percentage points** over unsteered generation.

papers.title: TIRE: Top-Down Formula Instantiation with Reliable Execution for Physics Problem Synthesis
papers.abstract: Advancing physics reasoning in large language models requires scalable training data that connect physical laws, concrete problem scenarios, and verifiable numerical answers. Expert-designed problems offer top-down control over physical laws, conditions, and scenarios, but require costly human effort. LLM-based synthesis from texts scales efficiently, but model-generated answers and assessments leave supervision vulnerable to hallucinations. We introduce TIRE, a framework for Top-Down Formula Instantiation with Reliable Execution that brings knowledge-driven problem construction to large-scale data generation. Top-down instantiation uses reusable physical formulas and their applicability conditions to control the physical relations and numerical configurations of generated problems. Reliable execution establishes reference answers before problem generation, providing a common numerical foundation for problem construction and teacher distillation. Together, these mechanisms combine control over problem content with execution-grounded supervision for both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Using TIRE, we construct TIRE-19k, spanning nine subfields of physics. Across 3 backbone LLMs and 4 benchmarks, TIRE-19k outperforms 5 representative datasets with equal amounts of SFT data, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.86 percentage points on average. Further GRPO raises Qwen3-8B's average accuracy by 1.52 percentage points over its TIRE-19k SFT checkpoint. These results demonstrate the value of generating physics training data from explicit physical knowledge with reliable execution.
papers.summary: Training LLMs on physics reasoning needs scalable problems with verifiable answers, but expert-written problems are expensive and LLM-synthesized ones suffer from hallucinated answers. `TIRE` (Top-Down Formula Instantiation with Reliable Execution) generates problems from reusable physical formulas and their applicability conditions, and it computes reference answers by execution before the problem text is written. The resulting `TIRE-19k` dataset spans nine physics subfields and, at equal SFT data size, **beats five representative datasets by 2.86 percentage points on average** across 3 backbones and 4 benchmarks. Further `GRPO` training lifts `Qwen3-8B` by another 1.52 points.

papers.title: HullProbe: Measuring Interventional Part Reliance in Maritime Vessel Classifiers
papers.abstract: Recognizing a vessel's type from an image supports maritime surveillance and sanctions monitoring, but a classifier can reach high accuracy by leaning on the generic hull instead of the more distinctive superstructure, and is then fooled when a vessel is re-hulled or occluded. De-biasing methods claim to remove such reliance, yet the field certifies them with worst-group accuracy, a proxy that needs group labels and only infers reliance from accuracy. We measure the reliance directly. HullProbe swaps a registered anatomical part of a vessel for another instance's and reads how much that part drives the decision, using a same-class swap to control for compositing artifacts. Because a surface vessel is a hull and a superstructure arranged along one axis, its parts form a 2x3 grid whose 2^6 = 64 swaps we evaluate exhaustively, and a single Walsh transform returns each part's interventional influence and its interaction spectrum. On planted shortcuts, where the true reliance is known, the measure tracks worst-group accuracy (r = -0.94 over 45 configurations), and replacing its learned segmenter with human annotations changes the hull-share by less than the audit's resolution. On the 26 vessel types of MARVEL, the classifier places about 46% of its corrected sensitivity on the generic hull yet follows the superstructure when the two conflict, and the group-label-free de-biasers available there do not detectably reduce the hull's share. The findings hold across three architectures and a second maritime dataset, and the method extends to fine-grained vehicle recognition on Stanford Cars.
papers.summary: Vessel-type classifiers used for maritime surveillance can reach high accuracy by relying on the generic hull rather than the distinctive superstructure, and de-biasing methods are usually certified only indirectly through worst-group accuracy. `HullProbe` measures part reliance directly by swapping registered anatomical parts between vessel images over a 2x3 part grid, evaluating all 64 swaps and applying a Walsh transform to get each part's influence and interactions. On planted shortcuts the measure tracks worst-group accuracy (r = -0.94). On `MARVEL`'s 26 vessel types, classifiers put **about 46% of their sensitivity on the hull**, and available group-label-free de-biasers do not detectably reduce it.

papers.title: Reflection-Guided Dynamics Rectification for Text-to-Image Generation
papers.abstract: Fine-grained rectification of existing generations under a limited additional budget remains a key problem in test-time optimization (TTO) for image generation. As for prior approaches, they could identify residual errors, but could not directly ensure that the model acts on the feedback during reasoning. Such errors stem from multiple sources, such as the initial noise or text prompt, and ultimately induce an execution gap of failing to handle potential deviations along the trajectory generating. However, classic models generally cannot remedy this gap. To narrow it, we propose Reflection-Guided Dynamics Rectification (RGDR), which turns reflections on completed outputs into corrective interventions on the process of sampling dynamics at the trajectory level. Specifically, RGDR could impact every sampling step by adapting to instantaneous intervention. Moreover, RGDR generates flexible candidates while adjudicating between them and the reference. As experiments show, rectification from RGDR starts from the existing base trajectory and reflection, and RGDR is substantially more effective than former trajectory exploration. Under matched budgets for additional image generation, RGDR's gain in the cross-model average final checklist score over the reference is $1.51\times$ that of TIR prompt refinement and $1.81\times$ that of Dynamic CFG.
papers.summary: Test-time optimization for text-to-image generation can identify residual errors in a generated image but cannot ensure the model acts on that feedback while sampling. `Reflection-Guided Dynamics Rectification` (`RGDR`) turns reflections on completed outputs into corrective interventions applied at every step of the sampling trajectory, starting from the existing base trajectory, and then adjudicates between the resulting candidates and the reference. Under matched extra-generation budgets, its gain in average checklist score is **1.51x that of `TIR` prompt refinement and 1.81x that of `Dynamic CFG`**.

papers.title: Spectral Adaptive Graph Transformer for Efficient and Scalable Traffic Forecasting
papers.abstract: Traffic forecasting models based on spectral graph convolution offer an interpretable account of how information is mixed between sensors, but they rely on an eigendecomposition of the graph Laplacian. It costs cubic time, is fixed by the road network, and provides a symmetric operator that cannot represent the directed propagation of traffic congestion. Attention-based spatio-temporal transformers remove these limitations but generate a dense sensor-by-sensor attention map at each layer and time step, so memory, rather than accuracy, becomes the binding constraint on large networks. We introduce the spectral adaptive graph transformer, whose spatial operator is learned rather than derived from the Laplacian, directed rather than symmetric, and conditioned on the current traffic state rather than a static state, at a cost linear in the number of sensors. A sparse road graph diffusion branch provides the strictly local propagation that a low-rank operator cannot express, and a zero-initialized gate learns the balance between the two. Before spatial mixing, a unit-mean-gain frequency-bin attention module reweights each sensor's short-term periodicities according to its identity and current context. Across six public benchmarks spanning 170 to 1843 sensors, evaluated over three random seeds, the proposed model attains the lowest error of any single end-to-end model on one benchmark and remains competitive with the strongest current attention models on the others, while using about a quarter of their memory and training about twice as fast.
papers.summary: Spectral graph models for traffic forecasting need a cubic-cost Laplacian eigendecomposition and a symmetric operator that cannot represent directed congestion, while attention-based transformers are limited by dense sensor-by-sensor attention memory. The spectral adaptive graph transformer learns a directed, state-conditioned spatial operator at linear cost in the number of sensors, adds a sparse road-graph diffusion branch with a zero-initialized gate, and reweights periodicities with frequency-bin attention. Across six benchmarks with 170 to 1,843 sensors it stays competitive with the strongest attention models **while using about a quarter of their memory and training about twice as fast**.

papers.title: PLANE: Plug-and-Play Fine-Grained Visual Experts for Hallucination Mitigation in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) commonly suffer from hallucinations, which appear as fabricating non-existent objects or outputting incorrect attributes and spatial relationships in images. Previous works empirically indicate that CLIP-style vision encoders tend to focus on primary objects while ignoring image details, which is one of the causes of hallucinations. To address this issue, we propose plug-and-play fine-grained visual experts (PLANE) comprising two components: LoRA visual experts operating on CLIP for multi-aspect image encoding, and an instruction-aware gate network for adaptive image feature fusion. During training, we construct a fine-grained image-caption pairs dataset, where images are described from three aspects: objects, attributes, and relations between objects. Image-caption pairs from different aspects are used to train the three fine-grained LoRA experts respectively. Aiming at comprehensively evaluate our method's capabilities, we manually annotate a fine-grained hallucination evaluation benchmark for LVLMs which is GPT4-independent during evaluation phase (GIFT). We conduct experiments both on popular hallucination evaluation benchmarks and GIFT. The results show that our method effectively reduces hallucinations across models of different types and sizes while introducing minimal inference latency. Compared to advanced baselines, our model also demonstrates superior performance.
papers.summary: Large vision-language models hallucinate objects, attributes, and spatial relations, partly because CLIP-style encoders focus on primary objects and miss detail. `PLANE` adds three LoRA visual experts on top of `CLIP`, each trained on fine-grained captions about objects, attributes, or relations, plus an instruction-aware gate that fuses their features. The authors also release `GIFT`, a manually annotated hallucination benchmark whose evaluation does not depend on GPT-4. The method **reduces hallucinations across models of different types and sizes with minimal added inference latency**.

papers.title: FHKAN: Fractional Hermite Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Data-Driven and Physics-Informed Learning
papers.abstract: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) replace fixed scalar weights by learnable univariate maps, yet most spectral KANs still rely on Chebyshev polynomials that live on a bounded interval and therefore require a saturating squashing of the pre-activation. We introduce the Fractional Hermite Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (FHKAN), a neural architecture that equips KANs with an adaptive, trainable fractional-order generalized Hermite basis. With a nonnegative shape parameter, the underlying generalized Hermite functions are orthonormal on the entire real line and uniformly bounded under a Gaussian envelope, so they act directly on unbounded pre-activations without any saturating map. We derive closed-form derivatives of the generalized, fractional, and scaled basis away from the origin and determine its order of differentiability at the origin, where the fractional power map creates a singular point. On synthetic regression, FHKAN attains the lowest test error at every network depth among nine fixed activations and the spline-based KAN. On image classification, image denoising, and sentiment analysis, the best-performing fractional Hermite block yields the highest accuracy or reconstruction quality. On physics-informed problems, FHKAN reaches mean absolute errors of order 10^-6 to 10^-5 on the Lane-Emden equation, residuals of order 10^-4 on the Burgers equation, and absolute errors below 10^-4 on a fractional delay differential equation.
papers.summary: Most spectral Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) use Chebyshev polynomials, which only work on a bounded interval and so require squashing the inputs to each layer. `FHKAN` replaces them with a trainable fractional-order generalized Hermite basis. This basis is orthonormal over the whole real line and bounded by a Gaussian envelope, so it can act directly on unbounded inputs. The authors derive closed-form derivatives of the basis and work out how smooth it is at the origin, where the fractional power creates a singular point. `FHKAN` has the lowest test error at every depth on synthetic regression, compared with nine fixed activations and a spline-based KAN, and it leads on image classification, denoising, and sentiment tasks. On physics-informed problems it reaches **mean absolute errors of 10^-6 to 10^-5 on the `Lane-Emden` equation**, with small errors on `Burgers` and a fractional delay differential equation as well.

papers.title: Learning without Overwriting: Structural Knowledge Fusion for Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Catastrophic forgetting in sequential deep learning arises from a fixed-capacity architectural constraint: parameter updates encoding new tasks perturb weight subspaces supporting prior representations. We introduce the Knowledge Fusion Network (KFN), which mitigates the stability-plasticity trade-off in class-incremental learning through novelty-gated structural expansion rather than parameter negotiation within a shared capacity budget. KFN decouples task acquisition from knowledge consolidation: each incoming task is learned in an isolated lightweight specialist network (2.8M parameters) and integrated into the global model via a Structural Fusion Module that allocates dedicated channel capacity conditioned on a quantitative novelty score. Dual structural isolation--channel-space separation with temporally phased gradient unfreezing--protects consolidated knowledge. On ten-task Split CIFAR-100, KFN achieves 11.94% minimum task accuracy and 71.16% task-10 accuracy, whereas shared-parameter baselines degrade severely: LwF to 9.07% average accuracy (0.00% min), Replay++ to 8.91% (85.08% forgetting), and Replay to 16.21% (73.44% forgetting); KFN's forgetting (57.92%) is 15.5 pp lower than Replay. Furthermore, KFN prevents logit-scale drift, maintaining near-symmetric task performance. Across CIFAR-100 and EuroSAT satellite imagery, KFN's class-incremental retention (72.7% and 42.5%) substantially exceeds the best baselines (29.6% and 0.94%). Crucially, KFN achieves parameter-efficient linear scaling, adding 25% of the base parameter count per step and requiring 25.1% of naive backbone duplication over ten tasks (28.1M vs 112.0M). With a 37.1% peak GPU memory reduction over full retraining, KFN establishes novelty-gated expansion as a practical path beyond fixed-capacity architectures.
papers.summary: Catastrophic forgetting in class-incremental learning happens when training on new tasks overwrites weights that earlier tasks depend on. The `Knowledge Fusion Network` (`KFN`) avoids this by learning each new task in a small isolated specialist network of 2.8M parameters. A Structural Fusion Module then merges the specialist into the global model, giving it dedicated channel capacity in proportion to how novel the task is, and unfreezes gradients in phases. On `CIFAR-100` and `EuroSAT` satellite imagery, `KFN` retains **72.7% and 42.5% class-incremental accuracy, against 29.6% and 0.94% for the best baselines**. It also forgets 15.5 percentage points less than `Replay` on ten-task `Split CIFAR-100`. Parameter count grows linearly, reaching about 25% of what full backbone duplication would need over ten tasks.

papers.title: Morpheus: a fully local, defense-in-depth de-identification engine for Greek clinical text - a benchmark evaluation
papers.abstract: Background and Objective: Clinical free text cannot leave the hospital without de-identification, yet no de-identification system or benchmark exists for Greek clinical text. We evaluated Morpheus, a fully local de-identification pipeline for Greek clinical documents, on 500 synthetic discharge summaries. Methods: The notes (300 cardiac surgery, 100 cardiology, 100 nephrology) were generated by a frontier large language model (Gemini 3.1 Pro) constrained to authentic Greek hospital document layouts. Notes were pre-annotated at generation; two clinicians then independently reviewed and corrected every note, blinded to each other, with disagreements arbitrated. Primary outcomes were recall over must-redact identifiers and over-redaction of clinical content, measured over must-survive probes. Secondary outcomes: residual leaks flagged by an independent egress-review layer, processing time and reproducibility. Results: Inter-annotator agreement was F1 = 0.998. The de-identification rate was 96.59% (7,666/7,937 identifier instances; 95% CI 96.16-96.96): 98.49% for direct and 93.42% for quasi-identifiers. No patient's own complete identifier survived in any note; of 271 residual instances, 199 (73.4%) concerned institutional identity, chiefly the hospital letterhead. The over-redaction rate was 2.82% (190/6,747 probes; 95% CI 2.45-3.24). The egress guard flagged 2 of 271 residuals, both complete telephone numbers. Two independent runs gave identical verdicts. Conclusions: A fully local, deterministic pipeline removed 98.5% of direct patient identifiers from Greek clinical text while altering under 3% of protected clinical content; most residuals concerned the institution, not the patient. To our knowledge this is the first benchmark evaluation of clinical-text de-identification for Greek and the first quantified evaluation of an independent egress-guard layer.
authors: Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children
papers.summary: No de-identification system or benchmark has existed for Greek clinical text, and such text cannot leave a hospital until identifiers are removed. The authors evaluate `Morpheus`, a fully local and deterministic de-identification pipeline. The test set is 500 synthetic discharge summaries generated by `Gemini 3.1 Pro` and annotated independently by two clinicians. The pipeline removed 96.59% of identifier instances overall and **98.49% of direct patient identifiers**, while altering only 2.82% of clinical content that should have been preserved. No patient's complete identifier survived in any note; most of the remaining leaks were institutional details such as the hospital letterhead. An independent egress-review layer, a final check on outgoing text, caught 2 of the 271 residual leaks.

papers.title: Do LLMs Reproduce the Age Gap in Loneliness? Evaluating Survey Simulation against European Survey Data
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often used to simulate survey respondents, but matching survey averages does not establish accurate demographic differences. We test whether LLM outputs reproduce within-country age gaps in loneliness using the 2022 EU Loneliness Survey, comparing adults aged 18-34 and 65 or older in France, Italy, Poland, and Sweden. We evaluate simulation with and without age information and direct distribution estimation against a probability-based sample, with a non-probability sensitivity reference. Both human samples show higher mean loneliness among younger adults. Under age-specified simulation with standard response-option order, Mistral Small 4 and GPT-5.6 Terra reverse this ordering under all three prompt framings in three and two countries, respectively, mainly by overestimating older-adult means. DeepSeek V4 Flash preserves the ordering everywhere but underestimates both group means, with errors largely cancelling in France and Italy. Against the probability-based reference, direct estimation has lower absolute age-gap error than simulation for Mistral and Terra in every country. For DeepSeek, simulation has lower gap error but direct estimation has lower group-mean error; these comparisons depend on low-validity older-adult simulation cells. Evaluating LLM outputs as proxies for age groups within countries therefore requires checking both group means and their contrast against human survey data.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are often used to simulate survey respondents, but matching overall averages does not show that they reproduce differences between demographic groups. Using the 2022 EU Loneliness Survey, the authors test whether LLMs reproduce the gap in loneliness between adults aged 18-34 and those 65 or older in France, Italy, Poland, and Sweden. In the human data younger adults are lonelier, but **`Mistral Small 4` and `GPT-5.6 Terra` reverse this ordering in several countries**, mainly because they overestimate loneliness among older adults. `DeepSeek V4 Flash` preserves the ordering but underestimates both groups, and in some countries these errors cancel out. The authors conclude that using LLMs as stand-ins for survey respondents requires checking both group means and the gaps between groups against human data.

papers.title: Legal Guidance in the Wild: How Users Seek Legal Help in Real-World LLM Conversations
papers.abstract: People ask conversational AI models about their legal rights, obligations, procedures, and personal situations that may have legal consequences. To study this behavior, we first need to distinguish requests for legal guidance from other legally themed discussions and unrelated conversations. We contribute a multi-axis taxonomy of legal queries capturing whether legal guidance is sought, how a request is formulated, and which legal domains it concerns; apply it to 2,122 naturally occurring WildChat-1M conversations; and create a human-reviewed gold evaluation set of 200 conversations. All annotations, model checkpoints, and evaluation code are publicly available. In this enriched sample, 71.1% of conversations containing legal content seek personalized or practical guidance. Rights-and-options advice is the most common primary request type among legal-content conversations, and 25.3% of guidance-positive conversations span multiple legal topics. The gold evaluation set supports a two-stage comparison of ModernBERT-base and ModernBERT-large against a TF-IDF cascade. Our framework supports large-scale studies of legal guidance in conversational AI, and the public release of the annotated data facilitates reproducible research and future model development.
papers.summary: To study how people seek legal help from chatbots, the authors build a multi-axis taxonomy of legal queries. It records whether guidance is being sought, how the request is phrased, and which legal domains it touches. They apply it to 2,122 real conversations from `WildChat-1M` and create a human-reviewed gold set of 200 conversations. In this sample, **71.1% of conversations with legal content seek personalized or practical guidance**; advice on rights and options is the most common request, and a quarter of guidance-seeking conversations span several legal topics. They compare `ModernBERT-base` and `ModernBERT-large` classifiers against a TF-IDF cascade on the gold set, and release all annotations, model checkpoints, and evaluation code.

papers.title: Indistinguishable Agents: Training Agent Privacy as Twin-World Indistinguishability
papers.abstract: LLM agents search, shop and send messages for their users, and every action is seen by some party. Existing privacy training rewards agents for not mentioning protected items, yet an observer can infer a private fact from what the agent does. Since an observer learns a fact only if its view changes with the fact, we propose \methodfull (\method), which trains on twin worlds that differ only in the private fact. A frozen distinguisher scores each observer's view by its log-likelihood ratio for the true world, and paired GRPO trains the agent on task success minus this ratio. We prove that this objective controls the Bayes success of every observer on every channel. On shopping and messaging tasks \method removes the leakage that disclosure judges and query-level rewards miss, while the agent still completes its tasks.
papers.summary: LLM agents that shop, search, and send messages can leak private facts through what they do, even when they never mention those facts. Existing privacy training only penalizes explicit mentions. The authors train agents on pairs of "twin worlds" that differ only in the private fact. A frozen distinguisher model scores how much each observer's view reveals which world is real, and paired `GRPO` (a reinforcement learning method) rewards task success minus that score. They **prove the objective bounds how well any observer on any channel can infer the private fact**. On shopping and messaging tasks, the method removes leakage that disclosure judges and query-level rewards miss, while the agent still completes its tasks.

papers.title: M-JEPA: Predictive Self-Supervised Learning for Molecular Graphs with Scaffold-Shift Evaluation on Tox21
papers.abstract: Self-supervised molecular representation learning is increasingly used to improve transfer on small, label-limited property prediction tasks, yet commonly used contrastive objectives can be sensitive to view construction and are often evaluated with protocols that report only discrimination. We adapt Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) to molecular graphs by masking chemically coherent connected subgraphs and training a context encoder to regress the masked target embedding produced by an exponential-moving-average (EMA) teacher. To evaluate predictive self-supervision under realistic distribution shift, we introduce a leakage-resistant, compute-matched three-phase protocol: (i) an 80-run objective screening on ESOL with fixed compute budgets, (ii) JEPA-only refinement of masking and augmentation choices, and (iii) per-assay Tox21 evaluation under Bemis-Murcko scaffold splits with joint discrimination-reliability analysis and attribution diagnostics. Under matched compute, M-JEPA achieves substantially lower ESOL proxy RMSE than a compute-matched InfoNCE baseline (mean RMSE 2.12 vs 3.75; mean paired dRMSE 1.61; 95% bootstrap CI [1.52, 1.72]; Wilcoxon p=2.4e-4) and typically completes runs faster (~15-25 min vs ~35-45 min on a single GPU under identical hardware), albeit with higher runtime variance. On Tox21, improvements in ROC-AUC/PR-AUC are assay-dependent and do not uniformly imply better calibration; reliability diagrams and Brier/ECE metrics reveal endpoints where fine-tuning improves ranking but leaves probabilities miscalibrated.
papers.summary: `M-JEPA` adapts Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) to molecular graphs for self-supervised learning. It masks chemically coherent subgraphs and trains a context encoder to predict the masked region's embedding, as produced by an exponential-moving-average (EMA) teacher network. The authors also introduce a three-phase evaluation protocol designed to prevent leakage and match compute across methods, ending with per-assay `Tox21` tests on scaffold splits that measure both ranking and calibration. With matched compute, **`M-JEPA` reaches a mean RMSE of 2.12 on `ESOL` versus 3.75 for an `InfoNCE` contrastive baseline**, and usually finishes runs faster. On `Tox21` the gains depend on the assay, and better ranking does not always come with well-calibrated probabilities.

papers.title: World Models, Trees and Foundation Models for Retail Forecasting: Evidence from Four Public Data Sets
papers.abstract: A retailer makes different decisions at different grains of the product, store and time hierarchy: store orders for an item in a store, supplier funding for an item across stores, category performance by store, and the financial plan for the chain. Which forecasting model to use depends on the grain. This paper compares models at each grain on four public data sets (M5, six Dominick's categories, Breakfast at the Frat, and Corporaci\'on Favorita, the last kept out of all development), over rolling forecast origins with paired tests and model confidence sets. It covers price and promotion through the plan inputs these data record, not product, assortment or place. The models are a world model that carries each item's state forward under the price and promotion plan, the same network without that state, LightGBM, the Temporal Fusion Transformer, TimesFM, Chronos-Bolt, Timestral, seasonal naive, and an equal-weight average of the world model, LightGBM and TimesFM given the plan. The answer changed with the grain. For an item by store and an item across stores, the average had the lowest error on seven and eight of nine data sets, and the 90% confidence set held a median of 1 and 2 models. For a category by store, a category and the chain total, the lowest-error model differed between data sets and a median of 4 of nine models were not separated by the four to six windows available. For category-by-store planning cost, the average or LightGBM was lowest on seven of eight data sets, and the world model was lowest only on M5; it was behind LightGBM item by store on six of eight. Every trained model used the plan, and on the weekly promotion-driven data pretrained models were less accurate without it. These results hold for these data sets; a forecast solved across all four Ps, or a retailer's own data, may give different results. Every model, test and change that lost is reported.
papers.summary: Retailers make forecasts at different levels of the product, store, and time hierarchy, and the authors test which model works best at each level on four public datasets: `M5`, `Dominick's`, `Breakfast at the Frat`, and `Corporación Favorita`. They compare a price-and-promotion-aware world model, `LightGBM`, `Temporal Fusion Transformer`, the pretrained models `TimesFM`, `Chronos-Bolt`, and `Timestral`, a seasonal naive baseline, and an equal-weight ensemble. At the item-by-store and item-across-stores levels, **a simple average of the world model, `LightGBM`, and `TimesFM` had the lowest error on most datasets**. At category and chain levels, no model was consistently best and most could not be statistically separated. The world model rarely beat `LightGBM`, and pretrained models were less accurate when they were not given the promotion plan.

papers.title: An Information-Geometric Framework for OCS-Reconfigurable Interconnect Topology in Large-Scale AI Clusters
papers.abstract: Optical Circuit Switches (OCS) make inter-pod wiring in AI clusters programmable, posing design questions on wiring choice, symmetry departure, and reconfigurations. We present a unified information-geometric framework to address these issues.A wiring is a point in a probability simplex over circuits within a degree polytope. Departure from a symmetric Fat-Tree prior $\mathbf{q}$ is measured by $\DKL(\cdot \,\|\, \mathbf{q})$. The cost $U$ is the smoothed DAG critical-path length, whose gradient equals path marginals of a Gibbs distribution via forward--backward recursion.For free energy $F_{\beta_1} = U + \beta_1^{-1} \DKL(\cdot \,\|\, \mathbf{q})$, we prove well-posedness, monotonic dependence on $\beta_1$, adaptation bounds via Jeffreys divergence, and a symmetry principle for static optimality. An entropic proximal-gradient method updates multiplicatively with a $|V|$-dim dual KL projection, achieving linear convergence.For time-varying traffic, a threshold policy yields regret $O(\sqrt{\Gamma C V_1 T})$ against the switching-free optimum. Traffic changes are detected by a multinomial GLR--CUSUM detector with non-asymptotic false-alarm bounds. Multi-job generalized-mean fairness aligns with $\alpha$-fairness ($\alpha \ge 2$). Experiments on pipeline, data, and MoE workloads validate the framework against integer programming.
papers.summary: Optical Circuit Switches (OCS) make the wiring between pods in AI clusters programmable, which raises the question of how to choose and reconfigure that wiring. The authors model a wiring as a probability distribution over circuits. They optimize a free energy that trades off the smoothed critical-path length of the training job's dependency graph against KL divergence from a symmetric `Fat-Tree` layout. They prove the problem is well-posed, give an entropic proximal-gradient method with **linear convergence**, and derive a threshold reconfiguration policy with sublinear regret when traffic changes over time. A change detector with false-alarm guarantees and a multi-job fairness criterion complete the framework, which they validate against integer programming on pipeline-parallel, data-parallel, and mixture-of-experts (MoE) workloads.

papers.title: Memory, Know Your PLACE: Governing Lifecycle State and Query-Time Eligibility in Persistent-Memory Agents
papers.abstract: Persistent memory turns prior interactions into durable agent state, but existing systems provide limited control over whether that state remains valid and whether it should influence a later query. We argue that reliable memory requires governance over both state formation and query-time influence. We introduce PLACE, a factorized governance layer that adds write-side state certification and read-side authorization to a memory backend. A factorial evaluation on Mem0 with Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-7B isolates the contribution of each mechanism. Results show that write-side governance substantially improves lifecycle state correctness, while read-side governance eliminates measured causal leakage from ineligible memory in the state-correct setting. Their combination achieves the strongest joint performance while preserving query-relevant support. These findings show that reliable persistent memory requires explicit control over both maintained state and query-time information influence.
papers.summary: Persistent memory gives agents state that lasts across interactions, but current systems give little control over whether a stored memory is still valid or whether it should affect a later query. `PLACE` adds a governance layer to a memory backend. On the write side it certifies stored state; on the read side it authorizes which memories may influence each query. A factorial evaluation on `Mem0` with `Qwen2.5-3B` and `Qwen2.5-7B` shows that write-side governance substantially improves state correctness. Read-side governance **eliminates measured leakage from ineligible memories** once stored state is correct, and combining the two gives the best overall results without removing memories relevant to the query.

papers.title: Dialogue Generation for Conversational Recommendation Using User Search Interactions and Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Large-scale conversational recommendation datasets typically require manual dialogue construction or annotation. We propose SearCl, which automatically generates conversational recommendation dialogues grounded in user search and click behaviors. SearCl segments user interactions into query sessions and derives each recommendation target from content selected after a search query. A configurable probabilistic state machine controls the dialogue flow, while two LLM agents acting as the seeker and recommender generate utterances according to turn-level constraints. To support recommendation, the recommender is provided with knowledge graphs constructed from metadata about the content items used in each dialogue, capturing their attributes and relationships. Using SearCl, we generate 3,538 dialogues from content search and click interaction data, covering 1,731 unique target items. Under an LLM-as-a-judge protocol, the resulting dialogues achieve higher quality scores than dialogues from existing benchmarks. These results demonstrate that SearCl enables controllable and knowledge-grounded dataset construction without human annotations.
papers.summary: Building conversational recommendation datasets usually requires writing or annotating dialogues by hand. `SearCl` generates them automatically from real user search and click logs. It splits interactions into query sessions and uses the item clicked after each query as the recommendation target. A configurable probabilistic state machine controls the dialogue flow, while two LLM agents play the seeker and the recommender, with the recommender drawing on a knowledge graph built from item metadata. The authors generate 3,538 dialogues covering 1,731 target items, and **an LLM judge rates them above dialogues from existing benchmarks**.

papers.title: Concept Representations in Vector Space: Toward an Interdisciplinary Study of Meaning Variation
papers.abstract: An increasing number of disciplines recognize the explanatory potential of meaning-bearing mental structures through which individuals interpret the world and guide their behavior. Concept representations constitute a core class of these structures, emerging from individuals' experiences with concept referents and encoding and organizing their understanding of them. Recognizing a private level of meaning, where concepts are not objectively defined by rules in the world but constitute subjective structures in individuals' minds, raises a fundamental question: do different individuals actually mean the same thing when they invoke the same concept? As latent structures, concept representations are difficult to access and model empirically. The present study introduces a measurement framework that makes such representations empirically accessible through textual traces elicited under standardized conditions. Using transformer-based sentence embeddings, the framework maps standardized responses elicited for concepts into a high-dimensional shared vector space, opening concept representations to the systematic analysis of interindividual variation. It develops three analytical avenues: (1) comparing representational sharedness across concepts, (2) identifying variables that correlate with representational variation, and (3) examining how focal actors or subpopulations deviate from a reference population. Each avenue is illustrated through an empirical proof-of-concept drawing on a large-scale free-association dataset. Together, the demonstrations show how researchers from across disciplines can move from a research question and data source to analysis and interpretation. An accompanying GitHub repository provides a ready-to-use implementation of the framework for existing and custom datasets.
papers.summary: Researchers in several disciplines are interested in whether different people mean the same thing when they use the same concept, but these mental representations are hard to measure. The authors propose a framework that embeds people's standardized text responses to concepts into a shared vector space using transformer sentence embeddings, so variation between individuals can be measured directly. They develop three analyses: comparing how widely shared each concept's representation is, finding variables that correlate with representational differences, and measuring how specific individuals or subgroups deviate from a reference population. Each is demonstrated on a large free-association dataset, and the framework is released as a ready-to-use implementation on GitHub.

papers.title: Reranking Answers of Large Language Models with Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract: Answering natural language questions over knowledge graph data is challenging due to the vast number of facts, which can be difficult to process and navigate. One potential solution for this issue is to use mined subgraphs related to the query, although this process still requires extracting these subgraphs. This research presents a solution for extracting subgraphs related to entity candidates from a question-and-answer set, which can be obtained by inferring a large language model by calculating the shortest paths between entities. The proposed approaches detail various features that can be extracted from the subgraphs and reranking models to select the most probable answers from a list of candidates. Experiments were conducted on Wikidata to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed approaches. This involved enumerating all the main feature types that can be extracted from mined subgraphs and a detailed analysis of the proposed features and reranking method combinations. In addition, a public web application that provides a useful web tool for studying the graph space between question and answer entities has been developed to work with subgraphs. This includes visualization of the extracted subgraph and automatic generation of natural language text to describe it.
papers.summary: To improve LLM answers to questions over knowledge graphs, the authors have an LLM propose candidate answers and then extract a `Wikidata` subgraph linking the question's entities to each candidate via shortest paths. They catalog the main types of features that can be computed from these subgraphs and evaluate many combinations of features and reranking models for picking the most likely answer. They also release a public web tool that visualizes the subgraph between question and answer entities and **automatically generates a natural-language description** of it.

papers.title: Sampling and Curvature in First-Exit Comparisons for Momentum SGD
papers.abstract: First-exit prediction for momentum SGD depends on sampling information that pointwise gradient laws omit. Strongly convex finite pools with identical pointwise laws and matched iid momentum dynamics can have different reshuffled exits; even analytic pools with uniformly close pointwise laws can have separated exit probabilities. For persistent sampling in one dimension, we establish an explicit $O(h)$ mean-exit comparison with a finite-rate switching process under nonvanishing component velocities and step-size conditions; iid sampling instead averages to an ODE. Retaining realized minibatches and sampled curvature yields finite-window exit brackets beyond this regime. In 32 trained ridge-logistic runs, 29 meet prespecified targets with rounding-certified brackets; an enclosure control explains most of the width advantage. Exact-real certificates establish finite means at the original tested radii for three ResNet-18 checkpoints and give local finite-mean conditions for tanh and ViT networks; their upper bounds remain loose, and original-radius ViT mean guarantees remain unresolved despite 128 fresh continuation paths. A two-network replication gives 32/32 successful seeds in each of four finite-path persistence comparisons. Independent equal-length controls retain slower exits after refresh resets than without resets, but the refresh-versus-random ordering reverses with update length at both networks. These interventions do not causally decompose raw momentum SGD. Neural step-size scaling does not validate the switching limit.
papers.summary: Predicting when momentum SGD leaves a region around a minimum (its "first exit") depends on how training examples are sampled, not just on the distribution of individual gradients. The authors show that data pools with identical gradient distributions can have different exit behavior under reshuffled sampling. For persistent sampling in one dimension, they prove an O(h) comparison between mean exit times and a finite-rate switching process, while iid sampling averages out to an ODE. By tracking the actual minibatches and sampled curvature, they compute certified bounds on exit time: **29 of 32 ridge-logistic runs meet their targets**, and checks on `ResNet-18`, tanh, and `ViT` networks give partial guarantees. The authors note these results do not causally explain raw momentum SGD and do not validate the switching limit for neural networks.

papers.title: Acharya 2.0: An AI Tutor for Self-Learning Subjects in Hindi
papers.abstract: Text processing is crucial for low-resource languages as it enables the development of tools and technologies that bridge the digital divide and provide equitable access to information and services. By empowering low-resource languages with robust text processing, we can preserve linguistic diversity, enhance education, improve communi- cation, and foster inclusivity in a rapidly digitizing world. Due to the lack of sufficient annotated datasets and lin- guistic resources, it is challenging to develop accurate and reliable language technologies for these low-resource languages. Large Language Models (LLMs) have attracted sig- nificant attention with their performance and the value they produce. However, with the ever-evolving language, adapting LLMs for a specific task is time-consuming and resource-intensive. Thus, Retrieval-Augmented Genera- tion (RAG) has overcome this limitation by augmenting LLMs with external knowledge, thereby improving their efficiency and extensive task-specific adaptation. Most applications of the RAG technique have been limited to English and has seen limited application in In- dic languages. This paper introduces the RAG-powered AI-Tutor application, Acharya 2.0, designed to produce academic assistance to Hindi-speaking students. The client-server-based web application integrates many fea- tures to support students in accessing and interacting with educational content.
papers.summary: `Acharya 2.0` is a web-based AI tutor for Hindi-speaking students. It uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), which supplies an LLM with relevant passages retrieved from a document collection, to answer questions about educational content. The authors motivate the work by the lack of annotated data and language tools for low-resource Indic languages and note that RAG has mostly been applied in English. They describe the client-server application and its features for accessing and interacting with study material.

papers.title: Shallow Probes Are Sufficient for Near-Oracle Personalization Depth Allocation in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Rather than proposing a new federated optimizer, we study whether a small client-specific measurement budget can support cost-aware personalization-depth decisions under a utility that trades Macro-F1 against deployment cost. Exhaustive evaluation of six depths defines an offline oracle that is not deployable. We audit the Probe Sufficiency Hypothesis: three shallow probes (P0--P2) may contain most decision-relevant information for approaching that oracle. FedPBA is a secondary learned instantiation for deep-action extrapolation. On CIFAR-10/100 and patient-disjoint PTB-XL (45 sessions; 900 clients; 2700 evaluations; GroupKFold), training-free greedy probing achieves regret 0.0071 and 98.3 percent oracle recovery, beating metadata-only policies and FedPBA (0.0110 / 97.3 percent). Aggregate shallow-best versus oracle correlation is 0.9818 but falls to 0.578 on deep-oracle rows; PTB-XL deep-oracle cases remain a high-regret boundary without a validated escalation gate.
papers.summary: In personalized federated learning, each client must decide how many layers to personalize, balancing Macro-F1 against deployment cost. Finding the best choice exhaustively is too expensive to deploy. The authors test whether three cheap, shallow probes give enough information to make nearly optimal choices. On `CIFAR-10/100` and patient-disjoint `PTB-XL`, a training-free greedy probing strategy **recovers 98.3% of the best achievable utility**, beating policies that use only metadata as well as a learned variant, `FedPBA`. The probes work less well when the best choice is a deep personalization depth, and those cases on `PTB-XL` remain a weak spot.

papers.title: ChronoChart: Setup-Agnostic Channel Charting for Label-Free Indoor Localization
papers.abstract: Accurate radio-based indoor localization remains challenging in multipath-rich and dynamic indoor environments. Supervised fingerprinting methods achieve high positioning accuracy by learning mappings from radio channel measurements to physical locations, but require costly position labels and frequent recalibration. Channel Charting (CC) addresses this limitation by learning low-dimensional representations of Channel State Information (CSI) without position labels, yielding channel charts in which nearby points correspond to nearby physical locations. However, prominent CC methods rely on setup-specific dissimilarity metrics, such as ADP-, CIRA-, or PDR-based distances, and on precomputed $O(n^2)$ distance matrices, limiting scalability and transferability across radio systems. We propose ChronoChart, a timestamp-supervised CC framework that requires only CSI and timestamps without prior knowledge for training. Our method jointly optimizes complementary objectives: a triplet loss using temporally derived positive and negative samples to establish coarse global structure, a temporal-proximity loss that promotes smooth trajectories in the chart, and a joint-embedding loss that enforces consistency between representations of different augmentations. Evaluated on real-world 5G, MIMO, and passive UWB data, our method matches or exceeds prior CC baselines that depend on tailored distance metrics, and remains scalable and applicable across heterogeneous radio systems.
papers.summary: Channel Charting (CC) learns maps of radio Channel State Information (CSI) without position labels, so that nearby points on the map correspond to nearby physical locations, which is useful for indoor localization. Existing CC methods depend on distance metrics designed for a specific radio setup and on O(n^2) distance matrices, which limits scalability and transfer to other systems. `ChronoChart` instead uses only CSI and timestamps. It combines a triplet loss built from samples that are close or far apart in time, a temporal-proximity loss that keeps trajectories smooth, and a consistency loss across data augmentations. On real 5G, MIMO, and passive UWB data, it **matches or exceeds CC baselines that rely on tailored distance metrics**.

papers.title: RAIL-5G: A Challenging Real-World Dataset and Benchmark for AI-Based 5G Indoor Localization
papers.abstract: Reliable radio-based indoor localization is essential for industrial automation, yet existing methods are often evaluated in environments that do not fully reflect the severe multipath and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions encountered in real deployments. This limits our understanding of how AI, i.e., modern geometric, unsupervised, and semi-supervised localization methods generalize to industrial 5G settings. We present RAIL-5G, a public real-world 5G NR channel impulse response (CIR) benchmark recorded in an operational railway maintenance facility. RAIL-5G covers an 811m$^2$ indoor area with eight distributed radio units, robot-mounted user equipment (UE) trajectories, high-accuracy iGPS reference positions, and severe metal-induced multipath caused by train compartments and maintenance infrastructure. We benchmark geometric time-difference of arrival (TDoA), supervised fingerprinting, unsupervised channel charting, and self-supervised wireless pretraining methods. Our results highlight the difficulty of RAIL-5G: on the full dataset, TDoA reaches 7.02m mean average error (MAE), the best unsupervised method reaches 2.46m, and supervised fingerprinting achieves 0.52m. Self-supervised pretraining reduces the labeling effort by up to one order of magnitude, but the remaining gap to supervised learning shows that robust AI-based localization under severe multipath remains an open challenge. The dataset and code are available at https://iis.fraunhofer.de/rail-5g.
papers.summary: `RAIL-5G` is a public dataset of real 5G radio channel measurements recorded in an operational railway maintenance facility. Metal train compartments and equipment there cause severe multipath and non-line-of-sight conditions. It covers 811 m² with eight radio units, trajectories from a robot-mounted receiver, and high-accuracy reference positions. The authors benchmark geometric time-difference-of-arrival (TDoA), supervised fingerprinting, unsupervised channel charting, and self-supervised pretraining. TDoA reaches 7.02 m mean error, the best unsupervised method 2.46 m, and **supervised fingerprinting 0.52 m**. Self-supervised pretraining cuts the number of labels needed by up to ten times, but a gap to fully supervised accuracy remains.

papers.title: ViCoR: Estimating Visual Necessity via Counterfactual Residuals for Multimodal Medical Data Selection
papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models often exhibit hidden stratification, where high overall performance masks failures on subtle visual findings and overlapping clinical conditions. We trace this failure mode to modality imbalance during fine-tuning, where strong linguistic priors can suppress visually grounded learning and induce plausible but weakly grounded rationales. Existing data selection methods usually score image-text pairs as holistic units, without separating visually necessary samples from shortcut-solvable ones. To address this problem, we propose ViCoR, a counterfactual-residual-based data selection method for Med-VLM fine-tuning. ViCoR estimates visual necessity through image-dependent optimization residuals, calibrates the resulting scores with medical supervision compatibility, and constructs a diversity-aware fine-tuning subset. Across two backbones, four external generalization benchmarks, and one multi-disease robustness benchmark, ViCoR-selected 20\% subsets achieve the strongest average performance compared with full-data fine-tuning and selection baselines. Gradient-level analysis and perturbation audits further show that ViCoR enriches image-dependent training signals and strengthens image-level and evidence-region dependence. The code will be available at https://github.com/htgan-ai/ViCoR.
papers.summary: Medical vision-language models can score well overall while failing on subtle visual findings, which the authors attribute to strong language priors crowding out visual learning during fine-tuning. `ViCoR` selects fine-tuning data by estimating how much each image-text pair truly needs the image. It does this by comparing optimization residuals with and without the image, adjusting for fit with the medical supervision signal, and enforcing diversity in the chosen subset. Across two model backbones and five benchmarks, **`ViCoR`-selected 20% subsets outperform full-data fine-tuning** and other selection methods. Gradient analysis and perturbation tests show that models trained this way rely more on the image and on the relevant image regions.

papers.title: A Thousand Faces: A Persuasion Benchmark with Experience-Grounded Persuadees Informed by Psychology and Pragmatics
papers.abstract: People can express the same beliefs and desires yet need different reasons to change their minds. What makes an argument relevant depends on how those views arose: experiences shape what a person finds credible, what matters to them, and what could prompt reconsideration. These personal grounds may also be expressed indirectly, through contextual clues in conversation. Benchmarks that specify beliefs and desires without these connections can reward arguments that match a description while overlooking whether they address the person's reasons. We introduce A Thousand Faces (ATF-Persu), with 1,000 personas across 200 topics and nine domains. Drawing on personality and attitude theories and conversational implicature, we construct five personas per factual context, linking experiences to judgments, expression, and grounds for revision. Evaluations show lower persuasion success than three comparison benchmarks under their respective protocols. Complete backgrounds yield broader use of supplied personal grounds and higher persona faithfulness than simplified specifications; blinded reviewers also rate ATF-Persu above CToMPersu on identifiable personal reasons, their influence on responses, and contextual expression. The dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Slandes/ATF-Persu.
papers.summary: Persuasion benchmarks usually describe a target's beliefs and desires but not the life experiences behind them, so an argument can match the description without addressing the person's actual reasons. `ATF-Persu` contains 1,000 personas across 200 topics. Drawing on personality and attitude theories and on conversational implicature (meaning conveyed indirectly), each persona links experiences to judgments, ways of expressing them, and conditions under which they would reconsider. **Persuasion success is lower than on three comparison benchmarks**, and full persona backgrounds lead to wider use of the supplied personal grounds and more faithful persona behavior than simplified descriptions. Blinded reviewers also rated it above `CToMPersu` for identifiable personal reasons and contextual expression.

papers.title: BrandEval: A Two-Track Multi-Agent Benchmark for Risk-Sensitive LLM Crisis Communication
papers.abstract: Evaluating LLMs for crisis communication requires more than judging isolated responses, because public feedback and competitor actions can reshape trust over time. Existing benchmarks remain largely static and single-turn, offering limited evidence about long-horizon risk-sensitive communication. We introduce \textbf{BrandEval}, a two-track benchmark for product-crisis communication, focusing on public brand responses to product-related safety, quality, service, and trust incidents. BrandEval-Static evaluates stakeholder-aware strategic analysis, while BrandEval-Dynamic stress-tests response policies in \textbf{BrandPolis}, a controlled multi-agent sandbox with consumer feedback, competitor responses, and trust-risk trajectories. We also construct \textbf{BrandSRD}, a Chinese crisis-response dataset, and instantiate a reference Strategic Agent using \textbf{Strategic Rationale (SR)}. Across proprietary and open-source models, we find that static strategic quality is informative but incomplete: it aligns with some end-state outcomes but does not reliably predict volatility and delayed recovery; dynamic stress tests further expose tail-risk failures under manipulative or weakly grounded policies. The code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/htgan-ai/BrandEval.
papers.summary: Most benchmarks for LLM crisis communication judge single responses in isolation. They miss how public reaction and competitor moves change trust over time. `BrandEval` covers product-crisis communication in two tracks. `BrandEval-Static` scores stakeholder-aware strategic analysis, and `BrandEval-Dynamic` stress-tests response policies in `BrandPolis`, a multi-agent sandbox that simulates consumer feedback, competitor responses, and trust-risk trajectories. The authors also release `BrandSRD`, a Chinese crisis-response dataset, and a reference agent built on `Strategic Rationale (SR)`. Across proprietary and open models, **static strategic quality matches some end-state outcomes but does not reliably predict volatility or delayed recovery**, and the dynamic tests expose tail-risk failures under manipulative or weakly grounded policies.

papers.title: NeuroAct: Advancing EEG Analysis and Decoding via Dual-Loop Autonomous Research
papers.abstract: EEG analysis and decoding underpin brain-computer interfaces, cognitive assessment, and sleep monitoring. Fixed pipelines and reward-driven search do not explicitly determine how signal structure, representations, predictor behavior, and training dynamics contribute to performance or generalization gaps, leaving intervention choice underdetermined. We introduce NeuroAct, an autonomous research agent framework for EEG analysis and decoding. NeuroAct implements dual-loop autonomous research across EEG foundation models, task-specific predictors, and model combinations. In an inner loop, research, development, and review roles use evidence on signal structure, representations, predictor behavior, and training dynamics to test hypotheses, select analyses or interventions, and refine candidates using performance, stability, and cost feedback. An outer loop distills outcomes into conditional, testable recommendations with task and model conditions, then validates and revises them on subsequent tasks.We evaluate four settings: (A) EEG General Analysis, (B) Cross-task Model Optimization, (C) Single-task Open Research, and (D) Collaborative Prediction. In Setting A, NeuroAct's 80.88 macro-average exceeds BrainAgent's 63.13 by 17.75 points. In Setting B, NeuroAct raises EEGPT's mean balanced accuracy (BA) by 7.34 points and HBN Pearson's (r) from 0.6894 to 0.7362; in Setting C, it improves ADFTD BA by 16.33 points; and in Setting D, it raises Workload BA from 79.69% to 85.02%. Experience reuse raises BCIC-IV-2a BA from 34.66% to 50.81% while reducing LLM tokens by 64.02%, indicating recommendations improve cross-task performance. NeuroAct enables evidence-guided EEG research improved by cross-task experience.
papers.summary: `NeuroAct` is an autonomous research-agent framework for analyzing and decoding EEG (electroencephalography) signals. It works across EEG foundation models, task-specific predictors, and combinations of models. In an inner loop, research, development, and review roles test hypotheses using evidence about signal structure, representations, predictor behavior, and training dynamics. An outer loop distills the outcomes into conditional recommendations that it validates and revises on later tasks. `NeuroAct` reaches an 80.88 macro-average on general EEG analysis against 63.13 for `BrainAgent`, and it improves `EEGPT` and several decoding tasks. Reusing past experience raises `BCIC-IV-2a` balanced accuracy from 34.66% to 50.81% **while cutting LLM token use by 64%**.

papers.title: Calibration-Free Early Stopping for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via E-processes
