papers.abstract: Reasoning large language models (LLMs) benefit from test-time scaling, motivating adaptive policies that spend tokens when they help and stop early otherwise. Existing rules halt when a confidence or stability signal crosses a threshold, but such thresholds rarely transfer across models and datasets, and validation-calibrated rules lose their guarantee under shifts in test-time horizon or signal dynamics. We reframe adaptive stopping as sequential evidence accumulation along the reasoning trajectory rather than threshold calibration on held-out data. Our framework runs two e-processes on a shared per-chunk signal: a commit stream tracks the signal's position relative to its slow trend, and an abstain stream tracks its signed velocity, making the two anti-correlated by construction. Under signal-level nulls on the per-chunk increments, Ville's inequality yields an anytime-valid signal-level false-alarm bound at user-specified significance levels, with no held-out calibration. Across various model--dataset combinations, the framework matches or exceeds calibration-based stopping on the token--accuracy Pareto front using zero calibration data, and the same significance level transfers unchanged across cells where calibration becomes infeasible.
papers.summary: Reasoning LLMs often keep generating tokens after extra thinking stops helping. Existing early-stopping rules rely on confidence thresholds that rarely transfer across models and datasets. The authors instead treat stopping as sequential evidence accumulation. Two anti-correlated e-processes run on a shared per-chunk signal: a commit stream tracks the signal's position against its slow trend, and an abstain stream tracks its signed velocity. Ville's inequality then gives an anytime-valid false-alarm bound at a user-chosen significance level. The method **matches or beats calibration-based stopping on the token–accuracy Pareto front using zero calibration data**, and the same significance level transfers unchanged across model–dataset pairs.

papers.title: LiftDiff: Guided Discrete Diffusion for Quantum Code Construction
papers.abstract: The realization of fault-tolerant quantum computation relies on Quantum Error-Correcting Codes (QECC). Of particular interest are codes that combine a high encoding rate with sufficient distance. Existing algebraic constructions, such as lifted product (LP) codes, build a large quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) code from a classical base matrix. In this work we introduce LiftDiff, a generative approach to the discovery of QECC. A discrete denoising diffusion model is trained to generate base matrices over the group algebra $\mathbb{F}_2[\mathbb{Z}_\ell]$, which are then expanded into LP codes. The reverse diffusion process is guided by an energy function that evaluates quantum code properties, including girth, degree, sparsity and decoding performance, steering the sampler toward matrices that yield LP codes with favorable parameters. Our method discovers codes with parameters such as $[[169,13,11]]$, $[[143,15,9]]$, and $[[260,24,10]]$, including a $[[247,19,14]]$ code that achieves the highest ${kd^2}/{n}$ among the baselines. Moreover, several discovered codes outperform the Gross code across a broad range of the tested physical error rates under both code-capacity and circuit-level noise.
papers.summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing needs quantum error-correcting codes that combine a high encoding rate with large distance. `LiftDiff` trains a discrete denoising diffusion model to generate base matrices over a group algebra, which are then expanded into lifted product (LP) quantum low-density parity-check codes. Sampling is guided by an energy function that scores code properties such as girth, degree, sparsity, and decoding performance. The method finds codes including **a [[247,19,14]] code with the highest kd²/n among the baselines**, and several of the discovered codes outperform the `Gross code` across a broad range of physical error rates under both code-capacity and circuit-level noise.

papers.title: Hidden Cartographer: Hidden State Guided Data Selection for Dual Budgeted Instruction Tuning
papers.abstract: Given the high cost of expert annotation and limited fine-tuning resources, effective data selection from large unlabeled pools under strict budgets has become a crucial step in adapting LLMs to specialized domains. Existing label-dependent methods risk distorted selection when using pseudo-labels, while traditional active learning methods do not explicitly characterize instruction-tuning dynamics. To address these limitations, we propose Hidden Cartographer (HC), a two-stage framework that uses hidden states to guide annotation and exact training dynamics to select the final training subset. The first stage is Progressive Candidate Expansion, which utilizes the proxy to iteratively select top unlabeled candidates for expert annotation, merging them to recompute training dynamics and update the proxy until the annotation budget is exhausted; the second stage is Exact Cartography Pruning, which ranks these annotated candidates by their exact dynamics scores to isolate a compact subset under the final training budget. Experiments across the medical, legal, and financial domains demonstrate that HC achieves the highest average accuracy among all budgeted baselines, requiring annotation for only 20--30% of the original pool and fine-tuning on just 10--15%.
papers.summary: Adapting LLMs to specialized domains is constrained by two budgets: how much expert annotation is affordable and how much fine-tuning compute is available. `Hidden Cartographer` uses hidden states as a proxy in two stages. In the first stage, it iteratively picks unlabeled candidates for expert annotation and updates the proxy with recomputed training dynamics until the annotation budget runs out. In the second stage, it ranks the annotated examples by exact training-dynamics scores to choose a compact final training set. Across medical, legal, and financial domains, it achieves the highest average accuracy among budgeted baselines **while annotating only 20–30% of the pool and fine-tuning on 10–15%**.

papers.title: DROD: Dual-Ratio Ordered Dropout for Federated Continual Learning on Heterogeneous Devices
papers.abstract: Federated learning for capacity-heterogeneous clients and federated continual learning are each well studied on their own, but their intersection -- clients holding differently sized models while every client's data stream also drifts over time -- remains underexplored. We study this setting directly, training a ResNet-18 fleet from scratch on Split-CIFAR-100 (10 tasks, class-incremental), and introduce DROD (Dual-Ratio Ordered Dropout), which builds on FjORD's Ordered Dropout by using two independent reduction axes to extract sub-models: a shortcut ratio and a branch ratio. On a shared parameter/FLOP budget ladder, DROD achieves the highest mean accuracy among the heterogeneous-model federated learning strategies we compare. Its advantage over the two strongest baseline geometries persists across every replay-buffer size we test and under ER, DER++, and BiC; under EWC, all three geometries collapse alike.
papers.summary: The authors study federated continual learning in which clients run models of different sizes and every client's data stream drifts over time. They train a `ResNet-18` fleet from scratch on class-incremental `Split-CIFAR-100`. `DROD` (Dual-Ratio Ordered Dropout) extends `FjORD`'s ordered dropout by extracting sub-models along two independent axes, a shortcut ratio and a branch ratio. On a shared parameter and FLOP budget ladder, **`DROD` achieves the highest mean accuracy among the heterogeneous-model strategies compared**, and its advantage holds across every replay-buffer size tested and under `ER`, `DER++`, and `BiC`. Under `EWC`, all three model geometries collapse alike.

papers.title: Assessing the Empirical Evidence for Loss of Control from Agentic General-Purpose AI
papers.abstract: Theoretical literature warns that advanced generalist agentic systems might pursue instrumental goals that are misaligned with human preferences, thus posing risks of irreversible loss of human control. The EU's Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI lists loss of control as a systemic risk that must be assessed, yet no structured assessment of the quality of the empirical evidence for this risk exists. This study fills that gap. We evaluate 19 recent empirical studies across eight properties identified from threat models (such as strategic deception, situational awareness, and autonomous replication), assessing the quality of evidence across three dimensions: construct validity, content validity, and external validity. Our central finding is that the current body of evidence supports a judgment of loss of control as "weakly plausible." In our framework, 'plausibility' denotes the strength and direction of available evidence, not a probability estimate. Emerging evidence exists across multiple properties. No study clears the validity thresholds for a stronger judgment that a property is present; a single study clears them only for a negative-direction judgment (against situational awareness). Validity gaps, particularly in external validity, are widespread. Therefore, our findings highlight the need for more rigorous evaluations of agentic general-purpose AI systems. However, for the most dangerous properties, high external validity may be structurally unachievable under responsible research practices, reflecting a ceiling on feasible evidence rather than absence of the capability. Furthermore, as AI capabilities advance rapidly, empirical assessments may systematically lag behind the capability frontier. Our framework provides a structured baseline for ongoing monitoring as capabilities advance.
papers.summary: The EU's Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI treats loss of human control as a systemic risk, but no one had systematically assessed the quality of the empirical evidence for it. The authors review 19 recent empirical studies across eight threat-model properties, including strategic deception, situational awareness, and autonomous replication. They grade each study's construct, content, and external validity. They conclude that **the current evidence supports loss of control only as "weakly plausible"**: no study clears the validity thresholds for a stronger judgment, and external-validity gaps are widespread. They also argue that for the most dangerous properties, high external validity may be structurally unachievable under responsible research practices.

papers.title: Estimating Causal Bounds from Observational Data With Neural Generative Models
papers.abstract: Identifying causal bounds from discrete observational data is a fundamental problem in causal inference. While exact analytical bounds exist for certain graphs, this is not generally the case. In this paper, we introduce a framework for estimating such bounds using neural generative models together with a new extrapolation procedure to estimate these bounds more accurately. Across multiple causal inference settings, it produces bounds that are consistently closer to the true bounds than those obtained with existing general neural approaches. We validate the framework on a range of benchmark problems for which exact bounds are available.
papers.summary: When causal effects cannot be identified exactly from discrete observational data, analysts can still bound them, but exact analytical bounds exist only for certain causal graphs. The authors propose a framework that estimates these bounds with neural generative models and adds a new extrapolation procedure to tighten the estimates. On benchmark problems where the exact bounds are known, **the framework's bounds are consistently closer to the true bounds** than those from existing general neural approaches.

papers.title: Improving the Expressive Power of Hybrid Sequence Models via Multi-Hop Retrieval
papers.abstract: Hybrid architectures offer a promising approach to efficient language modeling by combining a small number of full-attention layers with a larger number of efficient sequence layers, such as sparse attention and recurrent layers. While full-attention layers maintain a KV cache that grows linearly with sequence length, efficient layers typically rely on separate, fixed-size states rather than accessing this richer existing memory. Recent work has begun exploring ways to allow efficient layers access to the KV cache, but the theoretical benefits of such access, and the extent to which existing approaches can realize them remain poorly understood. We investigate these questions by analyzing the expressive power of individual hybrid blocks on function composition, a well-studied task in sequence-model expressivity associated with multi-hop reasoning. We first establish that both conventional hybrid blocks and those with top-$\kappa$ KV-cache access require $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ capacity to compute even two-function composition over a domain of size $n$. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the \emph{Multi-hop Retrieval Attention} (MuRA) hybrid block, a simple architecture that enables multi-hop retrieval from a shared KV cache while preserving asymptotic computational and memory efficiency. We prove that a single fixed size $m$-hop MuRA block can compute $m$-function composition, whereas computing $(m+1)$-function composition with the same retrieval depth requires polynomial model size, establishing a strict expressivity hierarchy in retrieval depth. Synthetic experiments support this hierarchy, showing that increasing retrieval depth enables learning progressively deeper compositions, substantially outperforming existing hybrid architectures. Together, our results identify multi-hop retrieval as a promising mechanism for improving the expressive power of efficient hybrid architectures.
papers.summary: Hybrid language models pair a few full-attention layers with many efficient layers, such as sparse attention or recurrent layers, which usually keep their own fixed-size states instead of reading the shared KV cache. The authors analyze expressivity on function composition, a proxy for multi-hop reasoning. They prove that conventional hybrid blocks, including those with top-κ KV-cache access, need Ω(√n) capacity to compose even two functions. They introduce `Multi-hop Retrieval Attention` (`MuRA`), which performs multi-hop retrieval from the shared KV cache while keeping asymptotic compute and memory efficiency. They prove that **a fixed-size m-hop `MuRA` block computes m-function composition, while m+1 functions require polynomial model size**, and synthetic experiments match this hierarchy.

papers.title: Persistent Representational Misalignment Induces Vision-Language Model Failures
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) fail at some tasks that are simple for humans---but why? We hypothesize that many such failures stem from VLMs' difficulties translating between vision and language representations, a misalignment the Platonic Representation Hypothesis predicts should disappear with scale. This paper is composed of two parts: in the first, we show that existing vision and language representations are linearly unalignable. This misalignment is an inherent property of the data and hence expected to persist regardless of either scale or the alignment's complexity. In the second, we demonstrate how this misalignment both leads to a predictably induced generalization failure and correlates with existing failure modes, where more representationally aligned VLM backbones accordingly exhibit fewer failures. Overall, these results imply representations will not become aligned simply given sufficient scale, providing evidence against a strong version of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) fail at some tasks that are easy for humans. The authors trace many of these failures to difficulty translating between vision and language representations. They show that existing vision and language representations are **linearly unalignable, a property of the data that should persist regardless of scale**, contrary to a strong version of the `Platonic Representation Hypothesis`. They then show that this misalignment predictably induces a generalization failure and correlates with known failure modes, with better-aligned VLM backbones failing less often.

papers.title: BatchParScale: Sparse Batch-Mixing for Sequence Models
papers.abstract: Recent test-time scaling methods improve model performance by increasing inference-time compute. One practical form of this is parallel scaling, where a model samples multiple independent reasoning streams and aggregates their answers using methods like voting, reranking, or verification. While effective, this approach leaves the streams uncoordinated, and a discovery made in one rollout cannot influence any other. Multi-Sequence Verifiers jointly score candidate answers after generation, but the reasoning streams remain independent during inference. ParScale takes a step toward model-internal parallel scaling by learning to aggregate multiple forward passes, but its streams still do not exchange information while processing a sequence. We introduce BatchParScale, an attention mechanism that allows parallel streams to exchange information through a small set of communication positions. We evaluate BatchParScale on a new Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval benchmark and in pretraining, fine-tuning, and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Across these settings, BatchParScale outperforms ParScale on language-model loss and remains competitive on coordination-sensitive MARL tasks. Masked pretraining runs beat an unmasked single-sequence baseline despite local sequence corruption, and LoRA fine-tuning shows the mechanism can be added to a pretrained Transformer. At the same time, fact retrieval performance for pretrained and finetuned BatchParScale models remains unclear.
authors: Hans Peter Lyngs{\o}e Raaschou-jensen (University of Copenhagen)
M. Onurcan Kaya (Technical University of Denmark)
papers.summary: In parallel test-time scaling, multiple reasoning streams run independently, so a discovery made in one rollout cannot help the others. `BatchParScale` is an attention mechanism that lets parallel streams exchange information through a small set of shared communication positions. The authors evaluate it on a new `Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack` benchmark and in pretraining, `LoRA` fine-tuning, and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. It **outperforms `ParScale` on language-model loss** and remains competitive on coordination-sensitive tasks. Fact retrieval by pretrained and fine-tuned models remains unclear.

papers.title: Emergent Sparsity: How Many Effective Variables Survive Coarse-Graining in AlphaEarth Embeddings?
papers.abstract: AlphaEarth encodes each 10 m land pixel as a 64-component vector intended to support diverse global mapping tasks. Yet many scientific applications work at coarser spatial supports, for which fewer than 64 effective variables may suffice. We ask whether these vectors can be reorganized into ranked global nonlinear coordinates, how many suffice at a chosen reconstruction accuracy, and whether that number decreases with spatial scale. We thus describe effective dimension as a two-control surface over tolerance and spatial scale, rather than one intrinsic number. At each scale, a $\beta$-VAE scan with a common architecture produces a rank--distortion envelope, giving the smallest retained count achieved within the scanned family at each reconstruction tolerance. At 3% validation tolerance, this number falls from 24 to 7 when the scale is increased from 10 m to 78.9 km, whereas the corresponding PCA rank falls only from 46 to 38. Repeating the analysis on unit-norm targets preserves this trend.
papers.summary: `AlphaEarth` encodes each 10 m land pixel as a 64-component embedding, but many scientific applications work at much coarser spatial scales. The authors use a `β-VAE` scan to measure how many nonlinear coordinates are needed to reach a given reconstruction tolerance at each spatial scale. They treat effective dimension as a surface over tolerance and scale rather than a single intrinsic number. At 3% validation tolerance, **the retained count drops from 24 to 7 as scale grows from 10 m to 78.9 km**, while the corresponding `PCA` rank falls only from 46 to 38.

papers.title: EasyResearch: Honest Regression, Forecasting and Signal Classification for Researchers Who Do Not Program
papers.abstract: EasyClassifier showed that researchers who do not program can obtain honest classification results when the correct evaluation is the default. Most applied studies, however, predict a number, forecast a series or classify recordings, and each task has its own way of producing scores that do not hold on new data. We present EasyResearch, open-source analysis cores for regression, time-series forecasting and signal classification, and EasyResearch Desktop, a Windows application that runs these three tasks and EasyClassifier's classification without code. All four follow the same rules: everything learned from data is learned on training data only, models keep their published defaults with fixed seeds, the selected model receives a separate final score, forecasts are never evaluated on shuffled data, and every run writes a report with a Methods paragraph and the references for every method used. We measured whether the reported scores are honest by keeping part of each dataset untouched. In regression (9 public datasets, 90 runs), the common practice overstated R^2 by +2.2 points and the best comparison score by +2.5, while EasyResearch's final score was -1.0; screening predictors on all rows before cross-validation, which EasyResearch does not offer, reported R^2 = 0.27 on pure noise against -0.44 on new data. In forecasting (15 series), shuffled cross-validation over windows of past values promised errors 19% smaller than its chosen models achieved in the untouched future, while EasyResearch's final-period score was unbiased to within 1.5%; the models EasyResearch chose had 14% lower future error, and on random walks shuffled cross-validation chose a machine-learning model in 5 of 5 series, each worse in the future than repeating the last value, which EasyResearch chose 4 times. In signal classification (4 UCR datasets) one method won every comparison and neither estimate was biased.
papers.summary: `EasyResearch` provides open-source analysis tools and a no-code Windows app for regression, time-series forecasting, and signal classification, aimed at researchers who do not program. Correct evaluation is the default: everything learned from data is learned on training data only, forecasts are never evaluated on shuffled data, and each run writes a report with a Methods paragraph and references. On held-out data, common regression practice overstated R² by about 2 points, and screening predictors on all rows reported R² = 0.27 on pure noise against −0.44 on new data. In forecasting, **shuffled cross-validation promised errors 19% smaller than its chosen models achieved**, while `EasyResearch`'s final-period score was unbiased to within 1.5%.

papers.title: Federated Learning for Malware Image Classification under Data Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Malware image classification (MIC), in which binary files are converted into visual representations and deep neural networks are trained to identify malware families, has recently emerged as an effective approach for malware detection. Federated learning (FL) enables malware image classifiers to be trained collaboratively by multiple clients without sharing raw data. However, a fundamental challenge in FL is data heterogeneity (non-IID), which is particularly relevant but understudied in the malware context. In this paper, we address this gap via three contributions. First, we present an empirical study of federated MIC under varying degrees of data heterogeneity across three popular malware image datasets (MalImg, Virus-MNIST, and MalNet). We show that while FL achieves strong accuracy under IID conditions, both accuracy and training stability degrade as data becomes increasingly non-IID. Second, we introduce a set of round-level statistics that characterize the data contributed by participating clients in each FL round, and demonstrate that class entropy (diversity of class labels present in a given round) exhibits strong positive correlation with global model accuracy. Third, leveraging this insight, we propose an entropy-aware client selection strategy that filters candidate client subsets based on class entropy, and show that our strategy outperforms standard random selection. Our results highlight the role of client composition in federated MIC and underscore the importance of distribution-aware classifier training under data heterogeneity.
papers.summary: Malware image classification converts binaries into images and trains neural networks to identify malware families. The authors study it under federated learning (FL), where clients train collaboratively without sharing data, and focus on non-IID data across clients. On `MalImg`, `Virus-MNIST`, and `MalNet`, accuracy and training stability degrade as client data becomes more non-IID. The authors find that **the class entropy of the data in each training round correlates strongly with global model accuracy**. They use this insight to propose an entropy-aware client selection strategy that outperforms random selection.

papers.title: SPARC: Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus
papers.abstract: Speech anonymization has focused on the acoustic signal, leaving open how much speaker information the transcribed words themselves retain. In this work, we study pairwise speaker and demographic-attribute verification from transcribed speech. We introduce SPARC (Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus), a benchmark built from two podcast corpora comprising over 12,500 speakers, 1.5M quality-filtered utterances, and speaker-level inferred or source-provided labels for sex, age, and accent, and evaluate five attribution models and three LLMs on identity- and attribute-verification trials with episode- and metadata-based topic proxies. LLM adversaries distinguish same-speaker pairs from text alone. Attribute-label agreement is harder to verify, but LLMs perform sex- and accent-label verification above chance. Finally, releasing only short probe texts (50 words) degrades the strongest adversaries the most, offering a partial reduction in observed linkage.
papers.summary: Speech anonymization usually targets the acoustic signal and ignores how much speaker information the transcribed words still carry. `SPARC` (Spoken Profile Authorship Recognition Corpus) is a benchmark built from two podcast corpora, with over 12,500 speakers, 1.5M utterances, and labels for sex, age, and accent. It evaluates five attribution models and three LLMs on identity- and attribute-verification trials. **LLM adversaries can tell same-speaker transcript pairs apart from text alone**, and they verify sex and accent labels above chance. Releasing only short 50-word probe texts partially reduces this linkage.

papers.title: EG-GRPO: Evidence-Guided Step-level Credit Assignment for Deep Search Agents
papers.abstract: LLM-based search agents demonstrate strong capabilities in long-horizon information seeking and reasoning, typically trained via reinforcement learning. However, existing approaches predominantly rely on trajectory-level outcome rewards, providing limited supervision for complex search and reasoning processes. Although step-level credit assignment offers a promising solution, obtaining reliable and task-grounded supervision for open-ended search remains challenging. In this paper, we propose Evidence-Guided Group Relative Policy Optimization (EG-GRPO), a framework that derives step-level supervision from the evidence annotations available in synthetic deep search data. EG-GRPO identifies the first supporting citation for each required evidence claim and uses the newly acquired evidence to construct step-level process rewards. By representing the accumulated evidence as an evolving knowledge state, EG-GRPO further performs state-conditioned relative advantage estimation and combines the resulting step-level signal with the standard trajectory-level outcome advantage. Experiments on five challenging deep search benchmarks show that EG-GRPO generally outperforms standard GRPO and existing reward-enhanced and step-level RL baselines across different model scales. These results demonstrate that task-grounded evidence annotations can provide effective process supervision for credit assignment in deep search RL.
papers.summary: LLM search agents are usually trained with reinforcement learning on trajectory-level outcome rewards, which give little guidance for long multi-step searches. `EG-GRPO` (Evidence-Guided Group Relative Policy Optimization) derives step-level process rewards from the evidence annotations in synthetic deep-search data: it identifies the step where each required piece of evidence is first cited. It represents the accumulated evidence as an evolving knowledge state, estimates state-conditioned relative advantages, and combines them with the standard outcome advantage. On five deep-search benchmarks, **`EG-GRPO` generally outperforms standard `GRPO` and existing reward-enhanced and step-level RL baselines** across model scales.

papers.title: Bridging Concepts: Multi-Agent Reasoning over Scientific Concept Graphs for High-Impact Research Prediction
papers.abstract: Within a research community, new topics often emerge when previously unconnected concepts are first studied together. We construct scientific concept graphs (SCGs)--domain knowledge graphs whose nodes are fine-grained research concepts extracted from paper text by LLMs and whose edges capture their co-occurrence in papers--and study the task of forecasting high-impact concept pairs, i.e., discovering concept pairs that are currently unconnected but will have high impact when connected. To this end, we introduce new benchmark datasets constructed from CIKM, KDD, and SIGIR conference papers, with varied prediction settings, including impact forecasting for emerging concepts unseen during training. We propose MiroGraph, a Multi-agent reasoning framework with scientific concept Graphs, in which a feature designer agent designs predictive features for a given concept pair from structural, semantic, and trend perspectives, and then three LLM agents compute the actual feature values from the enclosing subgraph of the concept pair. Using these feature values, a classifier designer agent constructs a classifier that predicts the final impact labels. MiroGraph outperforms various impact forecasting and temporal link prediction methods.
papers.summary: The authors forecast which currently unconnected pairs of research concepts will have high impact once studied together. They build scientific concept graphs from LLM-extracted concepts and their co-occurrence in papers, and release benchmarks drawn from `CIKM`, `KDD`, and `SIGIR` papers, including settings with emerging concepts unseen during training. `MiroGraph` is a multi-agent framework: one LLM agent designs structural, semantic, and trend features, three agents compute the feature values from the subgraph around each concept pair, and a final agent builds the classifier. **`MiroGraph` outperforms existing impact-forecasting and temporal link-prediction methods.**

papers.title: Data-driven forecasting of tropical cloud forest phenology: A dynamical systems and machine learning hybrid approach
papers.abstract:
Forecasting how species and ecosystems respond to climate change is a critical challenge in ecology, particularly in hyper-diverse tropical biomes. While traditional phenological models often rely on preconceived functional forms, this study introduces a data-driven hybrid approach that integrates dynamical systems theory with machine learning to forecast flowering and fruiting cycles.
  Using a robust 35-year dataset from a Venezuelan tropical cloud forest, we reconstruct the system's state-space using delay vectors inspired by Takens' theorem, incorporating climate forcing variables such as temperature and precipitation. The model was trained using Gaussian Process Regression, providing both point predictors and explicit uncertainty estimates.
  Our results clearly suggest that the synergy between dynamical systems and machine learning effectively captures the non-linear complexities of ecological time series. Specifically, the model achieved higher predictive accuracy for flowering and fruiting. This hybrid framework offers a scalable tool for anticipating phenological mismatches and informing conservation strategies in the face of global environmental change.
papers.summary: The authors forecast flowering and fruiting cycles in a Venezuelan tropical cloud forest using a 35-year dataset. They reconstruct the system's state space with delay vectors based on Takens' theorem, include temperature and precipitation as climate forcing, and train `Gaussian Process Regression` models that provide both point forecasts and uncertainty estimates. The authors report that **the hybrid of dynamical systems theory and machine learning achieved higher predictive accuracy for flowering and fruiting**, and they propose it as a tool for anticipating phenological mismatches under climate change.

papers.title: A discrete-continuous-time stochastic framework for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder-related symptom modeling and pharmacological intervention via methylphenidate
papers.abstract: This paper presents an original mathematical and computational framework for modeling the efficacy of methylphenidate as an optimal control policy acting on the nonlinear dynamics of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Neural processes in ADHD are conceptualized as stochastic processes with trajectories that inherently converge towards stable, yet dysfunctional patterns associated with clinical symptoms. The pharmacological intervention is mathematically formalized as an external control signal that reassesses the system's drift and redirects these trajectories towards neurotypical regimes. To bridge these theoretical stochastic models with empirical clinical data, latent representations are inferred using a novel deterministic hybrid deep learning architecture, combining a one-dimensional convolutional neural network and a Vision Transformer, trained on preprocessed functional magnetic resonance imaging data.
papers.summary: The authors model attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) as stochastic neural dynamics whose trajectories converge toward stable but dysfunctional patterns. They formalize methylphenidate as an optimal control signal that changes the system's drift and steers trajectories toward neurotypical regimes. To connect the theory to clinical data, they infer latent representations from functional MRI with **a hybrid deep learning architecture that combines a 1D convolutional network and a `Vision Transformer`**.

papers.title: Vision as Proprioception: Estimating Humanoid Robot Pose from Video
papers.abstract: Estimating a humanoid robot's internal state from video has a wide range of real-world applications but remains unexplored. During interactions with a robot, its onboard state information may be unavailable due to privacy, ownership, or communication constraints. Meanwhile, online and AI-generated robot videos provide rich sources of data but typically lack corresponding joint configurations, limiting their direct use in robot learning. To address these issues, we present HumanoidPose, a new framework that treats vision as proprioception to recover full-body joint configurations in world space from video alone. Specifically, we combine pretrained human-pose features with robot kinematics in a unified model that predicts each embodiment's joint configurations. We retarget human motions to sixteen different humanoid embodiments, enabling scalable learning entirely from synthetic data. To improve real-world generalization, we further leverage unlabeled online videos through self-training to develop a 2D robot-pose detector. In our evaluation, HumanoidPose improves joint-angle and joint-position accuracy over the evaluated baselines and reduces joint-angle error by 18-32% relative to the best-performing baseline on each of the three real humanoid platforms. We further show improved global localization and generalization to unseen embodiments. HumanoidPose enables visual understanding of other robots during interaction and extraction of robot motion from online and generated videos.
papers.summary: A humanoid robot's internal joint state is often unavailable to outside observers, and online or AI-generated robot videos lack joint labels. `HumanoidPose` recovers full-body joint configurations in world coordinates from video alone. It combines pretrained human-pose features with robot kinematics, trains on synthetic data from human motions retargeted to sixteen humanoid embodiments, and self-trains a 2D robot-pose detector on unlabeled online videos. On three real humanoid platforms, it **reduces joint-angle error by 18–32% relative to the best baseline**, and it improves global localization and generalizes to unseen embodiments.

papers.title: The Explainability Illusion: Must ViTs Exhibit Patch-Decoding Interpretability?
papers.abstract: Transformers are widely assumed to exhibit token-decoding explainability. In particular, in vision transformer (ViT) classifiers, decoding individual patch tokens has become a common diagnostic tool due to its tendency to yield human-interpretable outputs. In light of the increasing popularity of this approach, an important question is whether token-decoding explainability is an inherent property of transformers that should be expected to hold across architectures, scales, and training objectives, or merely an artifact of some implicit bias. In this paper we systematically study token-decoding explainability across diverse ViT settings, spanning architectures, scales, and training objectives, using both controlled experiments and real-world models. We find that while some models indeed exhibit aligned and interpretable token decodings, others exhibit either inverted explainability maps or a complete lack of correlation with the image semantics. As we show, these tendencies toward different explainability behaviors are not intrinsic to the architecture and can vary arbitrarily with changes in the optimization landscape. We provide theoretical support for these observations by demonstrating a setting where a single fixed toy transformer architecture can provably implement the optimal classification rule in multiple ways, which differ in their patch-decoding explainability patterns. Our results show that token-decoding explainability is not an inherent property of trained transformers, but rather an outcome contingent on the problem setting and thus should not be a-priori assumed to hold. Code can be found in https://ronensc.github.io/Explainability-Illusion/ .
papers.summary: Decoding individual patch tokens in vision transformer (ViT) classifiers is a popular way to diagnose them, because it often gives human-interpretable maps. The authors test whether this kind of interpretability is an inherent property of transformers by running controlled experiments and examining real-world models across many architectures, scales, and training objectives. Some models give aligned, interpretable decodings, while others give inverted maps or maps with no relation to the image content, and which behavior appears can change arbitrarily with the optimization landscape. A toy-model proof shows that a single fixed transformer architecture can implement the optimal classifier in several ways with different patch-decoding patterns, supporting the conclusion that **token-decoding explainability is not inherent to trained transformers and should not be assumed in advance**.

papers.title: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds
papers.abstract: Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control. Yet their latent worlds naturally lack a human-interpretable interface. In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction. To this end, we envision a four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding. Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored. Overall, this Perspective aims to call for a broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds.
papers.summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (`JEPA`s) are evolving from representation learners into latent world models used for prediction, planning, and control, but their latent states have no human-interpretable interface. This perspective argues that interpretability research should move beyond asking what latents encode and study how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive predictions. It proposes a four-stage agenda of **Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act**, and notes that existing JEPA interpretability work only addresses the first stage. Systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remain largely unexplored.
papers.highlight_summary:
JEPA-style latent world models predict and plan in an abstract representation space that humans can't read directly. This position paper argues that interpreting them means going past what latents encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction, and it proposes a four-stage `Ground–Structure–Verify–Act` agenda for that shift.

- The framework treats a JEPA as an encoder plus a predictor: **Ground** maps latent subspaces to world variables such as position, velocity, or contact; **Structure** recovers how those variables relate and evolve over time, including under actions; **Verify** tests whether the predictor actually depends on them by intervening on the latents and checking the prediction; and **Act** uses the verified mechanisms to steer, edit, or retrain the model and measurably improve it.
- The central claim is that **decodability is not understanding**: a probe that recovers velocity from a latent state doesn't show that the predictor uses velocity rather than a correlated shortcut such as background texture.
- When the authors place existing work in this framework (`V-JEPA 2` probing, `AIM`, `WorldModelLens`, and steering of non-JEPA World Action Models), they find that direct JEPA evidence sits **almost entirely at the Ground stage**; Structure, Verify, and Act remain largely unexplored.
- They argue that latent-world analysis could tell apart failures in state representation, dynamics, interaction, and multi-step rollout, separate real world structure from shortcuts, and flag predictions that shouldn't be trusted before a planner acts on them.
- As a perspective piece, it reports no experiments or quantitative results, and it names open problems itself: human-defined concepts may not match the model's internal ontology, and latent interventions can change entangled factors or produce implausible states. The authors call for controlled testbeds and shared infrastructure.

papers.title: Aligning Language Models with Indigenous Community Cosmovision through Constitutional AI
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are predominantly trained on corpora that reflect Western, anglophone worldviews. This asymmetry is not neutral: when a model answers questions about territory, community authority, or the relationship with nature, it does so from assumptions that may be alien to the communities using the system. This paper presents a system for aligning language models with the ethical principles of Indigenous communities in Latin America. Drawing on interviews with five Indigenous leaders and defenders, we built an operational cultural constitution grounded in an Indigenous cosmovision, with 12 principles. On this basis, we implemented a Constitutional AI (CAI) pipeline in two phases: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimization (DPO). The base models were Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. With only 24 preference pairs, improvements were modest but detectable in intergenerational transmission, linguistic caution, and consultation and consent. Qualitative analysis reveals that the SFT phase was responsible for the primary shift in alignment, while DPO refined specific categories. The system was deployed in a conversational interface with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that allows communities to feed the knowledge base, turning alignment into a participatory cycle. We argue the architecture is functional and will scale qualitatively once the corpus is expanded and computing constraints are resolved. The work constitutes a first iteration of an epistemic justice mechanism for value alignment in the Global South.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are trained mostly on Western, English-language corpora, so they can bring foreign assumptions to questions about territory, community authority, and nature. The authors interviewed five Indigenous leaders in Latin America to write a 12-principle cultural constitution. They then used it in a Constitutional AI (CAI) pipeline with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimization (DPO) on `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct` and `Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct`. With **only 24 preference pairs**, the gains were modest but detectable in areas such as linguistic caution and consultation and consent, and most of the shift came from the SFT phase. The system is deployed in a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) chat interface where communities can add to the knowledge base themselves.

papers.title: Learning When to Abort in Transformer Planning: A Mechanistic Study
papers.abstract: Planning does not by itself imply the ability to recognise errors, but recognising errors can improve planning capacity. In this paper, we study this phenomenon in Transformer planning. To analyze the inner mechanism, we follow the approach of Wang et al. (2024) and abstract planning as path-finding in graphs. In this setting, we train the model to detect the error of invalid transitions, i.e., after the model generates a next node that is not adjacent with the current node, the model should then generate a special abort token x. For expressiveness, we construct a Transformer with feed-forward width $O(|V|)$ for any fixed graph with node set $V$. It can detect all possible invalid transitions, and select a valid next node if the prefix is valid. We then propose a worst-case lower bound on feed-forward width, which makes the detector's linear width near-optimal up to logarithmic factors. In trained models, we demonstrate that invalid-transition detection increases previous-node attention, and most of the valid--invalid separation locates in the feed-forward network's output. This accords with our theoretical insights. Finally, we use this error detection to improve the model's performance: at inference, generating the abort token x will directly cause an external procedure to discard the attempt and restart from the original prompt. Experiments show that error detection combined with retry improves model's planning reliability on graphs, Countdown, and mazes.
papers.summary: The work studies whether transformers can learn to recognize their own planning errors, using path-finding in graphs as the setting. A model is trained to emit a special abort token when it generates a move to a node that is not adjacent to the current one. The authors construct a transformer with feed-forward width linear in the number of nodes that detects every invalid transition, and prove a lower bound showing this width is near-optimal up to logarithmic factors. In trained models, error detection increases attention to the previous node, and most of the valid-versus-invalid separation sits in the feed-forward output. At inference, **restarting the attempt whenever the abort token appears improves planning reliability** on graphs, `Countdown`, and mazes.

papers.title: Shared-Private Cross-Modal Discrepancy Learning for Imbalanced Multi-Source Audio-Visual Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: Audio-visual deepfake detectors are often trained under a single dataset or manipulation regime, but multi-source training collections may contain heterogeneous attacks and uneven source distributions. Training separate detectors for each source is inefficient, while a single shared detector may be biased toward dominant source-specific patterns. We study known-source imbalanced multi-source audio-visual deepfake detection using FakeAVCeleb and LAV-DF, where source identity is supplied during training and inference. To address this setting, we build on the Multi-Scale Cross-Modal Transformer Encoder (MSCT) and propose Pre-MSCT Shared-Private Feature Fusion. Our method routes \texttt{[CLS]}-augmented audio and visual tokens into a shared stream and source-specific private streams before the first MSCT block, while retaining its internal multi-scale self-attention (MSSA), differential cross-modal attention (DCA), and feed-forward operations. The shared stream models cross-source reusable evidence, while the private streams retain source-dependent residual variations. A domain-aware gated residual fusion module injects selected private evidence into the shared representation for the main fused prediction. Experiments under two controlled source-composition protocols show improved macro and worst-source AUC compared with the MRDF and MSCT baselines. These results support shared-private cross-modal discrepancy learning in the evaluated two-source setting with known source identity.
papers.summary: Audio-visual deepfake detectors trained on mixed collections of attack sources can become biased toward whichever source dominates the data. The authors study this imbalanced multi-source setting on `FakeAVCeleb` and `LAV-DF`, with source identity known at training and inference time. Their method extends the Multi-Scale Cross-Modal Transformer Encoder (`MSCT`): audio and visual tokens are routed into a shared stream and source-specific private streams, and a domain-aware gated residual module injects selected private evidence into the shared representation. Under two controlled source-composition protocols, it **improves macro and worst-source AUC over the `MRDF` and `MSCT` baselines**.

papers.title: Atoms, Not Knowledge: What Production-Scale Addressed-Memory Writes Deposit
papers.abstract: Deterministic hash-addressed conditional memory permits local post-hoc knowledge injection. Extending arXiv:2610.21553's bounded-feasibility audit rejecting under-specified generality claims with repaired probes and training-dose/capacity axes, we give, to our knowledge, the first production-scale write-content verdict. We test 124M-7B self-trained/publicly pretrained beds, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 (176.95B; 320,001,536 FP8 rows), and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Write coverage requires a sufficiently trained backbone prior, full-width readout, trainable gates; undertrained-bed intervention confirms a threshold, not a slope. At fixed budget, coverage falls from 98% (50 facts) to 12.7% (1,000); table size is not binding. Two-hop composition does not exceed the independent single-hop baseline (26% observed vs 25% expected; 15% lexical-distortion floor). Synergy remains absent across dose/load in two independent bed families. A 28-percentage-point in-context gap (given vs recalled intermediates) localizes failure to retrieval-for-reasoning, not gate access. Writes are independently retrievable, precisely addressable, reversible atoms, not composable into reasoning. A layered protocol, the first, to our knowledge, to cover compositionality in behavioral memory evaluation, separates baseline, synergy and distortion floor. Any addressed/key-value memory must report coverage, synergy ratio and distortion rate before deployment claims. Composition must be system-orchestrated; multi-constraint queries should explicitly chain written atoms. In-context controls show given intermediate entities are exploited at twice the implicit rate. Production load fits exponential interference ($R^2=0.98$); its mechanism, between budget dilution and write interference, remains open. All numbers are recomputed from archived raw logs/JSON; a fresh 52-target production rerun gives 52/52, exactly matching archived baselines.
papers.summary: Hash-addressed conditional memory lets facts be written into a language model after training. The authors audit what such writes actually store, testing models from 124M to 7B parameters as well as production-scale models such as `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8` and `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash`. Writes only work with a sufficiently trained backbone, full-width readout, and trainable gates, and at a fixed budget, coverage falls from 98% with 50 facts to 12.7% with 1,000. Two-hop composition does no better than chance combination of single hops (26% observed versus 25% expected), so **written facts are retrievable, addressable, and reversible atoms but do not compose into reasoning**. The authors propose an evaluation protocol that reports coverage, synergy ratio, and distortion rate.

papers.title: AdaFedXplain: Adaptive Federated Learning with Explainable AI for Ransomware Detection
papers.abstract: Attacks using ransomware have developed into complex multiphase campaigns that target vital infrastructure, resulting in annual damages of billions of dollars. Conventional detection techniques are ineffective against zero-day variations, and privacy issues are raised by centralized machine learning algorithms. Federated learning allows for cooperative model training without data sharing, however current FL approaches suffer from explainability issues, high communication cost, and non-IID data heterogeneity. In this study, we present AdaFedXplain, an explainable AI-based adaptive federated learning system for ransomware detection. Our approach includes progressive XGBoost complexity to avoid overfitting, a decaying learning rate schedule for stable convergence, and dynamic client grading based on ransomware prevalence and data sufficiency. Using 62,485 real-world ransomware samples from four OS-based non-IID clients, we compare AdaFedXplain against FedAvg, FedProx, and SCAFFOLD. According to experimental data, AdaFedXplain outperforms all baselines with 99.59% detection accuracy and 99.64% F1-score while cutting energy usage by 75%, latency by 65%, and communication overhead by 75%. The ablation investigation demonstrates that every element enhances performance. Security analysts can use SHAP explainability to identify important PE header characteristics that influence detection decisions. Our system provides a collaborative ransomware detection solution that is efficient and interpretable, while reducing privacy risks through federated learnings data-local training paradigm.
papers.summary: Ransomware detection has to cope with zero-day variants and with privacy concerns about centralizing training data, while existing federated learning (FL) methods struggle with explainability, communication cost, and non-IID (unevenly distributed) client data. `AdaFedXplain` combines progressively more complex `XGBoost` models, a decaying learning-rate schedule, and dynamic client weighting based on ransomware prevalence and data sufficiency. It uses `SHAP` to show analysts which PE header features drive each decision. On 62,485 real ransomware samples split across four operating-system-based clients, it reports **99.59% accuracy and a 75% reduction in communication overhead** compared with `FedAvg`, `FedProx`, and `SCAFFOLD`.

papers.title: Where and Why Search-Augmented LLMs Fail When Reasoning over Rapidly Evolving Knowledge
papers.abstract: As the world changes, new information is published while older records remain online. This complicates reasoning for large language models (LLMs), which must retrieve evidence and resolve conflicts to determine which information remains valid. Existing evaluations treat information seeking as a black box, revealing little about where and why LLMs fail. To address this gap, we introduce TREK, a suite of three components: TREKTRACE is a plug-and-play framework that attributes failures to specific stages of retrieval and reasoning. We apply it to TREKBENCH-WILD, a meta-benchmark of real-world questions that require complex reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge. Surprisingly, the main bottleneck is post-retrieval reasoning rather than retrieval: frontier models are often misled by conflicting evidence even after retrieving all the information needed to answer. To study this bottleneck, we build TREKBENCH-CTRL, a controlled benchmark with distractors spanning temporality, relevance, and trustworthiness, and show that benchmarks dominated by outdated distractors substantially underestimate task difficulty. Together, TREK provides a testbed for diagnosing and improving reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge.
papers.summary: Search-augmented LLMs have to reason over web evidence in which outdated and current information coexist, and existing evaluations treat the whole process as a black box. `TREK` addresses this with `TREKTRACE`, a framework that attributes failures to specific retrieval and reasoning stages, and two benchmarks: `TREKBENCH-WILD`, built from real-world questions, and `TREKBENCH-CTRL`, a controlled benchmark with distractors that vary in timeliness, relevance, and trustworthiness. The main bottleneck turns out to be **post-retrieval reasoning rather than retrieval**: frontier models are often misled by conflicting evidence even after retrieving everything needed to answer. The controlled benchmark also shows that benchmarks dominated by outdated distractors substantially underestimate task difficulty.

papers.title: Where Groups Split: A Probe Prior for Nonzero Within-Group Variance in RL Post-Training
papers.abstract: Group relative policy optimization learns from a prompt only when the rewards in the sampled group disagree. With a binary verifier, a group that is entirely correct or entirely incorrect has within-group variance zero and a zero advantage. Uniform sampling continues to spend rollouts on prompts that are unanimous now and stay unanimous as training goes on. Pass rate is a weak forecast of that future. Two prompts at the same pass rate can move apart: one into the range where a finite group splits, and one toward a ceiling where the group becomes unanimous again. Aperture estimates the later pass rate from a short probe. A small subset of the pool is trained with the same recipe, every prompt is scored on the base model and on the probe model, and the two pass rates are plugged into the probability that a group of the training size is all wrong or split. The resulting weight is a static prior. It can be used alone or multiplied by an online scheduler, and the GRPO update is left as it is. On mathematical and logical reasoning with 1.7B and 4B models, the prior improves greedy accuracy over uniform GRPO and raises the fraction of groups with a nonzero advantage. The same prior still helps when it is combined with dynamic sampling or with selective rollouts.
papers.summary: Group relative policy optimization (`GRPO`) learns nothing from a prompt when every sampled response is correct or every one is wrong, yet uniform sampling keeps spending rollouts on such prompts. The current pass rate is a poor predictor of which prompts will produce mixed groups later in training. `Aperture` trains a short probe on a small subset of the prompt pool with the same recipe and compares each prompt's pass rate under the base and probe models. It uses the two rates to estimate how likely a training-sized group is to split, and turns that into a static sampling prior that leaves the GRPO update unchanged. On math and logic reasoning with 1.7B and 4B models, it **improves greedy accuracy over uniform GRPO and increases the share of groups with a nonzero advantage**, and it still helps when combined with dynamic sampling or selective rollouts.

papers.title: Follow the Mixed Groups: Ridge-Tracking Gaussian Sampling for Zero-Variance Web Rollouts
papers.abstract: Group relative policy optimization learns from a question only when the sampled responses disagree. A group that is entirely correct or entirely incorrect has zero reward variance and a zero advantage. On the Web, that group has already spent its searches and page fetches. Gaussian curricula aim the next batch at pass rates where a finite group can still mix. A Gaussian on the latest empirical rate treats every all-fail history as the same point, and a center stepped by the average signed change of those rates is pushed by prompts already stuck at 0 or 1. RIDGE keeps the Gaussian curriculum and changes the coordinate, the center, and the width. Each prompt carries a Beta posterior. The sampling weight is the marginal of a Gaussian target under a Gaussian approximation of that posterior, divided by a prediction of tool-call cost. The center and the width are an exponential smooth of the posterior means of groups that just came back mixed. All-correct and all-incorrect groups refresh the posterior and do not move the center. The GRPO update itself is unchanged. On two math backbones and a retrieval-augmented question answerer, RIDGE raises average accuracy by 3.4 and 2.9 points over GRPO and average exact match by 3.7 points, at 29.6\% fewer math rollouts and 32.7\% fewer tool calls than dynamic sampling.
papers.summary: In `GRPO` training of web agents, groups whose responses are all correct or all wrong produce no learning signal, even though they have already used up searches and page fetches. `RIDGE` keeps a Gaussian sampling curriculum but tracks a Beta posterior for each prompt and divides each sampling weight by the predicted tool-call cost. It updates the curriculum's center and width only from groups that just came back mixed, so prompts stuck at 0% or 100% no longer drag the curriculum. Across two math backbones and a retrieval-augmented question answerer, it raises accuracy by 3.4 and 2.9 points and exact match by 3.7 points over GRPO, while using **32.7% fewer tool calls** and 29.6% fewer math rollouts than dynamic sampling.

papers.title: A Distribution-Free Separation Between Learned and Fixed Features
papers.abstract:
The success of neural networks is largely attributed to their ability to learn useful representations from training data. However, known results that prove a computational advantage of learned features over fixed ones are restricted to specific input distributions. We settle the COLT open question of Feldman, Kamath, and Srebro (2026) by showing that this advantage can persist in the distribution-free setting.
  We construct a family of hypothesis classes that can be efficiently learned by a natural gradient-based algorithm on a two-layer ReLU network, but cannot be represented by linear predictors over any fixed feature map with polynomial dimension (and runtime). Specifically, for any sufficiently small error and any sufficiently large runtime budget R (depending on the error), there exists a hypothesis class that the neural network learns under any input distribution to the desired expected classification error in time at most R, while the dimension complexity (governing the dimension needed by linear predictors) is superpolynomial in R.
papers.summary: Earlier proofs that learned neural-network features have a computational advantage over fixed features hold only for specific input distributions. This work resolves an open question from COLT posed by Feldman, Kamath, and Srebro by **proving that the advantage persists in the distribution-free setting**. The authors construct hypothesis classes that a natural gradient-based algorithm on a two-layer ReLU network learns efficiently under any input distribution. Linear predictors over any fixed feature map, by contrast, would need dimension superpolynomial in the network's runtime budget.

papers.title: Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention
papers.abstract: Multi-head attention is a central component of the transformer architecture, yet how its expressivity depends on the number of heads remains poorly understood. We study a one-layer, attention-only transformer with additive positional embeddings and define the head complexity $H^\ast(f)$ of a Boolean function $f$ as the minimum number of attention heads required to represent it. We derive an exact linear-fractional normal form for head complexity, prove a general threshold-degree lower bound, and give an explicit ten-bit function for which this bound is strict. For symmetric Boolean functions, we independently show that head complexity equals the number of times the function changes value between consecutive Hamming-weight levels, even when positional embeddings are allowed. This agrees with the concurrent characterization of Hsu and Xu (arXiv:2608.04243) in a model without positional embeddings. The symmetric lower bound combines our general threshold-degree bound with the classical result of Aspnes et al. (1994). These results were discovered and formalized by a frontier model through conjecture generation, theorem proving, and machine verification, while human researchers asked the high-level questions and reviewed the generated theorems. We make the Lean formalization and research traces publicly available to support agent-assisted theorem proving and formal verification in mechanistic interpretability. This work provides a proof of concept for using the capabilities of frontier models, grounded by formal verification, to develop an understanding of transformer architectures.
papers.summary: The study asks how many attention heads a one-layer, attention-only transformer needs to represent a given Boolean function, a quantity the authors call head complexity. It derives an exact normal form for head complexity, proves a general lower bound based on threshold degree, and shows that for symmetric functions **head complexity equals the number of value changes across Hamming-weight levels**. The results were discovered and formalized in `Lean` by a frontier model through conjecture generation, theorem proving, and machine verification, with humans posing the high-level questions and reviewing the theorems. The formalization and the model's research traces are released as a proof of concept for agent-assisted, formally verified research.

papers.title: Predicted Class Correction: Conformal Thresholds for Classes with No Calibration Data
papers.abstract: Class-conditional conformal prediction calibrates a separate score threshold for every class and therefore requires labelled calibration examples of every class. In long-tailed deployments these are exactly what is missing: rare classes are left with few or no held-out examples, and existing methods are either undefined for them or fall back to the shared marginal threshold. We ask whether the per-class correction can instead be predicted from descriptors of the class that require no labels at all. We propose Predicted Class Correction (PCC), which regresses the offset between the per-class and the marginal conformal quantile on geometric descriptors of the classifier head, shrinks the prediction by a scalar selected on the labelled classes, and refits a single marginal offset. The descriptors depend only on the model's weights, so a class with zero calibration examples still receives its own threshold, and since only one scalar is calibrated, split conformal's marginal guarantee is retained. On ImageNet, PCC improves worst-class coverage on such classes by 0.058 [0.006, 0.110] at matched average set size, 42% of an oracle that sees the test labels. Of eight baselines on the same splits, six change the statistic by exactly zero and the best reaches 0.016 with an interval containing zero, so PCC is the only one distinguishable from no improvement; the gain persists with only 100 labelled classes out of 1000. A second finding concerns evaluation: worst-class coverage becomes unmeasurable before it becomes unachievable. Below roughly 35 test examples per class no improvement can be shown even for an oracle, so a null result there reflects the evaluation set, not the method. Restricting evaluation above this depth recovers a significant improvement on Pl@ntNet-300K, where the effect had appeared absent.
papers.summary: Class-conditional conformal prediction needs labeled calibration examples for every class, which long-tailed deployments lack for their rare classes. Predicted Class Correction (`PCC`) predicts each class's threshold offset from geometric descriptors of the classifier head's weights, so classes with no calibration data still get their own threshold, and it keeps split conformal's marginal coverage guarantee. On `ImageNet`, PCC improves worst-class coverage on such classes by **0.058, about 42% of what an oracle achieves**, while none of eight baselines shows a gain distinguishable from zero. The authors also find that below about 35 test examples per class, improvements in worst-class coverage cannot be measured at all, and evaluating above that depth reveals a significant gain on `Pl@ntNet-300K`.

papers.title: Local Evidence, Global Failure: Diagnosing Speech-Vision Temporal Composition in Audio-Visual Language Models
papers.abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) can fail at full-video speech-vision decisions even when useful visual evidence is locally recoverable. We introduce Temporal Evidence Decomposition (TED), a training-free diagnostic framework that separates local visual verification from speech-relative aggregation. Automatic speech recognition supplies a transcript and utterance interval. TED queries audio-free windows with the transcript for Temporal Alignment and Forecasting, or answer candidates for Cross-Modal Temporal Binding, then aggregates evidence relative to that interval. Across four frozen AV-LLMs on SVHalluc, Temporal Forecasting accuracy rises from 29.3-33.7% under full-video questioning to 79.3-82.2% with TED. Query replacement reduces recovery; the observed anchor remains beneficial when temporal-region availability is held fixed. Physical-isolation and timing-shortcut controls test alternative explanations. The findings distinguish locally recoverable evidence from successful full-video decisions, motivating explicit separation of narration content, utterance timing, and time-indexed visual evidence.

papers.title: CHSM8: A Chess Transformer that Follows Natural-Language Style Prompts
papers.abstract: We present CHSM8, a 210M-parameter chess transformer that plays moves conditioned on a free-text description of a playing style, e.g. "go for the Sicilian Defense", "solid, safe, risk-free chess" or "You are Magnus Carlsen in his prime". The model is pretrained without search on 1.07B filtered Lichess games, using a factorized move representation and legal-move masking. It reaches 1837 Elo against a strength-limited Stockfish and, in 1,000-game matches, beat every other public model we tested that was likewise trained without preference tuning, rewards or search, including one with 13 times as many parameters. We then fine-tune it to follow text on a synthetic dataset: Gemma-4-31B describes the playing style of 3M game sides, a 1B Gemma-3 model distilled from the 2.4M of those descriptions that contradict nothing on the board labels the rest, and every one of 30M selected game sides gets five descriptions. Supervised fine-tuning attaches a frozen text encoder through gated cross-attention, and direct preference optimization (DPO) uses the same moves under a mismatched description as the rejected sample. After DPO, style adherence rises on every prompt we test (for example, queens traded early 53% -> 67%, pawn moves 29% -> 32% of all moves, queenside castling 97.3% -> 99.7%), and strength without a prompt stays within noise of SFT (1792 vs. 1797 Elo). Design choices at every stage were made by fixed-budget automated search loops on top of standard architectures and training recipes. We document the full pipeline and the decisions behind it, report the ablations that failed, and evaluate the models across many style prompts and kinds of games, with 1,000 games per setting. The work is fully open source and reproducible: weights, datasets with all training labels, prompts, configurations, inference code and playable demos are public and free to build on.
papers.summary: `CHSM8` is a 210M-parameter chess transformer that plays according to a free-text style prompt such as an opening name or a request for safe, risk-free play. Pretrained without search on 1.07B `Lichess` games, it reaches **1837 Elo against strength-limited `Stockfish`**, and it beat every other public model tested that was likewise trained without search, rewards, or preference tuning, including one 13 times larger. Style-following comes from synthetic style descriptions generated by `Gemma` models, supervised fine-tuning through gated cross-attention to a frozen text encoder, and direct preference optimization (DPO) that uses mismatched descriptions as rejected samples. DPO raises style adherence on every prompt tested without measurable loss of strength, and the weights, datasets, code, and failed ablations are all released openly.

papers.title: CD-OPD: Contextual Digest for On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Teacher takeover in on-policy distillation (OPD) can produce incorrect responses even when the student and teacher independently answer the same problem correctly, a failure we quantify using Collaboration Failure Rate (CFR). To address it, we propose Contextual Digest for On-Policy Distillation (CD-OPD). CD-OPD structures the earlier context of teacher guidance through a teacher-generated dependency graph, curating the required problem conditions and preceding reasoning as node summaries alongside the unchanged guidance in a Contextual Digest before student continuation. We further develop online meta-reweighting, which compares Digest segment gradients with a task gradient from independent student responses to improve student-only performance, favoring updates predicted to reduce task loss. Across eight benchmarks, CD-OPD improves average accuracy by 1.32--7.05 percentage points over representative existing OPD methods. It also reduces CFR by 27.4\%--56.4\% relative to existing takeover-based OPD methods.
papers.summary: In on-policy distillation (OPD), a teacher can take over part of a student's response, and the combined answer can be wrong even when both models would answer correctly on their own. The authors quantify this with a Collaboration Failure Rate (CFR). `CD-OPD` has the teacher build a dependency graph that summarizes the problem conditions and preceding reasoning into a Contextual Digest given to the student before it continues. An online meta-reweighting step then favors updates predicted to improve the student's performance on its own. Across eight benchmarks it improves average accuracy by **1.32 to 7.05 percentage points** over existing OPD methods and cuts CFR by 27.4% to 56.4% relative to takeover-based methods.

papers.title: Operator-Mismatch Contrastive Learning for World-Relative Trajectory Coherence
papers.abstract: World models are increasingly judged by how well they rank plausible futures, yet plausibility alone is the wrong target. The same scene can evolve under many latent rules, and a future that is smooth and physically valid under one rule can be incoherent under the rule actually in force. We formalize the resulting failure, operator-blindness, and show that it is systematically hidden by standard evaluation: a scorer can attain near-perfect generic ranking while separating current-world from other-world futures no better than chance. We introduce Operator-Mismatch Contrastive (OMC) learning, whose semantic hard negatives are valid-but-wrong-operator trajectories, and a matching protocol that measures world-relative coherence directly. On a controlled synthetic benchmark with in- and out-of-distribution operator parameters, across two trajectory-scoring backbones, and on feature-level external validation with CoPhy ballsCF, OMC raises operator-sensitive scoring far above a chance baseline that nonetheless achieves 0.99 generic top-1. We prove that the wrong-operator negative is necessary both for the protocol to detect the failure and for the objective to fix it, and position OMC as an auxiliary coherence signal (a trajectory-coherence scorer, not a generative model, planner, or control agent) that can be attached to existing world-model representations.
papers.summary: World models are usually evaluated on how well they rank plausible futures, but a future can be physically valid under one latent rule and incoherent under the rule actually in force. The authors call this failure operator-blindness and show that standard evaluation hides it: **a scorer can reach 0.99 generic top-1 ranking while separating current-world from other-world futures no better than chance**. Operator-Mismatch Contrastive (`OMC`) learning trains with valid trajectories generated under the wrong operator as hard negatives, and a matching protocol measures this world-relative coherence directly. OMC greatly improves operator-sensitive scoring on a synthetic benchmark and on `CoPhy ballsCF`, and the authors prove that wrong-operator negatives are necessary both to detect the failure and to fix it.

papers.title: Aligning Cultural Behaviors in Arabic Language Models via Preferences
papers.abstract: Arabic LLMs have improved rapidly, but aligning them with country-specific cultural behavioral preferences remains underexplored. Previous work has focused primarily on instruction-tuning for factual knowledge, overlooking nuanced cultural behaviors. We propose ArabPref, which to our knowledge is the first large-scale pan-Arab preference data set for the alignment of cultural behavior conditioned on the country. Our contribution includes two resources in English and Modern Standard Arabic: a culturally grounded preference dataset for training and evaluation, and a multiple-choice benchmark designed to assess culturally aligned behavior across nations. All test data are validated by native speakers to ensure authenticity. To optimize cultural alignment, we experiment with post-training methods across multilingual and Arabic-centric language models, evaluating performance on both generation tasks and our cultural multiple-choice benchmark.
