The resulting formulation remains compatible with standard Markov decision process (MDP) planning.
papers.summary: In many human-AI systems a proposed action is first evaluated by another decision-maker, possibly with a different objective, before it is executed. Standard decision frameworks hide this step inside the transition model. The authors introduce a framework with a joint action language and an interpretation function that maps each proposal and interaction context to a semantic outcome, from which transitions and rewards are derived. This separates **context-dependent evaluation, such as advisory or authorization patterns, from execution dynamics** while staying compatible with standard Markov decision process (MDP) planning, and it is illustrated in shared human-AI autonomy.

papers.title: Self-Distillation for Supervised Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning treats the expert demonstration or gold response as a one-hot target, suppressing valid alternative continuations that the model would otherwise assign probability to. We propose Gold-Conditioned Distillation (GCD), a method that turns expert demonstrations into model-native supervision. GCD uses one model as both teacher and student: the teacher conditions on a prompt containing the gold response in context, the student conditions on the original prompt as at inference, and the student is trained to minimize the forward KL divergence to the teacher's next-token distribution at each gold response token. This lets the model use its prior knowledge to teach itself the new task: correctness is anchored by the gold response, while the soft target preserves plausible alternatives. Across various training tasks on Qwen and Llama models, GCD improves new-task accuracy over SFT and generally reduces degradation on general benchmarks.
papers.summary: Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) treats the gold response as a one-hot target, which suppresses valid alternatives the model would otherwise consider. `GCD` (Gold-Conditioned Distillation) uses one model as both teacher and student. The teacher sees the gold response in its prompt, the student sees only the original prompt, and the student minimizes forward KL divergence to the teacher's next-token distribution at each gold token. Across tasks on `Qwen` and `Llama` models, GCD **improves new-task accuracy over SFT and generally reduces degradation on general benchmarks**.

papers.title: Assessing the AI Readiness of Construction Datasets: A Multidimensional Operational Framework
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in construction has increased the demand for datasets suitable for reliable model development, evaluation, and reuse. However, construction datasets vary widely in documentation, quality, governance, and evaluation support, and consistent criteria for assessing AI readiness remain limited. This study develops a Construction Dataset AI Readiness Framework with 30 attributes across four dimensions: Metadata Completeness, Data Quality and Representativeness, Data Governance and Accessibility, and AI Utility. The framework uses attribute-specific scoring, applicability screening, and automated and manual verification. It was evaluated using 21 publicly available datasets across seven data-type groups. Overall readiness scores ranged from 0.720 to 0.964, with a mean of 0.879. Hybrid verification achieved 90.5% agreement between automated suggestions and manually verified scores. The framework supports consistent assessment of heterogeneous construction datasets and identification of readiness gaps.
papers.summary: Datasets for AI in construction vary widely in documentation, quality and governance, and there are few consistent criteria for judging whether they are ready for AI use. The proposed framework scores 30 attributes across four dimensions: metadata completeness, data quality and representativeness, governance and accessibility, and AI utility. It combines applicability screening with automated and manual verification. Applied to 21 public datasets, readiness scores ranged from 0.720 to 0.964, and **automated suggestions agreed with manual scores 90.5% of the time**.

papers.title: Formal Raising: Embedding Verifiable Ethical Properties into the Development of AI
papers.abstract: Alan Turing proposed constructing a ``child machine'' and educating it rather than directly programming an adult-like intelligent machine. Recent work on model raising revives this developmental view for Large Language Models by arguing that moral values should accompany capability acquisition from the beginning rather than be added only through post-hoc alignment. This paper proposes Formal Raising (FR): selected moral values are represented as explicit, machine-checkable properties that participate in development, evaluation, and action selection. We present a C-based reasoning framework in which candidate actions are evaluated against prioritized ethical properties. Conflicts are resolved w.r.t. a given order, strict rules are non-defeasible, and underdetermination is reported explicitly. Exceptions are not encoded as special cases but emerge from the comparison of alternatives. We provide examples that cover conflicts involving life, truthfulness, harm, privacy, autonomy, and strict rules. We outline a property layer inspired by a Property Specification Language (PSL) for state and temporal requirements and discuss its integration into a raising process.
papers.summary: Building on Turing's idea of educating a child machine and on recent work on model raising, the paper proposes `Formal Raising`, in which selected moral values become explicit, machine-checkable properties used during development, evaluation and action selection. A C-based reasoning framework evaluates candidate actions against prioritized ethical properties. Conflicts are resolved by a given priority order, strict rules cannot be overridden, and underdetermined cases are reported explicitly. **Exceptions emerge from comparing alternatives rather than being hand-coded**, as shown in examples involving life, truthfulness, harm, privacy and autonomy, and the authors outline a temporal property layer inspired by the Property Specification Language (PSL).

papers.title: Steered Not Stirred: Effective Reward Tilting using Surrogate Reward Mixing
papers.abstract: Continuous-time generative models, from diffusion models, flow matching, and now flow maps, owe their practical value to high-fidelity generation and steerability. In many applications, a ground-truth latent ``oracle'' reward $R^*$ is unavailable or expensive to evaluate, e.g., human judgments or experimental measurements. Although the oracle reward is not directly observable, it can often be approximated through multiple cheaper surrogates that, individually, provide incomplete characterizations but collectively reveal substantial information about the downstream task. In this paper, we present a method for composing such surrogates to steer a pretrained model toward the distribution tilted by an unavailable $R^*$. Given a small feedback set of oracle rankings or numerical rewards, we introduce Mixing And Reward Tilting for INference-time Improvement (MARTINI), which learns a surrogate composition for plug-and-play use with standard inference-time steering methods. Our theory characterizes surrogate information limits and relates population recovery error to ideal-target KL at small tilt strength. For preferences, the bound additionally accounts for an irreducible mismatch between the Plackett-Luce population target and the conditional mean. Experiments demonstrate improved oracle-tilt fidelity in language generation and ImageNet alignment, and improved joint pose accuracy and validity in protein-ligand cofolding, without inference-time oracle queries.
papers.summary: Steering a pretrained diffusion or flow model toward a true oracle reward is hard when that reward, such as human judgment or a lab measurement, is unavailable or costly to query. `MARTINI` (Mixing And Reward Tilting for INference-time Improvement) learns how to combine several cheaper surrogate rewards from a small set of oracle rankings or scores. The combined reward then plugs into standard inference-time steering methods. The theory bounds how much information surrogates can carry and how recovery error relates to KL divergence from the ideal target. Experiments show **better fidelity to the oracle-tilted distribution without querying the oracle at inference**, across language generation, `ImageNet` alignment and protein-ligand cofolding.

papers.title: From Seeing to Reporting: A Theory of Reliable Visual Set Generation in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are asked to report what they see: to count objects, box them, parse a screen or pick a click target (GUI grounding). We argue that reporting is part of the visual task, not merely its formatting. In a dense scene with 173 shapes, GPT-6.1 lists 173 records that match every shape, yet the counts it states in the same response sum to 188. From Seeing to Reporting (FSR) is a theory of visual reporting and a set of inference-time procedures that improve the reports of frozen VLMs. It models reporting as a chain from responses to decoded records, constructed sets and task answers, linked by task-compatible matching. The chain gives exact relations for deleting records, averaging their coordinates and switching readouts, and it splits the error of one answer chosen among several calls into missing candidates, lost representatives and wrong choices. These relations guide procedures for counting, detection, document layout, screen parsing and GUI grounding that use the task specification and a shipped configuration, without requiring labels from the target task. On 50 dense synthetic scenes, a one-call reporting-and-decoding protocol cuts per-type count error by 85.2% for GPT-6.1 and 98.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5. On 600 ScreenSpot-Pro items, a GUI-grounding tier that combines three models lowers the miss rate from 13.67% for GPT-6.1's two-stage zoom to 9.33%, against 12.67% for three such zooms combined by a cluster vote at about the same cost. A plain vote over the same three models misses 12.33%: the other models supply the candidates, and selecting among them turns those candidates into fewer misses. We release the protocols, the stored responses and the analysis code.
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often see a scene correctly but report it inconsistently. In one dense scene, `GPT-6.1` lists 173 correct records yet states counts in the same response that sum to 188. `FSR` (From Seeing to Reporting) models reporting as a chain from responses to decoded records, constructed sets and answers, and uses that chain to derive training-free inference procedures for frozen VLMs on counting, detection, layout and GUI grounding. A one-call reporting protocol **cuts per-type count error by 85.2% for `GPT-6.1` and 98.8% for `Claude Sonnet 5.5`**. On `ScreenSpot-Pro`, a three-model GUI-grounding tier lowers the miss rate to 9.33%, from 13.67% for `GPT-6.1`'s two-stage zoom.

papers.title: Where Are Language-Specific Features Represented in Multilingual LLMs? Everywhere
papers.abstract: Previous work has argued that multilingual LLMs encode language-specific features most strongly in their initial and final layers, implying that intermediate layers support language-agnostic representations. This paper reconsiders this finding by performing four different experiments: three that undertake a fine-grained analysis of representations of Portuguese and Spanish, two closely related languages, and one large-scale language identification experiment that covers over 200 languages. The results of these experiments challenge the strict separation between language-specific and language-agnostic layers in multilingual LLMs, using Llama 3.2 1B as a test case. By analyzing and manipulating contextual sentence embeddings, we demonstrate that language identity remains strongly recoverable throughout the model rather than being restricted to initial and final layers. Moreover, we find that the model tends to classify ambiguous strings as closer to Spanish than to Portuguese, revealing a skew in model behavior that differs from human judgments.
papers.summary: Earlier work argued that multilingual large language models (LLMs) encode language identity mainly in their first and last layers, leaving the middle layers language-agnostic. Using `Llama 3.2 1B`, the authors run three fine-grained experiments on Portuguese and Spanish and one language-identification experiment covering over 200 languages. They find that **language identity remains strongly recoverable at every layer**, which challenges the strict layer separation. They also find that the model classifies ambiguous strings as closer to Spanish, unlike human judgments.

papers.title: KPI-Aware Multimodal Anomaly Detection for 5G and Open RAN Telemetry
papers.abstract: Reliable anomaly detection is a deployment bottleneck for 5G/Open RAN observability and emerging self-optimizing 6G systems, where hundreds of heterogeneous KPIs, severe class imbalance, and strict alert budgets make purely numerical scores brittle. We present KAC, a deployment-oriented KPI-aware multimodal anomaly-detection framework that uses KPI-level residual-text alignment to turn compact operator-style summaries into a learnable feedback signal over full-KPI temporal evidence. This gives the detector broad numerical coverage like modern time-series models, while retaining the sparse KPI-specific reasoning that makes operator feedback sustainable in a future operator-facing workflow. Across public telecom telemetry, enterprise-scale Open RAN observability data, and a Nokia benchmark built from real 5G RAN production packet traces with realism-hardened injected anomalies, KAC achieves strong threshold-based detection performance while remaining competitive on threshold-free ranking metrics. On TelecomTS, at a fixed 2.5 percent false-positive-rate operating point, KAC achieves the highest recall among the evaluated residual-based methods while maintaining comparable precision; across the evaluated benchmarks, it remains robust under substantial class imbalance. KAC is integrated in pre-production shadow mode with Nokia's GKE-based KPI construction pipeline, where it continuously scores telemetry windows alongside an internal packet-level anomaly detector for operational evaluation.
papers.summary: Anomaly detection on 5G and Open RAN (radio access network) telemetry must cope with hundreds of key performance indicators (KPIs), heavy class imbalance and strict limits on alert volume. `KAC` aligns per-KPI prediction residuals with compact operator-style text summaries, so that it covers all KPIs numerically while keeping sparse, KPI-specific reasoning that operators can review. On public telemetry, enterprise Open RAN data and a `Nokia` benchmark built from real production traces, it **achieves the highest recall among residual-based methods at a 2.5% false-positive rate on `TelecomTS`** with comparable precision. It is running in pre-production shadow mode in `Nokia`'s KPI pipeline.

papers.title: Dynamics-Aligned Representation Learning under Induced Partial Observability
papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) has enabled sample-efficient learning of continuous control policies from high-dimensional observations through learned latent dynamics models. These models are typically trained with observation reconstruction objectives, which provide strong supervision but can bias representations toward visual fidelity leading to an undertrained prior and unreliable long-horizon predictions. We propose a stochastic gating mechanism that induces controlled partial observability during training by sampling a spatial binary mask from a Beta--Bernoulli random field and applying it to the raw observation. The gate probability is resampled at each time step, exposing the encoder to conditions ranging from near-total occlusion to near-full visibility. Integration of our method requires minimal architectural changes from existing dynamics models: the gated observation and the binary mask are channel-wise concatenated and passed to the encoder as a single augmented input, with no modifications to the broader training pipeline. We evaluate the proposed approach on a set of pixel-based continuous control tasks selected from the DeepMind Control Suite. Using model predictive control for evaluation, which relies solely on open-loop model rollouts, we show that stochastic gating improves planning performance and data efficiency across tasks. Further analysis demonstrates that performance is robust to the spatial scale of the mask, and a balanced observability during training outperforms configurations biased toward either sparser or denser observations.
papers.summary: Latent dynamics models in model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) are usually trained to reconstruct observations, which can push representations toward visual detail at the expense of reliable long-horizon prediction. The authors add a stochastic gate that hides parts of each training observation using a spatial binary mask sampled from a Beta–Bernoulli random field. The masking rate is resampled every time step, so visibility ranges from almost fully hidden to almost fully visible. The masked observation and the mask are concatenated as encoder input, which requires only minimal changes to the architecture. On pixel-based `DeepMind Control Suite` tasks evaluated with model predictive control, **stochastic gating improves planning performance and data efficiency**. Results are robust to mask scale, and balanced visibility works better than training biased toward either sparse or dense observations.

papers.title: When Interpretations Persist: Downstream Influence in Gaze-Aware Assistants
papers.abstract: AI assistants may carry forward not only observations but also interpretations of what a person is doing or may do next across time. Once retained, these interpretations become context for later predictions and system-triggered outputs. We study whether this representation step changes later behavior in gaze-aware streaming assistance. Holding retrieved events, their order, and the target input fixed, we find that Free-form Interpretation amplifies historical influence in both directions: correct histories produce more helpful changes and wrong histories more harmful changes. Unsupported and broader interpretations about activity or future behavior are associated with greater harmful influence. Evidence-Bounded Interpretation preserves distinctions between observation, inference, uncertainty, and temporal scope, reducing unsupported and overcertain content and lowering wrong-source harmful influence while retaining most helpful influence. The same effect structure appears with a second model. These findings identify persistent interpretation as a consequential design choice for history-aware human-AI systems.
papers.summary: The authors examine what happens when gaze-aware streaming assistants store their interpretations of what a person is doing or will do next, and those stored interpretations shape later predictions. Retrieved events, their order and the target input are held fixed. Under that control, `Free-form Interpretation` **amplifies the influence of history in both directions**: correct histories produce more helpful changes, and wrong histories produce more harmful ones. An alternative, `Evidence-Bounded Interpretation`, keeps observation, inference, uncertainty and temporal scope separate. It reduces unsupported and overconfident content and lowers harm from wrong sources while keeping most of the helpful influence, and the same pattern appears with a second model.

papers.title: Bud ContextCompact 2.0: Context Compaction for Agent Success and Accuracy with Small Language Models and Constrained Context Windows
papers.abstract: Agents that work for many turns outgrow the context window of the model that serves them, and on small language models (SLMs) and constrained inference systems that window is small. Context compaction replaces older turns with a summary so a session can continue, but it is lossy, costs a model call, and can help or hurt depending on when it runs. We describe Bud ContextCompact 2.0, the compaction built into the Bud agent runtime, and evaluate it in two settings. On recall questions over recorded agent sessions, compaction to a 16K budget raised a 1.2B-parameter model's accuracy to 0.335, from 0.247 with truncation and 0.176 with its full 32K history (p < 0.001), and raised a 9B model from 0.515 (truncation) to 0.577 (p = 0.04). On 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks run end to end by a 27B reasoning model on a 49K-token window (556 graded sessions), compaction raised the resolve rate on long sessions from 41% to 53% (+12.3 points, 95% CI +1.6 to +23.0, McNemar p = 0.043), left short sessions unchanged, and used 13% fewer tokens per solved task at equal total cost. The main failure without compaction was not the history overflowing but a reasoning turn exhausting the room the history left. The gain has limits: it vanished under a 45-minute session budget, because each summary took a median of 161 s, and in a threshold study it appeared only when compaction triggered early enough to leave room. An 8B model submitted after about ten turns at 5-8K tokens and never needed compaction. We argue that the accuracy results transfer across hardware, including CPU inference, for an equivalent model and window, while the time cost scales with the hardware and must be budgeted for.
papers.summary: Long-running agents outgrow the context windows of small language models (SLMs). Context compaction addresses this by replacing older turns with a summary, but it is lossy and costs a model call. `Bud ContextCompact 2.0` is the compaction built into the Bud agent runtime. On recall questions over recorded agent sessions, compacting to a 16K budget raised a 1.2B model's accuracy from 0.247 with truncation to 0.335. On 100 `SWE-bench Verified` tasks run by a 27B reasoning model with a 49K-token window, it **raised the long-session resolve rate from 41% to 53%** and used 13% fewer tokens per solved task. The main failure without compaction was a reasoning turn running out of the room the history left, not the history itself overflowing. Gains disappeared under a 45-minute session budget because each summary took a median of 161 s, so the authors argue that time cost must be budgeted for on slower hardware such as CPUs.

papers.title: ATEST: Adaptive Resource-Aware Test-Time Scaling for LLM Inference
papers.abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling multiple answers, but fixed sampling budgets ignore both query difficulty and the changing energy cost of inference under GPU contention. We measure up to a 4.1-fold increase in energy for the same four-sample query as GPU load rises. We present ATEST, a resource-aware TTS framework that jointly considers the expected value of additional samples and their current GPU cost. ATEST-Online, its default mode, requires no offline calibration: it incrementally generates samples, estimates the stability of the plurality answer, monitors live GPU conditions, and learns step energy cost online to decide when to stop. ATEST-Calibrated instead selects a per-query budget using offline accuracy and cost models, favoring deployments with stable loads. We evaluate both modes on four reasoning and question-answering datasets using Phi-3-mini on an NVIDIA A100 under controlled varying load, and test transfer to an NVIDIA L40S and Qwen2.5-3B. Across the four A100 datasets, ATEST-Online answers every query without exceeding the energy budget, while achieving the highest or statistically tied accuracy and reducing sampling as load increases. On GSM8K at high load, it achieves 60.0% accuracy with no deferrals, versus 44.0% accuracy and 42.4% deferrals for ATEST-Calibrated. Ablations show that online cost learning drives adaptation to load. Including offline profiling, ATEST-Online uses 42 times less GPU time and 48 times less energy than ATEST-Calibrated for the evaluated workload. Online control trades higher tail latency and lower throughput on short tasks for robustness under varying load; offline calibration remains competitive under stable conditions.
papers.summary: Test-time scaling (TTS) samples several answers from a large language model to improve reasoning. Fixed sample budgets ignore both how hard a query is and how energy cost changes with GPU load, which the authors measure rising up to 4.1-fold for the same query. `ATEST-Online` generates samples one at a time, tracks how stable the plurality answer is, monitors live GPU conditions and learns per-step energy cost online to decide when to stop. A second mode, `ATEST-Calibrated`, instead picks a per-query budget from offline accuracy and cost models. Using `Phi-3-mini` on an A100, the online mode stays within the energy budget on every query. On `GSM8K` at high load it **reaches 60.0% accuracy with no deferrals, versus 44.0% for the calibrated variant**. Including offline profiling, it uses 48 times less energy than the calibrated mode, though at the cost of higher tail latency.

papers.title: When Empathy Misses the Goal: A Benchmark for Goal Displacement in LLM Advice
papers.abstract: Conversational large language models can respond with warmth and reassurance while failing to advance the user's stated goal. We conceptualize this failure as $\textbf{goal displacement}$, the substitution of persona-maintenance content for goal-relevant substance. To measure it, we introduce $\textbf{GDB}$ (Goal Displacement Benchmark), comprising 230 scenarios across nine domains and $4{,}134$ human-scored responses from 18 models. A $2 \times 2$ taxonomy crosses hard constraints with emotional distress, distinguishing failures to confront infeasible goals or combine empathy with practical guidance from reverse displacement, where unsolicited problem-solving replaces requested emotional support. A deletion-test rubric assesses whether substantive help remains after purely supportive sentences are removed. Independent raters achieve weighted $\kappa = 0.82$ against author scores for displacement severity. Trap displacement ranges from $0.0\%$ to $37.7\%$ and is strongly negatively correlated with Chatbot Arena Elo ($\rho = -0.706$, $n = 15$). Reverse displacement reaches $41.9\%$, including substantial rates in models with negligible trap displacement. A factorial probe supports a distinction from social sycophancy. Human-scored responses in the high-complexity, low-pressure condition exhibit $35.0\%$ sycophancy but $7.5\%$ displacement, with little association between the constructs. Matched OLMo-2 checkpoints show that mixed empathy-with-constraints displacement remains at $52.3\%$ after supervised fine-tuning and falls to $13.8\%$ after direct preference optimization. GDB provides a reproducible diagnostic of whether responses advance the operationalized user goal, supporting model comparison, post-training evaluation, and regression testing. We release the dataset, annotations, and rubric under CC-BY-4.0 and the evaluation code under MIT.
papers.summary: Chat models sometimes answer with warmth and reassurance but fail to advance the user's actual goal, a failure the authors call goal displacement. `GDB` (Goal Displacement Benchmark) contains 230 scenarios across nine domains and 4,134 human-scored responses from 18 models. It uses a taxonomy that crosses hard constraints with emotional distress, plus a deletion-test rubric that checks whether real help remains once purely supportive sentences are removed. Displacement rates range from 0% to 37.7% and are **strongly negatively correlated with `Chatbot Arena` Elo (ρ = −0.706)**. Reverse displacement, where unrequested problem-solving replaces the emotional support the user asked for, reaches 41.9%. Matched `OLMo-2` checkpoints show that direct preference optimization (`DPO`), rather than supervised fine-tuning, cuts mixed displacement from 52.3% to 13.8%, and a factorial probe separates the phenomenon from social sycophancy.

papers.title: FracTS: Hierarchical and Autoregressive Time Series Generation
papers.abstract: Time series are ubiquitous across different domains, and the growing use of synthetic data for privacy-preserving sharing, data augmentation, and stress testing makes time series generation increasingly important. Early generative approaches are predominantly autoregressive, which can suffer from low sample diversity, error accumulation, and difficulty modeling long-range dependencies. In this paper, we introduce FracTS, a hierarchical, coarse-to-fine autoregressive model for multivariate time series generation. Inspired by fractal generative modeling developed for images, FracTS adapts the paradigm from 2D to 1D sequences by learning a multi-scale representation that captures global trajectory structure at coarse scales and local dynamics at fine scales while following the autoregressive nature of time series. In contrast to unstructured images, time series are structured, allowing easy automated or designated temporal feature processing optimized for the model, and global (static) feature extraction describing the instances that generate the corresponding time series in the collection. We incorporate them in the generation process to further improve the generation quality. The design naturally handles multivariate dependencies and improves long-horizon temporal coherence without requiring fixed-length inputs. Experiments on five datasets (two conditional, three unconditional) conducted against seven baselines show that FracTS consistently outperforms baselines across marginal distribution and predictive ML utility, and correlation preservation in the unconditional setting. In particular, the predictive ML utility is averagely improved by 100.0% and 75.0-81.0% for unconditional and conditional time series datasets compared to the best baseline (relative error computed on dataset-averaged raw values). Code is available at: https://github.com/BetterdataLabs/fracts.
papers.summary: Autoregressive generators of synthetic time series can suffer from low sample diversity, accumulating errors and weak long-range coherence. `FracTS` adapts fractal generative modeling from images to 1D sequences. It builds a coarse-to-fine hierarchy in which coarse scales capture global trajectory structure and fine scales capture local dynamics, while the model stays autoregressive in time. The model also conditions on engineered temporal features and static per-instance features, and it does not require fixed-length inputs. Across five datasets and seven baselines, it **roughly doubles predictive ML utility over the best baseline on unconditional data** and improves it by 75–81% on conditional data.

papers.title: Breaking the 1/3 Barrier for Approximate Nash Equilibria in Symmetric Bimatrix Games
papers.abstract: We give the first unconditional family of polynomial-time algorithms that breaks the $1/3$ approximation barrier for symmetric bimatrix games. For every fixed $\delta>0$, an algorithm in this family computes a symmetric $(1-1/\sqrt{2}+\delta)$-approximate Nash equilibrium, improving on the previous best guarantee of $(1/3+\delta)$ due to Kontogiannis and Spirakis [2011].
papers.summary: The authors study how well polynomial-time algorithms can approximate Nash equilibria in symmetric two-player (bimatrix) games. They give the first unconditional family of polynomial-time algorithms that breaks the long-standing 1/3 approximation barrier for these games. For any fixed δ > 0, the algorithms compute a **symmetric (1 − 1/√2 + δ)-approximate Nash equilibrium, about 0.293**. This improves on the previous best guarantee of 1/3 + δ from Kontogiannis and Spirakis (2011).

papers.title: StopLoss: Teaching Agents to Predict Failure and Stop Early
papers.abstract: Coding agents keep working on runs that will fail verification, and asking a frontier model to watch for this is expensive in its own right. We introduce StopLoss, a small external monitor that learns failure recognition from completed trajectories and their verifier outcomes. The name is inspired by the stop-loss order in finance: StopLoss ends a run early when the run is likely to fail, which saves resources. Final outcomes label earlier local windows, so a fine-tuned language model can score the most recent tool steps in a single forward pass, and a threshold calibrated on successful runs turns that score into an abort decision without changing the executor. Trained on GPT-family SWE-rebench trajectories and evaluated on SWE-bench Verified and a SWE-bench Pro subset with GPT and Claude executors, StopLoss is compared against six general-purpose judges reading identical windows. Outcome supervision lifts failure prediction from near chance to a useful signal at the first check, at one to two orders of magnitude lower cost per check than any tested judge. This translates into savings: relative to completing every task, StopLoss lowers cost per retained solve by 4.5\% on Verified while preserving 99\% of successful runs, and by up to 31\% on the costlier Pro subset, reaching 48\% with a Qwen3-8B backbone, and in all four settings its cost per retained solve is below that of every judge policy. Outcome-trained small monitors can make failure recognition cheap enough for early stopping to pay for itself.
papers.summary: Coding agents often keep working on runs that will ultimately fail verification, and having a frontier model watch for this is itself expensive. `StopLoss` is a small external monitor trained on finished trajectories, with each run's final verifier outcome used as the label for its earlier windows. At each check, a fine-tuned language model scores the most recent tool steps in one forward pass. A threshold calibrated on successful runs turns that score into an abort decision without modifying the executor. It was trained on `SWE-rebench` trajectories and tested on `SWE-bench Verified` and a `SWE-bench Pro` subset with GPT and Claude executors. It **predicts failure usefully at one to two orders of magnitude lower cost per check than six general-purpose LLM judges**. Cost per retained solve drops by 4.5% on Verified while keeping 99% of successful runs, and by up to 48% on Pro with a `Qwen3-8B` backbone.

papers.title: From Clinical Risk Prediction to Operational Decisions: An Uncertainty-Aware Framework for ICU Staffing
papers.abstract:
Advances in electronic health records (EHR) and large-scale critical care databases have enabled the development of machine learning models for the early detection of patient deterioration. While these models often achieve strong predictive performance for outcomes such as sepsis and mortality, most studies evaluate them purely on discrimination metrics. This leaves a critical gap: how to systematically translate probabilistic clinical risk estimates into downstream operational decisions under real-world constraints, such as shift rigidity and hiring delays.
  This study proposes an uncertainty-aware anticipatory staffing framework that bridges short-term patient risk prediction and staff planning without altering the upstream predictive model. Instead of relying on naive deterministic aggregation or fixed safety buffers, the framework explicitly models dynamic predictive uncertainty and evaluates extreme shortage exposure using Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR). These aggregated, risk-calibrated demand signals are then embedded into an hourly rolling-horizon scheduling policy to generate delay-constrained staffing decisions.
  Evaluated on realistic trajectories from the MIMIC-IV database, the proposed framework demonstrates a favorable cost-shortage trade-off compared to deterministic and purely reactive baselines. Pareto frontier analysis illustrates how uncertainty-aware demand construction changes resource allocation under varying safety preferences, while stress testing confirms the framework's operational robustness even when subjected to systematic predictive bias in the form of calibration drift. By formalizing this translation layer, this work provides a principled, transparent pathway for safely integrating probabilistic AI outputs into high-stakes healthcare operational systems.
papers.summary: Clinical risk models for outcomes such as sepsis and mortality are usually judged only on how well they discriminate, leaving open how to turn their probabilities into operational decisions. The authors build an uncertainty-aware staffing framework on top of an unchanged predictive model. It models predictive uncertainty explicitly and measures exposure to extreme shortages using Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR). The resulting demand signals feed an hourly rolling-horizon scheduling policy that respects shift rigidity and hiring delays. On trajectories from `MIMIC-IV`, the framework achieves a **better cost-versus-shortage trade-off than deterministic and purely reactive baselines** and remains robust under calibration drift.

papers.title: Modaliff: A Unified Token Diffusion Model for Any-to-Any Generation
papers.abstract: Any-to-any generation seeks a single model that translates flexibly among text, image, and audio, yet existing approaches either require fully aligned multimodal tuples or a shared representation that suppresses modality-specific structure. We introduce Modaliff, a novel token-based diffusion model that learns from widely available bimodal pairs while preserving each modality in its native latent sequence. Modaliff assembles conditions and targets into a unified token sequence, with per-token attributes to disambiguate token identities and role-based positional embedding to preserve each modality's internal structure across sequence layouts. This design enables a single denoiser to support diverse generation tasks without task-specific architectural changes or a shared cross-modal latent space. Beyond one-to-one generation, Modaliff supports multiple conditions either by combining single-condition predictions at inference or by lightweight finetuning on captions that jointly describe multiple inputs. Experiments across text, image, and audio show that Modaliff achieves the best fidelity among any-to-any models on most generation tasks while using substantially fewer parameters and training data.
papers.summary: Any-to-any generation across text, image and audio has typically required either fully aligned multimodal training tuples or a shared latent space that suppresses modality-specific structure. `Modaliff` is a token-based diffusion model that learns from widely available bimodal pairs and keeps each modality in its native latent sequence. Conditions and targets are assembled into a single token sequence. Per-token attributes identify each token, and role-based positional embeddings preserve each modality's internal structure, so one denoiser handles many tasks without task-specific architecture. Multiple conditions can be combined at inference or through lightweight fine-tuning. The model **achieves the best fidelity among any-to-any models on most tasks while using substantially fewer parameters and less training data**.

papers.title: Residential Construction Image Dataset Using CSI Divisions for Deep Learning-based Object Detection
papers.abstract: Accurate recognition of construction site elements is essential for the application of deep learning (DL) in the construction industry. Despite rapid advances in computer vision, the adoption of DL in construction has been limited by the lack of structured, publicly available datasets aligned with established industry standards. To address this gap, we introduce the Residential Construction Dataset Using CSI Divisions (ResCD-CSI) image dataset, a manually labeled image benchmark organized according to the divisional structure defined by the Construction Specifications Institute (CSI). The dataset comprises high-resolution images collected from active residential construction sites across the United States, capturing diverse building components, materials, and equipment under real-world conditions. In total, 16,365 objects spanning 14 major CSI divisions were precisely annotated using bounding boxes, ensuring consistency and reliability for object detection tasks. By aligning with the CSI divisional framework, ResCD-CSI establishes a standardized resource that bridges construction practice with computer vision research and supports the development of Artificial Intelligence-driven solutions for residential construction monitoring.
papers.summary: Deep learning has seen limited use in construction partly because few public datasets follow industry standards. `ResCD-CSI` is a manually labeled image dataset from active U.S. residential construction sites, organized by the divisions of the Construction Specifications Institute (CSI). It contains **16,365 bounding-box-annotated objects spanning 14 major CSI divisions**, covering building components, materials and equipment under real-world conditions, for training object detection models.

papers.title: Auditing Tool Traces in Agentic LLMs: Source Localization and Counterfactual Dependence Testing
papers.abstract: Agentic LLMs increasingly support scientific prediction by grounding decisions in external evidence. In biology, they promise accurate, interpretable predictions for important problems by integrating complex experimental and computational evidence. However, serialized tool results can contain hidden label shortcuts, such as dataset identifiers or template artifacts, that create apparent success without biological reasoning. To address this risk, we introduce a two-stage audit. Stage 1, Per-Tool TF-IDF Decomposition (PT2D), localizes label-predictive patterns to individual tool results while avoiding signal dilution in the concatenated tool trace. Stage 2, Token-Class Redaction, counterfactually tests whether the frozen LLM depends on the localized shortcut. We apply this audit to TCR-pMHC binding, where tool augmentation substantially outperforms a no-evidence baseline. At face value, this suggests that the LLM has learned to use scientific evidence. The audit overturns this interpretation: PT2D localizes the strongest signal to identifiers in one tool result, and redacting them reduces performance to chance. These findings show how hidden label shortcuts can masquerade as scientific reasoning or discovery, motivating source-level audits before benchmark gains are trusted.
papers.summary: Tool results returned to agentic LLMs can contain hidden label shortcuts, such as dataset identifiers or template artifacts, that produce apparent success without genuine reasoning. The authors propose a two-stage audit. `Per-Tool TF-IDF Decomposition` (`PT2D`) traces label-predictive patterns to individual tool outputs. `Token-Class Redaction` then tests whether the frozen model actually depends on those patterns. On TCR-pMHC binding prediction, tool augmentation appeared to substantially beat a no-evidence baseline. However, the audit traced the strongest signal to identifiers in a single tool result, and **redacting them dropped performance to chance**. The authors argue that benchmark gains from tool use should be audited at the source level before they are trusted.

papers.title: Reinforcement learning on the EPRI AI-ccelerating Unit Commitment benchmark: diagnosing over-commitment and guiding MILP with learned policies
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly proposed as a fast solver for unit commitment (UC), but standalone agents remain far more expensive than mixed-integer linear programming (MILP). In the first study of RL on the 51-generator, 72-hour benchmark of the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) AI-ccelerating Unit Commitment competition, we trace this gap to the agents' own exploration, close most of it, and show that the resulting policy can accelerate an exact solver. In every configuration tested, Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) and an action-branching Deep Q-Network (DQN) trained from scratch committed about twice the units of a thermal-only MILP optimum, at 39-64% higher cost, whereas a merit-order rule came within 1.6-7% (10-24% when unserved energy is priced). When each unit's decision is sampled independently, spare units insure against random de-commitments. Consistent with this, injecting exploration noise during fine-tuning enlarged a lean policy's fleet, a reward without shaping terms did not remove the over-commitment, and under their training noise the agents outperformed the rule subjected to comparable noise. Imitating the MILP solutions and fine-tuning conservatively brought PPO within 2.6% of the optimum, and these policies had the lowest penalised cost of any evaluated (about 5%). Fixing the fine-tuned policy's confident decisions made the MILP 3.8-8.5 times faster within 0.10-0.25% of the best solution, with a smaller worst case than an imitation-only policy fixing as many variables (1.1% against 8.9%). Because dispatch method and benchmark scope alone shift the reported optimality ratio by up to 3.6% and 9%, we propose a reporting protocol.
papers.summary: Unit commitment (UC) is the problem of scheduling which power generators run when. The authors present the first study of reinforcement learning (RL) on the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) UC competition benchmark, which has 51 generators over 72 hours. `PPO` and an action-branching `DQN` trained from scratch consistently commit about twice as many units as the mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) optimum, at 39–64% higher cost. The authors trace this to exploration noise: when each unit's decision is sampled independently, keeping spare units on insures against random shutdowns. Imitating MILP solutions and then fine-tuning conservatively brings `PPO` within 2.6% of the optimum. Fixing that policy's confident decisions **speeds up the MILP solver 3.8–8.5× while staying within 0.10–0.25% of the best solution**. The authors also propose a reporting protocol, because dispatch method and benchmark scope alone shift reported optimality ratios by several percent.

papers.title: Beyond the record: evaluating probabilistic AI weather forecasts deep in the tail
papers.abstract: Can probabilistic artificial intelligence (AI) weather forecasts retain skill beyond their training domain? We compare four state-of-the-art AI models (ArchesWeatherGen, U-Cast, WeatherNext2 and GenCast-mini) with the physics-based IFS-ENS over land in 2022, at 1.5{\deg} resolution and lead times of 2--10 days. Monthly ERA5 records from 1979--2021 define common historical boundaries, and we characterize new records set in 2022 by their depth, i.e., the exceedance margin relative to local historical variability. Two proper scores, record-threshold weighted CRPS and Brier score, assess the magnitude and probability of record exceedances across all eligible cases, retaining both missed extremes and false alarms. Verified against ERA5, AI models outperform IFS-ENS for heat and cold records at almost every lead and depth. For heat, the advantage strengthens with depth, partly because IFS-ENS over-forecasts deep records, and largely persists for deeper records under HRES-fc0 verification. For wind, gains erode for deeper records and longer leads. Better tail scores can nevertheless coexist with aggregate probability deficits or surpluses, and some improvements arise chiefly on non-exceedances. Increasing underprediction on progressively more extreme observed subsets can also arise through outcome selection, even for an ideal conditional-mean forecast. These findings establish that native probabilistic AI ensembles retain, and for heat increase, their advantage over IFS-ENS as thresholds move beyond local records, although all advantages narrow with lead time. They caution against generalizing the extrapolation failure reported for deterministic AI forecasts to probabilistic systems, and motivate common verification conventions that separate comparative tail skill, performance on realized extremes, and probabilistic calibration.
papers.summary: The authors test whether probabilistic AI weather models keep their skill on extremes that go beyond the historical record. They compare `ArchesWeatherGen`, `U-Cast`, `WeatherNext2` and `GenCast-mini` with the physics-based `IFS-ENS` ensemble over land in 2022 at lead times of 2–10 days. New records are measured by how far they exceed the 1979–2021 `ERA5` records relative to local variability, and are scored with threshold-weighted CRPS and Brier scores. The **AI models outperform `IFS-ENS` for heat and cold records at almost every lead time and depth**, and their advantage on heat grows for deeper records, while for wind the gains erode. The authors caution against applying the extrapolation failures reported for deterministic AI forecasts to probabilistic ensembles, and they call for verification conventions that separate tail skill from calibration.

papers.title: EmotiQ: A Quantum Residual Specialist Framework for Text Emotion Classification
papers.abstract: Emotion classification from text is challenging because many affective states are distinguished by subtle linguistic signals and semantically overlapping boundaries. We investigate whether compact quantum modules can serve as targeted residual specialists that assist traditional classifiers on difficult emotion decisions. We introduce EmotiQ, a residual specialist framework for text emotion classification using a frozen transformer classifier as the primary decision maker, identifies challenging emotion boundaries from validation behavior, and trains boundary specialists, including quantum encodings, data re-uploading specialists, prototype and fidelity specialists, and kernel-based specialists. Specialists are permitted to intervene only when they satisfy validation-based admission criteria. We evaluate the framework across six text emotion classification datasets and establish traditional model baselines. Experimental results show that the admitted EmotiQ policy improves mean macro-F1 metrics over the baseline, and achieves positive gains on five of six datasets. Among the quantum components, ZZ interaction feature maps are the most consistently effective, yielding a mean macro-F1 improvement of +0.0030 and positive gains on four datasets. These findings suggest that current quantum NLP methods can be deployed as residual specialists that provide localized improvements under strong classical supervision.
papers.summary: `EmotiQ` tests whether compact quantum circuits can help a classical text emotion classifier on hard decisions between similar emotions. A frozen transformer classifier makes the primary decision. The framework identifies difficult emotion boundaries from validation behavior and trains boundary specialists, including quantum feature maps, data re-uploading circuits and kernel methods. A specialist may intervene only if it passes validation-based admission criteria. Across six datasets, the admitted policy improves mean macro-F1 on five. `ZZ` interaction feature maps are the most consistent quantum component, though with a **mean macro-F1 gain of just +0.0030**.

papers.title: Editing as Language: Teaching LLM Agents a Grammar for Native Context Editing
papers.abstract: A synopsis in novels folds a story into a few lines; a function in code gathers many steps with a single execution. Context editing is native to language itself. In this paper, we propose the Native Context Editing (NCE) framework, which gives language model agents a grammar for natively editing their own context. By encoding context-editing operations in a grammar of dedicated special tokens, we teach the agents to invoke edits through the language itself. We train agents on iteratively constructed trajectory segments, with each teacher edit conditioned on the evolving context. This establishes context editing as an atomic and inherent capability of LLM agents, enabling them to dynamically modify their context as they generate responses over long-horizon reasoning and interaction. Compared with context-editing methods that learn to generate tool-use code within specific external harness environments, our approach integrates context editing as an internal mechanism of the model's native generation process, enabling better generalization across diverse real-world workflows. On four long-horizon agentic benchmarks (Terminal-Bench 2.0, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Multilingual, and SWE-bench Pro), NCE improves the average task success rate over the base model by 5.6 percentage points for LongCat-Flash-Lite-Sparse and by 4.5 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, while reducing average token usage by 36% and 15%, respectively.
papers.summary: Native Context Editing (`NCE`) teaches language model agents to edit their own context directly through a grammar of dedicated special tokens, rather than by generating tool-use code inside a specific external harness. Agents are trained on trajectory segments built iteratively, with each teacher edit conditioned on the evolving context. Editing thus becomes a built-in part of generation during long-horizon tasks, which the authors argue generalizes better across workflows. On `Terminal-Bench 2.0`, `SWE-bench Verified`, `SWE-bench Multilingual` and `SWE-bench Pro`, `NCE` **raises average task success by 5.6 points for `LongCat-Flash-Lite-Sparse` and 4.5 points for `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B`**. It also cuts average token usage by 36% and 15%, respectively.

papers.title: Symbolic Constraint Agents: Mining Formal Tool-Call Constraints to Prevent Agent Errors
papers.abstract: Symbolic constraints (programmatic, deterministic checks for tool calls) enable deterministic verification of LLM agents' tool calls, but existing approaches primarily enforce predefined safety policies rather than tool dependencies in complex tool environments. We explore whether symbolic constraints can be mined from environments and observations beyond predefined policies, and whether they can improve end-to-end task performance. We present Symbolic Constraint Agents (SCA), a framework that mines symbolic constraints from API documentation, refines them against execution traces, and checks the agent's tool calls with an SMT solver at runtime. A violation triggers a natural-language warning or, when the valid replacement is uniquely determined, an automatic repair. On AppWorld, refinement raises error-detection F1 from 37.0 to 58.3 on GPT-5.5 traces and from 39.3 to 61.9 on Qwen3.5-27B traces. At runtime, repair raises GPT-5.4-mini's task success by 5.4 points under a 40-call budget and 9.8 points when environment errors are hidden, while removing 59--87\% of failed calls across models, and transfers to $\tau^2$-bench with gains of up to 5.6 points. These findings show that automatically acquired symbolic constraints can improve tool-calling reliability and task completion, particularly when failures are costly or difficult to diagnose.
papers.summary: Deterministic checks on LLM agents' tool calls usually enforce predefined safety policies rather than the dependencies between tools in complex environments. Symbolic Constraint Agents (`SCA`) mine such constraints from API documentation, refine them against execution traces, and check tool calls at runtime with an SMT solver. A violation triggers either a natural-language warning or, when the valid replacement is uniquely determined, an automatic repair. On `AppWorld`, refinement raises error-detection F1 from 37.0 to 58.3 on `GPT-5.5` traces. Runtime repair **raises `GPT-5.4-mini` task success by 5.4 points under a 40-call budget and removes 59–87% of failed calls** across models. The approach transfers to `τ²-bench` with gains of up to 5.6 points.

papers.title: Narrow Decision Models: A System-1 Architecture for Calibrated, Typed Decisions
papers.abstract: System One models, introduced with TypeSafe's Jev, answer typed questions about a state with calibrated probabilities instead of generated text: choosing among options described in natural language (Choice), placing the state on an ordered scale (Score), or judging a yes/no statement (Noul). Jev is general-purpose: one set of weights, served as an API and adapted to a domain only through the request. We study the other end of the design space. A Narrow Decision Model (NDM) offers the same interface but is trained for the decisions of one organization, is small enough to run on its own infrastructure, and has an open architecture whose properties can be stated and tested. The state can be any text or structured record about which decisions are made; our running case is the routing of court communications. The architecture serializes a request as a prefix tree (the state, then each question, then each option) and runs a bidirectional encoder under a block attention mask with logical positions, so that each answer is, by construction, invariant to the order of its options and independent of the other questions asked. Routing through an organization chart is a composition of Choice decisions with an explicit "none of these" option. We describe training with proper scoring rules through a curriculum, calibration and abstention, decisions composed by rubrics, and a protocol that accepts or rejects the mechanism before held-out data is opened. A minimal validation on public and fictitious data shows that the invariances hold to rounding in a trained model, that a small instance routes on organization charts it has never seen well above lexical retrieval, and that, at equal compute, the block architecture reaches a lower loss than a pairwise cross-encoder. A first instance trained on real legal documents agrees with the LLM classifier in production on 91% of held-out documents.
papers.summary: Narrow Decision Models (`NDMs`) answer typed questions about a state with calibrated probabilities instead of generated text: choosing among options, placing the state on a scale, or judging a yes/no statement. Each model is trained for a single organization's decisions and is small enough to run on its own infrastructure. The architecture serializes a request as a prefix tree and runs a bidirectional encoder under a block attention mask. By construction, each answer is invariant to the order of its options and independent of the other questions asked. The authors cover training with proper scoring rules, calibration and abstention, and routing court communications through an organization chart. A small instance routes on unseen organization charts well above lexical retrieval, and a model trained on real legal documents **agrees with the production LLM classifier on 91% of held-out documents**.

papers.title: FTFM: Factorized Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are becoming a powerful alternative to conventional tabular learning, adapting to new datasets in context without task-specific training. Current architectures, however, face a trade-off: models that preserve cell-level representations are expensive because they repeatedly attend across rows and columns, while faster models collapse each row into a fixed embedding and lose this fine-grained state. We introduce Factorized Tabular Foundation Models (FTFM), which preserve cell representations while factorizing their computation through one contextual latent per row and one per column. Cells no longer attend to one another directly; instead, each cell is updated through the interaction of its row and column latents, reducing repeated attention while retaining feature-specific information. FTFM achieves competitive predictive performance in tabular classification on major benchmarks such as TabArena and BeyondArena.
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) adapt to new datasets in context, but face a trade-off. Models that keep per-cell representations are expensive because they repeatedly attend across rows and columns, while faster ones collapse each row into a single embedding. `FTFM` keeps cell representations but factorizes the computation through one contextual latent per row and one per column. Each cell is updated through the interaction of its row and column latents instead of attending to other cells directly. The model **achieves competitive classification performance on `TabArena` and `BeyondArena`** while avoiding repeated cell-to-cell attention.

papers.title: Learning Which Device to Call: Online Tool Grounding for LLM Agents in IoT
papers.abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) gives large language model (LLM) agents access to physical observations, but one requested capability is usually offered by several devices, and the agent's plan does not say which one to call. Existing work retrieves relevant tools and checks plan feasibility, without learning which eligible device returns a useful observation. Unlike previous works, we study online tool grounding: binding an already specified tool call to one physical endpoint under service cost and device participation constraints. We propose a framework that learns which physical device should execute each agent-issued call. It formulates selection as a contextual bandit problem and combines adaptive context partitions with hierarchical endpoint trees, so that execution feedback is reused across related requests and devices. Selection balances task success against service cost while respecting device capability, authorization, battery reserves, and availability. Gaussian reward aggregation provides an optional mechanism for protecting individual feedback values. Theoretical results establish a finite-horizon regret bound and differential privacy for released reward statistics under fixed, reward-independent assignments. In a simulated loading-dock workload, the proposed router achieves higher step success and better cost-adjusted service, at lower simulated device energy and latency, than nearest-device, advertised-quality, UCB1, and LinUCB selection.
papers.summary: In the Internet of Things (IoT), a capability that an LLM agent requests is often offered by several physical devices, and the agent's plan does not say which one to call. The authors define online tool grounding as the problem of binding an already-specified tool call to one device. They solve it as a contextual bandit, using adaptive context partitions and hierarchical endpoint trees so that feedback is reused across related requests and devices. The selection balances task success against cost while respecting device capability, authorization, battery and availability. The authors prove a finite-horizon regret bound and differential privacy for released reward statistics. In a simulated loading-dock workload, the router **achieves higher step success and better cost-adjusted service than nearest-device, `UCB1` and `LinUCB` selection** at lower energy and latency.

papers.title: Concurrent two-scale topology optimization of printable bone scaffolds via rectified-flow generation and exact latent-space refinement
papers.abstract: Bone scaffolds must reconcile a macroscale mechanical response with microscale geometric feasibility, yet conventional approaches to their design restrict attainable constitutive properties. This work presents a concurrent two-scale topology optimization framework; a conditional rectified flow generates periodic lattice microstructures, which are then refined in latent space by exact finite-element homogenization sensitivities. The resulting unit-cell geometries and their spatial assignments are jointly optimized under mechanical and feature-size constraints. In a distal rabbit femur benchmark, all eight flow-started refinements produce printable cells with maximum relative errors under 1\% across six prescribed engineering moduli. Constructing the implant from a single tiled cell reproduces intact whole-femur compliance within 0.1\% and regional strain energy within 0.35\% under four loading conditions. In human femoral reconstruction, multiscale concurrent optimization produces a cortical mid-shaft scaffold with porosity 63\% while satisfying the compliance constraint within 2\% under walking and stair-climbing loads. It achieves an 84\% porosity on a proximal cancellous scaffold with strain-energy deviations below 0.25\% under the same loads. Analysis of the learned representations reveals distinct architectural families in latent space. Further, the attention heads of the rectified-flow transformer specialize for spatial shifts -- learning the analogue of a finite-difference stencil -- and coordinate symmetries, with ablations showing their influence on generated topologies. These results establish a route to printable, mechanically constrained scaffold designs. The framework is general enough for extending to many other multiscale structural design applications including topology-microstructure co-design in metal additive manufacturing.
papers.summary: Bone scaffolds have to match a target mechanical response at the scale of the whole bone while staying printable at the scale of their internal lattice, and conventional design methods limit which material properties can be reached. The authors propose a concurrent two-scale topology optimization framework. A conditional `rectified flow` model generates periodic lattice unit cells, which are then refined in latent space using exact finite-element homogenization sensitivities, and the cell shapes and their placement are optimized jointly under mechanical and feature-size constraints. On a rabbit femur benchmark, all eight refinements produced printable cells within 1% of six target moduli. In human femur reconstruction, a cancellous scaffold reached **84% porosity with strain-energy deviations below 0.25%**. Analysis of the model also shows that its transformer attention heads specialize in spatial shifts, acting like a finite-difference stencil, and in coordinate symmetries.

papers.title: Flattening Fantasies: Analyzing Stereotypes in Pornographic Discourse
papers.abstract:
This study presents a large-scale quantitative analysis of 5.4 million video
  titles from xHamster, the world's fourth most visited pornography platform, to
  examine linguistic patterns used to describe different dimensions of
  identities (e.g., race and gender). Specifically, we investigate how
  nationalities, ethnic groups, and gender identities are portrayed in
  pornographic discourse, focusing on stereotypes and deviations from implicit
  norms of pornography. The results show the dominance of American pornography
  over other groups, which acts as the de facto norm for the adult industry. We
  identify persistent ethnic stereotypes reflecting colonial power dynamics,
  religious fetishization, and the sexualization of cultural taboos. The
  analysis reveals gendered representational differences across cultures, with a
  prevalent Madonna-Whore dichotomy in the portrayal of women and stereotypical
  depictions of men in physically dominant roles.
papers.summary: The authors run a large-scale quantitative linguistic analysis of **5.4 million video titles** from the pornography platform `xHamster` to study how nationalities, ethnic groups, and gender identities are described. They find that American pornography acts as the default norm for the industry. They also report persistent ethnic stereotypes that reflect colonial power dynamics, religious fetishization, and the sexualization of cultural taboos. Across cultures, women tend to be portrayed through a Madonna-Whore dichotomy, while men are cast in physically dominant roles.

papers.title: Design and Cross-Domain Evaluation of an Agent Execution Harness
papers.abstract: Completing complex tasks with language-model agents requires coordinating planning, execution, and review so the final result addresses the user's original objective. We present an agent execution harness that keeps the original objective separate from a revisable plan and an execution record. A planner assigns scoped tasks, workers produce outputs and artifacts, and a reviewer examines results against the original request before submitting or requesting additional work. Reusable domain-specific instructions guide these roles and are refined during construction using task inputs and execution trajectories, without official grading feedback. We evaluate complete harness configurations across terminal tasks, clinical responses, application building, and scientific questions. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, the harness passes 83 of 89 instances (93.26%); on HealthBench Professional, a Fable-configured system achieves a length-adjusted rubric score of 69.63 across 525 tasks. In a 53-task paired HealthBench comparison, the Fable-configured harness achieves an aggregate score 19.89 points higher than direct completion, despite a $-1.46$-point median task-level change; mean inference cost rises from \$0.29 to \$2.13 per task. We combine these outcomes with latency, documented instruction revisions, and reviewer decisions. Evaluating outcomes alongside execution trajectories and resource use clarifies how coordination supports task completion, where it introduces regressions, and at what cost.
papers.summary: The authors describe an execution harness for language-model agents that keeps the user's original objective separate from a revisable plan and an execution record. A planner assigns scoped tasks to workers, and a reviewer checks results against the original request before submitting or asking for more work. Reusable domain-specific instructions guide each role and are refined from task inputs and execution trajectories, without using official grading feedback. The harness passes **83 of 89 instances (93.26%) on `Terminal-Bench 2.1`** and scores 69.63 on `HealthBench Professional`. In a 53-task paired comparison it beats direct completion by 19.89 aggregate points, although the median per-task change is slightly negative and mean cost rises from $0.29 to $2.13 per task.

papers.title: Representations in Motion: Layer-wise Rotation and Trajectory Divergence in LLMs
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that activation dynamics--how representations change during inference--might be more revealing about language model behavior than static readouts from individual layers. In this work, we investigate the layer-wise evolution of representations of factuality, using true and false statements when the model is prompted to either lie or to be honest. We report a geometric phenomenon in which the factuality directions extracted from the lying and honest conditions appear to rotate away from each other across layers. We find that such layer-wise rotation also occurs in a task that requires the model to take different visual perspectives in the 3D world, suggesting that the rotation phenomenon might be indicative of manipulating conceptual spaces in general, rather than unique to factuality. We then investigate the "real time" transformation of conceptual representations on a trial-to-trial basis. We show that it is possible to make strong predictions about the model's target task and behavior from trajectories alone. In addition, diverging points in single-trial trajectories correspond to the onset of rotation in aggregated-trial analysis. Finally, we show that both rotation and divergent trajectories occur in more naturalistic settings in which models are not overtly prompted to "lie" but rather report false statements in the course of completing a different task.
papers.summary: The authors study how a language model's internal representation of factuality changes from layer to layer when the model is told either to lie or to be honest about true and false statements. They find that the factuality directions from the lying and honest conditions **rotate away from each other across layers**. The same rotation appears in a 3D visual perspective-taking task, which suggests it reflects a general way the model manipulates conceptual spaces rather than something specific to lying. Single-trial activation trajectories alone predict the model's task and behavior well, the point where trajectories diverge matches the onset of rotation, and both effects also appear when models produce false statements without being explicitly told to lie.

papers.title: Benchmark for Structured Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Perovskite Photovoltaics
papers.abstract: While retrieval-augmented language models increasingly serve as literature assistants in the physical sciences, existing benchmarks evaluate them primarily on qualitative text overlap or through model-based scoring rather than against verified experimental ground truth. In experimental materials disciplines such as perovskite photovoltaics, however, the most critical inquiries are inherently quantitative and aggregate measurements across dozens or hundreds of papers. Here, we present a quantitative question-answering benchmark where all 755 ground-truth answers are computed directly from 45,441 measured device records (40,889 human-curated records through 2021 and 4,552 records extracted from 2022-2026 literature). Benchmarking six retrieval architectures over 158,274 passages from 25,662 papers using an open 14B model on a single 24 GB GPU, standard passage retrieval tops out at 16-23% accuracy (compared to 1.6-6.5% zero-shot). In contrast, equipping the language model with read-only SQL execution over the structured device table elevates accuracy to 51.5% on historical and 50.8% on prospective literature -- a 33.01.8 percentage-point advantage over hybrid text retrieval. Aggregate queries spanning extrema, distributions, and filtered record counts prove virtually unsolvable via text retrieval alone, demonstrating that systematic table extraction is an operational prerequisite for literature-scale quantitative inquiry.
papers.summary: The authors build a quantitative question-answering benchmark for perovskite photovoltaics in which all 755 answers are computed from 45,441 measured device records, rather than judged by text overlap or by another model. They compare six retrieval architectures over 158,274 passages from 25,662 papers, using an open 14B model on a single 24 GB GPU. Standard passage retrieval tops out at 16-23% accuracy. Giving the model read-only SQL access to a structured device table raises accuracy to **51.5% on historical and 50.8% on newer literature**, roughly 33 percentage points above hybrid text retrieval. Aggregate questions about extremes, distributions, and filtered record counts are almost impossible to answer with text retrieval alone.

papers.title: Finite Interaction Lens: Structured Precision Sharing for Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Identifying which visual interventions interact in a vision-language model requires comparing their joint and separate effects. The resulting four-output difference can be small enough for rounding error to obscure it. We introduce the Finite Interaction Lens (FIL), a mixed-precision method for evaluating finite intervention families. At each selected linear projection, FIL decomposes each candidate's input into a native state, two single-intervention components, and a full-dimensional mixed residual. It projects the single-intervention components at higher precision and reuses the same numerical contributions in the joint candidates, while retaining every mixed residual and nonlinear trajectory. We derive a local cancellation identity and a conditional bound on error propagation through a smooth nonlinearity. In one MLP of Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, FIL reduces final interaction MSE by 94.4% on 16 synthetic families and by 99.85% and 99.35% in two separate four-image COCO studies, relative to a control that has the same nominal BF16-product budget and higher-precision single interventions but projects each joint candidate independently. One image accounts for most of the absolute gain in each COCO study. Higher-accuracy multi-product BF16 arithmetic on all candidates gives lower aggregate error at similar total query times. Single-product BF16 already recovers the reference choices in both candidate-selection tasks we tested. On these development inputs, FIL improves interaction fidelity at a fixed nominal precision budget. Its practical value depends on a task that needs the extra fidelity.
papers.summary: To find out which visual interventions interact inside a vision-language model, you compare their joint effect with their separate effects, but that difference can be small enough for rounding error to hide it. The `Finite Interaction Lens` (`FIL`) is a mixed-precision method that splits each candidate's input at a linear projection into separate components. It projects the single-intervention components at higher precision and reuses them across the joint candidates, while keeping every mixed residual. In one MLP layer of `Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct`, `FIL` cuts interaction mean squared error by **94.4% on synthetic families and over 99% in two `COCO` studies** compared with a control at the same nominal `BF16` budget. However, plain single-product `BF16` arithmetic already recovers the correct answers in the candidate-selection tasks the authors tested.

papers.title: CVTA: Cross-Variable Temporal Attention for Multivariate Irregular Time Series Prediction
papers.abstract: Irregularly sampled multivariate time series arise in many real-world domains such as healthcare, climate science, and large-scale monitoring systems. Characterized by asynchronous observations and heterogeneity across variables, such time series pose significant challenges for forecasting. In this work, we introduce Cross-Variable Temporal Attention (CVTA), a short-term, continuous-time forecasting framework that learns prediction functions from its compact, interpretable state summarizing recent temporal dynamics across variables. CVTA uses Variable-Conditioned Embeddings to project heterogeneous variables into variable-specific latent spaces, and applies temporal attention to capture cross-variable dependencies from this state. Furthermore, we demonstrate that CVTA can be integrated as an auxiliary module into existing state-of-the-art prediction models through a dynamic meta-decision model. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world benchmarks show that CVTA achieves strong short-term predictive accuracy, supports efficient online inference, improves existing prediction models when used as an auxiliary module, and learns attention patterns that align well with domain knowledge.
papers.summary: Forecasting multivariate time series is hard when variables are sampled irregularly and asynchronously, as is common in healthcare and climate data. `Cross-Variable Temporal Attention` (`CVTA`) is a short-term, continuous-time forecasting framework that maps each variable into its own latent space using `Variable-Conditioned Embeddings`, then applies temporal attention over a compact state to capture dependencies between variables. `CVTA` can also be plugged into existing forecasting models as an auxiliary module through a dynamic meta-decision model. Experiments on several real-world benchmarks show **strong short-term accuracy and efficient online inference**, improvements when added to existing models, and attention patterns that match domain knowledge.

papers.title: Assertion and Belief: Moore's Paradox in Language Models
