papers.abstract: Moore's paradox \citep{moore1942} concerns sentences such as ``It is raining, but I don't believe that it is,'' which may well be true yet cannot be sensibly asserted. The absurdity lies not in the content but in the act, since to assert is to vouch for one's own belief. This makes the paradox a test of whether language models take the speech act into account when computing meaning. We present the first test of Moore's paradox in LLMs, evaluating 12 models on a curated set of Moorean sentences in varied contexts. We find that models largely recognize the infelicity of Moorean sentences, and that the judgement is not tied to a memorized form and tracks the speech act. Using the Rational Speech Act framework (RSA; \citealt{goodmanfrank2016}), we then test whether these judgements arise from a listener reasoning about a speaker. We find the models' own listeners do not reason about their own speakers, and their reasoning traces suggest that they instead recall knowledge about the paradox and apply rules therein. The models thus appear to have learned the paradox as a fact about sentences, not as a requirement on speakers.
papers.summary: Moore's paradox concerns sentences such as "It is raining, but I don't believe that it is", which can be true but cannot sensibly be asserted, so they test whether a model accounts for the act of speaking when it interprets meaning. Across 12 language models and a curated set of Moorean sentences, the models largely recognize that these sentences are odd, and their judgments depend on the speech act rather than on a memorized surface form. Tests based on the `Rational Speech Act` (`RSA`) framework show, however, that the models' listeners do not reason about their speakers. The authors conclude that **models learned the paradox as a fact about sentences rather than as a requirement on speakers**, and the models' reasoning traces show them recalling and applying rules about the paradox.

papers.title: Divergence based Ranked Preference Alignment for LLMs
papers.abstract: Alignment of large language models typically relies on pairwise preference feedback, though ranked feedback can capture more comprehensive information across multiple responses within a single annotation. However, ranked-preference alignment is underexplored in practice compared to simpler pairwise approaches, potentially resulting in suboptimal behavior. Concurrently, recent research has conceptualized large language model alignment objectives as divergence estimators between aligned (preferred) and unaligned (less-preferred) response distributions, resulting in a family of objectives with an interpretable theoretical foundation and strong empirical performance. This work unifies these perspectives by introducing $f$-RPO, a $f$-divergence objective for ranked preference optimization that extends divergence-based alignment to ranked feedback and recovers pairwise preference alignment as a special case. Our theoretical analysis establishes rank-order consistency, showing that $f$-RPO preserves the underlying preference ordering at convergence. Empirical results indicate that total-variation and reverse-KL variants of the proposed objective consistently outperform ranked-alignment baselines in both ranking and generation quality across Qwen, Llama, & Gemma models ranging from 0.5B to 8B parameters.
papers.summary: Language-model alignment usually relies on pairwise preferences, even though rankings over several responses carry more information per annotation. `f-RPO` extends divergence-based alignment objectives, which treat alignment as estimating a divergence between preferred and less-preferred response distributions, to ranked feedback. Pairwise preference alignment falls out as a special case. A theoretical analysis shows that the objective preserves the true preference ordering at convergence. **The total-variation and reverse-KL variants consistently beat ranked-alignment baselines** on both ranking and generation quality across `Qwen`, `Llama`, and `Gemma` models from 0.5B to 8B parameters.

papers.title: Distributionally-Robust Policy Learning with Observational Data
papers.abstract: Policy learning from observational data is fundamental to applications ranging from personalized medicine to welfare-program targeting, but standard approaches optimize empirical performance and may fail when the deployment distribution differs from the training distribution. We study \emph{distributionally-robust policy learning}: given observational data, we seek a policy $\pi \in \Pi$ that maximizes the worst-case policy value over an $f$-divergence ball of radius $\rho$ around the data-generating distribution. We propose an estimator built on cross-fitted doubly-robust scores for the conditional treatment effect, paired with a DRO solver that handles \texttt{KL}, $\chi^2$, and \texttt{CVaR} ambiguity sets. We establish two convergence guarantees. First, the estimated policy attains the standard $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$ rate on its DRO regret, and inherits the doubly-robust property -- the rate continues to hold whenever either the outcome model or the propensity model is consistently estimated, even at slow nonparametric rates. We then propose a sample-splitting bias-correction algorithm derived from the Lagrangian dual, and show that under a Tsybakov-style margin condition on the treatment-effect, the estimator attains a fast rate of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-(1+\alpha)/(2+\alpha)})$ , interpolating between $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{n})$ and $\widetilde{O}(1/n)$ as the margin parameter $\alpha$ ranges over $[0,\infty)$. To our knowledge, this is the first work to incorporate a margin condition into the analysis of distributionally-robust policy learning, and the first to obtain fast rates in this setting. Empirically, on synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments calibrated to a welfare-to-work program, distributional robustness yields meaningful improvements over empirical welfare maximization when training and test distributions differ.
papers.summary: Policies learned from observational data, for example in personalized medicine or welfare targeting, can fail when the deployment population differs from the training population. The authors learn a policy that maximizes worst-case value over an f-divergence ball around the data distribution. Their estimator combines cross-fitted doubly-robust treatment-effect scores with a distributionally robust optimization solver that supports `KL`, chi-squared, and `CVaR` ambiguity sets. It achieves the standard root-n regret rate while remaining doubly robust. With a bias-correction step and a Tsybakov-style margin condition, it achieves **the first fast rates for distributionally robust policy learning**, and experiments calibrated to a welfare-to-work program show gains over empirical welfare maximization when the distribution shifts.

papers.title: Cognitive Map in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: It has long been proposed that animals construct cognitive maps to support flexible behavior in novel environments. We tested whether large language models form similar representations using relational reasoning tasks and causal "mosaic experiments" that manipulate internal activations in open-weight language models. Models beyond the ten-billion-parameter scale successfully inferred unstated relationships between entities and generalized to synthetic entity names. Across model and task families, models generated abstract representations of relational structure and combined them additively with representations of entity identity, binding entities to roles within that structure. Models stored observed relationships as pairwise links that they composed retrospectively when queried, rather than prospectively positioning each entity in a global coordinate system. Binding was mediated by a sparse, distributed set of key--value pairs; by perturbing these pairs, we implanted "false memories" that altered model behavior in predictable ways. Overall, our findings reveal an internal organization analogous to a cognitive map that explains how language models reason with limited information.
papers.summary: Animals are thought to build "cognitive maps" for flexible behavior, and the authors test whether language models build something similar, using relational reasoning tasks and causal "mosaic" experiments that swap internal activations in open-weight models. Models above about ten billion parameters inferred unstated relationships and generalized to made-up entity names. They represent relational structure abstractly and add it to entity identity, binding each entity to a role. Rather than placing entities in a global coordinate system, **models store pairwise links and compose them only when queried**. The binding runs through a sparse set of key-value pairs, and perturbing those pairs implanted "false memories" that changed model behavior in predictable ways.

papers.title: Text Dominance in Paralinguistic Conflict: Tracing Suppression Through Audio LLM Circuits
papers.abstract: Audio LLMs deployed in settings such as crisis hotlines and customer support are only useful beyond speech-to-text pipelines if they use acoustic cues rather than the transcript alone. We test whether they prioritise transcript content over paralinguistic cues (emotion, speaker identity, sarcasm) and trace the mechanism when they do. Across six audio LLMs under LISTEN-style conflict conditions, the mean text-dominance rate on mismatched text+audio items is 0.78 (0.86 excluding sarcasm). In the most text-dominant screened model, probing shows speaker identity remains linearly decodable at ceiling at the language model's input, so the failure is not perceptual. Back-patching, reported to repair lexical text dominance, has no measurable effect here; but it also fails on its own source task in our replication (n=300), so we treat its null as uninformative rather than as evidence of non-transfer. Attention knockout partially restores audio-grounded output by blocking the claim from propagating through intermediate tokens during open-ended generation, whereas blocking the answer position's direct connection to the conflicting claim has no effect. The claim's influence therefore travels through an intermediate relay rather than a single severable edge. The effect appears only in free-form generation and not in closed-set multiple choice, suggesting that benchmarks relying on that format may be systematically blind to interventions of this kind. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/AdvayRoongta/audio-llm-mech-interp.
papers.summary: Audio language models only add value over speech-to-text pipelines if they use acoustic cues such as emotion, speaker identity, and sarcasm instead of just the transcript. Across six audio LLMs, given text and audio that conflict, the models follow the text **78% of the time on average**, even though probing shows that speaker identity is still perfectly decodable at the language model's input. Back-patching, a fix previously reported for text dominance, had no effect, but it also failed to replicate on its original task. Attention knockout partially restored audio-grounded answers by blocking the conflicting claim from spreading through intermediate tokens, and this effect appears only in free-form generation, so multiple-choice benchmarks may miss interventions like this entirely.

papers.title: When Better Opportunities Backfire: Service Worker Responses to Parallel AI Deployment in Customer Acquisition
papers.abstract: As AI voice agents get deployed in high-volume contact centers, firms can route low-intent leads to AI and allocate high-intent leads to human workers. Drawing on sequential search theory, we posit that AI-induced task allocation reshapes work, enriching opportunities facing human workers but also raising their reservation value for continuing with the lead in hand, making them less willing to persist. We study the effects of an AI voice-agent deployment at a Chinese online health-insurance brokerage using more than a half million customer outreach records surrounding the rollout. Adopting a regression-discontinuity-in-time design, we trace how worker behavior changes across the workday. Results show that the enrichment of human-facing opportunities concentrates early in the workday, raising the probability that a call is a high-intent lead by about 23 percentage points on the first three calls and fading to zero later. However, customer acquisition by human workers declines precisely where the enrichment is greatest, falling about 5 percentage points on the first three calls and flattening over the day. Consistent with the theorized reservation value mechanism, workers reallocate their earliest leads about 8 percentage points more often and persist less with them, shortening those calls by about 13%. A calibrated decomposition analysis further shows that the modest gain from improved lead ordering is outweighed by a much larger negative behavioral response. By reshaping the quality and within-workday distribution of opportunities, parallel AI deployment alters how workers pursue tasks, highlighting opportunity distribution as an important service operations state variable beyond workload and congestion.
papers.summary: The authors study what happens to human sales agents when a firm sends low-intent leads to AI voice agents and keeps high-intent leads for people. They use more than half a million outreach records from a Chinese online health-insurance brokerage and a regression-discontinuity-in-time design. After the rollout, the first three calls of each workday were about 23 percentage points more likely to be high-intent leads. Yet **human customer acquisition on those same calls fell by about 5 percentage points**, as workers reassigned early leads more often and kept those calls about 13% shorter. A decomposition shows that this behavioral response outweighs the small gain from better lead ordering, which is consistent with richer opportunities making workers less willing to persist with the lead in hand.

papers.title: Adversarial Post-Training of Foundation Models for High-Frequency Trading
papers.abstract: While autoregressive foundation models trained on limit order book (LOB) data show state-of-the-art performance for market simulation, pre-training with cross-entropy neither penalizes the compounding of sampling errors over free-running rollouts nor targets desired market properties. We introduce a post-training method for LOB foundation models using a Wasserstein generative adversarial network (GAN) objective. A critic, trained online on rollouts through the true, non-differentiable matching engine, guides updates from evolution strategies over rank-4 LoRA perturbations of the pre-trained generator, under a KL trust region. For efficiency, we use EGGROLL (Evolution Guided GeneRal Optimisation via Low-rank Learning), a memory-efficient variant of evolution strategies. On a held-out panel, adversarial post-training improves LOB-Bench realism by 17.6% (WS-21) and 17.0% (Mean-$L_1$), while selection-matched random-perturbation and compute-matched continued-pre-training controls yield no improvement. Post-training is thus a necessary stage that more pre-training does not replace. Per-position divergence measurements show that it slows error accumulation over 500-message rollouts from $3.1\times$ to $2.3\times$. Adversarial post-training is also inexpensive, requiring under 50M training tokens and 12 GPU-hours per seed, three orders of magnitude below the 48B-token pre-training budget. Ablations over critic inputs, optimizers, and the population-rollout trade-off, together with an analysis of reward hacking, yield practical design guidelines for adversarial post-training.
papers.summary: Autoregressive foundation models trained on limit order book (LOB) data simulate markets well, but cross-entropy pretraining neither penalizes errors that compound during long rollouts nor targets the market properties people care about. The authors post-train such models with a Wasserstein GAN objective. A critic, trained on rollouts through the real non-differentiable matching engine, guides updates found by evolution strategies (`EGGROLL`) over rank-4 `LoRA` perturbations, with a KL trust region keeping the model near its starting point. This improves `LOB-Bench` realism by **about 17%** and slows error accumulation over 500-message rollouts, while compute-matched continued pretraining gives no improvement. It needs under 50M tokens and 12 GPU-hours per seed.

papers.title: PRISM: Prior Relational Information for Self-supervised Modeling to Enhance Solubility OOD Generalization
papers.abstract: Solubility depends on intermolecular interactions between solutes and solvents, and is central to drug discovery, chemical and materials process engineering. Its prediction requires out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization to unseen solutes, solvents, and solvent mixtures, where supervised methods suffer from data scarcity, and existing self-supervised methods do not explicitly learn chemically meaningful relations. Learning chemically meaningful relational information without labels can alleviate data scarcity and improve OOD generalization, but remains challenging. We introduce Prior Relational Information for Self-supervised Modeling (PRISM) and apply it to solubility OOD generalization. PRISM is a label-free pretraining framework that converts expert-defined chemical priors into relational teachers. For solubility prediction, it trains four encoders to preserve the population-level relational information from priors capturing hydrophobic, electrostatic, polarizability, and substructural effects, using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence to match distance-based neighborhood distributions during pretraining. Across scaffold, solute, and solvent OOD settings, PRISM matches or surpasses supervised and self-supervised baselines. Under mixed-solvent OOD, freezing the four PRISM encoders and training a lightweight fusion-and-composition head outperforms strong baselines and substantially reduces run-to-run variation. Ablations and control studies confirm that gains stem from chemically meaningful relational structures baked into the encoders by PRISM. We expect this strategy of turning relational priors into self-supervision signals to extend beyond solubility prediction to domains where chemically or biologically meaningful relational priors are available.
papers.summary: Solubility prediction has to generalize to solutes, solvents, and solvent mixtures that were not seen in training, where labeled data is scarce. `Prior Relational Information for Self-supervised Modeling` (`PRISM`) is a label-free pretraining framework that turns expert chemical priors into relational teachers. It trains four encoders, covering hydrophobic, electrostatic, polarizability, and substructural effects, to match each prior's neighborhood distributions using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. `PRISM` matches or beats supervised and self-supervised baselines on scaffold, solute, and solvent out-of-distribution splits. On unseen solvent mixtures, **frozen `PRISM` encoders with a lightweight head outperform strong baselines** and vary much less from run to run.

papers.title: Safety Offset Learning: When Benign Fine-Tuning Misaligns LLMs
papers.abstract: Safety risks from fine-tuning are commonly characterized by the harmfulness of the training data:harmful fine-tuning is considered dangerous, while benign fine-tuning is often assumed to preservealignment. We argue that this view misses a more fundamental factor-the behavioral transition inducedby supervision. Harmful fine-tuning and safety-degrading benign fine-tuning can both be understoodas learning the same refusal-to-compliance transition, but on different data distributions. We studywhether such a transition learned on benign inputs can generalize to harmful requests. We constructbenign examples that an aligned model initially tends to refuse and pair them with their originalharmless responses, creating a discrepancy between the model's initial refusal and the supervisedanswer. Fine-tuning on these examples increases harmful compliance, but only when two conditionshold together: the discrepancy is large enough, and it cannot be resolved through a narrow surface-levelshortcut. With the induced discrepancy matched, varying only whether it is localized changes harmfulcompliance by an order of magnitude; raising the discrepancy does not help while a shortcut remainsavailable, and removing the shortcut does not help while the discrepancy is small. Building on thisobservation, we introduce SAFEOFF, a dataset of benign instructions rewritten to raise the alignedmodel's refusal likelihood and paired with their original answers. Across three aligned LLMs and threesafety benchmarks, SAFEOFF substantially weakens safety alignment despite containing no explicitharmful supervision, suggesting that fine-tuning safety depends not only on what data a model sees, butalso on which behavioral boundary the supervision moves.
papers.summary: The authors argue that fine-tuning risks depend less on how harmful the training data is and more on whether the training pushes the model from refusing to complying. They build benign examples that an aligned model tends to refuse and pair them with their original harmless answers. Fine-tuning on these examples raises harmful compliance, but only when the gap between the model's refusal and the target answer is large and cannot be closed by a narrow surface-level shortcut. Their resulting dataset, `SAFEOFF`, **substantially weakens safety alignment across three aligned LLMs and three safety benchmarks despite containing no harmful supervision**.

papers.title: Curriculum Learning Teaches LLMs Long-Horizon Implicit Reasoning, Up To A Limit
papers.abstract: LLMs "reason" by externalizing intermediate steps as tokens through chain-of-thought (CoT), yet even frontier reasoning models hit abrupt performance cliffs on long-horizon tasks. Implicit reasoning (reasoning within a single forward pass) is useful during CoT generation, as the model can "search ahead" to decide the correct next move without explicit search. Models with weak implicit reasoning are more likely to commit to wrong paths and must attempt to recover via backtracking, while models with strong implicit reasoning identify the correct proof strategy directly, shortening the CoT. However, prior work shows LLMs struggle to reason implicitly beyond shallow depths, with no relief from scale. We investigate whether curriculum learning can extend this depth by fine-tuning on examples with progressively increasing vocabulary size and lookahead (the number of steps a model must search ahead to identify the correct next move). At matched compute, curriculum-trained models achieve lookaheads where no-curriculum training fails. Qwen3-0.6B reaches 98% accuracy on problems with lookahead up to 256 with curriculum, compared to 45% without. However, progress slows as fine-tuning continues, following a saturating exponential that suggests a maximum intrinsic lookahead to which models can learn to reason implicitly. Larger models reach higher fitted ceilings, fine-tuning pretrained models far outpaces training from scratch, and curriculum step sizes that are too large stall progression. Finally, the capability acquired on synthetic data transfers to natural language reasoning, with curriculum-trained models outperforming models trained without curriculum at matched compute on 11 natural language reasoning benchmarks.
papers.summary: Language models struggle to reason implicitly, that is, to search ahead within a single forward pass, beyond shallow depths, and scale alone does not seem to help. The authors fine-tune on a curriculum of examples with steadily increasing vocabulary size and lookahead, meaning the number of steps the model must search ahead to pick the correct next move. At matched compute, **`Qwen3-0.6B` reaches 98% accuracy at lookahead up to 256 with the curriculum versus 45% without**. Gains follow a saturating curve that points to a maximum learnable lookahead, which is higher for larger models. The acquired skill transfers to 11 natural-language reasoning benchmarks.

papers.title: CheXFuse: Guided Differential Joint Attention Fusion for Robust Multimodal Chest X-Ray Classification in Data-Scarce Medical Settings
papers.abstract: A central challenge in multimodal learning is how to fuse modalities that differ substantially in predictive strength. When one modality provides a much stronger representation than another, indiscriminate cross-modal interaction can introduce weak, redundant, or unstable signals, limiting or even degrading performance relative to the strongest unimodal representation. To address this problem, we propose CheXFuse, a multimodal fusion framework based on Guided Differential Joint Attention (GuDJA). CheXFuse combines image and text token representations within a joint multimodal sequence, where learned token guidance emphasizes informative representations and differential attention reduces less useful attention responses. We evaluate CheXFuse on the Indiana University (IU) Chest X-ray dataset, using binary (normal vs. abnormal) classification as the downstream task. Experiments are conducted under both original-report and masked-report settings, with the latter serving as a controlled stress test under reduced textual informativeness. CheXFuse with GuDJA achieves the strongest mean overall performance across the evaluated baselines and ablations, reaching 95.73% accuracy, 95.79% F1-score, 96.54% recall, and 95.28% sensitivity at 95% specificity (Sens@95Spec) with original reports, and 95.58%, 95.60%, 95.60%, and 94.34%, respectively, under masked reports. These results suggest that GuDJA provides a promising fusion strategy under asymmetric or partially reduced modality informativeness.
papers.summary: When one input modality is much more informative than another, naive fusion can perform worse than the strongest single modality. `CheXFuse` uses `Guided Differential Joint Attention` (`GuDJA`), which puts image and text tokens in one joint sequence, applies learned token guidance to emphasize informative tokens, and uses differential attention to suppress less useful attention responses. On normal-versus-abnormal classification on the `Indiana University (IU) Chest X-ray` dataset, it reaches **95.73% accuracy with the original reports**. Accuracy stays at 95.58% when the reports are masked to reduce how informative the text is.

papers.title: Weighted State Souping for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval
papers.abstract: State space models (SSMs) combine fast inference and fixed state size with competitive language-modeling performance. Recently, state souping has been proposed as a procedure whereby an SSM independently encodes chunks of tokens like documents, tool definitions, or memory records. The resulting state encodings may be cached and recombined to cheaply construct a context for downstream queries. However, both state souping and vanilla SSMs deteriorate on long, crowded contexts, limiting their utility for long-horizon domains. To address this issue, we propose weighted state souping, a simple method that learns query-dependent weights for composing cached states. The resulting models improve long-context performance substantially across both single- and multi-hop document question answering, needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, variable tracking, and tool use. Our method can be further adapted into an efficient sparse variant, yielding near-constant encoding cost with respect to context length while preserving (and sometimes improving) performance. We also present simple theoretical arguments that illustrate why souping works and when it may fail, and discuss informally the advantages of weighted souping. Weighted state souping thus combines reusable context representations with selective retrieval, offering an efficient approach to language modeling over large collections of documents, tools, and other forms of structured context that increasingly dominate modern agentic workloads.
papers.summary: State space models (SSMs) can encode chunks such as documents, tool definitions, or memory records independently, cache those states, and later combine them ("state souping") to build a context cheaply, but the approach degrades on long, crowded contexts. Weighted state souping learns query-dependent weights for combining cached states. It **substantially improves long-context performance** on single- and multi-hop document QA, needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, variable tracking, and tool use. A sparse variant keeps encoding cost nearly constant as context grows while preserving accuracy. The authors also give simple theoretical arguments for when souping works and when it fails.

papers.title: Zephyrus-R1: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Weather Reporting
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key method for training AI models in scientific applications, but RL remains difficult when outputs cannot easily be verified against a known ground-truth answer. Natural-language weather forecast reports are one such domain: they translate atmospheric data into assessments of weather evolution, hazards, and uncertainty for both the general public and key decision-makers. Unlike numerical weather-analysis questions, they admit many valid outputs, which limits deterministic verification. To address this, we develop Zephyrus-R1, a practical framework for RL on scientific weather forecast reporting. We focus on three key components of the agentic RL pipeline: reward design, curriculum learning, and an analysis of human-expert alignment. To encourage both report legibility and factual accuracy, we design a reward function that combines a meteorological rubric with bidirectional claim entailment, both evaluated against National Weather Service reference reports. Our framework optimizes this reward in a simulated tool-calling environment, enabling vision-language agents to gather and analyze forecast evidence across regions and lead times before producing a report. We use annotations from three meteorologists to audit the claim labels produced by our LLM judges. Finally, a curriculum helps small models first develop tool use and scientific reasoning through RL on verifiable weather-analysis questions, then optimize the open-ended report reward. After training Qwen3.5-4B with Zephyrus-R1, we improve the mean across six judge-metric scores by 26% over the base model and achieve results competitive with frontier open-weight models. For Qwen3.8-27B, we improve the same mean by 13% over the base model, by 6.7% over Kimi-K3, and by 2.7% over GPT-5.6-Luna.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is hard to apply when outputs, such as natural-language weather forecast reports, cannot be checked against a single correct answer. `Zephyrus-R1` trains vision-language agents in a simulated tool-calling environment to gather forecast evidence across regions and lead times before writing a report. The reward combines a meteorological rubric with bidirectional claim entailment against National Weather Service reference reports, and three meteorologists audited the LLM judges' claim labels. A curriculum first trains tool use on verifiable weather-analysis questions. Training **improves `Qwen3.5-4B` by 26% over its base model** on the mean of six judge metrics, and the trained `Qwen3.8-27B` edges out `Kimi-K3` and `GPT-5.6-Luna`.

papers.title: MapSteal: Map-based Autonomous Knowledge Stealing Attack Against Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Knowledge acquisition from black-box large language models (LLMs) offers a practical approach to adapting smaller student models. However, many existing methods rely on predefined queries or student feedback to guide acquisition, leaving autonomous expansion of knowledge targets an important challenge. We propose \textbf{MapSteal}, a student-independent framework for structured recursive knowledge acquisition. Starting from a small set of initial roots, MapSteal represents acquisition targets using structured states and recursively expands them through teacher-proposed directions. Question realization, proposal admission, and deduplication constrain the acquisition process, while root-aware scheduling organizes exploration under a fixed QA budget. The resulting question--answer pairs are used to adapt student models without requiring student feedback during acquisition. Experiments with Qwen3.5 students at 2B, 4B, and 9B scales show competitive downstream performance across six medical and cybersecurity benchmarks. On the 4B medical evaluation, Full MapSteal improves average accuracy by 1.17 percentage points over a simplified recursive acquisition variant. Cross-domain evaluations show that gains depend on the domain and evaluation panel. These results demonstrate the feasibility of structured, student-independent recursive acquisition while highlighting the distinction between generating acquisition targets and obtaining useful training supervision. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/LabRAI/Mapsteal} {https://github.com/LabRAI/Mapsteal}.
papers.summary: Smaller student models can be adapted by harvesting knowledge from black-box large language models (LLMs), but most existing methods rely on predefined queries or on feedback from the student to decide what to ask. `MapSteal` starts from a few seed topics, represents what to acquire as structured states, and recursively expands them along directions the teacher proposes. Question realization, admission filtering, deduplication and root-aware scheduling keep the process within a fixed budget of question-answer pairs, and the resulting pairs are used to fine-tune the student without any student feedback. Across six medical and cybersecurity benchmarks, `Qwen3.5` students at 2B, 4B and 9B reach competitive performance, with the full method adding **1.17 percentage points of average accuracy over a simplified recursive variant on 4B medical evaluation**; gains in cross-domain evaluation depend on the domain and the benchmark panel.

papers.title: Conditional Average Treatment Effect Distillation for Hypothetical State-Intervention Targeting Under Budget Constraints
papers.abstract: Personalized public-health targeting must capture heterogeneous intervention benefits while remaining interpretable under resource constraints. Flexible causal-effect models can be hard to operationalize, while coarse subgroup policies may lose individualized effect information. We study budget-constrained hypothetical state interventions in observational data without a logged historical decision policy. For obesity, elevated glucose, and lifetime smoking-history states, causal-structure-informed pretreatment covariates are prespecified, with capacity capped at 70% of those observed in the adverse state. We evaluate causal distillation where Causal Forest and Bayesian Causal Forest teachers estimate conditional average treatment effects (CATEs), which decision tree and random forest students approximate. We compare individualized policies with unsupervised K-means subgroup policies and supervised causal-tree policies with leaf counts matched to K-means cluster counts. Observational policies are assessed on held-out data using a doubly robust estimator, bootstrap uncertainty, and decision-focused teacher-student fidelity measures. Across PIMA obesity and glucose and NHANES smoking-history experiments, each distilled student was within 0.011 absolute utility of its teacher, with allocation Jaccard similarities of 0.738-0.937. K-means and causal-tree policies were also competitive, with the highest point-estimate policy varying by application. Prespecified paired comparisons were nonsignificant after Holm adjustment, while near-budget-boundary agreement was less stable than global fidelity for some teacher-student pairs. Findings support causal distillation for translating flexible effect models into simpler budgeted targeting rules, although observational estimates depend on causal-identification assumptions and require longitudinal or prospective validation.
papers.summary: Public-health targeting under a fixed budget needs policies that capture individual differences in treatment benefit while staying interpretable. The authors use `Causal Forest` and `Bayesian Causal Forest` teachers to estimate conditional average treatment effects (CATEs), then distill them into decision-tree and random-forest students. They compare these students with K-means subgroup policies and causal-tree policies for hypothetical interventions on obesity, glucose and smoking history in the `PIMA` and `NHANES` datasets, with capacity capped at 70%. **Each distilled student came within 0.011 absolute utility of its teacher**, with allocation Jaccard similarities of 0.738 to 0.937. Simpler subgroup policies were also competitive, and paired comparisons were not significant after Holm correction.

papers.title: Selecting and Composing Agent Design Patterns: Industrial Case Evidence and Controlled Reference-System Experiments
papers.abstract: Agent pattern catalogs describe architectural alternatives, but engineers also need evidence for selecting and composing them. We extend a cognitive-function--execution-topology framework with an evidence-driven selection procedure and explicit composition contracts. The study combines two industrial case accounts, a contributor's collaboration design, seven practitioner workshops, and executable fault-injection experiments. Three local reference systems use SQLite state, shared artifact files, and a file-backed map-publication surrogate. A 2 x 2 ablation separates function-specific contracts from execution controls across 36 scenario families, with ten input variants per family. Under equal family weighting, composition correctly completes or safely refuses 11 of 12 families in each system, compared with 2, 2, and 1 for the simple baselines. These are constructed challenge-suite results, not production success rates. Recovery without consumer-side verification increases false-success cases in the map surrogate. All composed systems still fail a boundary case in which trusted evidence is wrong. An audit of a frozen six-arm language-model pilot reproduces its scores but confirms an evaluator-dependent ranking reversal. The contribution connects industrial failure, pattern selection, executable treatment, external acceptance, and revision. Selection is demonstrated rather than evaluated against an alternative procedure; catalog admission rests on separate criteria. The results support bounded composition mechanisms, not a claim that the framework improves engineers' design decisions over an equally informative conventional method.
papers.summary: Catalogs of agent design patterns describe alternatives but give engineers little evidence for choosing and combining them. The authors extend a framework that maps cognitive functions to execution topologies, adding an evidence-driven selection procedure and explicit composition contracts. They support it with industrial case accounts, practitioner workshops, and fault-injection experiments on three local reference systems. In a 2×2 ablation over 36 scenario families, **composed systems correctly completed or safely refused 11 of 12 families, versus 1 to 2 for simple baselines**, although every composed system still failed when trusted evidence was wrong. The authors stress that these are constructed challenge-suite results rather than production success rates.

papers.title: The Forward/Inverse Duality of Controlled Emergence:A Computational Design Program from Explanation to Engineering
papers.abstract: The macroscopic capabilities of intelligent systems arise from the local interactions of many simple units. When such systems are deployed in the real world, their behaviour must nevertheless be constrained, leaving designers caught between releasing adaptability and preventing loss of control, yet without formal tools to resolve the dilemma. This paper proposes a unified research program for controlled emergence that restates this tension as a pair of dual problems: the forward problem explains macroscopic behaviour from local rules, and the inverse problem solves for controllable rules and readout mechanisms from a desired target. We take an augmented quintuple as the formal object shared by both ends, and decompose ``engineering'' into three independently measurable coordinates: controllability, reproducibility, and degree of formalizability. On this basis we give three testable working hypotheses (critical scale; the cooperation and trade-off between constraint and adaptability; minimal constraint) and one feasibility criterion, which reduce inverse design from unconstrained optimization to interval checking. The program takes explicit failure boundaries as its premise, does not pursue complete control, and always preserves the system's room for self-organization. The reduced pilot experiment attached to this paper serves only to verify the executability of the research protocol and does not constitute a statistical test of the working hypotheses. This design language generalizes to multi-agent artificial intelligence, the industrial internet, and emergency response systems, all of which must confront emergence and controllability at once.
papers.summary: Designers of systems whose capabilities emerge from many simple interacting units face a tension between allowing adaptability and keeping control, without formal tools to manage it. The authors propose a research program that splits this into a forward problem (explaining macroscopic behaviour from local rules) and an inverse problem (deriving controllable rules from a desired target), built on a shared augmented quintuple formalism. They break engineering down into controllability, reproducibility and degree of formalizability, and state three testable hypotheses plus a feasibility criterion that **reduces inverse design from unconstrained optimization to interval checking**. The attached pilot experiment only shows that the protocol can be executed and does not test the hypotheses statistically.

papers.title: Clean Forcing: Drift-Resistant Autoregressive Video Diffusion with a Frozen Base
papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate streaming video of arbitrary length by conditioning each new chunk of frames on those already generated. However, they suffer from exposure bias, where a model trained on clean context must continue from its own imperfect outputs, and errors compound until quality collapses within seconds (drift). Existing methods either require cluster-scale base retraining, apply training-free inference corrections with inconsistent results, or train frozen-base correctors for sampling and cache errors. We instead find that drift is largely deterministic and therefore learnable, as holding the noisy state fixed while varying only the history reveals a counterfactual velocity gap that is ~95% systematic across noise seeds. Based on this observation, we introduce Clean Forcing, which trains a 5.9M-parameter LoRA corrector on the frozen base model to regress this gap, with a closed-loop stage that adds DAgger-style aggregation and a drift-contraction objective to expose the corrector to its own rollouts. Because the clean histories can be the base model's own single-shot generations, training needs no real videos, and the merged corrector adds no inference cost. In 50 s text-to-video generation, Clean Forcing reduces {\Delta}-drift from +11.3 to +1.65 without real video and to -0.16 with 40 real clips, improving on the best published result of +3.57 with over 150x less data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Clean Forcing outperforms prior methods in aesthetic quality and data efficiency with reduced drift for long-horizon video generation.
papers.summary: Autoregressive video diffusion models can stream video of any length, but because they continue from their own imperfect outputs, errors compound and quality collapses within seconds (drift). The authors find that drift is about 95% systematic across noise seeds, which makes it learnable. `Clean Forcing` trains a 5.9M-parameter `LoRA` corrector on a frozen base model to regress this gap, using a DAgger-style closed-loop stage and a drift-contraction objective. It can be trained on the base model's own generations without real video and adds no inference cost once merged. In 50-second text-to-video generation, **drift falls from +11.3 to +1.65 with no real video and to −0.16 with 40 real clips**, beating the best published result of +3.57 with over 150× less data.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Gated SHAP-Dirichlet Refinement for MRI-Based Depression Classification
papers.abstract: Structural MRI-based classification of major depressive disorder (MDD) remains challenging due to subtle, heterogeneous anatomical changes. We propose uncertainty-gated SHAP-Dirichlet refinement, a post-hoc reliability layer that improves predictions without retraining the classifier. The method retrieves similar labeled SHAP explanations, constructs Dirichlet class evidence, and selectively refines uncertain predictions through probabilistic fusion, while allowing unreliable cases to be deferred for expert review. We evaluate five classifiers on 504 SRPBS subjects (252 controls and 252 MDD patients) using 159 anatomical features and repeated nested cross-validation. Refinement improved accuracy across all 8 repetitions for TabM and ResNet, yielding mean gains of 1.04 and 0.45 percentage points (sign test p=0.008), while modifying at most 8.3% of predictions. Gains were concentrated among low-confidence cases, with significant improvements in calibration. The method also benefited an RBF support vector machine but not logistic regression or random forests. Ablations confirmed the importance of uncertainty gating and soft fusion. Dirichlet evidence identified baseline errors (AUROC 0.62), while deferring 50% of cases increased retained-case accuracy to approximately 75%. These findings support selective explanation-guided refinement as a practical approach to improving prediction reliability and facilitating expert triage in MDD classification.
papers.summary: Classifying major depressive disorder (MDD) from structural MRI is hard because the anatomical changes are subtle and vary between patients. The proposed post-hoc layer retrieves similar labeled SHAP explanations, builds Dirichlet class evidence from them, and refines only uncertain predictions, without retraining the classifier and with the option to defer unreliable cases to experts. On 504 `SRPBS` subjects, refinement improved accuracy in all 8 repetitions for `TabM` and `ResNet` (mean gains of 1.04 and 0.45 points) while changing at most 8.3% of predictions, and it also helped an RBF SVM. **Deferring 50% of cases raised accuracy on the retained cases to about 75%**.

papers.title: ACorD: Adaptive Correspondence Discovery for Medical Image Registration
papers.abstract: Medical image registration is a fundamental task for aligning anatomical structures across images. Exhaustively searching for point-wise correspondences is prohibitively expensive in both computation and memory, particularly for high-resolution 3D medical images. Most recent learning-based methods directly predict correspondences in a coarse-to-fine manner, but often propagate intermediate estimates across scales without explicitly weighting correspondence evidence, which can allow coarse-scale errors to persist during refinement. To address these challenges, we propose ACorD, an adaptive correspondence discovery framework designed to mitigate error propagation with an attention-guided process. ACorD first predicts multiple potential correspondence candidates through Correlation-guided Cross-scale Offset Prediction (CCOP), which combines correlation maps as spatial matching priors with cross-scale features as global deformation context. Then, Multi-Head Deformable Aggregation (MHDA) aggregates these candidate correspondences using attention, producing a learned, non-uniform weighting over competing matches rather than treating them equally. The multi-head design further captures complementary deformation patterns, ensuring both global alignment and local precision. By integrating adaptive offset prediction with selective, attention-based aggregation of correspondence evidence, ACorD enables accurate deformation refinement. Extensive experiments on four public medical registration benchmarks demonstrate that adaptive correspondence discovery within a multi-scale refinement framework improves registration robustness across diverse anatomical structures.
papers.summary: Learning-based medical image registration usually refines correspondences from coarse to fine, which can let errors at coarse scales carry through to the final result. `ACorD` predicts several candidate correspondences with Correlation-guided Cross-scale Offset Prediction (`CCOP`), which combines correlation maps with cross-scale deformation context. Multi-Head Deformable Aggregation (`MHDA`) then weights these candidates non-uniformly with attention rather than treating them equally. Experiments on **four public medical registration benchmarks** show improved robustness across diverse anatomical structures.

papers.title: Think, Compress, Answer: Reinforcement Learning for Multimodal Grounding via Reasoning Compression
papers.abstract: Extended reasoning has substantially improved multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on tasks requiring compositional and relational inference. However, multimodal grounding imposes a distinct requirement: reasoning must ultimately converge on a target-specific compact representation that supports precise localization. As reasoning trajectories grow longer, they often expand into broad scene narratives and peripheral relational details, which can dilute grounded perceptual evidence and lead to ambiguous or incorrect predictions. Motivated by the information bottleneck principle, we propose Think-Compress-Answer (TCA), a reinforcement learning framework that decomposes multimodal grounding into three phases: free-form reasoning, target-aware context compression, and answer generation conditioned on the compressed context. TCA is optimized through a multi-stage Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with progressive rewards that establish the structured output protocol, minimize reasoning-specific information while preserving target-relevant content, and directly improve localization accuracy. This staged design enables MLLMs to retain the benefits of extended reasoning while distilling it into the minimal context required for grounding. Experiments across six multimodal grounding benchmarks show that TCA attains substantial zero-shot performance gains, demonstrating the effectiveness of reasoning compression.
papers.summary: Long reasoning chains help multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with relational inference, but in visual grounding they tend to drift into broad scene descriptions that dilute the evidence needed to localize the target. Motivated by the information bottleneck principle, `Think-Compress-Answer` (`TCA`) splits grounding into free-form reasoning, target-aware compression of that reasoning, and answer generation conditioned only on the compressed context. The model is trained with multi-stage Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) and progressive rewards for output format, compression and localization accuracy. Across **six multimodal grounding benchmarks**, `TCA` reports substantial zero-shot gains.

papers.title: Sampling of Signals on Multigraphs: From Removable and Uniqueness sets to Spectral Proxies
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the sampling of bandlimited signals on multigraphs, where several graphs with different shift operators are defined on the same set of nodes. Since the shift operators do not commute in general, they admit only a joint block diagonalization, and the frequencies of the multigraph signal model are matrices rather than scalars. Relying on a formal algebraic convolutional signal model, we introduce a notion of frequency and bandwidth for multigraph signals that does not depend on any individual layer, and we extend the notions of removable and uniqueness sets to multigraphs. We prove that the optimality of a sampling set is determined exclusively by the common Fourier basis and its invariant subspaces, and not by any individual layer, although the individual layers provide computable sufficient conditions that certify a sampling set as a uniqueness set. Since identifying which layers provide reliable certificates requires spectral information, we propose an aggregate operator that pools the information of all the layers, is computable directly from the shift operators, and certifies uniqueness without any assumption on the individual layers. This operator leads to a greedy sampling algorithm that does not require computing the joint block diagonalization. Numerical experiments on multigraphs whose layers order the frequencies inconsistently show that the proposed algorithm selects better-conditioned sampling sets and attains lower reconstruction errors than single-layer methods.
papers.summary: The authors study sampling of bandlimited signals on multigraphs, where several graphs with non-commuting shift operators share the same nodes, so frequencies become matrices that come from a joint block diagonalization. Using an algebraic convolutional signal model, they define frequency and bandwidth independently of any single layer and extend removable and uniqueness sets to this setting. They prove that **whether a sampling set is optimal depends only on the common Fourier basis and its invariant subspaces**, not on any individual layer. They also propose an aggregate operator, computable directly from the shift operators, that certifies uniqueness and drives a greedy sampling algorithm which avoids the block diagonalization and achieves lower reconstruction error than single-layer methods.

papers.title: Spherical Fixed-Point Reasoners: Adaptive Loop Halting on the Hypersphere
papers.abstract: Looped (weight-tied) transformers enable adaptive computation by allocating more iterations to harder inputs. Fixed-Point Reasoners (FPRM) achieve this with a damped fixed-point solver, but operate in an unbounded Euclidean residual space with coupled rescaling and relative-norm halting. We introduce Spherical Fixed-Point Reasoners (SFPRM), which perform the same computation on the unit hypersphere of normalized transformers (nGPT). Input injection, damping, and halting become geodesic operations, yielding boundedness by construction and eliminating coefficient coupling. We prove fixed-point existence, local convergence under an explicit step-size condition, and global convergence under strong injection. On Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, and Mini-ARC, SFPRM achieves 96.6%, 87.9%, and 59.1% test accuracy, respectively, outperforming FPRM and other baselines while allocating test-time compute more effectively. Its converged geometry is also interpretable: token-input angles capture puzzle structure and predict correctness.
papers.summary: Looped (weight-tied) transformers can spend more iterations on harder inputs. Fixed-Point Reasoners (`FPRM`) do this with a damped fixed-point solver in an unbounded Euclidean space. Spherical Fixed-Point Reasoners (`SFPRM`) instead run the computation on the unit hypersphere of normalized transformers (`nGPT`), turning input injection, damping and halting into geodesic operations that are bounded by construction. The authors prove fixed-point existence and convergence under stated conditions. `SFPRM` reaches **96.6% on `Sudoku-Extreme`, 87.9% on `Maze-Hard` and 59.1% on `Mini-ARC`**, outperforming `FPRM` while allocating test-time compute more effectively, and the angles between tokens and inputs at convergence predict whether an answer is correct.

papers.title: Consistency Training Suppresses Cue Following Without Teaching Cue Selectivity
papers.abstract: Language models often change answers because of a cue, a hint such as "I believe the answer is B" that gives no valid evidence. Consistency training (CT) trains a model to answer the same with and without the cue. Four CT methods apply this idea to output tokens (BCT), residual activations (ACT), attention patterns (AttCT) and sampled-answer rates (RMCT). Prior work suggests some learn different solutions. We train all four on Gemma-2-2B-it and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with the same data. We test predictions written in advance and inspect the models with a known circuit that carries cues to the answer. All four make the trained cue less effective, and their fixes share three properties. First, correct cues lose about as much influence as wrong ones. Second, the fix is usually large for cues before the answer options, as in training, and much smaller after them. Llama RMCT depends least on position. Third, the circuit heads still carry most remaining cue-induced errors. Making BCT targets depend on the cue's correctness mostly weakens the fix. CT thus weakens the trained cue without teaching models when a cue is right. Evaluations with only wrong cues at the trained position miss the first two properties.
papers.summary: Language models often switch answers in response to non-evidential cues such as "I believe the answer is B". Consistency training (CT) counters this by training the model to answer the same way with and without the cue. The authors train four CT variants, acting on output tokens, residual activations, attention patterns and sampled-answer rates, on `Gemma-2-2B-it` and `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`, then test preregistered predictions and inspect a known cue-carrying circuit. All four reduce the trained cue's effect in similar ways: **correct cues lose about as much influence as wrong ones**, the fix is much weaker when the cue appears in an untrained position, and the original circuit heads still carry most of the remaining cue-induced errors. CT therefore suppresses cue following without teaching the model when a cue is right, and evaluations that use only wrong cues miss this.

papers.title: OPDArena: Understanding Learning and Forgetting in On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly used for language model post-training, yet how teacher supervision shapes learning and forgetting remains unclear. We present OPDArena, a framework comparing supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and OPD across five pretrained models and diverse teacher sources. It jointly evaluates mathematical learning, general capability retention, and predictive distribution changes. Teacher choice strongly shapes retention: students of RLVR-trained teachers improve on the target task while retaining prior capabilities, whereas students of SFT-trained teachers incur greater capability loss. Across post-training methods, out-of-domain (OOD) distribution change shows a more consistent positive association with forgetting than in-domain change. To understand how teacher choice affects these changes, we examine the additional information teachers provide relative to the student's pretrained model. Controlled teacher comparisons show that the task-specific preferences teachers acquire through post-training make student updates more concentrated in-domain.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly used to post-train language models, but it is unclear how the choice of teacher affects what a student learns and what it forgets. `OPDArena` compares supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and OPD across five pretrained models and several teacher sources. It measures math learning, retention of general capabilities, and shifts in the predictive distribution. **Students of RLVR-trained teachers improve on the target task while retaining prior capabilities, whereas students of SFT-trained teachers forget more**. Across methods, distribution change on out-of-domain data tracks forgetting more consistently than in-domain change, and controlled teacher comparisons show that post-trained teachers concentrate student updates in-domain.

papers.title: A "feature ODE" describing the learning behavior of shallow MLPs on simple functions
papers.abstract: We study the gradient flow training dynamics of two-layer multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) on anisotropic Gaussian data. Even in this simple setting, solving the dynamics in full is notoriously difficult, so we try something different. We propose a "feature ODE" that might be intuitively expected to describe the learning dynamics of a shallow MLP. We find that MLPs trained to learn simple target functions (low-order Hermite polynomials and staircase functions) actually roughly follow the loss trajectories from this feature ODE. This agreement is a surprise because of the size of the simplification and the fact that it does not come from a rigorous chain of approximations. We discuss this surprise and speculate on its reasons and uses.
papers.summary: Fully solving the gradient-flow training dynamics of two-layer MLPs is notoriously hard, even on anisotropic Gaussian data. Rather than derive the dynamics rigorously, the author proposes a heuristic "feature ODE" that one might intuitively expect to describe how a shallow MLP learns. Surprisingly, **MLPs trained on low-order Hermite polynomials and staircase functions roughly follow the loss trajectories this ODE predicts**, even though the ODE is a large simplification and does not come from a rigorous chain of approximations. The paper discusses possible reasons for the agreement and how it might be used.

papers.title: Beyond Leaderboards: A Method for Application-Specific Capability Profiling of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Public leaderboards rank large language models (LLMs) in general, but an engineer has to choose a model for a specific application, architecture and cost. This paper presents a method for application-specific capability profiling of LLMs and its realization as a containerized testbed. The method treats each application as a unit of extension: an Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration agent, a documentation-grounded chatbot or an enterprise-support automation agent runs in its own container behind a small contract, brings its own dataset, evaluator and owned attributes, and is onboarded together with its dashboards. Measurements accumulate in a versioned, sparse metamodel of every model. The method separates the model under test from judges and agents, freezes and hashes plans, refuses to compare values from different contexts, diagnoses the instrument before the system, and applies a null-agent check and a noise rule whose operating characteristics are quantified by simulation. In the evaluated automation conditions, model choices produced larger differences on selected observable outcomes than framework choices, although the experimental design does not establish a general causal ranking of these factors. The experiments also show that instruction tuning is deployment-specific and that system-reported success can exceed independently observed success: of 216 migration units checked against a real Oracle database, 108 were demonstrably correct. These measurements establish application-specific observations, not a universal model ranking.
papers.summary: Public leaderboards rank large language models (LLMs) in general, but engineers have to choose a model for a specific application, architecture and cost. The authors present a containerized testbed in which each application, such as an Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration agent, a documentation chatbot or a support-automation agent, brings its own dataset and evaluator. Results accumulate in a versioned metamodel, with safeguards that include frozen and hashed test plans, separation of the model under test from judges, a null-agent check and a simulated noise rule. In the evaluated automation conditions, model choice affected outcomes more than framework choice, and system-reported success overstated real success: **only 108 of 216 migration units were demonstrably correct against a real Oracle database**.

papers.title: Knowledge Manifold Optimization for Scientific Discovery
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion and specialization of scientific literature make it increasingly difficult to identify not only what is known, but where new and still supportable knowledge may emerge. We introduce Knowledge Manifold Optimization (KMO), a discovery-oriented extension of the Knowledge Manifold framework that treats scientific discovery as a multiobjective search over a continuous, literature-derived knowledge space. Candidate locations are evaluated using four complementary objectives: persistent knowledge-regime boundary strength, band-pass white-space novelty, semanticgradient magnitude, and evidential support. Rather than collapsing these criteria into a single weighted score, KMO identifies Pareto-optimal Supported Knowledge Gaps, defined as corpus-relative unoccupied regions that remain sufficiently supported by surrounding literature. The method is demonstrated on a 99-paper corpus in aerodynamics and aerodynamic design. On a 21 x 21 grid, exact Pareto analysis produced 19 non-dominated points, of which 16 formed the practical front after excluding points with zero white-space score. These solutions exhibited distinct discovery modes, including methodology bridges, aero-structural topology/FSI integration, functional aerodynamic-device integration, and rear-wake/vehicle flow-control integration. A distance-maximization baseline preferentially selected extrapolative regions with substantially lower support and reliability, demonstrating why emptiness alone is insufficient. Representative Pareto locations were converted into auditable evidence packages and then verbalized by a constrained large language model into candidate research hypotheses. The results show that scientific discovery can be formulated as structured multi-objective search in an explicit knowledge space, while keeping novelty corpus-relative and separating numerical discovery from downstream language generation.
papers.summary: Knowledge Manifold Optimization (`KMO`) treats scientific discovery as a multi-objective search over a continuous knowledge space built from the literature. It scores candidate locations on four criteria: boundary strength between knowledge regimes, novelty of white space, semantic gradient, and evidential support. Instead of combining these into a single score, it finds Pareto-optimal "Supported Knowledge Gaps". On a 99-paper aerodynamics corpus, the Pareto analysis yielded **16 practical non-dominated gaps** in distinct discovery modes. A baseline that simply maximizes distance picked extrapolative regions with much weaker support, and selected gaps were turned into evidence packages that a constrained LLM then phrased as research hypotheses.

papers.title: Can Metadata Fix the Gauge? Calibration Turns Sparse Multi-Source Learning from Sparse PCA into Sparse Mean Recovery
papers.abstract:
Source labels tell us where a sample came from, but not how that source oriented its coordinates. In a sparse Gaussian multi-source model with source-specific sign gauges, that distinction changes the learning problem. Without calibration, pooling across sources erases the mean signal, and the source-labelled experiment reduces to sparse PCA. With task-independent relative-gauge metadata, synchronization aligns sources and the same observations become a sparse mean problem. We formalize the value of metadata through AlignedMass, which quantifies how much first-order signal a metadata-induced alignment restores. Source labels create only limited AlignedMass, whereas valid calibration can create AlignedMass proportional to the full sample size. This yields a statistical separation in micro-source regimes and, under standard sparse-PCA hardness assumptions, a computational separation as well. Synthetic experiments check the predicted scaling; controlled real-feature
  and physical sensor studies examine sign cancellation, separately
  acquired calibration, and reuse across tasks.
papers.summary: In a sparse Gaussian multi-source model where each source may flip the signs of its coordinates, source labels identify where a sample came from but not how that source oriented its data. Without calibration, pooling across sources cancels the mean signal and the problem reduces to sparse PCA; with task-independent calibration metadata, the sources can be aligned and the same data become a sparse mean-recovery problem. The authors quantify this effect with `AlignedMass`, the amount of first-order signal that an alignment restores, and show that **valid calibration can recover AlignedMass proportional to the full sample size, whereas source labels alone cannot**. This yields a statistical separation and, under standard sparse-PCA hardness assumptions, a computational one, which they check on synthetic data, real features and physical sensors.

papers.title: Arbitrage-Free Implied Volatility Surface Reconstruction via Additive Martingales
papers.abstract: This work focuses on reconstructing a continuous implied volatility (IV) surface from a small number of option quotes, a fundamental task for option pricing and risk management. We propose Additive Martingale (AddMart), a few-shot IV surface reconstruction framework that satisfies static no-arbitrage conditions by construction. Rather than predicting IVs directly, AddMart maps sparse quotes to non-negative increment densities of an exponential additive martingale, from which valid risk-neutral marginals and IVs are recovered. By incorporating the no-arbitrage structure directly into its architecture, rather than enforcing it through regularization in the learning objective, AddMart produces IV surfaces that satisfy static no-arbitrage conditions throughout the domain. Extensive experiments on ten real-option datasets demonstrate that AddMart achieves competitive reconstruction accuracy with no material static arbitrage violations, while directly enabling the estimation of VaR, CVaR, and crash probabilities.
papers.summary: Reconstructing a continuous implied volatility (IV) surface from a few option quotes is central to option pricing and risk management, but learned models can produce surfaces that admit arbitrage. `AddMart` maps sparse quotes to non-negative increment densities of an exponential additive martingale, from which valid risk-neutral marginals and IVs are recovered. Because the no-arbitrage structure is built into the architecture rather than added as a penalty in the loss, **the resulting surfaces satisfy static no-arbitrage conditions throughout the domain**. On ten real option datasets the method reaches competitive accuracy and directly supports estimates of VaR, CVaR and crash probability.

papers.title: HyperTaxa: Multiscale Genome Representations for Generalized Microbial Taxonomic Inference
papers.abstract: Reliable microbial taxonomic inference is challenged by the rapid growth of newly sequenced organisms and incomplete reference coverage. While alignment- and database-driven tools remain essential for reference-backed identification, they are not designed for learned inference over species absent from genome-level training. We introduce HyperTaxa, a taxonomy-aligned representation learning framework for open-set microbial taxonomic inference. HyperTaxa encodes whole genomes as multiscale hyperspectral k-mer transition fields and aligns these representations to a taxonomy-derived semantic space using a two-stage Node2Vec-to-MDS procedure that combines local graph structure with global hierarchical distance preservation. The resulting space supports zero-shot inference over species excluded from genome-level training but represented in the taxonomy, generalized zero-shot inference over seen and unseen species, and cascaded genus-to-species prediction. Across benchmark and large-scale disjoint-species evaluations, HyperTaxa improves taxonomic prediction over pseudo-image and transformer-graph baselines, with the strongest gains at higher taxonomic ranks. Ablations further show that multiscale transition encoding and taxonomy-aware alignment are key contributors to generalization. These results position HyperTaxa as a complementary taxonomy-aware representation and candidate-generation framework for microbial identification under incomplete reference coverage and open-set uncertainty.
papers.summary: Alignment-based microbial identification tools struggle with newly sequenced species that are missing from reference databases. `HyperTaxa` encodes whole genomes as multiscale hyperspectral k-mer transition fields and aligns them to a semantic space derived from the taxonomy, built with a two-stage `Node2Vec`-to-MDS procedure. This supports zero-shot and generalized zero-shot prediction for species unseen during genome-level training, as well as cascaded genus-to-species prediction. Across benchmark and large disjoint-species evaluations, it outperforms pseudo-image and transformer-graph baselines, **with the largest gains at higher taxonomic ranks**.

papers.title: LIRQuant: An Efficient Locally Isolated Rotation Quantization Method for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) enables efficient deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet activation outliers remain a key challenge for low-bit quantization. Existing global transformation methods overlook heterogeneous channel sensitivity to quantization noise, leading to suboptimal accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. To address this, we propose \textbf{Locally Isolated Rotation Quantization (LIRQuant)}, a sensitivity-aware framework that selectively applies transformations. LIRQuant identifies sensitive channels using a noise-weighted sensitivity metric, applying expressive learnable rotations only to these channels and lightweight fixed rotations to the remaining ones. This decoupled design reduces optimization complexity without sacrificing outlier smoothing capability. Extensive experiments across the LLaMA-2/3, Mistral, Qwen3, and Mixtral families demonstrate that LIRQuant achieves state-of-the-art accuracy under the challenging W4A4KV4 setting. Meanwhile, LIRQuant calibrates LLaMA-3-8B in only 25 minutes with 20.3 GB peak GPU memory, achieving the fastest calibration and the lowest memory footprint among recent learnable-rotation methods, and its fused inference kernels deliver up to $2.3\times$ prefill speedup and $3.5\times$ memory saving over FP16.
papers.summary: Activation outliers make low-bit post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models (LLMs) difficult, and global rotation methods treat every channel the same even though channels differ in how sensitive they are to quantization noise. `LIRQuant` uses a noise-weighted sensitivity metric to find sensitive channels, applies learnable rotations only to those, and uses cheap fixed rotations for the rest. Across the `LLaMA-2/3`, `Mistral`, `Qwen3` and `Mixtral` families it reports state-of-the-art accuracy in the 4-bit weight, activation and KV-cache (W4A4KV4) setting. It calibrates `LLaMA-3-8B` in 25 minutes with 20.3 GB of peak GPU memory, and its fused kernels deliver **up to 2.3× prefill speedup and 3.5× memory savings over FP16**.

papers.title: Neither Over- nor Under-Constrained: Evaluating LLM Personalization under a Constraint Qualification Audit
papers.abstract: Accurate evaluation of LLM personalization is hindered by current evaluation paradigms that over- or under-constrain the response space, yielding frequent false rejections and false acceptances. To reduce these false rates, we introduce ConQual-Audit, an audit-based framework that evaluates LLM personalization through a three-stage process: (1) extracting semantic constraints from user profiles and task-grounded reference; (2) qualifying constraints by pruning unnecessary constraints and recovering missing constraints; and (3) verifying candidate responses against the audited constraints via natural language inference. Across PrefEval and LaMP, ConQual-Audit outperforms nine baselines, attaining top AUCs (0.88 and 0.90) and the lowest false rate (0.21) on the leanest constraint sets at an amortizable audit cost. Crucially, this constraint audit is portable: integrating it into ExPerT and PREF helps revise smaller, higher-quality constraint sets to reduce their evaluation false rates.
papers.summary: Current ways of evaluating LLM personalization either over- or under-constrain acceptable responses, so they frequently reject good answers and accept bad ones. `ConQual-Audit` extracts semantic constraints from user profiles and task references, prunes unnecessary constraints and recovers missing ones, then checks candidate responses against the audited constraints using natural language inference. On `PrefEval` and `LaMP` it beats nine baselines, with **AUCs of 0.88 and 0.90 and the lowest false rate (0.21)**. The audit step also transfers to the existing evaluators `ExPerT` and `PREF`, where it reduces their false rates.

papers.title: Cross-Pollination Retrieval: Finding Transferable Ideas Across Fields in Scientific Literature
papers.abstract: Many scientific advances come from cross-pollination, carrying an idea from one field over to a problem in another. Yet retrieving papers across fields remains underexplored, with existing benchmarks confined to a narrow range of fields. We study cross-pollination retrieval, the problem of identifying transferable ideas across research fields, and introduce CPR-Dataset, a large-scale dataset constructed by mining cross-topic citations. Its evaluation split CPR-eval has 1,300 queries in 26 fields, and its training split CPR-train has 10,573 pairs. On CPR-eval, the best of eleven existing retrievers reaches a Recall@10 of only 0.26, whereas an LLM reranker reaches 0.81. Standard contrastive fine-tuning on CPR-train raises Recall@10 to as high as 0.70. The gain carries over to domains held out from training and to analogy and reasoning-intensive retrieval. On AnaloBench, it raises nDCG@10 by up to 33% over the untrained retriever, whereas training on three existing retrieval datasets lowers it. On BRIGHT, it raises nDCG@10 by up to 70%, more than twice the gain from those datasets. CPR-Dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/CPR-Dataset, and the code at https://github.com/SeokwonJung-Jay/Cross-Pollination-Retrieval.
papers.summary: Cross-pollination retrieval is the task of finding papers in other research fields whose ideas could transfer to a given problem. The authors build `CPR-Dataset` by mining citations that cross topics. Its evaluation split, `CPR-eval`, has 1,300 queries across 26 fields, and its training split, `CPR-train`, has 10,573 pairs. The best of eleven existing retrievers reaches a Recall@10 of only 0.26, while an LLM reranker reaches 0.81. Contrastive fine-tuning on `CPR-train` lifts retrievers to as high as 0.70, and the gains carry over to held-out fields and to analogy and reasoning-heavy benchmarks, including **up to a 70% nDCG@10 improvement on `BRIGHT`**.

papers.title: LOOP: Recovery-Aligned Iterative Layer Pruning via On-Policy Distillation
