In particular, we leverage reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts, and further model each patient's deviation from cohort prototypes as a structured drift signal encoding fine-grained individual heterogeneity. These cohort- and drift-aware representations are incorporated into the foundation model to enable reasoning that is simultaneously informed by population-level patterns and sensitive to individual-level variation. Extensive experiments on real-world electronic health record (EHR) benchmarks demonstrate that CODA achieves consistent effectiveness and strong generalizability across diverse clinical tasks, including closed-QA, open-QA, and report generation.
papers.summary: Clinicians reason about a patient by comparing them with similar patient cohorts and noting how they deviate, while most multimodal clinical models treat each sample in isolation. `CODA` uses reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts and models each patient's deviation from the cohort prototype as a structured "drift" signal. These cohort and drift representations are fed into a foundation model. On real-world electronic health record (EHR) benchmarks, the authors report **consistent gains across closed-ended QA, open-ended QA, and report generation**.

papers.title: Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation for Parameter-Efficient MCI Conversion Prediction
papers.abstract: Allocating limited trainable capacity across convolutional layers is a central challenge in parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of pretrained three-dimensional (3D) networks. We propose Residual-Guided Adaptive Tucker Rank Allocation, which jointly selects input- and output-channel ranks under a fixed adapter-parameter budget while preserving the spatial kernel modes. To guide rank selection, we learn task-specific proxy updates from downstream training data and approximate them using candidate Tucker rank pairs. A perturbation analysis bounds the output discrepancy between the fixed proxy network and its Tucker approximation in terms of layerwise reconstruction residuals, motivating residual-based allocation. We normalize each squared residual by the corresponding proxy-update energy to compare relative approximation errors across layers. Dynamic programming minimizes their sum under a global budget constraint that accounts for both channel factors and the Tucker core. This yields a globally optimal allocation over the specified candidate rank pairs. We evaluate the method on the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort for predicting conversion from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease within 36 months, using hippocampal segmentation pretraining. Across five random seeds, the proposed method achieves a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.7706, compared with 0.7239 for fixed-ratio Tucker adaptation and 0.7430 for full fine-tuning. The total number of trainable parameters is limited to approximately 0.618 million, accounting for only 1.45% of the full model. Adaptive Tucker rank allocation thus provides an effective approach to parameter-efficient transfer learning in 3D medical imaging.
papers.summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of pretrained 3D convolutional networks has to decide how to spread a limited parameter budget across layers. This method learns task-specific proxy weight updates, measures how well candidate Tucker rank pairs reconstruct them, and uses dynamic programming to choose ranks that are globally optimal under a fixed budget. Predicting conversion from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease on the `ADNI` cohort, it reaches **a mean AUC of 0.7706, versus 0.7239 for fixed-ratio Tucker adaptation and 0.7430 for full fine-tuning**, while training only 1.45% of the parameters.

papers.title: Learning to Reason Efficiently with Interventional Step Credit
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models often produce lengthy chain-of-thought (CoT) traces mixing useful intermediate steps with unnecessary ones. Recent methods explore step-level signals such as attention mass and step entropy to identify and suppress unnecessary steps. Despite their effectiveness, such signals reflect the model's behavior at a step rather than that step's contribution to the answer. To address this, we propose the interventional step credit (ISC), which takes a causal-intervention view and assesses step importance to the reasoning through targeted parameter-level interventions. Building on ISC, we further propose IGPO, which uses ISC to guide fine-grained advantage rescaling in reinforcement learning, reducing redundant steps while preserving the important ones. Experiments across two model scales and nine benchmarks show that IGPO achieves up to 62% average token reduction and better overall performance among compared methods.
papers.summary: Large reasoning models produce long chain-of-thought (CoT) traces that mix useful steps with redundant ones. Existing step-level signals such as attention mass or entropy describe the model's behavior at a step, not how much that step contributes to the answer. Interventional step credit (`ISC`) estimates a step's importance through targeted parameter-level causal interventions. `IGPO` then uses `ISC` to rescale reinforcement-learning advantages step by step, suppressing redundant steps and keeping important ones. Across two model scales and nine benchmarks, `IGPO` achieves **up to 62% average token reduction** and the best overall performance among the methods compared.

papers.title: DeltaTrace: Efficient Signed Attribution for Reasoning Language Models
papers.abstract: We study how words in the context support or oppose a language model's response and present DeltaTrace, a novel attribution framework that explains the effect of input tokens on a fixed model response. DeltaTrace measures how the response's log-probability changes when the context tokens being explained are masked. To distribute this difference among source tokens, it constructs operator-specific local rules for finite changes and composes them backward through the computational graph using effective secant slopes. Each token is assigned a signed attribution as the inner product of its embedding displacement and the corresponding backward-propagated slope. Local conservation makes these contributions sum to the measured score difference and preserves their meaning when aggregated over sentences or passages. DeltaTrace supports both attention and linear-attention models, with auxiliary memory growing linearly with sequence length at fixed model dimensions and chunk size. On the evaluated attention model, DeltaTrace achieves the lowest deletion-faithfulness scores (RISE and MAS) on most retrieval and reasoning tasks and the highest needle-in-a-haystack Recall, exceeding FlashTrace by 5.67-24.33 percentage points. On the evaluated hybrid attention and linear-attention model, DeltaTrace lowers RISE on 9 tasks and MAS on 12 relative to FlashTrace.
papers.summary: `DeltaTrace` attributes a fixed model response to individual context tokens by measuring how the response's log-probability changes when those tokens are masked. It splits that change among tokens using finite-difference rules propagated backward through the network. Each token gets a signed score showing whether it supports or opposes the response, and the scores sum exactly to the measured change, so they stay meaningful when aggregated over sentences or passages. The method works for both attention and linear-attention models, with memory that grows linearly in sequence length. On an attention model it gets the best deletion-faithfulness scores (`RISE`, `MAS`) on most tasks and **exceeds `FlashTrace` by 5.67–24.33 points on needle-in-a-haystack recall**.

papers.title: Asynchronous On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Unlike on-policy distillation (OPD), which depends on a separate teacher model, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) leverages a single language model acting simultaneously as the student and the teacher, with the teacher conditioned on privileged information. Despite this architectural simplicity, synchronous rollout generation dominates overall training time, creating a severe systems bottleneck when scaling OPSD. To address this, we introduce Asynchronous On-Policy Self-Distillation (AsyncOPSD), a framework that decouples rollout generation from learner updates to improve training throughput. Since the teacher and student share parameters, AsyncOPSD eliminates the multi-model coordination overhead inherent to OPD architectures in asynchronous training. As the student policy evolves, buffered trajectories generated by older policies become stale, potentially degrading performance. To mitigate this, we introduce a distillation objective based on staleness-aware policy control and token-level entropy weighting. Across three model sizes and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, AsyncOPSD improves the training throughput by $1.96$--$2.25\times$ over synchronous OPSD while increasing average benchmark accuracy.
papers.summary: In on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), one language model acts as both student and teacher, with the teacher given privileged information. Generating rollouts synchronously dominates training time. `AsyncOPSD` decouples rollout generation from learner updates. Because the teacher and student share parameters, it avoids the multi-model coordination that asynchronous training with a separate teacher would require. To handle stale buffered trajectories, it uses a distillation objective with staleness-aware policy control and token-level entropy weighting. Across three model sizes on math reasoning benchmarks, it **improves training throughput by 1.96–2.25×** over synchronous OPSD and also raises average accuracy.

papers.title: Learn the Interface, Not the Implementation: Output Representation Dominates Training Regime in LLM-Based RTL Generation
papers.abstract: Large-language-model register-transfer-level (RTL) generation has concentrated on how to train the model: fine-tuning, continued pre-training, and reinforcement learning from a verifier. We argue this is the second-order question. On a bounded, formally specifiable task of generating single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting (SECDED) ECC memory wrappers, we hold the task, data, and correctness oracle fixed and vary two axes independently: the training regime (seven settings) and the output representation (four levels, from fully expanded flat Verilog to an eight-field configuration expanded by a deterministic generator). Because a reference generator exists, correctness is decided by formal equivalence over a design space of approximately ten million points, rather than sampled from a hand-written testbench. Two results follow. First, representation dominates: every representation close to raw RTL reaches a pass rate of at most 0.17, while the configuration reaches 0.83 with no training at all. Once the model emits the configuration, every training regime achieves a pass rate between 0.89 and 1.00. Second, raw RTL hits a hard output-length limit: a 512-bit design requires 44,237 tokens of flat Verilog compared with just 69 tokens for the configuration. Consequently, raw generation becomes infeasible above 32-bit data words rather than merely inaccurate. A model trained from scratch with fewer than 50 million parameters, combined with the verified generator, achieves 0.89 formal equivalence, compared with 1.00 for a 32-billion-parameter fine-tuned model, while using approximately 1600 times less inference energy per correct design. Inference energy also dominates amortized training energy. The lesson is to learn the interface, not the implementation.
papers.summary: Work on LLM generation of register-transfer-level (RTL) hardware code has focused mainly on training methods. This study instead holds the task fixed (SECDED error-correcting memory wrappers, checked by formal equivalence) and varies the training regime and the output representation independently. Representation dominates: outputs close to raw Verilog reach at most a 0.17 pass rate, while **emitting an eight-field configuration expanded by a deterministic generator reaches 0.83 with no training** and 0.89–1.00 under every training regime. Raw RTL also hits a hard length limit (44,237 tokens versus 69 for a 512-bit design). A model under 50M parameters trained from scratch and paired with the generator reaches 0.89 using about 1600× less inference energy per correct design than a fine-tuned 32B model.

papers.title: Manifold-Constrained Residual Adaptation with Frame-Adaptive Layer Aggregation for Speaker Verification
papers.abstract: Large self-supervised speech models provide powerful representations for speaker verification, but full fine-tuning is expensive. Most conventional adapters insert small trainable modules to modify the output of each layer, while keeping the original residual connections unchanged. Building on our preliminary study of manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections in speaker encoders, we explore parameter-efficient adaptation of both residual paths and feature selection across layers. We first propose a Manifold-Constrained Residual Adapter (MCRA), which splits the hidden dimensions of each Transformer residual state into N groups and uses a small Sinkhorn-normalized matrix to exchange information among them. A learnable gate controls the balance between the original and mixed residual paths. The gate adds only one scalar parameter at each residual connection and initially favors the original path, allowing gradual adaptation. We further propose Frame-Adaptive Layer Aggregation (FALA), an attention-based aggregation method that uses a single learned query shared across all utterances to compute layer weights separately for each speech frame. Because the layer representations depend on the input, the resulting weights vary across both utterances and frames, unlike the fixed weights of a conventional layer-weighted sum. Compared with a frozen WavLM baseline using a fixed layer-weighted sum, our method achieves relative EER reductions of 22.4% on VoxCeleb1-O and 2.9% on CN-Celeb, with trainable adaptation parameters equivalent to only 0.0009% and 0.0016% of the WavLM-Large parameters, respectively.
papers.summary: Fully fine-tuning large self-supervised speech models for speaker verification is expensive, and most adapters leave residual connections unchanged. The Manifold-Constrained Residual Adapter (`MCRA`) splits each Transformer residual state into groups, mixes them with a small Sinkhorn-normalized matrix, and uses a one-scalar gate that starts out favoring the original path. Frame-Adaptive Layer Aggregation (`FALA`) uses a single learned attention query to weight layers separately for each frame. Compared with a frozen `WavLM` baseline, the approach cuts equal error rate (EER) by **22.4% relative on `VoxCeleb1-O`** and 2.9% on `CN-Celeb`, while training only about 0.001% of `WavLM-Large`'s parameters.

papers.title: Motor compound fault diagnosis using an attention-based cross-talk architecture
papers.abstract: As physical AI increasingly relies on sensing to understand physical systems, reliable condition monitoring of industrial machinery has become more important. Motors are ubiquitous in industrial systems, and increasing system complexity raises the likelihood of simultaneous faults. Accordingly, compound fault diagnosis that identifies multiple fault components and their severities is increasingly required. Because different fault components jointly affect the same vibration signal, their severity classification can be formulated as related tasks, making multi-task learning (MTL) suitable for exploiting shared information. However, conventional shared-trunk architectures force tasks to share a common representation, potentially causing negative transfer because fault components are characterized by different time-frequency regions. To address this issue, this study proposes a Residual Neural Dimension Reductor with Time-Frequency Channel Attention (RNDR-TFCA), an attention-enhanced cross-talk architecture for multi-output compound fault diagnosis. RNDR-TFCA preserves task-specific feature extractors while selectively exchanging information across tasks. Time-frequency attention emphasizes informative intra-task regions, while channel attention enhances useful inter-task information after nonlinear feature fusion. Experiments on a rotor-bearing system with inner-race fault, outer-race fault, misalignment, and unbalance showed that RNDR-TFCA achieved a macro F1 score of 0.898, outperforming single-task, multi-class, shared-trunk, and cross-talk baselines. Ablation experiments confirmed the benefit of jointly applying both attention mechanisms. RNDR-TFCA required 713 K parameters and 170.42 MMACs, only slightly higher than RNDR. Channel-expanded baselines still underperformed RNDR-TFCA, indicating that the gain was not simply attributable to increased model capacity.
papers.summary: Diagnosing compound motor faults means classifying the severity of several fault components that all show up in the same vibration signal. Shared-trunk multi-task learning (MTL) can cause negative transfer here, because each fault type lives in different time-frequency regions. `RNDR-TFCA` keeps a separate feature extractor per task and exchanges information across tasks using time-frequency attention within each task and channel attention across tasks. On a rotor-bearing system with four fault types, it reaches **a macro F1 score of 0.898**, beating single-task, multi-class, shared-trunk, and cross-talk baselines with only a small increase in parameters.

papers.title: When Should AI Chime In? Benchmarking Timely Contribution of Proactive Agents in Multi-Party Chat
papers.abstract: Proactive agents can support group collaboration by surfacing useful information without waiting to be asked, but even relevant contributions can be disruptive if poorly timed. In this work, we isolate the timing question: given a fixed candidate contribution such as a clarification or relevant fact, when should an AI agent chime in? We introduce PITCH (Proactive Intervention Timing in CHat), to our knowledge the first benchmark with large-scale human judgments of proactive agent timing collected from participants in the same unscripted multi-party conversations they took part in. To collect high-quality judgments, we design a novel interface in which 2-4 people chat synchronously, author candidate AI contribution messages, place their own and others' contributions into the chat history, and then deliberate as a group about the best placement for each message. PITCH contains 384 candidate contributions and 1,091 judgments, each marking an ideal turn, an acceptable window, or that a contribution should not appear, from 89 participants engaged in 35 conversations. Evaluating 15 models across 28 configurations, we find that while models can place contributions well when given the entire conversation history, they systematically chime in too early when asked to decide live as the conversation unfolds: best-turn accuracy falls from 57.8% to 19.0%, with nearly half of placements occurring before every participant's acceptable window. In comparison, lay humans deciding live are more accurate (23.7% vs 19.0%), and fewer of their placements are premature (39.7% vs 46.4%). Model reasoning traces show that 93% of intervention justifications cite relevance, while almost none consider waiting. By providing a human-grounded benchmark, our work reveals gaps in agents' ability to integrate into group settings and points towards proactive agents that can reason explicitly about appropriate timing.
papers.summary: Even a relevant contribution from a proactive AI agent can be disruptive if it arrives at the wrong moment in a group chat. `PITCH` (Proactive Intervention Timing in CHat) collects 1,091 human judgments of where 384 candidate AI messages should be placed, gathered from the participants of 35 unscripted multi-party conversations. Across 15 models, placement is reasonable when models see the whole conversation, but when they must decide live, **best-turn accuracy drops from 57.8% to 19.0%** and nearly half of placements come too early. Lay humans deciding live do better, and 93% of model justifications cite relevance while almost none consider waiting.

papers.title: Budgeted Attack Scheduling for LLM Red-Teaming: The Roles of Static Priors, Semantic Guidance, and Online Feedback
papers.abstract: As jailbreak attacks against large language models (LLMs) become increasingly diverse, red-teaming has come to rely on large libraries of jailbreak prompts and attack strategies to evaluate the robustness of victim models and their defense settings. However, attack effectiveness is highly condition-dependent: an attack that succeeds under one victim-defense setting may fail under another, while exhaustively evaluating the full attack library for each setting incurs substantial token and monetary costs. This motivates studying how jailbreak attacks should be prioritized under a limited attempt budget for efficient robustness evaluation. In this work, we formalize this problem as budgeted attack scheduling over a fixed attack library and investigate three complementary signals under a fixed victim-defense condition: (1) static historical attack success rate (ASR) priors; (2) semantic guidance from LLMs; and (3) online feedback from earlier queries. Building on these signals, we design four scheduling strategies and evaluate them across three victim models and three defense settings on GPT-5.2. Extensive experiments clearly characterize the conditions under which each signal is most effective. Historical ASR provides a strong initialization, but its reliability degrades under defense-induced distribution shifts. Semantic guidance consistently improves or matches static prior-based scheduling in the cold-start regime, while online feedback becomes particularly valuable when transferred priors become stale. Semantic guidance and online feedback can also partially compensate for missing historical priors. Taken together, these findings characterize budgeted red-teaming as an attack scheduling problem in which historical priors, semantic guidance, and online feedback play complementary roles.
papers.summary: Red-teaming LLMs against jailbreaks now draws on large attack libraries, but running every attack for every combination of victim model and defense is costly, and which attacks work depends on that combination. The authors frame this as budgeted attack scheduling and test three signals: historical attack success rate (ASR) priors, semantic guidance from LLMs, and online feedback from earlier queries. They combine these into four scheduling strategies and evaluate them across three victim models and three defense settings. **Historical ASR gives a strong starting point but becomes unreliable when defenses shift the distribution.** Semantic guidance helps most at cold start, online feedback matters most when transferred priors go stale, and the two can partly make up for missing priors.

papers.title: SWE-Residual: Evaluating Starting-State Robustness of Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Software engineering (SWE) benchmarks are the primary way to measure the capabilities of coding agents: an agent is placed in a code repository or machine environment, given a request, and judged by hidden tests. These benchmarks almost always start the agent from a clean state that contains no earlier work on the task. In practice, however, agents often continue work that a developer or another agent has already done and reported as complete, with no indication of what remains incorrect or missing. We introduce SWE-Residual, a benchmark for Starting-State Robustness: the ability to maintain performance on a task when the starting state already contains earlier work on that task. SWE-Residual contains 198 Residual States drawn from 111 tasks in DeepSWE and Terminal-Bench, where the earlier work modifies a code repository or a whole machine environment. Each Residual State is the state a predecessor agent left behind after submitting its work as complete, although the hidden tests still fail. The evaluated agent receives only the original request and this state, without the predecessor's trajectory or any sign that the attempt failed; because the request and hidden tests are unchanged, the starting state is the only difference from the source benchmark. Across five frontier agents, success drops by 20.6--53.5 percentage points on DeepSWE and 20.6--34.9 points on Terminal-Bench relative to a Clean Start, and agent rankings on DeepSWE reverse. Failed continuations show a pattern we call acceptance bias: agents treat the inherited work as the definition of what remains to be done instead of checking it against the request. On DeepSWE, in 58.9--88.2% of failed runs, they submit with exactly the same tests failing, although they pass most of these tests from a Clean Start. SWE-Residual thus exposes a capability gap that clean-start evaluation does not capture.
papers.summary: Coding-agent benchmarks almost always start the agent from a clean repository, but in practice agents often pick up work that a developer or another agent has already reported as complete. `SWE-Residual` measures this "Starting-State Robustness" with 198 residual states drawn from 111 `DeepSWE` and `Terminal-Bench` tasks. Each state is what a predecessor agent left behind after declaring success while the hidden tests still failed, and the evaluated agent sees only the original request and that state. Across five frontier agents, success drops by **20.6 to 53.5 percentage points on `DeepSWE`** compared with a clean start, and agent rankings reverse. The authors trace failures to "acceptance bias": in 58.9–88.2% of failed runs, agents submit with exactly the same tests still failing, even though they pass most of those tests when starting clean.

papers.title: Out-of-Distribution Detection in Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Out-of-distribution detection in continual learning (OOD-CL) is highly challenging, as it requires (i) learning a sequence of tasks without catastrophic forgetting, and (ii) identifying unknown samples (OOD) without access to known (in-distribution (ID)) data from past tasks, where standard confidence-based OOD scores tend to degrade. Existing methods largely rely on a rehearsal buffer of past data or assume closed-world settings, limiting their scalability and reliability in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we propose a novel OOD detection framework for rehearsal-free continual learning, inspired by Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN), which mitigate catastrophic forgetting via their inherent local neuroplasticity. To better leverage KAN in OOD-CL, we introduce a task-adaptive classifier architecture, TA-KAN, which mitigates recency bias and enhances ID--OOD separability through task-specific control of activation locality. Furthermore, we propose a geometry-guided OOD score that complements TA-KAN classifier confidence without relying on past ID data. Our method significantly improves OOD detection while maintaining strong ID classification performance, achieving state-of-the-art results in OOD-CL.
papers.summary: Detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs during continual learning is hard because the model must avoid forgetting earlier tasks and also flag unknown samples without access to old in-distribution data. Most existing methods depend on a rehearsal buffer of past data or assume a closed world. The authors propose a rehearsal-free approach built on Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (`KAN`), whose local plasticity limits forgetting. It combines a task-adaptive classifier, `TA-KAN`, which reduces bias toward recent tasks, with a geometry-guided OOD score that needs no past data. They report **state-of-the-art OOD detection in continual learning** while keeping strong in-distribution classification accuracy.

papers.title: An Analysis of Semantic and Spatio-Temporal Co-evolution for Edge Classification on Dynamic Text-Attributed Graphs
papers.abstract: Dynamic edge classification on text-attributed Web graphs, such as review networks, community forums, and news-derived knowledge graphs, requires high quality, adaptive semantic representations in the context of network evolution. Existing dynamic graph architectures typically initialize text feature vectors with pretrained language models and hold them static during training to preserve their semantic structure, forgoing the potential benefits of allowing them to co-evolve with network topology. In this work, we investigate the effects of enabling such co-evolution with a unified text-graph alignment framework that integrates a lightweight Transformer adapter to update token-level text representations via spatio-temporal gradients from a contrastive pretraining objective. To prevent detrimental semantic distortion, a language model maintenance objective anchors the evolving text embeddings to their original semantic structure. Evaluations on the Dynamic Text-Attributed Graph Benchmark demonstrate that this anchored text-graph co-evolution consistently improves upon the edge classification performance of frozen-text baselines across diverse Web-related domains. Representational analyses reveal that the framework reduces anisotropy, improving the linear separability of text embeddings, and effectively encodes structural and temporal information into the semantic space. A computational efficiency analysis confirms that this beneficial semantic and spatio-temporal co-evolution is achieved without incurring the prohibitive computational overhead typical of end-to-end joint training.
papers.summary: Dynamic graph models for text-attributed Web graphs, such as review networks and forums, usually encode text once with a pretrained language model and keep those features frozen during training. This work instead lets the text representations evolve along with the graph's structure and timing. A lightweight Transformer adapter is trained with a contrastive objective, and a separate language-model objective anchors the embeddings so their original meaning is not distorted. On the `Dynamic Text-Attributed Graph Benchmark`, this anchored co-evolution **consistently beats frozen-text baselines on edge classification** across domains. Analysis shows the resulting embeddings are less anisotropic and encode structural and temporal information, and the method avoids the heavy compute cost of full end-to-end joint training.

papers.title: CALM: Consistency-Aware Logit Masking in Decoding Space for Mitigating Overthinking of Large Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved strong performance on challenging mathematical and scientific tasks through long chain-of-thought reasoning, but they often suffer from overthinking with unnecessary reasoning steps. Existing truncation-based methods typically detect consecutive trial-answer agreement and force early exit, yet such local stopping signals do not necessarily indicate final-answer stability and can disrupt useful subsequent reflection or verification, potentially leading to performance degradation. We propose consistency-aware logit masking (CALM), a training-free decoding intervention for mitigating overthinking in LRMs. CALM first monitors trial answers at step boundaries and then applies logit masking to action transition point (ATP) tokens such as "Wait", "Alternatively", and "Hmm", suppressing redundant transitional reasoning while allowing the model to continue its thought process more naturally. Experiments across four advanced LRMs and five benchmarks show that CALM reduces token consumption by 18.6%-25.0% compared with full CoT reasoning while maintaining performance, and can even improve accuracy by 0.07%-1.48% by reducing redundant reasoning. LLM-as-a-Judge results also demonstrate that CALM provides more coherent and concise results.
papers.summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) often overthink by producing unnecessary reasoning steps, and existing early-exit methods can cut off useful verification and hurt accuracy. Consistency-aware logit masking (`CALM`) is a training-free decoding intervention that tracks trial answers at step boundaries. Once the answers stabilize, it suppresses "action transition point" tokens such as "Wait" and "Alternatively" instead of forcing the model to stop. Across four LRMs and five benchmarks, `CALM` **cuts token usage by 18.6–25.0% while maintaining accuracy**, and in some cases improves accuracy by up to 1.48%.

papers.title: FisherEdit: Fisher Information Guided Knowledge Editing for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Sequential knowledge editing in Large Language Models (LLMs) often leads to a degradation of general capabilities due to cumulative parameter interference. In this paper, we revisit prominent projection-based methods like AlphaEdit and reveal a surprising mismatch: their robustness is primarily driven by update regularization rather than the intended null-space projection. Based on this insight, we propose FisherEdit, a theoretically grounded method built on Fisher geometry, which replaces coarse activation-space projections with importance-aware regularization in parameter space. It penalizes changes to sensitive parameters more strongly while retaining flexibility for new facts, and admits an efficient row-wise closed-form solution. Experiments on Llama-3, Qwen2.5, and Olmo-3 across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that FisherEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance while better preserving model stability and downstream task accuracy.
papers.summary: Editing many facts in a large language model one after another tends to erode its general capabilities as parameter changes accumulate. Re-examining projection-based editors such as `AlphaEdit`, the authors find that their robustness comes **mainly from update regularization, not from the intended null-space projection**. Building on this, `FisherEdit` uses Fisher information to apply importance-aware regularization in parameter space, penalizing changes to sensitive parameters more heavily. It has an efficient row-wise closed-form solution. Experiments on `Llama-3`, `Qwen2.5`, and `Olmo-3` show state-of-the-art editing performance with better preservation of downstream task accuracy.

papers.title: Secure Agentic Coding through Counterexample-Grounded Feedback
papers.abstract: As coding models and agent harnesses become more capable, reliable security verification is becoming a central bottleneck. Improving secure code generation requires a signal whose reported progress remains aligned with actual program behavior under optimization; otherwise, an optimizer can improve the signal's verdict without removing the underlying vulnerability. Existing model-based approaches require models to either infer program behavior from source code or specify correct outcomes for adversarial tests, placing substantial reasoning demands on the security signal. We introduce \falcon{}, a counterexample-grounded verification framework that separates attack exploration from behavioral verification and connects them through execution traces of the program under test. In test-time repair, \falcon{} yields substantially stronger held-out functional-security gains than alternative security signals across secure code generation benchmarks, while preserving or improving functionality. As an RL reward, \falcon{} also outperforms static-analysis and learned rewards on held-out functional-security, even when all policies successfully optimize their respective training rewards. Combining \falcon{} with either proxy reward further improves held-out performance, suggesting that execution-grounded feedback can mitigate reward overoptimization while preserving useful guidance from existing security signals.
papers.summary: Improving secure code generation requires a security signal that cannot be gamed: an optimizer should not be able to satisfy the signal while leaving the vulnerability in place. `Falcon` is a counterexample-grounded verification framework that separates attack exploration from behavioral verification, connecting the two through execution traces of the program under test. Used for test-time repair, it delivers substantially larger held-out functional-security gains than alternative signals while preserving functionality. Used as a reinforcement learning reward, it **outperforms static-analysis and learned rewards on held-out security even when every policy fully optimizes its own training reward**, and combining it with those proxy rewards improves results further.

papers.title: LEAPS: Long-context Evaluation of Adaptive Pattern Learning and State Tracking
papers.abstract: Long-context language models (LCLMs) power agents that act over long trajectories, from improving a codebase to running research experiments to forecasters that condition on lengthy histories. These applications draw on three distinct long-context capabilities: recall, where the answer is a fact present in the context; state tracking, where the outcome can be computed by performing a series of transformations to a specified state; and pattern learning, where the goal is to make a prediction by sampling from a distribution inferred from many observations. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on the first capability. In this work, we introduce LEAPS (Long-context Evaluation of Adaptive Pattern learning and State tracking), a collection of 12 novel datasets, spanning agentic workflows, behavioral modeling, and forecasting of market and world events. By construction, LEAPS is resistant to data contamination, extends to millions of input tokens, and uses reliable metrics. We evaluate 30 API and open models from 8K to 512K input tokens. LEAPS distinguishes models that perform near perfectly on recall tasks, finding that such models' state tracking and pattern learning abilities can vary significantly and degrade much more dramatically with increasing input lengths--even for pattern learning, where more observations should make learning a theoretically easier task. Moreover, thinking models often underperform their base counterparts, exhausting their generation budget or oversimplifying the task. We hope LEAPS can guide the development of the next generation of LCLMs.
papers.summary: Long-context benchmarks mostly test recall of facts present in the context, but agents and forecasters also need to track state through a series of transformations and to learn patterns from many observations. `LEAPS` (Long-context Evaluation of Adaptive Pattern learning and State tracking) provides 12 new contamination-resistant datasets covering agentic workflows, behavioral modeling, and market and world-event forecasting, with inputs that scale to millions of tokens. Evaluating 30 models from 8K to 512K input tokens, the authors find that models near-perfect at recall **vary widely in state tracking and pattern learning, and degrade sharply as input length grows**. Thinking models often underperform their base versions because they run out of generation budget or oversimplify the task.

papers.title: Maestro: Agentic Formal Proof Development by Coordination
papers.abstract: Lean is increasingly used to verify mathematical proofs and software produced by LLM agents, but writing formal proofs remains hard. Existing prover systems take a divide-and-conquer approach that recursively decomposes hard proof obligations into easier lemmas and splits again any lemma that resists proof. However, a lemma can resist proof for different reasons, including insufficient guidance, a false statement, or a flaw in the decomposition that produced it. Existing systems cannot tell these apart as a failed attempt reports little beyond its failure, and responses are confined to the failing node without considering the rest of the proof or revising the plan above it. The system may thus keep decomposing obligations along a flawed proof direction until the budget runs out, causing the whole proof attempt to fail. We introduce Maestro, a Lean prover harness that handles failures through global coordination. Provers report why they failed, not just that they failed, and a coordinator that sees the whole proof chooses an appropriate response, such as guiding a stuck prover, correcting a false lemma, or retracting a flawed subtree and replanning it. The same harness extends to verified code synthesis, where a checked counterexample sends the code back for repair. We evaluate Maestro with four frontier LLMs on seven mathematics and three software verification benchmarks. It proves more targets than each model's native coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) on every benchmark the agent has not already saturated, with the largest gains on research-level mathematics. With Claude Opus 5, it discovers its own proofs of 34 of the 48 theorems in the June 2026 release of arXivLean, against 19 for the native agent. It also outperforms all published prover systems on every benchmark they share, solving 669/672 PutnamBench, 59/60 Lean-IMO-Bench, and 6/6 IMO 2026.
papers.summary: LLM-based Lean provers typically decompose hard proof goals into lemmas recursively, but a failed lemma only reports that it failed. As a result, they cannot tell a missing hint from a false statement or a flawed decomposition, and they can waste their budget along a bad proof direction. `Maestro` is a prover harness in which provers report why they failed and a coordinator with a view of the whole proof chooses a response: guiding the prover, correcting a lemma, or retracting and replanning a subtree. The same harness also supports verified code synthesis. With four frontier LLMs, it beats the native `Claude Code` and `Codex` agents on every unsaturated benchmark. With `Claude Opus 5` it proves 34 of 48 `arXivLean` theorems versus 19 for the native agent, and it **solves 669/672 `PutnamBench`, 59/60 `Lean-IMO-Bench`, and 6/6 IMO 2026 problems**.

papers.title: UtilityBench: Measuring Language Model Utility When Errors Have Different Costs
papers.abstract: As language models are increasingly deployed in real-world scenarios with important outcomes, the impact of their mistakes often extends far beyond what correctness can capture. In domains like medicine, a single error can lead to serious consequences and put patient safety at risk. However, mainstream evaluation protocols still treat all errors as equal, overlooking the spectrum of real-world costs. To address this, we propose a utility-based evaluation paradigm that explicitly incorporates the varying consequences of errors. Guided by this principle, we develop UtilityBench, a large-scale benchmark of 15,000 instances with verifiable answers, quantifying error severity using Best-Worst Scaling to elicit meaningful, data-driven cost estimates. These quantified utilities shape when a model should answer or abstain, guiding it to make decisions that align with the true importance of each scenario. As another merit, we introduce UtilityAUC, a metric that measures the area under the utility curve determined by a model's response ordering, thereby enabling utility preference alignment beyond error frequency. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that UtilityAUC can distinguish between models where standard accuracy and AURC fall short. Empirically, evaluating 20 state-of-the-art models, we find that greater accuracy or more advanced architectures do not reliably translate to higher UtilityAUC, highlighting a gap between problem-solving ability and responsible decision-making in language model evaluation.
papers.summary: Standard language model evaluations count all errors equally, even though some mistakes, such as those in medicine, are far more costly than others. `UtilityBench` contains 15,000 verifiable instances whose error severities are estimated with Best-Worst Scaling. These costs determine when a model should answer and when it should abstain. The authors also introduce `UtilityAUC`, the area under a utility curve built from the order in which a model ranks its responses, and show theoretically that it distinguishes models that accuracy and the area under the risk-coverage curve (`AURC`) cannot. Across 20 models, **higher accuracy or more advanced architectures do not reliably yield higher `UtilityAUC`**.

papers.title: TESS: LLM-guided Translation, Exploration, Simulation, and Search for Embodied Task Planning
papers.abstract: In this work we focus on the problem of embodied task planning, which requires an agent to accomplish a complex task by separating it into atomic actions. Recent studies have developed LLM-based methods to address this problem. However, the executability and correctness of the generated plans remain suboptimal in complex environments and tasks. On the other hand, classical search algorithms have the potential to solve the planning problems perfectly, yet they require fully observable environments, known state transitions and goal state, which are often unattainable in general task domains. Therefore, we propose to implement an LLM-guided search algorithm that makes the search process possible and efficient by incorporating LLMs' commonsense knowledge. Our method leverages LLMs to (1) translate natural language instructions into formatted goal conditions, (2) facilitate efficient exploration in partially observable environments, (3) implement a rule-based world simulator, and (4) prune the space of candidate actions to improve search efficiency. Experimental results on VirtualHome and ALFWorld demonstrate its superior performance.
papers.summary: LLM-based embodied task planners often generate plans that cannot be executed or are wrong. Classical search could solve these problems, but it needs full observability, known transitions, and an explicit goal. `TESS` combines the two by using an LLM to translate instructions into formal goal conditions, guide exploration in partially observable environments, build a rule-based world simulator, and prune candidate actions during search. Experiments on `VirtualHome` and `ALFWorld` report **better performance than prior LLM-based planners**.

papers.title: EvoSkill v2: Fully Agentic Skill Evolution from Benchmark Adaptation to a Stateful Evolver
papers.abstract: EvoSkill v2 is a three-agent system that edits the instructions (skills) an agent is given, leaving its model and harness intact. The user starts a run by describing a benchmark and supplying a grader, which a benchmark adaptor turns into a benchmark-specific plugin. A solver attempts the tasks, and an evolver reads the solver's training rollouts and rewrites the skills at each epoch. We implement the evolver as one stateful coding agent with a bash tool for the whole run, unlike the two most common designs among the skill optimizers we surveyed: a sequence of single model calls, as in SkillOpt, and an agent that starts afresh each round, as in SkillBoost. We also measure how much the solver's rollouts vary from one attempt to the next, give the evolver several attempts per training task, and accept every epoch's skills instead of selecting among them on noisy scores. With fine-grained ground truth, EvoSkill v2's skills raised the held-out pass rate above the stronger of SkillOpt and SkillBoost by 7.7 percentage points on SpreadsheetBench v2 and by 5.4 on $\tau^3$-bench banking. In both benchmarks and both feedback settings, EvoSkill v2's evolver cost less per percentage point of held-out pass rate gained than either baseline's optimizer. EvoSkill v2 also enables a less capable model to improve its own skills, demonstrated by a gain of up to 21.5 percentage points in the $\tau^3$-bench banking experiment where Claude Haiku 5.5 powers both solver and evolver.
papers.summary: `EvoSkill v2` improves an agent by rewriting its instruction files (skills) while leaving the underlying model and harness unchanged. It uses three agents: an adaptor that turns a benchmark description and grader into a plugin, a solver that attempts the tasks, and an evolver that reads the solver's rollouts and rewrites the skills each epoch. Unlike prior optimizers, the evolver is a single stateful coding agent with a bash tool that persists for the whole run. It also accounts for variation between solver attempts and accepts every epoch's skills rather than picking among noisy scores. It beats the stronger of `SkillOpt` and `SkillBoost` by 7.7 points on `SpreadsheetBench v2` and 5.4 points on `tau^3-bench` banking at lower cost per point gained, and it lets **`Claude Haiku 5.5` improve its own skills by up to 21.5 percentage points**.

papers.title: Keep the Lineages Alive: Diversity-Preserving SMC for Diffusion LLM Decoding
papers.abstract: Inference-time sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding can improve the reasoning accuracy of masked diffusion language models (diffusion LLMs) without post-training by resampling a population of partial generations according to a reward. Its effectiveness therefore depends on the resampling step, which must concentrate computation on promising candidates while retaining enough diversity to explore alternative reasoning paths. The reward can be internal, the decoder's own confidence on the committed prefix, or external, a process reward model scoring that prefix. Under either reward, multinomial resampling can disrupt this balance by duplicating high-weight particles and discarding lineages that may still reach a correct solution. The effective sample size (ESS) does not register this loss: multinomial resampling resets it to its maximum even as distinct lineages disappear. To retain such lineages, we introduce lineage-preserving SMC (LP-SMC), which combines Chopthin resampling with an input weight floor. Instead of equalizing weights, Chopthin bounds the ratio between the largest and smallest weights it returns and carries the unequal weights forward. The floor limits how far below the maximum a weight may fall before resampling so that lineages with low early weight keep a chance to recover. Across mathematical-reasoning and code-generation benchmarks on two base models, LP-SMC raises oracle coverage, the fraction of problems with at least one correct particle, in every setting, by 1.8 to 25.6 points, and raises end-to-end accuracy under a common reward-model selector in eleven of twelve settings, by up to 7.9 points on LLaDA-1.5 and 18.3 on Dream-7B. The coverage gain persists under the external reward model, which suggests that diversity-preserving resampling and the guidance signal contribute separately to inference-time search.
papers.summary: Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding improves reasoning in masked diffusion language models at inference time by resampling a population of partial generations according to a reward. Standard multinomial resampling, however, can wipe out lineages that might still reach a correct answer, and the effective sample size metric does not reveal this loss. Lineage-preserving SMC (`LP-SMC`) combines Chopthin resampling, which bounds the ratio between the largest and smallest weights instead of equalizing them, with a floor on how low a weight can fall. On math and code benchmarks with `LLaDA-1.5` and `Dream-7B`, it **raises the share of problems with at least one correct candidate in every setting, by 1.8 to 25.6 points**, and improves end-to-end accuracy in eleven of twelve settings, by up to 18.3 points.

papers.title: The KV-Surgeon: Compensation-Aware Offline KV-Cache Compaction
papers.abstract: Offline compaction of the key--value cache (KV-cache) reduces the cost of repeatedly querying a fixed context by constructing a smaller cache once and reusing it subsequently. The central challenge of compaction is deciding which cache entries to delete and which to retain. Existing methods score each candidate for deletion on its own, with the rest of the cache being held fixed. However, softmax renormalization of the attention operation couples these decisions in a nonlinear manner: removing one entry changes the attention weights of every remaining one. In this work, we introduce KV-Surgeon, which uses calibration data to take interactions into account in a tractable way. We derive a quadratic surrogate that admits closed-form expressions for jointly making the optimal greedy removal decision as well as compensation within the remaining entries. On QuALITY, LongHealth, and Long Code Arena, and at every evaluated compaction ratio, KV-Surgeon substantially advances the cost--accuracy Pareto frontier of dense and mixture-of-experts models from 4B to 30B parameters. At $50\times$ compaction, KV-Surgeon improves question-answering accuracy by up to four points over attention matching (Zweiger et al., 2026), the state of the art, at comparable cost. Lastly, we introduce an even faster variant, which also exceeds the state of the art while requiring only two fifths of its cost.
papers.summary: Offline compaction of a key-value cache (KV-cache) builds a smaller cache once so that repeated queries over a fixed context cost less. Existing methods score each entry for removal in isolation, ignoring that softmax renormalization makes removing one entry change the attention weights of all the others. `KV-Surgeon` uses calibration data and a quadratic surrogate to derive closed-form expressions that jointly select the best greedy removal and compensate the remaining entries. On `QuALITY`, `LongHealth`, and `Long Code Arena`, with dense and mixture-of-experts models from 4B to 30B parameters, it improves the cost-accuracy trade-off at every compaction ratio, including **up to four points higher accuracy than attention matching at 50× compaction**. A faster variant also beats that prior state of the art at two-fifths of its cost.

papers.title: MITRA-lexicon: Lexica of attested translations from Sanskrit into English, Tibetan and Chinese
papers.abstract: The standard Sanskrit lexica are monumental and indispensable, but they cite their attestations as abbreviated references to editions, without links to the digitized texts now widely available and without a translation of the passage, and they naturally do not reflect translations made after them. To address these gaps, we present MITRA-lexicon, a family of corpus-grounded lexica based on span annotations of translation equivalents with Sanskrit as the pivot: Sanskrit-English, derived from the Mitrasamgraha corpus, as well as Sanskrit-Tibetan and Sanskrit-Chinese, derived from the MITRA-parallel corpus of Buddhist literature. In total, the resource comprises 2.18 million headword entries in six directional lexica. Headwords are lemmas and compounds from silver annotations that follow the Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS). Senses are ranked by frequency, and each of the 10.4 million attestations includes its sentence pair, with character offsets of the word and its equivalent. We propose a multi-step pipeline based on grammatical annotation models, fine-tuned large language models, and a teacher-student setup to produce the alignments. We evaluate the lexica against reference dictionaries and manually corrected gold alignments. We release the lexica and the fine-tuned span annotation model, together with a web interface for looking up headwords and their attested senses.
papers.summary: Standard Sanskrit dictionaries cite their sources as abbreviated references, without links to digitized texts or translations of the cited passages. `MITRA-lexicon` is a family of corpus-grounded lexica that use Sanskrit as the pivot language for English, Tibetan, and Chinese, built from the `Mitrasamgraha` and `MITRA-parallel` corpora. It contains **2.18 million headword entries and 10.4 million attestations across six directional lexica**, each linked to its sentence pair. The alignments come from a pipeline of grammatical annotation models, fine-tuned LLMs, and a teacher-student setup, and are evaluated against reference dictionaries and hand-corrected alignments.

papers.title: Global probabilistic forecasting of air pollution
papers.abstract: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) refers to particulate matter with an aerodynamic diameter of 2.5 micrometre or less. It comes from human activities, such as traffic and industry, and from wildfires, desert dust and gases emitted by vegetation. Short-term exposure to it accounts for about a million deaths a year. Operational forecasts run on grids tens of kilometres wide, which hide the pollution breathed by nearly two hundred million people a day. Machine learning has transformed weather forecasting, but data-driven forecasts of air pollution still blur extremes and lose skill as the air travels. Here we introduce Foehn, a generative model that learns from global kilometre-scale estimates of PM2.5 and computes where the air comes from. Over a year of retrospective forecasts, it outperforms the operational forecast at three stations in four and forecasts at the scale of this hidden exposure. Its ensembles are calibrated, and their mean detects local pollution extremes four days ahead as well as the operational forecast does one day ahead. Such forecasts could warn the millions whom coarse maps miss, once kilometre-scale data are available in real time.
papers.summary: Operational forecasts of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) run on grids tens of kilometres wide, which hide the local exposure of nearly two hundred million people. Existing data-driven forecasts also tend to blur extremes. `Foehn` is a generative model trained on global kilometre-scale PM2.5 estimates that explicitly computes where the air comes from. Over a year of retrospective forecasts, it beats the operational forecast at three out of four stations and produces calibrated ensembles. Its ensemble mean **detects local pollution extremes four days ahead as well as the operational forecast does one day ahead**.

papers.title: Speech LLMs That Breathe: Modeling Non-Verbal Vocalizations in Dialogue
papers.abstract: The user experience of speech interaction models has improved, benefiting from the modeling of paralinguistic attributes and advances in speech reconstruction paradigms. However, human communication follows extensive norms regarding non-verbal vocalizations (NVVs) spanning respiratory, affective, and discourse. The omission of these events imposes inherent limitations on the naturalness of current approaches. In this work, we cover 13 major types of NVVs and construct a natural dialogue dataset that conforms to human conversational norms through an automated synthesis pipeline. We enhance the ability of speech interaction models to generate contextually appropriate NVV events through multi-stage fine-tuning and NVV-aware GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). Based on distinct modeling paradigms, we substantially improve the expressiveness of VocalNet and VITA-Qinyu in empathy interactions and role-play dialogues, and further discuss the architectural necessity for achieving high-quality natural speech generation.
papers.summary: Speech interaction models generally omit non-verbal vocalizations (NVVs) such as breathing, laughter, and discourse sounds, which limits how natural they sound. The authors cover 13 NVV types and build a natural dialogue dataset that follows human conversational norms using an automated synthesis pipeline. They then train models to produce contextually appropriate NVVs through multi-stage fine-tuning and an NVV-aware version of Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`). This **substantially improves the expressiveness of `VocalNet` and `VITA-Qinyu`** in empathetic and role-play dialogue, and the paper discusses which architectures are needed for natural speech generation.

papers.title: Policy Search in Code Space for Multi-Agent Pathfinding
papers.abstract: Developing coordination policies for complex multi-agent systems relies on either labor-intensive algorithm design or opaque task-specific reinforcement learning. With recent advances in autonomous coding agents, we show that policy search directly in code space offers a compelling third path that combines automated optimization with explicit interpretability. We investigate a human-directed workflow in which coding agents iteratively propose, implement, evaluate, diagnose, and eventually refine algorithms guided by simulation feedback and explicit correctness verification. We conducted two case studies and found that this workflow robustly outperformed any manually engineered solutions. On a challenging map in the 2024 League of Robot Runners competition, a two-day search discovered a policy that exceeds the stronger locally reproduced competition entry by 35.0% on the densest instance and generalizes to unseen map instances. In simulated real-world warehouses with irregular lanes, continuous robot geometry, and asynchronous motion, a week-long search discovered an entirely new class of multi-agent pathfinding algorithm that outperforms a calibrated proprietary solution in throughput by 58.9%. Under stated assumptions, we further prove that the new algorithm is collision-free and completes, in finite time, every accepted goal that is not withdrawn or replaced. Together, the studies show that policy search in code space powered by state-of-the-art coding agents offers a highly competitive path to building real engineering solutions that are both effective and analytically tractable.
papers.summary: Coordination policies for multi-agent systems are usually either hand-designed or learned as opaque task-specific reinforcement learning policies. This work explores a third option: a human-directed workflow in which coding agents propose, implement, evaluate, diagnose, and refine algorithms in code, guided by simulation feedback and correctness checks. On a map from the 2024 `League of Robot Runners` competition, a two-day search found a policy that beats the strongest reproduced entry by 35.0% on the densest instance. In simulated warehouses, a week-long search discovered a new class of multi-agent pathfinding algorithm that **beats a calibrated proprietary solution in throughput by 58.9%** and is proven collision-free under stated assumptions.

papers.title: Claim Laundering: When Agent Decision Models Trust Records Over Reality
papers.abstract: Agent decision models select actions in a single forward pass from inputs that combine environmental observations with the agent's own record of previous actions. When an action fails silently, these sources can conflict: the record reports success, but the environment shows that the step did not take effect. We ask which source determines the next decision. Across Android screen traces, ALFWorld, and WebShop, we construct paired states that independently vary the observation, the logged action, and an explicit success claim. In all 12 configurations of four decision models and three domains, records have a larger average effect on commitment decisions than observations; after claimed-but-failed steps, the models still stop, advance, or purchase in 53-100% of cases. Yet the relevant evidence is often represented internally: linear probes on intermediate hidden states distinguish successful from failed steps on held-out apps, tasks, and goals (AUROC 0.77-1.00), and activation patching reveals increasing influence from records in later layers. We use this signal in EVIGATE, an intermediate-layer veto that requires no additional forward pass and adds 0.04-2.0% serving latency. Under injected silent failures, EVIGATE improves task success by 18.7 points in live ALFWorld agents, 5.0 in WebShop, and 5.1 in a phone simulator, and in WebShop and the simulator it also outperforms random vetoes at the same rate. Its effectiveness depends on representative calibration states: gates calibrated on offline counterfactual states do not transfer reliably to live agent trajectories.
papers.summary: When an agent's action fails silently, its own log may report success while the environment shows that nothing changed. This study asks which of the two sources drives the agent's next decision. Using paired states across Android screen traces, `ALFWorld`, and `WebShop`, the authors find that **records outweigh observations in all 12 model-domain configurations**: after a claimed but failed step, models still stop, advance, or purchase in 53–100% of cases. Linear probes show that intermediate hidden states do encode whether the step failed, and the authors use this signal in `EVIGATE`, a veto at an intermediate layer that adds at most 2% latency. Under injected silent failures, `EVIGATE` improves task success by 18.7 points in live `ALFWorld` agents, but gates calibrated only on offline counterfactual states do not transfer reliably to live trajectories.

papers.title: OrderGPT: Generation Order as a Learnable Modeling Choice
papers.abstract: Generative modeling of discrete data has two popular paradigms: autoregressive models such as GPT, which factorize a sequence in a left-to-right (L2R) order, and masked diffusion models, which are essentially any-order autoregressive modeling. Rather than competing methods, these are the two extreme points of a single axis -- the generation order. For structured discrete domains without a natural traversal, both extremes may be suboptimal, yet the intermediate choice -- a single well-adapted order -- remains largely unexplored. We introduce OrderGPT, which builds on Any-Order GPT to learn a task-level generation order without canonical-order supervision. Our key observation is that predicting variables from randomly sampled reveal prefixes produces recurring attention patterns in the backbone that provide a model-dependent signal of predictive dependencies. We aggregate this signal into a reciprocal dependency graph and use a spectral teacher to derive continuous generation priorities. A lightweight OrderMLP integrated into the GPT backbone learns to predict these priorities from attention, incorporating order learning into the architecture within a single training run. Training gradually shifts toward the learned order, which is then frozen for subsequent autoregressive training and generation. The same mechanism adapts across modalities: adaptively it recovers near-L2R dependency structure in language, learns anatomically organized factorizations on human pose, and discovers a factorization on tabular data that places statistically and semantically related fields nearby, while improving downstream modeling metrics across all domains. The code is available at https://github.com/Chenhe-yang/OrderGPT/.
papers.summary: Left-to-right autoregressive models and masked diffusion models sit at the two extremes of a single design choice, the generation order. For structured data without a natural order, a single well-adapted order in between may work better than either. `OrderGPT` builds on `Any-Order GPT` and learns a task-level generation order without supervision. It aggregates recurring attention patterns into a dependency graph, uses a spectral teacher to derive generation priorities, and trains a lightweight `OrderMLP` to predict those priorities within one training run. The learned order recovers near-left-to-right structure for language and anatomically organized orders for human pose, groups related fields in tabular data, and **improves modeling metrics in all domains tested**.

papers.title: AdaExploreBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Proactive Exploration and Test-time Adaptation in Evolving Environments
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in unfamiliar and evolving environments, requiring them to proactively explore, understand, and adapt to environmental dynamics. However, existing benchmarks rarely test whether agents can proactively discover how an environment works and adapt as it evolves. To address this gap, we introduce AdaExploreBench, a benchmark for proactive exploration and test-time adaptation in evolving environments. By instantiating environmental dynamics as hidden rules, AdaExploreBench requires agents to actively acquire evidence and infer the rules. Under implicit rule drift, the latent rule changes without announcement, requiring agents to detect from degraded performance that prior knowledge is stale and re-explore. Experiments on eight leading LLMs show that proactive and adaptive exploration remain challenging: GPT-6 Sol achieves only 61.9% calibrated accuracy, while providing sufficient evidence or removing rule drift improves average performance significantly by close to 10%. These results reveal a critical bottleneck in current LLM agents: they can often reason effectively from informative evidence once it is available, but struggle to actively acquire the right evidence and recognize when previously acquired evidence is no longer valid.
papers.summary: Few benchmarks test whether LLM agents can work out on their own how an unfamiliar environment behaves and adapt when it changes. `AdaExploreBench` encodes environment dynamics as hidden rules that agents must infer by gathering evidence. Under implicit rule drift, the rules change without notice, so agents must notice falling performance and re-explore. Across eight leading LLMs, **the best model, `GPT-6 Sol`, reaches only 61.9% calibrated accuracy**, and supplying sufficient evidence or removing drift raises average performance by close to 10%. The authors conclude that current agents reason well once they have informative evidence but struggle to collect it and to recognize when what they learned is out of date.
papers.highlight_summary:
LLM agents in unfamiliar settings need to discover how an environment works on their own and notice when it quietly changes. The benchmark encodes environment dynamics as hidden action-to-outcome rules that agents must find by probing, and those rules drift partway through an episode without any announcement.

- **How it works:** the benchmark has 256 evaluation and 1,000 training episodes, generated by an LLM pipeline across finance, healthcare, cybersecurity and manufacturing, with hidden rules drawn from four families (`additive`, `conjunctive`, `disjunctive`, `lexicographic`); agents choose when, what and how much to probe with self-designed cases, while past evaluation cases are masked so the only evidence they hold is what they collected themselves.
- **Main results:** all eight models score below **70% calibrated accuracy**, with `Gemini-3.8-Flash` best at **67.3%** and `GPT-6-Sol` at **61.9%**; giving agents enough evidence raises average accuracy by **9.4 points**, and removing rule drift raises it by **6.2 points**.
- **Exploring more doesn't mean exploring better:** `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` sends about **24×** as many probes as `Llama-3.1-8B` yet trails both top models, and forcing all models to probe more lowers average accuracy by **2.0 points**, which points to probe informativeness as the bottleneck.
- **Damage from drift:** accuracy falls by an average of **26.9 points** right after a rule change and never fully recovers; agents report identical rules before and after the change in **36.3%** of episodes and catch factor replacements far more reliably than reversals of a factor's direction.
- **Limitations:** the rule-based environments are a simplified abstraction, exploration quality is only measured indirectly through ablations, and drift is limited to within-family factor replacements and direction reversals.

papers.title: CXBench: A Benchmark for Process-Compliant LLM Agents in Regulated Customer-Experience Workflows
papers.abstract:
Tool-using language agents increasingly perform regulated customer-service workflows, where a correct final state is insufficient: agents must also provide disclosures, obtain consent, and follow required procedures. Existing tool-agent benchmarks largely score final business states, accepting trajectories that reach correct outcomes through non-compliant processes.
  We introduce cxbench, a benchmark that evaluates outcome and process compliance separately across six regulated domains. Each task combines a customer request, a tool-based environment, and explicit process requirements. Rule cards link cited regulatory obligations to observable trace evidence. A hybrid grader combines deterministic checks for ordering and authority with an LLM judge for semantic requirements. We define a false-pass as an outcome-pass run that fails process checks.
  Across seven models and 120 tasks, 55.5% of the 840 retained executions are false-passes, representing 80.1% of outcome-passing runs; only 13.8% pass both checks. Process-inclusive evaluation changes the observed model ordering and exposes differences hidden by outcome-only scoring. cxbench makes these failures inspectable through trace-linked criteria.
papers.summary: Tool-using agents in regulated customer-service settings must reach the correct end state and also follow required procedures such as giving disclosures and obtaining consent. Existing benchmarks mostly score only the final state. `CXBench` scores outcome and process compliance separately across six regulated domains, using rule cards that tie regulatory obligations to evidence in the agent's trace. A hybrid grader combines deterministic ordering and authority checks with an LLM judge for semantic requirements. Across seven models and 120 tasks, **80.1% of runs that reached the correct outcome failed process checks**, only 13.8% of runs passed both checks, and adding process scoring changed the model rankings.

papers.title: Productive State-Space Exploration for Multi-turn RL in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) for Large Language Model (LLM) agents in multi-turn, long-horizon environments remains challenging due to inefficient action selection and repetitive behavioral patterns. In particular, agents often become trapped in high-confidence yet unproductive behaviors, repeatedly executing invalid actions or entering action loops that hinder task completion. We observe that these frequently violate environment preconditions, revealing a mismatch between the agent's representation of the internal state and the dynamics of the underlying environment. In addition, repetitive high-confidence actions lead to cyclical behaviors that provide little to no progress towards the goal. We argue that addressing these challenges requires more productive task-aligned exploration to improve the agent's understanding of environment dynamics. Motivated by intrinsic curiosity-driven exploration, we propose a conditional state-space exploration framework that balances task completion with intrinsic information-seeking behavior. Specifically, we introduce an intrinsic reward that penalizes actions whose observation duplicates prior state memory. This provides the benefit of reducing redundant behaviors and encouraging state-space coverage without relying on a general information-theoretic measure. Strong experimental results demonstrate that our approach substantially improves policy learning in multi-turn environments, mitigating invalid actions and repetitive loops.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents trained with reinforcement learning (RL) in multi-turn, long-horizon environments often get stuck in confident but unproductive behavior, such as repeating invalid actions or looping through the same states. The authors trace this to a mismatch between the agent's internal state representation and the environment's actual dynamics. They propose a conditional state-space exploration framework that balances task completion against curiosity-style information seeking. Its core is an **intrinsic reward that penalizes actions whose observations duplicate earlier states in memory**, which the authors report substantially improves policy learning and reduces invalid actions and loops.

papers.title: EmbodiedWorld-200K: Toward Embodied World Agents via Embodied-Planning Dataset and Interactive World Models
papers.abstract: Building embodied agents that can perceive, reason, and act across diverse 3D worlds is a central research direction toward artificial general intelligence. Yet most existing work remains confined to specific tasks in a single scene and transfers poorly to new environments, leaving general embodied agents for open-world settings under-explored. We refer to such agents as Embodied World Agents (EWAs), whose defining property is the ability to understand diverse visual environments and execute general actions in open-world conditions. To advance EWA research, we study open-world embodied navigation-planning and release EmbodiedWorld-200K, a large-scale dataset of over 200K samples spanning diverse scenes. Each example is equipped with multi-level annotations, ranging from low-level camera-motion trajectories to high-level semantic instructions. The dataset also provides unified evaluation splits and task-specific metrics, supporting offline pretraining and fair evaluation of EWAs. Beyond offline supervision, a defining characteristic of an EWA is its interaction with the environment; training solely on offline data is therefore insufficient, especially for generalizing to scenes not covered in the training distribution. Building dedicated real interactive environments, however, is often prohibitively expensive. To address this, we propose a novel training scheme that employs a video world model as a low-cost environment proxy and performs interactive reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training of the EWA within it. Empirically, pretraining on EmbodiedWorld-200K substantially improves the open-world embodied planning ability of the EWA, and further RL post-training inside a world model yields clear gains on out-of-distribution scenes. The dataset, baseline checkpoints, and training and evaluation code are available at https://xiaokunfeng.github.io/EmbodiedWorld-200K/.
papers.summary: The work targets embodied agents that can plan and navigate across diverse, open-world 3D scenes rather than a single task in a single scene. It releases `EmbodiedWorld-200K`, a dataset of **over 200K navigation-planning samples** with annotations ranging from low-level camera-motion trajectories to high-level semantic instructions, plus unified evaluation splits and metrics. Because real interactive environments are expensive to build, the authors also use a video world model as a low-cost stand-in environment for reinforcement-learning (RL) post-training. Pretraining on the dataset improves open-world planning, and RL inside the world model further improves results on out-of-distribution scenes.

papers.title: PaceVLA: Adaptive Temporal Action Quantization in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Fast and reliable manipulation is crucial for practical robot deployment. Although Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently shown remarkable progress as generalist robot policies, their execution often remains temporally inefficient. A key source of this inefficiency is that policies learn fine-grained temporal patterns from teleoperated demonstrations, requiring many low-level action steps. Temporal action quantization offers a simple way to accelerate execution by aggregating consecutive low-level actions into temporally coarser actions. However, applying action quantization without considering when fine-grained control is required introduces a speed-accuracy trade-off: accelerated actions may efficiently reduce redundant steps in some phases, while discarding critical motion details in precision-sensitive interactions.
