papers.abstract: Neural solvers for the Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling Problem (FJSP) typically refresh graph representations and update feasibility after every operation--machine decision. However, only feasibility must remain exact at every step, whereas graph encoding is substantially more expensive and can potentially be refreshed less frequently. We present CoRS, which decouples them: an interval-level graph representation is reused across multiple sequential decisions, while a stepwise feasibility state is updated after every action. This two-timescale design amortizes graph encoding without parallelizing action generation or relaxing scheduling constraints. CoRS further develops a feasibility-preserving composite-interval decoding scheme with dynamic constraint tracking and boundary state synchronization, which reduces representation refresh frequency while maintaining continuous feasible schedule construction. Furthermore, to alleviate representation staleness caused by interval-level state reuse, CoRS introduces enhanced static features as a compensation mechanism. By providing more comprehensive structural information of the scheduling problem, these features improve the model's perception of overall problem characteristics. Extensive experiments on synthetic and multiple public FJSP benchmarks demonstrate that CoRS significantly reduces inference time while maintaining competitive solution quality, achieving favorable speed-quality trade-offs under tight wall-clock budgets and low-latency scenarios.
papers.summary: Neural solvers for the Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling Problem (FJSP) usually re-encode the whole scheduling graph after every operation-to-machine decision, even though only the feasibility state needs to be exact at each step. `CoRS` separates the two: it reuses one interval-level graph encoding across several sequential decisions while still updating feasibility after every action. Constraint tracking at interval boundaries keeps schedules feasible, and richer static features compensate for the encoding going stale between refreshes. On synthetic and public FJSP benchmarks, it **substantially cuts inference time while keeping solution quality competitive**, which helps under tight time budgets.

papers.title: Machina Pauliana: A neuro-symbolic approach to the actio pauliana in Dutch insolvency law
papers.abstract: Applying a legal provision frequently requires both structured rule-based reasoning and sensitivity to open-textured terms developed in case law. The actio pauliana of Article 42 of the Dutch Bankruptcy Act (Faillissementswet, Fw), which allows an insolvency practitioner to avoid transactions that prejudice creditors, requires both. We present a neuro-symbolic model of Article 42 Fw. Its symbolic core is written in Catala in a literate style that keeps statute and formalisation aligned and was developed through pair programming, with open-textured terms represented as boolean inputs where neural components couple to the symbolic solver. A neural routine structures a case's natural-language facts into boolean and date inputs. Neural subroutines resolve the open-textured terms through case-based reasoning over Dutch civil judgments, retrieved through a pipeline that filters on the requirement being resolved and expands along the procedural chain of a case. Segmenting and labelling those judgments attains high precision and recall against a manually annotated gold standard of 100 judgments. On ten hand-annotated cases the neuro-symbolic model handles most criteria reasonably but struggles with the knowledge requirement. Retrieval depth shows no clear quantitative effect, although retrieved judgments provide explicit grounding in prior case law.
papers.summary: Applying the actio pauliana in Article 42 of the Dutch Bankruptcy Act, which lets insolvency practitioners undo transactions that harm creditors, requires both rule-based reasoning and interpretation of open-ended terms shaped by case law. The authors encode the statute in `Catala` as a symbolic core, with open-ended terms left as boolean inputs that neural components fill in. One neural routine turns a case's natural-language facts into structured inputs, and others resolve open-ended terms by case-based reasoning over retrieved Dutch civil judgments. Judgment segmentation and labeling reach high precision and recall on a 100-judgment gold standard; on ten hand-annotated cases the system handles most criteria reasonably but **struggles with the knowledge requirement**.

papers.title: RECAP: Reciprocal Sparse Attention and Hierarchical Caching for Efficient Video Diffusion
papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos but remain computationally expensive. Sparse attention and temporal caching reduce computation within and across denoising steps, respectively, offering a natural composition. However, predictions produced with sparse attention become sources for temporal reuse, coupling their errors along the sampling trajectory. We observe that improving the accuracy of these sources recovers fidelity without changing the reuse schedule, and that sparsification errors remain directionally aligned across nearby steps, suggesting that correction information can be shared rather than recomputed. These observations motivate RECAP, a training-free method that couples sparse attention with hierarchical caching through reciprocal correction, adaptively coordinated by online error feedback. Cached dense refinement corrects omitted interactions in current sparse estimates, while fresh sparse statistics track input changes and regulate the aging correction. The resulting predictions then renew the sources for whole-step prediction reuse, allowing prediction history to advance between dense refreshes. We evaluate RECAP on multiple video diffusion models against sparse-attention methods, caching methods, and their direct compositions. On HunyuanVideo at 720p 5-second generation, RECAP achieves a 3.05x speedup and outperforms all tested direct compositions in both fidelity and inference speed.
papers.summary: Video diffusion transformers are expensive, and the two main speedups, sparse attention within a denoising step and caching across steps, interact badly: errors from sparse attention get reused and compound along the sampling trajectory. `RECAP` is a training-free method in which cached dense-attention refinements correct sparse estimates, fresh sparse statistics keep those corrections from going stale, and online error feedback coordinates the two. It relies on the observation that sparsification errors point in similar directions across nearby steps, so corrections can be shared instead of recomputed. On `HunyuanVideo` at 720p for 5-second clips, it **achieves a 3.05x speedup** and beats every tested direct combination of sparse attention and caching in both fidelity and speed.

papers.title: Beyond Static Leaderboards: Capability-Focused Evaluation with Structural Diversity for Time Series Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Static public benchmarks for time series foundation models (TSFMs) typically have fixed and narrow test distributions. Their repeated reuse encourages benchmark-specific tuning, making reported performance reflect adaptation to the fixed test set rather than genuine forecasting generalization. In addition, a single aggregate score cannot fully characterize model capabilities across distinct temporal structures and input relationships. We propose CaFE (Capability-Focused Evaluation), a refreshable evaluation extension grounded in original benchmark data that enriches static benchmarks with structural diversity and enriches single-score black-box evaluation with multi-dimensional, capability-oriented assessment. CaFE first profiles the original benchmark and defines eight Structural Features (SFs) that characterize its temporal structure. For each SF, it resamples the original data according to its structural support, removes edge-of-distribution samples, and augments the retained samples by varying the SF's salience, producing samples with different structural profiles. After filtering out out-of-distribution samples while preserving diversity, CaFE yields a refreshed evaluation set. TSFMs are then evaluated on this set using both conventional forecast-error metrics and intervention-response metrics, giving each model a per-feature capability profile alongside endpoint accuracy. Experiments on GIFT-Eval and FEV-Mini20 show that CaFE yields stable evaluation results and reveals per-feature strengths and weaknesses that a single aggregate score hides. Moreover, on genuine data filtered by structural condition, models selected by CaFE outperform those chosen by the aggregate leaderboard. CaFE therefore makes model selection conditional on the structural response of interest.
papers.summary: Static benchmarks for time series foundation models (TSFMs) have narrow, fixed test sets that invite benchmark-specific tuning, and a single aggregate score hides how models handle different temporal structures. `CaFE` (Capability-Focused Evaluation) profiles a benchmark along eight structural features, then resamples and augments the original data to vary each feature, filtering out out-of-distribution samples to produce a refreshed test set. Models get a per-feature capability profile from both forecast-error and intervention-response metrics. On `GIFT-Eval` and `FEV-Mini20` the results are stable, and on real data filtered by structural condition, **models selected by `CaFE` outperform those picked by the aggregate leaderboard**.

papers.title: SEAM: Spectral Embedding Alignment and Merging for Low-Resource TTS
papers.abstract: Expanding the vocabulary of conditional text-to-speech (TTS) models typically requires extensive fine-tuning with paired audio, creating a major bottleneck for low-resource and cross-lingual adaptation. To address this, we introduce SEAM, a zero-audio initialization method that constructs embeddings for unseen tokens from known subtokens. Unlike standard pooling strategies that ignore sequential structure, SEAM applies a spectral filter to preserve temporal phonetic order and uses closed-form ridge regression to align the new embeddings with the pretrained conditioning manifold. Across three languages and two TTS architectures, SEAM approaches or matches baseline performance using up to four times less training data, reducing sample complexity by 75\% compared to random initialization and mean pooling. Our approach provides a lightweight, reproducible, and theoretically grounded solution for vocabulary expansion in low-resource speech synthesis.
papers.summary: Adding new tokens to a conditional text-to-speech (TTS) model's vocabulary normally requires heavy fine-tuning on paired audio, which is a bottleneck for low-resource and cross-lingual adaptation. `SEAM` builds embeddings for unseen tokens from known subtokens without any audio, using a spectral filter to preserve phonetic order and closed-form ridge regression to align the new embeddings with the pretrained embedding space. Across three languages and two TTS architectures, it approaches or matches baseline quality with up to four times less training data, **reducing sample complexity by 75%** compared with random initialization and mean pooling.

papers.title: LOCU: Lowdin-Orthogonalized Constraint Updates for Multi-Constraint Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: We investigate multi-constraint policy optimization in constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs), where interactions among constraint gradients often yield ill-conditioned update directions, causing numerically fragile steps and unintended cancellation or redundant overlap in constraint corrections. To address this, we propose LOCU, which mitigates numerical instability arising from constraint interactions by applying symmetric Lowdin orthogonalization to the natural gradients of the reward and constraints under the Fisher-Rao metric. Combined with Fisher-geometric screening and near-collinear compression, LOCU yields a compact reduced space in which the trust region becomes a Euclidean ball and constraints are handled symmetrically through a low-dimensional active-set solve. For infeasible iterates, LOCU constructs a Pareto-descent direction which preserves the local feasibility of satisfied constraints within the same reduced formulation. Experiments show that LOCU remains stable under high constraint coupling, narrow feasible regions, and infeasible starts, and generalizes across different cost critic architectures.
papers.summary: In constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) with many constraints, the gradients of different constraints interact and produce ill-conditioned update directions, so corrections can cancel each other out or overlap redundantly. `LOCU` applies symmetric Löwdin orthogonalization to the natural gradients of the reward and constraints under the Fisher-Rao metric. It then screens and compresses near-collinear directions, producing a compact reduced space where the trust region becomes a Euclidean ball and the constraints are handled by a small active-set solve. When a policy violates its constraints, the method builds a Pareto-descent direction that keeps already-satisfied constraints locally feasible, and experiments show it **stays stable under high constraint coupling, narrow feasible regions, and infeasible starts**.

papers.title: AudioScorer: Learning Question-Aware Token Relevance for Large Audio Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) reason over speech, environmental sounds, music, and other acoustic information. However, their audio encoders produce dense token sequences that make long-form audio costly to process. Existing audio pruning methods reduce this cost using heuristics such as attention, representation similarity, or temporal sampling, but do not explicitly learn which tokens are most useful for a given question. We propose AudioScorer, a lightweight model that scores audio tokens according to the user question. It is trained by distilling the ranking of audio tokens under the frozen LALM's answer-gradient saliency, together with downstream answer supervision. Compared with other pruning methods, AudioScorer achieves the best or tied-best result at 10% token retention on 7 of 10 semantic and acoustic tasks, including speech recognition, emotion recognition, and audio-scene classification.
papers.summary: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) process dense sequences of audio tokens, which makes long recordings expensive, and existing pruning methods choose tokens with heuristics rather than by relevance to the user's question. `AudioScorer` is a lightweight model that scores each audio token conditioned on the question. It is trained by distilling the token ranking from the frozen LALM's answer-gradient saliency, together with supervision on the downstream answer. Keeping only 10% of tokens, it achieves **the best or tied-best result on 7 of 10 tasks** compared with other pruning methods, including speech recognition, emotion recognition, and audio-scene classification.

papers.title: REFLEX: RNA Ensemble Generation via Flexibility-Calibrated Stochastic Bridge
papers.abstract: RNA molecules often function through multiple experimentally observed conformational states. A central challenge is to capture ensemble diversity without sacrificing structural fidelity: samples may collapse toward averaged representative structures or drift into unsupported conformational regions. We introduce REFLEX (RNA Ensemble generation calibrated by FLEXibility), a sequence-conditioned generator for RNA backbone-frame ensembles based on a heteroscedastic stochastic bridge on SE(3). During training, experimental B-factors calibrate residue-wise bridge widths, exposing each observed conformer through local perturbation neighborhoods with residue-specific scales while keeping constrained regions sharper. A learned flexibility condition guides the bridge-field network to recover target conformer-specific frames from these calibrated noisy states. At inference, REFLEX uses only the input sequence, requiring no MSA-subsampling heuristics. On a multi-conformer RNA benchmark, REFLEX achieves the best precision-recall trade-off for ensemble coverage across evaluation thresholds, while recovery-stress ablations indicate gains in target-frame recovery under stronger perturbations.
papers.summary: RNA molecules often adopt several functional conformations, and generative models tend either to collapse to an averaged structure or to drift into conformations the data does not support. `REFLEX` generates RNA backbone-frame ensembles from sequence alone, using a heteroscedastic stochastic bridge on SE(3). During training, experimental B-factors set a separate noise width for each residue, so flexible regions are explored more widely while constrained regions stay sharp, and a learned flexibility condition guides recovery of the specific conformers. No multiple-sequence-alignment subsampling heuristics are needed at inference, and on a multi-conformer RNA benchmark it achieves **the best precision-recall trade-off for ensemble coverage across thresholds**.

papers.title: A Pitfall in the Evaluation of Gene Perturbation Models
papers.abstract: Gene perturbation models aim to predict transcriptional responses to unseen genetic interventions, but comparisons rely on heterogeneous evaluation metrics and differentially-expressed (DE) gene subsets. We investigate the consequences of these choices using eight methods across six single-gene perturbation datasets under a unified evaluation protocol. Varying the number of top DE genes reveals substantial instability in Precision-based rankings, with the winning method changing $86.7\%$ of the time, while rankings based on the rest of the metrics remain comparatively stable. Investigating this discrepancy exposes that repeating a single predicted expression profile across cell-level rows, a standard practice for many methods, can inflate significance estimates and produce excessively large predicted significant-DE sets. Specifically we found that $67.1\%$ of tested perturbation--gene pairs pass the significance threshold despite some of them having minuscule effects. We derive an inflation factor showing that replicated predictions can amplify the standardized Mann--Whitney statistic even after correction for tied ranks, without adding independent information. This artifact changes Precision mainly as the number of DE genes increases because for smaller cutoffs, most of the genes are already significant due to the effect-based ordering. Taking this pitfall into account in our benchmark comparison, we find that a random forest using Gene Ontology features achieves the best overall results.
papers.summary: Gene perturbation models predict how gene expression responds to unseen genetic interventions, but they are compared using inconsistent metrics and different subsets of differentially-expressed (DE) genes. Evaluating eight methods on six single-gene perturbation datasets under one protocol, the authors find that Precision-based rankings are unstable, with **the winning method changing 86.7% of the time** as the number of top DE genes varies. They trace this to a common practice: repeating a single predicted expression profile across cell-level rows inflates the Mann-Whitney significance statistic, which they formalize with a derived inflation factor, and as a result 67.1% of tested perturbation-gene pairs pass the significance threshold even when effects are tiny. Once this artifact is accounted for, a random forest on `Gene Ontology` features gives the best overall results.

papers.title: Physics-anchored residual quantum neural networks for cloud-cover parameterization
papers.abstract: Compact quantum neural networks have been explored for cloud-cover parameterization, but their predictive value depends on how physical knowledge is incorporated and which classical models provide the reference. We investigate an offline residual formulation that retains a fitted \XR\ cloud-cover estimate and learns a correction to its logit in transformed target space. Using released ICON/DYAMOND-derived data, we compare ten model variants in six- and eight-input settings, with three matched replicates and 10,000 training samples per replicate. All quantum circuits use local Z readout and noiseless exact expectation values. Under a common 30-epoch protocol, residual prediction reduced physical-space test mean squared error relative to direct QNN prediction by 54.3\% and 38.8\% for six-input XYZ and ZZXY circuits, and by 49.2\% and 38.9\% for their eight-input versions. Residual QNNs also outperformed the selected compact residual multilayer perceptron in every paired replicate. A larger, longer-trained Grundner-Q1 adaptation nevertheless achieved lower error: residual Q1 reached mean MSEs of 0.00778 and 0.00791, compared with 0.01124 and 0.01082 for residual XYZ. The results support residual prediction for compact simulated QNNs within the tested budget and establish a clear boundary set by stronger classical references. They do not establish computational quantum advantage or online climate-model skill.
papers.summary: Compact quantum neural networks (QNNs) have been tried for cloud-cover parameterization in climate models, and this study tests whether they work better when they learn a correction to a fitted physical estimate rather than predicting cloud cover directly. Using `ICON`/`DYAMOND`-derived data and noiseless simulated circuits, the authors compare ten model variants with six and eight inputs. Residual prediction **cut test mean squared error by 38.8–54.3% relative to direct QNN prediction**, and residual QNNs beat a compact residual multilayer perceptron in every paired replicate. A larger, longer-trained classical `Grundner-Q1` model still achieved lower error, and the authors explicitly claim no quantum advantage or online climate-model skill.

papers.title: Trust Your Targets: Is Target Propagation Block-Diagonal Gauss-Newton?
papers.abstract: Target propagation (TP) is a backpropagation alternative in which local targets carry the global learning signal. Prior works claim that TP performs Gauss-Newton (GN) optimisation on these targets, but the correspondence has only been established under unrealistic assumptions where hitting them exactly is trivial. Practical variants instead descend on a least-squares problem via a single gradient step. In this paper, we rederive TP from a trust region under an implicit, previously unexamined norm, and introduce CGTP (Conjugate Gradient Target Propagation), which uses conjugate gradients to solve the layer-local subproblems in parallel. A single adaptive parameter jointly controls this trust region and a matching bound on the weight update; KFAC emerges exactly as the special case where the per-sample Jacobians are replaced by their batch mean, giving its factored damping a variational grounding. On MNIST and Fashion-MNIST MLPs, CGTP matches the accuracy of ADAM and KFAC while needing orders of magnitude fewer outer iterations than ADAM (about 10x fewer backward-pass-equivalents overall), while remaining stable across depth.
papers.summary: Target propagation (TP) is an alternative to backpropagation in which local per-layer targets carry the learning signal, and earlier claims that it performs Gauss-Newton optimization relied on unrealistic assumptions. The authors rederive TP from a trust region under a previously unexamined implicit norm and introduce `CGTP` (Conjugate Gradient Target Propagation), which solves the layer-local subproblems in parallel with conjugate gradients. A single adaptive parameter controls both the trust region and the weight-update bound, and `KFAC` emerges exactly as a special case when per-sample Jacobians are replaced by their batch mean. On `MNIST` and `Fashion-MNIST` multilayer perceptrons, `CGTP` matches the accuracy of `Adam` and `KFAC` with **about 10x fewer backward-pass-equivalents than Adam** and remains stable as depth increases.

papers.title: Learning SOCP Solver Dynamics with Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Second-order cone programs (SOCPs) are a fundamental class of convex optimization problems widely applied across engineering domains. Classical interior-point methods are robust and accurate, but their iterative nature can be costly in real-time or repeated-solve settings. This has motivated learning-based solvers that approximate optimizer solutions with neural networks. Recent work has increasingly studied graph neural networks (GNNs) for linear, quadratic, and second-order cone optimization, leveraging their ability to model sparse relational structure among variables, constraints, and objective functions. Most existing GNN-based solvers compress the optimization process into a single forward pass, predicting the optimizer directly without using the intermediate trajectory produced by classical solvers. We introduce SOCPNet, a recursive GNN framework that uses solver trajectories to learn an iterative SOCP solution procedure. A shared GNN model is applied repeatedly, refining the current iterate at each step and enabling inference for a variable number of iterations. Rather than predicting the solution in a single pass, SOCPNet learns from intermediate iterates to progressively refine its estimates using a trajectory-regularized training procedure. We evaluate SOCPNet on multiple datasets spanning standard SOCP problem classes and show that it consistently reduces the final solution error relative to a SOCP-GNN baseline. Finally, we demonstrate how trained SOCPNet models can be used in a hybrid optimization pipeline by warm-starting a classical interior-point solver, reducing solver iterations without loss of accuracy.
papers.summary: Second-order cone programs (SOCPs) are typically solved with interior-point methods, which can be too slow when the same kind of problem must be solved repeatedly or in real time. Most existing graph neural network (GNN) solvers predict the solution in a single forward pass. `SOCPNet` instead applies one shared GNN recursively, training it on intermediate iterates from classical solver trajectories so that it refines its estimate step by step and can run for a variable number of iterations. It consistently reduces final solution error relative to an `SOCP-GNN` baseline across standard problem classes, and **warm-starting an interior-point solver with its output reduces solver iterations without loss of accuracy**.

papers.title: Toward Online Robust Zero-Sum Markov Games with Function Approximation
papers.abstract: Online robust zero-sum Markov games pose a coupled operator-learning and game-solving problem: from nominal interaction data, the learner must recover a worst-case minimax Bellman operator while maintaining strategic coverage and controlling stage-game approximation error. Existing robust reinforcement-learning theory does not yet provide such an operator-learning perspective beyond specialized multi-agent settings. We develop an optimistic dual robust Bellman framework that combines dual robust Bellman fitting, optimistic minimax planning, backward-validated confidence sets, and exploiter-mix data collection. Our analysis is organized around the robust Bellman residuals induced by the candidate value class and yields a regret reduction that separates exploration complexity, robust operator-estimation error, stage-game solution error, and misspecification. Under explicit interpretable assumptions, we obtain conditional theorem interfaces for general and projected function approximation, together with closed results in several structured regimes, including tabular, epochwise cross-fit linear, self-normalized pure-online linear / finite-rank kernel, and projected RKHS truncation. Small-scale numerical experiments illustrate robustness calibration, strategic coverage, and the return-gap trade-off predicted by the framework.
papers.summary: In online robust zero-sum Markov games, a learner must recover a worst-case minimax Bellman operator from interaction data with a nominal environment while also solving each stage game and exploring strategically. The authors propose an optimistic dual robust Bellman framework that combines dual robust Bellman fitting, optimistic minimax planning, backward-validated confidence sets, and exploiter-mix data collection. Its main result is **a regret bound that separates exploration complexity, robust operator-estimation error, stage-game solution error, and misspecification**, with closed-form results for tabular, linear, finite-rank kernel, and projected RKHS settings. Small-scale numerical experiments illustrate the predicted trade-offs between robustness calibration, strategic coverage, and return gap.

papers.title: Robotic Photography System based on Vision-Language-Action Model
papers.abstract: Modern robotic photography requires understanding photographic intent, planning camera motions, and producing aesthetically pleasing images in complex environments. We present RoboPhoto-VLA, a unified Vision-Language-Action framework that jointly models perception, reasoning, and camera control for autonomous robotic photography. RoboPhoto-VLA incorporates PhotoCoT for structured action planning and Aesthetic Direct Preference Optimization (ADPO) to align camera behaviors with human aesthetic preferences. To facilitate training and evaluation, we construct OpenPhotography, a robotic photography dataset with language-guided demonstrations. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that RoboPhoto-VLA produces photographs better aligned with human aesthetic preferences while generalizing effectively to unseen subjects, viewpoints, poses, and complex photographic instructions.
papers.summary: Autonomous robotic photography requires a system to understand what the user wants photographed, plan camera motions, and produce aesthetically pleasing shots. `RoboPhoto-VLA` is a Vision-Language-Action framework that handles perception, reasoning, and camera control together, using `PhotoCoT` for structured action planning and Aesthetic Direct Preference Optimization (`ADPO`) to align camera behavior with human aesthetic preferences. The authors also build `OpenPhotography`, a dataset of language-guided robotic photography demonstrations. In real-world experiments, the system **produces photos better aligned with human aesthetic preferences** and generalizes to unseen subjects, viewpoints, poses, and complex instructions.

papers.title: Answering While You Type: Optimizing Time-to-Answer with Streaming Generation
papers.abstract: Work on efficient large-language-model inference has concentrated almost entirely on reducing the cost of decoding once a request is complete. The quantity a user experiences, however, is the interval between submitting a request and receiving a usable response, and that interval can be shortened without making decoding itself faster. While a request is being composed it is already partially specified, yet conventional deployments begin no computation until submission. We propose and study streaming generation, a decoding regime in which the model begins producing a response from an incomplete request and revises it as the remaining input arrives, so that only a small residue of the answer remains to be computed once the request is submitted. We evaluate the regime on autoregressive and diffusion language models, characterise the conditions under which it reduces user-visible latency, and analyse the mechanism responsible.
papers.summary: Work on efficient LLM inference has focused on making decoding faster once a request is complete, but users actually experience the delay between submitting a request and receiving a usable answer. The authors propose streaming generation, in which the model starts producing a response while the request is still being typed and revises it as more input arrives, so **only a small residue of the answer remains to be computed at submission time**. They evaluate the approach on both autoregressive and diffusion language models, characterize the conditions under which it reduces user-visible latency, and analyze the mechanism behind the savings.

papers.title: CAST: Cast-Admissible Generative Design and Shape Optimization with Paired Depth Images
papers.abstract: Deep generative design can produce complex geometries, but unconstrained representations may create undercuts that prevent release from a two-part mold. We present CAST, which reformulates three-dimensional shape generation under a selected mold-opening constraint as a two-dimensional image generation problem using paired top and bottom depth images. Each valid depth pair defines one material interval along a selected mold-opening direction, so reconstructions exclude undercuts in that direction by construction. Diffusion models generate candidate shapes in this representation, and a finite element analysis (FEA) guided optimizer refines the same two boundaries. We evaluate diffusion-based generation with limited training data comprising 211 SimJEB bracket designs. On SimJEB brackets, FEA-guided refinement with a volume penalty reduced compliance in 193 of 200 generated candidates. The median reduction across all candidates was 36.8 percent in the optimization FEA model. Reconstruction of existing brackets revealed a mass--stiffness trade-off: filling occluded regions increased material volume and reduced displacement under the evaluated loads. Paired depth images thus connect generative exploration and structural refinement in a shared design space that preserves the selected pull-direction restriction.
papers.summary: Deep generative design can produce shapes with undercuts, which prevent the part from being released from a two-part mold. `CAST` turns 3D shape generation under a chosen mold-opening direction into a 2D problem by representing each shape as a pair of top and bottom depth images; because every valid pair defines one material interval along that direction, undercuts are excluded by construction. Diffusion models generate candidate shapes in this representation, and an optimizer guided by finite element analysis (FEA) refines the same two boundaries. Trained on only 211 `SimJEB` bracket designs, FEA-guided refinement **reduced compliance in 193 of 200 generated candidates, with a median reduction of 36.8%**.

papers.title: The Scheduler Is a Hidden Retriever: How Asynchrony Shapes Evidence Acquisition in Search Agents
papers.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly solve complex tasks through parallel reasoning and asynchronous information gathering. Controlled replay across two model families and three benchmarks shows that delivery timing redirects search decisions made before all results arrive, despite identical initial evidence. Acquisition disagreement reaches up to 24 percentage points above same-order repeat variation. This dependence persists after all initial evidence arrives and through a second search, turning temporary differences in what agents have seen into lasting differences in what they acquire. An acquisition-regret bound with a matching construction shows that invariance at a fixed early arrival count can limit the use of evidence already received. We introduce Confluent Evidence Acquisition (CEA), which instead releases local reasoning when each subquestion's evidence is complete and allocates shared search independently of completion order. For a fixed plan and stable conditional response law, we prove joint invariance of decisions, acquisitions, and answers. With question-only plans across three benchmarks, CEA brings acquisition disagreement to within 1.0 percentage point of repeat variation and achieves accuracy comparable to complete-input controls, improving over early commitment by up to 12.6 percentage points. Replacing CEA's fixed allocation with first-ready allocation under contention adds 21.6 percentage points of acquisition disagreement, while local query-target disagreement remains near repeat variation. Timed comparisons show that CEA reaches decisions earlier and responds faster than the same program waiting for all initial evidence.
papers.summary: Search agents increasingly gather information asynchronously and in parallel, and this study shows that the order in which results arrive changes what an agent decides to search for next, even when the initial evidence is identical. In controlled replays across two model families and three benchmarks, **acquisition disagreement reached up to 24 percentage points above same-order repeat variation**, and the divergence persisted through later searches. The authors prove an acquisition-regret bound and introduce Confluent Evidence Acquisition (`CEA`), which resumes local reasoning only when a subquestion's evidence is complete and allocates shared search independently of completion order. `CEA` brings disagreement to within 1.0 point of repeat variation, matches the accuracy of waiting for all evidence, improves over early commitment by up to 12.6 points, and still responds faster than waiting for all initial evidence.

papers.title: Selective Transfer through Sequence Distillation: From Benchmark Knowledge to Backdoor Behaviour
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation is widely used to transfer capabilities from teacher models to student models, but recent work shows that it can also transfer unintended teacher properties. We study whether different hidden teacher properties survive the same distillation channels. Specifically, we compare two properties: benchmark-associated knowledge and refusal backdoors, and show that distillation treats them very differently. Teachers fine-tuned on benchmark data successfully pass that knowledge to students through all four distillation channels we test, including when students are trained only on teacher-generated number sequences containing no natural language or domain content whatsoever. Refusal backdoors tell the opposite story: backdoored teachers achieve near-perfect triggered refusal, yet sequence-distilled students inherit essentially none of this behaviour. Logit-based distillation transfers it substantially, reaching up to 85.5\% triggered refusal in students that saw zero backdoor examples. Distillation is therefore selective, and the selection criterion is not what data the student sees, but what structure the teacher's property has. The code is available at https://github.com/MJonibek/kd-leakage.
papers.summary: Knowledge distillation can transfer unintended properties from a teacher model to a student, and this study asks whether different hidden properties survive the same distillation channels. Teachers fine-tuned on benchmark data pass that knowledge to students through all four channels tested, even when students train only on teacher-generated number sequences with no natural-language content. Refusal backdoors behave the opposite way: students distilled from teacher-generated sequences inherit almost none of the behavior, while **logit-based distillation yields up to 85.5% triggered refusal in students that never saw a backdoor example**. The authors conclude that what transfers depends on the structure of the teacher's property, not on which data the student sees.

papers.title: StrucChunk: Structure-Aware Retrieval for Legal Document RAG
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can ground LLM outputs in domain-specific knowledge, but legal documents are hard: standard chunking fragments hierarchical argument structure, and generic embeddings struggle with both precise citation matching and semantic understanding. We propose StrucChunk (Structure Aware Chunking) with hybrid dense-sparse retrieval for hierarchically structured legal documents. It treats documents as directed acyclic graphs of provisions, preserves clause boundaries, resolves cross-references before embedding, and combines BM25 with BGE-M3 via Reciprocal Rank Fusion. We evaluate on five corpora, three legal traditions and two languages. StrucChunk reaches 100% boundary precision (vs. 7.7% for recursive splitting on CrPC), preserves 97.6% of documented cross-references (vs. 0%), and matches section coverage with 40.3% fewer chunks on GDPR. On LegalBench-RAG (6,858 query-passage pairs), it achieves Char-Recall@8 of 48.18% vs. 23.59% for the best baseline (+104%), surpassing the published state of the art by +83%. On 501 queries each for CrPC and CPC (Indian law), Recall@5 improves from 0.557 to 0.804 (+44.4%) and from 0.158 to 0.259 (+64.6%); chunking accounts for 88% and 73% of the gain. On 501 GDPR queries, Recall@5 is 0.868 with R@1 improving +59%. On NitiBench-CCL (3,730 Thai financial law queries), HR@5 is 0.856 vs. 0.594 for naive chunking (+44.1%), showing that section-boundary alignment is the dominant factor across languages, and cross-reference augmentation adds +2.3% on cross-reference queries. We release the implementation, 5,256 evaluation queries across five legal corpora, annotation methodology and chunking quality metrics. Code: github.com/SinghSuryaDeep/legal-rag-strucchunk-1
papers.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) over legal documents suffers because standard chunking breaks up hierarchical provisions and generic embeddings handle exact citations poorly. `StrucChunk` treats each document as a directed acyclic graph of provisions, preserves clause boundaries, resolves cross-references before embedding, and fuses `BM25` with `BGE-M3` using Reciprocal Rank Fusion. On `LegalBench-RAG` it reaches **Char-Recall@8 of 48.18% versus 23.59% for the best baseline**, and it also improves recall on Indian criminal and civil procedure codes, `GDPR`, and Thai financial law (`NitiBench-CCL`). Across all five corpora, aligning chunks with section boundaries accounts for most of the gain.

papers.title: MCDA: Multi-View Graph Contrastive Learning with Dynamic Topology Augmentation for Functional MRI Analysis
papers.abstract: Resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) is a vital non-invasive tool for diagnosing brain disorders and uncovering pathological mechanisms. However, existing graph contrastive learning (GCL) methods often underexploit augmentation histories across training epochs and the relationships among different augmented views. In this paper, we introduce a topology-guided Multi-view graph Contrastive learning framework with Dynamic graph topology Augmentation (MCDA) for fMRI analysis. Unlike traditional GCL that uses fixed noise or edge-dropping, MCDA employs a Dynamic Augmentation Update (DAU) module that iteratively refines the augmented topology. Specifically, we incorporate self-aware and cross-sample augmentation strategies to simultaneously capture individual-specific functional signatures and inter-subject heterogeneity. We then design a topology-guided multi-view graph contrastive learning scheme that explores interrelationships not only between the original network and its augmented views, but also across different augmented views to maximize structural information preservation. We characterize the score-level optimization directions and establish a lower bound for the contrastive objective. The framework combines classification and contrastive losses for brain disorder diagnosis and examines discriminative functional connectivity patterns as potential biomarkers. Experiments on two public rs-fMRI datasets comprising 1,236 subjects demonstrate that MCDA outperforms the state-of-the-art methods. The code has been made publicly available at: \url{https://github.com/goodcodingagoodboy/MCDA}.
papers.summary: Graph contrastive learning on resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) brain networks typically uses fixed augmentations such as random noise or edge dropping, and it ignores how augmentations evolve across training epochs and how different augmented views relate to one another. `MCDA` adds a Dynamic Augmentation Update module that iteratively refines the augmented graph topology, using both subject-specific and cross-subject augmentation. It then contrasts the original network with every augmented view and also the augmented views with each other, and the authors derive a lower bound on the contrastive objective. On two public datasets totaling 1,236 subjects, **`MCDA` outperforms state-of-the-art methods for brain disorder diagnosis**.

papers.title: TriScore: Post-Hoc Out-of-Distribution Detection with Energy, Boundary Probes, and Transform Consistency
papers.abstract: Post-hoc out-of-distribution detection usually relies on a single signal extracted from a frozen classifier, such as confidence, energy, features, or gradients. This dependence becomes fragile under classifier-level adversarial shift, where the shift can preserve the detector's chosen cue while changing the model's decision behavior. We investigate whether this failure mode can be mitigated by combining complementary detection criteria instead of selecting a single score. We introduce TriScore, a post-hoc OOD detector that combines three ID-calibrated signals from the same frozen backbone: an energy prior, a boundary-fragility score, and a transform-consistency score. These signals are standardized on ID validation data and fused by an input-dependent ID-residual gate, requiring no OOD labels, auxiliary model, training, or stored feature bank. Across four ImageNet-scale backbones, TriScore achieves the best mean AUROC among 15 post-hoc baselines under a non-adaptive adversarial-shift protocol, while remaining competitive on standard OOD benchmarks. Ablations show that the gains come from combining complementary cues rather than optimizing a single detector signal. These results support multi-criterion post-hoc detection as a practical route toward more robust OOD detection under classifier-level shift. The source code is publicly available at github.com/gursoyege/TriScore.
papers.summary: Post-hoc out-of-distribution (OOD) detectors usually rely on a single signal from a frozen classifier, which becomes fragile when an adversarial shift preserves that signal while changing the model's decisions. `TriScore` combines three signals from the same backbone, an energy prior, a boundary-fragility score, and a transform-consistency score, each standardized on in-distribution validation data and fused by an input-dependent gate. The method needs no OOD labels, auxiliary model, training, or stored feature bank. Across four ImageNet-scale backbones, it achieves **the best mean AUROC among 15 post-hoc baselines under adversarial shift** while remaining competitive on standard OOD benchmarks.

papers.title: The Control Layer Behind Rule-Following Agents Trading Across Market Conditions
papers.abstract: Trading discipline often fails people. Our study tested whether four AI trading agents followed their strategies and risk rules. Offering traders the evidence and an agent evaluation toolkit to separate luck from following the rules, before giving agents meaningful autonomy or capital. Our study analysed 2,627 closed positions from 12 February to 27 August 2026 across the same asset universe and execution conditions. Most positions were simulated against live prices with a 0.09% round-trip fee; 18% involved real Hyperliquid orders. Each position declared a strategy, stop and target, with a limit of five open positions per agent. The fleet finished net positive after fees. Rule adherence was high across all four agents, including the unprofitable one. Profitability tracked how often agents won relative to their break-even win rates. Institutional-style controls ran by default and contained losses through a 29% market drawdown and recovery, with documented exceptions. The discipline held for all four agents. Agents kept 97.5% of gross loss within declared stops, and typical losses closed at declared levels. Declared risk remained stable after losses and broadly stable across calm and volatile months. Twenty-three of 24 runs respected the position limit; logs identify the exception's size and duration. The same live data produced different results across assigned strategies. The trade-log tests can be rerun from the published trade snapshot; regime tests also require the published Bitcoin prices and regime labels. Section 3.5 specifies the stop-breach tolerance. These trade-level results are not account-level returns or proof of a lasting edge. Our study provides an evaluation toolkit to help traders distinguish rule-following from luck before committing capital. For anyone considering allocating capital to agents to trade, discipline should be the entry test, not the only test.
papers.summary: This study tests whether four AI trading agents actually followed their declared strategies and risk rules, analyzing 2,627 closed positions from February to August 2026. Most positions were simulated against live prices, and 18% were real orders on `Hyperliquid`. All four agents showed high rule adherence, including the unprofitable one, and **kept 97.5% of gross loss within their declared stops** through a 29% market drawdown, while 23 of 24 runs respected the position limit. The authors release an evaluation toolkit and trade snapshot for separating rule-following from luck, and they note that these trade-level results do not represent account-level returns or prove a lasting edge.

papers.title: Typed Decision Models under Prevalence Shift: Decision Training, Calibration, and Implicit Priors
papers.abstract: Typed decision models (TDMs) return a probability over caller-defined options, and Jev is described by its vendor as calibrated. But in deployment class frequencies change, so calibration measured on a fixed test set need not hold where thresholds are applied. Existing evaluations leave two gaps: the gains of vendor decision training have not been separated from those of the backbone under an identical readout, and TDMs have been tested only at the test set's class distribution. We ask whether decision training improves a model over its own backbone, and whether a TDM's calibration and thresholds withstand prevalence (label) shift as well as a fine-tuned classifier's. We compare three TDMs (Jev, Tev1-4B, Nimble-9B), their base models and two trained classifiers on identical decisions from five public datasets under simulated shift, with 35 paired tests fixed before any test was computed. First, decision training is not uniformly beneficial: Nimble-9B, which differs from Qwen3.5-9B only by a LoRA adapter, is better calibrated on intent tasks but 12.0 Macro-F1 points worse on financial sentiment. Second, under moderate shift Jev's expected calibration error (ECE) and threshold risk grow significantly more than a fine-tuned DeBERTa's only on financial sentiment, by 1.7 and 2.5 percentage points; averaged over 2,000 shift scenarios (exploratory), the gap is at most one point on every dataset. Third, EM prior correction with the model's mean development prediction as its prior needs no labels and lowers Jev's ECE under shift by 2.7 and 1.8 points on the two datasets where it is highest, although labelled recalibration lowers it far more. The three TDMs we tested are neither uniformly better than their backbones nor uniquely fragile under shift; for calibration, their main weakness is the miscalibration they already have without shift. We release all inputs, code and outputs.
papers.summary: Typed decision models (TDMs) return probabilities over caller-defined options, but it is unclear whether their vendor decision training improves on the underlying backbone and whether their calibration holds when class frequencies shift after deployment. The authors compare three TDMs (`Jev`, `Tev1-4B`, `Nimble-9B`), their base models, and two fine-tuned classifiers on five public datasets under simulated prevalence shift, using 35 pre-registered paired tests. Decision training is not uniformly beneficial: **`Nimble-9B` is 12.0 Macro-F1 points worse than its `Qwen3.5-9B` base on financial sentiment**, even though it is better calibrated on intent tasks. Under shift, `Jev` degrades only slightly more than a fine-tuned `DeBERTa`, and label-free EM prior correction reduces its expected calibration error, though labeled recalibration helps far more.

papers.title: CIS-Transolver: A Cross-Layer Incremental-State Neural Operator for Fine-Scale Automotive Aerodynamic Flow Prediction
papers.abstract: Neural operators offer an efficient data-driven approach to rapid prediction of complex automotive aerodynamic flows. However, spectral bias and other factors limit accurate reconstruction of fine-scale flow variations near complex geometries. Existing studies improve the representation and fitting of fine-scale information mainly through information extraction and training objectives. Further study is needed to determine how extracted local details can be used continually in subsequent operator computations and contribute effectively to the overall flow-field representation. We propose CIS-Transolver, a cross-layer incremental-state neural operator that extends fine-scale modeling from local information extraction to its use across layers. The method extracts fine-scale information through local multiscale analysis and encodes it as geometric moment states that are propagated and updated across layers. By combining information from previous layers with feedback to the value representations in Physics-Attention, the method allows local details to contribute continually to subsequent modeling of global physical correlations. We systematically evaluate CIS-Transolver on three public automotive aerodynamics benchmarks, ShapeNet-Car, AhmedML, and DrivAerNet++, covering surface pressure fields and volumetric pressure and velocity fields. CIS-Transolver achieves the lowest mean relative L2 error among the evaluated methods for all five prediction metrics across the three benchmarks. The relative error reductions average 8.72% across the five metrics compared with the best baseline for each metric, reaching 16.38% for ShapeNet-Car pressure prediction and 15.60% for AhmedML velocity prediction. These results provide a new approach to fine-scale flow prediction for complex geometries.
papers.summary: Neural operators can quickly predict automotive aerodynamic flows, but spectral bias makes it hard for them to reconstruct fine-scale variations near complex geometry. `CIS-Transolver` extracts local fine-scale information through multiscale analysis and encodes it as geometric moment states, which are propagated and updated across layers and fed back into the value representations of `Physics-Attention`. On the `ShapeNet-Car`, `AhmedML`, and `DrivAerNet++` benchmarks, it achieves the lowest relative L2 error on all five prediction metrics, with **an average 8.72% error reduction over the best baseline** and up to 16.38% on `ShapeNet-Car` pressure.

papers.title: Large-Scale Biomedical RAG: Corpus Scaling, Document Representation, and Efficiency Trade-offs
papers.abstract: We present a controlled, large-scale evaluation of how corpus scale, document representation, and reranking affect the effectiveness and efficiency of biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. Retrieval collections were progressively expanded while retaining the relevant source documents, enabling consistent comparisons across corpus sizes. We compared abstract, flat full-text, and hierarchical full-text representations across first-stage retrieval, reranking, and end-to-end multiple-choice question answering. Configurations selected on development data were evaluated on five external biomedical benchmarks and a held-out test set, while retrieval latency and index storage were measured to quantify operational cost. Performance patterns observed with small or controlled collections did not consistently persist as collections grew, and the usefulness of reranking depended on the corpus and retrieval setting. RAG improved three of four model configurations across the external benchmarks, with mean gains of up to 9.6 percentage points, and improved all four configurations on the held-out test set by 10.2-30.3 points. Abstract retrieval performed best when reference evidence was abstract-aligned, whereas full-text representations were generally more effective when richer evidence was needed. Hierarchical representation matched or outperformed flat full-text retrieval in most end-to-end comparisons while requiring 67% fewer indexed units and 44-56% less storage. These findings show that corpus scale should be treated as an explicit evaluation variable in biomedical RAG, and that the most appropriate design depends on evidence format, model behavior, and operational constraints.
papers.summary: This controlled study examines how corpus size, document representation, and reranking affect both accuracy and cost in biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The authors progressively enlarge the retrieval collections while keeping the relevant documents, and they compare abstract-only, flat full-text, and hierarchical full-text indexing on five external benchmarks and a held-out test set. Patterns observed with small collections often did not persist at scale, and whether reranking helped depended on the corpus and setting. RAG improved held-out accuracy by 10.2–30.3 points, and **hierarchical full-text indexing matched or beat flat full-text while using 67% fewer indexed units and 44–56% less storage**.

papers.title: A Generic On-Board AI Processing Chain for Earth Observation: From Application Development to Embedded Deployment and Mission-Level Orchestration
papers.abstract: Earth observation satellites acquire more data than they can downlink. Extracting information on board with artificial intelligence (AI) turns the satellite into a data-reduction stage that downlinks compact products, such as masks or detections, instead of full scenes; deploying it in a mission, however, involves the whole processing chain and not only the neural network. We present a generic on-board AI processing chain along three axes, with wildfire segmentation as the worked example among ship detection and cloud segmentation. (i) The AI model is tuned (spectral-band selection, input normalization), quantized to 8-bit integers (int8) and ported to an AMD Versal VCK190, with its excellent segmentation performance preserved on the board. (ii) A modular tiler-inference-mosaicer workflow, reused unchanged across applications, brings the tile-level model to scene level, turning a full acquisition into a scene-level mask or detection list. (iii) Each step is packaged as a unikernel and orchestrated on board by ORCHIDE, a cloud-native orchestrator. The chain is characterized end to end, from the standalone execution on the target to its execution under orchestration with parallel workflows on a representative test bench. Beyond AI inference on individual tiles, this approach aims at increasing the maturity of on-board AI deployment by addressing a complete processing chain, from the acquired scene to the mission-level execution.
papers.summary: Earth observation satellites collect more data than they can send to the ground, so running AI on board lets them downlink compact products such as masks or detection lists instead of full scenes. The authors describe a reusable on-board processing chain, using wildfire segmentation as the main example alongside ship detection and cloud segmentation. The model is tuned, quantized to 8-bit integers (int8) and ported to an `AMD Versal VCK190` board. A modular tiler-inference-mosaicer workflow turns tile-level predictions into scene-level outputs, and each step is packaged as a unikernel and orchestrated on board by the cloud-native `ORCHIDE` orchestrator. The authors characterize the chain end to end, from standalone execution to parallel orchestrated workflows on a representative test bench, and report that **segmentation performance is preserved after int8 deployment on the board**.

papers.title: VibeTraining-Bench: Data-Trainer-Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires agents to diagnose system bottlenecks and coordinate improvements across training and inference. We refer to the agents' capability to jointly optimize training data, the trainer, and the inference harness as cross-component co-design. We introduce VibeTraining-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating this capability across tasks spanning terminal operation, software engineering, multi-turn tool use, and mathematical reasoning. Within each task, research agents start from an identical initial agent system under a fixed resource budget. Guided by validation feedback, they iteratively refine data, trainers, and inference harnesses, then select and submit a final agent system for evaluation on the test set. To prevent reward hacking, we enforce three safeguards: test data isolation, separate research and grading containers, and network restrictions for research agents. Our evaluation results show that frontier research agents substantially improve target agent systems. For example, on SWE-bench Verified, GPT-6-Astra raises the target agent system's performance from 32.9% to 53.7%, comparable to the human-developed instruct model's 55.4%. However, there is still room to improve their ability to co-design and iteratively refine data, trainer, and harness to achieve cumulative performance gains. We hope that VibeTraining-Bench will serve as a unified platform for advancing RSI, deepening our understanding of cross-component optimization for agent systems. Code and data are available at https://github.com/D2I-ai/VibeTrainingBench.
papers.summary: `VibeTraining-Bench` measures whether AI research agents can jointly improve a target agent system's training data, trainer, and inference harness, a capability the authors call cross-component co-design and treat as a step toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). Tasks span terminal operation, software engineering, multi-turn tool use, and math reasoning. Each research agent starts from the same initial system under a fixed resource budget and refines it using validation feedback. Test-data isolation, separate research and grading containers, and network restrictions guard against reward hacking. Frontier agents substantially improve their targets: on `SWE-bench Verified`, `GPT-6-Astra` raises the target system **from 32.9% to 53.7%, close to the 55.4% of the human-developed instruct model**. Their ability to compound gains across iterations of co-design remains limited.

papers.title: CARRS: A Constraint-Aware, Real-Time Routing System for Emergency Vehicles in Urban Environments
papers.abstract: Emergency vehicles such as police vehicles, fire engines, and ambulances require a stable and efficient route optimization to reach life-critical events in the shortest times possible. However, the dynamic nature of urban traffic makes this ideal scenario much more challenging, causing critical life-threatening delays. Traditional civilian navigation systems cannot account for real-time traffic changes alongside vehicle-specific constraints, creating inadequate routing scenarios. This research presents the Constraint-Aware Real-Time Routing System (CARRS), a unified software architecture tailored for emergency coordination. The CARRS architecture is engineered to fuse together classical pathfinding algorithms such as A*, Dijkstra, and Bidirectional A*, with Constraint Satisfaction Problem methodologies. The Design Science Research Methodology is the research framework, and prototyping is the iterative process. The artifact was empirically evaluated using OpenStreetMap data for major metropolitan road networks, combined with simulated dynamic traffic scenarios. Performance metrics focused on route optimality, constraint adherence, rerouting responsiveness, and the potential for future system scalability. Findings revealed the system's capability to generate optimal routes for operationally relevant subgraphs in under 35 seconds, with incremental rerouting responsiveness below 20 seconds. Furthermore, the system achieved more than 90% adherence to vehicle-specific constraints, making the CARRS architecture viable for real-time dynamic routing requirements. This study delivers a routing platform that bridges artificial intelligence-driven optimization with software engineering operational compliance, presenting a practical transformative step toward adaptive emergency vehicle coordination in dynamic urban environments.
papers.summary: `CARRS` (Constraint-Aware Real-Time Routing System) is a software architecture for routing emergency vehicles through changing urban traffic while respecting vehicle-specific constraints. It combines classical pathfinding algorithms (`A*`, `Dijkstra`, Bidirectional `A*`) with constraint satisfaction methods, and was developed iteratively under the Design Science Research Methodology. Evaluated on `OpenStreetMap` road networks with simulated dynamic traffic, the system produces optimal routes for operationally relevant subgraphs in under 35 seconds, reroutes incrementally in under 20 seconds, and achieves **more than 90% adherence to vehicle-specific constraints**.

papers.title: Logit Averaging During Training Sets a New State of the Art for Non-Invasive Speech BCI
papers.abstract: Non-invasive brain-computer interfaces are in practice limited by signal-to-noise ratio, and recent state-of-the-art methods address this limitation by aggregating over repeated trials of the same stimulus. Yet multi-trial aggregation has been treated inconsistently across the literature: some work averages brain signals at the model's input, other work averages predictions at the model's output, and neither treats aggregation as an architectural choice in its own right. We provide the first systematic comparison of aggregation strategies for non-invasive neural decoding, evaluating six paradigms (including logit averaging during training and three attention-based variants we introduce) across three datasets, four tasks, and two group sizes. We find that aggregation choice matters substantially: training-time logit averaging, the simplest method we propose, outperforms all others in 6 of 7 settings. On the phoneme classification setting of the 2025 PNPL competition, it sets a new state of the art, significantly outperforming the competition winner by 17.4 absolute percentage points in balanced accuracy. We further draw a theoretical connection between logit averaging and joint ensemble training, which has been shown to underperform independent ensembling in the deep learning literature; our results call into question recent explanations of why joint ensemble training fails. Together, these findings establish multi-trial aggregation as a key design choice for non-invasive neural decoding and identify training-time logit averaging as a simple, effective default.
papers.summary: Non-invasive brain-computer interfaces suffer from low signal-to-noise ratio, and prior work has combined repeated trials of the same stimulus in inconsistent ways, averaging either the input signals or the output predictions. The authors compare six aggregation paradigms, including three new attention-based variants, across three datasets, four tasks, and two group sizes. Averaging logits during training, the simplest method they propose, wins in 6 of 7 settings. On phoneme classification in the 2025 `PNPL` competition it **beats the competition winner by 17.4 absolute percentage points in balanced accuracy**. The authors also connect logit averaging to joint ensemble training and argue that their results challenge recent explanations of why joint ensemble training underperforms.

papers.title: PhyPro-FM: A Physics and Prompt-Guided Graph Foundation Model for Contingency Analysis
papers.abstract: The continuous evolution of next-generation power systems, characterized by the high penetration of renewable energy resources and dynamic topology variations, poses formidable challenges to traditional N-1/N-2 contingency analysis in terms of computational efficiency and scalability. While deep learning-based methods offer accelerated inference, existing studies predominantly treat contingency analysis as a pure regression problem, often overlooking the physical essence of grid operation and engineering requirements of real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes a physics and prompt-guided graph foundation model (PhyPro-FM) for generalizable and engineering-viable contingency analysis. The proposed architecture integrates graph neural networks with a learnable global query mechanism and, notably, introduces a prompt-guided learning paradigm. By leveraging historical snapshots as few-shot prompts, the model dynamically captures correlations between target and historical operating conditions, significantly enhancing generalization capabilities under unseen topologies. Furthermore, we design a physics-informed training mechanism that prioritizes branch power flow errors over nodal voltage errors, aligning the optimization objective with critical grid security constraints. To ensure engineering applicability, a physics-informed inference mechanism is also developed, incorporating a residual-based correction module and a specialized post-processing strategy for singular branches to circumvent numerical instability. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that PhyPro-FM outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy and generalization, validating its superior physical consistency and robustness for practical engineering applications.
papers.summary: Power grids with many renewable sources and frequently changing topologies make traditional N-1/N-2 contingency analysis slow, and existing deep learning approaches treat it as plain regression that ignores grid physics. `PhyPro-FM` is a graph foundation model that combines graph neural networks with a learnable global query mechanism. It uses historical grid snapshots as few-shot prompts to generalize to unseen topologies. Physics-informed training weights branch power-flow errors above nodal voltage errors, and at inference a residual-based correction plus special handling of singular branches avoids numerical instability. The authors report that it **outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy and generalization**, with better physical consistency.

papers.title: GAIDA: Generative AI for Human-in-the-Loop Document Annotation
papers.abstract: Document annotation is a fundamental yet labor-intensive step in building document information extraction systems. While Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Large Language Models (LLMs) can automate parts of this process, we argue that annotation systems should be judged not by how completely they remove human effort, but by how effectively they redirect it toward review and correction. We propose a modular human-in-the-loop architecture that integrates OCR-based extraction, LLM-based semantic pre-annotation, and human validation in a single editable workflow, and present \textbf{GAIDA}, a research prototype serving as its reference implementation. GAIDA supports interchangeable OCR engines, LLM backends, and prompt configurations, and enables stage-specific measurement of annotation effort. In an initial single-annotator, stage-specific study on the FUNSD scanned-form and WildReceipt retail-receipt benchmarks, OCR assistance reduced region-creation and transcription time by up to \textbf{80.9\%}, and reviewing LLM pre-annotations reduced semantic-labeling time by up to \textbf{73.7\%}, despite imperfect pre-annotations of 78.86\% and 86.98\% Micro F1 on FUNSD and WildReceipt, respectively. Finally, we reuse the same implementation, adapting only OCR and prompt configuration, to build and openly release \textbf{AraReceipt}, a manually annotated dataset of 100 Arabic receipt images labeled with 25 key-information classes. The results indicate that imperfect automated outputs provide practical value when presented as editable suggestions under human control.
papers.summary: The authors argue that document annotation tools should be judged by how well they redirect human effort toward review and correction, not by how fully they remove it. `GAIDA` is a modular human-in-the-loop prototype that chains Optical Character Recognition (OCR) extraction, Large Language Model (LLM) semantic pre-annotation, and human validation in one editable workflow, with swappable OCR engines, LLM backends, and prompts. In a single-annotator study on `FUNSD` and `WildReceipt`, OCR assistance cut region-creation and transcription time by up to **80.9%**, and reviewing LLM pre-annotations cut semantic-labeling time by up to 73.7%, even though the pre-annotations were imperfect. The same system was reused to build and release `AraReceipt`, a dataset of 100 Arabic receipts labeled with 25 key-information classes.

papers.title: Autonomous intelligence for mining productivity: a multi-agent AI approach to operational value creation
papers.abstract: Integrated Remote Operation Centres (IROCs) are emerging as the architectural frontier of Industry 4.0 for capital-intensive sectors such as mining, oil and gas, and energy. Yet two intertwined gaps constrain their evolution towards full autonomy. First, no integrated agentic architecture has been proposed for mining IROCs that orchestrates Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition systems, digital twins, predictive analytics and human-machine interfaces under safety-critical constraints. Second, no evaluation framework jointly addresses the real-time, Health-Safety-Environment, regulatory-auditability and cost-per-decision requirements that govern industrial agentic deployments. This paper makes four contributions. It synthesises industry needs and quantified gains documented in analogous industries that motivate an agentic approach to mining IROCs. It introduces EI2ROC, a three-tier multi-agent architecture combining a Large Language Model orchestrator with specialised monitoring and production-capacityprediction agents communicating through a Model Context Protocol-style tool interface. It provides a critical review of agentic evaluation along six orthogonal dimensions and identifies the industrial blind spot of current benchmarks. Finally, it proposes a multi-dimensional benchmarking framework for industrial agentic AI comprising scenario library, harness, metrics and humancalibration protocol. The paper states explicitly which components are implemented in the current prototype, which belong to the proposed reference design and which remain future work, and reports preliminary cost and latency observations from an operating site. Together, EI2ROC and the benchmarking framework constitute a methodological blueprint transferable across CAPEX intensive industries.
papers.summary: Integrated Remote Operation Centres (IROCs) in mining lack both an agentic architecture that coordinates control systems, digital twins, and analytics under safety constraints, and an evaluation framework suited to industrial requirements. The paper proposes `EI2ROC`, a three-tier multi-agent architecture in which a Large Language Model orchestrator directs specialized monitoring and production-capacity-prediction agents through a Model Context Protocol-style tool interface. It also reviews agentic evaluation along six dimensions and proposes a benchmarking framework covering real-time, safety, auditability, and cost-per-decision requirements. The authors state explicitly which parts are implemented, which are design proposals, and which are future work, and report **preliminary cost and latency observations from an operating mine site**.

papers.title: An Empirical Study of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods are critical for adapting large models under resource-constrained settings. However, as mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, which offer efficient inference at massive parameter scales, gain increasing prevalence in the community, a critical gap arising from the lack of systematic recipes for applying PEFT to MoE models. To narrow this gap, we conduct a large-scale systematic study that investigates a set of essential design recipes, including which modules should be adapted, which granularity should be used to adapt MoE modules, which PEFT method to use, and to what extent should the load-balancing objective be used, across three MoE backbones on downstream tasks and general knowledge tasks. Our experiments yield several key insights. First, adapting MoE experts alone achieves the highest downstream performance with competitive general capability retention under a comparable parameter budget. Second, native expert-weight updates offer a better downstream--retention trade-off than adapters that bypass experts or entire MoE modules. Third, LoRA and DoRA together define the strongest operating region for high downstream accuracy among the evaluated PEFT methods. Fourth, no nonzero load-balancing coefficient Pareto-dominates the zero baseline. We finally evaluate a weight-level redesign of MoE$^2$-LoRA on Qwen3. Moving its module-level bypass pool into native expert weights improves all four upstream endpoints by 2.4 to 17.9 points with 17% fewer trainable parameters and a 3.2-point average downstream cost.
papers.summary: There are no established recipes for applying parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) to mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models. The authors systematically study which modules to adapt, at what granularity, with which PEFT method, and with how much load-balancing loss, across three MoE backbones. **Adapting only the experts gives the best downstream performance while keeping general capabilities competitive**, and updating native expert weights beats adapters that bypass the experts. `LoRA` and `DoRA` form the strongest operating region among the methods tested, and no nonzero load-balancing coefficient Pareto-dominates turning it off. A weight-level redesign of `MoE²-LoRA` on `Qwen3` improves all four upstream endpoints by 2.4 to 17.9 points with 17% fewer trainable parameters, at an average downstream cost of 3.2 points.

papers.title: CTLite: Lightweight Irregular Multivariate Time Series Forecasting with Reusable Continuous-Time Summaries
papers.abstract: Irregular multivariate time series forecasting (IMTSF) requires capturing temporal dynamics and cross-variable dependencies from sparse, asynchronous observations. Existing methods often rely on learned temporal encoders, coupling historical representation construction with model optimisation and repeatedly processing the same observations. We propose CTLite, a lightweight forecasting framework that decouples historical summarisation from learned prediction. Specifically, a parameter-free continuous-time moment encoder summarises local levels and trends at multiple temporal scales while suppressing poorly supported slope estimates. A compact readout combines damped local extrapolation with a low-rank cross-variable correction that accounts for observation freshness, target availability, and forecast horizon. Since the historical summaries are independent of trainable parameters and forecast queries, they can be reused across optimisation steps and repeated predictions for an unchanged history without altering predictions or parameter gradients. Experiments on four real-world benchmarks show that CTLite achieves the best or second-best mean MSE and MAE among the evaluated methods with only 88-2,537 trainable parameters.
