We address these challenges by reconstructing order-level LOBSTER-format data from Polymarket and training agents in JaxMARL-HFT on 417 real markets. We enrich the baseline market maker's observation space with the book and recent flow, redesign its actions and inventory controls, and propose a cooperative multi-agent decomposition into a quoter and a risk manager trained using recurrent Independent Proximal Policy Optimisation (IPPO) with RNN policies. We investigate reward shaping, particularly reward blending and post-fill markout, to mitigate credit-assignment difficulties between the agents. Our redesigned single-agent market maker quotes more frequently and incurs smaller held-out losses than the retrained JaxMARL-HFT baseline, although the contributions of jointly changed observations, actions and risk constraints are not separately identified. Decomposition alone performs poorly; careful reward design substantially improves the desk relative to the unshaped split and yields our best result. Models are evaluated on realised end-of-episode portfolio value on held-out markets. None establishes positive average portfolio value in periodic held-out evaluation, and each configuration was trained with one seed. The environment, data and protocol lay a foundation for makers that quote many linked markets at once.
papers.summary: Market makers trained with multi-agent reinforcement learning are studied on `Polymarket` prediction markets, whose thin order books make adverse selection, delayed consequences of quotes, and missing order-level data especially difficult. The authors reconstruct order-level data in `LOBSTER` format, train in `JaxMARL-HFT` on 417 real markets, and split the market maker into a cooperating quoter and risk manager trained with recurrent Independent Proximal Policy Optimisation (`IPPO`). A redesigned single agent quotes more often and loses less than the retrained baseline. Splitting the agent in two works poorly on its own, but reward blending and post-fill markout shaping produce the best desk. However, **no configuration achieves positive average portfolio value on held-out markets**, and each was trained with a single seed.

papers.title: Training with ML-labeled Data via Stochastic First- and Zeroth-Order Optimization
papers.abstract: Training a machine learning (ML) model is an optimization process that typically requires a set of examples with ground-truth labels beforehand. Obtaining these ground truths usually requires laborious human effort and can be costly. The scalability of human labeling becomes a concern when there are a large number of data points that need to be labeled. To address this practical issue, we consider an optimization setting where a subset of samples has ground-truth labels, while the remaining data points were labeled by an ML predictor, which could potentially assign incorrect labels to those points. We propose both first-order and zeroth-order stochastic optimization methods for training on datasets consisting of a mix of true-labeled and ML-labeled samples. We further conduct comprehensive empirical studies from training a linear regression model to fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) to showcase the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms for training with ML-labeled data.
papers.summary: Human labeling becomes expensive at scale, so many training sets mix a small human-labeled subset with a larger set of samples labeled by an ML predictor that may be wrong. The authors propose both first-order and zeroth-order stochastic optimization methods designed for training on such mixed datasets. Empirical studies range from linear regression up to **fine-tuning a large language model**, showing the methods work across this range.

papers.title: SOMA: Continuous Monitoring and Intervention for System Two Reasoning with System One Models
papers.abstract: Reasoning models often run into problems without noticing them, even when symptoms are visible in their own text. In humans, metacognition separates monitoring from control: fast, intuitive signals keep watch while slow, deliberate reasoning unfolds and help decide whether to continue, change course, or stop. System One (S1) decision models, such as Jev, are a natural candidate for this role: they return a calibrated probability for a natural-language question about a text in one fast call, yet they are used only as gates before reasoning. We introduce SOMA (System One Metacognitive Awareness), in which an S1 model continuously monitors a System Two (S2) reasoning model and intervenes when needed. SOMA has three layers: a scenario layer states each objective in natural language with predefined actions, an awareness layer lets S1 judge whether the described behavior appears, and a control layer accumulates these judgments, first reminds S2, and takes over only if the behavior persists. Sharing one S1 model and one controller across tasks, without training, SOMA addresses two different failures on two reasoning models: on overthinking, it cuts reasoning tokens by up to 36\% while improving average accuracy, and on unanswerable questions, it raises abstention from 70.5\% to 87.2\%.
papers.summary: Reasoning models often fail to notice problems even when the symptoms appear in their own output. `SOMA` (System One Metacognitive Awareness) uses a fast System One decision model such as `Jev`, which returns a calibrated probability for a natural-language question about a text, to continuously monitor a slower System Two reasoning model. It has three layers: scenarios describe objectives and predefined actions in natural language, an awareness layer judges whether the described behavior is occurring, and a control layer first reminds the reasoner and takes over only if the behavior persists. With one shared monitor and controller and no training, it **cuts reasoning tokens by up to 36% on overthinking while improving average accuracy**, and it raises abstention on unanswerable questions from 70.5% to 87.2%.

papers.title: On Data Scaling in Tabular ML: More Data, Better Generalization?
papers.abstract: Recent work in tabular machine learning has emphasized the importance of diverse and realistic evaluation settings. The niche of large-scale (1M+) data, however, remains under-explored. To study training-data scaling, we assemble eight real-world tabular datasets with up to around ten million training examples, retaining the natural distribution shifts of the tasks and using random-split evaluation as a control. We find that GBDTs and MLP-based models show broadly similar scaling trends, with gains from both additional training data and algorithmic improvements. Tabular foundation models show more varied scaling behavior, with recent versions benefiting more consistently from larger contexts even under distribution shift. However, scaling training data under distribution shift introduces new challenges: in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance mostly improve together at smaller scales but can diverge at larger scales. We examine this through MLP capacity sweeps and comparisons of the validation distributions used for tuning and early stopping in MLPs and GBDTs. We also compare common practices of using validation data, contrasting its use for model selection in MLP pipelines with using it for in-context fitting in tabular foundation model pipelines. Under stronger shifts, MLPs selected using validation representative of the evaluation conditions generally maintain or improve performance as training data grows. In contrast, including such examples in context improves foundation-model performance, but does not prevent deterioration with increasing training size in our experiments.
papers.summary: Tabular machine learning has rarely been studied at the scale of a million or more training examples. The authors assemble eight real-world datasets with up to roughly ten million examples, keep their natural distribution shifts, and use random splits as a control. Gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) and MLP-based models scale similarly, while tabular foundation models vary more, with recent versions benefiting more consistently from larger contexts. A key finding is that **in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance improve together at smaller scales but can diverge at larger ones**. Under strong shift, MLPs tuned on validation data that matches the evaluation conditions keep improving, whereas putting such examples into a foundation model's context helps but does not stop performance from degrading as training size grows.

papers.title: Two hidden layer suffice: the caterpillar net
papers.abstract: Every continuous piecewise linear (CPWL) function is a finite signed sum of maxima of affine functions, making maximum representation a central problem in the study of the expressiveness of ReLU networks. A now-disproved conjecture predicted logarithmic depth for maxima. Inspired by the proof by Brunck et al. (2026) that two hidden layers suffice for general CPWL functions, we give the Caterpillar Net, a nonrecursive construction for the maximum of $N$ inputs with two hidden layers of widths $O(N^2)$ and $2^{O(N\log N)}$. The construction has a direct geometric interpretation.
papers.summary: Every continuous piecewise linear function is a signed sum of maxima of affine functions, so how deep a ReLU network must be to compute a maximum is a central question in the study of network expressiveness. Building on a recent proof that two hidden layers suffice for general piecewise linear functions, the authors give the `Caterpillar Net`, a **nonrecursive two-hidden-layer construction for the maximum of N inputs**. Its hidden layers have widths O(N²) and 2^O(N log N), and the construction has a direct geometric interpretation.

papers.title: Teacher Supervision, Fixed Representations and Calibration: Exact Risk Calculations for Candidate-Scoring Decision Models
papers.abstract: Candidate-scoring decision models return a probability distribution over a presented set of answers. Public documentation of one such system, Jev, and of an open counterpart, JevAny, describes three training ingredients that determine what these probabilities estimate: soft targets from larger models, a frozen pretrained backbone and temperature calibration. We analyze each ingredient in Gaussian surrogates where the finite-sample risk can be computed exactly. A student trained on teacher targets inherits the teacher's bias, which more student data does not remove and agreement with the teacher does not reveal. A fixed representation lowers the risk only below an explicit sample-size threshold. In a probit model the exact recalibration map is a temperature scaling, which removes all excess risk only when the teacher's coefficient has the correct direction and otherwise leaves a residual that calibration diagnostics do not detect. Under Luce's choice axiom, candidate scores are coherent across refinements of an event if and only if they aggregate by log-sum-exp. On 231,521 credit card complaints from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, where the decision is whether a complaint ends in monetary relief, a student trained on a logistic teacher's probabilities ends at the teacher's decision cost while a student trained on outcomes goes 8% below it, a 30B model read zero-shot remains worse than the teacher after recalibration, and that model departs from the coherence condition by 17.5 decibans. Pretrained representations reduce the labeled data required and calibration corrects the scale of the probabilities, but neither corrects a biased teacher, so the probabilities have to be checked against realized outcomes.
papers.summary: Candidate-scoring decision models such as `Jev` and its open counterpart `JevAny` are built from soft teacher targets, a frozen pretrained backbone, and temperature calibration. The authors analyze each ingredient in Gaussian models where finite-sample risk can be computed exactly. They show that **a student inherits its teacher's bias, which neither more data nor calibration removes**, that a fixed representation helps only below a specific sample-size threshold, and that scores stay coherent under refinement of events only if they aggregate by log-sum-exp. On 231,521 consumer credit-card complaints, a student trained on outcomes ends 8% below the teacher's decision cost while a teacher-trained student matches it, and a 30B model used zero-shot remains worse than the teacher even after recalibration.

papers.title: Learning to Refer: Inference-Time Collaboration in Decentralized Federated Learning
papers.abstract: In decentralized federated learning, heterogeneous clients may develop complementary expertise, yet each query is typically evaluated only by the client where it arrives. To exploit this distributed expertise without global coordination, we formulate inference-time collaboration as budgeted local expert referral, a graph-constrained routing process in which a query can move only between neighboring clients and only visited clients contribute to its final prediction. EdgeDRM implements this framework by learning a density-based routing potential for each client: differences between neighboring potentials provide the comparisons used to select successive referrals, while local task models generate predictions that are aggregated along the resulting route. Both training and inference are decentralized, using only neighbor-local information without a central router or graph-wide client scoring. We establish estimation guarantees for the learned comparisons and characterize how local improvement and graph structure govern prior-weighted density gains from referral. Experiments on benchmark and real-world medical data show that EdgeDRM outperforms graph-matched decentralized baselines in most settings, with the clearest benefits under sparse connectivity.
papers.summary: In decentralized federated learning, clients develop complementary expertise, yet each query is normally answered only by the client that receives it. The authors frame inference-time collaboration as budgeted expert referral, in which a query can move only between neighboring clients and the clients it visits contribute to the final prediction. `EdgeDRM` learns a density-based routing potential per client, picks referrals by comparing neighbors' potentials, and aggregates the visited clients' predictions, using only neighbor-local information for both training and inference. Theoretical guarantees cover the learned comparisons, and on benchmark and real medical data the method beats graph-matched decentralized baselines in most settings, **with the clearest gains under sparse connectivity**.

papers.title: Mise-en-Video: Fine-Grained 3D Control for Multi-Shot Video Generation
papers.abstract: Recent advances in text-to-video generation have enabled high-fidelity single-shot synthesis, yet practical storytelling creation requires multi-shot videos with both strong inter-shot consistency and fine-grained controllability. Existing multi-shot video generation approaches achieve strong consistency but still fall short in controllability. In this paper, we propose Mise-en-Video (MeV), a highly controllable multi-shot video generation framework that allows video creators to conduct staging the multi-shot in the 3D space and then generate the corresponding multi-shot video. To achieve this, our framework combines a hierarchical attention mechanism for multi-level narrative consistency with 3D-aware layout guidance for precise, per-shot spatial control. To support training and evaluation, we develop standardized annotation pipelines and construct a 160K-video dataset with hierarchical multi-shot texts and oriented 3D bounding boxes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MeV consistently outperforms strong baselines in video quality, inter-shot consistency, and subject-level controllability.
papers.summary: Storytelling with generated video requires multi-shot clips that stay consistent across shots while allowing fine-grained control, and existing multi-shot methods are consistent but hard to control. `Mise-en-Video` (`MeV`) lets creators stage each shot in 3D space and then generates the matching video. It combines hierarchical attention for consistency across narrative levels with 3D-aware layout guidance for per-shot spatial control. The authors also build a **160K-video dataset annotated with hierarchical multi-shot text and oriented 3D bounding boxes**. Experiments show `MeV` outperforming strong baselines on video quality, consistency across shots, and subject-level controllability.

papers.title: Scaling Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Brain Encoding
papers.abstract: Brain encoding models aim to predict neural responses to stimuli. The most widely used approach fits readouts from frozen pretrained backbones. Using neural data to train large models from scratch or fully fine-tune them after task-pretraining has proven difficult because neural data is costly and limited. We show that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables us to effectively adapt very large pretrained backbones for brain encoding with a small number of trainable parameters. To make it computationally practical, we exploit the backbone's causal structure to predict multiple timepoints in a single pass instead of using sliding windows, significantly reducing feature-extraction cost. This enables efficient fine-tuning of multimodal backbones with up to 104B parameters, the largest model adapted for brain encoding to our knowledge. Trained with a low-rank adapter (LoRA) and a lightweight readout, our approach consistently improves brain encoding performance across nine diverse multimodal backbones. On the same Qwen3-Omni backbone as the prior state-of-the-art (SoTA), our method BrainLoRA achieves the best published performance on the Algonauts 2025 Challenge. We also show the adapted multimodal backbones remain interpretable: modality attribution recovers the canonical sensory topography that prior work often obtains by construction from separate unimodal encoders, and neural adaptation increases the contribution of audio inputs and cross-modal mixing within the backbone. To scale out the number of adapted models, we develop a multi-LoRA kernel that accelerates joint training of multiple LoRAs on a shared backbone. This enables an ensemble of 200+ adapted models that ranks first on the public Algonauts post-challenge leaderboard at the time of writing. Together, our results highlight PEFT as an efficient and powerful paradigm for brain encoding.
papers.summary: Brain encoding models predict neural responses to stimuli. Neural data is scarce, so most work fits readouts on frozen pretrained backbones rather than fine-tuning them. `BrainLoRA` uses parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) with a low-rank adapter (`LoRA`) and a lightweight readout. It exploits the backbone's causal structure to predict many timepoints in one pass instead of using sliding windows, which makes it practical to adapt multimodal backbones of up to 104B parameters. The method improves encoding across nine backbones and achieves the best published result on the `Algonauts 2025` Challenge with `Qwen3-Omni`. A custom multi-LoRA kernel enables an **ensemble of 200+ adapted models that ranks first on the public post-challenge leaderboard**, and attribution analyses show the adapted models still recover the canonical sensory layout of the cortex.
papers.highlight_summary:
Brain encoding models usually fit a readout on top of a frozen pretrained backbone, because there is too little neural data to fine-tune large models. This work shows that low-rank adaptation (`LoRA`) lets fMRI data reshape multimodal backbones of up to 104B parameters, and that this beats frozen-backbone approaches while training only a small number of parameters.

- Because the backbone is causally masked, each 149 s window is encoded in a single forward pass rather than with overlapping sliding windows, which cuts feature-extraction cost by **~350×** (from about 700 to 2 GPU-hours); a 60 s context lead recovers the small accuracy loss this causes.
- `BrainLoRA` combines rank-16 `LoRA` in the attention layers of `Qwen3-Omni` with a lightweight linear or cross-attention readout and a closed-form ridge re-fit, and it improves all nine tested backbones (4.7B–104B) by **0.032–0.066** Pearson r over frozen baselines.
- On `Algonauts 2025` it reaches **0.327 ID / 0.228 OOD** with 61M trainable parameters, beating the single-model `MIRAGE` (0.310 / 0.217), which trains a 1.1B readout, with **~5%** of the parameters; full fine-tuning of 20.3B parameters does no better.
- A batched multi-`LoRA` kernel trains 32 adapters **29.8×** faster than training them one after another, and an ensemble of 261 adapted models scores **0.343 ID / 0.248 OOD**, first on the public post-challenge leaderboard; the authors find that ensemble accuracy depends jointly on individual model quality and diversity, with diversity coming mainly from varying the readout architecture or the backbone.
- Shapley-based modality attribution recovers the canonical cortical topography, and shows that adaptation raises the audio contribution by 39% and increases cross-modal mixing from 8.9% to 15.3%; the adapters also transfer to a held-out subject (97% of the gain) and zero-shot to `NNDb`, but all evaluation stays within narrative film viewing with only four training subjects.

papers.title: Safety Mid-Training: Internalizing LLM Safety as a Foundational Capability
papers.abstract: Safety alignment for large language models (LLMs) is primarily performed during post-training, while recent work has also begun incorporating safety data into pre-training. Yet safety can degrade when later training no longer includes safety data, and gains in safety often come at the cost of general capability. This tension suggests that safety and general reasoning should not be treated as separate training goals. We instead view safety as an LLM capability that can be learned through a reasoning structure shared with general tasks. Both require the model to understand intent or task goals, apply relevant knowledge, and reason about potential consequences. We introduce safety mid-training, a stage between pre-training and post-training that jointly develops safety and general reasoning through this shared structure. Given safety and utility prompts, the base model generates structured documents and reasoning traces that are then used for mid-training. Safety mid-training reduces average attack success rate (ASR) by 72% to 81% relative to Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B base models, while also improving general capability. The benefits persist through subsequent post-training. After general-only SFT, mid-trained models largely retain their safety, achieving lower ASR than the baselines without sacrificing general capability. They also retain safety under general-only GRPO without safety rewards, while subsequent RL reaches a better safety-utility frontier when initialized from the mid-trained models. Together, these results suggest that learning safety and general reasoning within a shared mid-training stage can reduce the safety-utility trade-off and make safety more robust to subsequent training.
papers.summary: LLM safety training usually happens in post-training. Those gains can erode when later training omits safety data, and they often cost general capability. The authors add a "safety mid-training" stage between pre-training and post-training. In it, the base model generates structured documents and reasoning traces for both safety and utility prompts, so that safety is learned through the same reasoning structure as general tasks. On `Qwen3` 1.7B, 4B, and 8B base models, this **reduces average attack success rate (ASR) by 72–81% while also improving general capability**. Most of the safety survives later general-only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and `GRPO`, and safety-focused RL started from mid-trained models reaches a better safety-utility trade-off.

papers.title: Next Best Action: Causal Constrained Offline RL for Business Action Targeting
papers.abstract: Next Best Action (NBA) systems must select among customer interventions (e.g., discounts, promotions, and lifecycle actions), maximize long-term economic value, satisfy complex operational constraints, and remain causally grounded. Existing approaches lack a rigorous framework for meeting these requirements jointly. We address this gap by formulating NBA as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP). We then integrate off-policy causal correction of the estimated customer dynamics directly into the Linear Programming (LP) formulation of the CMDP. The resulting policy selects actions based on customer states to maximize long-term value while explicitly enforcing business guardrails. Furthermore, the LP formulation yields shadow prices that quantify the economic trade-offs of operational constraints (e.g., fairness and user welfare), enhancing policy interpretability. We validate our proposed offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework on an industry case study involving rideshare coupon targeting, where customer states are defined by Recency, Frequency, and Monetary (RFM) stages. We evaluate performance using model-based off-policy evaluation, with causal dynamics estimated from a temporal holdout. Under the observed coupon budget and RFM state representation, our optimized policy improves customer lifetime value (LTV) by 19% over the estimated behavior policy and 8% over a myopic baseline. Although the demonstrated action space is binary, the proposed framework is action-agnostic, yielding a general-purpose decision module for targeting systems that manage multiple interventions.
papers.summary: Next Best Action (NBA) systems pick customer interventions such as discounts and promotions. They need to maximize long-term value while respecting operational constraints and staying causally grounded. The authors frame NBA as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) and build off-policy causal correction of the estimated customer dynamics directly into the CMDP's linear programming formulation. The resulting shadow prices quantify what each constraint, such as fairness or a budget, costs. In a rideshare coupon-targeting case study with Recency, Frequency, and Monetary (RFM) customer states, the offline RL policy **improves estimated customer lifetime value by 19% over the behavior policy** and by 8% over a myopic baseline.

papers.title: ASTOR: Benchmarking and Improving Autoformulation for Soft-Constraint Optimization with a Formal Grammar
papers.abstract: Real-world decision problems combine two qualitatively different kinds of constraints: requirements that must be satisfied, called hard constraints, and preferences that can be violated, called soft constraints. Because these problems are often posed to decision-makers in natural language, large language models offer a natural tool for assisting with their solution. This has given rise to autoformulation, which focuses on using LLMs to translate natural-language descriptions of decision problems into executable mathematical optimization models. However, this research often neglects soft constraints like those proposed by consumers, managers, and planners, despite the fact that many practical problems require modeling them explicitly. We introduce ASTOR, an inference-time framework that maps a natural-language decision problem to a grammar-guided abstract syntax tree (AST) before deterministically compiling the resulting representation into executable optimization code. We also introduce SoftOR, a unified benchmark of natural language problems which focuses on soft constraint formulations. On SoftOR, ASTOR achieves the best aggregate accuracy among comparable single-request and multi-agent LLM methods while remaining competitive on standard autoformulation benchmarks that include only hard constraints. Code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/astor-softor-iclr-E34C/README.md.
papers.summary: Autoformulation uses LLMs to turn natural-language decision problems into executable optimization models, but prior work largely ignores soft constraints: preferences that may be violated at a cost. `ASTOR` is an inference-time framework that has the LLM produce a grammar-guided abstract syntax tree (AST), which is then deterministically compiled into optimization code. The authors also release `SoftOR`, a benchmark of natural-language problems that centers on soft-constraint formulations. `ASTOR` achieves **the best aggregate accuracy on `SoftOR` among comparable single-request and multi-agent LLM methods** and stays competitive on standard hard-constraint-only benchmarks.

papers.title: AfriBED: a Speech Recognition Bias Evaluation Dataset for Low Resource African Languages
papers.abstract: Despite advancements in automatic speech recognition systems (ASR), current systems exhibit speaker-attribute bias, i.e., their speech recognition performance is biased against certain speakers based on their demographic attributes such as gender, accents, and speaker type. However, accurately assessing speaker attribute bias in a given ASR system requires the availability of a bias evaluation dataset with comparable speech across subgroups of a speaker attribute. In this paper, we introduce African speech Bias Evaluation Dataset (AfriBED), a novel speech recognition bias evaluation dataset for two low resource African languages, Bemba and Nyanja, to detect and estimate gender and speaker-type bias for ASR systems. The dataset comprises 9 hours of speech with 3928 utterances recorded by 80 speakers for Bemba, while the Nyanja set includes 6260 utterances with approximately 18 hours of speech recorded by 127 speakers. The results of our baseline experiments demonstrate that the datasets are useful for examining gender and speaker-type attribute bias in the target languages.
papers.summary: Measuring demographic bias in automatic speech recognition (ASR) requires comparable speech across speaker subgroups, and such data barely exists for low-resource languages. `AfriBED` (African speech Bias Evaluation Dataset) targets gender and speaker-type bias in Bemba and Nyanja. It contains **about 9 hours of Bemba speech from 80 speakers and about 18 hours of Nyanja speech from 127 speakers**. Baseline experiments indicate the dataset can detect and estimate attribute bias in ASR systems for these languages.

papers.title: SpecMRL: Redesign Matryoshka Representation Learning within Parametric Spectrum
papers.abstract: Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) is designed to support flexible representation sizes by jointly optimizing nested prefixes. While effective, this design lacks an explicit constraint to ensure that the leading portion provides a suitable compact encoding. To address this, we propose SpecMRL, which reorganizes the feature space to enable more effective prefix readout. Specifically, we extend MRL with a parameter-derived spectral basis organized with feature importance. SpecMRL otherwise follows standard MRL, with prefix readout performed in the learned spectral space. Experiments on MTEB show that SpecMRL outperforms MRL at all evaluated reduced dimensions, with larger gains under more aggressive compression. These results suggest that the learned spectral basis better prioritizes informative directions, enabling more effective representation compression. Notably, SpecMRL extends the performance frontier of MRL, surpassing full-dimensional MRL with only half the embedding dimensions.
papers.summary: Matryoshka Representation Learning (`MRL`) trains nested prefixes of an embedding so it can be truncated to smaller sizes, but nothing explicitly forces the leading dimensions to be the most informative. `SpecMRL` adds a parameter-derived spectral basis ordered by feature importance and reads prefixes out in that learned space, otherwise following standard `MRL`. On `MTEB` it outperforms `MRL` at every reduced dimension evaluated, with larger gains under heavier compression, and **surpasses full-dimensional `MRL` using only half the embedding dimensions**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Standard Matryoshka Representation Learning (`MRL`) truncates embeddings to their leading coordinates, but nothing forces those coordinates to carry the most useful information. `SpecMRL` keeps the `MRL` objective unchanged and reads prefixes in a learned spectral basis instead: it uses the eigenvectors of the Gram matrix of a learnable projection `W_Proj`, ordered by eigenvalue, so the leading dimensions hold the most important directions.

- The basis comes from an over-parameterized `W_Proj` of size D×128D, and each training step refreshes it with one warm-started power iteration followed by QR orthogonalization rather than an exact eigensolver, which cuts the training-throughput cost to **0.5–0.7%** (versus 3.4–8.4% for `torch.linalg.svd`/`eigh`) and avoids the gradient instability that exact eigenvectors have when eigenvalues are close together.
- On `MTEB`, using `Qwen3-0.6B`, `Qwen2-0.5B` and `Llama3.2-1B` backbones, `SpecMRL` beats `MRL` at every reduced dimension, and the gap grows as compression increases, reaching **+3.80 points at 16× compression** on `Qwen3-0.6B` (58.53 vs 54.73).
- Using only half the dimensions, `SpecMRL` (**61.61**) outperforms full-dimensional `MRL` (60.97), and that half-size embedding gives up to a **1.86× retrieval speedup** in `FAISS` while adding only **0.36%** to encoding time, the cost of one extra D×D projection.
- The gains persist on `Qwen3-4B` (**+3.31** at 128 dimensions), under longer training, and under sparse nested supervision (**+7.29** at 64 dimensions), and `SpecMRL` also beats `ESE (L2C)`, `MIPIC (SIA)`, a feature-derived basis (`FeatMRL`), and ablations that keep only the Gram-matrix reparameterization or only orthogonality.
- At full dimension `SpecMRL` is slightly worse than `MRL` (−0.03 to −0.42 points), which the authors trace to the smallest-eigenvalue spectral bands degrading isotropy, and the experiments cover only backbones up to 4B parameters, English `MTEB`, and training on roughly a fifth of the `KaLM` fine-tuning data.

papers.title: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution
papers.abstract: Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano and MemT-1.0-Flash, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately $1.86\times$ end-to-end inference speedup and a $66\times$ reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.
papers.summary: `MemT-1.0` is a family of "memory foundation models" that build memory into the model's computation instead of relying on an external store or the full context. Building on `Metis`, it uses `Gated DeltaNet-2` with a stable token-level memory update, plus a `Mixture-of-Storage` design that scales memory capacity. Training uses 34B tokens of continued pre-training and post-training data. The released `MemT-1.0-Nano` and `MemT-1.0-Flash` models beat parametric-memory baselines on average, remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, and largely preserve general capabilities. At a 128K-token history, `Nano` delivers **about 1.86× end-to-end inference speedup and 66× less persistent storage than a full-context KV cache**, and internalizing retrieved procedural experience improves success on agentic tasks.

papers.title: RefCraft: Benchmarking Visual-Reference-Conditioned Agentic Generation through Web Development
papers.abstract: Beyond basic tool use and coding skills, effectively incorporating visual references into agentic generation is equally essential for applying AI agents to real-world productivity tasks. We study this crucial capability through webpage development, a practical and readily evaluable setting in which existing benchmarks remain largely idealized: they typically focus on reconstructing visual targets or generating webpages from textual instructions alone, overlooking the more common workflow of developing from visual examples. Specifically, we introduce RefCraft, a benchmark comprising 300 realistic multimodal webpage-development tasks that combine natural-language instructions with screenshots from one to five reference webpages. Agents must selectively interpret and utilize these references while rendering, visually inspecting, and iteratively refining their outputs. We evaluate the resulting open-ended artifacts using independently verifiable keypoints and complementary programmatic and VLM judges. Across nine frontier (M)LLMs, the strongest system achieves an overall score of only 52.12 out of 100, revealing that visual-reference-conditioned agentic generation remains a substantial challenge for current models in practical webpage-development settings.
papers.summary: Existing web-development benchmarks either ask agents to reconstruct a visual target or work from text instructions alone. That skips the common real-world workflow of building from visual examples. `RefCraft` contains 300 realistic tasks that pair natural-language instructions with screenshots of one to five reference webpages. Agents must selectively use the references while rendering, visually inspecting, and iteratively refining their output. The open-ended results are scored with verifiable keypoints plus programmatic and vision-language model (VLM) judges. Across nine frontier (multimodal) LLMs, **the best system scores only 52.12 out of 100**.

papers.title: KEEP-Bench: Evaluating Evidence Preservation in Context Compression
papers.abstract: Context compression improves long-context efficiency but may introduce faithfulness issues through an information bottleneck. Existing evaluations rely on QA metrics, but a reader can still answer correctly from an unfaithful compression, so these metrics underestimate such loss. To bridge this gap, we introduce KEEP-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that directly assesses compression faithfulness with 4,102 cases across three challenging settings that require keeping evidence for plausible reference resolutions, explicit qualifiers, and minority perspectives. Experiments show that even with tailored prompting, the strongest models remain unreliable: despite context windows exceeding 100K tokens and inputs averaging only 3.1K tokens, the best open-weight model (31B) preserves all required evidence in only 66.8% of cases, and the best proprietary model in only 61.6%. Performance also varies sharply across evidence structures, so conclusions from limited structures may be biased. We further introduce a metric, Evidence Preservation Return (EPR), to relate evidence recall to inference FLOPs, and find that it peaks at moderate scales (4B-8B), where recall remains low. Additional output budget mainly benefits already strong models and widens capability gaps, yet the stronger preservation of these models comes at a steep computational cost. These findings highlight the importance for future work to investigate compressors with strong information preservation under a small computation budget, rather than relying on a large output budget or model scaling.
papers.summary: Context compression saves long-context compute but can silently drop evidence. Question-answering (QA) metrics understate this loss, because a reader can still answer correctly from an unfaithful compression. `KEEP-Bench` measures faithfulness directly with 4,102 cases that require preserving evidence for reference resolution, explicit qualifiers, and minority perspectives. Even though inputs average only 3.1K tokens, **the best open-weight model (31B) preserves all required evidence in just 66.8% of cases, and the best proprietary model in 61.6%**. A new metric, Evidence Preservation Return (`EPR`), relates evidence recall to inference FLOPs and peaks at 4B–8B models, where recall is still low. Extra output budget mainly helps models that are already strong.

papers.title: Agent World Model in the Wild: Computer-Use Agent Environment Synthesis
papers.abstract: Agent learning is shifting from learning from human data toward learning through interaction with the world. However, scaling such learning directly in real-world computer systems is challenging and can introduce substantial security risks. We therefore propose Agent World Model in the Wild (WildAWM), a scalable pipeline for synthesizing controllable environments and tasks for training general computer-use agents (CUAs). Whereas existing approaches typically specialize in a single agent interaction interface, we construct executable environments that jointly support graphical user interfaces, model context protocol services, and command-line interfaces, allowing agents to flexibly combine visual interaction, tool use, and code execution. WildAWM is entirely powered by open-source models, demonstrating that high-quality computer-use environments can be generated without proprietary frontier models. Beyond environments, we address three recurring challenges in task synthesis: ensuring solvability, maintaining sufficient difficulty, and producing reliable verifiers, by introducing execution-based quality gates that combine heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes of judgment robustness. The resulting pipeline synthesizes 341 long-horizon environment-task pairs that can require over 100 agent steps to solve and remain challenging even for frontier models, with GPT-6-Astra solving only 60% of them. We train two Qwen models of different sizes exclusively in these synthetic worlds. Both models achieve substantial gains across 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, demonstrating that learning in WildAWM's synthesized worlds generalizes broadly to unseen computer-use tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/WildAWM.
papers.summary: Training computer-use agents (CUAs) directly on real systems is hard to scale and carries security risk. `WildAWM` is a pipeline built entirely on open-source models that synthesizes executable environments supporting graphical user interfaces, model context protocol (MCP) services, and command-line interfaces together. Its task synthesis uses execution-based quality gates (diverse agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes) to keep tasks solvable, difficult, and reliably verifiable. The pipeline yields 341 long-horizon environment-task pairs, some needing over 100 steps, and `GPT-6-Astra` solves only 60% of them. Two `Qwen` models trained only in these synthetic worlds achieve **substantial gains on 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks** spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents.

papers.title: ProteinGeoBench: Frontier Structural-Biology Agents Are Fluent at Lookup but Lost in Geometry
papers.abstract: Frontier agents retrieve structural metadata well and compute geometry from coordinates less reliably. We ask how much of a benchmark score reflects that gap and how much reflects the evaluation configuration around the model. We study ProteinGeoBench, a suite of 131 protein-structure tasks, using 4,249 rollouts from four frontier models and 4,486 further trials across 26 models. Three of the four frontier models fall within 0.031 of one another (0.785 to 0.816) with no difference between them resolved, while the fourth scores 0.707 and all three gaps to it exclude zero. Three of the four do better on metadata lookup than on numeric calculation. The fourth is slightly better on numeric. Numeric tasks are 28 of the 131 but half of the twelve tasks that all four models fail. The ranking also depends on the evaluation budget: with one run per task, 23.9% of bootstrap replicates put a different model first. On a selected 15-task slice, removing network access lowers scores more than blocking eight structural-database domains, but the two contrasts were graded in different passes and cannot be cleanly decomposed. Swapping in each model's own command-line agent changes scores by -0.071 to +0.086, a comparison too small to rule out moderate harness effects. Across 26 models, numeric performance rises with non-numeric performance rather than staying flat. The experiments use different task subsets, so they cannot rank model, harness, access and task composition against one another. Evaluations should report results by task family, along with the number of runs, the harness and the access conditions.
papers.summary: Using `ProteinGeoBench`, a suite of 131 protein-structure tasks, the authors examine how much of a benchmark score reflects the model itself versus the evaluation setup. The analysis covers 4,249 rollouts from four frontier agents and 4,486 trials across 26 models. Most frontier models do better at retrieving structural metadata than at computing geometry from coordinates. Three of the four are statistically indistinguishable, and **with one run per task, 23.9% of bootstrap replicates put a different model first**. Network access, the agent harness, and task composition also shift scores. The authors recommend reporting results by task family along with the number of runs, the harness, and access conditions.

papers.title: Competing Learning in Hybrid Architectures
papers.abstract: Many modern language models have adopted hybrid architectures that incorporate both linear-time recurrence and softmax attention. Modern recurrence layers provide a highly expressive mixing mechanism while ensuring high throughput by compressing contextual information into a fixed-size state, but underperform softmax attention in contextual information retrieval. In this paper, we reveal a Competing Learning phenomenon where different kinds of mixers compete to learn the same function, and when any layer learns a function, it suppresses the corresponding learning signal for other layers. Layer attribution analysis reveals that under typical data distributions, modern recurrence learns retrieval functions faster than softmax attention, causing attention to fail to learn retrieval in most cases. Stopping weight updates in recurrence in the middle of training helps attention learn retrieval. Based on these results, we propose a staged training procedure for pre-training hybrid architectures on natural language. Empirical results on models up to 1B parameters show that our method results in substantial improvement in language modeling loss, common-sense reasoning, as well as a wide range of retrieval-related tasks across different context lengths.
papers.summary: Hybrid language models mix linear-time recurrent layers with softmax attention. The authors identify a "Competing Learning" phenomenon in which the two kinds of layers compete to learn the same function, and whichever learns it first suppresses the learning signal to the other. Under typical data distributions, recurrence learns retrieval faster, so **attention often fails to learn retrieval at all**. Freezing the recurrent weights partway through training lets attention pick up retrieval. A staged pre-training procedure based on this finding improves language-modeling loss, common-sense reasoning, and a wide range of retrieval tasks in models up to 1B parameters.

papers.title: Supervised Learning with Quantum Hamiltonian Embeddings
papers.abstract: Machine learning is widely regarded as a promising application in which quantum computing could offer a computational advantage. However, general quantum machine learning models with provable guarantees on performance, trainability, and efficient inference remain limited. In this work, we introduce quantum Hamiltonian embeddings, a supervised learning framework in which a classical training dataset is encoded into a single effective, parameterized Hamiltonian. Training optimizes the parameters of this data-dependent Hamiltonian, whose approximate ground state defines the classification rule. Once the ground state has been approximated using a quantum algorithm, inference can be performed either classically using a classical representation of the learned state, or with a quantum representation of the state. We establish efficient methods for gradient estimation and prove favorable generalization guarantees. Furthermore, under standard cryptographic assumptions, we show that Hamiltonian embeddings can realize hypothesis functions beyond the reach of efficient classical algorithms. We then demonstrate the framework at scale on IBM Heron processors using a standard benchmark dataset. Together, these results establish Hamiltonian embeddings as a new framework for quantum machine learning, combining theoretical guarantees with a path for experimental investigations at scale on quantum hardware.
papers.summary: Quantum machine learning has few general models with provable guarantees on performance, trainability, and efficient inference. In this framework, quantum Hamiltonian embeddings, a classical training set is encoded into a single parameterized, data-dependent Hamiltonian whose approximate ground state defines the classifier. Once that state is prepared, inference can run classically or on quantum hardware. The authors give efficient gradient estimation and generalization bounds, and show that **under standard cryptographic assumptions the framework can realize hypotheses beyond efficient classical algorithms**. They demonstrate it at scale on `IBM Heron` processors with a standard benchmark dataset.

papers.title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention
papers.abstract: We propose KronLSTM, a linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule, a novel update rule for associative matrix memories. KronLSTM extends the xLSTM family with a memory-revision mechanism that corrects targeted associations while modifying the memory only along a single direction in matrix space. This minimally invasive memory revision reduces interference with previously stored information compared with delta-rule updates, making it particularly well suited for long-context language modeling. The resulting memory dynamics can be mathematically described as a Markov chain that converges to a steady-state distribution, while the expected norm of the memory matrix remains uniformly bounded throughout the entire input sequence. Hence, KronLSTM ensures stable memory dynamics without requiring additional normalization and stabilization mechanisms for the memory state. Experiments show that KronLSTM is competitive with, and often outperforms, existing linear attention architectures, including models of the (Gated) DeltaNet family, with particularly strong performance on long context benchmarks. These results establish the Kronecker Delta Rule as an effective and analytically tractable foundation for stable associative memory in recurrent linear attention architectures. Our code (https://github.com/NX-AI/KronLSTM) and models (https://huggingface.co/collections/NX-AI/kronlstm) are open-source.
papers.summary: `KronLSTM` extends the `xLSTM` family of linear-attention models with the Kronecker Delta Rule, an update rule for associative matrix memories. The rule corrects targeted associations by changing the memory along only a single direction in matrix space, which causes less interference with stored information than standard delta-rule updates. The memory dynamics form a Markov chain with a steady state and a uniformly bounded expected norm, so **no extra normalization or stabilization of the memory state is needed**. Experiments show it is competitive with, and often better than, `DeltaNet` and `Gated DeltaNet` models, especially on long-context benchmarks. Code and models are open source.
papers.highlight_summary:
Linear-attention memories need bounded growth for stable training, but the delta rule used by `Gated DeltaNet` edits memory along a direction that depends on what is already stored, so it disturbs every association whose key overlaps the new key. The **Kronecker Delta Rule** instead corrects only the scalar association strength vᵀSk toward a gated target. It writes along the single matrix direction vkᵀ, so an update disturbs a stored pair only if both the keys and the values overlap.

- Vectorized, the update is a Widrow–Hoff delta rule on the Kronecker feature k⊗v; the paper proves the memory converges to a unique stationary distribution centered on the least-squares solution, with an expected memory norm bounded at every step by a constant that depends only on the data distribution.
- `KronLSTM` puts this rule into a standard mixer block with three separate gates: a per-key-channel forget gate, a sigmoid erase gate β, and a sigmoid write target c; L2-normalized keys and values make every update non-expansive, so it needs none of `mLSTM`'s normalizer or stabilizer states and stays stable in high-learning-rate stress tests where `mLSTM`'s gradient norm spikes.
- At 1.5B parameters trained on 100B `FineWeb-Edu` tokens, the pure linear model averages **59.72%** over six commonsense and `LAMBADA` tasks, **+1.6 points** over the strongest baseline `KDA`, with `LAMBADA` perplexity of **11.72** against 12.54 for the best baseline; it also leads the `SWA` hybrid setting and has the best average on the real-world recall suite (**30.31** linear, **37.40** hybrid).
- Its retrieval lead grows with context length: after extending the context to 32k it beats `GDN-2` on every RULER task at 32k and keeps the higher reasoning average (**60.19 vs 58.75**), and it trains **11–18% faster** than `GDN-2` (36.8–44.5K tokens/s on one H100), though plain `GDN` remains the fastest.
- On the synthetic `S-NIAH-1` task, where noise sentences repeat, `KronLSTM` falls well behind the baselines (66.2% vs about 100% for `GDN` at 4k); the authors attribute this to residuals accumulating for recurring keys, and state tracking only matches `GDN`, with `Mamba-3` better on modular arithmetic.

papers.title: Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy
papers.abstract: LLM agents that compute the right answer can still answer wrongly. Agent harnesses increasingly keep long tool outputs out of the context window, saving them to files that the agent searches or reads on demand. We ask where this costs accuracy with a real scientific tool: PHREEQC, a widely used geochemistry simulator from the USGS, whose reports reach 846.8k characters and whose determinism lets every printed value be traced. Agents use it to answer 158 execution-verified multiple-choice items. When agents read the simulator's report through a section index rather than in context, GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 lose 11.3 and 7.9 points of accuracy, while Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 show no detectable cost. Re-running all 11,007 logged simulator calls shows that both GPT models compute the keyed value about as often as before; what changes is the evidence they answer from. Under retrieval they often skip the report, answer from their own higher-precision output files, and misround to a neighboring option, a failure we call evidence substitution. With the simulation held fixed, retrieval still costs GPT-5.2 9.4 points. For GPT-5.4, more frequent correct simulations mask an evidence-use loss of about ten points, leaving a net change indistinguishable from zero. Naming the authoritative output raises accuracy by 6.3-7.9 points over plain retrieval for the three GPT models; for GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2, inlining outputs that fit works as well, while asking for correct rounding does not. Context-management choices in agent harnesses should be judged by where accuracy is lost, not only by final accuracy.
papers.summary: Agent harnesses increasingly keep long tool outputs out of the context window and save them to files the agent reads on demand. The authors measure what this costs using the `PHREEQC` geochemistry simulator, whose reports reach 846.8k characters, across 158 execution-verified multiple-choice items. Reading reports through a section index instead of in context costs `GPT-5.1` and `GPT-5.2` 11.3 and 7.9 points of accuracy, with no detectable cost for `Claude Opus 4.6` and `Claude Sonnet 4.6`. Replaying all 11,007 simulator calls shows the GPT models still compute the right value about as often. **The loss comes from "evidence substitution": the models answer from their own higher-precision output files and misround to a neighboring option.** Naming the authoritative output recovers 6.3–7.9 points.

papers.title: Newton-Based Methods for Bilevel Optimization Beyond Lower-Level Strong Convexity
papers.abstract: Bilevel optimization provides a framework for machine learning tasks such as hyperparameter optimization, data reweighting, and meta-learning. Existing Newton-based bilevel methods typically rely on the classical hypergradient formula, which is generally unavailable when lower-level solutions are nonunique and the lower-level Hessian is singular. We develop two Newton-based methods beyond lower-level strong convexity by exploiting curvature shared by the lower-level and multiplier updates. Newton-based GALET handles potentially singular lower-level curvature under a positive spectral-gap condition, exploiting its range structure to avoid the squared-Hessian multiplier system used in GALET. Newton-based BAMM uses a strongly convex aggregation model when the lower-level objective is convex and the upper-level objective is strongly convex in the lower-level variable. We establish convergence guarantees and improved complexity bounds relative to GALET and sl-BAMM under the corresponding assumptions. We further introduce GNBO, a generalized Newton-based framework that captures the shared-curvature structure of the proposed methods and several existing Newton and quasi-Newton bilevel methods. Experiments on synthetic problems, data hyper-cleaning, and GPT-2 data reweighting evaluate the proposed methods across different bilevel learning tasks.
papers.summary: Newton-based bilevel optimization methods usually rely on a hypergradient formula that breaks down when the lower-level problem has non-unique solutions and a singular Hessian. The authors propose two methods for this setting. `Newton-based GALET` handles singular curvature under a positive spectral-gap condition, and `Newton-based BAMM` uses a strongly convex aggregation model. Both come with convergence guarantees and **improved complexity bounds relative to `GALET` and `sl-BAMM`**. A generalized framework, `GNBO`, unifies these and several existing Newton and quasi-Newton bilevel methods. Experiments cover synthetic problems, data hyper-cleaning, and `GPT-2` data reweighting.

papers.title: LatComm: Reusable Context Compression for Latent Communication between Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Systems that combine several large language models (LLMs) often use one context for many questions. When the context is passed between models as text, the receiving model processes all of its tokens again for every question. Avoiding this cost requires a context representation that is compact, reusable across questions, and readable by a different LLM. Existing compression and latent communication methods each provide only some of these properties. We introduce LatComm, a Latent Communication interface that provides all three by separating encoding from reading: the context is encoded once without the question, and the receiver selects what to read for each question. A frozen context encoder LLM compresses the context into a fixed-size packet and sends it to a different frozen receiver LLM, which reads the packet through cross-attention, with gates computed from its prompt. On 12 multiple-choice question-answering datasets, LatComm improves average accuracy over single-vector baselines by up to 10.2 points. On QuALITY, it reduces the receiver's input by 57x and answers the questions of an article 3x faster.
papers.summary: When several LLMs share a context as text, the receiving model reprocesses every token for each question. `LatComm` (Latent Communication) avoids this with a context representation that is compact, reusable across questions, and readable by a different model. A frozen encoder LLM compresses the context once, without seeing the question, into a fixed-size packet. A different frozen receiver LLM reads the packet through cross-attention, with gates computed from its prompt. On 12 multiple-choice QA datasets it improves average accuracy over single-vector baselines by up to 10.2 points, and on `QuALITY` it **cuts the receiver's input 57× and answers an article's questions 3× faster**.

papers.title: AnyGoal: On World Model Generalization Beyond Expert Rollouts
papers.abstract: The goal of a world model is to capture the dynamics of an environment. This has the great appeal that it allows agents to plan and simulate a course of actions with the help of a world model. For these uses to be reliable, however, the learned dynamics must behave well beyond the specific state-action combinations observed in expert rollouts. Despite this, the relationship between data coverage, dynamics generalization, and downstream planning performance remains underexplored. We study this relationship through the lens of compositional generalization: can a world model recombine familiar state and action factors into valid dynamics? To answer this, we introduce AnyGoal, a benchmark of goal-shifted task variants built from widely used world-model environments, together with an open-source library. Each task is designed to be within reach of a world model that has learned the underlying dynamics: individual state factors and actions remain within their training support, but their combinations are underrepresented in expert trajectories. Across multiple environments and world model families, we find that current models consistently exhibit failures under these recombinations. By examining dynamics and representation failures across model families, interaction regimes, and evaluation metrics, we study where current world models generalize and where challenges remain for goal-shifted prediction and planning. Together, this framework, benchmark, and analysis provide a basis for evaluating progress toward world models that generalize to new planning tasks.
papers.summary: World models are used for planning, which only works if their learned dynamics hold up beyond the state-action combinations seen in expert rollouts. `AnyGoal` tests this through compositional generalization. It is a benchmark of goal-shifted task variants built from widely used world-model environments, with an open-source library. Each individual state factor and action stays within the training distribution, but their combinations are underrepresented in expert trajectories. Across multiple environments and model families, **current world models consistently fail under these recombinations**, and the authors analyze where the failures in dynamics and representations occur.
papers.highlight_summary:
`AnyGoal` tests whether world models trained on expert rollouts learn reusable action-conditioned dynamics, or only the behavior biases in that data. It builds goal-shifted task variants in which every state factor and action is familiar on its own, but their combinations are rare in the training trajectories, so a model with correct dynamics should generalize to them.

- The benchmark derives **eight variants** from four common world-model environments (`TwoRoom`, `Push-T`, `DMC Insert-Peg`, `OGBench Cube`), with **400 episodes per variant**; for example, `Avoid-T` asks a `Push-T`-trained model to steer around the block using the same 2D navigation it already knows.
- Range, Mahalanobis and KDE checks confirm that each variant stays within the training data's marginal support, and a full-dimensional joint KDE measures how far its state–action combinations fall into the under-covered "combinatorial gap".
- All five end-to-end models fail under these recombinations: the JEPA-style `LeWorldModel`, `Sensorimotor WM` and `DINO-WM`, and the generative `DriftWorld` and `IRASim`. Oracle-state predictors, which take ground-truth state instead of learning a visual encoder, show the failure is not only about representation: in contact-rich variants, rollout error rises by **one to three orders of magnitude** even with true state, while free-space variants hold steady or improve on planning.
- An action-intervention test finds that models become **less sensitive to the supplied action** in state regions where the expert's behavior is strongly goal-biased. This suggests they learn a behavior-policy shortcut rather than the action's actual effect. End-to-end models also degrade on `TR-Route`, where the observations stay visually in-distribution, which points to unfavorable latent geometry.
- The work is diagnostic and proposes no fix; the authors argue only theoretically that sparse, regime-specific transition mechanisms could generalize without needing every state–action combination covered. Prediction errors are measured in each model's own space (latent, pixel or state), so comparisons across model families are only rough.

papers.title: Train An Imaginative Agent
papers.abstract: A seemingly reasonable push in Sokoban can make the puzzle unsolvable. To avoid such mistakes, an agent has to anticipate the consequences of its actions before execution, especially when feedback from the real environment is sparse or actions are irreversible. We introduce Agentic Imagination (Agima), a training framework that trains an agent to imagine before acting, i.e. to be imaginative. Agima trains a single omni model to propose actions, generate images of their outcomes, and then reason over these imagined futures to decide what to execute in the real environment. Rather than committing to a single plan, the agent can simulate a sequence of actions, explore alternatives, and compare possible futures. We first use supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to unify policy and world modeling within a single omni model. This enables the agent to predict future outcomes and perform basic forms of imagination, such as forward thinking and counterfactual branching. We then use agentic reinforcement learning (RL) to teach the agent to reason with its imagined futures and use them effectively for planning. Across four environments spanning Maze2D, Sokoban, Pacman, and PushT, Agima generalizes to harder settings unseen during training. Trained with SFT alone on two-box Sokoban, Agima solves 40% of four-box puzzles while seeing the real board only once every five moves, compared with an action-only planner that only solves 2%. After RL, new behaviors emerge in how Agima uses its imagination: it learns a new unified format that was unseen during the SFT stage, learns to conduct forward thinking only when necessary, and branches more frequently at critical decision points. An agent that can picture where its actions lead can learn when and where to look ahead, that is, to plan. Project page: https://agima.net/.
papers.summary: `Agima` (Agentic Imagination) trains a single omni model to propose actions, generate images of their outcomes, and reason over these imagined futures before acting. This matters in settings like Sokoban, where one bad push makes a puzzle unsolvable. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) first unifies the policy and world model so the agent can think ahead and branch on counterfactuals, and agentic reinforcement learning (RL) then teaches it to use these imagined futures for planning. Trained with SFT only on two-box Sokoban, **`Agima` solves 40% of four-box puzzles while seeing the real board only once every five moves, versus 2% for an action-only planner**. After RL, it learns to look ahead only when necessary and branches more often at critical decision points, across `Maze2D`, `Sokoban`, `Pacman`, and `PushT`.

papers.title: WeAct: Dynamic Weight Switching as Agent Actions
papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents must learn heterogeneous capabilities from interleaved trajectories. Updating shared parameters to learn new capabilities can degrade previously acquired ones, resulting in catastrophic forgetting. As a trajectory unfolds, different stages may require different capabilities, yet conventional joint training and static adapter merging maintain a fixed parameter configuration throughout execution. We introduce WeAct (Weight-level Internal Actions), which trains independent capability-specific LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone and adds adapter selection to the agent's action space. These internal actions use the model's native tool-calling interface for on-demand capability composition in a shared context. Across eight deep-research benchmarks, Qwen3-32B with WeAct improves average accuracy by 6.2% relative to full fine-tuning counterparts despite using less compute, and by 27.5% relative to the strongest static LoRA-merging method. WeAct also supports modular continual adaptation, by adding a new code computation adapter to expand the agent's capabilities and updating the existing writing adapter to improve report quality. Both updates leave the backbone and other adapters unchanged, supporting modular continual adaptation in agents.
papers.summary: Long-horizon agents need different capabilities at different stages of a task, but jointly training shared weights causes catastrophic forgetting, and static adapter merging fixes one configuration for the whole run. `WeAct` (Weight-level Internal Actions) trains independent capability-specific `LoRA` adapters over a frozen backbone. It adds adapter selection to the agent's action space through the model's native tool-calling interface. Across eight deep-research benchmarks, `Qwen3-32B` with `WeAct` **improves average accuracy by 6.2% relative to full fine-tuning while using less compute**, and by 27.5% relative to the strongest static `LoRA`-merging method. New or updated adapters can be added without touching the backbone or other adapters, which supports modular continual adaptation.

papers.title: Where is Physical RSI capability from? An Observational Scaling Law of LLM-as-policy
papers.abstract: In this paper, we systematically investigate the mechanisms, scaling behavior, and generalization of physical Recursive self-improvement. We introduce PhysRSI-eval to quantify physical RSI through a five-axis metric: First-Attempt Performance, Efficiency, Success, Budget and Improvement from failure. Different VLMs are evaluated on 18 manipulation tasks under a fixed interaction budget. The analysis of experimental results motivates the Physical Barrel Hypothesis: different capabilities may constrain different parts of improvement. The five-axis metrics also distinguish systems with close public benchmark averages and show that high scores need not come with early or efficient gains. We study observational scaling from two perspectives: predicting the relative performance of VLM agents from their public capabilities, and forecasting later progress from early physical feedback. Together, these analyses ask how quickly and how far an agent can improve. Moreover, we conduct workspace interventions and then analyze what improvement leaves behind. Removing history reduces late-round success, frozen workspaces remain useful on unseen layouts, and three cross-task cases achieve success earlier. The results suggest that scene-specific adaptation and reusable experience can coexist.
papers.summary: The authors study physical recursive self-improvement (RSI): how well an agent driven by a vision-language model gets better at physical tasks by learning from its own attempts. They introduce `PhysRSI-eval`, which scores different VLMs on 18 manipulation tasks under a fixed interaction budget. It measures five things: first-attempt performance, efficiency, success, budget use, and improvement after failure. These five measures separate systems that score about the same on public benchmarks, and **high final scores do not necessarily come with early or efficient gains**. This leads to the authors' 'Physical Barrel Hypothesis', the idea that different capabilities limit different parts of the improvement process. Scaling analyses predict agent performance from public capability scores and from early physical feedback. Workspace interventions show that removing interaction history hurts late-round success, while frozen workspaces still help on unseen layouts.

papers.title: CoopUQ: Robust Multi-Robot Social Navigation via Uncertainty-Aware Cooperative Forecasting
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning enables mobile robots to make fast and scalable navigation decisions in constrained human-shared environments. However, directly extending single-robot approaches to multi-robot settings often fails to ensure safety and efficiency, especially under occlusions and out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios, where individual robots may overlook potential risks or make inaccurate predictions. Leveraging cooperation effectively for both prediction and navigation remains a major challenge. We propose CoopUQ, a multi-robot social navigation framework that bridges uncertainty-aware cooperative occupancy forecasting and robust decision making. CoopUQ predicts future occupancy grid maps through cross-robot spatiotemporal feature fusion and further leverages forecasts and their uncertainty to guide policy via constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning, where the cost penalizes navigation through regions predicted to be occupied or highly uncertain. This design enables the policy to adapt its risk sensitivity under distribution shifts. Experimental results across multiple Unity3D-based simulation environments with both in-distribution and OOD settings, including diverse layouts, pedestrian densities, and rushing behavior, demonstrate improved prediction performance and safety over representative baselines. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate its robustness across various scenes. Our code and videos are available at https://coopuq.github.io/.
papers.summary: Mobile robots that share space with people often navigate unsafely when single-robot methods are extended to teams, especially when views are blocked or the situation falls outside the training distribution (OOD). `CoopUQ` combines the features robots observe across space and time to forecast future occupancy grid maps, along with how uncertain those forecasts are. These forecasts feed a constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning policy whose cost penalizes moving through regions predicted to be occupied or highly uncertain, so the policy can adjust how cautious it is when conditions shift. In `Unity3D` simulations with varied layouts, crowd densities, and rushing pedestrians, both in-distribution and OOD, it **improves prediction accuracy and safety over representative baselines**, and real-robot tests show it holds up across different scenes.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning with Visually Attributable On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides reliable task-level supervision, yet offers limited guidance for localizing errors in visual reasoning. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) complements this supervision with dense token-level corrections from a privileged teacher equipped with an evidence-centered visual view. However, the resulting corrections may conflate visual evidence with non-visual shifts induced by linguistic priors, response style, or the privileged view itself. We formalize this phenomenon as privileged-correction contamination: a token-level correction is contaminated when its update direction cannot be consistently attributed to the privileged visual evidence. Directly distilling contaminated corrections may therefore reinforce erroneous token-level updates. To address this issue, we propose reinforcement learning with visually attributable on-policy self-distillation, an evidence-consistent paradigm that augments task-level RLVR supervision with privileged token-level corrections grounded in visual evidence. We instantiate this paradigm with Visual-Attribution Gating (VAG), which uses the verifier-derived advantage as the optimization anchor and validates each privileged correction against the contrast between evidence-present and evidence-degraded teacher views. By admitting only corrections directionally supported by this visual contrast, VAG preserves visually grounded guidance while suppressing inconsistent residuals. Experiments across six visual reasoning benchmarks show that VAG consistently outperforms GRPO and OPSD methods, establishing new state-of-the-art average performance.
papers.summary: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) gives reliable feedback on whether a whole answer is correct, but it does little to show where visual reasoning went wrong. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) adds token-by-token corrections from a teacher that gets a privileged, evidence-focused view of the image. The authors argue that some of these corrections are 'contaminated': they reflect language priors, response style, or the privileged view itself rather than actual visual evidence. Their method, `Visual-Attribution Gating` (VAG), keeps only the corrections whose direction is supported by comparing the teacher's output with the evidence present against its output with the evidence degraded, while the verifier-derived advantage anchors optimization. Across six visual reasoning benchmarks, VAG **consistently outperforms `GRPO` and OPSD methods and sets a new state-of-the-art average**.

papers.title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations.
