Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7-8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.
papers.summary: A controlled study across 22 benchmarks finds that simply giving multimodal large language models (MLLMs) a larger inference budget brings only modest gains on visual tasks that need grounded perception, external knowledge, or measurements. `OpenVLHarness` wraps a model with a capability layer that gives it a consistent interface to many different tools and converts their outputs into observations the model can read. It also keeps a persistent multimodal memory of images, structured data, and web references, plus a coding interface that runs generated programs over the stored results. With eight open and proprietary backbones, it **raises average scores by 9.7–12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines**. Using `GPT-6 Luna` at medium reasoning effort, it beats the base model, `Codex`, and `Visual Sketchpad` at maximum effort by 7.7–8.5 points while using at most 37% of their model-token cost.
papers.highlight_summary:
Multimodal models plateau on tasks that need grounded perception, external knowledge, or precise measurement: moving GPT-6 Luna from xhigh to max reasoning effort multiplies its token spend by 2.7 but adds only 0.7 points. `OpenVLHarness` gives the model evidence it can actually work with instead. A capability layer turns the outputs of different tools into observations the model can read, and a persistent multimodal memory keeps the underlying images, data, and web references available for reuse later in the same query.

- The capability layer wraps nine tools behind task-level interfaces, so a backend such as `SAM 3` or `Grounding DINO` can be swapped without changing calls. It also renders raw outputs (masks, depth arrays, retrieved webpages) into annotated images, short descriptions, and compact structured data.
- The memory registers each artifact under a reusable handle such as `input_image_3` or `webpage_url_1`, and a `Python Coding Agent` runs generated code directly on the stored values. For example, it can combine grounding masks with a depth map to measure the depth of each detected object.
- Across 22 benchmarks and eight backbones, it raises average scores by **9.7–12.6 points** over no-tool baselines, including `Qwen3-VL-8B` from 34.2 to **45.4** (13.6 points above `OctoTools`) and `GPT-6 Astra` from 60.3 to **70.2**, with gains on all 22 benchmarks. On `Qwen2.5-VL-7B` it also beats fine-tuned agents such as `DeepEyesV2` (**33.5 vs. 25.0**) without any weight updates.
- `GPT-6 Luna` at medium effort with the harness scores **56.5**, while the base model, `Codex`, and `Visual Sketchpad` score 48.0–48.8 at max effort, and the harness costs **at most 37%** of their model tokens. `Codex` at medium effort (43.8) actually falls below the no-tool baseline (45.8). In ablations, adding image handles to text-only memory adds **+3.1/+4.5** points on the 8B and 32B models, compared with +0.7/+0.3 for text-only memory.
- Several limitations remain. Counting in scenes with more than 25 objects is still hard, and incorrect tool outputs cause 75% of grounding failures. Gains on `Qwen3-VL-8B` are uneven, for example `FREAK-VQA` drops from 44.7 to 37.1. GPT-6 results are single runs, and the cost figures exclude tool execution.

papers.title: Can It Actually Work? Synthesizing Functional CAD Mechanisms
papers.abstract: While LLM agents can generate visually plausible CAD assemblies, these designs often fail to fulfill their intended physical functions. We study functional CAD design, a setting where agents interpret underspecified requests to construct and iteratively revise mechanisms that satisfy functional requirements in physical simulation. Verifying these requirements is nontrivial: different candidate mechanisms may realize the same function through entirely different components, controls, and operating sequences. To bridge this gap, we propose FunCAD-Harness, a framework that translates abstract requirements into candidate-specific physical tests and uses simulation feedback to guide design revisions. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce FunCADBench, a benchmark spanning 46 mechanism families with interdependent and multi-step operations. Experiments across frontier LLM agents show that FunCAD-Harness exposes subtle mechanical failures invisible to visual inspection, substantially improving functional success rates over standard simulation-augmented baselines. Ultimately, our work marks a step toward CAD agents capable of translating human intent into working mechanisms.
papers.summary: LLM agents can produce CAD assemblies that look plausible but often fail to do the physical job they were designed for. The authors frame functional CAD design as building and iteratively revising mechanisms from underspecified requests until they meet functional requirements in physical simulation. Because different mechanisms can achieve the same function in very different ways, `FunCAD-Harness` turns abstract requirements into physical tests tailored to each candidate design and uses the simulation results to guide revisions. On the new `FunCADBench`, which spans 46 mechanism families with interdependent, multi-step operations, the harness **exposes mechanical failures that visual inspection misses and substantially improves functional success rates** over standard simulation-augmented baselines across frontier LLM agents.

papers.title: Text-to-Image Generative Modeling Without Language Pretraining
papers.abstract: Modern text-to-image (T2I) systems use internet-scale language pretraining for text-conditioned image generation. We ask whether language pretraining is necessary for strong T2I generation. We introduce Halcyon, a family of early-fusion multimodal autoregressive models pretrained entirely from scratch on GPIC, a dataset of 100M image-text pairs. Halcyon-0.52B outperforms LlamaGen-XL/8 (48.0 vs. 63.3 gFD) with 18.2$\times$ less pretraining compute. Further, Halcyon-1.6B outperforms JiT-T2I-XXL/8++ (35.3 vs. 41.0 gFD) with 275$\times$ less pretraining compute. Controlled experiments show that text-only pretraining does not improve T2I generation. Halcyon also learns image captioning by replacing caption dropout with I2T supervision, maintaining competitive T2I generation quality under the same pretraining budget. We show that strong T2I systems can be trained from scratch without internet-scale language pretraining. Code and models are available at https://cs.stanford.edu/~keshik/halcyon
papers.summary: The authors ask whether text-to-image (T2I) generation actually needs internet-scale language pretraining. They train `Halcyon`, a family of early-fusion multimodal autoregressive models, entirely from scratch on `GPIC`, a dataset of 100M image-text pairs. `Halcyon-0.52B` beats `LlamaGen-XL/8` (48.0 vs. 63.3 gFD) with 18.2× less pretraining compute, and `Halcyon-1.6B` beats `JiT-T2I-XXL/8++` (35.3 vs. 41.0 gFD) with **275× less pretraining compute**. Controlled experiments show that text-only pretraining does not improve T2I generation. Swapping caption dropout for image-to-text supervision lets the model also learn captioning while keeping competitive generation quality under the same budget.
